# To the KING. <note>The monarch addressed here is George II, who ascended the British throne in June 1727, shortly before this work was published.</note>

### May it please Your MAJESTY,

<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut initial 'Y' decorated with scrolling floral and vine motifs.</image-desc>

YOUR Majesty’s gracious kindness <note>original: "Condescension." In this period, the term was a compliment, referring to a monarch's willingness to "descend" from their high rank to show favor to a subject.</note> in approving of my plan <note>original: "Design"</note> to publish this *History of Japan* encourages me, with the deepest respect and humility, to lay this work at Your Majesty’s feet.

# D E D I C A T I O N.

It gives an Account of a mighty and powerful Empire, which owes its Greatness to itself, and the flourishing Condition it is in, to its being debarred <note>The author refers to *Sakoku*, the isolationist policy of the Tokugawa Shogunate which restricted nearly all foreign contact and trade for over 200 years.</note> all Communication with other Nations: It unfolds the Rules and Maxims of a Government, where the mutual checks, jealousies and mistrusts of Persons invested with Power are thought the most effectual Means to oblige them to a faithful discharge of their respective Duties: It shows a long Series of Ecclesiastical Emperors <note>This refers to the *Tennō* or Mikado, the Japanese Emperors who were seen as divine or spiritual leaders rather than day-to-day administrators at this time.</note>, all descended of one Family, who swayed the Scepter of *Japan* for upwards of two thousand Years, and still keep up their Titles, Rank and Grandeur, though dispossessed of the supreme Power by the Secular Monarchs <note>This refers to the *Shōgun*, the military dictators who held the actual political and administrative power in Japan during the Edo period.</note>: It describes a valiant and invincible Nation, a polite, industrious and virtuous People, enriched by a mutual Commerce among themselves, and possessed of a Country, on which Nature hath lavished her most valuable Treasures.

These, and many other remarkable particulars, relating to the Religions, Sects, and Natural History <note>In the 1700s, "Natural History" was a broad field covering the study of plants, animals, minerals, and the environment.</note> of a Country, of which we had hitherto but an imperfect Knowledge, give me some hope, that

### THE
# Author’s PREFACE.

<image-desc>A large square decorative woodcut initial 'G' featuring a child or putto figure amidst leafy vine scrolls.</image-desc>
GERMANY was still embroiled in war with the Ottoman Empire <note>original: "Ottoman Porte"; the central government of the Ottoman Empire.</note> and the King of France <note>original: "most Christian King"; a traditional title for the French monarch, in this context referring to Louis XIV.</note> when the Swedish Embassy, which I had the honor of attending as Secretary, was dismissed by the Persian Court. It best suited my own inclinations to undertake a further journey; I chose to lead the restless and difficult life of a traveler rather than return home and be forced to share in the series of disasters then afflicting my native country. Therefore, I took my leave of the Ambassador and his retinue (who did me the honor of accompanying me for a mile outside of Isfahan <note>original: "Ispahan"; the capital of the Safavid Empire in modern-day Iran.</note>) with a firm resolution to spend several more years seeing other Eastern courts, countries, and nations. I was never accustomed to receiving large sums of money from home; I had supported myself through my own industry until then, and those same means sustained me afterward for as long as I remained abroad. This allowed me to serve the Dutch East-India Company, albeit in a less prestigious position. These descendants of Japhet <note>Kaempfer uses a common 17th-century biblical framework where Europeans were seen as the descendants of Japheth, one of the sons of Noah.</note> enjoy, more than any other European nation, the blessing of Noah: to live in the "tents of Shem" and to have "Canaan as their servant" <note>This is a theological justification for European presence and commerce in Asia (Shem) and the use of local or enslaved labor (Canaan).</note>. God has so blessed their bravery and leadership that they have expanded their trade, conquests, and possessions throughout Asia to the very edges of the East. There has never been a lack of prudent and capable men among them who have promoted their interests and welfare to the best of their abilities. But let us come to the point.

<summary>In this preface, Engelbert Kaempfer explains his decision to extend his travels in Asia by joining the Dutch East India Company, seeking to avoid the wars plaguing Germany. He frames the Dutch colonial success in the East through a providential and biblical lens.</summary>
<keywords>Engelbert Kaempfer, Dutch East India Company, Isfahan, Swedish Embassy, 17th-century travel, biblical geography, VOC, Persia</keywords>

--- Page 22 ---
<meta>This page continues the Author’s Preface. In the preceding section, Kaempfer explained his decision to leave the Swedish embassy in Persia to enter the service of the Dutch East India Company (VOC), seeking to explore the Far East rather than return to a war-torn Germany.</meta>

->ij<-
->**The Author’s P R E F A C E.**<-

It was by the gracious leave, and under the protection of this honorable Company <note>The Dutch East India Company (VOC).</note>, that I have often obtained my goals in the *Indies*, and have had the satisfaction at last to see the remote Empire of *Japan*, and the Court of its powerful *Monarch*. It is the present state of this Court and Empire which I herewith offer to the public, ahead of my other works which I have lately promised in the Preface to my *Exotic Pleasures* <note>original: "Amœnitates Exoticæ"; Kaempfer's 1712 book detailing his botanical and professional observations in Asia.</note>. I can assure the *Reader* that both my description and representations of things, though perhaps less elegant and perfect, are yet strictly agreeable to truth, and without embellishments, just as they occurred to me.

I must own that as to the more private affairs of the *Empire*, I could not procure information that was full and ample enough. It is known how difficult a matter it is for a foreigner to do so in any *Country*, and I found by experience that it is much more so in *Japan*. Ever since the *Roman Catholic Religion* was extirpated <note>Referring to the 17th-century suppression of Christianity in Japan under the Tokugawa Shogunate.</note>, the *Dutch* and *Chinese Merchants* have been, in a manner, imprisoned, and the whole *Empire* shut up to all *Commerce* and communication with foreign nations. The natives must be extremely cautious and reserved in their behavior toward those foreigners who are permitted to trade and are tolerated among them.

Those in particular who are more immediately concerned with our affairs are all obliged, by a solemn oath, not to converse with us, nor to discover anything to us regarding the condition of their *Country*, the *Religions* established there, the private transactions at *Court* and in the *Empire*, or other things. They are so strictly required to be on their guard that, by the same oath, they are bound to watch and to betray one another. To further ensure this, this oath is renewed to them every year. In so low a condition is the credit of foreigners currently held in *Japan*. The *Dutch*, who are suffered to trade there, have found this through long experience, and are of the opinion that it is impossible for them to procure any information concerning the present condition of the *Empire*, because they have neither proper opportunities nor enough liberty for it. *Mr. Cleyer* <note>Andreas Cleyer (1634–1697), a German physician and merchant who served as the VOC Opperhoofd (Chief) in Japan.</note>, who was himself *Director* of our trade there and our *Ambassador* to the *Emperor’s Court*, complains of this in a letter to the learned *Scheffer* <note>Johannes Schefferus (1621–1679), a noted German-born humanist scholar.</note>. The diffi-

->iij<-
->**The Author’s PREFACE.**<-

...difficulties <note>The word begins as a fragment, "culties," continuing from the previous page's "difficulties."</note>, I must admit, are great and significant, but not entirely impossible to overcome. They can be managed with the right approach, even despite all the precautions the Japanese government <note>The Tokugawa Shogunate, which ruled Japan during this period of isolation.</note> has taken to prevent it. The Japanese are a wise and brave people; they are not easily bound by an oath taken to the various gods or spirits that many worship but few truly understand. If they do follow such oaths, it is more out of fear of the certain punishment that would follow if they were betrayed. Furthermore, putting aside their pride and warlike nature, they are as civil, polite, and curious as any nation in the world. They are naturally inclined toward trade and friendship with foreigners, and they are excessively eager to learn about foreign histories, arts, and sciences. 

However, because we are merely merchants—whom they rank in the lowest class of society <note>In the Edo-period social hierarchy (Shinōkōshō), merchants were officially placed at the bottom, below samurai, peasants, and artisans.</note>—and because the strict supervision we live under naturally makes them suspicious, there is no other way to gain their friendship or win them to our side than by being willing to fulfill their requests, being generous enough to satisfy their greed, and being humble enough to flatter their vanity.

It was by these means that I developed such a friendship and closeness with our interpreters and the officials of our island <note>The artificial island of Dejima in Nagasaki harbor, where the Dutch were confined.</note>, who come over to visit us daily. I believe no one before me could boast of such a connection since these strict regulations were first put in place. By generously assisting them with my medical advice and medicines, providing information on **Astronomy** and **Mathematics**, and offering a sincere and plentiful supply of European liquors <note>Probably wine, brandy, or gin, which were highly prized by Japanese officials.</note>, I was able, in turn, to freely ask them whatever questions I liked. 

I questioned them about the affairs of their country, whether relating to the government in <term>Civil or Ecclesiastical affairs</term> <note>This refers to the distinction between secular governance (the Shogun) and religious or ritual matters (the Emperor and various priesthoods).</note>, the customs of the natives, or the natural and political history. There was no one who ever refused to give me all the information he could—even when we were alone—concerning things they were otherwise strictly commanded to keep secret. These private reports I gathered from those who came to visit me were of great use in collecting materials for my intended history of this country; yet, they were still not entirely sufficient or satisfactory.

<summary>Engelbert Kaempfer explains how he overcame Japanese secrecy by befriending officials and interpreters through his medical expertise, scientific knowledge, and gifts of European alcohol. This allowed him to gather clandestine information about Japanese society and government despite the strict isolationist laws of the Shogunate.</summary>

<keywords>Dejima, Shogunate, social hierarchy, interpreters, medical diplomacy, scientific exchange, Dutch East India Company, Tokugawa Japan, isolationism</keywords>

--- Page 24 ---
<meta>This page continues the Author’s Preface from page iij. In the previous section, Kaempfer described how he gained the trust of Japanese officials through generosity and humility, overcoming the strict surveillance imposed on the Dutch at Dejima.</meta>

->iv<-
->**The Author’s PREFACE.**<-

I likely would not have been able to achieve my goal had I not, by good fortune, encountered other opportunities—specifically the assistance of a sensible young man. Through him, I was richly supplied with whatever information I required concerning the affairs of Japan. He was approximately twenty-four years old, highly skilled in both the Chinese and Japanese languages, and very eager to improve his education. 

Upon my arrival, he was assigned to serve as my assistant and, at the same time, to be instructed by me in <term>medicine|Originally 'physick,' referring to the general practice of healing</term> and surgery. The <term>Ottona|A Japanese official who served as the headman or chief officer of the island of Dejima</term>, who is the primary official of our island, allowed the young man to remain in my service during my entire stay in the country, which lasted two years. This was because the young man had successfully treated the Ottona for an <term>illness|Originally 'distemper'</term> under my supervision. 

He also accompanied me on our two journeys to the <term>Imperial Court|The Shogun's court in Edo (modern Tokyo), rather than the Emperor's court in Kyoto</term>. Consequently, he traveled with me four times almost from one end of the Empire to the other. This was a favor seldom granted to young men of his age, and certainly never for such a long period of time. Since I could not have successfully reached my goal without giving him a solid grasp of the Dutch language, I taught him with such success that within a year he could read and write it better than any of our official interpreters. I also gave him all the instruction I could in anatomy and medicine, and further provided him with a generous annual salary to the best of my ability. 

In exchange, I employed him to gather the most detailed accounts possible concerning the current state and condition of the country, its government, the Imperial Court, the religions established in the Empire, the history of former ages, and noteworthy daily events. There was no book I wished to see on these or other topics that he did not bring to me and explain whatever I needed to know from it. Because he was often required to inquire, borrow, or buy items from other people, I always provided him with additional funds for these purposes on top of his yearly pay. Such is the expense and difficulty for foreigners to obtain any information about Japan since the <term>closing of the Empire|Referring to the Sakoku policy, which restricted foreign relations and prohibited most foreigners from entering Japan</term>. What I have managed to accomplish, I share freely with the public in this current history.

# Life of the AUTHOR.
## By the TRANSLATOR.

<image-desc>A decorative initial letter 'E' in a square woodcut block, depicting a figure standing in a landscape with trees and distant hills.</image-desc>ENGELBERT KÆMPFER was born on the 16th of September 1651, at Lemgo, a small town in the <term>Circle of Westphalia|An administrative region of the Holy Roman Empire</term>, belonging to the Count of Lippe. His Father, John Kæmpfer, was Minister of the Church of St. Nicholas in that town, and his Mother, Christiana Dreppers, was a daughter of Joachim Drepper, formerly a Minister of the same Church. He received, as far as his Father's circumstances would permit, a very liberal education, suited to the profession he was intended for, which was that of <term>medicine|Originally 'Physick,' the traditional term for the practice of healing and internal medicine</term>. He began his studies at the school of Hameln, in the Duchy of Brunswick, and was sent from there to Lüneburg, Hamburg, and Lübeck; at all these places he distinguished himself by his industrious application and ready progress in the learned languages, History, Geography, and Music, both vocal and instrumental. He stayed for some time at <term>Danzig|Historical 'Dantzick,' now Gdańsk in Poland</term>, where he gave the first public demonstration of his proficiency with a dissertation titled *On the Division of Sovereignty* <note>original: "De Majestatis Divisione"</note>, defended in 1673, and then went to Thorn. He stayed three years at the University of Kraków in Poland, studying Philosophy and foreign languages; having taken his degree of Doctor of Philosophy at that place, he repaired to Königsberg in Prussia, where he spent four years in close application to the study of medicine and Natural History, his Father's

He went from Prussia into Sweden, where his learning and discreet behavior quickly brought him into great reputation, both at the University of <term>Upsal|Now known as Uppsala, the oldest university in Sweden</term>, and at the Court of Charles XI, a munificent patron of men of learning. He was held in such high regard that very advantageous offers were made to him to establish himself in that Kingdom, which he thought fit to decline; he was always desirous of seeing foreign countries, and chose instead to take the position of Secretary of the Embassy, which the Court of Sweden was then sending to the King of Persia. 

The main design of this Embassy was to settle a trade agreement between the Kingdoms of Sweden and Persia, though at the request of the Emperor Leopold <note>Leopold I, the Holy Roman Emperor</note>, the Ambassador, Luis Fabritius, had orders, by a separate article, to engage, if possible, the King of Persia into a military break with the <term>Ottoman Porte|The central government of the Ottoman Empire</term>. As the first and chief goal—the settling of commerce—could not well be achieved unless their <term>Czarian Majesties|The Tsars of Russia</term> (Ivan and Peter, who then jointly governed the Russian Empire) would consent to allow passage for both European and Persian goods through their dominions on reasonable terms, the Ambassador was ordered first of all to travel to the Court of Moscow, and there to make an agreement concerning that matter. It is outside my present purpose to enter into the specific details or the success of Mr. Fabritius’s negotiations, except in how they lead me to follow Dr. Kaempfer through <term>Muscovy|An archaic name for the Grand Duchy of Moscow or the early Russian Empire</term> into Persia.

He set out from Stockholm, with the presents for the King of Persia, on the 20th of March 1683, <term>O. S.|Old Style, referring to the Julian calendar used in many Protestant and Orthodox countries at the time</term>, and went through Aaland, Finland, and Ingermanland to Narva, where he met the Ambassador with a retinue of thirty persons. After a dangerous passage over the *Caspian* Sea, where they were like to have been lost, through the violence of an unexpected storm, and the unskilfulness of their Pilots, (the ship having two Rudders, and consequently two Pilots, who did not understand each other’s language) they got safe to the Coasts of *Persia*, and landed at *Nisabad*, where they staid for some time, living under tents after the manner of the natives. Two other Ambassadors to the *Persian* Court, one from the King of *Poland*, and another from their *Czarian Majesties*, having landed at *Nisabad* much about the same time, they proceeded jointly to *Siamachi*, the Capital of the Province of *Schirwan*, in the *Media* of the Ancients, or, as it is now call’d, *Georgia*, where they arrived about the middle of December, and staid till the Governor of that Town and Province had sent notice of their arrival to the *Persian* Court, and received orders from thence after what manner they were to be treated, and which way to be sent to Court. *Dr. Kæmpfer*, in the mean time, did not sit idle, but went all about the neighbourhood of *Siamachi*, <term>herborizing|The practice of collecting and studying plants</term> and observing what was remarkable in nature and art, so far as otherwise his affairs, and a successful and not unprofitable practice of <term>Physick|The 17th-century term for the practice of medicine</term>, which the reputation of his being an *European* Physician quickly brought him into in that populous place, would permit. Mr. Fabritius <note>Ludvig Fabritius, the Swedish ambassador</note> had the honor of being introduced to his audience before the rest, and indeed during the whole time of his stay at Isfahan <note>modern Isfahan, then the capital of the Safavid Persian Empire</note>, which was nearly two years, he had very particular and distinguished honors shown to him, whereby it appeared that neither his person nor his business had been disagreeable to the Persian Court. Dr. Kaempfer, whose curious and inquisitive disposition suffered nothing to escape unobserved, made all possible advantages of so long a stay in the Capital of the Persian Empire. His main and favorite inquiries indeed, here and everywhere in his travels, tended chiefly to the improvement of Physick <term>Physick: the early modern term for medicine and the study of the human body's health</term> and Natural History in their several branches, and he has abundantly shown, by his *Exotic Entertainments* <note>original: *Amœnitates Exoticæ*, Kaempfer’s most famous scientific work</note>, that his endeavors in that way have not been unsuccessful. But he did not absolutely confine himself to this subject, though it was large and extensive enough: The Political History of a Country, the succession and remarkable actions of its Princes, the state of their Court and Government, their personal qualities, vices or virtues, the customs, manners, and inclinations of the natives, their way of life, trade, and commerce, the remains of antiquity, the modern buildings, whether sacred or civil, the flourishing or low condition of arts and sciences, and many other things of the like kind, equally exercised his industry and attention. As to the Persian affairs in particular, he was not a little assisted in his researches by the Reverend Father du Mans <note>Raphaël du Mans (1613–1696), a French Capuchin monk who lived in Isfahan for decades and served as a bridge between Persia and the West</note>, Prior of the Convent of Capuchins <note>a Catholic religious order of friars</note> at Isfahan, who had served the Court of Persia as an Interpreter for thirty years and upwards, and had acquired, beyond any European before him, a thorough knowledge of the Persian language, government, and customs, and a deeper insight into the state of that Court and Kingdom. And certainly, Dr. Kaempfer’s account of Persia (as delivered in his *Exotic Entertainments*) for accuracy and preciseness may rival the most significant accounts written before or since.

Mr. Fabritius having brought his negotiations at the Persian Court to a conclusion towards the latter end of 1685, and preparing to return to Europe, Dr. Kaempfer, for the reasons alleged in his Preface to this History of Japan, did not think fit to go back with him. The unhealthiness of Gamron, due to the sultry heat of the air and the want of water, is such that few Europeans can live there any considerable time without great prejudice <note>harm or damage</note> to their health; and even the natives are obliged, in the hot season, to retire up into the mountains. Dr. Kaempfer felt the effect of it soon after his arrival, falling into a malignant fever of which he lay delirious for some days; however, it pleased Providence to spare him. His fever abating, it flung him into a dropsy <term>dropsy: an old medical term (edema) for swelling caused by excess fluid in body tissues</term>, and that into a quartan ague <term>quartan ague: a form of malaria where the fever returns every fourth day</term>, and it was by these dangerous and unusual steps he recovered his health, but not his former strength and vigor. As soon as he found himself in a condition to move, he retired into the country for the change of air and the recovery of his strength, as well as in quest of new discoveries and observations, chiefly on those things which, because of the unhealthiness of the climate and other difficulties, had not been before thoroughly and so accurately enquired into.

He did not leave Gamron till the latter end of June 1688. The Fleet, on board which he went, having orders to touch at most *Dutch* settlements in *Arabia the Happy* <note>original: "Arabia Felix"; the fertile southern region of the Arabian Peninsula, including modern Yemen and Oman</note>, the Great *Mogul*'s Country <note>The Mughal Empire in India</note>, upon the Coasts of *Malabar*, in the island *Ceylon* <note>modern Sri Lanka</note>, in the Gulph of *Bengale*, and the island of *Sumatra*, he had an opportunity of seeing all these several Countries, every where with the same spirit of industry, and the same thirst of knowledge. Had his stay there been greater, his observations also would have been more numerous.

He had most certainly many qualifications necessary to make a good Botanist: a competent knowledge of that science, so far as it was improved in his time, a body enured to hardships, a great stock of industry and application, and which in my opinion is no less material, an excellent hand at drawing. With all these advantages he did not barely confine himself to the curious part of this science—an accurate description of the Plants and their parts—which though never so necessary, is yet thought too dry a subject by most readers. He endeavour'd to make his observations useful to mankind, and took a great deal of pains to enquire into the manifold uses of the Plants he describes, whether relating to **Physick** <term>Physick: the 17th-century term for the art of healing or the administration of medicinal drugs</term>, Agriculture, Manufactures, and the like, as also into the way of cultivating and preparing them to make them serve for these several purposes. The scarce superable difficulties, enough to deter even the most industrious, spurr'd him on to more painful searches, and he willingly sacrificed his time, art and money, to procure, for himself and others, a thorough information of a Country, of which, till then, no satisfactory account had been given: With what success he hath done it, is left to the publick to determine.

He quitted **Japan**, in order to his return into **Europe**, in November 1692, and **Batavia** <note>modern Jakarta</note> in February 1693. He staid near a month at the **Cape of Good Hope**, and arrived at **Amsterdam** in the month of October following. In April 1694, he took his degree of **Doctor in Physick** <note>Doctor of Medicine</note> at the **University of Leyden**, and on this occasion, as it is customary in foreign Universities, for Gentlemen aspiring to the like promotions, to give a publick proof of their ability, by what they call *Inaugural Theses* <note>original: "Inaugural Theses"; the formal public defense of a research paper required to graduate</note>, he communicated to the learned world ten very singular and curious observations, he had made in foreign Countries, on the celebrated *Scythian Lamb* <note>original: "Agnus Scythica"; also known as the "Borometz," a legendary Central Asian creature believed to be half-plant and half-animal. Upon his return to his native Country, he intended immediately to organize his Papers and written Memoirs into proper order, and to share with the public what he had observed in his travels; and certainly, it would have been then the best time for it, when everything was still fresh in his mind: But his reputation and experience, and the honor which the Count *de Lippe*, his Sovereign Prince, did him, by appointing him Physician to himself and his family, quickly involved him in such an extensive practice, that along with a variety of other business, he was prevented from pursuing this praiseworthy design with the vigor he himself desired, and which its own nature and importance deserved. For these reasons it was chiefly, that the *Exotic Delights* <note>original: "Amœnitates Exoticæ," Kaempfer's most famous work published during his life</note> did not appear in print until the year 1712. That work, which was only intended as a *Sample* <note>original: "Specimen"</note> and *Forerunner* <note>original: "Prodromus"</note> of others, was met (as indeed for the number and uniqueness of new and curious observations it well deserved) with general applause, and inspired in all lovers of learning an earnest request for his other works promised in the Preface—namely, his *History* of *Japan*, which is here offered to the public; his *Herbarium of the Regions Beyond the Ganges* <note>original: "Herbarium Ultra-Gangeticum"</note>, or the description and figures of the Plants observed by him in several Eastern Countries beyond the Ganges; and lastly, a complete account of all his Travels.

He was married in 1700, to *Maria Sophia Wilstach*, only daughter of *Wolfrath Wilstach*, an eminent Merchant at *Stolzenau*, and had by her issue one son and two daughters, who all died in their infancy.

The long course of his Travels, the fatigues of his profession, and some private misfortunes in his family, had very much impaired his constitution; and in the latter part of his life he was often troubled with the *Colic*, of which he had two very severe attacks, one in November 1715, and another at the

He was buried in the Cathedral Church of St. Nicholas <note>original: "S. Nicolas"</note> at Lemgow.

# INTRODUCTION

## By the TRANSLATOR.

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial letter 'I' decorated with a figure amidst blooming vines and leaves.</image-desc>

IT would be unnecessary to offer any excuse or *justification* for publishing the following *History of Japan*. There is something in all *travel books* that is both *useful* and *entertaining* to people of every rank and profession. As for this *History* specifically, the Author has already proved his learning, judgment, and integrity through a previous work (titled *Exotic Delights* <note>original Latin: *Amœnitates Exoticæ*</note>, published in *Lemgo* <note>original: Lemgow, a Hanseatic town in Germany</note> in 1712). Even without that reputation, the inherent interest and value of this subject—the distance of the country described in such detail, which has been little known until now—along with the many frustrating obstacles the Author faced during his research (as he mentions in his Preface and as will be seen throughout the work), would be enough to ensure it is well received. 

The *original manuscript in High German* was essentially ready for the press when the *Exotic Delights* was printed, and the preface of that book promised it would be released soon. However, his required duties in the practice of *medicine* <term>Physick: an archaic term for the practice of medicine</term>—specifically for the family of the Count *of Lippe*, where he served as the *primary resident physician* <term>Physician in ordinary: a doctor who serves a royal or noble household on a regular basis</term>—along with many other responsibilities, a lack of skilled engravers, and likely a lack of financial support, delayed its appearance until, ultimately, his illness and death brought a complete halt to this and some other intended works. <meta>catchword: works</meta>

<header>INTRODUCTION.</header>

...many other works of his, the result of many years of tireless effort and industry. Upon hearing of *Dr. Kaempfer’s* death, and knowing from his *Inaugural Theses* <term>Inaugural Theses: academic dissertations required for a university degree</term> and his *Exotic Delights* <note>original Latin: *Amœnitates Exoticæ*</note> that he must have collected and brought many natural and man-made curiosities back to *Europe*, *Sir Hans Sloane* asked *Dr. Steigerthal*—his Majesty's chief physician—to investigate what had happened to them during one of his trips to *Hanover*. This gentleman was kind enough to travel to *Lemgo* <note>original: Lemgow</note> himself. When he learned they were for sale, he immediately informed *Sir Hans*, who then purchased them for a significant sum of money, along with all of *Kaempfer’s* drawings and manuscript memoirs. 

It is thanks to *Sloane's* care and generous support that this *History of Japan*—the original *High German* <term>High German: the standard literary form of the German language</term> manuscript of which was bought at the same time—is now being published for the first time in *English*. It was at *Sloane's* suggestion (which I consider as binding as a command) that I agreed to translate it, as another gentleman of greater skill who intended to do the work was called away on different business. I began the task with great enthusiasm because, in his well-known spirit of sharing and his tireless effort to promote all useful knowledge—especially natural history—*Sir Hans* was pleased not only to grant me access to his library (which I dare say is the most complete of its kind in *Europe*), but also gave me permission to copy from his priceless collection of natural and artistic treasures anything that might help illustrate and improve this book. For these favors, and the many other signs of friendship he has shown me since I arrived in this country, I take this opportunity to express my most sincere and grateful thanks. 

My goal in this *Introduction* is to provide a brief overview of this work, highlight its particular strengths, and add a few remarks to clarify certain points based on the latest discoveries or explain things that have previously been overlooked. Since translating and publishing this *History* led me to research the Empire of *Japan* further, and to see what other authors have written on the subject, I thought it would be helpful to include a list of those authors, along with some observations I made while reviewing their various editions and translations. It has been very much doubted by some of the latest geographers whether or not the Empire of **Japan** is contiguous to the neighboring country of **Jesso** <note>Jesso: an early European name for Hokkaido, the northernmost of Japan’s main islands</note>, as the **Japanese** call it, and consequently whether it is to be reckoned among the islands or peninsulas. **Monsieur de l'Isle** <note>Guillaume Delisle (1675–1726), a prominent French cartographer known for his scientific approach to map-making</note>, a member of the **Royal Academy of Sciences** at **Paris** and geographer to the **King** of **France**, seemed rather inclined to think that it is contiguous to **Jesso**. He gave the reasons for his conjectures in a letter which was published in the third volume of the **Collection of Voyages to the North** <note>original: "Recueil des Voyages au Nord"</note>, (*p.* 32). It will not be out of place on this occasion to offer some observations which will serve to clear up this doubt and to show that it actually is an island. 

In the first place, it must be observed that **Monsieur de l'Isle** lays the greatest stress of his conjectures on the uncertainty which the **Japanese** themselves are in regarding the connection of their empire with a neighboring continent. He also cites some passages taken out of a letter from **Father Luis de Froes** <note>Luís Fróis (1532–1597), a Portuguese Jesuit missionary who wrote extensive accounts of Japan</note> and the memorable embassies of the Dutch to the **Emperors** of **Japan**, wherein it is positively asserted that they are contiguous. He admits these are of no small weight in leading one to think that it is an island, especially as this opinion is further supported by most accounts from those parts. 

As to what he quotes from **Tavernier** <note>Jean-Baptiste Tavernier (1605–1689), a French gem merchant and traveler whose reliability was often questioned by his peers</note> regarding a ship which he affirms, in the third volume of his travels, to have sailed all around **Japan**, that indeed might be easily dismissed, even if it were positively asserted. Although the *Japanese Monarchy* was founded long after the *Chinese*, the first Emperor of *Japan* having begun to reign in the year before Christ 660 <note>This refers to the legendary ascension of Emperor Jimmu, the traditional founder of Japan.</note>, yet the *Japanese*, led by a vanity, which they have in common with most *Eastern* nations, boast of a greater antiquity, than even the *Chinese*, and begin their *Annals*, with two *Successions* of *Deities*, supposed to have governed their Country many millions of years ago. As affairs now stand in *Japan*, there are properly two Emperors, an *Ecclesiastical* <term>Ecclesiastical Emperor: The *Tennō* (Mikado), who held spiritual and symbolic authority.</term> and a *Secular* <term>Secular Emperor: The *Shōgun*, the military dictator who held actual political and administrative power.</term>. For many Centuries the *Ecclesiastical* Monarchs were possess'd of an absolute and unlimited authority both in *Church* and *State* affairs, and it is an instance, I believe, not to be parallel'd, that the *Imperial Diadem* continued in one family for upwards of two thousand years: Even although in *Succession* of time, the *Crown Generals* <note>The *Shogunate* or *Bakufu*.</note> wrested the Government of *Secular* affairs entirely out of their hands, yet their rank and splendor, their ancient title and magnificent way of life, their authority in *Church* affairs, and one very considerable prerogative of the supreme Power, the granting of titles and honours, were left entire. The History of these Princes, during a *Succession* of CXIV <note>114</note> of them, who reigned from the year before Christ 660, to the year 1690, taken out of their own *Annals*, together with some remarks on their Court, and on the Chronology of the *Japanese*, necessary to make it intelligible, is the chief subject of the second Book of this *History of Japan*, and indeed not the least considerable, no attempt of this kind having ever been made, though I find it mention'd in *F. Couplet* <note>Philippe Couplet (1623–1693), a Jesuit missionary to China.</note>, that the Chronological Tables of the *Japanese Monarchy*, printed in *Chinese* characters, were, in his time, in the Library of the King of *France*, and that its beginning was therein likewise fixed to the year before Christ 660. At the end of the second Book is a list of the *Secular Monarchs*, from *Joritomo* <note>Minamoto no Yoritomo (1147–1199), the founder of the first shogunate.</note> to *Tsinajos* <note>Tokugawa Tsunayoshi (1646–1709), the fifth Shogun of the Tokugawa dynasty, who was in power during Kaempfer's residency.</note>, who was possess'd of the Throne, when the *Author* was in *Japan*.

The *Religions* now flourishing, or tolerated, in *Japan*, that in particular, which was of old established in the Country, and which very materially differs from the rest, are described, in the third Book, with that accuracy, which is observable throughout the *Author's* works.

In the fourth Book the Reader will find a complete and accurate description of *Nagasaki*, the only place in *Japan* now open to foreigners,

The *Japanese*, in their Annals, thankfully ascribe it to the powerful protection of their Gods, who enraged at this signal insult offered them by the *Tartars*, excited a most furious tempest, whereby their ships were sunk, and their numerous army totally destroyed, that but few escaped to bring back the tidings of this melancholy defeat to *China*. *Marco Polo* confirms the dreadful effects of this storm, and moreover adds, that the dissensions and misunderstandings which arose between the two *Tartar* Generals, was one of the chief causes of the ill success they met with, and of the loss even of what they had already made themselves masters of. my, but the *Venetian* fleet being defeated, he was taken prisoner himself and carried to *Genoa*. There, owing to his personal character and the vast knowledge and experience he had gained in foreign countries, he was treated with great honor. It was in *Genoa* that a nobleman, whose name has unfortunately been lost to history, wrote down the account of Polo’s travels and his observations on Eastern countries. This was done directly from Polo’s own spoken account and recorded in *Latin* sometime around the year 1298. 

A short time later, the work was translated into *Italian*. However, because the original *Latin* manuscript soon became extremely rare, *Francesco Pipino* of *Bologna*, a friar, produced a new translation. This version was printed in *John Huttich’s New World of Regions* <note>original: "Johan. Huttichii novus orbis Regionum"</note>, published at *Basel* in 1532 and again in 1555. Yet, this version was so poorly executed and differed so greatly from the original that *Giovanni Battista Ramusio*, having recovered one of the early *Italian* copies, believed it would be a public service to print it in that language. He included it in the second volume of his distinguished collection of voyages and travels, adding many fascinating remarks regarding the family of *Marco Polo* <note>original: "Marc Paul"</note> and his adventures after returning to *Venice*. 

In 1671, another *Latin* edition of this author was published in *Cologne* by *Andreas Müller*, featuring several different readings <note>The text uses "various lections," meaning alternative wording found in different manuscript versions.</note> from a manuscript in the Library of the Elector of *Brandenburg*, along with Müller’s own insightful commentary. Before I move on from this celebrated traveler, upon whom I fear I have dwelt for quite some time, it is worth noting that three maps of the Eastern countries—composed primarily from his accounts—appear in that rare and famous edition of *Ptolemy’s Geography*. This was published in *Lyons* in 1535 by *Michael of Villeneuve* (also known as *Michael Servetus*), who was later burned at *Geneva* as a heretic <note>The original text uses "Atheist," though Servetus was specifically executed for his non-trinitarian views during the Reformation.</note>.

<margin>How much the description of Japan in Marco Polo’s writings contributed to the discovery of America.</margin>

From the time of *Marco Polo*, through the ignorance and cultural decline of those middle ages, this important discovery of the East lay neglected. Indeed, all his writings were essentially buried in oblivion for nearly two hundred years. It was only with the restoration of learning and the invention of the printing press that they were brought to light once more, along with many other rare and valuable manuscripts. Very fortunately for the world, these writings fell into the hands of *Christopher Columbus*, that immortal discoverer of the Western World. He had long contemplated his great plan, influenced by many factors which led him to conclude that there must exist a country to the west of *Europe* that was yet to be discovered,

It is very much to the honor of Marco Polo that his writings, and in particular his account of the Island of *Zipangri* <note>Zipangri, or Cipangu, was the name used by Marco Polo to refer to Japan, based on the Chinese name 'Ze-pen-kuo'.</note>, at least supported Columbus in his hopes and conjectures. The wealth and riches for which Marco Polo says that island was famous, even in his days, made an attempt of that kind worth undertaking. Supposing (though erroneously, as appeared by later discoveries) that the Empire of China lay fifteen hours <note>In historical geography, longitude was often measured in hours rather than degrees; fifteen hours represents 225 degrees of the Earth's circumference.</note> eastward of Europe, and consequently *Zipangri* even further, it was but natural for him to conclude that the way there must be shorter sailing westward from Europe than by going eastward all round Africa. Perhaps also he might have received some hints from a sea chart and a map of the world, which it is said Marco Polo brought with him into Europe, and wherein were represented many countries in the East Indies which were afterwards discovered by the Portuguese. The success of this enterprise of Columbus none of my readers can be ignorant of, and I will only add that these several considerations above-mentioned made so strong an impression on his mind that when he landed at *Hispaniola* <note>The island currently shared by Haiti and the Dominican Republic.</note>, he thought it was the very *Zipangri* of Marco Polo.

<margin>Discovery of Japan by the Portuguese.</margin>

Meanwhile, as a new world was being added to the Monarchy of Spain by the discovery and conquest of America, the Portuguese, on their side, enlarged their dominions as successfully in the East Indies. The discovery of Japan, though it was but accidental, is one of many for which the honor is due to that nation. It is not indeed agreed on all hands in what year that discovery was made; some authors bring it as early as the year 1535, others to 1542, others to 1543, and some still later. In this uncertainty of opinions, that of Diego do Couto, the celebrated continuator of João de Barros’s *Decades* <note>The 'Decades of Asia' (Décadas da Ásia) is a monumental history of the Portuguese discoveries in the East.</note>, seems to me to deserve most credit. That gentleman, who was Historiographer to Philip II, King of Spain and Portugal, and spent the best part of his life in the Indies, had in his custody the Archives of Goa. From these, he collected the materials for that great work of his concerning the discoveries, conquests, and remarkable actions of the Portuguese in the Indies, which he brings down to the end of the sixteenth century. This author informs us in the *Fifth Decade of Asia* <note>original: "Decada quinta da Asia"</note>...

<margin>Their first establishments there.</margin>
The *Portuguese*, wherever they came to settle in the *Indies*, either by conquest or treaties, turned their thoughts and utmost endeavors chiefly to two things: the increase of their trade and the propagation of the Gospel. I believe it may be asserted that they met nowhere with so sudden and unexpected a success in both as they did in the Empire of *Japan*. As to the first, indeed, the flourishing condition of their trade and the immense wealth they gained by it, their own writers are largely silent about—perhaps for fear of discovering so valuable a branch of commerce to other nations. But the latter, the propagation of the Gospel, was thought too worthy and deserving a subject not to be enlarged upon in a variety of accounts still in existence. In these accounts, its early foundation, its surprising progress, the persecutions raised against it, the fervor of the new converts, their unparalleled constancy and resolution, and the final extirpation <term>extirpation</term> <note>The total destruction or rooting out of something; here, the complete suppression of Christianity in Japan through execution and expulsion.</note> of Christianity—effected by no less means than a cruel butchery of all those who would not renounce it—are considered in all their wide extent and most minute circumstances.

<margin>III. The writers on the Empire of *Japan*:</margin>
This leads me to the list I proposed to give of what authors I encountered in the library of the worthy *Sir Hans Sloane* <note>Sir Hans Sloane (1660–1753) was a royal physician whose massive collection of books and specimens provided the foundation for the British Museum.</note>, relating to either the ecclesiastical, political, or natural history of *Japan*.

<margin>Letters of the *Jesuits*.</margin>
Among the ecclesiastical writers, the letters of the *Jesuits* deserve to be mentioned first. It is well known that these Fathers are ordered once a year to send to their General <note>The Superior General, the high-ranking leader of the Society of Jesus (Jesuits) in Rome.</note> an account of what passed in their missions. Although their letters turn chiefly upon religious matters—their progress in the conversion of non-believers, the difficulties they meet with, claimed miracles, and the like—many remarks are nonetheless included relating to the condition, government, religion, and natural history of the countries where they are stationed, together with the manners and customs of the natives. In the Macanese port of the Chinese Kingdom, in the house of the Society of Jesus, with the permission of the ordinary and superiors, in the year 1590, Quarto.* <note>original: "De Missione Legatorum Japonensium ad Romanam Curiam, rebusque in Europa ac toto Itinere animadversis, Dialogus, ex Ephemeride ipsorum Legatorum collectus, & in Linguam Latinam versus ab Edvardo de Sande..."</note> *This rare and curious Treatise, which was printed at Macao in China, both in Latin and Japanese, lays open, at once, the state of Europe and the Indies, as it was at that time. # INTRODUCTION.

of the favourable reception they had met with in *Europe*, and the remarkable things they had seen in their voyage and return. And certainly it contains as complete an account, as it was then possible to give, of the state of *Europe*, its size and divisions, and its governments—whether *Monarchical*, *Aristocratical*, or *Democratical*. It describes the pomp and magnificence of the *European* Princes, the splendor of their Courts, their riches and power; the manners, customs, and way of life of the nobles and the common people; the flourishing condition of trade and commerce; and the methods of carrying on war in *Europe*, both by sea and land.

The account details the principal towns in *Europe*, particularly *Lisbon*, *Evora*, *Villaviziosa*, *Madrid*, *Pisa*, *Florence*, *Rome*, *Naples*, *Padua*, *Verona*, *Mantua*, *Cremona*, *Milan*, and *Genoa*—these being the places which the Ambassadors themselves had passed through, and where they had been shown, in the most ample manner, whatever was curious and remarkable. It speaks of the power and authority of the Pope at *Rome*, the magnificence of his Court, and the ceremonies observed upon his death and burial, as also upon the election of a new Pope, the splendor of his Coronation, and the pomp of his procession to take possession of the Church of *St. John Lateran* <note>The Archbasilica of Saint John Lateran is the cathedral church of the Diocese of Rome and the official ecclesiastical seat of the Pope.</note>. 

It further describes the power and grandeur of *Philip II*, then King of *Spain*, and the vastness of his dominions in *Europe* and both the *Indies* <note>Philip II (1527–1598) ruled one of the largest empires in history, including Spain, Portugal, Naples, Sicily, and territories in the Americas and Asia.</note>; the Republic of *Venice*, the nature of its government, and the situation, riches, and antiquity of that town and commonwealth; the numerous conquests and discoveries of the *Portuguese* in the *Indies*; several countries in the *East Indies*, particularly the Empire of *China*; and a variety of other things, too many to be mentioned here. 

The work was written in the form of dialogues, wherein the Ambassadors *Mancius* and *Michael*, their two companions *Martinus* and *Julian* <note>These refer to the four young Japanese noblemen of the Tenshō Embassy: Mancio Itō, Miguel Chijiwa, Martinho Hara, and Julião Nakaura.</note>, *Leo* (a brother of the Prince of *Arima*), and *Linus* (a brother of the Prince of *Omura*) are introduced as speakers <term>Interlocutors: the participants in a dialogue or conversation</term>. The author has not omitted, in proper places, to give some account of the Empire of *Japan* itself, and particularly to compare the manners and customs of that country with those of *Europe*. In short, were the whole work now reprinted, I do not doubt that it would still meet with a favourable reception.

But to proceed: there are many letters from the *Jesuits* written after the several collections mentioned above, and many other writers on the same subject. A list of these is subjoined below, arranged as nearly as possible in chronological order.

The "Abbé de T." was a pseudonym for the Jesuit Jean Crasset.</note> This is the *History* of the Church of *Japan* by *Father Solier*, put into better *French*, enlarged from several other *Memoirs*, and continued to the death of the Emperor *Toxogunsama* <note>Iemitsu</note>, which happened in 1658. <margin>Dutch Writers.</margin>
The *Dutch* having not only used the trade to *Japan* as early as the year 1609, but having enjoyed it exclusive of all *European* Nations ever since 1640, it is but natural to expect more ample and satisfactory accounts from their *Writers*, whom I proceed now to take into consideration.

***Jan Huyghen van Linschoten*** <note>original Latin: "Linscotanus"</note> is the first I meet with. He was a native of *Enkhuysen*, and went into the *Indies* with *Vincent Fonseca*, *Archbishop* of *Goa*, in 1583, some time before the establishment of the *Dutch East India Company*. It would be foreign to my purpose to mention all the differing editions and translations of his *Travels*; I will only observe that they make up the *second, third,* and *fourth* parts of *De Bry's India Orientalis*, and that ***Bernardus Paludanus***, a noted *Physician* at *Enkhuysen*, has added some remarks, particularly on those things which relate to *Natural History*. His account of *Japan*, which is but short and not without considerable mistakes, goes no farther than the information the *Portuguese* at *Goa* were then able, or willing, to give him.

The account of *Japan* by ***Francis Caron***, who was *Director* of the *Dutch Trade* there, is in proportion to its shortness, beyond question one of the best extant, though not altogether without mistakes. *For those individuals employed in spreading the Gospel, who could not hope for any success unless they were skilled enough to speak and debate with the local people, it may seem strange that so little has been done to make the language easier to understand. There is, in fact, a sample of the characters at the end of the second edition of <term>Maffei's</term> <note>Giovanni Pietro Maffei (1533–1603), a Jesuit historian.</note> collection of letters (see page 32 of this Introduction), and another in the works of <term>Purchas</term> <note>Samuel Purchas (c. 1577–1626), an English cleric who published vast compilations of travel reports.</note>, which is a copy of the privileges granted by the Emperor <term>Ongoschiosama</term> <note>A European rendering of Tokugawa Ieyasu’s posthumous name or title.</note> to the English; however, these were intended more as curiosities than for actual use. Father <term>Diego Collado</term>, a Franciscan, is the only one who published a Grammar of the Japanese Language, as well as a Dictionary in Latin, Spanish, and Japanese in two volumes, and also a guide for conducting confession for a Japanese person. All of these were printed in Rome in 1632, in <term>quarto</term> <note>A book size where the printing sheet is folded twice to create four leaves.</note>, at the expense of the <term>Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith</term> <note>original: "congregation de propaganda fide," the Vatican department overseeing missionary work</note>. However, the Japanese words in all these works are written only using the Latin alphabet.*

*Besides the information found in various parts of this History of Japan regarding the nation's language, I have added (in Table 45) three alphabets of the simple characters and some examples of the compound ones. * *Osacca mono Gattari:* <note>The *Osaka Monogatari* (Tale of Osaka).</note> *A Discourse of the affairs of* Osacca. *This is an ample account of the internal civil wars which arose in* Japan *upon the death of* Taicosama <note>Toyotomi Hideyoshi (1537–1598), the "Great Unifier" of Japan.</note>, *between the Counsellors of state appointed by that Monarch, and* Ongoschiosama <note>Tokugawa Ieyasu (1543–1616), the founder of the Tokugawa Shogunate.</note>, *whom he had made Guardian to* Fide Jori <note>Toyotomi Hideyori (1593–1615), Hideyoshi's son.</note>, *his only Son and Heir. This* Ongoschiosama *is the same Emperor who granted the liberty of trading in* Japan *to both the* English *and the* Dutch.

* *Simabaraki, or Simabaragasen,* <note>The *Shimabara-ki*, a chronicle of the Shimabara Rebellion (1637–1638).</note> *an account of the war at* Simabara. *The rebellion of the* Christians *of* Arima, *who retreated—numbering 37,000—into a Castle upon the Gulf of* Simabara; *the siege and surrender of this Castle, and the unparalleled slaughter of the besieged, by which the* Christian Religion *was totally suppressed in* Japan, *are the subjects of this discourse. Among many other writings of Dr.* Kæmpfer, <note>Engelbert Kaempfer (1651–1716), a German physician and naturalist known for his detailed descriptions of Japan.</note> *now in the possession of* Sir Hans Sloane, <note>Sir Hans Sloane (1660–1753), whose collection became the foundation of the British Museum.</note> *is a translation of these two works.*

*The History of* Abino Sime <note>Abe no Seimei (944–1005), a legendary cosmologist and folk hero.</note>, *Son of the Emperor* Abino-Jassima.

*Sin dai ki.* <note>The *Shindaiki* (Chronicle of the Age of the Gods).</note> *A History of all the Gods of the* Japanese, *as they were worshipped in the Country in ancient times.*

*Tensinki.* <note>Likely the *Tenjin-ki*, a biography of Sugawara no Michizane, deified as Tenjin.</note> *A particular History of the life and heroic actions of* Tensin, *who is the chief of the* Sintos <note>Shinto.</note> *Gods of the* Japanese.

*Nippon Idsumi no kuni Oojafijro,* <note>Possibly a reference to the Izumi Province and the "Great Shrine" (O-yashiro) of Izumo, though listed here as Izumi.</note> *that is, the wars of the Gods in* Oojafijro *in the Province* Idsumi.

* *Dai fanja Firamitz.* <note>The *Daihannya Haramitta* (Great Perfection of Wisdom Sutra), a central Buddhist text.</note> *A Treatise of all the Gods worshipped by the* Budsdioists <note>Buddhists.</note>.

*Sikki moku.* <note>The *Goseibai Shikimoku*, a legal code issued in 1232.</note> *The Laws and Constitutions of the* Japanese Empire.

*Kiusaj.* <note>Possibly *Kyūsai* or similar, referring to ritual or social relief/customs.</note> *A Treatise of the civil Customs and Ceremonies of the* Japanese.

*Shogaku* <note>Original: *Soogakf*. The *Xiaoxue* or "Elementary Learning," a fundamental Neo-Confucian text on ethics and social behavior.</note>. *A Treatise containing the precepts of morals, as taught and practiced by the <term>Shutoists (Neo-Confucian philosophers)</term> of Japan: It is divided into five parts.*

*Honcho Oin Hiji* <note>Original: *Fontsjo O in fisi*. Literally "Japanese Tales from the Shade of the Cherry Tree."</note>, *that is, in the literal sense, the artifice of the Shadow of the Japanese Cherry-Tree. It is a Treatise of the art of governing by <term>Itakura Suo-no-kami</term> <note>Itakura Katsushige (1545–1624), a prominent judge and governor of Kyoto.</note>, Governor of <term>Miaco (Kyoto)</term>, who in the decline of his life retired from business, and wrote this Book under a large Cherry-Tree in his Garden, whence also he has borrowed that Title.*

*Tsurezuregusa* <note>Original: *Tsure dsure Iofijdano Kenko*.</note>, *that is, the "Essays in Idleness" by Yoshida no Kenko, who was once a Soldier in the Emperor’s service, but retired afterwards into a Convent, and turned Monk. It is a Collection of moral Sentences, very conducive to regulate the behavior of mankind in various scenes of life.*

*Hyakunin Isshu* <note>Original: *Faku nin Isju*.</note>, *that is, the verses of an hundred men. It is a Book of Poetry, composed by an hundred persons of the Court of the <term>Dairi (the Imperial Court in Kyoto)</term>, every one of whom furnished his quota.*

*Kojogun*. *A Treatise of the Government of Japan.*

* *Nihon Shoki* <note>Original: *Nipponki*. The "Chronicles of Japan," the earliest official history of the nation.</note>. *An account of the most remarkable things to be met with in the Empire of Japan.*

* *Setsuyoshu* <note>Original: *Sitzi Jossu*. A popular dictionary and cultural encyclopedia of the period.</note>. *A Geographical description of the Empire of Japan, translated in Chapter 5 of the first Book of this History of Japan.*

* *Ise Monogatari* <note>Original: *Isje mono Gattari*.</note>. *A discourse of the affairs of Ise, by <term>Ariwara no Narihira</term>, a Person of the Imperial Court.*

* *A description of the Court of the <term>Dairi</term>, or the Emperor of Japan, together with one hundred different dresses of the Persons composing that Court.*

* *Edo Kagami* <note>Original: *Jedo Kagami*, the "Mirror of Edo."</note>. *A description of the Court of the Secular Monarch <note>The Shogun.</note> at <term>Jedo (Tokyo)</term>, with a list of all the Officers, and their Revenues.*

*Shiki* <note>Original: *Sikki*. The *Shiji* or "Records of the Grand Historian" by Sima Qian.</note>. *A Chinese Chronicle, containing a description of the most remarkable occurrences in the Empire of China.*

*Man’nen Goyomi* <note>Original: *Mannengojomi*.</note>, *that is, an almanac for ten thousand years, wherein it has been calculated, what days are fortunate or unfortunate, according to the influence of the celestial signs.*

* *Jokyo-reki* <note>Original: *Dsiookivi*. A calendar system introduced in 1684.</note>. *An Almanac. They are commonly eight Inches in height, and five feet in length.*

# I N T R O D U C T I O N.

<margin>Conclusion.</margin>
*Having thus gone through what I proposed to treat of in this Introduction, it may now at last be reasonably expected, that I should say something on my own behalf: I am very sensible, that this performance is far from being without Faults, in excuse of which, although I could alledge several things, yet I will rather rely on the candour of my readers, in hopes, that the difficulties, which inevitably attend the translating of a work of this kind, and which were not a little encreased by something very intricate and obscure in the author’s stile <note>Engelbert Kaempfer wrote his original manuscripts in a complex, 17th-century High German.</note>, together with the consideration, that I was to translate into a Language, which is not my mother tongue <note>The translator, John Gaspar Scheuchzer, was Swiss-born and spoke German as his first language.</note>, will be a means to soften the censures of some, and that the pains, I have been at in many other respects, will make amends with more impartial judges, for what imperfections still remain. What I chiefly aimed at, was to express the sense of the author, in as clear and intelligible a manner, as was not inconsistent with the nature of the subject, and the genius of the English Language; and being conscious of my own insufficiency, I have, for a farther satisfaction, desired some of my friends to peruse my translation, and to correct what they found very much amiss therein. As to the <term>Cuts</term> <note>original: "Cuts." A historical term for woodcuts or copperplate engravings used for illustrations.</note>, but very few were left finished by the Author: All the rest I have drawn with my own hand, either from his unfinished originals, or from the prints and drawings of the Japanese, in the Collection of Sir Hans Sloane <note>Sloane was a renowned physician whose massive collection of curiosities and manuscripts formed the foundation of the British Museum.</note>, and if they should appear to some to fall short in point of elegance, though even as to that I have taken all possible care, I have the satisfaction at least, that I can vouch for the truth and accuracy of them, and their conformity with the originals. But there is one thing, which I cannot forbear taking notice of, before I conclude, and that is, that the Author hath repeated, in some places, what he had already mentioned in others: I intended at first to leave out all these repetitions, but upon second thoughts, and for some other reasons, I resolved to give the whole History, as it had been delivered to me: the rather, as the said repetitions, which the Reader is desired candidly to excuse, are in the end not altogether useless, both as they serve to refresh the memory, and to give, in some places, a more ample explanation of such things as were but occasionally touched upon in others.*

->May 1. 1727.<-

<margin>The reason for the Author’s voyage.</margin>
After I had stayed for some time in *Batavia* <note>Modern-day Jakarta, Indonesia, which served as the headquarters for Dutch operations in Asia.</note>, the capital of the Dutch *East-India* Company <note>The Vereenigde Oostindische Compagnie (VOC), a powerful chartered trading company.</note> in the *Indies*, and the residence of the Director General located on the great island of *Java*, an opportunity arose for sailing to *Japan* on board a Dutch ship called *De Waelstroom* <note>Dutch for "The Whirlpool."</note>, bound for that country. I was offered the position of physician to the Embassy, which the Company sends once a year to the Japanese Emperor’s Court. It has now been almost a century since this Empire has been, as it were, shut up and kept from all commerce with foreign nations, except for the Dutch. Because the Dutch are looked upon as the most sincere of all foreigners, they are admitted and tolerated for this reason, though under very strict inspection, and are allowed this particular

This is the only Opportunity at present, an European can have of going thither, and viewing the Majesty of that Court and Empire. Our Ship was bound first to *Siam* <note>Modern-day Thailand.</note>, there to dispose of Part of her Cargo, and to take in Goods of that Country, whereby I had an Opportunity of seeing also this famous Kingdom and its magnificent Court.

<margin>Departure from Batavia.</margin>
I went on Board on *Sunday* the Seventh of *May* 1690 early in the Morning. We weigh'd Anchor the same Day and set Sail with a small, but favourable Breeze. About Noon we made the small Island *Eidam* <note>Now Pulau Edam, located in the Bay of Jakarta.</note>, lying a few Leagues <note>A league is a historical unit of distance, roughly equivalent to three miles.</note> off *Batavia*, along which we coasted till late at Night, when we lost sight of it.

<margin>S. Paul.</margin>
On *Monday* the Eighth we lost Sight of the high Land of *Java*, but not of the neighbouring Islands. We were becalm'd in the Afternoon and advancing but slowly, cast Anchor in Twenty nine Fathoms <note>A unit of depth equal to six feet.</note>, lest the Currents, which run here very strongly, should carry us too much out of our Course. About half a League off us we saw a small Portuguese Vessel at Anchor, with Chinese Sailors on board, which set Sail from *Batavia* two days before. She was call'd the *St. Paul*, and had the Image of this Apostle painted upon her Stern. She had been in *Japan* about five Years ago, notwithstanding that by order of the Japanese Emperor all Portuguese whatever are forbid entring his Dominions under Pain of Death and Forfeiture of their Ships and Goods <note>Following the Shimabara Rebellion in 1638, the Tokugawa Shogunate strictly banned the Portuguese from Japan due to their association with Catholic proselytizing.</note>. I flatter myself the Reader will not be displeas'd to be inform's of the Occasion and Event of this Voyage, which I particularly enquir'd into at *Batavia*, the rather since it bears a near relation to the main Subject of this History.

About six Years ago, a Japanese Vessel was forc'd away, in a violent Storm, from the Coasts of *Japan* towards *China*, and having suffer'd many Incommodities, was at last wreck'd near *Macao*, a famous trading Town in *China*, belonging to the Portuguese. The Portuguese Government at *Macao* thought this an excellent Opportunity, to recommend themselves to the Japanese Emperor, and perhaps, which they had more at heart, to recover their former advantageous Trade. For this reason it was resolv'd to relieve the twelve Japanese, whose Lives had been sav'd, to treat them with kindness and civility, and generously to send them back to *Japan* on board one of their own Ships. But the Event fell far short from answering their Expectation; for when they got into the Harbour of *Nagasaki* <note>Original: "Nangasaki." The only port open to limited foreign trade during this era.</note>, all the Japanese without exception were committed to Prison, and the Portuguese Vessel strictly guarded, without permitting any Body to set foot on shore, till the Governors of *Nagasaki* could give an Account of this delicate <note>Original: "nice." Used here in the historical sense of a precise, sensitive, or politically complicated matter.</note> Affair to the Imperial Court at *Edo* <note>Original: "Jedo." The Portuguese were like to be put to Death and to have their Ship burnt, pursuant to the standing Imperial

# Chap. I. The History of JAPAN.

Imperial Orders on this head; but the Severity of the Court being somewhat allay'd, partly by length of time, partly by the intercession of Mr. *Buteman* <note>Nicolaas de Buytenhem, the Dutch Resident (Opperhoofd) in Nagasaki from 1684–1685 and 1689–1690.</note>, then Resident of the Dutch East-India Company, they at last, in consideration of their good Intention, obtain'd leave to return to *Macao* <note>A Portuguese settlement in southern China.</note>, and Provisions were offer'd them consisting chiefly in Rice and Water. The unhappy *Japanese*, after a rude Imprisonment of two years, were set at Liberty, and under a strict Guard sent to their native Towns. One of our Residents, upon his return from *Jedo* <note>Modern-day Tokyo, then the seat of the Tokugawa Shogunate.</note> to *Nangasaki* <note>Modern-day Nagasaki, the only port open to Dutch trade.</note>, met some upon the road. Thus this Voyage ended without the least advantage to the City of *Macao*. But to proceed on our own Voyage.

We weigh'd anchor after midnight, and on the Ninth in the Morning made the Thousand Islands <note>Known today as Kepulauan Seribu, a chain of islands north of Jakarta's coast.</note>, as they are here call'd. We were in Sight of the high Land *Lampon* <note>Lampung, at the southern tip of Sumatra.</note>, in *Sumatra* opposite to *Bantam*. We saw likewise the Western Mountains both of *Java* and *Sumatra*, and particularly one in *Sumatra*, remarkable for its height, which to our great Grief we had had so long in Sight, some Months before in our Voyage from *Atjin* <note>Modern-day Aceh, at the northern tip of Sumatra.</note> to *Batavia*. The Wind was variable, mostly S. We were almost becalm'd in the afternoon, and could not make the Island *Norderwachten* <note>Dutch for "North Watcher," now known as Pulau Jaga Utara.</note>, that is *Northern Guard*, before Evening. After Sunset a fresh favourable Gale sprung up.

It was cloudy all the Tenth. The Wind E. S. E. We steer'd North out of sight of Land or Islands, excepting some few of the highest Mountains in *Sumatra*, the tops of which we perceiv'd indistinctly through the Clouds. We cast Anchor late at Night in six Fathoms, to avoid running against Land in the Night, which was seen from the great Mast the evening before, and suppos'd to be the Island *Lucipara*, lying at the mouth of the Strait of *Banca* <note>The Bangka Strait, separating Sumatra from Bangka Island.</note>.

On the Eleventh of *May* we weigh'd anchor early in the morning, but a Calm ensuing forc'd us to drop it again, and to lie by for some hours. About two hours after Sun rising, a brisk Gale sprung up at S. and we steer'd North between Land, which we saw last evening, and found to be the Island *Lucipara*, and the Coasts of *Sumatra* towards the Straits of *Banca*.

<margin>*Voyage from Batavia to Siam dangerous.*</margin>
Before I proceed further, I cannot forbear observing in general that the Voyage from *Batavia* to *Siam* is attended with no small difficulties and dangers, because of the many small low Islands, Rocks, Shoals and Sands. A careful and prudent Pilot must always keep at a due distance from Land, that is, neither too near it, nor too far off, that in case of strong stormy Winds and Turnado's <note>An archaic term for violent squalls or thunderstorms common in these waters, not necessarily a modern tornado.</note>, which frequently and unawares arise in this Passage, he may have an opportunity of coming to an anchor, and by this means preserve the Ship from running a-ground, or from being cast away too far out of her Course. For this Reason Ships commonly lie at anchor over night, the rather if Land was seen the day before, or some Signs appear'd of its be**ing**, <meta>catchword: ing,</meta>

[Draw]ing near. The most dangerous passage because of its narrowness, shoals, and rocks, are the Straits of *Bangka* <note>The Bangka Strait separates the island of Bangka from the eastern coast of Sumatra.</note>, formed by an island of this name and the coasts of *Sumatra*. The coasts of *Sumatra* all along the straits are low, without hills or mountains, but well stored with woods. *Bangka*, on the contrary, is ragged and broken with high hills and mountains in some parts, and low verdant ground in others. It seems in the main to be a very fruitful island. All the ships bound for the eastern coasts of *Malacca*, for *Siam*, *Cambodia*, *Cochinchina* <note>An old name for the region of central and southern Vietnam.</note>, *China*, and *Japan*, pass these straits. The coasts of *Sumatra*, opposite to *Bangka*, have two or three remarkable points running out into the straits. We got within half a league of the said coasts because there is a good soft clay at the bottom and even ground in six fathoms of water and more. We reached the second point of the coasts of *Sumatra* before sunset, and lay by until the next morning.

On the twelfth of *May* we weighed anchor before sunrise, and this morning got as far as the third and furthest point of the coasts of *Sumatra*. The *St. Paul* (mentioned above) which was until now far behind us, had now moved considerably ahead of us. We steered along the coasts to the North-North-West. The sky was thick and cloudy, the wind variable, mostly from the South. The coasts of *Sumatra* and *Bangka* appeared much as they did yesterday. In the afternoon the wind turned against us, which made us take in part of our sails and tack about for a while.

On the thirteenth of *May* in the evening, we safely reached the end of the straits, between the mouth of the River *Palembang* <note>Original: "Palimbang"; a major river in southern Sumatra.</note> on our larboard <note>The left side of a ship (modern "port").</note>, and a very high rock called *Monapin* <note>Now known as Tanjung Kalian or Mount Menumbing near Muntok.</note>, upon the extremity of *Bangka* to the starboard <note>The right side of a ship.</note>. 
<margin>Palembang River.</margin>

We could see no land beyond it, whether because of its vast extent or because of the dusk of the evening. # Chap. I. The History of JAPAN.

<margin>Pulau Saya <note>original: "Puli Saya." Kaempfer uses "Puli," a corruption of the Malay word "Pulau," meaning "Island."</note></margin>
We made considerable progress throughout the night, and on the morning of the fifteenth, we left *Pulau Saya* so far behind us that we could barely see the peak of one of its mountains, which is notable for its great height. Around noon, we reached *Pulau Lingga* and safely crossed the **Equator** <note>original: "Æquinoctial Line."</note>. The weather cleared up then, following a heavy rain the previous night. We were nearly becalmed in the afternoon, moving very little; however, at about four o'clock, we encountered a fierce **storm** <note>original: "Turnado." In this context, a sudden, violent tropical squall.</note> with the wind blowing hard from the Northwest. We sailed with incredible speed through these dangerous waters for about two hours until the wind died down. We then dropped anchor, having been blown significantly off our intended course.

We set sail again on the morning of the sixteenth with light, shifting winds and clear weather following another rainy night. Our progress was slow, and we did not lose sight of *Pulau Lingga* until evening, when we again anchored.

On the seventeenth of *May*, we weighed anchor two hours before sunrise. We steered Northwest but saw no land all day. The ocean currents carried us with great force toward the North and North-Northeast. Since there was little wind, we anchored toward evening in thirty-four fathoms of water and set sail again around ten at night.

The wind remained unpredictable throughout the eighteenth, occasionally blowing hard. We steered Northwest without any sight of land. We initially decided to pass by *Pulau Tioman*—where, according to the East India Company’s instructions, our ships usually stop for wood and water—choosing instead to take advantage of the favorable southerly winds to sail directly north toward *Siam* <note>Modern-day Thailand.</note>.

<margin>Pulau Tinggi</margin>
<margin>Pulau Aur</margin>
We remained under sail all night. On the morning of the nineteenth, spotting the peak of a mountain on our **port side** <note>original: "Larboard." The left side of the ship.</note>, we hoped it was the island of *Pulau Tinggi* and steered directly toward it. Our hopes were confirmed, and in the afternoon, we sighted *Pulau Aur* (also called *Pulau Oor*) and soon after, *Pulau Pisang*.

<margin>Pulau Tioman</margin>
On the twentieth of *May*, at about eight in the morning, we anchored off the island of *Pulau Tioman*, which lay to the Northeast by East. I went ashore with several others, partly to survey the island’s geography and partly to observe the plants and other natural wonders it produces. Throughout my travels, this has always been one of my primary interests and pastimes.

*Pulau Tioman* is one of the largest islands located near the eastern coast of *Malacca* <note>The Malay Peninsula.</note>. It is subject to the King of *Johor*, who lives at *Siperka* on the mainland of *Malacca*. He governs the island through two **local officials** <note>original: "Orang Kay's." From the Malay "Orang Kaya," which literally means "rich person" but serves as a title for a local leader or nobleman. Kaempfer mistakenly translates it here as "woodman."</note>, one on each side of the island. *Orang Kaya* in the Malay language literally means a "man of wood," or someone tasked with the oversight of forests. The inhabitants are a group of **outlaws** <note>original: "Banditto's."</note> who have occupied this island for a long time. Their numbers have recently grown so much that a few years ago, one of their leaders who came aboard one of our ships claimed they numbered no fewer than two thousand, though the actual count is likely not even half of that.
