## The History of J A P A N. Book I.

They live apart from one another in humble, small cottages, which consist of only a single room with one small window and a door for entry. These huts are no more than five or six paces long and two or three wide. The only furniture inside consists of a bench running around the room for sitting or sleeping. Outside, there are a few <term>Pinang</term> (Areca palm) trees. Although the island consists of almost nothing but rocky cliffs, the inhabitants choose to live in places where they can find a bit of flat ground around their cottages specifically to plant Areca and other trees.

The inhabitants are quite lively and well-proportioned. They are somewhat darker in complexion than the **Javanese** <note>original: "Javans."</note>, as they live closer to the **Equator** <note>original: "Æquinoctial Line."</note>; some of them appeared to me to have a very unhealthy complexion. They pluck out their beard hairs, as do the people of **Malacca** and **Sumatra**, which makes both the men and women look like ugly old women. They are all **Muslims** <note>original: "Mahometans."</note>, as this religion has spread across almost the entire East. Their clothing consists of a piece of coarse cloth made from tree bark, which they wear around the waist. They also wear a piece of the same cloth twisted like a garland around their heads; some wear hats made of <term>Gabbe Gabbe</term> (Sago palm) leaves. The <term>Gabbe Gabbe</term> is a common tree throughout the East Indies and is not unlike the palm tree. The inhabitants make <term>Sago</term> <note>original: "Saga." A starch harvested from the pith of palm stems.</note> from it, which they eat instead of bread.

The inhabitants came out to our ship in small boats just large enough to hold a single person, and so light that one man can easily haul them onto the shore. The rower sits in the middle with his goods stowed behind him. The oars are longer than a man's height and shaped so that the rower, holding them in the center, rows with both ends on either side of the boat. They also have larger boats that can comfortably hold four people; with these, they venture as far as the coast of **Malacca**.

They brought us exceptionally large **mangoes**, larger than any I had ever seen before. They also brought **bananas** <note>original: "Pisangs (Indian Figs)." At this time, Europeans often referred to bananas as "figs of the Indies."</note> of an unusual size—about a span and a half long and a span in circumference <note>A "span" is roughly 9 inches (23 cm), meaning these fruits were over 13 inches long.</note>. We also saw very large <term>Soursops</term> <note>original: "Suursacks." A tropical fruit with a tart, creamy white pulp.</note>, pineapples, small lemons, poultry, and a very peculiar breed of ram. These animals are reddish in color with long hair and a large tusk on each side <note>Kaempfer is likely describing the Babirusa, or "deer-pig," an Indonesian mammal known for its upward-curving tusks, though he classifies it here as a type of sheep.</note>. They brought no manufactured goods on board except for bags made of neatly woven banana fiber and small mats made of the same material or Sago palm leaves, which were also very skillfully crafted.

They would not accept money for their goods; instead, linen, shirts, rice, iron, and other trinkets <note>original: "Bawbles."</note> were very welcome to them. They seem to have no knowledge of money at all; when we showed them some coins, they asked for ten times the value of a small mat. On the contrary, for a small piece of coarse linen—perhaps not worth three farthings <note>A farthing was a British coin worth a quarter of a penny.</note>—they would readily trade food worth two or three shillings. We climbed up the rocky shores to look for watering places, though not without some difficulty and danger; we were helped by the roots of trees that grow near the top and hang down to the ground for ten, twenty, or even more **fathoms** <term>A unit of length equal to six feet, originally based on the span of a man's outstretched arms.</term>, serving us as ropes to hold onto. Between the heaps of rocks and ruins—for so I might well call them—you very frequently find small lakes or ponds of fresh water. In some places, this water is so cold that after I went for a swim, I felt quite unwell for several days. We found one river large enough to power a couple of mills; it cascaded down from the mountain peaks, rushing over rocks and stones with such speed and roaring that we could hardly hear each other speak while standing beside it. The water was clear and cool, though it seemed to me to have a somewhat bitter taste. I did not have enough time to make all the observations I would have liked regarding the plants on this island. *Terum Lauk* <note>Likely the 'Sea Indigo' (*Guettarda speciosa*), a common coastal tree in the Indo-Pacific.</note> is a medium-sized shrub with oblong leaves about two or three inches long and an inch and a half wide. The seed was exceptionally beautiful, entirely green and shaped like a seven-rayed star. Three, four, or five of these starry seeds grew close together, creating a very handsome appearance.

<margin>*Maanbu*</margin>
*Maanbu*. A fairly large tree with several rounded, tender leaves that are soft to the touch. They lack a central vein and cluster together at the ends of the branches. I had seen this same tree at **Edam**, but I did not have the good fortune then to find its flowers and fruit, which I saw here in full perfection. <margin>Fine Iris.</margin>

Upon our arrival in the morning, a gun was fired to invite the inhabitants to trade with us. In the evening, after the ship had taken in a good store of wood and water, the same signal was given for those of us who had gone ashore to return on board.

We set sail after supper with a brisk, favorable wind. Puli Timon, which in the morning—bearing North East by East—appeared small and narrow, now made a much handsomer and larger appearance, bearing East North East at about **half a league** <term>A league is roughly three miles; half a league is approximately 1.5 miles or 2.4 kilometers.</term> distant. It seemed to be about four leagues long and two broad.

On the twenty-first of May in the morning, we lost sight of Puli Timon and discovered the high mountains of **Malacca** <note>The Malay Peninsula.</note> at a considerable distance ahead. We steered to the North West and North West by West to draw diagonally near the land, which we came in sight of before sunset. This was the main continent of Malacca and some small neighboring islands. We passed these islands in the night, and on the morning of the twenty-second of May, we got within a good league of the coast of Malacca, along which we pursued our course to the North with a fine, favorable land breeze. The coasts of Malacca seemed to me to be not unlike the coasts of **Ceylon** <note>Modern-day Sri Lanka.</note>: very much broken and rocky near the sea, with steep high mountains further inland, otherwise green and full of timber, and to all appearance very fruitful.

The weather continuing fair and the wind favorable all day long, we reached the two islands of **Puli Capas** <note>Modern-day Pulau Kapas, which translates to "Cotton Island."</note> after sunset.

On the Twenty-fourth of *May* we made the Mouth of a River, and a small village upon the Continent of *Malacca*, in Portuguese Maps called *Bufe*. The Inhabitants, who are all Fishermen, called it *Terchannu* <note>Modern-day Terengganu, Malaysia.</note>. The village seemed to consist of about Fifty Houses or Cottages, built along the Shore. A Portuguese Ship, which, as we were told by the Inhabitants, came from **Macao** <note>A Portuguese trading post on the south coast of China.</note>, lay there at anchor with her Colours flying. The Inhabitants speak both **Siamish** <note>Thai</note> and **Malayan** <note>Malay</note>. Three of them came on board in one of their boats to sell us fish; and for a coarse Table-cloth we had as much fish as Twenty hungry people could eat, and amongst others what they call King's Fish, which is a Fish not unlike a Pike, and about three foot long, **Korkuades** <term>Derived from the Portuguese *corcovado*, meaning "hunchbacked"; these are likely Lookdown fish or Moonfish.</term> called by the Dutch Horse-heads, because of their figure, red **Steenbrasfems** <note>Dutch: *Steenbrasem*, a species of sea bream.</note>, **Salammets** <note>Likely the *Ikan Selamat*, a local Malay name for certain edible fish.</note>, and **Jacobs Ewertzen** <note>A Dutch mariner's name for the threadfin or similar ornate fish.</note>. We were becalmed in the afternoon, and cast anchor in sight of some small Islands called the **Redans Islands** <note>The Redang Islands off the east coast of Malaysia.</note>. Some of the Ships Company diverted themselves, as usual, with fishing, and one of them caught a very fine **Starfish with nine Rays** <note>Likely a species of Luidia or similar multi-armed sea star.</note>. The main body held four Inches in Diameter, and each Ray was near one span and a half long, so that the Diameter of the whole Creature was three spans at least. The upper surface was rough to the Touch, as it were full of small Scales. The thickness of the main body was two Inches representing a separate Star with nine short Rays raised above the substance of the body, in the Centre of which was a round hole, or mouth, pretty large and edged with two rows of fibres. The larger Rays were square in circumference, and of the thickness of a finger, straight, running into a point, of a whitish, pale colour, and marked on the upper surface with Spots running across like Clouds, resembling those of a Tyger's skin. Both sides of the upper part were lined up to the point with a row of prickles joining very close and growing still closer, as they run on towards the point. The under surface of this Creature was something softer to the touch or of a white colour, and each Ray lined on each side with a row of small feet like an **Indian Millepes, or Fortyleg** <term>An archaic term for a millipede or centipede.</term>, which in moving confusedly together afforded an odd and diverting sight. In the main body was a cavity tolerably deep, from which Issued a channel along each Ray. The inward substance was white, hard and so brittle that some of the Rays broke in my hands. (see **Table 1. Figure 1.** <note>original: "Tab. 1. Fig. 1.", referring to the engraved plates accompanying the original manuscript.</note>)

### The History of JAPAN. Book I.

...making but little progress, and at last cast anchor in sight of the said Cape. We had several fishermen come on board, who sold us fish in exchange for Linen. Among the rest, they brought us some of those animals which our <margin>Sea Cats.</margin> sailors call *Sea Cats*, and which are true *sea cucumbers* <note>original: *Ichthyothuria*; a classification of marine invertebrates that includes sea cucumbers and starfish, which Kaempfer correctly observes lack a traditional bony skeleton.</note>, having neither bones nor fibers like other fish. We caught an abundance of them during our voyage to *Japan*, a subject to which I will refer the reader for a more particular description later. It is worth observing here that linen is what the inhabitants of *Malacca*—both on these coasts and on the opposite side toward the Straits of *Malacca* and the Gulf of *Bengal*, as well as the inhabitants of the neighboring islands—desire most. They willingly exchange the products of their country, food, and manufactured goods for it, to the great advantage of seafaring people. 

These people are for the most part fishermen and admirable swimmers, as they spend the best part of their lives at sea. <margin>Nicobar Islands.</margin> I was told by several of our seamen, who had traveled that way and were eyewitnesses to the fact, that the inhabitants of the *Nicobar* Islands—which lie in the Gulf of *Bengal* and are commonly encountered when traveling from *Malacca* to *Bengal*—are such proficient swimmers that they will follow a ship even when she has all her sails crowded <note>Sails "crowded" means all available sails are set to achieve maximum speed.</note> and can actually keep pace with her. While swimming, they frequently leap out of the water. They tie their goods around their necks and sell them on board for fish-hooks, small knives, and other such trinkets, but chiefly for linen if they can obtain it. They climb up the ship wherever they happen to reach it with great swiftness and dexterity. They are for the most part strong and well-built, with wide mouths and large teeth. When a gun was fired for amusement, they would all jump overboard, only to climb back up again a short while later. The Portuguese frequently stop at these islands to trade with the inhabitants. They speak a unique language of their own, yet they understand some **Malay**, **Portuguese**, and **Dutch** words. They are said to be so savage and cruel that if a European has the misfortune to fall into their hands, they will greedily devour him; yet they are considered inferior in barbarity and fierceness to their neighbors, the inhabitants of the <margin>Andaman Islands.</margin> *Andaman* Islands, which also lie in the Gulf of *Bengal*. The **Brahmins** <note>original: *Bramines*; the priestly caste of India.</note> say that the inhabitants of these *Andaman* Islands are devils in human form, animated by the souls of wicked and wretched men. These islands are not easy to reach because of the shallow shoals and rocks that surround them.

<margin>Remarkable Shipwreck in sight of Great Varella.</margin> <note>original: *Vi-ssa Grande*; likely a reference to Pulo Varella or a similar landmark along the Malay coast.</note> On the twenty-ninth of *May*, we set sail before sunrise. We had not been under sail for long when a storm arose out of the north, hitting us so suddenly that we could not **furl** <note>To roll up and secure a sail.</note> our sails without some difficulty. The storm passed in about two hours, but the wind continued to be contrary, keeping us at anchor until the morning of the thirtieth. In the meantime, I beg leave to make a short digression and provide an account of a remarkable shipwreck and the wonderful survival of a native of *Japan* who was a passenger on our ship from *Batavia* <note>Modern-day Jakarta, Indonesia.</note> to *Siam* <note>Modern-day Thailand.</note>, which

**which I had from himself.** His name was *Hanjemon*. He was an honest and industrious man, and in addition to his native language, he was well-versed in the Chinese, Vietnamese <note>original: *Tunquinese* and *Cochinchinese*; referring to the northern and southern regions of Vietnam</note>, Malay, and Siamese languages. He was born at *Hirado* <note>original: *Firando*</note> in *Japan*, and after leaving his home country, he settled in the Kingdom of *Siam* <note>modern-day Thailand</note>. In 1682, he boarded a large Siamese junk <note>a traditional sailing vessel</note> bound for *Manila* in the Philippine Islands. The pilot of this junk, which carried sixty-four other people besides himself, was Portuguese. After a reasonably good voyage, the ship ran aground in fair weather on a rock about two leagues <note>roughly 6 miles or 10 kilometers</note> away from a small, low island called *Visia Grande* <note>Portuguese for "Great View"</note> by the Portuguese. The pilot and several others took the boat and, after drifting for six days, reached the coast of *Vietnam*, from where they eventually returned to *Siam*. Most of the crew were swept out to sea and undoubtedly died. *Hanjemon* and thirteen others were cast upon the aforementioned island, which was no more than two leagues distant from the spot where they were stranded. It was fortunate for them that the weather remained fair and the sea calm; otherwise, they all would have inevitably perished. *Visia Grande* belongs to the Philippine Islands, located not far from the large island of *Luzon* (or *Manila*). It is a low, flat island without hills or forests, though it is not without plants and *bamboo*. It was measured to be 357 fathoms broad and 363 fathoms long <note>roughly 700 yards or 650 meters in each direction</note>.

*Hanjemon* and his unfortunate companions found a large number of birds for their survival on the island. These birds were so tame that the men could catch them by hand whenever they pleased. The birds had long beaks and were observed to belong to only four different species. One species in particular, which was black and white and called *Parginje* <note>likely a corruption of the Portuguese *Pardela*, referring to shearwaters or petrels</note> by the Portuguese, proved most useful to them because of their eggs. These eggs were nearly as large as chicken eggs and were available to eat throughout the year. Along the coasts, they caught large *tortoises* <note>sea turtles</note>, which sustained them for six months of the year. Among the plants, they found the *Dracontium* <note>Dragon-root</note>; the large root of this plant is eaten in the *Indies* after its bitter, stinging juice has been squeezed out. 

They diligently gathered whatever wood washed up on the island. After building a type of raft from it, they went out in calm weather to retrieve whatever wood, iron, and other tools they could recover from the shipwreck. These items later proved very useful for catching fish and providing themselves with other necessities. They started fires in the Indian fashion by rubbing two dry sticks of *bamboo* together. Since their clothes had all worn out, they replaced them with the skins and feathers of the birds they killed, stitching them together as best they could. The large shells which the Dutch in the *East Indies* call *Vader Noachs Schulpen* <note>Dutch for "Father Noah's Shells," referring to the Giant Clam (*Tridacna gigas*)</note> served as pots for cooking their food. However, they discovered that these shells would not last long when placed over a fire. To fix this problem, they smeared the shells with the blood of the birds they killed...

upon the island, having observed by chance, to their great joy, that when coated in this way <note>original: "daub’d"; likely referring to containers or wood being smeared with resin, clay, or fat to make them more durable or watertight</note>, they would last longer. In short, they lacked little for the support of their lives except for fresh water. To supply this need, they dug holes in the ground in several places on the island to collect rainwater, which they afterwards stored for use in the previously mentioned large shells. They also took particular care to gather and save whatever pieces of wood were washed up on the coasts from time to time.

They survived in this manner for nearly eight years, having lost three of their companions during that time; they thought of nothing else but ending their days in this solitude. But at last, the desire to return to their wives, relations, and friends prevailed with them so strongly that they unanimously resolved to build a boat—or rather, a monster of a boat—from their supply of wood. They decided to trust themselves once more to the mercy of the waves rather than lead any longer such a comfortless and miserable life on a destitute, uninhabited island. 

So they all went to work, and having finished their boat, eleven of them embarked, not knowing where their fate and good fortune would carry them. After thirty-one whole days of drifting and enduring many hardships, they finally reached the Bay of Tonkin <note>original: *Tunquin*; the northern region of modern-day Vietnam</note> on the coasts of the island of Hainan <note>original: *Haynam*</note>. As luck would have it, they landed on the part of the island facing Canton <note>modern-day Guangzhou</note>, which belongs to the Chinese; the other side toward Cochinchina <note>the southern region of modern-day Vietnam</note> was inhabited by a merciless and savage people. 

The Chinese Governor of this island received them with all imaginable kindness, clothed them, and sent them to *Macao*. From there, three of them boarded a Portuguese ship to *Batavia* <note>modern-day Jakarta, Indonesia</note>, where one of them remained. *Hanjemon* and his companion returned to *Siam* <note>modern-day Thailand</note> on board our ship. The latter learned, to his great grief, that his wife—unable to wait through his long and tedious absence and having lost all hope of ever seeing her husband again—had married a Portuguese man, by whom she already had a child.

We made very little progress on the 30th. On the 31st, we met with a small accident, being suddenly hit by a strong <term>Turnado; a violent tropical squall or whirlwind</term>. As we were taking in our sails, we lost our foremast, which split to pieces and fell partly onto the deck and partly overboard. Two of our men, who were standing at the topmast, fell overboard. One of them swam back to the ship directly and was saved with ropes and wooden bars that were lowered to him. The other missed the ship but managed to catch hold of the towline that tied our small boat to the ship. He held on tight, even though the ship was moving very fast, until two men stepped into the boat and pulled him up with great difficulty. Neither of them seemed to be outwardly hurt or bruised, but one complained of great pains in his side, and the other in his chest. It was fortunate for us that the rigging of the foremast broke, because otherwise it might have endangered the mainmast as well. No sooner had we dropped anchor and taken our sails in than the storm blew over; we remained there until the next day repairing our foremast.

On June 1st, the wind shifted to the south-southwest, southwest, and south. We spread all the sails we could and, to keep the ship balanced, hoisted both sprit-sails <note>Sprit-sails are small square sails set on a yard under the bowsprit, used primarily for maneuvering and balance.</note>.

<margin>Ligor,</margin>
<margin>Puli Cornam.</margin>
<margin>Puli Sancorij.</margin>
<margin>Puli Bordia</margin>
Having repaired our foremast and set it back in place, and with the wind remaining favorable, we made good progress within sight of flat, low land along the coasts of *Ligor* <note>Nakhon Si Thammarat, a province in southern Thailand.</note>. On June 4th, we sighted three large islands at ten degrees North latitude belonging to the Kingdom of *Ligor*. In the morning, we saw the first, marked on maps as *Puli Cornam* <note>likely Ko Samui; "Puli" is a variation of the Malay "Pulau," meaning island</note>; around noon, the second, *Puli Sancorij*, which lies exactly at the tenth degree of North latitude; and soon after, the third, *Puli Bordia*. By nightfall, we had left them all behind. We were extremely pleased to have entered the jurisdiction of *Siam*, for on June 5th, we reached the region of *Kui* <note>Kui Buri</note>, with the wind still favorable from the south and southwest. The coasts here are very steep and rocky—reminding me of the coasts of *Sweden*—with many dangerous shoals, rocks, and small islands, some inhabited and some not. I was surprised by this, as there is not the slightest hint of such features on our maps. Indeed, I cannot help but observe that most sea charts are so poorly made that I wonder accidents do not happen more often, as their accuracy cannot be relied upon at all. 

*Monproncena*, a Siamese merchant, gave me some information about these coasts, with which he was well acquainted. He had been the late King’s factor <note>A commercial agent or representative</note>, but during the recent revolution in *Siam* (which I will describe more in the next chapter), he was taken prisoner by the *French*. They seized the goods entrusted to him by the King, as well as some of his own property, and set him ashore at *Paliakatta* <note>Pulicat, on the Coromandel Coast of India</note>. There, the Governor received him kindly and sent him and his family to *Batavia* <note>modern-day Jakarta</note>. He identified the largest of the aforementioned rocks and small islands as *Samajotn*, and named several places between there and the mouth of the River *Meinam* <note>The Chao Phraya River; "Meinam" or "Menam" simply means "river" in Thai</note>. He generally referred to the various rocks and islands we saw on our port side as *Pran* or *Pranj*. Continuing up the coast, he said the next places were *Czam* (or *Ce’am*), then *Putprik*, then *Isan*, then *Mayaklon*, then *Satzyn*, and finally the mouth of the *Meinam*, which in the Siamese language is called *Pagnam Taufia* <note>Paknam, meaning "river mouth."</note>.

<margin>Arrival in the road of Siam.</margin>
On the evening of June 6th, we arrived safely at the road <note>An open but sheltered anchorage for ships</note> of *Siam*. After announcing our arrival by firing five guns, we dropped anchor. The mouth of the *Meinam* lay directly North, about nine miles off.

On the morning of June 7th, I went ashore with Mr. *Gudward* and *van Lookn*. From the anchorage to the river mouth, the bottom consists of soft muddy clay where all types of ships can safely anchor. As we traveled, we noticed that markers had been placed in several areas to help ships navigating the river avoid the shallow spots. We also encountered several fishing boats with men busy at their work. At the mouth of the river, we could scarcely

We sent our boat back again to fetch four chests of silver from on board.

On the ninth of June, we sailed up the river in our own boat, and along the way diverted ourselves by shooting at monkeys, which are frequently seen on the banks of the river climbing the trees. 
<margin>Bangkok.</margin>
At *Bangkok*, we saw the new fort—which had been raised by the French on the right bank—completely demolished. The banks above *Bangkok* are quite well inhabited and stocked with houses and villages. I do not mention the names of particular places here because I have recorded them on a map of this river, which I had the opportunity to make during this journey upstream, and which I corrected later in several places as we traveled back down to return to the ship. On the morning of the tenth, we came to a small island washed by two arms of the river, where there are several temples and dwellings of the *Talapoins* <note>A term used by early European travelers to refer to Buddhist monks.</note>. I went ashore and noticed in one of the temples three large seated gilded idols and one standing, wearing Mandarin-style caps. About forty smaller idols kept them company, standing at their feet. We cast anchor at night a few miles from the capital.

In the afternoon, the director of our factory was notified to keep his people indoors the next morning because his Majesty intended to go abroad. On the Twelfth of *June*, at four in the afternoon, the *Berklam's* <note>The *Phra Khlang*, or Minister of Foreign Affairs and Trade, who acted as a Chancellor.</note> or Chancellor's of *Siam*, who hath also the direction of foreign affairs, his Mother was buried with great pomp and solemnity. The *Siamites* <note>The Siamese (Thai) people.</note> call also their Nurses mothers, and those brothers and sisters, who sucked the same Breasts. This was only the *Berklam's* Nurse, for his Mother died, and was buried about Fifteen months before. The burials of *Siamites* of quality are pompous and magnificent beyond expression. The Corpse is carried to the burial place by water in a stately Prow <note>A type of boat or barge; in this context, a ceremonial royal barge.</note>, as they are here called; which is sometimes gilt all over, the Drums beating and the Music playing all the while. The Corpse is either laid on the face in a coffin, or placed in an open chair exposed to the view of the Spectators, though often it smells intolerably, by reason of the time and delay the preparations for their burial require. And yet persons of quality esteem it one of their chief cares, as soon as they are taken ill of a violent, or lingering sickness, to order the necessary preparations for their funeral to be got ready betimes.

The Coffin is a sort of an oblong-square Chest, or box, not unlike the German Coffins, gilt, or covered with gilt paper. It is placed under a stately hearse with a ceiling, which is likewise gilt and curiously adorned with fine columns and cornices, supporting several arched, bended roofs in proportion to the deceased's quality. At the side of the boat which carries the dead corpse is rowed another of equal length, with a beautiful gilt pyramid, built in form of a steeple. Before and behind are several other prows, with high poles of Bamboos in the middle, hung with eight or ten gilt crowns made of paper. The annexed figures (see *Table I Figures 2. 3.*) will give the Reader a much better Idea, than could be expected from the most accurate description. All these several prows lie along the banks of the River till the funeral is over.

After this manner the Corpse is brought to the burial place, accompanied by <term>Talapoins: a term used by early European travelers to refer to Buddhist monks</term>, the Music playing all the while, and there burnt together with the coffin. The remaining bones and ashes are gathered together, and interred, and a stately Pyramid <note>A *Chedi* or *Stupa*, a bell-shaped monument containing relics or ashes.</note> erected over them, instead of a Monument, the height and magnificence of which are again proportionable to the deceased's quality. The place, where the Berklam's mother was interred, was seated between two branches of the River opposite to the City, and enclosed with a square row of Banners, Flags and other Ornaments disposed in form of palisades. On each side of the chair stood a <term>Scimeter|Scimitar</term> and Pike, gilt and adorned with precious stones as badges of their authority, which all the Mandarins cause to be carried after them upon solemn occasions. These state scimitars have handles fixed to them at least a man's length, so that one may cut and beat with them as with scythes. The chairs are composed of several pieces. Entering the court, we noticed to the left an open house or room, almost square and without walls; its floor was covered with boards and full of people, some sitting, some walking and conversing together.

A large elephant, completely harnessed, stood in the stable to the right.

Opposite to the entry was a stone staircase leading to the *Berklam's* house, where we were to have our audience.

We went up the stairs and then pulled off our shoes.

This house has but one single room, or rather a lofty hall, like a church. It is white inside and full of dust and cobwebs.

Seven square pillars on each side supported the ceiling, which was raised under the third roof and neatly enough painted with red floral patterns <note>original: "branch’d work"</note>.

About the middle of each pillar hung a large plate of Chinese copper.

In the wall between the pillars were long openings with shutters instead of windows.

There were two entries into the hall, with a window between them.

Bamboo poles were fixed to the pillars on each side of the hall, hung with white cloth. Behind these, between the pillars and the wall, were the *Berklam's* servants and household staff <note>original: "domesticks"</note> without any specific order—some sitting, some lying on the ground.

In front sat the Mandarins, such as *Oja Tewejaata* <note>Likely 'Ok-ya' Tevejat.</note>, a Muslim who is set over the <term>Querry|Equerry; an officer in charge of the royal stables.</term> of the King's elephants, sitting next to the *Berklam* on his right; and *Oja Pipat* <note>Likely 'Ok-ya' Pipat, a deputy minister.</note>, the Deputy *Berklam*, to his left. Both had golden *Boefets* before them.

<margin>*Boefets.*</margin>
<term>Boefets|Ceremonial cubical boxes used to hold betel nut supplies, serving as an official insignia of rank.</term> are cubical boxes made of *Pinang* wood. They are marks of the King's favor, which he presents to his Mandarins when he grants them their names and raises them to that dignity. This is never done without first asking the advice of his astrologers.

## The History of JAPAN. Book I.

<margin>Siamese, Chinese, and Muslim officials</margin>
Beside these two, several other Siamese, Chinese, and Muslim officials <note>original: "Mandarins"</note> were seated. I counted twenty-three to the Berklam’s right, and twenty-one to his left. Seven of the highest-ranking officials on each side, sitting in the primary positions, had golden ritual bowls <note>original: "Boesets"; these were likely decorative containers for betel nut or ceremonial items</note> standing before them, while the two officials seated next to them had silver ones. The Letters, along with the purses, the basin, and other ornaments, were placed about four or five paces in front of the Berklam. We sat in the middle between the two rows of officials. A tray <note>original: "baſon"</note> containing minced betel nut <note>original: "Betel and Pinang"</note>, with jasmine and other flowers laid around the borders for decoration, was set before each of us. 

The Berklam, representing the person of the King, sat in a private enclosed area at the upper end of the Hall. He was positioned behind an embroidered carpet draped over a bamboo pole, raised about two or three feet above the ground, so that only the upper part of his body was visible. Two gilded umbrellas were placed before him, one on each side. Behind him were two golden daggers resting on cushions, and a ceremonial sword <note>original: "ſtate Scimeter"</note>, as described previously, stood at each side. Two European paintings hung on the wall behind him, framed with decorative branch-work instead of traditional frames, according to the local fashion. 

Once we had all seated ourselves, the Berklam asked Mr. van Hoorn, through the interpreter, how the Governor-General of our East India Company was doing, how long he had been in the Indies, what troops we currently had at Batavia <note>modern-day Jakarta, Indonesia</note> and at Bantam, which of the two was the better country, and also who we—the Captain and I—were. After these and several other questions were answered, the purses containing the diplomatic letters were opened. Having passed through the hands of several of the officials present, the letters were read aloud. Because the interpreter did not understand some of the Malay expressions, Mr. Moses and Daniel were asked to assist him. The audience lasted about three-quarters of an hour. We were then conducted by the Berklam’s son—who until then had remained behind his father—through his other house to our boats <note>original: "prows"</note>, and from there to a dinner that had been prepared for us.

<margin>Siamese forbidden to wash themselves in the River.</margin>
Nothing else remarkable happened during our stay at Siam, except that toward the end of this month, an order from the King was made public, forbidding his subjects from washing themselves in the river. I later saw several Siamese people washing themselves in their boats using river water, as it is impossible for this nation to live without it.

<margin>Venomous Water Lizard.</margin>
The reason for this order was that several people had recently been bitten by a venomous water snake or lizard and died a few hours later. I was told that these snakes do not exceed a finger in length or a leech in thickness, that they are patterned with brown and blue, and that they infest the river only once every eight or ten years. To ensure the people strictly complied with this order, it was decreed at the same time that the relatives or heirs of any person who died from the bite of this creature would be required to pay a fine of fifteen taels <note>original: "Thails"; a unit of currency and weight used in Southeast Asia</note>.

# CHAPTER II.

->*The present State of the Court of Siam, with a description of Ayutthaya, the Capital City and Place of the King's Residence.*<-

---

<margin>Present state of the Court of Siam.</margin>
The Kingdom of Siam is the most powerful, and its Court the most magnificent, among all the nations of Southeast Asia <note>original: "black Nations of Asia"; a historical term used by 17th-century Europeans to categorize various non-European peoples.</note>. The present *Tsiaufa* <term>Sovereign; from the Siamese title *Chao Fa*, meaning "Lord of the Sky"</term>, or Sovereign, is *Petraatia* <note>King Phetracha, reigned 1688–1703</note>, who, upon the death of his predecessor *Pro Narees Naray e pintsiav* <note>King Narai the Great, reigned 1656–1688</note>, seized the scepter by cruelly exterminating all those who had a stronger legal claim to the succession. He possessed the power to achieve this because he served as Captain General during the late King's lifetime. Furthermore, the King had entrusted him with the chief administration of the Kingdom during a long illness which, despite hopes of recovery, eventually proved fatal. The discovery of a conspiracy formed by a Minister of State named *Constantin Faulcon* against the rightful heirs to the crown and their supporters provided him with a perfect opportunity to achieve his goals. I will briefly relate the history of this conspirator and the details of the conspiracy itself.

<margin>History of Constantine Phaulkon</margin>
*Faulcon* (or *as he signed himself, Phaulkon*) was Greek by birth. He was a man of great intelligence, with a pleasing appearance and an eloquent tongue, despite having received no formal education. He spent his younger years mostly at sea among various nations—particularly the English—whose languages he had learned. While serving the English as a boatswain <term>original: "Cookswain" or Coxswain; the officer in charge of a ship's boat and its crew</term>, he arrived in *Siam* and obtained a position at Court.

<margin>His rise.</margin>
His natural talents, quick apprehension, and success in the tasks entrusted to him—which were initially minor but grew increasingly significant—raised him within nine years to the highest level of influence and authority. He was placed at the head of the Kingdom’s finances and also directed the King’s household. Almost all public affairs of the greatest importance were decided by his advice, and anyone who had a petition was obliged to apply to him. To better secure his authority, he thought it necessary to support his position with a foreign power; he judged the French nation to be the most suitable for supporting his designs, which appeared to even aim at the royal dignity itself.

<margin>He conspires against the Heirs to the Crown.</margin>
To this end, he led his Sovereign to believe that, with the assistance of the French, he could modernize <note>original: "polish"</note> his subjects and bring his dominions to a flourishing condition.

# The History of J A P A N. Book I.

Accordingly, an embassy was sent from Siam to France, which resulted in two return embassies from France to Siam. Jesuits, artists, and military officers were invited from there.

<margin>Puts the French in possession of Bankok.</margin>
General des Fargues <note>The commander of the French expeditionary forces sent by Louis XIV</note>, having arrived with several hundred soldiers, was placed in possession of the fortress of Bangkok by Phaulkon. This fortress was the key to the kingdom, situated on the great River Menam <note>original: "Meinam"; the Chao Phraya River. The name comes from the Thai *Mae Nam*, meaning "river"</note> six leagues from the harbor. The French soldiers, along with other troops raised within the country, were stationed there as a garrison, and the place was made stronger with new fortifications. Once these preparations were complete, Phaulkon entered into secret agreements with the French General and certain Mandarins <note>High-ranking officials or bureaucrats</note>, or officers of the Crown, whom he trusted. Monpi Totso <note>Mom Pi, the adopted son of King Narai</note>, the King’s son-in-law and his protégé—a dependent of both Phaulkon and the French—was intended to be placed on the throne as soon as the sick King died; the King's increasing dropsy <note>A historical medical term for edema, or severe swelling caused by fluid retention</note> threatened him with a sudden death. Phetracha <note>original: "Petraatia"</note> and his sons, along with the King’s two brothers as presumptive heirs to the crown, and whoever else was likely to oppose the conspirators' designs, were to be eliminated.

Pursuant to this scheme, Monpi’s father and relations had already raised fourteen thousand men, who lay dispersed throughout the country. To better facilitate the execution of this design, Phaulkon persuaded the sick King—having found a way to introduce himself into the King's private apartments—that it would be very much for his personal security during his ill state of health to send for the French General and part of his garrison to come up to Louvo <note>original: "Livo"; modern-day Lopburi</note>, where the King then was. Louvo was a city fifteen leagues north of Ayutthaya <note>original: "Judia"; the capital of the kingdom</note> and was the King’s usual place of residence, where he spent most of his time.

<margin>The Conspiracy discovered.</margin>
While General des Fargues was on his way there, the conspiracy was discovered by Phetracha’s own son <note>The future King Sanphet VIII, often called the "Tiger King"</note>. He happened to be with two of the King’s concubines in an apartment adjoining the one where the conspirators were meeting and had the curiosity to listen at the door. Having heard the bloody resolution they had taken, he immediately went to his father to tell him of it. Phetracha, without losing any time,

# Chapter II: The History of **JAPAN**.

The sick King, heartily sorry for the untimely end of his dearest *Mom Pi* <note>Mom Pi was the King’s favorite and adopted son</note>, earnestly desired that the deceased's body might not be exposed to any further shame but decently buried, which was accordingly carried out. *Mom Pi’s* father was seized by a trick upon his estate between Ayutthaya <note>original: "Judia"; the historic capital of the Kingdom of Siam</note> and Lopburi <note>original: "Livo"; the King's summer residence</note>, and all their followers were scattered. 

<margin>The execution of Phaulkon.</margin> 
Constantine Phaulkon, after having been tortured and starved for fourteen days—reducing him almost to a skeleton—finally had his irons removed. He was carried away after sunset in an ordinary chair, unaware of what his fate would be. He was first taken to his house, which he found had been ransacked. His wife lay prisoner in the stable; far from saying goodbye to him, she spit in his face and would not even allow him to kiss his only remaining son, who was four years old (another son having recently died and remained unburied). 

From there, he was carried out of town to the place of execution where, despite all his resistance, he was beheaded. His body was cut into two parts and covered with a little earth, which dogs scratched away during the night to devour the corpse down to the bones. Before he died, he took his seal, two silver crosses, and a relic set in gold which he wore on his breast (a present from the Pope), as well as the Order of *St. Michael* (which was sent to him by the King of France), and delivered them to a Mandarin <note>A high-ranking Siamese official</note> standing by, asking him to give them to his little son. These were presents, indeed, that could be of no great use to the poor child, who to this day goes begging from door to door with his mother, as nobody dares to speak up for them.

<margin>What happened to the French General.</margin>
General *des Fargues* <note>Commander of the French troops in Siam</note>, having arrived at Lopburi in the meantime with a few men, could not help but be extremely surprised by this unexpected turn of affairs. He was, to all appearances, well-received and presented in the King’s name with the usual gift of a golden *Boeset* <note>An ornate container or casket</note> or betel nut box <note>original: "Pinang's box"; *Pinang* is the Malay word for the areca nut used in betel chewing</note>. However, before he was permitted to return to Bangkok, he was forced to promise to surrender that city to the Siamese and to leave his two sons and twelve of his countrymen as hostages at Lopburi. 

Upon his return there, the General—enraged by this disappointment—acted in total contradiction to his promises. He threw the watermen who had brought him down the river into prison, fired at the Siamese from the fortress, and discharged his guns at their ships as they passed by. On this occasion, when two members of his garrison who were natives appeared less ready to fight than he wished, he had them hanged on the ramparts in sight of their countrymen and committed every sort of hostility imaginable. This conduct was likely to provoke the Siamese to perform a bloody tragedy upon him and his sons; accordingly, they had already begun to build forts on the banks of the river to cut off his retreat by water. However, his temper soon cooled. After he laid all the blame for his conduct on his men, claiming they would not obey his commands, the Dutch Resident <note>The local head of the Dutch East India Company (VOC)</note> persuaded the Court that it would be more for their honor to take revenge on him by generously overlook-

Three other Jesuits, who had settled at Lopburi near the temple of *Wathniak prani Waan*, under the pretense of learning the Siamese <term>Pali</term> <note>The sacred language of Theravada Buddhism</note>—the language of their holy books—from the priests, also conformed to their ways by shaving their heads and adopting their dress and lifestyle. These three disappeared suddenly, and it was never discovered what became of them. During these troubles, the Dutch were assured of Phetracha’s <note>original: "Petraatia"; the General who led the revolution and later became King</note> favor and protection by his order. Orders were also sent down to Bangkok <note>original: "Bankock"</note> to let their ships and boats pass by unmolested.

...in <margin>The King dies.</margin> October 1656, he had replaced his uncle, *Pracitama Ratia* <note>original: "Pracitama Ratia"; likely referring to King Sri Suthammaracha</note>, who had succeeded his father and was only in the third month of his reign when his nephew took possession of the throne. What added even more to the King’s <note>King Narai</note> misery was that he had always regarded *Petraatia* <note>Phetracha, the leader of the 1688 revolution</note> as his most intimate friend. Phetracha was his sister’s son, and his own sisters and daughters were the King’s wives; furthermore, Phetracha had always expressed such a hatred for the burdens of a crown that the King never suspected him of such a cruel betrayal. Consumed by this grief, the King died two days later, on the eleventh of July 1689—or according to the *Soncarad* <term>the Chula Sakarat, or Siamese civil era, which begins in 638 AD</term> 2232—in the fifty-fifth year of his age and the thirty-second of his peaceful reign.

<margin>Petraatia ascends the Throne.</margin>
In this manner, *Petraatia* took control of the administration with the title of *King of Siam*, *Tanassari* <note>Tenasserim</note>, *Sucketa* <note>Sukhothai</note>, and *Poiseluke* <note>Phitsanulok</note>, as well as the *Protector of Cambodia*, *Jehoor* <note>Johor</note>, *Pattany* <note>Pattani</note>, and *Queda* <note>Kedah</note>.

<margin>Laws relating to the Succession to the Throne.</margin>
According to the ancient laws of *Siam*, upon the death of a King, the crown passes to his brother; upon that brother’s death, or if there are no brothers, it passes to the eldest son. However, this rule has been broken so frequently, and the right of succession has fallen into such confusion, that currently, upon a King's death, the crown is claimed by whoever is most powerful within the Royal Family. Consequently, it rarely happens that the lawful heir ascends the throne or is able to maintain a peaceful possession of it.

<margin>Rebellion of a Prince of Maccassar.</margin>
This uncertainty regarding succession sometimes even allows strangers, who have no legitimate claim, to aspire to the throne. I will briefly recount two recent examples. A Prince from the royal family of *Maccassar* <note>Makassar, in modern-day Indonesia</note>, having fled to *Siam* for protection some years ago with many of his countrymen, settled near the camp of the *Malagans* <note>Malays</note>, which the King of *Siam* had assigned to them as their residence. (*It should be noted here that the various plots of land where the Malays, Chinese, Japanese, Portuguese, Dutch, and other nations live in Siam—which are shown in detail in the attached map of the King's residence—are called "Camps."*) This Prince formed a plan, with the help of the *Malagans* (who, like him, follow the *Mahometan* <note>Muslim</note> religion), to seize the capital city and take the throne for himself. However, his plot was discovered before it could be carried out. The Prince was summoned to court to surrender and beg for mercy, but he refused with the characteristic stubbornness of the *Maccassar* people. After a bloody battle in which they defended themselves bravely and killed many *Siamites* <note>Siamese people</note>, the Prince and all his countrymen were cut to pieces, except for his eight-year-old son. The *Malagans* who had assisted him submitted in time and escaped this severe punishment; they were pardoned and restored to their positions, as the King was of a merciful nature. This occurred in the year 1687, during the late King's lifetime.

# The History of **JAPAN**. Book I.

<margin>Rebellion of a Priest from Pegu.</margin>
In the year 1689, a Priest from *Pegu* <note>Pegu was a powerful kingdom in modern-day Myanmar; many Peguan refugees and captives lived in the Siamese capital</note>, who had been formerly held in custody at *Juthia* <note>Ayutthaya, the capital city of Siam</note> and was well-acquainted with the affairs of the Court, made a similar attempt at rebellion. He traveled throughout the country, claiming that he was the eldest of the late King’s brothers—those who had been killed by the order of *Petraatia* <note>King Phetracha</note>—and was therefore the rightful heir to the Crown. This story was so widely believed that in a short time he drew about ten thousand men to his cause, though most were an untrained mob. Having learned that the Prince Royal was traveling to a certain location for recreation with his court, the priest went there and hid in the woods. His plan was to murder the entire party, surprise the city, and then kill the King and all his servants. However, his scheme failed; when the Prince saw such a large crowd and suspected a plot, he abandoned his silver plate <note>Valuable tableware and ceremonial items</note> to them as loot and fled back to the Court. The King quickly gathered an army of twelve thousand men and sent them to meet the undisciplined multitude as they marched toward the city. This unexpected resistance terrified the rebels; they immediately scattered and fled so fast that only about one hundred were killed. Three hundred were taken prisoner, and the victors prevented their escape by burning the soles of their feet. A few days later, the priest himself was found sleeping under a tree in the woods with only a boy for company. He was brought to *Juthia*, where he was chained by his neck and chest to a post and displayed as a public spectacle for several days. Afterward, while still alive, his belly was cut open and his intestines were given to the dogs to tear and devour.

<margin>Officers of the King’s Court.</margin>
The King’s Court consists of the following great Officers of the Crown:

**1.** *Peja Surusak* <note>Phraya Surasak, the King’s son and future King Sanphet VIII, often called "The Tiger King"</note>, also called *Peja Wani-a* and *Fairwani*, to whom the King has assigned the affairs of the Crown—specifically the management of criminal courts and the confiscation of property. This is considered the most odious <note>hateful or unpopular</note> part of the royal power. It is generally thought the King gave him this role to make him unpopular with the people, though others claim it was done to secure his succession to the throne.

**2.** *Peja prah’ klam* <note>The Phra Khlang, the Minister of Trade and Foreign Affairs</note> (foreigners pronounce it *Berklam*), who serves as High Chancellor and manages foreign affairs. He is a more handsome man with a better appearance than I have usually seen among this dark-skinned race, who are generally short in stature and look almost like monkeys <note>The author displays the typical Eurocentric prejudices of the 17th century</note>. He possesses a sharp mind and a lively manner; for this reason, he was sent as an Ambassador to *France* a few years ago <note>This refers to Kosa Pan, who led the famous Siamese embassy to the court of Louis XIV in 1686</note>. He would often speak to us of that country, its government, and its fortresses. The hall of his house, where we had a private audience with him, was decorated with portraits of the French Royal Family and European maps, though the rest of his furniture was nothing but dust and cobwebs.

The Siamese have no hereditary family names, but receive their denomination from the fancy of others, particularly their superiors. Great men are called after their employments, and such are the names above related. Court titles and dignities go in this order:

1. ***Peja*** and ***Oja*** is as much as a Prince. 
2. ***Opera***, who are about forty in number both at Court, and in the country, are like Lords or Barons. 
3. ***Oluang***, or ***Luang*** are their noblemen or gentry. This title the King bestows also on his <term>interpreters</term> <note>original: "Truchemans," from the word 'dragoman,' meaning a professional translator or intermediary</note>. 
4. ***Okucen***, are persons descended of great families. 
5. ***Omucen***, inferior officers of distinction. 
6. ***Majalacks***, pages and young gentlemen.

<margin>Names of the Kingdom of Siam.</margin>
The Kingdom of **Siam** is by the natives called ***Muan Thai***, which is as much as to say, the ***Land Thai*** <note>Literally "The Land of the Free"</note>. In their books it is found with this epithet, ***Krom Thep Pramma haa Ikoon***, which translates to the **Circuit of the Visitations of the Gods** <note>original: "Circuitus visitationis Deorum"</note>. The Malays and Peguans call it ***Tziam***, from whence comes the European name **Siam**.

<margin>Its situation.</margin>
Its Northern latitude about the middle of it, or where the capital city is situated, is fourteen degrees eighteen minutes, and its longitude according to the common maps is 138, but according to the late observations of the Jesuits, 120 degrees. Eastward it borders upon the kingdoms of **Tonkin** <note>original: "Tunkin"</note>, **Cochinchina** <note>original: "Cosynsina"</note>, and **Cambodia**; on the South it is limited by the sea, and the countries of **Malacca**, of which the King of Siam possesses **Ligor** <note>original: "Ligoor"</note>, **Tenasserim** <note>original: "Tanasseri"</note>, and some other small provinces. On the West is the Kingdom of **Pegu**, and on the North that of **Laos**.

<margin>Extent.</margin>
Considering its extent, it is but indifferently peopled, being best inhabited only along the banks of the rivers. The great quantity of deer and buffalo skins...

<margin>Its Division.</margin>

This is further evidenced by the fact that these animals are only hunted in the nearby areas, as the presence of tigers and marshes prevents hunters from venturing deep into the forests. This Kingdom contains twelve large provinces, each of which is governed by an <term>Oja</term> <note>A high-ranking Siamese title of nobility, often transliterated as Ok-ya</note>, or Prince, acting as the King's Lieutenant. He has several <term>Opera’s</term> <note>A subaltern official rank, transliterated as Ok-pra</note>, or subordinate officers, under his command. Additionally, there is an <term>Oja</term> at Court for every province who manages its interests and keeps a watchful eye over the conduct of the commanding Lieutenant. The late King had added a thirteenth province to the original twelve, which he conquered from the Kingdom of **Laos**; in all probability, he would have conquered more if the flooding of a large river had not halted his progress. However, a few years later, that province was retaken from him. As a result, the only benefit of an expedition undertaken in such a remote country and at such great expense was the creation of a lasting jealousy between the two nations, which ruined their former trade and moved it to **Cambodia**.

<margin>Account of the Kingdom of Laos.</margin>
Since I have mentioned **Laos**, it is appropriate to share with the reader the account I received of this Kingdom, which is otherwise little known because it is a landlocked country far from the sea. **Laos** is situated in the same northern climate as <term>Tunquin</term> <note>Tonkin, a historical region in northern Vietnam</note> and is a large and powerful kingdom separated from neighboring states by forests and deserts. It lies a month's journey north of <term>Judia</term> <note>Ayutthaya, the capital of the Kingdom of Siam</note>. Traveling there by land is very difficult and troublesome due to the high mountains; traveling by river is equally difficult because of the rocks and cataracts. Consequently, the vessels—or <term>Prows</term> <note>From 'proa,' a type of multi-hulled sailing vessel</note> as they call them—are built so that they can be taken apart and carried over high ground to continue the journey by water.

It is a fruitful country. The soil is a rich clay which grows so hard and firm in the summer that the inhabitants use it as a floor to thresh their rice to separate it from the husks, whereas in other places they use a wooden trough. It produces an abundance of the best kind of rice and supplies **Cambodia** with the finest <term>Benzoin</term> <note>A fragrant balsamic resin used in incense and perfume</note> and <term>Gum Lac</term> <note>A resin secreted by lac insects, used to make shellac and red dye</note>, though both commodities also grow in that country. It also yields highly valuable musk, some gold, and precious stones—chiefly rubies—along with pearls, which the Siamese call <term>Muk</term> <note>original: "Muk"</note>. This presence of pearls is quite remarkable, as I could not find any report of a salt sea within the country. Their religion is the same as that of **Siam**, and they do not differ much in their language and writing, except that the inhabitants of **Laos** cannot pronounce the letters *L* and *R*. They write upon leaves, similar to the <term>Peguans</term> <note>People from Pegu, in modern-day Myanmar</note> and <term>Malabarians</term> <note>People from the Malabar Coast of India</note>, and in the same style that the Siamese use for their religious books. However, civil affairs are written upon a type of coarse paper using clay styluses. They boast that the Siamese learned the art of writing and the language of their holy books from them. In physical appearance and demeanor, they resemble the Chinese, but they are more tawny and slender, and...

<margin>Description of *Judia*.</margin>
But not to wander too far from our subject, we will return to *Futhia*, or *Judia* <note>Ayutthaya, the historic capital of the Kingdom of Siam</note>, the capital city and place of residence of the King of *Siam*, which in some travel descriptions is wrongly called *India*, perhaps by a printing error. This city in ancient times stood at the place which is now called *Bankok*, on the west bank of the great River *Menam* <note>The Chao Phraya River; "Mae Nam" is the Thai word for river</note>. From there, it was later moved to the location where it now stands: a low island formed by the aforementioned river. This island, with the city upon it, is shaped like the sole of a man's foot, with the heel turning westward, and is about two *German* miles <note>A German mile was a historical unit roughly equal to 7.5 kilometers; the circumference was thus about 15 kilometers</note> in circumference. It is situated in a completely flat country as far as the eye can reach, on low ground cut through by many canals coming from the river. These canals divide the area into so many islands and squares that one cannot go far without the help of boats. It is surrounded by a brick wall which, on the south and north, is four and a half fathoms <note>Approximately 27 feet or 8.2 meters</note> high, clean, well-maintained, and adorned with battlements; however, the rest of it is lower, neglected, and decaying. This wall is open in many places where there are small gates facing the river. On the inside, ramparts are raised against it at different distances for placing cannons. At the lower end of the city, a large bastion projects into the water, alongside several smaller ones. The first is equipped with cannons to defend against incoming ships. To protect the city wall against the erosion of the current, a narrow bank or quay is left, which has been built upon in many places. Several great canals flow from the river directly through the city—some from east to west, others from north to south—and many smaller canals branch off from the main ones. Consequently, ships may come from the river up into the town and dock near the principal houses and palaces. The streets run in straight lines along the canals. Some of them are reasonably large, but the majority are very narrow and, generally speaking, all are foul and dirty. Some are also overflowed at high tide. Considering the size of the city, it is not very populous and is only thinly inhabited in some parts, particularly on the west side due to its remoteness, and towards the

The first street upon entering the city is that which runs westward along the curve of the wall: it has the best houses, among which are those that formerly belonged to the **English**, **Dutch**, and **French**, as also that in which **Faulcon** <note>Constantine Phaulkon (1647–1688), a Greek adventurer who became the primary counselor to King Narai of Siam</note> resided. The **Mandarins** <note>High-ranking government officials</note> or **Ministers** of State and **Courtiers** live in separate palaces, with courtyards attached to them, which are very dirty. The buildings in general, though raised with lime and stone, are but mediocre, and the apartments are neither clean nor well furnished. The booths, or shops of the town, are low and very ordinary; however, they stand in good order and in a straight line, as the streets do. The many canals necessitate a great number of bridges. Those which are laid over the great canal are of stone, with balusters of the same, but as there are no wagons nor carts in this place, they are narrow; in the middle they are high and eighty paces long; but the bridges over the side canals have no specific architecture and are for the greatest part made of wood. Only boats are allowed to come upon the great river as far as it runs by the walls of the palace. The gates and other avenues of the palace are crowded with swarms of men, whose tawny skin is painted with black checkered figures, applied in the same manner as the images at the Holy Sepulchre in *Jerusalem* <note>A reference to the practice of pilgrims getting tattoos in Jerusalem to commemorate their journey</note>. <margin>Palace of the Prince Royal.</margin>
These men are the King's guards, doorkeepers, and watermen, who carry short thick clubs instead of arms, roving and sauntering about the palace like idle vagrants. The second palace, called the *foremost palace*, is situated in the northeast part of the city towards its edge. It is square in shape, but not nearly as large as the first. It was the ancient residence of former kings, but at present, in 1690, it is inhabited by the Prince Royal, who is twenty years of age.

<margin>Palace of the Equerry of the King's Elephants.</margin>
The third and last palace is smaller than either of the other two, and is situated in the west and least inhabited part of the city. In this lives at present a Prince of the Royal Blood; it is called the Palace of the Equerry <note>An officer of a royal household in charge of the stables and horses, or in this case, elephants</note> of the King's Elephants, as the said Prince is the conductor and manager of the elephant that carries the King. The Prince does not ride upon the elephant's neck as is usual, but lies upon its crupper <note>The hindquarters of the animal</note> behind the King, from where he governs the beast by certain signs to which it is accustomed.

<margin>Temples and Schools.</margin>
After the palaces, I shall take notice of the temples and schools of this city. They are great in number, for as the whole country is stocked with priests and monks, this city in particular abounds in all parts with temples. The courts of these temples are sized in regular proportion with the streets and are full of pyramids and columns of various shapes, all gilded over. They do not equal our European churches in size, but far exceed them in outward beauty because of their many tiered roofs, gilded frontispieces, elevated steps, columns, pillars, and other ornaments. Within, they are adorned with many images as large as life or larger, skillfully formed of a mixture of plaster, resin, oil, and hair; the outside of these is first varnished with black and then gilded. They are placed in several rows on an elevated platform where the altar stands. In some temples, they also sit along the walls in single rows, with their legs crossed and bodies naked except for the waist, around which is tied a dark yellow cloth; over the left shoulder down to the navel hangs another piece of cloth of the same color, twisted closely together. Their earlobes are slit and are so long that they reach the shoulders. Their hair is curled and tied over the crown in two knots, so that one cannot distinguish whether it is a cap or some other ornament. The right hand rests upon the right knee, and the left lies in the lap.

The <term>Siamites</term> <note>people of Siam, modern-day Thailand</note> call him *Prah*, meaning the Saint, or *Prah Pudi Dfiau* <note>original: "Prah Pudi Dfiau"; likely Phra Phuttha Chao, or "Lord Buddha"</note>, the Saint of high descent, or by the specific name *Sammona Khodum* <note>Gautama Buddha</note>, which the <term>Peguans</term> <note>people from Pegu, in modern Myanmar</note> pronounce *Sammond Khutama*, meaning "a man without passions." The Japanese and Chinese call him *Siaka* or *Saka* <note>Shakyamuni</note>, and those in Ceylon <note>Sri Lanka</note> call him *Budhum* and *Budha*. This *Prah*, or *Khodum*, is represented in a monstrous <note>in this context, meaning "gigantic" or "immense"</note> size in some temples. In a Peguan temple outside the city, called in the Peguan language *Tfianpnum Tfiun*, there sits an idol on a raised platform, heavily gilded. Its proportions are so massive that it would be 120 feet tall if it were standing. Later, we will encounter another *Siaka*, or idol, in *Miaco* <note>Kyoto</note>, the capital of Japan and the residence of its ecclesiastical hereditary emperor <note>the Emperor, or Tenno</note>, which is not inferior to the one at *Judia* <note>Ayutthaya, the former capital of Siam</note> in either size or beauty. The posture of this idol is the same as that in which Buddha and his disciples placed themselves when they were deep in religious meditation. Even today, the monks who follow him are required by their rules to sit daily at specific times in the posture of their master, practicing their devotions of meditation and religious fervor. They also go about in the same style of dress, though with their heads shaved, and they shield their faces from the sun with a fan made of palm wood and leaves.

<margin>Houses of the Monks.</margin>
Next to the temples are the living quarters of the monks, which are humble houses. Beside them, they have a public hall or oratory called a *Prabkdi* <note>likely an "Ubosot" or "Vihara," a sacred hall for assembly and preaching</note>, which is usually a fairly large wooden building much like the temples. The edges of the roof are gilded, and a few steps lead up to the entrance. It is furnished with many wooden shutters instead of windows to allow air to pass through during their public assemblies or lectures. Inside, the ceiling is supported by two rows of columns, and the room is divided into various sections and benches. In the center, raised several steps above the floor, stands a desk or pulpit, intricately carved and gilded, much like those in our own churches. At certain hours, an old monk appears there and reads holy words to the audience in a slow, clear voice from large palm leaves inscribed with black characters. The audience consists mainly of divinity students or young monks. When certain words or names are spoken, the listeners clap their hands together above their foreheads. However, for the most part, they show little attention or devotion; I myself saw some cutting *Pinang* <note>betel nut, commonly chewed in South and Southeast Asia</note>, others grinding powders, or mixing mercury with the juice of herbs, or keeping their hands busy with other pastimes. Near the pulpit, or in another spot, one can see the idol of *Amida* <note>Amitabha, the Buddha of Infinite Light</note> standing upright on the <term>lotus</term> flower—also known as *Tarate*, the <term>Egyptian bean</term> <note>original Latin: "Faba Aegyptiaca"</note>, or the <term>great crimson water-lily</term> <note>original Latin: "Nymphea magna incarnata"</note>. They believe *Amida* to be the intercessor for the souls of the departed. Around the hall are hung paper flowers, crowns, banners, and other gilded ornaments hanging from bamboo reeds, which they also carry in funeral processions.

<margin>Suburbs of Siam <note>referring to Ayutthaya, the then-capital of the Kingdom of Siam</note>.</margin>
Around the city lie many suburbs and villages. Some of these consist of inhabited ships or vessels rather than houses, containing two, three, or more families each. They move these from time to time and float them particularly when the waters are high to places where fairs are held, <margin>Inhabited boats.</margin> in order to sell their goods and earn their living. (*See Table III. Figures 4, 5, 6.*) The houses in the common villages that stand on firm ground are generally built of bamboo, reed, planks, and other ordinary materials. Some of the houses in the villages along the riverbanks stand on piles a fathom <note>about six feet</note> high, so that the floodwaters—which overflow the country for several months—may pass freely under the houses. Each house is equipped with stairs or a ladder to descend during dry weather, and with a boat to move about during high water. (*See Table III. Figure 7.*) Other villages stand on higher and dry ground; consequently, not being subject to those floods, their houses require neither such stairs nor boats. On these elevations also stand temples, monasteries, burial places where they inter their dead, and yards where they burn the bones and ashes, erecting costly pyramids over them. <margin>Remarkable Tree with Birds' nests</margin>
Before I leave this subject, I must take notice of a tree of a strange nature. One encounters it when leaving the city toward these two squares, over the dyke recently built to close off the southern arm of the great river. It is about the size of an apple tree, with narrow leaves and long, spreading branches. At the very tips and smallest twigs of these branches hang birds' nests, ingeniously twisted together from dry grass and other materials in the shape of a purse with a long, narrow neck. The openings of these nests face the northwest, so that no south wind or rain can enter. I counted over fifty of them on this single tree, and I never found the like on any other. The birds were of a dark yellowish color, not unlike canary birds, and chirped almost like sparrows—which are otherwise very plentiful in this country. Another extraordinary thing about this tree is that its trunk and larger branches are covered in rugged growths or "warts" of different shapes, which the inhabitants use as a <term>Medicine</term> against certain illnesses.

<margin>Religion of the Siamese</margin>
The religion of these people is the <term>Pagan</term> doctrine of the *Brahmins* <note>referring to the Indian roots of Buddhism</note>. For many centuries, this faith has been practiced among all the nations from the River Indus to the farthest reaches of the East. The exceptions are the Court of the Great Mughal <note>The Mughal Empire in India</note> and his major cities, as well as in Sumatra, Java, Sulawesi <note>original: *Celebes*</note>, and other neighboring islands, where *Islam* <note>original: *Mahometism*</note> has gained so much ground that it seems to prevail. This general "Paganism"—which should be distinguished from the religion of the ancient *Persians* <note>Zoroastrianism</note> who worship the sun and are now almost extinct—is divided into various sects and opinions according to different customs, languages, and interpretations. # The History of JAPAN. Book I.

<margin>Origin.</margin> The people of Siam <note>The Siamites, or people of Thailand</note> represent the first teacher of their pagan faith in their temples as a large, seated black figure of enormous size. His hair is curled and his skin is black, though it is often covered in gold leaf out of respect. He is accompanied on each side by one of his chief companions, and both in front of and around him are his other apostles and disciples, all depicted with the same skin color and mostly in the same posture. They believe, following the teachings of the Brahmans <note>The priestly caste of India</note>, that the Deity dwelt within him, which he proved through his teachings, his way of life, and divine revelation. For *Vishnu* <note>original: "Wistnu"</note>, by which they mean the Deity, having already assumed different forms and visited the world eight different times over many hundreds of thousands of years, appeared for the ninth time in the person of this black-skinned teacher. For this reason, they style him *Prahpuditfau* <gloss>the Saint of high descent</gloss>; *Sammana Khutama* <gloss>the Man without Passions</gloss> <note>Sanskrit: Shramana Gautama</note>; *Prah bin Tfjau* <gloss>the Saint who is the Lord</gloss>; or simply *Prah* <gloss>the Saint</gloss>, or *Buddha* (or *Phutha* in one syllable, pronounced with a guttural sound). The people of Ceylon <note>Modern-day Sri Lanka</note> call him *Budhum*. <margin>Siaka</margin> The Chinese and Japanese call him *Sacka*, or *Siaka* <note>Shakyamuni</note>, or simply *Fotoge* <gloss>the Spirit or Deity</gloss> <note>Japanese: Hotoke</note>, and use the honorable title *Si Tfun* <gloss>the Great Saint</gloss> <note>Chinese/Japanese: Shizun, meaning "World-Honored One"</note>.

<margin>Where born.</margin> Regarding his origin and native country, I find that the accounts of these diverse peoples do not agree. The people of Siam call the country of his birth *Lanca*, which is the island of *Ceylon*, from where they say their religion was first brought to them and later spread through neighboring countries as far as *China* and *Japan*. Accordingly, there are still traces of their religion to be seen—both the faith they practiced before and the one that replaced it—on the top of a high mountain in the island of *Ceylon* which Europeans call *Pico d' Adam* <note>Adam's Peak</note>. They consider this mountain holy and place it at the center of the world in their maps. The people of Ceylon themselves call his birthplace *Macca desia* <note>Likely referring to Madhyadesa, the "Middle Country" of India</note>, meaning the Kingdom of *Siam*, for they use the *Pali* language—the religious language of the Siamites—which the people of Pegu <note>Modern-day Myanmar</note> call *Maccatapasa*. They write this in their *Khom* <note>The sacred script used in Thailand for Pali texts</note>, or the language of the *Khomuts*, acknowledging that they received it from the Siamites. The Chinese and Japanese claim that this Saint and the doctrine he revealed originated in the country of *Magatta*, or as the Japanese call it, *Tensik Magatta Kokf* <gloss>the Celestial Kingdom of Magadha</gloss>. According to their description, this is the continent of *India*, including *Pegu* and *Siam*. They add that *Siaka* was the son of the King of those countries. It seems the inhabitants of each region attribute the origin of their teacher to another, as a prophet is always thought greater when he comes from a foreign land. The *Banians* <note>Indian merchants/Hindus</note> and learned *Brahmans* believe that *Buddha* had neither father nor mother, and consequently admit they know nothing of his birth or native country. They represent him in the form of a man with four arms, and they have few other legends concerning his miracles and actions beyond a tradition of his adorable
