### Chap. II. The History of JAPAN.

...piety, having now sat upon a <term>Tarate flower<gloss>Lotus</gloss></term> for 26,430 years, and praising the supreme God for the last 21,639 years (counting from the current year of 1690). This began when he first appeared and revealed himself to the world. However, the <term>Siamites<gloss>people of Siam/Thailand</gloss></term> and other nations further to the East have entire books filled with stories of the birth, life, and miracles of this God, whom they call *Prah* or *Siaka*. I am uncertain how to reconcile these various and conflicting accounts that I have gathered in these countries, unless I adopt what I believe to be the true explanation: that the people of Siam and other Eastern nations have confused a more recent teacher with the original *Budha* <note>The author distinguishes between the historical Buddha and an older, perhaps mythological, figure</note>. This confusion of gods and their names is quite common in the histories of the Greeks and Egyptians. 

<margin>
*Siaka and Budha are not the same Person.*
</margin>

Therefore, *Prah* or *Siaka* is not the same person as *Budha*, and certainly not the same as *Ram* or *Rama*, as he is called by Father <term>Kircher<gloss>Athanasius Kircher</gloss></term> in his book <italic>China Illustrated</italic> <note>original: "Sina Illustrata"</note>. Rama appeared many hundreds of thousands of years earlier, whereas this figure was likely a new <term>Impostor<gloss>pretender or religious innovator</gloss></term> who emerged only about five hundred years before the birth of Christ. Furthermore, many circumstances make it probable that *Prah*, or *Siaka*, was not an Asian or Indian at all, but rather a prominent Egyptian priest—likely from <term>Memphis</term>—and a <term>Moor<gloss>a historical term for a dark-skinned person from Africa</gloss></term>. It is possible that he and his followers, after being expelled from their native country, brought the Egyptian religion to the Indies and spread it there, for the following reasons:

<margin>
*Eastern Paganism derived from the worship of the Egyptians.*
</margin>

1. There appears to be a significant agreement on several key points between this Eastern faith and ancient Egyptian <term>Paganism</term>. The Egyptians represented their gods, just as these people do now, in the forms of various animals and human-animal hybrids. In contrast, their neighbors in Asia—such as the Persians, Chaldeans, and other nations of similar faiths—worshipped the celestial bodies, particularly the Sun and Fire as its earthly image. It is probable that before the introduction of current Eastern religions, the Indians followed the same worship as the neighboring Chaldeans and Persians. Since it is unlikely that such <term>sensible<gloss>rational or perceptive</gloss></term> nations lived without any religion at all (unlike the <term>Hottentots<gloss>an archaic and derogatory term for the Khoikhoi people of South Africa</gloss></term>), it is highly probable they revered divine power by worshipping the Sun and other stars, as these parts of creation most affect the senses and fill the mind with wonder. To this day, there remain some remnants of this <term>Chaldean<gloss>Babylonian/Mesopotamian</gloss></term> religion among these people, seen in their respect for the Sun and stars. While this is not officially taught by their priests, it is tolerated as a form of extra devotion, much like how certain ancient pagan customs and superstitions—specifically the <term>Bachanals<gloss>festivals of Bacchus/Dionysus</gloss></term>—persist even under Christian governments. Two major tenets of the Egyptian religion that were strictly maintained were the <term>Transmigration of Souls<gloss>reincarnation</gloss></term>...

# The History of JAPAN. Book I.

and a deep respect for cows, particularly for the <term>holy Cow<gloss>The author refers to the bull Apis as a cow, though in Egyptian tradition Apis was male</gloss></term> at *Memphis*, called *Apis*, or *Serapis*, which received divine honors and was served by priests. Both of these practices are still observed among the *Asian* pagans, particularly those who live on the west side of the *Ganges* river. In those regions, no one dares to kill even the smallest and most harmful insects, believing they are inhabited by a <term>transmigrated human soul<gloss>the belief that after death, a soul moves into a new body, whether human or animal</gloss></term>. Furthermore, the cows—whose souls they believe have become almost divine through frequent transmigrations—are served and tended with great devotion. Their dung is burned to ashes to be used as a holy salve, their urine serves as holy water, and an image of a cow occupies a special chapel in front of their temples, where it is honored daily with fresh flowers and anointed with sweet-smelling oil. 

It is also noteworthy that the closer these people are to *Egypt*, the greater their zeal for these two practices; the further away they are, the more these customs diminish. Thus, in *Siam* <note>modern-day Thailand</note> and the kingdoms further east, even the priests themselves have no problem eating the meat of cows, provided they did not cause or consent to the animal's death. Nor does the belief in the transmigration of souls hold as much sway there as it does among the <term>Benjans<gloss>Banyans; a term used for Hindu merchants or Hindus in general</gloss></term> in <term>Hindostan<gloss>Northern India</gloss></term>, for the inhabitants on the east side of the *Ganges* show no mercy to the fleas or flies that bite them. I will only briefly mention that among these *Asian* pagans, we find not only the major deities of the Egyptians but also the minor ones, though they are disguised by different names and mythical stories; however, these connections could easily be clarified and reconciled.

2. It is notable that twenty-three centuries ago—or, according to the most precise calculation, in the 536th year before the birth of Christ—<term>Cambyses<gloss>Cambyses II, King of the Persian Empire</gloss></term>, the *Persian* tyrant, overthrew the religion of the Egyptians. He killed their *Apis*, or *holy cow*, which was the protector of their worship, and either murdered or exiled their priests. Now, if one considers that the people of Siam calculate their <term>Soncarad<gloss>Sakaraj; the Siamese era or calendar system</gloss></term>, or ecclesiastical <term>Epoch<gloss>a fixed point in time used as the start of an era</gloss></term>, from the death of their great Saint, their 2233rd or 2234th year coincides with our current year of 1690. From this, it appears that their era matches that specific time. One might conclude from this that a prominent priest of *Memphis*, whom they called *Budha*, *Siaka*, or "the great Saint," fled with his followers into *India*. There, he shared his teachings, which were so well received that they spread to the farthest reaches of the East.

3. Because this Saint is depicted with curled hair like a <term>Negro<gloss>a 17th-century descriptor for African physical features, particularly tight, curly hair</gloss></term>, there is reason to conclude that he was not a native of *India*, but was born in the hot climate of *Africa*. This is based on the fact that the climate in *India* does not produce that "curled wool" texture on its black inhabitants, but rather long, black, and very straight hair with very little curl. ### Chap. II. The History of J A P A N.

...curls of an African person, and consequently it is more probable that <term>Budha<gloss>The Buddha, the founder of Buddhism</gloss></term> was of African extraction rather than <term>Siamite<gloss>Siamese, relating to modern-day Thailand</gloss></term> origin.

The Siamese people in general are a straightforward and kind-hearted people. Their
<margin>Clergy of Siam.</margin>
clergymen lead a quiet and disciplined life; for they aim at a state of perfection in this world that is acceptable to Heaven and rewarded with eternal blessings. They achieve this by subduing their passions and suppressing their desires, following the doctrine and example of their great Master. They never marry as long as they remain in their religious order, but live together in monasteries near the temples. They go almost naked, wearing only a cloth, or apron, of a dark yellow color tied about their waist, and another piece of cloth hanging down from the left shoulder in narrow pleats. In bad rainy weather, they open and spread this cloth over their shoulders and the upper part of the body. Their heads are never covered, but are shaved close; in their hands they carry a fan made of palm leaves or shavings of wood. There are different ranks and degrees among them. 

(1) The youngest call themselves <term>Dsiaunces<gloss>derived from the Thai 'Chao-nen', referring to novice monks</gloss></term>, or Friars and students of divinity. After reaching their twentieth year and undergoing a rigorous examination, they are promoted to the dignity of <term>Dsiaukus<gloss>derived from 'Chao-khu', a title for fully ordained monks</gloss></term>, or Fathers, an occasion celebrated with a great feast. The <term>Peguans<gloss>people from the Mon kingdom of Pegu, in modern Myanmar</gloss></term> call them <term>Talapoi<gloss>a term used by early Europeans for Buddhist monks in Southeast Asia</gloss></term>. This name first became known to foreigners, and they now apply it indifferently to all the priests and clergy of this "Symbolic Religion" in <term>Pegu<gloss>Bago, Myanmar</gloss></term>, <term>Siam<gloss>Thailand</gloss></term>, <term>Camboja<gloss>Cambodia</gloss></term>, <term>Aracan<gloss>Rakhine State, Myanmar</gloss></term>, <term>Parma<gloss>Burma</gloss></term>, <term>Laos</term>, <term>Tunkin<gloss>Tonkin, northern Vietnam</gloss></term>, and <term>Cochintsina<gloss>Southern Vietnam</gloss></term>. 

(2) <term>Dsiauku</term> are the common priests or fathers who live together in societies, inhabiting one or more buildings like monasteries near certain temples. Each such monastery is governed by (3) a Prior, whom they call <term>Luangwad<gloss>from 'Luang Wat', meaning the head or superior of a temple</gloss></term>, which means the Head of the Temple, or <term>Sompan<gloss>from 'Chao Omphan', a title for a senior monk or abbot</gloss></term>, meaning "The Noble." All the monasteries in each province are overseen by one (4) <term>Prabkhru<gloss>from 'Phra Khru', a monastic rank above an abbot, similar to a bishop</gloss></term>, who acts like a Bishop or Metropolitan. These leaders, along with all the rest of the clergy in the kingdom, are under the authority of (5) the <term>Prah Sankara<gloss>the Phra Sangkharat, the Supreme Patriarch of the Thai Buddhist order</gloss></term>, who serves as the Primate and High Priest. He lives in the capital and the King’s residence, <term>Judia<gloss>Ayutthaya, the former capital of Siam</gloss></term>, and his authority is so great that even the King himself is obliged to bow to him. 

These clergymen do not belong to a specific race or caste like the <term>Brahmans<gloss>the hereditary priestly caste in Hinduism</gloss></term>, but anyone who wishes to do so and can qualify may become a monk; even married men may leave their wives and go to live in the monastery. The clergy, as long as they remain in their orders, cannot be punished by the <term>secular arm<gloss>the civil or non-religious legal system</gloss></term> for any offense whatsoever. For this reason, they are first "degraded" (stripped of their rank) and deprived of their monastic robes before they are delivered to the civil courts for justice. However, out of respect for the religious character they once held, they are treated with much less severity than ordinary people. Sometimes, even for capital crimes, the King will only banish them to an uninhabited island called <term>Coccatsian<gloss>Koh Sichang</gloss></term>, where he also sends his <term>Mandarines<gloss>high-ranking government officials</gloss></term> and ministers of state if they fall into disgrace. There are also nuns among

The Siamese begin their <term>Soncarad<gloss>Sakarat; an era or epoch in the Thai calendar</gloss></term>, or *Era*, from the death of their great God <term>Sammona Khutama<gloss>Sommonacodom, a transcription of Samana Gautama, the historical Buddha</gloss></term>, otherwise called *Prab*, and *Budha*. <margin>*Their Months.*</margin>
It appears by this List of the twelve Years, that <term>Pije<gloss>Pi; the Thai word for year</gloss></term> signifies a Year in general. The Year is divided into twelve Months, which are Lunar, of twenty nine, and thirty Days, alternatively. Every third Year they tell thirteen Months, one of the twelve being repeated twice. The general name of the Month is <term>Duan<gloss>Duan; the Thai word for month</gloss></term>, to which word is added the number, as they follow one another, for the names of particular Months, as for instance, *Duan Aey*, the first Month, *Duan Gie*, or *Dzi*, the second Month, and so on, *Saem*, for the third, *Sie*, for the fourth, *Ha*, for the fifth, *Hook*, for the sixth, *Tset*, or *Tsiet* for the seventh, *Pet*, or *Peijt* for the eighth, which is told twice every third Year, *Cau*, or *Knau* for the ninth, *Sieb*, or *Sib*, for the tenth, *Siebeet*, for the eleventh, and *Sieb Song* for the twelfth. <margin>Their Festival Days.</margin> The <term>Siamites<gloss>The people of Siam, modern-day Thailand</gloss></term> celebrate the first and fifteenth day of every month, being the days of the new and full moon. Some also go to the <term>Pagods<gloss>Temples or Stupas, referred to locally as Wat</gloss></term> every first day of the quarter, which in some measure answers to our Sunday. They have besides several yearly solemn festivals, as for instance, one at the beginning of the year, call'd <term>Sonkraen<gloss>Songkran; the traditional Thai New Year</gloss></term>, another call'd <term>Kitimbac<gloss>Kathin Bok; a ceremony involving the presentation of new robes to monks, performed via a land procession</gloss></term>, or *Ktimbac*, that is to say, the procession by Land, on which, as I have been inform'd, the King goes to make his offering at a famous Temple at *Napathat*, in a Siamese Coach, drawn by men; another call'd <term>Ktinam<gloss>Kathin Nam; the water-borne version of the Kathin ceremony</gloss></term> when the King attended with a magnificent train goes by water to make his devotions and offerings at a stately temple call'd *Banihin*, situated below <term>Judia<gloss>Ayutthaya, the capital city</gloss></term>, and according to the opinion of the common people to cut the waters, which about the time of this solemnity are highest, and to command them to withdraw <note>This ritual reflects the king's role in managing the annual monsoon floods</note>. The beginning of the festival days in general is by the Siamites call'd <term>Kaupasa<gloss>Khao Phansa; the beginning of the three-month Buddhist Lent or Rains Retreat</gloss></term>, and the end thereof <term>Oppasa<gloss>Ok Phansa; the end of the Buddhist Lent</gloss></term>.

<margin>The Author travels down the River Meinam.</margin>
<margin>Banibijn, a Temple.</margin>
On the evening of July 4, 1690, I went with the Captain of the ship and others of our company in a boat, in order to travel down the <term>River Meinam<gloss>The Chao Phraya River; "Mae Nam" is the Thai word for river</gloss></term> to our ship. The vessel lay at anchor two days' journey from here, and four leagues from the mouth of the river. After traveling two leagues, we arrived at the famous temple *Banibijn*, called the *Golden Pagoda* by foreigners. Every year, when the water levels are at their highest, the King travels there with great pomp and a numerous attendance to perform his devotions and to make his offerings to the priests. The common people call this solemnity <term>Ktinam<gloss>Likely the 'Thot Kathin' ceremony or the 'Royal Barge Procession'</gloss></term>, which means "the Cutting of the Water," based on an erroneous tradition they have that the King, on that occasion, cuts the water with a knife in order to make the floodwaters recede. It may be that this custom was practiced in ancient times, but at present there is nothing extraordinary in this ceremony beyond the magnificence of the procession, which is conducted by water.

On July 5, we proceeded slowly because of a headwind, which gave me frequent opportunities to go ashore and gather <term>simples<gloss>Medicinal plants or herbs</gloss></term> that I found there.

<margin>Bangkok.</margin>
On the morning of July 6, we arrived at *Bangkok*, having advanced very little during the night because of the difficulties we had to struggle against. We found the old fort, which sits on an island, in good condition; however, the new fort that had been built by the French on the eastern shore was quite demolished <note>The French were expelled from Bangkok following the 1688 revolution</note>. Before evening, we reached the

<margin>Amsterdam.</margin>
Dutch settlement and storehouse called *Amsterdam* <note>The VOC trading post known as Baan Hollanda</note>, which is only two leagues distant from the sea. It is built on piles made of bamboo, according to the fashion of the country. Stores of deer and <term>buffalo<gloss>original: "Buffle"</gloss></term> skins were kept in the lofts.

<margin>Description of the Meinam.</margin>
*Me Nam*, or *Meinam* <term>Me Nam<gloss>Thai: "Mae Nam," meaning "Mother of Water" or "River"</gloss></term> in the *Siamite* Language signifies *Mother of humidities*, which name hath been given to this River by reason of the abundance of its water, which renders the whole Country fruitful. For it is the only River in it, very deep, rapid, full of water, and broader than the *Elbe*; but below *Judia* <note>Ayutthaya, the former capital</note>, down to the Sea, it divides it self into several branches. The account, which the Natives give of its source, differs from what is represented in our maps; for they say, that it takes its rise like the *Ganges* of *Bengale* in the high mountains of *Imaas* <note>The Himalayas; historically referred to in Latin as the *Imaus* mountains</note>, where it spreads it self into several arms, which run through *Cambodia*, *Siam*, and *Pegu* into the Sea; and they pretend, that these arms are again joyn'd by several smaller branches, not only with each other, but also with the *Ganges* it self, if they are not rather to be look'd upon altogether, as so many branches deriving from that very River. If it was not for the vast pains it would require to trace out its several Channels, through the Forests and Desarts, and to open a navigation, it might perhaps be made possible for Vessels to go from hence into *Bengale*. I will not stand to the truth of this account; but as for what relates to the description of the River from *Judia* to the Sea, and the draught I have given of it, this wants no support; forasmuch as I have had sufficient opportunity, and leisure, to observe it myself in sailing up and down. <margin>Remarkable Particulars observed in the Meinam.</margin>
Several remarkable particulars are to be observed in this River. <note>The "Meinam" is the Chao Phraya River, the primary waterway of Thailand.</note>

1. It overflows its branches like the *Nile* in *Egypt*, though at contrary times, and by setting the Country under water, renders it fruitful. This overflowing begins with the Month of *September* or sooner, when the Sun entering the **Tropic of Cancer**, by its approach dissolves the Snow on the high Mountains to the North. To this also contributes not a little the rainy Season, which falls in with that time, and is observed in all Countries situated between the two Tropics, when the Sun passes over the Heads of their Inhabitants. A most remarkable Instance of the Wisdom and Goodness of the Omnipotent Creator. In *December* the Waters begin to fall by degrees, and at last confine themselves to their former Channel.

2. Though the Water in the Earth appears upon digging the Ground to be regularly level with the River-water, yet it is observed to rise sooner, and to flow over the Surface of the Land, even before the River begins to swell, or can let any Water run over the Banks into the flat Country.

3. All the Water that appears upon digging the Ground hath a <term>nitrous</term><note>In this context, "nitrous" refers to a salty or mineral-heavy taste common in brackish groundwater near the delta.</note>, not a salt, taste all over the Country, and is consequently not fit for drinking, whereas the River-water, though muddy, yet is always sweet, fit for drinking and wholesome.

4. Whereas all Waters naturally run towards the Sea, as lying lowest, with respect to the Land, yet it is observed, that this **Inundation** does not so much affect the Country near the Sea-shore, as it does the upper and middle Parts of the Kingdom.

5. The Waters by overflowing the Fields that are sown, make the **Rice** grow so quickly, that the Stalks grow as fast as the Water rises, and the Ears keep above the Surface, which when ripe, are cut off by the Reapers in Boats, and gathered, but the Straw, which often is of an incredible length, is left in the Water. <note>This describes "floating rice," a traditional variety adapted to deep seasonal flooding.</note>

6. When the Waters fall and return to their former Channel, which happens about the beginning of the **North Season**, as it is called, when the Northerly Winds drive the Water down, and forward its running off, they are apprehensive, that a great mortality will ensue among Men and Cattle. To avert which Calamity a solemn Festival is kept throughout the whole Country, in order to appease the destroying Spirits, which remain after the Water is run off. The Ceremonies are lighting **paper Lanterns** near the chief Temples, in the King's Palace, and the Houses of Persons of Distinction and the Priests singing their Offices or Prayers in their Convents. <note>This festival is likely a description of *Loy Krathong*, where lanterns are floated on water to honor the water spirits and wash away sins/misfortune.</note> Our Europeans have observed, that if the Northerly Winds, which commonly blow very strong at that time, are not high enough to push the Water forward, and that consequently it goes off but slowly, there appears a slime left on

<margin>Banks of the Meinam.</margin>
The banks of this river are low, and for the greater part marshy, yet reckoning from *Judia* <note>Judia is Ayutthaya, the former capital of Siam (Thailand).</note> to *Bankok* <note>Bangkok, which at this time was a smaller fortified settlement downstream from the capital.</note>, which makes at least three parts in four of the way to the Seashore, they are pretty well inhabited. Along them appear many villages, the houses of which are rais'd on piles, but built of poor flimsy materials, and sometimes fine Temples and Habitations of the priests, with abundance of Trees some bearing fruit, some not. But from *Bankok* to the Harbour there is nothing but Forests, Deserts and Morasses; and every where there is plenty of *Bambous* <note>Bamboo</note>, and *Gabbe Gabbe*, (a Shrub with leaves like those of the Palm Tree) furnishing the Inhabitants with materials to make Houses, Hedges and Roofs.

<margin>Monkeys.</margin>
Three sorts of animals afford much diversion to Travellers sailing on this River. First are to be seen incredible numbers of Monkeys of a blackish Colour, some of which are of a very large size, and some less of the common sort, and a grey colour, which walk about tame, and as it were for pleasure sake along the shore, or climb up the Trees, but towards evening perch themselves upon the highest Trees on the shore in great numbers like Crows. The she ones hold their young so fast on their breasts, that they would not let them go, even when they were shot down. They are fond of this part of the Country on account of finding their food there on large Milk Trees, call'd *Tjaak* <note>The Nipa palm (*Nypa fruticans*), known locally as *Chak*.</note>, growing there in great plenty, with light green leaves of an oval shape, and a fruit not unlike our Apples as to their bigness and form, except that they seem compress'd, and are of a very harsh taste.

<margin>Glowworms</margin>
The Glowworms (<term>Cicindela</term> <note>original Latin: "Cicindela" refers to the firefly or glowworm.</note>) represent another shew, which settle on some Trees, like a fiery cloud, with this surprizing circumstance, that a whole swarm of these Insects, having taken possession of one Tree, and spread themselves over its branches, sometimes hide their Light all at once, and a moment after make it appear again with the utmost regularity and exactness, as if they were in a perpetual <term>Systole and Diastole</term> <note>original Latin: "Systole and Diastole" are medical terms for the rhythmic contraction and expansion of the heart; here used to describe the synchronized flashing of fireflies.</note>.

<margin>Gnats very troublesome to Travellers.</margin>
What is remarkable in the third place, are the common Gnats, or Flies, which in the day time appear but sparingly upon the water, but at night in such swarms like Bees, that it is difficult to guard against them. There is a sort like these in *Russia*, with which Travellers are pester'd, but they are smaller, have a less sting, and consequently do not hurt so much. This Vermin renders this Journey by water, which would be otherwise pleasant enough, very troublesome and disagreeable.

<margin>Return on board.</margin>
On the Seventh of *July*, being Friday, at break of day we left the River and the Land, and with a favourable North-wind arriv'd at eight of the clock on board our Ship, which lay at anchor four Leagues from the mouth of the River in six fathom of water. This harbour, or road, is the end of a bay between the Countries of *Cambodia* and *Siam*:

The Captain, a civil and good natur’d Man, (a Character, which is very rare among the Dutch Seamen,) forthwith took care to set them to rights, by laying some of them in irons, and prepar’d to set sail the next day.

<margin>Monsoons.</margin>
On the 8th of *July*, when we were busy with lading the last part of our Cargo of Hides <note>Animal hides, particularly deer and ray skins, were among the most profitable exports from Siam to Japan at this time.</note>, there came two Officers of the Dutch Factory at *Judia* <note>Ayutthaya, the capital of the Kingdom of Siam.</note> on board to review our Ships Company according to Custom. The wind blowing at South West from Shore, they left us on the 11th, and return’d to the Shore in their boat, being saluted by us, with a treble discharge of five Guns. With the said Wind we steer’d South East, in order to get upon the Main, and to make use there of the Southern Trade-wind, with which we were to steer North, North-East along the Coasts of *Cambodia*, *Cotfinfina* <note>Cochinchina, a historical region encompassing the southern part of modern-day Vietnam.</note>, and *China* towards the Harbours of *Japan*. The Reader will observe, that in these Eastern Parts from *Malacca* to *Japan*, there are Winds constantly blowing South and South West for four months together, which time is call’d the South or West Season, or *Monsoon*, then again North and North East for four other months, which is call’d the North or East Season, or *Monsoon*. Between these two Seasons there are two months, during which the wind is always variable, shifting from one of the said quarters, till at length it settles in that, which is opposite. It happens however in some years, that, to the great disappointment of sea-faring people, these trade-winds fix sooner or later than ordinary, by some weeks. These Seasons obtain also in other parts of the *Indies*, with this difference only, that according to the situation of the Countries, the Shores and the Seas, the winds blow more or less constant from East or West, for which reason those months are call’d the East or West *Monsoons*. By these *Monsoons* all navigation in the *Indies* and *Asia* must be directed. This sort of Fish <note>The description indicates a shark.</note> is very frequent in all the Seas of the Indies: Its full length is ten or twelve foot, and its flesh hard, and unpleasant of taste. It is reckon'd the fiercest of all Sea animals, and a great enemy to mankind, against which sailors are oblig'd to be very much upon their guard, when they go a bathing. This is the reason, why *Athenæus* <note>A Greek rhetorician and grammarian of the 2nd–3rd century AD.</note> calls it *Anthropophagos*, or the Man-eater <note>Original Greek: *Anthropophagos*</note>. He hath a wide mouth, not in the foremost part of the head, but a little lower, for which reason he is obliged to turn upon the back, when he takes in food from above.

<margin>Sucking Fish</margin>
Three things appear'd to me remarkable in them. 1. A strange small Fish sticking to one's side, and holding the flesh so fast with its mouth, that it requir'd some strength to pull it off; this little Fish the seamen call *Sucker* <note>The Remora, known for its dorsal fin that acts as a suction cup to hitch rides on larger animals.</note>. 2. There were in one's belly six young ones alive, each one span and half long. It is said, that these young ones creep in and out of the old one's belly, before they grow bigger. I was not able to examine into the possibility and truth of this assertion, the sailors cutting and mangling it too quickly, and hurrying it to the kitchen. 3. In the back part of the head of those two Fishes next to the head there lay a good quantity of a white substance like Crabs-eyes <note>In early modern medicine, "Crabs-eyes" were calcified stones from the stomachs of crayfish; here, Kaempfer refers to the shark's otoliths or ear-stones.</note> wrapt up in a thin membrane, which they carefully preserv'd, as an approv'd remedy against the stone <note>Kidney or bladder stones.</note> and hard labour in women.

Soon after was catch'd by another, a very fine Sea-star, with nine rays, which being not unlike that we catch'd upon the coasts of *Malacca*, in our voyage from *Batavia* <note>Modern-day Jakarta, Indonesia.</note> to *Siam*, and which I have given an account of in my Journal of that voyage, I need not repeat the description here.

<margin>Sea cats.</margin>

The Dutch call them *Sea Cats*, after the name which is given them in the Country Language, which implies as much <note>Likely referring to the cuttlefish or squid, known in Dutch as "zeekat."</note>. The fore part resembles a *Polypus marinus* <note>Original Latin for a marine polyp or octopus.</note>, provided as it were with snouts, about nine in number of different length. The belly is quite empty, open above, and may be blown up; the flesh is transparent without bones or nerves. If I remember right, *Bontius* <note>Jacobus Bontius (1592–1631), a Dutch physician and pioneer of tropical medicine.</note> gives the figure and description of them, to which I refer, adding only, that between the jaws the mouth is cover'd with a membrane, under which are two black, thick and crooked teeth, one above the other, strong enough to break the hardest object.

...province of **China**. On the 12th of **August** in the morning, we found ourselves two leagues off the coasts of **China**, where the aforementioned mountains end, and at noon we were near a famous sandbank, along which the ships coming from **China** and **Japan** sail toward **Batavia** <note>Present-day Jakarta, Indonesia, which was the headquarters of the Dutch East India Company.</note>. A little before this, we were boarded by a **proa** <note>Original: "Prawe," a type of swift sailing vessel used in Southeast Asia.</note> sent from a Chinese **junk** <note>Original: "Yonk," a classic Chinese sailing ship.</note>, which offered to sell us a parcel of tobacco. This evening we altered our course to avoid the **South Lamos** <margin>*South Lamos.*</margin>, which we guessed to be near, being two or three low rocks marked on the maps at 23° 10’. On the 13th of **August**, being **Sunday**, we discovered these rocks at a distance of one small league to our larboard <note>The left side of the ship, now called port.</note>, and steered past them with the help of the current, as the sea and air were calm. In the evening, we saw other such rocks on the same side, which we bypassed in the same manner, and then steered Northeast by East. I mention these islands and rocks to make the reader sensible of the danger of our voyage, particularly at night and during storms, and to show that our slow progress and frequent changes of course proceeded only from caution. On the 14th of **August**, four fishermen came on board—contrary to their usual habit—bringing **sharks** <note>Original: "Hayes," from the Dutch word *haaien*.</note> and **rays** <note>Original: "Beggers," likely referring to a type of sea bream or ray.</note>. As the goods they offered were of no value, we bought none but dismissed them after giving each a glass of brandy for their trouble. This civility invited others to us, from whom we took some fish. They refused to accept rice or linen in exchange, preferring brandy and pepper, which led us to conclude that they are not in great need. They carried watermelons with them to quench their thirst. Their dress consisted of straw hats and dark brown gowns reaching down to the knees and tied with a sash. They performed strange antics and made a noisy chattering like the **Malabarians** <note>People from the Malabar Coast of southwest India; Kaempfer is comparing the sound of the Chinese dialect to the Dravidian languages he encountered earlier in his travels.</note>. The latitude this day was 23° 58’, in a place marked on the maps as 24° 10’. We steered Northeast and North by East under favor of the current, the weather being almost calm. The coasts were low with a few hills. around the 27th degree of latitude, I observed a yellowish-green substance floating on the surface of the sea. This appeared for two days, where the depth was fifty fathoms and the seabed consisted of sandy clay mixed with seaweed.

<margin>*Strange birds.*</margin>
For several days, various black birds also arrived and perched on different parts of the ship, allowing themselves to be caught by hand. One day, a **woodcock** was found among them. <margin>*Remarkable storm.*</margin>
On the 26th of **August**, the storm increased with thunder and lightning. Having encountered shallows at thirty-two fathoms, we turned to the other side toward the South-East and South-East-by-East. On the 27th of **August**, being **Sunday**, the storm continued from the North-East-by-East. We found the depth to be thirty-six fathoms and steered to the other side toward the East-South-East. We took the height of the sun at noon and found ourselves at 29° 50'. This evening at nine o'clock, a **Chinese Junk** <term>Junk<gloss>A traditional Chinese sailing vessel characterized by its high stern and fully battened sails.</gloss></term>, with all her sails crowded and full before the wind, rushed past our side to seek shelter in a harbor. The seamen on this coast recognize certain signs by which they foresee an impending storm and retire in time to the nearest harbor they can reach. 

On the 28th of **August**, the storm increased with such vehemence that before evening we were forced to tie our rudder fast, pull in the **main sheet** and **mizzen** <note>The mizzen is the sail on the mast nearest the stern (back) of the ship.</note>, and let the ship drive with the current. Some **Cajan** <term>Cajan<gloss>Also known as Indian Vetches or pigeon peas; a type of legume commonly used for food on long voyages.</gloss></term> and rice boiled in water were set down on the deck for our dinner. However, the tossing of the ship was so violent that only two of the sailors, who held the bowl, were able to snatch and swallow any of it; the rest of us had enough to do just to crawl on all fours to prevent ourselves from being injured. This evening we found the depth to be fifty-six fathoms. 

On the 29th of **August**, the wind having turned that night into a perfect and furious storm, the tossing became intolerable, so much so that it was impossible to stand on one's legs. We attempted to use the rudder, but the approaching night soon forced us to tie it fast again. We were not much better for it, however, as the massive waves beat with such force against the ship that even before daybreak we were compelled to take in our sails again—which were starting to be torn to pieces—to keep the rudder tied up, and to leave our ship to the mercy of the two raging elements. The sails were brought in, contrary to expectation, by taking a lucky opportunity. ### Chap. III. *The History of* J A P A N.

...pieces. The **cramp-irons** <term>Cramp-Irons: heavy metal clamps or brackets used to fasten large timbers or equipment together</term> and ropes with which the chests were fastened broke, and the goods were thrown from one side of the ship to the other. It was resolved to bring to the **mizzen** <term>Mizzen: the sail on the mast nearest the stern (back) of the ship</term>, but when the sailors were working on it, the wind caught it and tore it to pieces. What made our condition even more lamentable was the darkness of the air, which was also full of water; this seemed to me to come from something other than just the rain and the breaking of the waves, which the wind mixed into the air. We could not see each other at half the ship’s length, and the confused noise of the wind, the sea, and the ship made it impossible to understand one another. The waves covered us like so many mountains; they beat the doors open without intermission, and the water ran over the deck into the cabin in such quantity that everything was filled with it. Besides this, the ship began to leak, so that we were obliged to bail the water out with pails and add a second pump to the first one, which was already playing continually.

During this noise, we heard a continual thumping at the stern of the ship, as if everything was to be staved to pieces. We had no opportunity to find out the cause of it until the afternoon, when the storm shifted to the East; we then saw that the hinges of the **rudder** were broken, the cramp-iron pulled out, and the rudder was draggling behind. This misfortune increased the danger we were in, and though we endeavored as well as we were able to fasten the rudder to its chains, the thumping continued with such force that we had reason to fear the ship would be broken to pieces and sunk within a few hours.

All the while, we were driving back to the **South-West** and **West-South-West** toward the fatal islands of *China*. This was a new and formidable appearance of danger, which was further heightened by the great confusion of our men, who would not listen to the commands of their officers. The officers were as much disordered by strong liquors as the men themselves; for since no drinking water could be reached in the hold, and all their food was merely some boiled rice, they were obliged to keep up their spirits with **Arrack** <term>Arrack: a potent distilled spirit, often made from fermented sap of coconut palms or sugarcane</term> and brandy. This eventually so disordered them that any sober man would tremble at the complication of so many dangers. 

To complete it all, a dreadful night came on, which however seemed to be more comfortable than the daylight, as it served to hide from our eyes the horrors of our impending destruction. The most important point was to save the ship from the terrible blows she received from the rudder every time it was lifted up by a swelling wave. In order to do this, the rudder either had to be disengaged and taken in, or some other method had to be tried. Accordingly, the ship’s carpenter and his assistants went into the cabin provided with levers, hatchets, ropes, and other tools. They loosened tables and seats, broke through the hatches in the floor into the room under it, and—being tied with ropes—were let out through the cabin windows. But all their pains to mend the rudder were in vain; it was im-

On the 30th of *August*, early in the morning, the storm began to die down and the waves to subside. The master carpenter was lowered down on a rope and fixed a new beam to the rudder; in short, the whole job was finished by noon. When the sky cleared, the cook was finally able to light a fire, and the sailors took the measurement of the sun’s altitude and found our latitude to be 28° 31'. We hoisted the sails again and steered northeast with a fair wind.

On the 31st of *August*, having thus escaped this danger, we were comforted at daybreak by the bright appearance of the sun, though the wind still continued to blow very hard. After five days of fasting, we were very hungry and quite dispirited by the great fatigue. We were in expectation of refreshing ourselves with a hearty meal and good drink, but our foolish steward—who was rarely sober on land and always drunk at sea—had drunk every last drop of our wine. Furthermore, a fat hog and all our poultry had died from the bad weather. The cook had nothing to give us but boiled rice, **pigeon peas** <note>original: "Cajan"</note>, and old bacon. We feasted on this for lack of better delicacies, hoping to catch some fresh fish during the next calm. The first and most difficult part of this day’s work was to tighten the **shrouds** <term>Shrouds: the heavy ropes supporting a mast from the sides</term> <note>original: "shrewds"</note>, which had been loosened so much by the constant tossing in the late storm that they were unable to hold up the masts. Meanwhile, others were busy trying to find leaks in the ship, though they haven't discovered any yet. Some bales of silk and hides that had gotten wet were brought onto the deck to dry, as were our clothes and bedding; this task took up the next two days. Our course was to the northeast and north-northeast, with the wind coming from the east and east-by-north. Our latitude was 29° 20', and the depth in the evening was 43 **fathoms** <term>Fathom: a unit of water depth equal to six feet</term>. At noon, we calculated our **altitude** <note>In this context, altitude refers to the sun's height used to determine the ship's latitude, or distance from the equator.</note> at 30° 9', and in the evening, we measured a depth of 23 **fathoms** <term>Fathom: a unit of length equal to six feet, used to measure water depth</term>. On the second of *September*, our altitude was 30° 20' with a depth of 90 fathoms. On the third of *September*, which was *Sunday*, the altitude was 31° 16' and the depth 26 fathoms. On the fourth of *September*, the weather became so stormy that no altitude could be measured. Throughout the day, we found depths between 25 and 32 fathoms, with the sea floor consisting of white sand. On the fifth of *September* at noon, the altitude was 31° 15', and by evening the depth was 26 fathoms. That evening, several **Sea-devils** <note>Original: "Sea-devils, or Rays." These were likely manta rays or large stingrays, which were often viewed with superstition by early sailors.</note> passed by our ship; these are flat fish, two or three fathoms long and of a frightening appearance.

<margin>Second storm.</margin>
On the sixth of *September*, the altitude was 31° 30'. This afternoon, we unexpectedly encountered a most imminent danger, quite different in nature from what we had experienced in the previous storm. We were steering *Southward* with a gentle gale blowing from the **E. S. E.** (East-South-East) when we noticed lightning to the *North*. Soon after, massive, hollow waves began tumbling over each other like clouds, rolling toward our ship with incredible speed. The ship was thrown into such a disordered and confused motion that we almost lost our senses, not knowing how to react. Because the waves of the **Southerly Monsoon** <term>Monsoon: a seasonal wind and weather system in South and Southeast Asia</term> were pushing against our course, the ship could not move forward quickly. Since the wind was light and hitting us at an angle, the immense force of these opposing waves struck the **stern** <term>Stern: the back part of a ship</term> directly. Two hours after sunset, two of these waves—appearing like mountains—hit us almost simultaneously from behind. They overwhelmed the entire ship with such force that they pushed her deep under the water. Every person standing on the **quarter deck** <term>Quarter deck: the elevated deck at the rear of the ship, usually reserved for officers</term>—myself included—was submerged, and we all believed we were sinking to the bottom of the sea. This impact was accompanied by such a terrifying cracking and noise that it seemed as if the entire stern had been torn off and shattered. Our Captain and his Mate, both over sixty years old, along with other veteran sailors, admitted they had never encountered anything like it in their entire lives. They immediately checked the **rudder** and found it still attached to its hinges, though a few planks had been snapped off. We started the pump, but no leaks were found. However, in the cabin, almost everything was destroyed or soaked with salt water. Our drunken steward was nearly drowned in his bed, even though he slept below deck in what was supposed to be one of the safest places. The deck was covered in knee-deep water, and the **tackling** <term>Tackling: the ropes and rigging used to control the sails</term> was floating about. Although we quickly opened the holes to let the water drain, it had already soaked into many of our belongings. To my great grief, I found that the water had penetrated my papers and written memoirs. A brisk wind blowing from the North, accompanied by rain and a storm, hurried our ship towards the South and East. This actually protected us from the fury of those massive waves, though we suffered through terrible tossing which lasted all night and through the next day, the seventh of September. Even though the storm itself had ceased and the weather was manageable, the ship was still in some peril. It was notable that on this day the wind blew from every direction of the compass, moving in a direction opposite to the path of the sun. We were unable to calculate our **altitude** <note>The height of the sun above the horizon, used to determine the ship's latitude.</note> this day, but measured the water's depth at 30 to 40 **fathoms** <term>Fathom: a maritime unit of depth equal to six feet.</term>. On the eighth of September at noon, our altitude was 31° 11', and in the evening the depth was 42 fathoms. The sea remained very rough, causing heavy tossing and a difficult night. On the ninth of September, the altitude was 31° 5', and the depth ranged from 42 to 48 fathoms.

<margin>*Third storm.*</margin>
On the tenth of September, which was a Sunday, our altitude was 30° 20', but we could find no bottom with our measuring lines. This afternoon we were once again battered by a violent storm from the North. We were forced to turn the ship, lower the sails, tie down the **rudder** <note>The steering blade at the rear of the ship.</note>, and simply let the vessel drift wherever the wind took her, placing our trust in Providence. On the eleventh of September toward evening, the storm finally abated after lasting twenty-four hours. We hoisted the main sail again and returned to using the rudder. At noon, we found our altitude to be 29° 55', and in the evening the depth was 60 fathoms. By this point, we had encountered three different storms between *China* and *Japan*, during which many of our goods had been damaged by the constant tossing and tumbling. The ship's crew began to show signs of reluctance and discontent regarding this difficult voyage, especially since there seemed little hope of reaching *Japan*. The "North Season" <note>Referring to the onset of the winter monsoon winds, which blow from the north and would make sailing toward Japan from the south nearly impossible.</note>, which blew directly against our course, appeared to be fully settled. For this reason, it was decided on the twelfth of September to let the ship drift more with the wind, allowing it to move more easily back toward the South-West by West. This day at noon our altitude was 29° 30', and in the evening the depth was 62 fathoms.

On the 13th of September, early in the morning, while the crew was **careening** <term>Careening: the practice of leaning a ship on its side to clean or repair the hull, or in this context, inspecting the ship's sides while at sea.</term> the ship, it was noticed that the clamps—which serve as the ribs and braces of this floating body—had become loose during the accident on the sixth of September. This discovery discouraged both the officers and the common sailors, making them weary of continuing to struggle against the wind. It was considered most advisable to head for a harbor in *China* to take on fresh water, as we had less than a month's supply remaining, and then return to **Batavia** <note>Modern-day Jakarta, Indonesia, which served as the headquarters for the Dutch East India Company in Asia.</note>. Several passengers and others who had influence with the ship’s council tried to persuade them to accept this proposal. It likely would have been approved if the Mate had not raised objections. As for myself, I had in my possession a journal of a voyage to *Japan* which I had received from a reliable source; I consulted it and found that some years

### Chap. III. The History of JAPAN.

Before a **Dutch** ship had safely arrived in **Japan** toward the end of **September**, I went privately to the Captain. First, I put it to his consideration that the wet hides <note>The ship’s cargo of animal skins, which were a primary trade good.</note> would likely rot in the humid air of **Batavia** <note>Modern-day Jakarta, the headquarters of the Dutch East India Company in Asia.</note> if we returned now. He would later be held accountable for that damage, which would be seen as the result of his faint-heartedness and hasty retreat. I then showed him a specific passage in the Journal, which startled him. Having read it three times over, he immediately changed his mind and decided to continue without further objection. 

On the fourteenth of **September**, our **elevation** <note>The height of the sun above the horizon, used to calculate latitude.</note> was 29° 36', and in the evening we measured a depth of 41 to 46 **fathoms** <term>Fathom: a maritime unit of depth equal to six feet.</term>. On the fifteenth of **September**, we found the altitude to be 29° 57' and the depth 36 fathoms. On the sixteenth of **September**, the altitude was 30° 13' and the depth 38 fathoms. On the 17th of **September**, which was a Sunday, we could not take an elevation, but the depth was 47 fathoms. On the eighteenth of **September**, the weather being stormy, we could take no elevation; the depth was 34 fathoms. On the nineteenth of **September**, the altitude was 30° 31', and the depth in the evening was 45 fathoms. On the twentieth of **September**, the altitude was 30° 36', the depth in the evening 58, and at night 70 fathoms. This morning we killed a **Dolphin**, or **Dorado**, with a javelin. Its color was a yellowish blue, and its length was six spans; its flesh was very delicious and a welcome meal for our sick stomachs.

<margin>Matsima.</margin>
On the twenty-first of **September**, we reached a latitude of 31° 30'. According to common maps, this is the latitude of the rocky island of **Matsima** <note>Likely referring to the Uji Islands or similar rocky outcrops near Kyushu.</note> located in the **Japanese** Ocean. Like a **Hermes** <note>original: "Hermes"; referring to a *herma*, a classical stone pillar used as a boundary marker or signpost for travelers.</note>, this island is watched for by sailors traveling to or from **Japan**. We sighted it two hours after taking our noon measurement, at a distance of nine or ten leagues to the North-East. From this, we concluded that it actually lies a bit further North, near 32° latitude. A little before sunset, this long-wished-for landmark appeared five leagues to the North. Six hours later, under bright moonlight, the island sat a league off our port side. We observed that it consisted of about seven pointed rocks—rough, bare, and clustered together. They were covered in most places with bird droppings, appearing to be inhabited only by **sea-mews** <note>An old name for seagulls.</note>, which we saw there in great numbers. We made the same observation two years later when we sailed past it on our return from **Japan**. We had the good luck to catch another **Dorado**, and in the evening, we found the depth to be 78 fathoms over a bottom of sandy mud. 

On the twenty-second of **September**, early in the morning, we saw **Matsima** lying far to the West-South-West, so distant we could hardly make it out. Shortly after, we spotted a **Chinese Jonk** <note>A traditional Chinese sailing vessel.</note> from **Nanking**, and then two more which appeared to be Chinese by their construction; all were coming from **Japan**.

### Chap III. The History of JAPAN.

On the neighboring mountains stand guard-houses with guards in them, who, using their telescopes <note>original: "spying Glasses"</note>, observe everything that happens at sea. They provide immediate information to the government at **Nagasaki**, and by this method, they had notice of our arrival already two days earlier, on the morning of the 22nd. Along the shore at the foot of those mountains that surround the harbor, there are various round bastions. On these, I observed only rails or palisades painted red—seemingly for ornament—but saw no cannons. Besides these, on two hills on both sides of the city near the shore, there are two imperial main guards. These are draped with cloth for decoration and to prevent people from seeing the number of cannons and men inside. When we passed them, we saluted each guard with twelve large guns. After arriving at our assigned place, we dropped anchor about three hundred paces from the city.

<margin>Deshima</margin>
We were just as far from **Deshima**, which is the residence of the Dutch. It is a separate island built specifically for this purpose near the shore outside the city. Then two **Bugyō** <term>Bugyō: High-ranking Japanese officials or governors appointed by the Shogunate to oversee trade and local administration.</term>—gentlemen sent by the governors on official business—came to us. They were accompanied by many subordinate clerks, interpreters, and soldiers.

<margin>Japanese come on board</margin>
They called all those who had newly arrived and made them pass in review before them one after another, according to the list provided to them. They inspected everyone from head to toe, writing down each person's name, age, and occupation with a brush <note>original: "pencil". In the 17th and 18th centuries, the word "pencil" (from the Latin *penicillus*) often referred to a small fine-haired brush used for writing or painting.</note> on paper.

<margin>Their procedures.</margin>
In addition, about six more people were examined individually regarding our voyage: where we came from, when we set out, how long we had been traveling, whether we had landed anywhere else, etc. Their various answers were carefully recorded. Many questions were asked regarding the deceased steward, and those answers were also noted. His chest and the rest of his skin were narrowly inspected to see if there was any cross or other mark of the **Catholic religion** <note>original: "Popish Religion". Following the suppression of Christianity in Japan, the authorities were intensely vigilant, searching for any Christian symbols or hidden "Kirishitan" converts.</note> upon it. Through our repeated requests, we managed to have the corpse taken away that same day, but none of us were permitted to accompany it or see where it was buried.

Once this review was over, soldiers and clerks were stationed in every corner, and the entire ship and its cargo were, in a sense, taken into possession by the Japanese. The boat and skiff were left to our men only for that day so they could tend to their anchors. However, they demanded and took into custody our pistols, cutlasses, and other arms. These were followed the next morning by the gunpowder packed in barrels. In short, if I had not been previously informed of their usual procedures, I could not have helped thinking we had entered a hostile country or had been mistaken for spies. I must also mention here that during our voyage, as soon as we sighted this land, everyone was required—according to an official order and long-standing custom—to surrender his prayer-book and other books of divinity, as well as all European...

The chief purpose of these orders was that every one of us ought to behave soberly and discreetly with respect to the natives, and the laws and customs of the country. A paper containing these orders, having been read publicly, was—according to the custom of Japan—posted on board the ship for everyone to read. In the afternoon I went on shore to **Dejima**, on which occasion one is obliged to take out a passport from the Japanese Ship-Guard to those on shore, and upon the return, another from the Land-Guard to those on board. Finding that eating the raw garden fruit sent to us yesterday had caused me great pain, I was obliged to hasten back to our ship. From there, I went on the 26th of September with my belongings to live in the habitation assigned to me at **Dejima**.

### CHAPTER IV.
### Of the Empire of Japan in general, as to its situation, and the size of its several Islands.

<margin>The Japanese Empire and its names.</margin>
This Empire is called *Japan* by the Europeans. The natives give it several names and characters. The most common, and most frequently used in their writings and conversation, is *Nippon*, which is sometimes pronounced *Nihon* <note>original: "Nifon"</note> in a more elegant manner particular to this nation. The inhabitants of **Nanjing** <note>original: "Nankin"</note> and the southern parts of China call it *Sijppon*. It signifies the *foundation of the sun*, being derived from *Ni*, meaning fire—and in a more sublime sense, the sun—and *Pon*, meaning the ground or foundation of a thing.

### Chapter IV. The History of Japan.

There are still several other names and epithets for the country which are rarely mentioned in conversation but appear more frequently in their writings. These include, for example:

1. ***Tenka*** <term>Tenka: A term meaning "all under heaven," historically used in East Asian spheres to refer to the realm of the Emperor or the known civilized world.</term>, which means the *Subcelestial Empire*, as if it were the only one existing under Heaven. Because of this, the Emperor is called ***Tenkasama***, the *Subcelestial Monarch*. In former times, this name was unique to the Empire of *Japan* alone. However, since commerce has made other countries known to them, they now condescend to honor those nations with the same epithet—particularly those whose inhabitants are admitted and tolerated among them. Thus, they call the Empire of *China* ***To Sin Tenka*** <note>original: "To Sin Tenka," referring to the Qing or "Tang" (To) dynasty's realm.</note>, and the united Provinces of the *Netherlands* (known to them by the name of *Holland*) they call ***Hollanda Tenka***.

2. ***Fino Motto*** <note>original: "Fino Motto," modern: "Hi no Moto"</note> is much the same as ***Nippon***, and signifies, strictly speaking, the *Root of the Sun*. *Fi* signifies the *Sun*, and *Motto* means a *Root*; *No* is simply a particle used to combine these two words together.

3. ***Awadsissima*** <note>original: "Awadsissima," modern: "Awaji-shima"</note> is the original name of this country, which translates to *Terrestrial Scum Island*. *Awa* signifies *Scum*, *Dsi* means the *Earth*, and *Sima* is an *Island*. This name is based on a legendary tradition recorded in their histories regarding the origin and first creation of the various islands that make up this mighty Empire. In ancient times, due to a lack of communication with other countries, the natives looked upon these islands as the only inhabited part of the globe. According to their creation myth, the supreme of the seven first celestial spirits (discussed further in Chapter VII of this book) stirred the Chaos—the confused mass of the early Earth—with a staff. When he withdrew the staff, drops of muddy scum fell from it, which clumped together to form the Japanese islands. One of these islands, the fourth in size, still retains this name, being specifically called ***Awadsissima***.

4. ***Sin Koks*** <note>original: "Sin Koks," modern: "Shinkoku"</note> or ***Camino Kuni*** <note>original: "Camino Kuni," modern: "Kami no Kuni"</note>, which means the *Country* or *Habitation of the Gods*. *Sin* and *Cami* refer to the gods <note>The author refers here to the Shinto deities, or kami.</note> who were originally and specifically worshipped in *Japan*, while both *Koks* and *Kuni* signify a *country*.

5. ***Akitsima*** or, according to common pronunciation, ***Akitsussima*** <note>original: "Akitsussima," often translated as "Dragonfly Island," a poetic name for Japan found in the Nihon Shoki.</note>, is another ancient name for this country, frequently found in their chronicles and legends.

6. ***Tontsio***, the *True Morning*.

7. ***Sio***, meaning *All*—referring to all the various islands subject to the Emperor of *Japan*.

8. ***Jamatto*** <note>modern: "Yamato"</note>, a name also given to one of its central provinces.

I will refrain from mentioning several others, such as ***Asijwara*** <note>modern: "Ashihara," or the "Plain of Reeds."</note>, ***Asijwara Koks***, ***Qua***, or ***Wa***, to avoid being tedious on such a minor subject.

<margin>Its geographical situation.</margin>
The Empire of *Japan* lies between 31 and 42 degrees of Northern Latitude. In a recent map of *China* corrected by astronomical observations, the Jesuits place it between 157° and 175° 30' of Longitude. <note>Early modern longitude was often measured from the Canary Islands (Ferro Meridian) rather than Greenwich, explaining these high degree numbers.</note> The country extends to the Northeast and East-Northeast. It is irregularly broad, though generally quite narrow compared to its length. From one end of the province of ***Fisen*** <note>modern: "Hizen," located on the island of Kyushu.</note> to the furthest point of the province of ***Osiu*** <note>modern: "Oshū," or Mutsu Province in northern Honshu.</note>, the distance is estimated to be two hundred German miles <note>A German mile (geographical mile) was significantly longer than an English mile, roughly equivalent to 7.5 kilometers.</note>.

# The History of JAPAN. Book I.

<margin>Japan is not unlike Great Britain.</margin>
In various respects, Japan may be compared to the Kingdoms of *Great Britain* and *Ireland*. It is structured in much the same way, though to a more significant degree—it is divided and broken up by corners and headlands, arms of the sea, great bays, and inlets that run deep into the country, forming several islands, peninsulas, gulfs, and harbors. Furthermore, just as the King of *Great Britain* is sovereign over three kingdoms—<margin>Its division.</margin> *England*, *Scotland*, and *Ireland*—so too does the Japanese Emperor hold supreme jurisdiction over three separate large islands. 

The first and <margin>Nippon.</margin> largest is called ***Nippon*** <term>Nippon: The primary name for Japan, often translated as "Sun's Origin."</term>, taking its name from the whole Empire. It runs lengthwise from East to West in the shape of a jawbone, with its curved part turned toward the North. A narrow channel or strait, full of rocks and islands—some inhabited and some not—separates it from the second island. This second island is next in size and, because of its location to the Southwest of *Nippon*, is called ***Saikoku*** <note>original: "Saikokf," modern: Saigoku</note>, which <margin>Saikoku.</margin> means the *Western Country*. It is also called ***Kyushu*** <note>original: "Kiusiu"</note>, or the *Country of Nine*, as it is divided into nine large provinces. It measures 148 *German* miles <term>German Mile: A historical unit of distance, roughly equal to 7.5 kilometers or 4.6 miles.</term> in circumference; according to the Japanese, it is 140 of their own miles in length and between 40 and 50 in breadth. 

The third island lies between the first and the second. It is nearly square in shape, and because it is divided into four provinces, the Japanese call it <margin>Shikoku.</margin> ***Shikoku*** <note>original: "Sikokf"</note>, which means the *Country of Four* (referring to the provinces). These three large islands are surrounded by an almost inconceivable number of others. Some are small, rocky, and barren, while others are large, rich, and fruitful enough to be governed by petty princes, as will be shown more clearly in the next chapter, where I intend to provide a more accurate geographical description of this Empire.

<margin>Divided into 7 tracts of land.</margin>
All these various islands and territories that make up the mighty Empire of *Japan* were divided by the ecclesiastical hereditary monarch, ***Sujin*** <note>original: "Siusin," referring to Emperor Sujin, though the date 590 AD provided by the author suggests a later period or different ruler.</note>, into the ***Goki-shichido*** <note>original: "Gokisitzido," referring to the Five Home Provinces and Seven Circuits, the traditional administrative units of Japan.</note>, or seven large tracts of land, in the year of Christ 590. Many years later, in the year of Christ 681, ***Tenmu*** <note>original: "Ten Mu," referring to Emperor Tenmu (r. 673–686 AD).</note> divided these seven chief tracts <margin>Sixty-eight provinces.</margin> into 66 provinces, appointing many lords of his court to command and govern them as princes or as his lieutenants. Two additional islands, ***Iki*** and ***Tsushima*** <note>original: "Tsussima"</note>—which formerly belonged to the Kingdom of ***Korea*** <note>original: "Corea"</note>—were conquered in the last century and added to the Empire of *Japan*, bringing the total to 68 provinces. 

While both of these divisions of the Japanese Empire still exist today, the misfortunes of time have caused these 68 provinces to be <margin>Six hundred and four districts.</margin> carved into 604 smaller districts since their first creation. In the earliest and happiest ages of the Japanese monarchy, every prince enjoyed the government of the province entrusted to him by the Emperor in peace and tranquility. However, in the miseries of the following eras, frequent quarrels and contentions arose among the chief branches of the Imperial Family regarding...

### Chap. IV. *The History of J A P A N.*

The succession to the throne gradually dragged the entire Empire into bloodshed and confusion. Its Princes took different sides, and as soon as weapons were introduced among them as the most powerful and certain way to resolve their disagreements, everyone tried to use them to keep hold of the lands they held entirely through Imperial generosity. Those who had not been provided for by the Emperor took it upon themselves to provide for themselves. The Princes divided their inherited territories among their sons, who—though they possessed only a fraction of their father’s estate—would not be outdone in grandeur and magnificence. It is no wonder, then, that the number of princedoms and territories increased perpetually. 

The Emperors of the family currently in power <note>This refers to the Tokugawa Shogunate (1603–1867). While the author calls them "Emperors," they were military dictators who ruled in the name of the ceremonial Emperor in Kyoto.</note>, who are themselves usurpers of the throne they now hold, do not believe this great division of the Empire’s provinces is in any way harmful to their government. Instead, they find it helpful, as it makes them better acquainted with the true state of their wealth and tax revenues. Therefore, far from returning these territories to their original size, they continue to tear and divide them even more as they please or as their interests require; there are several recent examples of this. The Province of *Chikuzen* <note>original: "Tsikusen"</note> was not long ago divided into two governments, *Yanagawa* and *Kurume*, and the Prince of *Chikugo* <note>original: "Tsikungo"</note> was ordered by the Court to surrender part of his territories to the Prince of the two islands mentioned above, *Iki* and *Tsushima*, who until then owned no land on the mainland of *Japan*.

<margin>Its Borders.</margin>
The borders of this Empire are its rocky, mountainous coasts and a stormy sea. Because the water is shallow, it allows only small vessels to pass, and even then at great risk. The depth of most of its gulfs and harbors is still unknown, and others—which the local pilots are better acquainted with—are unsuitable for anchoring ships of any significant size. Indeed, it seems Nature intentionally designed these islands to be a kind of "little world," separate and independent from the rest, by making them so difficult to access and by providing them so generously with everything required to make the lives of their inhabitants both delightful and pleasant, enabling them to survive without trading with foreign nations.

<margin>Neighboring Countries subject to the Emperor of Japan.</margin>
Besides the various islands and provinces already mentioned, there are some more distant countries that do not, strictly speaking, belong to the Empire of Japan, but either recognize the authority of the Emperor or live under his protection. I think it is necessary to provide a brief preliminary account of these before I proceed to a more detailed description of the Japanese Empire itself. They are: 1. The islands of *Ryukyu* <note>original: "Riuku" or "Liquejo"</note>, whose inhabitants call themselves subjects not of the Emperor of *Japan*, but of the Prince of *Satsuma*, who defeated and conquered them. 2. *Chosun* <note>original: "Tsiosin," referring to the Kingdom of Korea</note> is the third and

<margin>The Ryukyu Islands</margin>
I. The **Ryukyu** Islands <note>original: "Liquejo"</note>, as they are marked on our maps, or the Islands of **Riuku**, as they are called by the inhabitants, must not be confused with the **Leucanian Islands** <note>original: "Insulæ Leuconiæ"</note> or the **Philippine** Islands. They lie to the southwest of the Province of **Satsuma**, which is located on the continent of **Kyushu** <note>original: "Saikokf"</note>, and the neighboring Island of **Tana** or **Tanegashima**; according to our maps, they reach down almost to the 26th degree of Northern latitude. If we believe the **Japanese**, these islands are so fertile that they produce a rice harvest twice a year. The inhabitants, who are mostly either farmers or fishermen, are a good-natured, merry sort of people. They lead an agreeable, contented life, entertaining themselves after their work is finished with a glass of rice beer and playing upon their musical instruments, which they carry out into the fields for this purpose. 

Based on their language, they appear to be of **Chinese** descent. During the late great revolution in **China**, when the **Tartars** <note>The Manchu conquest that established the Qing Dynasty in 1644.</note> invaded and took possession of that mighty Empire, the natives fled in great numbers and were dispersed all over the **East Indies**. Not a few fled to these islands, where they applied themselves chiefly to trade, being skilled in navigation and well-acquainted with those seas. Consequently, they still carry on commerce with **Satsuma** and travel there once a year. Some centuries ago, these islands were invaded and conquered by the Prince of **Satsuma**, whose successors still keep them in submission through their <term>Bugyō</term> <note>original: "Bugios"; these were magistrates or governors appointed by the Shogunate to oversee trade and administration.</note>, or Lieutenants, and strong garrisons. 

However, because of their distance from **Satsuma**, the inhabitants are otherwise treated with great respect and kindness; they are required to give their Sovereign only one-fifth of the produce of their country, while his own natural subjects, the **Satsumese**, are taxed at two-thirds. But besides what they pay to the Prince of **Satsuma**, they collect a contribution among themselves to be sent as a gift, once a year, to the Tartar Monarch of **China** <note>The Qing Emperor</note> as a sign of loyalty and submission. Like the **Tonkinese** and **Japanese**, they have a <term>Dairi</term> of their own, or an ecclesiastical hereditary monarch, to whom they pay great respect, believing him to be directly descended from the Gods of their country. He resides at **Yaeyama** <note>original: "Jajama"</note>, one of the main islands in this group, located not far from the island of **Oshima**, which is the second largest.

As he had only lately come to the throne, he did not doubt that he could find the time to fully settle and secure his possession of it if he could send some of the most powerful **Princes of the Empire** <note>The daimyo, or regional lords, who might have posed a threat to his new rule.</note> abroad upon such a military expedition, and by this means remove them from the Court and the Country. 

He therefore gladly seized this opportunity and resolved to renew and support his pretensions to the Kingdom of **Korea**. He gave out that his main design was to open for himself a way through this kingdom to the conquest of the great Empire of **China** itself. Accordingly, he sent ambassadors over to **Korea** to desire the natives to acknowledge the supremacy of the Japanese Emperor and to give tokens of their loyalty and submission. But the **Koreans**, instead of an answer, killed the Emperor’s ambassadors; by this hostile act, they gave him just reason to prosecute them with war. 

Accordingly, a numerous army was sent over without further delay, under the command of those Princes of the Empire whose presence he had the most reason to be apprehensive of. This war lasted seven years, during which time his Generals, with great difficulty <note>original: "much a do"</note>, finally broke through the strong opposition made by the natives and their allies the **Tartars**. After a brave defense, the country was again made tributary to Japan.

### Chap IV. The History of JAPAN.

The southern coasts of this island <note>Referring to Ezo, modern-day Hokkaido.</note> were secured to ensure the inhabitants would never again have the power to attempt such an uprising. The local Prince is now required to send an annual embassy to *Matsumae* with gifts valued at one <term>Mangoku <note>A "Ten-Thousand Koku" unit; a koku is the traditional measure of rice (about 180 liters) used to define the wealth of a domain or the status of a lord.</note></term>. This island is situated at 42 degrees Northern Latitude, to the North-North-East, directly opposite the great Province of *Oshu* <note>original: "Ooſiu"</note>. There, two promontories named *Tsugaru* <note>original: "Sugaar"</note> and *Tappisaki* <note>original: "Taajaſaki"</note> extend far into the sea, forming a large gulf that faces the island directly. 

The crossing to this island is said to take one day, though it cannot be made at all times due to the strong currents that run sometimes East and sometimes West. Otherwise, the distance is only forty <term>Japanese water leagues <note>A traditional maritime measurement; one league is roughly 2.4 miles or 3.9 kilometers.</note></term>, and in some places it is no more than five or six <term>German miles <note>A historical unit of distance, significantly longer than an English mile, roughly equivalent to 4.6 miles or 7.4 kilometers.</note></term> from the Japanese coast. It is said to be as large as the island of *Kyushu*, but it is so densely covered in woods and forests that it produces nothing of use to the Japanese, except for some pelts and furs—items which even the inhabitants of Southern Japan have little need for. 

The people of Ezo bring nothing else to trade except those furs and the famous fish called *Karasaki* <note>Likely referring to dried salmon or a specific northern cod species.</note>, which is caught in great abundance around the island. The Japanese consider this fish a great delicacy, boiling and eating it much like cod. 

As for the shape of the island, I could not determine anything certain, neither from the accounts of the Japanese nor from the maps I found in the country, as they differ greatly from one another. Some represent it as nearly round, while others give it a very irregular shape with large promontories, gulfs, and bays. In several places, the sea reaches so far inland that one might easily believe it is composed of several different islands. I am inclined to believe that the land discovered by the explorer *de Vries* <note>Maarten Gerritsz de Vries, a Dutch explorer who mapped these northern waters in 1643.</note> to the north of Japan was part of this island. I noticed that on some Japanese maps, the larger southwest portion is called *Matsuki*, but these were generally so poorly drawn that I would be at a loss to say whether it is an island on its own or joined to the rest. 

According to the Japanese descriptions of the inhabitants <note>The Ainu people.</note>, they are a strong but "savage" people with long hair and beards. They are highly skilled with bows and arrows and in fishing, as the majority of them live almost entirely on fish. The Japanese further describe them as very dirty and "nasty," but the truth of this accusation should not be strictly relied upon; the Japanese themselves are so extremely meticulous and superstitious regarding the frequent washing and cleaning of their bodies that they have found the very same fault with the Dutch. The language of *Ezo* <note>original: "Jedſo"</note> is said to share some characteristics with the language spoken in *Korea*.
