...the strait of *Anian* <note>The Strait of Anian was a semi-legendary passage sought by early explorers, believed to separate Asia from North America; it corresponds roughly to the modern Bering Strait.</note>, or the so long-wished-for passage out of the North Sea into the great Indian Ocean—supposing such a thing exists—or whether the land is closely joined either to *Tartary* <note>A historical name used by Europeans for North and Central Asia, from the Caspian Sea to the Pacific Ocean.</note> or *America* without any intermediate strait or passage at all. I made it my business, both in my travels through *Muscovy* <note>An archaic name for the Grand Duchy of Moscow or the Tsardom of Russia.</note> and *Persia*, and during my stay in *Japan*, to enquire with all the diligence I was capable of into the true state of those Northern Countries. Though, in the main, this was to very little purpose, as I hardly met with anything worth the notice of the public. 

At *Moscow* and at *Astrakhan*, I spoke to several people who had picked up what few and uncertain pieces of information they could, either during their travels through *Siberia* and *Kataya* <note>Cathay, an old name for Northern China.</note> into *China*, or during their stay in *Siberia*, where they had been banished by the *Czar* and lived for many years. However, I could learn nothing further than that Great *Tartary* is joined by an isthmus, or neck of land, to a neighboring continent which they supposed to be *America*. From this, they concluded that, in all probability, there is no such thing as a communication between the Icy Sea and the Indian Ocean. 

In a map of *Siberia*—which was carved into wood by a man banished there, with the names of places marked in Slavic characters <note>original: "Sclavonian"</note>—there were several considerable promontories which stood out into the sea from the eastern coasts. One of these, which was too large to be fully contained on the map's surface, was cut off at the edge. The man who showed me this map told me at the same time that, according to the accounts gathered from the *Tartars* living in those parts, this very promontory is nothing but an isthmus that runs toward a neighboring large continent where it terminates. He added that it is composed of high, rough, and almost inaccessible mountains, and that in his opinion, even if there had once been a passage there for the first inhabitants of the world to cross over into *America* and people 그 continent, such an undertaking would be utterly impossible at present. 

This map of *Siberia*, such as it was—which is to say, extremely poorly made and without any scale of distances or degrees of longitude or latitude—was nonetheless the first that could give the *Czar* of *Muscovy* some notions, however imperfect, of the great extent of his Tartarian dominions to the north. And it is from this same map that my particular friend, the ingenious Mr. *Vinius* <note>Andrei Vinius (1641–1716), a high-ranking Russian official and cartographer of Dutch descent who oversaw the postal and apothecary departments.</note>—who was appointed by the *Czar* as Inspector General over the apothecaries and druggists' shops in *Muscovy*—made the first rough sketch of his map of *Russia* and *Tartary*. He afterwards considerably corrected and expanded this map using several accounts procured from different parts, and finally reduced it to the necessary degrees of longitude and latitude.

During my stay at the Court of *Moscow*, it happened that he served as our interpreter. However, I found him too distrustful and secretive; he was very unwilling to share the observations he had made during his journey. 

<margin>*Nicolaus Witsen*</margin> 
The late, illustrious *Nicolaus Witsen*, <term>L.L.D.</term> <note>Doctor of Laws.</note> and Mayor of *Amsterdam*—a man to whom the public is greatly indebted—met with much better success in his own inquiries. During his last embassy to the Court of *Muscovy* <note>The Tsardom of Russia.</note>, through his extraordinary conduct, great learning, and friendliness, he gained the favor of the *Czar* and the high officials of his court. As a result, whatever accounts they had gathered from all parts of *Russia* were shared with him without reservation. This enabled him to create that excellent and accurate map of the entire *Russian* Empire and Great *Tartary* <note>A historical region covering North and Central Asia.</note>, detailing its mountains, rivers, lakes, cities, and provinces—most of which were unknown until then. This work, because of its great usefulness, greatly pleased those interested in geography. 

However, as accurate as Doctor *Witsen's* map was—and it later proved very useful to Mr. *Isbrand Ides* <note>Evert Ysbrants Ides, a traveler and diplomat who led a Russian embassy to China.</note> on his overland journey to *China* as an ambassador—the full extent of the eastern coasts of *Siberia* and Great *Tartary* remains undetermined. We are still in the dark regarding how they relate to the neighboring continent, which is likely that of *Oku Jeso* <note>Literally "Deep Ezo" or "Further Ezo"; a term used for the lands north of Hokkaido, likely Sakhalin or the Kuril Islands.</note>.

<margin>*Accounts which the Japanese give of Oku Jeso.*</margin>
The *Japanese*, for their part, are just as poorly informed about the state and size of that country which lies behind the island of *Jeso Gasima* <note>Hokkaido.</note> and which they call *Oku Jeso*. They say only that it is 300 *Japanese* miles <note>The "ri," a unit of distance roughly equal to 2.44 miles or 3.9 kilometers.</note> long, but I cannot say what evidence they have to support this claim. 

A ship having been accidentally cast upon the coasts of that continent some years ago, the crew met among the rude and savage inhabitants some people dressed in fine *Chinese* silk. From this, one can probably guess that the natives have some communication with the neighboring *Daats* <note>A Japanese term likely referring to the "Tatars" or the people of the Amur River region in mainland Asia.</note>, or *Tartary*—at least suggesting that these countries are not very far from each other. A <term>Jonk</term> <note>A junk, a traditional Chinese or Japanese sailing vessel.</note> that was sent there specifically for discovery around the year 1684 returned after a three-month voyage and brought back the exact same report. An experienced *Japanese* pilot, who knew the seas around *Japan* well from having sailed everywhere around the Empire, could give me no other satisfying answer to my questions except that between *Japan* and *Jesogasima*, the currents run alternately, sometimes East and sometimes West, and that behind *Jesogasima*...

<margin>Discovery of a New Island</margin>

On the shores, they found an incredible quantity of fish and crabs, some of which were from four to six feet long.

As long as they remain on this island, they must work for their livelihood. ### C H A P. V.

#### *The Division and Sub-division of the Empire of Japan into its several Provinces; as also of its Revenue and Government.*

<margin>Division of the Empire of Japan.</margin>
IN the general Geographical Description of *Japan*, which I have laid down in the preceding Chapter, I took notice that this Empire hath been divided into seven great Tracts of Land, which were again sub-divided into 68 considerable Provinces, and these into 604 smaller Districts, or Counties, as one might call them. I proceed now more particularly to consider the largeness, extent, fertility, produce, and revenues of each Province, as I found them in a *Japanese* description of this Empire, publish'd in *Japan*, by the title of *The Seven Circuits Guide* <note>original: *Sitzi Jossu*; likely the *Shichido Yōshū*, a historical geographical gazetteer.</note>.

<margin>Crown Lands.</margin>
But before I proceed to a particular consideration of the seven large Tracts of Land, which the Empire of *Japan* hath been divided into, and of their several Provinces, I shall take notice of the *Five Home Provinces*, or the *Five Provinces of the Capital Region* <note>original: *Gokinai*, or *Gokinai goka Kokf*</note>, that is the five Provinces of the Imperial revenues, so call'd, because all the revenue, of these five provinces is particularly appropriated for the support and maintenance of the Imperial Court. They amount to 148 *Ten-Thousands* <note>original: *Man*; a Japanese counting unit for 10,000.</note>, and 1200 *Koku* <note>original: *Kokf*; a unit of volume for rice, roughly 5 bushels, which was the standard for measuring wealth and taxes.</note> of Rice. The Reader is desir'd to observe in general, that all the revenues in this Country are reduc'd to these two measures in Rice. A *Man* contains 10000 *Koku*, and a *Koku* contains 3 <note>The OCR transcription reads "3000," but in the original 1727 text and historical context, one *koku* is equivalent to approximately 3 to 5 bales or bags of rice.</note> bales or bags of Rice. *Tanboku* and *Tannan*. 4. **Izumi**, also known as *Senshū*, is a very large province, though only moderately fertile. It spans one hundred Japanese miles <note>The "Japanese mile" mentioned here refers to the *Ri*, which is approximately 2.44 miles or 3.9 kilometers.</note> from south to west. The southern parts are quite warm, while the northern regions are colder and more abundant in what the locals call <term>Gokokf</term> <note>original: *Gokoku*; literally the "Five Grains," typically referring to rice, barley, beans, and two types of millet.</note>, which are the five primary types of grains and legumes eaten in this country. It is divided into 13 districts: *Sumiyoshi*, *Kudatsu*, *Higashinari*, *Nishinari*, *Hatchō*, *Shimashimo*, *Shimakami*, *Teshima*, *Kawanobe*, *Muko*, *Awara*, *Arima*, and *Nose*.

<margin>*Seven great tracts of Land.*</margin>
I shall now proceed to the seven large tracts of land <note>This refers to the *Gokishichidō* system, or "Five Provinces and Seven Circuits."</note> into which the Japanese Empire was divided by the Emperor *Sushun*.

<margin>*TŌKAIDŌ*</margin>
I. The first is **Tōkaidō**, which means the *South Eastern Circuit*. As I noted previously, these seven large tracts were further divided by the Emperor *Tenmu* into 68 provinces (including the five provinces mentioned above), to which two more were added some centuries later. The *Tōkaidō* consists of 15 of these 68 provinces, which are:

<margin>*Iga*</margin>
1. **Iga**, otherwise called *Ishū*, which is bounded on the south and east by the sea. To the north, it is separated from neighboring provinces by a ridge of high mountains. It is a warm country but only moderately fruitful, producing some plants, trees, and bamboo. It is divided into four districts: *Ahai*, *Yamada*, *Iga*, and *Nabari*.

<margin>*Ise*</margin>
2. **Ise**, otherwise called *Seishū*, is a three-day journey in length from south to north. It is almost entirely surrounded by the sea and is extremely fertile, featuring a pleasant variety of hills and plains. It is divided into 15 districts: *Kuwana*, *Asake*, *Suzuka*, *Ichishi*, *Anki*, *Take*, *Nishikishima*, *Gofasuma*, *Inabe*, *Mie*, *Ano*, *Itaka*, *Watakei*, *Ino*, and *Taki*.

<margin>*Shima*</margin>
3. **Shima**, or *Sishō*, is but a small province that one can travel across in half a day. It is a very barren land, but the neighboring sea supplies it with an abundance of fish, oysters, shells, and similar resources. It has only three districts: *Tōshi*, *Ako*, and *Kameshima*.

<margin>*Owari*</margin>
4. **Owari**, otherwise called *Bishū*, is an inland province entirely separate from the sea, yet it is one of the most fertile provinces in the entire empire and is densely populated. It is a three-day journey in length from south to north and is divided into nine districts: *Ama*, *Nakashima*, *Kaguri*, *Niwa*, *Kasugai*, *Yamada*, *Aichi*, *Chita*, and *Tōshijima*.

<margin>Tōtōmi</margin>
6. **Tōtōmi**, also known as *Enshū* <note>original: "Sensju"</note>, is a very good and fruitful country. It is considered one of the most pleasant provinces due to its curious variety of hills, rivers, fertile plains, towns, and villages. Its length is estimated to be a two-and-a-half-day journey when traveling from east to west. It is divided into 14 districts: *Hamana*, *Fuchi*, *Aratama*, *Nagakami*, *Nagashino*, *Suchi*, *Hamana* <note>The author repeats the name Hamana here.</note>, *Kikugawa*, *Haibara*, *Toyota*, *Yamana*, *Sano*, and *Iwata*.

<margin>Suruga</margin>
7. **Suruga**, or *Sunshū* <note>original: "Siufju"</note>, likewise deserves praise for the variety of its towns, villages, hills, and fruitful plains. It is the same length as Tōtōmi, traveling from east to west, and is divided into seven districts: *Abuta*, *Mashizu*, *Udo*, *Ihara*, *Fujikawa*, *Fuji*, and *Abe* <note>original: "Suringa"</note>.

<margin>Kai</margin>
8. **Kai**, otherwise known as *Kaishū* or *Kōshū* <note>original: "Ksjooku"</note>, is a flat country that abounds in rice fields, pasturage, plants, and trees. It also breeds some cattle, especially horses. It is a two-day journey long from south to north and is divided into four districts: *Yamanashi*, *Yatsushiro*, *Koma*, and *Tsuru*.

<margin>Izu</margin>
9. **Izu**, or *Zuishū* <note>original: "Toosju"</note>, is a long peninsula almost entirely surrounded by the sea. It provides a large quantity of salt and all sorts of fish, and is generally considered a reasonably good country. It is quite mountainous with some flat ground and a few rice fields. It has only three districts on the mainland of *Nippon*: *Tagata*, *Naka*, and *Kamo*, to which are added two neighboring islands, *Ōshima* and *Niijima* <note>original: "Firakasima"</note>.

<margin>Sagami</margin>
10. **Sagami**, or *Sōshū*, is a three-day journey long. It is a flat and barren country that provides hardly anything for human sustenance except for tortoises, fish, and crabs from the sea, along with a good quantity of timber from its large forests. It is divided into eight districts: *Ashigara-kami*, *Ashigara-shimo*, *Ōsumi*, *Yurugi*, *Aikō*, *Takakura*, *Kamakura*, *Miura*, and *Enoshima* <note>original: "Jesima"</note>.

<margin>Musashi</margin>
11. **Musashi**, or *Bushū*, is a very large province with a circumference of about a five-and-a-half-day journey. It is a flat country without woods or mountains, but it is very fruitful, abounding in rice, <term>Gokoku</term> <note>The "Five Grains," a traditional grouping of essential Japanese crops including rice, barley, and beans.</note>, garden fruits, and plants. It is divided into 21 districts, which are: *Kuraki*, *Tsuzuki*, *Tama*, *Tachibana*, *Kura*, *Iruma*, *Toshima*, *Hiki*, *Yokomi*, *Saitama*, *Kodama*, *Chichibu*, *Haba*, *Hanzawa*, *Naka*, *Kami*, *Adachi*, *Chichibu*, *Ebara*, *Toyoshima*, and *Ōsato*.

<margin>Awa</margin>
12. **Awa**, otherwise known as *Bōshū* <note>original: "Foosju"</note>, is a moderately good country with mountains, hills, rivers, and plains, providing both rice and corn. It is tolerably well-inhabited and plentifully supplied by the neighboring sea with fish and oysters; the inhabitants use the oyster shells to manure their ground. It is a one-and-a-half-day journey long from south to north and is divided into four districts: *Heguri*, *Awa*, *Asai*, and *Nagasa*.

<margin>Kazusa</margin>
13. **Kazusa**, otherwise known as *Jōshū* <note>original: "Koosju"</note>, is a three-day journey long from south to north. It is a reasonably good country, though not without high, rough mountains. Many of the inhabitants earn their living by weaving <term>hemp-stuffs</term> <note>original: "Cannis," likely referring to hemp cloth (*asa*).</note>, a craft they understand very well. It is divided into 11 districts: *Suisū*, *Amaha*, *Ichihara*, *Unakami*, *Habu*, *Mōki*, *Isumi*, *Hanyū*, *Nagara*, *Yamane*, and *Musa* <note>original: "Mufsa"</note>.

<margin>Hitachi</margin>
15. **Hitachi** <note>original: "Fitats"</note>, or **Jōshū** <note>original: "Sjoo"</note>, is a very large province. <margin>Ōmi</margin>
II. **Tōsandō** <note>The "Eastern Mountainous Tract."</note> contains eight large provinces within its borders:
1. **Ōmi**, an extraordinarily good and fruitful country, featuring a variety of mountains, hills, rivers, and fertile fields. It produces both rice and corn, and rewards the laborer a thousand-fold (to use my Japanese author’s way of describing the country’s richness). It is three and a half days' journey in circumference and is divided into 13 districts: *Shiga*, *Kurimoto*, *Yasu*, *Gamō*, *Kanzaki*, *Inukami*, *Sakata*, *Echi*, the upper and lower *Azai*, *Ika*, *Takashima*, *Kōka*, and *Yosuizumi*.

<margin>Mino</margin>

It produces plenty of rice, corn, and <term>Gokoku<note>The "Five Grains," a traditional grouping of essential Japanese staples: rice, barley, beans, and two types of millet.</note></term>, as well as other necessities of life. It is a three-day journey from South to North and is divided into 18 districts: *Ishizu*, *Fuwa*, *Anpachi*, *Ikeda*, *Ōno*, *Mototsu*, *Mushiroda*, *Katakata*, *Atsumi*, *Kagami*, *Yamagata*, *Mugi*, *Gujō*, *Kamo*, *Kaka*, *Toki*, *Ena*, and *Taki*.

<margin>Hida</margin>

It abounds in woods and forests and yields a great quantity of firewood and timber for building. It has only four districts: *Ōhara*, *Mashita*, *Amano*, and *Araki*.

<margin>Shinano</margin>
4. **Shinano**, or **Shinshū**, is a very cold country. Salt and fish are very scarce here because it is so far from the sea, and there is little livestock due to the lack of pastures. It is otherwise reasonably fertile and produces a good quantity of mulberry trees, silk, and <term>Hemp<note>original: "Cannib," likely referring to hemp (kanna) used for textiles.</note></term>, for which several good factories are established. It is said to be a five-day journey from South to North and is divided into 11 districts: *Mizuchi*, *Takai*, *Hanishina*, *Chiisagata*, *Saku*, *Ina*, *Suwa*, *Chikuma*, *Azumi*, *Sarashina*, and *Shina*.

It is said that Spring arrives here fifteen days earlier than in other provinces. It formerly belonged to **Mutsu** but is now a separate province, divided into 12 districts: *Akumi*, *Kawanobe*, *Murayama*, *Oitama*, *Okatsu*, *Hiraka*, *Tagawa*, *Dewa*, *Akita*, *Senboku*, *Mogami*, and *Yamamoto*. It is a journey of two and a half days in length from East to West and is divided into four districts: *Hakui* <note>original: "Bagui"</note>, *Noto*, *Fugeshi* <note>original: "Fukeesund"</note>, and *Suzu* <note>original: "Sfus"</note>.

It is divided into four districts: *Tonami*, *Imizu* <note>original: "Imidfu"</note>, *Nei* <note>original: "Mebu"</note>, and *Niikawa* <note>original: "Nijkawa"</note>.

# The History of JAPAN. Book I.

...and the number of idols worshipped by the inhabitants is often discussed. The yearly revenue of these two islands <note>Referring to the islands mentioned at the end of the previous page, likely part of the Izu or surrounding chains.</note> amounts to 30,000 and 5,000 koku. <note>The original text uses "3 Man," where "Man" is the Japanese term for 10,000.</note>

<margin>Revenue of the Empire of Japan.</margin>The total revenue of all the islands and provinces belonging to the great Empire of Japan amounts to a yearly sum of 23,286,200 koku, <note>A "koku" (original: "Kokf") was a unit of volume—roughly 180 liters of rice—used to measure the wealth of a domain based on its agricultural productivity.</note> according to the accounts provided above. However, my Japanese source records it as only 22,570,000 koku. <note>original: "2257 Mangokf"</note>

<margin>Government of Japan.</margin>While this is not the most suitable place to detail the specific governance of the Japanese Empire, its provinces, and its districts, it seems necessary for the better understanding of my history to say something on this subject before I proceed further. The entire Empire is governed by the Emperor with absolute monarchical power. Likewise, every individual province is ruled by a Prince who enjoys authority over that territory under the Emperor's sovereignty. <margin>The Emperor Tsunayoshi, now reigning.</margin>The present **Kubo**, <note>The "Kubo" refers to the Shogun, the secular military dictator who held actual political power, as opposed to the Mikado or spiritual Emperor in Kyoto.</note> or secular monarch, is **Tsunayoshi**, <note>original: "Tsinajos"</note> the fourth successor and great-grandson of **Ieyasu**, <note>original: "Jejassama," referring to Tokugawa Ieyasu (1543–1616), the founder of the Tokugawa Shogunate.</note> the first Emperor of the currently reigning family. He seized the throne from the lawful heir and began his reign at the start of the 17th century. **Tsunayoshi** is characterized as a severe but just and prudent monarch. Along with the crown, he inherited from his ancestors an absolute and unlimited power over all his subjects, from those of the lowliest birth to the highest rank. Even the greatest Princes and Lords of the Empire are his vassals to such an extent that he can disgrace, exile, or deprive them of their lives and territories as he pleases, or as he deems necessary for the peace and welfare of the Empire, or as their crimes may deserve.

<margin>Daimyo, Princes of the Empire.</margin>Specific provinces are governed by hereditary Princes called **Daimyo**, <note>original: "Daimio"</note> which signifies *High-named*—that is, Princes and Lords of the highest rank. Some of these have found ways to enlarge their territories through force of arms. For instance, the Prince of **Satsuma** <note>original: "Satzuma"</note> made himself master of the two neighboring provinces, **Ōsumi** <note>original: "Oosumi"</note> and **Hyūga**, <note>original: "Fiugo"</note> and the Prince of **Kaga** <note>original: "Canga"</note> took the neighboring province of **Noto**. For this reason, these two Princes are said to be the most powerful in the Empire.

<margin>Shomyo, Lords.</margin>The Lords of smaller districts are called **Shomyo**, <note>original: "Siomio"</note> meaning *Well-named*, who are Lords of an inferior rank. Their domains—whether they be islands like **Goto**, **Hirado**, <note>original: "Firando"</note> **Amakusa**, **Matsusaki**, and several others, or located on the mainland of the three chief islands that compose the Japanese Empire—are included in the list of the 66 great provinces, appearing under the specific province to which they belong or where they are situated. All the **Shomyo** are subject to the Emperor to the extent that they are allowed to stay in their hereditary domains for only six months of the year. The other half of the year must be spent in the imperial capital, **Edo**, <note>original: "Jedo," modern-day Tokyo.</note> where their wives and families are kept year-round as hostages to ensure their loyalty. <note>This refers to the "Sankin-kotai" or "alternate attendance" system, a central tool of control used by the Tokugawa Shogunate.</note>

<header>Chapter V. The History of JAPAN.</header>

<margin>How the Crown Lands are governed.</margin>
Some of these smaller districts are Imperial estates, or Crown Lands. This is either because they were set aside long ago to support the monarchy, or because, as opportunities arose over time, they were seized from their hereditary owners as punishment and annexed to the crown. It has always been a primary political strategy of the Emperors of Japan <note>The author uses "Emperor" here to refer to the Shogun, the secular military ruler of the period, rather than the spiritual Emperor in Kyoto.</note> to maintain their peaceful hold on the throne by splitting large territories into several smaller ones. By doing so, they aim to weaken the power and authority of the regional Princes. The largest of these Crown Lands are managed by officials called **Bugyō**, <term>Bugyō: high-ranking governors or commissioners appointed by the central government to oversee important cities or regions.</term> who act as lieutenants. The smaller areas are overseen by **Daikan**, <term>Daikan: local administrators or stewards responsible for managing smaller estates and collecting taxes.</term> or stewards. All tax revenues from these lands must be paid directly into the Emperor’s treasury.

# CHAPTER VI.

->**The Author’s opinion on the true Origin and Ancestry of the Japanese.**<-

<margin>An examination of different opinions regarding Japanese ancestry.</margin>
It has been the long-standing opinion of most European geographers that the Japanese are originally of Chinese descent, coming from the inhabitants of that massive empire. This belief is based on the following two stories, which were brought back from the East by European travelers.

<margin>A conspiracy in China.</margin>
The first story is this: It is said that in China, several families once conspired against the Emperor. When the plot was discovered, it was ordered that everyone involved be executed without mercy. However, the number of accomplices was so vast that the executioners eventually grew weary of the endless bloodshed. The matter was brought before the Emperor again, who then decided to change their death sentences to transportation and exile to the neighboring islands of Japan—which were then wild and uninhabited. These exiles populated the islands and became the ancestors of the large and powerful nation that lives there today.

<margin>The search for a universal medicine.</margin>
The second story is reported as follows: One of the Emperors of China was unwilling to give up his empire and all the grandeur and power he possessed within the short span of a human life. He sought to discover a "universal medicine"—an elixir that could grant him immortality. To this end, he sent skilled and learned men to every corner of the world. Among them, one of his lead physicians convinced him that the necessary ingredients for such a medicine could be found in the...

<sig>X</sig>
<meta>catchword: neighbor-</meta>

<summary>This page describes how the Shogunate manages its private lands through governors and stewards to maintain control over regional lords, then begins an investigation into the legendary origins of the Japanese people, focusing on Chinese exile and immortality myths.</summary>

neighboring Islands of *Japan*, but that they were of so tender and singular a structure, that they would wither, and lose their virtues, if touched by any other, but chaste and pure hands. And the better to execute this design, he proposed that 300 young men, and as many young women, all of a strong and healthful constitution, should be carried over thither, which accordingly he did himself, though far from having any real intention to satisfy his Sovereign, but rather out of a desire to escape his Tyranny, to settle in happier climes, and to people these then uninhabited islands. As to the first of these two stories,

<margin>Linschoten refuted.</margin>
Linschoten <note>original: "Linſchoot"; referring to Jan Huyghen van Linschoten (1563–1611), a Dutch traveler and historian whose accounts of the East were highly influential in Europe.</note> is the author of it; but he not acquainting his reader, what authority he had for it, or how he came by it, and there being not the least mention made, neither in *Chinese*, nor *Japanese* histories, of any such conspiracy, it deserves no credit, but ought to be entirely rejected, as forged and fabulous.

<margin>A Chinese Physician comes over with a Colony to Japan.</margin>
But as to the second, the coming over of a *Chinese* Physician with so many young men, and young women, the same is not at all denied by the *Japanese*; nay, far from it, they still show a place upon *Kumano* <note>original: "Khumano"</note> (so they call the southern coasts of the provinces) in *Kii* <note>original: "Kijnokuni"; Kii Province is located on the Kii Peninsula on Honshu.</note>, and some neighboring provinces, where he landed, and afterwards settled with his gallant colony; they even point to the remains of a temple which was there erected to his memory, for having brought over to them from *China* good manners, and useful arts and sciences.

<margin>Sikwo, Emperor of China.</margin>
<margin>His Tyranny and profuseness.</margin>
As to the occasion of his coming over, it is recorded in *Japanese* histories, that there was great search made after an universal medicine <note>This refers to the "Elixir of Life" or "Elixir of Immortality," a central pursuit in ancient Chinese alchemy.</note>, during the reign of the Emperor *Si*, or *Sikwo*, or as the vulgar pronounce it, *Sino Sikwo* <note>Refers to Qin Shi Huang (r. 221–210 BCE), the first emperor of a unified China.</note>. This Emperor was one of the three *Chinese Neros*, along with *Sinosko*, *Ketzuwo*, and *Thuwo*, whose memory will be forever abhorred. He not only governed his empire with unparalleled tyranny, but lived with the greatest pride, and most profuse magnificence imaginable, of which there are several remarkable instances mentioned in the history of his life. He caused once a large spot of ground to be dug up for a lake, and having ordered it to be filled with *Chinese* beer <note>Likely referring to rice wine or "huangjiu."</note>, he sailed over it in stately barges. He caused a stately palace, named *Kojaku* <note>The Epang Palace, a legendary and massive palace complex built by Qin Shi Huang.</note>, to be built for his residence, the floors whereof were paved with gold and silver, and the whole building of such an extent, that the Emperor *Kooll*, who usurped the throne upon his grandson (whom he put to death, with all the Imperial Family), having set it on fire, it burnt into ashes for the space of three months. This memorable event gave birth to a proverb, whereby the *Japanese* express the sudden changes, and short duration, that human grandeur and happiness are liable to.

<margin>Conjectures about the origin of different Nations taken from their languages.</margin>
It is unquestionably true, that languages, and their proprieties, are as sure and certain marks, as perhaps it is possible to produce, whereby to discern, and trace out, not only the true origin of a Nation, but likewise to find out, how in success of time it increased, by being, as it were, incorporated with other Nations. Of this most *European* Nations afford us evident proofs. Thus, for Instance, we may easily find by the language alone, that the *Polanders*, *Bohemians* and *Muscovites* are of *Slavonian* <note>The Slavic language family.</note> extraction; that the *Italians*, *French* and *Spaniards* descend from the *Romans*; that the *Germans*, low *Dutch*, *Danes* and *Swedes*, are the offspring of the ancient *Goths*. Nay, we may go still further, and assert, that the languages alone of several nations, and proper considerations thereupon, will qualify and enable us to form probable conjectures, what revolutions happened among them, whether, and what neighbouring nations they were conquered by, as also, whether, and how from time to time they increased by fresh supplies and colonies from foreign parts: For it may be laid down as a constant rule, that in proportion to the number of strangers, who come to settle and live in a Country, words of the tongue spoke by them will be brought into the language of that Country, and by degrees, as it were, naturalized, and become so familiar to the Natives, as if they had been of their own growth. The number of *German*, *French*, and *Danish* words, in the *English* language, doth it not evidently prove, that *England* was successively conquered by the *Danes*, lower *Saxons* and *French*. Not even the *Latin* Tongue was able to preserve its purity, but *Greek* words were freely, and in great number, adopted into it, after the *Romans* became Master of that Country, then the seat of learning and politeness. The language now spoke in *Transylvania* hath a considerable mixture both of the *Latin* and neighbouring *Hungarian*. The language of the Inhabitants of *Semigallia* <note>A historical region in present-day Latvia.</note>, (a small Country near *Russia*) is composed of the *Lettish* <note>The Latvian language.</note>, *Slavonian* and *Latin*. The same observation holds true in other parts of the World, as well as in *Europe*. *John de Barros* <note>João de Barros (1496–1570), a Portuguese historian famous for his "Decades," documenting the Portuguese Empire in the East.</note> in his *Decades*, and *Flaccourt* <note>Étienne de Flacourt (1607–1660), a French governor of Madagascar who wrote a detailed history of the island.</note> in his *History of Madagascar* assure us, that the language spoke by the Inhabitants of that large *African* Island, is full of *Javan* and *Malayan* words, as remaining proofs of the trade and commerce, which these two Nations, about 2000 years ago the richest and most powerful of *Asia*, had

By their neighbors, I mean chiefly the *Chinese*, who inhabit the Eastern maritime provinces of that Empire and carry on trade with *Japan*. These conclude no more for an original descent of the *Japanese* from *China* than some few *Portuguese* words—such as bread <note>original: "Pan"</note>, palm <note>original: "palma"</note>, cake <note>original: "bolan"</note>, cloak <note>original: "Cappa"</note>, flask <note>original: "frasco"</note>, glass <note>original: "bidou"</note>, much <note>original: "tante"</note>, and a few more still left there—would be allowed as sufficient proof that the *Japanese* were originally descended from the *Portuguese*. Nor was the number of *Chinese* who came from time to time to settle in *Japan* ever considerable enough to cause any remarkable alteration in the mother-tongue of the *Japanese*, though they could, and actually did, communicate and introduce among them the arts and sciences which had long before flourished in *China*. They even introduced the knowledge of the learned and significant character-based language <note>The Chinese writing system (Kanji), which uses symbols to represent concepts rather than sounds.</note> of that country, which is likewise received in *Korea*, *Tonkin* <note>Modern-day northern Vietnam.</note>, and other neighboring Kingdoms, much in the same way that Latin is used in most European countries.

But besides this, there are two other essential properties of a language—construction and pronunciation—which in the *Japanese* language are so entirely different from those of the *Chinese* that there is no room left to think that these two Nations gave birth to each other. And first, as to the construction and way of writing: the *Chinese* set their characters one below another in a row, without any intermediate particles to connect them. The Chinese are peaceable, modest, great lovers of a sedate, speculative and philosophical way of life, but withal very much given to fraud and usury. <margin>Japanese are Descendents of the Babylonians.</margin>

### Chapter VI. The History of JAPAN.

[...our linguistic] examination to be entirely free, contrary to what we find in all European and most Eastern languages known to us. These other languages seem to have been from their very beginning so thoroughly mixed and confounded, that there is scarce any that does not have some words of another, however remote. If then our Japanese colony did reach that part of the world which Divine Providence assigned for their future abode as soon as the Chinese, the people of Tonkin <note>original: "Tunquinese," referring to the historical region of northern Vietnam.</note>, and other neighboring nations did theirs, it must be supposed that they fortunately fell in with such a road as could with safety and speed bring them to the eastern extremities of Asia, from whence there is but a short passage over to **Japan**.

In order therefore to trace out what road it is probable they took, we must consider the first Babylonians <note>The author uses the biblical account of the Tower of Babel as a historical starting point for human migration and the origin of distinct ethnic groups.</note> in the condition they were in after that dreadful confusion of languages, wholly disappointed from going on with their vain design, and brought to the fatal necessity to part with each other and to be dispersed all over the world. And in order to this, let us suppose:

1. That among the different parties there arose in all likelihood a strong emulation to choose for their future abode such countries as were not only fruitful and delightful, but thought to be less exposed to the invasion of other parties—either because of their commodious situation toward the sea, or between large rivers and high mountains, or by reason of their great distance. And in this regard, it is highly probable that such countries as were very remote, but situated under a temperate climate, became not the last inhabited. This seems to be the case of the Empire of **Japan**, whose remoteness, as well as its fruitfulness and pleasant situation between 30 and 46 degrees of northern latitude, could fully answer all the expectations of a first colony.

2. But secondly, let us suppose that the chief care of these first colonies, in their search for a country fit for their habitation, must needs have been to follow such roads and tracts of land where, in the meantime, they could be provided with the necessities of life. This intention could scarce be answered more effectually than by traveling either along the seacoasts or, and with more probability, along great rivers and lakes. There they could be supplied with fish for their own nourishment, with sweet water to quench their thirst, and where they were like to meet with good pasture ground for their cattle, until at last they alighted at a country where they thought they could settle with safety and convenience.

Having discovered the mainland of *Nippon* by this means, they surely resolved to cross over (which they could easily do even in ordinary fishing boats) and choose that country for their future home. ### The History of JAPAN. Book I.

These are my theories—for I offer them only as such—concerning the true original descent of the Japanese Nation.

<margin>The growth of the Japanese nation is primarily due to their own population.</margin>
Before I conclude this chapter, it is worth saying something about the growth of this first Japanese colony. Once they had decided to stay and populate the country, they likely led a simple and impoverished life for many ages before making significant improvements in agriculture and other arts and sciences. They survived on their livestock, the plants, roots, and fruits the earth produced, and the fish and crabs provided by the sea. It was undoubtedly and primarily due to their own efforts that, over the passage of time, they became such a numerous and powerful nation. The present inhabitants of *Japan* should generally be viewed as descendants of those who, after the confusion of languages at *Babel* <note>A biblical reference to the origins of different languages and the dispersal of humanity across the earth.</note>, traveled here and settled in these islands.

<margin>But also through other colonies.</margin>
On the other hand, it cannot be denied that from time to time new colonies were sent over, mainly from *China* and *Korea* <note>original: "Corea"</note>, and perhaps also from other neighboring countries. The Japanese themselves frequently mention learned Chinese people in their histories who brought over their books and the knowledge of useful arts and sciences. However, this did not occur until more recent ages, when the Japanese monarchy had already become a powerful empire. Indeed, since so few foreign words have been introduced into the Japanese language—so few that it is hardly noticeable that any change has been made at all—and since their religion and ancient customs persist to this day, it is clear that whatever foreign colonies came to *Japan* (whether voluntarily or by chance), their numbers must have been very small compared to the total Japanese population.

<margin>Due to shipwrecks.</margin>
Considering further that the islands of *Japan* are surrounded by a dangerous and stormy sea, it is highly probable that from time to time ships from foreign countries were stranded on the Japanese coasts. If any of the crew were lucky enough to save their lives, they likely chose to stay in *Japan* and settle among the natives rather than trust themselves to the mercy of the sea again and risk a dangerous return to their own country. Although navigation has greatly improved by now, similar accidents still happen very frequently. Hardly a year goes by without some ships being forced onto the coasts of *Japan*, sometimes coming from countries so remote or entirely unknown that one can hardly guess where they are from, based on the appearance, language, or customs of the crew.

# Chapter VI. The History of JAPAN.

<margin>Genkaisima; an Island formerly inhabited by Blacks.</margin>
The Japanese, having some centuries ago accidentally discovered the island of *Genkaisima* <note>Now known as Genkai Island, located in the Genkai Sea north of Fukuoka.</note>, situated to the north of *Japan*, found it inhabited—as their histories relate—by *Oni* <note>original: "Oni"; supernatural creatures in Japanese folklore, often translated as demons, ogres, or devils.</note>, that is, *Black Devils*. It is highly probable that these black inhabitants had been forced onto the coasts of this then-uninhabited island during a storm. It is further observed in the history of this war that they wore long hair spread over their shoulders and that they possessed a strange sort of household goods, including, among other items, high European hats. As for the Japanese calling them "Devils," we need not wonder at it, considering either their black skin or the natural pride of the Japanese nation, which so far despises all other countries that they call them *Umakokf* <note>original: "Umakokf"; likely a transcription of *Onigoku*, meaning "Land of the Devils."</note>, that is, the "Countries of Devils."

<margin>More instances of shipwrecks on the Japanese coasts.</margin>
Not long before my arrival, and during my stay in *Japan*, several ships stranded upon the coasts, coming from remote and unknown countries. In such cases, the entire ship’s company—both the survivors and the bodies of those who drowned when thrown ashore—as well as all the ship’s tackle and the boat (if any), must be brought up to *Nagasaki*. This is the place appointed for a general inquiry into maritime affairs. The governors of this place examine every minute circumstance of the unhappy accident with that care and jealous circumspection which is peculiar to this nation. This is done to discover, if possible, what country the ship came from and what language the survivors speak. This examination is sometimes made in the presence of the *Dutch Resident*, who did me the favor, upon these occasions, to carry me along with him. It is a duty incumbent on every Prince of the Empire to take care, if any ships strand upon the coasts of his province, that they be sent up to *Nagasaki* as mentioned before; out of respect for the Emperor, this is commonly done at great expense. 

Not long ago, a <term>junk</term> <note>A type of sailing ship common in East and Southeast Asia.</note> coming from *Manila*, on board which were some <term>Topassians</term> <note>original: "Topassians"; Luso-Asians or people of mixed Portuguese and Indian/Asian descent, often serving as soldiers or sailors.</note> (a sort of black Christians), was wrecked upon the coasts of *Satsuma*. Most of the ship’s company were drowned, some died on shore, and only three were brought up alive to *Nagasaki*. The last of these died there in prison after having taken some <term>medicine</term> <note>original: "physick."</note> ordered for him by a *Japanese physician*. Of another ship which stranded upon the same coasts, only three black sailors were saved. They could not pronounce one distinct word besides that of *Tobacco*. After having lain for some time in prison, they were delivered to us to be transported on board our ships. 

Another ship was brought to *Nagasaki* which had been forced upon the northern coasts of *Japan* without anybody on board. The odd, uncommon structure of this vessel and the remains of three *Chinese characters* upon the stern made the *Japanese* conjecture that it came from the extremities of *Jeso* <note>Ezo, the historical name for the northern island of Hokkaido.</note>.

<margin>Pygmy Island.</margin>
If we believe the *Japanese*, there is another unknown nation—very different from theirs in customs, shape, and language—which inhabits the island of *Kubitejima* <note>original: "Kubitefima"; likely a reference to mythical or poorly understood northern islands like those of the Ainu</note>, one of the most northern islands belonging to *Japan*. <margin>The Japanese differ in shape and complexion.</margin>
Taking everything into account, the wide difference still observed between the *Japanese* inhabitants of various provinces regarding their physical appearance strongly suggests that, over time, different and new branches were grafted onto the original tree of this nation. For although the *Japanese* in general—particularly the common people of *Nipon* <note>The main island of Japan, modern-day Honshu.</note>—have a very plain appearance, being short-statured, strong, thick-legged, and tawny, with somewhat flat noses and thick eyelids (though the eyes do not sit as deep in the forehead as those of the *Chinese*), the descendants of the oldest and noblest families, including the princes and lords of the empire, have something more majestic in their shape and countenance, being more similar to *Europeans*. 

The inhabitants of the provinces of *Satsuma*, *Osumi*, and *Hyuga* <note>original: "Satzuma, Oosijmi, and Fiuga"</note> are of medium height, strong, courageous, and manly, yet otherwise civil and polite. The same is observed of the inhabitants of some of the northern provinces on the great island of *Nipon*, with the exception of those from the large province of *Oshu* <note>original: "Osju"</note>, who are said to be more cruel and unmerciful than others. The inhabitants of some provinces of *Saikoku* <note>The island of Kyushu.</note>, particularly *Hizen* <note>original: "Fifen"</note>, are short and slender but well-shaped, with a handsome appearance and extreme politeness. The inhabitants of the great island of *Nipon*, particularly its eastern provinces, are distinguished from others by their large heads, flat noses, and muscular, fleshy complexions.

### CHAP. VII.

## Of the Origin of the *Japanese*, according to their own fabulous Opinion.

<margin>The *Japanese* trace their origin from their deities.</margin>
THE *Japanese* fancy themselves highly affronted by the endeavors of some who busy themselves to draw the original descent of their nation from the *Chinese* or others of their neighbors. They pretend that they arose within the compass of their own Empire, though not out of the Earth, like mice and worms, as the proud *Athenians* <note>Refers to the Athenian claim of being "autochthonous," or born directly from the soil of their homeland.</note> for that same reason were upbraided with by that Cynic *Diogenes* <note>Diogenes of Sinope, a Greek philosopher known for mocking social pretenses.</note>. They claim a birth much higher and nobler, and esteem themselves no less than offspring of their very deities, whom otherwise they do not look upon as eternal, but suppose that in the first motion of the Chaos <note>original: "Chaos"; referring to the Greek concept of the void or primordial state of the universe before creation.</note>, out of which all things were formed, their Gods also were brought forth by its invisible power.

<margin>Of which there are two successions.</margin>
They have two differing genealogies of their deities. The first is a succession of Celestial Spirits, of beings absolutely free from all manner of mixture with corporeal <note>Physical or bodily.</note> substances, who ruled the *Japanese* world during an undetermined and incomprehensible series of centuries. The second is a race of Terrestrial Spirits, or God-men, who were not possessed of that pure being peculiar only to their predecessors. They governed the *Japanese* Empire by a lineal succession, each for a long but limited number of years, till at last they begot that third race of men, which *Japan* is now inhabited by, and who have nothing left of the purity and perfections of their divine progenitors.

There is no province or town throughout the Empire that does not have at least one temple where **Tensio Dai Dsin** is worshipped. In the hope of obtaining temporal blessings through his power, he is worshipped with much more dedication and devotion than any of their other gods. <margin>The origin of these two successions of Deities.</margin>
These are the two successions of divine and semi-divine beings from which the Japanese trace the original descent of their nation. The account they give of how these Gods were created, and how they fathered one another, is no less fantastical and legendary. They say the first of the seven great Celestial Spirits was the very first thing to emerge from the **Chaos** <note>The formless state of the universe before creation.</note>, being its purest, invisible part and power. His son and heir emerged from him in a manner beyond human understanding—or, as some attempt to explain it to make it intelligible, through the motion and active power of the Heavens and the elements below them. Thus were born the seven great Celestial Spirits of the first succession. It was the last of them <note>Referring to Izanagi.</note> who, knowing his wife in a physical manner, fathered the second succession of "God-men"—beings who were half divine and half human. These, although they fell far short of the perfection of their ancestors, still possessed divine qualities that allowed them to preserve their lives and continue their rule through their descendants (whom they fathered in a more understandable way) for an immemorial time, far exceeding the lifespan to which humans are now limited.

<margin>How the third race of Men was fathered.</margin>
At last, all these beings passed away with the person of **Awase-Dsuno**, the last of this second race, who himself became the first parent of the third race: the current inhabitants of **Japan**. To those of this third race who descend directly from the first-born son of **Awase-Dsuno-Mikoto**, and so on down through their heirs, the Japanese attribute a supernatural, almost divine power and unlimited authority over their fellow creatures. This is expressed to some degree by the grand titles and high-sounding epithets they give to this entire family, but particularly to its head and Prince. Such titles include: **Oodai** <note>Meaning "Great Generation" or "Great Era."</note>; **Mikaddo** <term>Mikado<gloss>A title for the Emperor of Japan, literally "Honorable Gate," referring to the imperial palace.</gloss></term> (Emperor—the title *Mikotto* <note>Modern: *Mikoto*, meaning "Lord" or "Augustness."</note> being reserved only for the first and second successions of Gods and God-men); **Tenoo** <term>Tenno<gloss>The modern title for the Emperor, meaning "Heavenly Sovereign."</gloss></term> (Heavenly Prince); **Tensin** <term>Tenshin<gloss>Meaning "Son of Heaven."</gloss></term> (Son of Heaven); **Tee** (Prince); and **Dairi** <note>Technically referring to the inner palace, but used here to describe the Emperor and his court.</note>, a name frequently used to denote the whole court of the ecclesiastical hereditary Emperor. # The History of JAPAN. Book I.

<margin>Some Remarks on this fabulous Tradition of the Japanese.</margin>
Thus far I have recounted the common tradition of the Japanese regarding the original descent of their nation. This account is esteemed as sacred among them, carrying as much authority as the Holy Scriptures do among Christians. It would be unnecessary to disprove it, as its nature is so clearly weak that it cannot withstand the scrutiny of even the most basic reasoning. 

Some people might think it possible that these two successions of Gods and "God-men" are actually allegorical accounts—perhaps obscure versions of the Gold and Silver Ages described by Greek writers, or the ages of the world before and after the Great Flood. However, how could one reconcile the infinite amount of time during which the Japanese claim these spiritual beings governed the world with the much shorter number of years passed since the Creation, according to the divine account provided to us in the Holy Bible? 

The Japanese, it seems, did not want to be outdone by the Egyptians, Chaldeans, <term>Brahmins<note>A high-ranking social class in India, here referring to the ancient scholars and priests of the East.</note></term>, and their other neighbors in the East. Driven by the pride and vanity common to Eastern nations, they dated their origins as far back as possible, believing it glorious to display a long line of monarchs who ruled over them. 

Their primary goal, however, seems to have been outdoing their neighbors, the Chinese. In their historical writings, they place **Tensio Dai Sin** <note>original: "Tensio Dai Sin"; modern: *Tenshō Daijin*, the Sun Goddess Amaterasu Omikami, the supreme deity in Shinto.</note>, the first ancestor of the Japanese nation, many thousands of years before the person they call the fictitious founder of the Chinese nation, **Sinkwosi** <note>original: "Sinkwosi"; likely referring to *Shennong*, the legendary "Divine Farmer" of Chinese mythology.</note>, or **Tien Hoamtsij** <note>original: "Tien Hoamtsij"; Chinese: *Tiánhuángshì* (Celestial Sovereign), a primordial deity.</note> in the Chinese pronunciation. 

To ensure they were cleared of any suspicion of being descended from the Chinese, they added a preceding succession of great celestial spirits, which they trace back to the very beginning of Creation. They are, however, at a loss for an answer when asked how **Awase Dsuno** <note>original: "Awase Dsuno"; modern: *Ugayafukiaezu*, the last of the earthly deities and father of the first human emperor.</note>—the last of their earthly Gods and a being endowed with the many supernatural qualities they attribute to him—could father a race as poor and miserable as the current inhabitants of Japan. 

They have just as little to say regarding the state of their country or the history of their ancestors before the time of **Sinmu** <note>original: "Sinmu"; modern: *Jimmu*, the legendary first Emperor of Japan, traditionally said to have founded the empire in 660 BCE.</note>, their first monarch. For this reason, several of their own writers have ventured to call Japan **Atarasikoks** <note>original: "Atarasikoks"; from the Japanese *Atarashiki-koku*, meaning "New Country."</note> and **Sinkoks** <note>original: "Sinkoks"; from the Japanese *Shinkoku*, meaning "Divine Country" or "Land of the Gods."</note>, as if it had been newly discovered and populated during the reign of their first Emperor. 

It is true that genuine Japanese history only begins with the reign of this first monarch, who lived about 660 years before Christ. In this regard, the Chinese have surpassed them; they began recording the history of their country at least 2,000 years earlier. The Chinese can show something that I believe no other nation can boast: an unbroken succession of monarchs, including accounts of their lives, governments, and significant actions, stretching back over 4,000 years to the present day. It must be owned

<meta>This page continues the author’s analysis of Japanese origins, transitioning from mythical genealogies to a more grounded historical perspective. # Chap. VII. The History of JAPAN. 101

It is certain, however, that the Japanese nation must have existed and lived in the country for a considerable time before their first **Odai**, **Mikado**, or Emperor. By the time he was raised to the throne, the population was already very numerous. Soon after, as recorded in their histories, great wars broke out among them, and many thousands perished from plague and famine. Such developments would be impossible unless one assumes they arrived all at once from another country or sprang out of the earth like mushrooms—notions which are either absurd or improbable. 

I am more inclined to believe that from the time their ancestors first arrived in the country, they led a wandering life for many ages, moving from place to place with their families and cattle. The very geography of the country—divided as it is by mountains, seas, and rivers—seems to have necessitated such a lifestyle. This continued until the blessed **Ninus Dsin Mu Ten Oo** <note>original: "Ninus Dſin Mu Ten Oo"; a variation of *Jimmu Tennō*, the legendary first Emperor of Japan who is said to have founded the imperial line in 660 BCE.</note> civilized them and brought them into a better social order, becoming their first monarch, whether by force or by choice. 

Since that time, the Japanese have been accurate and faithful in writing the history of their country and the lives and reigns of their monarchs. To conclude: just as **Dadshijno Mikotto** <note>original: "Dadſijno Mikotto"; likely referring to *Izanagi-no-Mikoto*, a creator deity in Japanese mythology.</note> is believed by them to have been the greatest of the first succession of Celestial Spirits, and **Tenshō Dai Jin** <note>original: "Ten ſio Dai Dſin"; the Sun Goddess Amaterasu, from whom the imperial family claims descent.</note> the greatest of the second succession of God-men, so they look upon **Jimmu Tennō** as the greatest of the third race—the human inhabitants living now. 

In his family, the hereditary right to the crown, held with a more than human authority, was continued down to **Kinsan Kiwotei** <note>original: "Kinſan Kiwotei"; referring to Emperor Higashiyama, who reigned from 1687 to 1709.</note>, the present 114th Mikado. This spans a period of 2,360 years, calculating up to the year of Christ, 1700. I say "the hereditary right to the crown," for the actual government of the Empire itself has lately passed into secular hands <note>This refers to the *Bakufu* or Shogunate, the military government that exercised real political power while the Emperor remained a symbolic and ritual figurehead.</note>, as will be shown more particularly in another place.

# The History of J A P A N. Book I. 102

### C H A P T E R VIII.

## Concerning the *Climate* of *Japan*, and its *Produce* regarding *Minerals*.

<margin>Climate of Japan. Its Air.</margin>
JAPAN enjoys a pleasant and healthy climate. The air is quite variable and prone to sudden changes. In winter, the land is covered with snow and subject to sharp frosts, while in summer—especially during the **Dog-days** <note>The "Dog-days" refers to the hottest period of the summer, historically associated with the rising of the star Sirius, the Dog Star.</note>—it becomes oppressively hot. 
<margin>Rains.</margin>
It rains frequently throughout the entire year, but most heavily during the months of June and July. For this reason, these months are called *Satsuki*, which means the "Water-months." <note>Satsuki (皐月) is the traditional name for the fifth month of the lunar calendar, which roughly corresponds to June.</note> However, the rainy season in Japan does not follow the same predictable regularity seen in the hotter regions of the East Indies. Thunder and lightning are also very frequent occurrences.

<margin>Sea.</margin>
The sea surrounding the islands of Japan is very rough and stormy. Combined with many rocks, cliffs, and shoals—both above and below the water—this makes navigation extremely hazardous. There are two re-
<margin>Whirlpools.</margin>
markable and dangerous whirlpools. The first is called *Faifaki* <note>original: "Faifaki"; likely the Hayasaki Strait, known for its powerful tidal currents.</note> and is located near **Shimabara**, below **Amakusa**. It is most dangerous when the tide turns; at high tide, it becomes level with the surface of the sea, but as soon as the tide begins to recede, the water churns violently and suddenly drops. I was informed it reaches a depth of fifteen fathoms <note>A fathom is a unit of length equal to six feet (about 1.8 meters), used primarily to measure water depth.</note>, forcefully swallowing any ships, boats, or other objects that happen to be caught nearby at that fatal moment. These are dashed to pieces against the rocks at the bottom. Sometimes the shattered wreckage remains underwater; other times, it is thrown out again several **German miles** <note>A German mile (Geographische Meile) was a historical unit roughly equal to 4.6 English miles or 7.4 kilometers.</note> away. The other whirlpool lies near the coast of the Province of **Kii** <note>original: "Kijnokuni"; Kii-no-kuni.</note>. It is called *Narrotto* <note>The Naruto whirlpools in the Naruto Strait.</note>, and because of its proximity to the Province of **Awa**, it is also called *Awano Narrotto*, which means "the rushing of Awa." This name is given because the water rushes with a thunderous, boisterous noise around a small rocky island, which is kept in a state of perpetual trembling by the violence of the motion. Though it looks terrifying, it is considered less dangerous than the first whirlpool because its roar can be heard from a great distance, allowing it to be easily avoided. Japanese authors, especially poets, frequently reference the unique nature and motion of this *Narrotto* in their writings, as do the priests in their sermons.

Waterspouts are also frequently observed rising in the Japanese seas and moving toward the coast. The Japanese imagine these to be a type of **Water Dragon** with long, watery tails, flying up into

...the air with a swift and violent motion, for which reason they are called *Tatsmaki* <note>original: "Tatsmaki" (竜巻); literally "spiraling dragon," the Japanese term for a waterspout or tornado.</note>, that is, spouting dragons.

<margin>*Soil.*</margin>
The soil of Japan, in itself, is for the most part mountainous, rocky, and barren. However, through the tireless care and industry of the natives, it has been made fruitful enough to supply them with all manner of necessities, in addition to what the neighboring sea affords in the way of fish, crabs, and shells. Even the most rocky and uncultivated places yield plants, fruits, and roots for the sustenance of the inhabitants. Their impoverished ancestors learned through experience how to dress and prepare these resources, so as to make them not only fit for food but also pleasing and agreeable to the taste. Considering this and the frugal way of living of the Japanese in general, we need not wonder that this vast and populous empire is so abundantly provided with all the necessities of human life. Japan exists as a world unto itself, which Nature seems to have purposely separated from the rest of the globe by encompassing it with a rocky and tempestuous sea; it can easily subsist on its own without any assistance from foreign countries, so long as arts and agriculture are followed and improved by the natives.

<margin>*Rivers and Fresh Waters.*</margin>
The country, moreover, is plentifully supplied with fresh water, as there are many springs, lakes, and rivers throughout the empire. Some of the rivers in particular are so large and rapid—due either to the steep, high mountains and rocks where they originate, or because of the profuse rain showers which fall frequently—that they cannot be crossed without danger. Some are so impetuous that they can support no bridges. Some of the most famous rivers are:

1. <margin>*Ujingava River.*</margin> **Ujingava**, that is, the **River Ujin** <note>Likely the Ōi River or the Uji River, famous historical crossing points on the journey to Edo.</note>. It is about a quarter of a German mile (or an English mile and a half) broad. As there is no bridge built over it, it must be forded. The force and rapidity with which this river falls down from the mountains is such that even when the water is low and scarcely knee-deep, five strong men who are well acquainted with the riverbed must be employed to lead a horse through. This, combined with the many large stones lying at the bottom, makes the passage equally difficult and dangerous. The people whose business it is to ford passengers through this and other similar rivers are made answerable for the passengers' lives by the laws of the country, lest they should fail to take due care. This is the reason why few unlucky accidents happen. 

<margin>*Oomi River.*</margin> 
2. The **River Oomi** is famous for its surprising beginning; for it is recorded in Japanese histories that it sprang up suddenly in one night in the year 285 BC <note>This refers to the legend that Lake Biwa and Mount Fuji were formed simultaneously by a massive seismic event.</note>. It borrowed its name from the province where it arises. 

<margin>*Askagava River.*</margin> 
3. The **River Askagava** <note>The Asuka River.</note> is remarkable because the depth of its bed alters perpetually; for this reason, it is frequently alluded to by Japanese authors, especially poets <note>In Japanese poetry, the shifting shallows of the Asuka River are a common metaphor for the uncertainty and constant change of life.</note>.

# The History of JAPAN. Book I 104

<margin>Earthquakes.</margin>
*Japan* is very much subject to Earthquakes, which happen so frequently, that the Natives dread them no more, than we Europeans do an ordinary storm of thunder and lightning. They are of opinion, that the cause of Earthquakes is a huge large whale’s creeping under ground <note>Early Japanese folklore often attributed earthquakes to a giant fish or dragon; by the 18th century, the "namazu" or giant catfish became the most common culprit, though Kaempfer here records it as a whale.</note>, and that they signify nothing. Sometimes however the shakes are so violent, and last so long, that whole Cities are thereby destroy’d, and many thousand of the Inhabitants buried under the ruins. Such a dreadful accident happen’d, as Father *Lewis de Froes* <note>Luis Frois (1532–1597), a Portuguese Jesuit missionary who wrote extensively about Japan.</note> relateth (in the *Work on Japanese Affairs collected by John Hay* <note>original Latin: "opere de Rebus Japonicis collecto a Joh. Hayo"</note>) in the year 1586, he himself being then in *Japan*. (a) The like accidents happen’d frequently since that time. In 1704, I had a letter from *Batavia* <note>Modern-day Jakarta, then the capital of the Dutch East Indies.</note>, from a friend of mine, then lately arrived from *Japan*, wherein among other things he gave me an account of such a violent shock, which happen’d there in 1703, whereby, and by a great fire, which broke out at the same time, almost the whole City of *Jedo* <note>Edo, modern-day Tokyo.</note>, and the Imperial Palace itself, were destroy’d and laid in ashes, and upwards of 200,000 Inhabitants buried under the ruins. It is remarka-

<margin>Places free from Earthquakes.</margin>
ble, that some particular places in *Japan* are observ’d to be free from all manner of succussions <note>Violent shakings or tremors.</note>. The Japanese reason variously upon this Phænomenon. Some attribute it to the holiness and sanctity of the place, and to the powerful protection of its Genius, or tutelar God. Others are of opinion, that these places are not shook, because they immediately repose upon the unmov’d Center of the Earth. The fact itself is not call’d in question, and there are noted for having this singular Privilege, the Islands of *Gotho*, the small Island *Sikubusima* <note>Chikubu-shima in Lake Biwa.</note>, on which stands a most stately Temple of <term>Bonzes</term> <note>A term used by early Europeans to describe Buddhist monks.</note>, being one of the first that was built in the Country, the large mountain *Kojasan* <note>Mount Koya, the headquarters of Shingon Buddhism.</note> near *Miaco* <note>Kyoto, the then-capital and residence of the Emperor.</note>, famous for the number of its convents, Monasteries and Monks, besides some few others.

From the Province *Sacaja* <note>Sakai.</note> as far as *Miaco* the Earth trembled for forty days successively. In the Town of *Sacaja* sixty Houses were thrown down. At *Nagafama* <note>Nagahama.</note>, a small Town of about a thousand houses in the Kingdom *Oomi* <note>Omi Province.</note>, the Earth gaped and swallowed up one half of that place, the other half was destroy’d by a Fire. A strong Castle in the Kingdom of *Mino*, built at the top of a high hill, after several violent shocks sunk down and disappeared of a sudden, the earth gaping, that not the least footstep remained, a lake quickly filling the place, where the foundations of the Castle had been. Another accident of this kind happened in the Province *Ikeja* <note>Likely Iga or Ise.</note>. His palaces were strongly shook, but not thrown down.

### Chap VIII. The History of JAPAN.

<margin>The wealth of Japan and its sources.</margin>
The greatest riches of the Japanese soil—and those in which this Empire surpasses most known countries—consist of all sorts of minerals and metals, particularly gold, silver, and copper. The many hot springs in several parts of the Empire, and the various smoking and burning mountains, show what a vast stock of sulfur is hidden in the bowels of the earth. Sulfur is considered the "mother" and main ingredient of mineral and metallic bodies; in addition to these volcanic signs, vast quantities of this substance are dug up in several places.

<margin>Volcanoes.</margin>
Not far from Firando <note>Modern-day Hirado.</note>, where we had our factories and warehouses before we moved to Nagasaki, lies a small rocky island. It is one of those which, because of their great number, are called by the Japanese *Kiukiu Sima*—that is, the *Ninety-nine Islands*. Although it is very small and surrounded by the sea, this island has been burning and trembling for many centuries. Another small island opposite to *Satzuma* [Satsuma] is called *Fuogo* <note>Portuguese for "Fire."</note> by the Japanese, a name they borrowed from the Portuguese and have retained ever since. It is marked on our maps by the name *Vulcanus* [Vulcan]. This island has a fire-spewing mountain which has likewise been burning at different intervals for many ages. At the top of a mountain in the Province of *Figo* [Higo] can be seen a large cavern, formerly the mouth of a volcano, but the flame ceased recently, probably for want of combustible material. In the same province, there is another place called *Aso*, famous for a temple called *Asa no Gongen*, or the "Temple of the Jealous God of Aso." Not far from there, an almost perpetual flame issues from the top of a mountain, which is more visible at night than during the day. 

Another burning mountain lies in the Province of *Tsikusen* [Chikuzen], not far from a place called *Kujanoffe* [Kuyanose]. It was formerly a coal mine, which accidentally took fire through the carelessness of the miners and has continued burning ever since. Sometimes a black stench and smoke are observed to issue from the top of the famous mountain *Fesi* [Mount Fuji] in the Province of *Suruga*. In height, it is surpassed only by the Peak of Tenerife, but in shape and beauty, I think it has no equal. Its top is covered with everlasting snow which, being frequently blown into flakes by the violence of the wind and dispersed, looks like a "smoking hat." Japanese histories mention that its summit used to burn, but that the flame ceased soon after a new opening was made by the violence of the fire on the side of the mountain. *Unsen* [Mount Unzen] is a deformed, large, but not very high mountain near *Simabara* [Shimabara]. Its top is always bare and whitish from the color of the sulfur, and it resembles a worthless residue <note>original: "Caput Mortuum"; an alchemical term for the useless remains left after a chemical process or distillation.</note> or a burnt-out solid mass <note>original: "Massa"</note>. It smokes little; however, I could discern the smoke arising from it at three miles' distance. Its soil is burning hot in several places and is so loose and spongy that, except for a few spots where trees stand, one cannot walk over it without constant fear because of the cracking, hollow noise perceived underfoot. ## The History of JAPAN. Book I.

The sulfurous smell is so powerful that no birds can be seen for many miles around. When it rains, the water bubbles up, and the entire mountain appears as if it is boiling. Many cold springs and hot baths arise on and around it. Among these is a famous hot bath believed to be an infallible cure for venereal disease <note>Likely referring to syphilis, often called "the pox" in this era.</note>, provided the patient bathes for only a few moments a day over several days. The treatment must begin at another, slightly milder hot bath called *Obamma* <note>Modern-day Obama Onsen in Nagasaki Prefecture.</note>, located a few leagues away. While using the waters, the patient must follow a "warming" diet and, immediately after leaving the bath, go to bed and cover themselves well to encourage sweating.

Not far from this hot bath is a monastery of the *Tendai* sect <term>Tendai: A major school of Japanese Buddhism that emphasizes the Lotus Sutra</term>. The monks there have given specific names to each of the nearby hot springs based on their characteristics—the nature of the froth on top, the sediment at the bottom, or the noise they make emerging from the ground. They have designated these springs as "purgatories" for various types of tradesmen and craftsmen whose professions supposedly relate to the springs' qualities. For example, they "lodge" dishonest beer and sake brewers <note>original: "Sackibrewers"</note> at the bottom of a deep, muddy spring; cooks and pastry-makers are assigned to one known for its white froth; and those who are argumentative or quarrelsome are placed in a spring that rushes from the earth with a terrifying murmuring sound. In this way, by imposing upon the "blind and superstitious" common people, the monks extract large sums of money, convincing them that their prayers and intercession can deliver the deceased from these places of torment. During the horrific persecution of Christians in Japan <note>A reference to the suppression following the Shimabara Rebellion (1637–1638), which took place in this very region.</note>—which has no equal in history—new converts were brought here and tortured with these scalding waters to force them to abandon their new faith and return to the paganism of their ancestors.

Of the other hot baths in Japan, the one called *Obamma* is among the most prominent and effective. It lies about three miles west of Mount *Usen* <note>Mount Unzen.</note> and is said to have extraordinary virtues in curing various external and internal ailments <note>original: "distempers"</note>. Through bathing and sweating, it is used to treat the "pox," though it is observed that the disease frequently returns—likely because the locals are not skilled enough to manage the condition or do not understand the proper medicinal use of baths in general.

The Province of *Figo* <note>Higo Province, modern-day Kumamoto.</note> has several hot springs where, according to my reports, camphor trees <note>original: "Camphire trees"</note> of an uncommon size grow, some being hollow and filled with water. The most significant spring for its healing properties is a hot bath located near the previously mentioned temple of *Asano Gongen* <note>Aso-no-Gongen, the deity of Mount Aso.</note>.

There are also several hot springs in the Province of *Fifen* <note>Hizen Province, modern-day Saga and Nagasaki.</note>, including one in the village of *Takijo* <note>Likely Takeo Onsen.</note> and another in the village of *Urisino* <note>Modern Ureshino Onsen.</note>. Both would prove very beneficial in curing several ailments...

<margin>Sulfur</margin>
The greatest quantity of sulfur <note>original: "Sulphur"</note> is brought from the Province of Satsuma <note>original: "Satzuma"</note>. It is dug up on a small neighboring island, which, due to the great plenty of this substance it affords, is called *Iwogasima*, or the Sulfur Island. It is not above a hundred years since they first ventured there. Before that time, it was thought to be wholly inaccessible because of the thick smoke which was observed continually to arise from it. Due to several specters and other frightful, uncommon apparitions people fancied they saw there—chiefly at night—it was believed to be a dwelling place of devils. This lasted until a resolute and courageous man offered himself and obtained leave to go and examine its state and situation. He chose fifty resolute fellows for this expedition, who, upon going ashore, found neither Hell nor devils, but a large flat spot of ground at the top. This was so thoroughly covered with sulfur that wherever they walked, a thick smoke issued from under their feet. Ever since that time, this island has brought in to the Prince of Satsuma about 20 chests of silver per year <note>original: "per annum"</note>, arising only from the sulfur dug up there, besides what he gets from the trees and timber growing along the shore. The country of Shimabara <note>original: "Simabara"</note>, particularly around the hot baths mentioned above, also affords a fine, pure native sulfur. However, the inhabitants dare not venture to dig it up for fear of offending the protective spirit <term>tutelar genius: a guardian deity or supernatural protector of a specific place</term> of the place, they having found upon trial that he was not willing to spare it. I pass over in silence several other places for want of thorough information.

<margin>Gold</margin>
Gold, the richest of all metals, is dug up in several provinces of the Japanese Empire. The greatest quantity of it is smelted out of its own ore <note>original: "oar"</note>. Some they wash out of gold sand, and a small quantity is also contained in the copper. The Emperor claims the supreme jurisdiction of all the gold mines—and indeed all other mines in the Empire—none of which may be opened and worked without his express leave and consent. Of the produce of all the mines which are worked, he claims two-thirds, and one-third is left to the Lord of the Province in which the mine lies. The latter, however, as they reside upon the spot, know how to improve their third parts so as to share the profits pretty equally with the Emperor. The richest gold ore, which yields the finest gold, is dug up in Sado, one of the northern provinces <note>Sado is an island province off the coast of Honshu.</note> in the great island of Honshu <note>original: "Nipon"</note>. Some of the veins there were formerly so rich that one *catti* <term>catti: a unit of weight used in East Asia, approximately 1.3 lbs or 600 grams</term> of the ore yielded one, and sometimes two *thails* <term>thail: also known as a tael; a weight used for silver and gold currency, roughly 37 grams</term> of gold. But of late, as I was informed, the veins there, and in most other mines, not only run scarcer, but yield not
