For this reason, the Emperor <note>The Shogun.</note> has given strict orders not to work it, for fear that such a great treasure should be exhausted too soon. 

A mountain on the Gulf of **Omura** <note>original: "Ookus, in the district of Omura"</note>, which had leaned to one side for a considerable time, happened some years ago to collapse into the sea. At the bottom of the place where it had stood, a gold sand was found that was so rich that—as I was credibly informed—it yielded one-half pure gold. It lay somewhat deep and had to be recovered by divers. However, this rich harvest did not last long; a few years later, during a great storm and an extraordinarily high tide, the sea overflowed the entire spot and covered these priceless riches with mud and clay to a depth of several fathoms. The poor people in the neighborhood still busy themselves washing the sand around this mountain, which contains some gold, but in such an insignificant quantity that they can hardly make a livelihood from it. 

There is another gold mine in the province of **Chikugo** <note>original: "Tfikungo"</note>, not far from a village called Toffino, but it is so full of water that they cannot continue working it. However, the layout of the mine is such that by cutting into the rock and making an opening beneath the mouth of the mine, the water might be easily drained off. This was attempted accordingly, but as they went to work, there suddenly arose such a violent storm of thunder and lightning that the workmen were forced to stop and fly for shelter. This led the local people <note>original: "superstitious vulgar"</note> to believe that the <term>Tutelar God<note>A guardian deity or spirit of a specific place.</note></term> and protector of the site—unwilling to have the "bowels of the earth" committed to his trust thus rifled—had raised this storm on purpose to show how much he was displeased by the undertaking. No further attempts have been made since, for fear of provoking his anger and wrath still more. 

A similar accident, which had the same effect, happened at the opening of a gold mine on the island of **Amakusa**; it was so suddenly filled with water, which broke out of the mountain and destroyed all the works, that the miners barely had time to escape with their lives.

### Chap. VIII. The History of J A P A N. ###

<margin>*Silver.*</margin>
There are several silver mines in the province of **Bingo** <note>Modern-day eastern Hiroshima Prefecture.</note>. Others, much richer, are located at a place called **Kattami** in one of the northern provinces. There are others in various locations which I will not mention due to a lack of sufficient information. The two islands **Ginsima** and **Kinsima**—that is, "Gold Island" and "Silver Island"—which lie to the east of Japan and which I discussed in the fourth chapter of this book, deserve mention here. This is especially true if the Japanese claims regarding their immense wealth and riches are accurate, as their names and written characters suggest.

<margin>*Copper.*</margin>
Copper is the most common of all metals extracted in Japan, and the output of these copper mines enriches several provinces of the Empire. Today, it is primarily mined in the provinces of **Suruga**, **Atsingo** <note>likely Echigo, modern Niigata Prefecture.</note>, and **Kijnokuni** <note>Kii Province, modern Wakayama Prefecture.</note>. The copper from Kijnokuni is the finest, most malleable, and best suited for craftsmanship of any in the world. That from Atsingo is coarse, and seventy <term>catties<note>A traditional unit of weight; one catty is approximately 1.3 pounds or 600 grams.</note></term> of it must be mixed with thirty catties of the Kijnese <note>Copper from Kii Province.</note> copper to make it workable and fit for use. The copper from Suruga is not only exceptionally fine and without flaws, but it is also infused with a significant amount of gold. The Japanese now separate and refine this gold much better than they did in the past, which has led to great complaints among the refiners and <term>Brahmins<note>Kaempfer likely refers to Indian merchants or metal workers on the Coromandel Coast who previously profited from extracting gold from imported Japanese copper.</note></term> on the **Coromandel Coast** of India. 

There are also copper mines in the province of **Satsuma** <note>original: "Satzuma"</note>, which the Emperor <note>The Shogun.</note> very recently granted permission to work. All copper is brought to **Sakai** <note>original: "Saccai"</note>, one of the five Imperial Towns, where it is refined and cast into small cylinders about a span and a half long <note>roughly 12 inches</note> and a finger thick. As many of these cylinders as equal one <term>picul<note>original: "pickel"; a unit of weight equal to 100 catties, or approximately 133 pounds.</note></term> (125 pounds weight) are packed into square wooden boxes and sold to the Dutch for twelve to thirteen <term>mace<note>original: "Maas"; a unit of currency based on a weight of silver.</note></term> per picul. It is one of the primary commodities the Dutch purchase in Japan, and they maintain a large trade in it. There is also a coarser type of copper cast into large, flat, roundish lumps or cakes; this is much cheaper than the other kind, as it is inferior in quality and appearance. Brass is very scarce in Japan and much more expensive than copper; the calamine stone <note>A zinc ore used to make brass.</note> must be imported from **Tonkin** <note>original: "Tunquin"; northern Vietnam</note> in flat cakes and sold at a very high price.

<margin>*Tin.*</margin>
The province of **Bungo** produces a small amount of tin, which is so exceptionally fine and white that it almost rivals silver. However, there is very little use made of this metal within the country.

<margin>*Iron.*</margin>
Iron is mined only on the borders of the three provinces of **Mimasaka**, **Bitchu**, and **Bizen**. It is found there in very large quantities. It is refined on-site and cast into bars or cylinders two spans long. Japanese merchants buy it at the source and export it throughout the Empire. Its price is similar to that of copper; in fact, iron tools are just as expensive, or perhaps more so, than those made of copper and brass. Household goods, hooks, cramp-irons for buildings and ships, and other tools that are made of iron in other countries, are made in

### The History of Japan. Book I. ###

Old vessels of this kind are highly prized and purchased at great expense; they possess a unique shape and craftsmanship that modern artisans have lost the ability to replicate.

<margin>*Coals.*</margin>
There is no shortage of coal in Japan; it is excavated in great quantities in the province of **Tsikufen** <note>Chikuzen Province, in modern-day Fukuoka Prefecture.</note> near **Kujanisse**, as well as in most of the northern provinces.

<margin>*Salt.*</margin>
Salt is produced from seawater in several coastal provinces. The process is as follows: they enclose a plot of ground and fill it with fine, loose sand, then pour seawater over it and allow it to dry. They repeat this several times until the sand is thoroughly saturated with salt. Then, they remove the sand and place it into a large trough with holes at the bottom. By pouring fresh seawater over it, they allow the brine to filter through the sand. This liquid is then boiled until it reaches a thick consistency, and the resulting salt is heated in earthen pots until it becomes white and ready for use or sale.

<margin>*Agates.*</margin>
<margin>*Jaspers.*</margin>
Various types of agates—some remarkably fine and of a bluish tint resembling sapphires—as well as cornelians and jaspers, are brought from the **Tsugaar** mountains <note>Tsugaru, in the northernmost part of Honshū.</note> located at the northern edge of the great province of **Osju** <note>Mutsu Province.</note>, opposite the land of **Jedo** <note>Likely referring to Ezo (modern Hokkaido), though spelled similarly to the capital, Edo.</note>.

<margin>*Pearls.*</margin>
Pearls, called *Kainotamma* <note>original: "Kainotamma"; from the Japanese *kai no tama*, literally "jewels of the shell."</note> by the Japanese, are found almost everywhere around **Saikokf** <note>Saikoku, referring to the "Western Provinces" or Kyushu.</note> in oysters and various other seashells. Anyone is permitted to fish for them. Historically, the natives placed little value on them until they were informed of their worth by the Chinese, who would pay high prices. Chinese women are very fond of wearing pearl necklaces and other ornaments. 

The largest and finest pearls are found in a small species of oyster called **Akoja** <note>The Akoya pearl oyster (*Pinctada fucata martensii*).</note>, which is similar to the Persian pearl shell. It has much the same shape, with both shells closing tightly; it is about a hand's breadth wide, extremely thin and brittle, and has a black, smooth, and shiny exterior. The interior is somewhat rough and uneven, whitish in color, and glitters like mother-of-pearl. These shells are found only in the waters around **Satzuma** <note>Satsuma Province.</note> and in the Gulf of **Omura**. 

Some of these pearls weigh between four and five <term>condonins<note>Also known as candareens; a traditional East Asian unit of weight for precious metals and gems.</note></term>, and these sell for a hundred <term>colans<note>Likely referring to the Koban, a large oval gold coin.</note></term> each. The inhabitants of the **Riuku Islands** <note>Ryukyu Islands/Okinawa.</note> purchase most of the pearls found near Satzuma, as they trade frequently with that province. Conversely, those found in the Gulf of Omura are sold primarily to the Chinese and <term>Tunquinese<note>People from Tonkin, in modern-day northern Vietnam.</note></term>. It is estimated that they purchase about 3,000 <term>thails<note>Taels; a unit of weight used for silver currency.</note></term> worth of pearls annually. This significant profit led to strict orders recently issued by the Princes of both Satzuma and Omura, decreeing that in the future, these specific oysters should no longer be sold in common markets alongside ordinary oysters, as was previously the custom.

### Chap. VIII. The History of JAPAN. 111 ###

I procured some in private from **Omura** <note>Ōmura, a region in Nagasaki Prefecture</note>, though not without great difficulty. I was told a very extraordinary thing regarding this sort of pearl, and was strongly assured of its truth: that they possess a reproductive quality. It is claimed that when some of the largest are placed into a box filled with a particular Japanese cheek-varnish made from another shell called **Takaragai** <note>original: "Takaragai"; likely the cowry shell, *Cypraeidae*</note> (which I shall describe in another place), one or two "young" pearls will grow on the sides, and when they reach maturity—which takes about three years—they drop off. These pearls, because they are so scarce, are kept in private families as heirlooms, and the owners seldom part with them except in cases of urgent necessity. All of this, however, I report only from hearsay, as I have not seen this specific type of pearl myself.

There is another shell which sometimes yields pearls, found in abundance upon all the Japanese coasts, and called by the natives **Awabi** <note>The abalone, specifically *Haliotis gigantea*</note>. It is a univalve, almost oval in shape, quite deep, and open on one side where it clings to the rocks at the bottom of the sea. It has a row of holes that grow larger as they reach the edge of the shell. The outer surface is rough and limy, frequently with corals, sea-plants, and other shells sticking to it, but the inside has an exquisite, shimmering mother-of-pearl finish. Occasionally, this interior is raised into whitish pearly growths, similar to those observed in the common Persian pearl-shell. A large mass of flesh fills the cavity of this shell; for this reason alone, they are sought after by fishermen, as they are a very good commodity for the market. They use a tool specifically designed to pry them off the rocks to which they stick so closely.

Another shell, the name of which I could not learn, yields a very large pearl that sometimes weighs between five and six **Condonins** <note>A unit of weight used in East Asia, approximately 0.37 grams</note>, but these are of a dirty yellow color, poorly shaped, and worth very little. A fairly good type of pearl is sometimes found growing directly in the flesh of a shell called **Tairaggi** <note>The pen shell or fan mussel, *Atrina pectinata*</note> by the natives. It is found in the Gulf of **Arima**, between **Yanagawa** and **Isahaya**. It is a flat, oblong shell, almost triangular and slightly curved on each side. It is about a span and a half long <note>approximately 13.5 inches</note> and a span broad at its widest point; it is thin, transparent, and polished like horn, but very brittle.

<margin>*Naphtha*.</margin>
**Naphtha**, of a reddish color, called by the Japanese **Tsutsono Abra** <note>original: "Tſutſono Abra"; likely *Tsuchi-no-abura*, meaning "earth oil"</note>, which signifies *red Earth*, is found in a river in the province of **Echigo** <note>original: "Jetſingo"</note>. It is collected in places where the water has little or no current, and the natives burn it in lamps instead of oil.

<margin>*Ambergris*</margin>
Some **Ambergris** <note>A waxy substance produced in the digestive system of sperm whales, highly valued for perfume</note> is found upon the coasts of **Satsuma** and the **Ryukyu Islands**. A much greater quantity comes from the coasts of **Kumano**, as they call them, which refers to the southern coasts of **Kii**, **Ise**, and some neighboring provinces. It is found chiefly in the intestines of a whale which is caught frequently upon the Japanese coasts, called by the natives **Hyaku-hiro** <note>original: "Fiakfiro"; literally "hundred-fathoms fish"</note>, because of the immense length of its intestines, which is...

## The History of JAPAN. Book I. ##

supposed to equal that number of fathoms <note>A fathom is a unit of length equal to six feet, used primarily for measuring water depth or the length of cables</note>. It is found, as I observed, in the intestines of this whale, particularly in the lower guts, mixed with chalky, limy excrements, almost as hard as stone. It is from the hardness of these excrements that they conjecture, upon dissecting the animal, whether or not they are likely to find **ambergris**. The natives have given a very despicable name to this precious commodity—a name, however, becoming the meanness of its origin—for they call it *Kusurano su* <note>original: "Kusurano su"; likely a transcription of *Kujira no kuso*, literally "whale excrement"</note>, that is, *the excrement of whales*. 

The ambergris, as it is torn off by the waves from the bottom of the sea and thrown upon the coasts before it is swallowed by the whales, is a deformed, flat, slimy substance, not unlike a cow-turd, and moreover of a very disagreeable, ungrateful smell. People who find it thus floating on the surface of the water, or lying upon the coasts, take several small pieces and squeeze and press them close together into the form of a round ball, which as it grows dry becomes also more solid and weighty. Others mix and knead it with meal, or flour of rice-husks, by which means they not only increase the quantity but heighten and improve the color. However, ambergris thus adulterated is easily detected; for if you take any quantity and burn it, there will remain a coal <note>a charred residue</note> proportional to the quantity of the material mixed with it. It is observed, besides, that worms quickly infest this spurious sort of ambergris. Others adulterate it by mixing it with a certain powdered rosin <note>resin</note> of a very agreeable scent, but this cheat also is easily discovered; for upon burning a piece of it, the mixture of resin will evidently appear by the very color, smell, and quality of the smoke. 

The Chinese have another way of trying whether it be genuine: they scrape some of it very fine upon hot boiling tea-water; if genuine, it will dissolve and diffuse equally, which the adulterated sort does not. The natives use it only as an ingredient in other well-scented substances, in order, as they say, to fix their volatile smell. In general, they value it but little, and it is owing entirely to the Dutch and Chinese—who would buy it up at any price—that they have now learned to prize it. And yet, everyone is at liberty to take it up where he finds it and to sell it as his own property. During my stay in **Japan**, there was a piece to be sold of 140 <term>Cattis<gloss>A "catty" is a traditional East Asian unit of weight, approximately 1.3 pounds or 600 grams</gloss></term> weight, and of a grayish color. It was too large for any single person to purchase, for which reason they sold it by retail, from sixty to seventy <term>Thails<gloss>A "thail" or "tael" refers to a unit of weight for silver, used as currency</gloss></term> per Catti. I bought some for myself, for about thirty Thails, of that which was blackest. (*A more particular account of the ambergris is inserted in the Appendix.*)

<margin>Minerals not found in Japan.
Antimony. Salarmoniac. Quick-silver. Borax.
Sublimate.
Cinnabar.</margin>
It remains to say something of the Minerals and Mineral substances, which have not as yet been found in *Japan*, and are imported from beyond Sea. *Antimony* <note>A metallic element used in alloys and medicine</note> and *Salarmoniac* <note>Sal ammoniac, or ammonium chloride; used in metalwork and medicine</note> are absolutely wanted, nor are their qualities and uses in the least known to the natives. *Quick-silver* <note>Liquid mercury</note> and *Borax* are imported by the *Chinese*. I met however with two sorts of *Borax*, growing naturally in *Japan*, but they are so thoroughly mix'd with heterogeneous <note>varied or foreign</note> substances, that the Inhabitants don't think it worth their while to pick them up. *Sublimate Mercury* <note>A highly toxic mercury compound used as a disinfectant or in specialized medicines</note> is very much ask'd for by some private People, who will give an extravagant price for it. They use it as the chief Ingredient of a Mercurial water, which is in great vogue among them for the cure of ulcers, cancers, and other cutaneous <note>skin-related</note> diseases. Native *Cinnabar* <note>The bright red ore of mercury</note> is by them given inwardly, in several distempers. The artificial *Cinnabar* they make use of for a colour. Both are imported from *China*. The buying and selling of this Commodity is in the hands of private Merchants, who monopolize it by virtue of Letters Patents <note>Official documents granting exclusive rights</note> from the Emperor. The native *Cinnabar* in general, is of a beautiful red colour, but some of it is so exquisitely fine, that it is sold for more than its weight in Silver.

## C H A P. IX.
### Of the Fertility of the Country, as to Plants.

<margin>Fruitfulness of Japan.</margin>
IT is not in the least surprising, considering either the peculiar happiness of the Japanese Climate, or the industry of its laborious Inhabitants, that the Country affords so large a stock, and such an infinite variety of plants and fruits, both wild and cultivated, as it may deservedly boast of. Most of these their Forefathers, indigent and frugal as they were, used for their food and sustenance. In succeeding ages, as wealth and riches encreas'd, the taste also became more refined, and their tables more sumptuous and magnificent. In this present Chapter, I will take notice only of such Plants as are of a more extensive use, and as to the rest refer the more curious Reader to my *Exotic Pleasures* <note>original: "Amœnitates Exoticæ"; Engelbert Kaempfer’s famous 1712 work documenting the botany and history of the regions he visited</note>, wherein I have given a Catalogue, and begun a more accurate and botanical Description of them.

-># The History of JAPAN. Book I.<-

<margin>Mulberry-Trees.</margin>
Among the trees, the **Mulberry-tree** rightfully holds the most important place. Even though its fruit—both the black and white varieties—is quite tasteless and not suitable for eating, this lack is more than made up for by its incredibly useful leaves, which serve as the primary food for silkworms. It grows throughout most of Japan, but is especially abundant in the northern provinces. In these regions, many cities and villages rely almost entirely on the manufacture of silk for their livelihood, even though the silk produced there is not of the highest quality. The finest and most exquisite fabrics are actually made by exiled high-ranking officials on the island of *Fatfinfo* <note>original: "Fatfinfo"; referring to Hachijō-jima, an island historically used as a place of exile for political prisoners and disgraced nobles</note>. For these exiles, weaving is their main pastime, though they use fine silk imported from abroad to create their work.

<margin>Paper-tree.</margin>
The *Kadsi* <note>The paper mulberry, *Broussonetia papyrifera*</note>, or **Paper-tree**, is a relative of the Mulberry. Although it grows wild throughout the country, it is transplanted and farmed in many places because it is so useful. It is known to grow with astonishing speed and to spread its branches quite wide. It produces a large amount of bark, which is used to make paper, as well as ropes, fuses, fabrics, clothing, and various other items. I have provided a more detailed description of this tree and the very difficult and slow process of making paper from its bark in my book, *Amœnitates Exoticæ* <note>Latin: "Exotic Delights" or "Exotic Pleasures"; Kaempfer's 1712 work on the flora and medicine of the East</note>. (The account mentioned by the author has been included in the appendix of this volume.)

<margin>Varnish-tree.</margin>
The *Urusi* <note>Urushi, the Japanese lacquer tree (*Toxicodendron vernicifluum*)</note>, or **Varnish-tree**, is another of the most noble and useful trees in the country. It produces a milky sap that the Japanese use to varnish—or "japan," as we call it—all their household items, including wooden dishes and plates. This practice extends from the Emperor himself down to the humblest peasant. Even at the Imperial Court and the Emperor's own table, lacquerware sets are preferred over those made of gold or silver. Another type of varnish tree with narrow leaves is called the *Faasi* <note>The Japanese wax tree, *Toxicodendron succedaneum*</note>; it grows wild on hills and mountains. It only yields a small amount of sap, which is of very poor quality, so the locals rarely find it worth the effort to collect. The true *Urusi* is a species unique to this country. It grows in the provinces of *Figo* <note>Higo Province, modern Kumamoto</note> and *Tfikoku* <note>Likely Chikugo Province or the island of Shikoku</note>. However, the variety grown in *Jamatto* <note>Yamato Province, modern Nara</note> is considered the best for use, yielding a higher quality varnish than any other region. 

The Indian varnish tree, which I believe to be the true *Anacardinus* <note>A botanical term referring to the *Anacardiaceae* family, which includes cashews and the marking nut tree</note>, is a completely different tree from the Japanese *Urusi*. In Siam <note>Modern-day Thailand</note>, it is called the *Rack-tree*. It grows and produces fruit in most Eastern countries, but it is noted that it does not produce its milky sap west of the Ganges River—perhaps due to poor soil, or the neglect and ignorance of the locals who do not know how to cultivate it. The largest supply of sap from this Indian varnish tree is brought from the kingdoms of Siam and Cambodia and is sold very cheaply throughout the East Indies. It is even imported into Japan, where the locals use it to lacquer inexpensive items or as a filler in their rarer, high-quality varnishes. (The Japanese Varnish-tree is described and illustrated in *Exotic Delights*, page 792.)

### Chapter IX. The History of JAPAN.

<margin>Bay-trees.</margin>
<margin>Spurious Cinnamon-Tree.</margin>
**Laurels**, or **Bay-trees** of several kinds grow in *Japan*. The variety that bears red berries is a *Cannelifera spuria* <note>Latin: "false cinnamon-bearer"</note>, or rather, because of its stickiness, a *Cassia lignea* <note>Latin: "wood cinnamon"; referring to *Cinnamomum cassia*, which is related to but distinct from "true" cinnamon</note>. It exactly resembles the **Cinnamon-tree** in its shape and the form and texture of its leaves. However, the bark is nowhere near as sweet and pleasant as the bark of the true Cinnamon, having more of the spicy sharpness of a *Costus* <note>An aromatic root used since antiquity in perfumes and medicine</note>. I believe this imperfection is entirely due to the quality of the soil where it grows. I have also observed that the bark of the cinnamon trees from the **Malabar Coast**, **Sumatra**, and **Java** (the latter of which is completely ignored) does not have nearly the same high degree of sharpness or pleasant taste for which the true **Ceylonese** <note>From modern-day Sri Lanka</note> Cinnamon is so highly and deservedly valued. Furthermore, these other varieties tend to lose their aromatic quality quickly, or their sharp, biting particles are so trapped in a sticky substance that they are completely unworthy of even being called "Cinnamon." True cinnamon is expected to produce a fine, pleasant, and fragrant oil, which no *Cassia lignea* <note>wood cinnamon</note> ever will. (*See Exotic Delights, p. 772.*)

<margin>Camphor-tree.</margin>
The **Kusu** <note>The Camphor tree, *Cinnamomum camphora*</note>, or **Camphor-tree**, is also a member of the Laurel family. It bears black and purple berries. Camphor is prepared by the country people in the province of **Satsuma** and on the **Goto Islands** through a simple process of boiling down the roots and wood, which have been cut into small pieces. It is extremely cheap; one can buy 80 to 100 *catties* <note>A traditional unit of weight in East Asia, roughly 1.3 pounds or 600 grams</note> of this Japanese boiled camphor for the price of a single *catty* of the true **Bornean Camphor**. The Bornean variety is said to be a natural substance gathered from the stumps of old camphor trees on the island of **Borneo**, found in cuts made between the bark and the wood. (*The Japanese Camphor-tree is described and illustrated on page 770 and following of the Exotic Delights.*)

<margin>Tea.</margin>
**Tfianoki** <note>Japanese: *Cha-no-ki*; the tea plant, *Camellia sinensis*</note>, which is the **Tea-shrub**, is one of the most useful plants growing in *Japan*. Despite its usefulness, it is only allowed to grow around the borders of rice and cornfields, or in other barren places unsuitable for growing other crops. The common drink of the Japanese is brewed from the larger leaves of this shrub. However, the young and tender leaves are dried, ground into a powder, and mixed in a cup of hot water to create a kind of soup; this is drunk in the homes of the nobility before and after their meals. It is also the custom of the country to offer friends who come to visit one or more dishes of tea, both when they arrive and when they depart. (*A complete description of this shrub, its cultivation, growth, etc., has been included in the Appendix.*)

<margin>Sanfio.</margin>
**Sanfio** <note>Japanese: *Sanshō*; the Japanese prickly ash or Sichuan pepper relative, *Zanthoxylum piperitum*</note> is a medium-sized tree covered in prickles. They use its bark and husks as a substitute for pepper or ginger, and they eat the leaves because of their pleasant aromatic taste. They also eat the *Riches* <note>Likely referring to the seeds or fruit of the plant</note> that grow in the country. (*See Exotic Delights, p. 892, where this tree is described and illustrated.*)

<margin>Fig-trees.</margin>There are three different sorts of **Fig-trees** growing in *Japan*. One is called **Kaki** <note>The Japanese Persimmon (*Diospyros kaki*)</note>; if it may otherwise be called a Fig-tree, it differs from it in several particulars. It grows very plentifully in all parts of the Empire. It is a very ugly, deformed sort of a tree to look at, much like a short, old Apple-tree. It has long oval leaves, without notches <note>meaning the leaf edges are smooth, not serrated</note>. The fruit resembles a reddish Apple both in shape and color, and its fleshy part has the taste of a delicate Fig. The seed is of a hard, and almost stony substance, and not unlike Gourd-seeds. It is no less commendable for its great fruitfulness than it is for its extensive use, for the fruits of it, when dried, afford a pleasant and agreeable food for rich and poor alike. The Chinese preserve them with Sugar. The second sort of Figs is not unlike that which grows with us in Europe, only it grows on a tree with broad, oblong, rough leaves without notches. Our European Fig-tree makes up the third sort. It was brought into the country and planted there by the *Portuguese*. It bears a very large fruit, bigger than ours, and I think better tasted. But it is very scarce. I need not mention anything here of the <margin>Wild Fig-tree.</margin>**Sycomorus**, or **Wild-fig-tree**, because its fruits are not eaten in the country, though it grows there very plentifully. (*The first two sorts of the Fig-tree are described and illustrated on page 803 and following of Exotic Delights* <note>Latin: *Amoenitatum Exoticarum*, Kaempfer’s scholarly work published in 1712</note>.)

<margin>Chestnut trees.</margin>**Chestnut-trees** grow in great plenty in *Japan*, particularly in the Province of **Tfikufen** <note>Chikuzen Province, located in modern-day Fukuoka Prefecture</note>, and they bear Chestnuts much larger and better than ours. Apple-trees, such as we have them in Europe, they know nothing of. Nor have they more than one sort of Pears, of that kind <margin>Pears.</margin>which we call **Winter-pears**. They grow in great plenty and come to an extraordinary size, the smallest weighing seldom less than a pound: But they are not fit to be eaten raw.

<margin>Wallnut-trees.</margin>**Walnut-trees** grow chiefly in the Northern Provinces. In the same provinces grows a certain tall kind of **Taxus** <note>A genus of yew trees</note>, called by the Japanese <margin>Kaja.</margin>**Kaja** <note>The Kaya tree, or Japanese Nutmeg-yew (*Torreya nucifera*)</note>, with oblong nuts enclosed in a fleshy pulp, and not unlike, in size and shape, to the **Arrack-nut** <note>The Areca nut or Betel nut</note>. These nuts are not very agreeable to the taste when fresh, even when taken out of their pulp, for they have something astringent <note>a harsh, mouth-drying quality</note> in them: They taste better when dried. They have a gentle purging quality, which is owing to their sweet oil, and for their many medicinal virtues, they are served at the table along with the dessert. The oil expressed out of these nuts is very sweet and agreeable, and tastes not unlike the oil of sweet Almonds. It is much commended for its medicinal virtues and is also used to dress victuals <note>prepare food</note>. The smoke of the kernels of these nuts is the chief ingredient of the best and most expensive Japanese **Ink**. (*This kind of Taxus is described and illustrated on page 814 of Exotic Delights.*)

Bramble berries.
Raspberries.
Strawberries.
Plums.
Cherry-trees.
</margin>
They plant but few **Vines**, because they observe that the grapes will not easily ripen. **Bramble-berries** and **Raspberries** are not very agreeable to the taste. **Strawberries** are entirely tasteless and are not eaten. With **Peaches**, **Apricots**, and **Plums**, they are plentifully supplied. Of plums particularly, they have two sorts, both different from ours: one white, the other purple, both textured like mulberries and used as ingredients in the pickles they call **Atsiaer**. **Cherry-trees** and the like are kept only for the sake of their flowers; this is also true for some who keep **Apricot** and **Plum-trees**, which they improve greatly by cultivation so that the flowers become as large as roses. In the spring, when they are in full blossom, they afford a most delightful sight around their temples, in their gardens, and along walks, the trees being as thickly covered with flowers as if with snow.

<margin>
Firs.
Cypress-trees.
</margin>
**Firs** and **Cypress-trees** are the most common trees in their woods and forests. There are several different sorts of both. Houses and ships are built of this wood, and it is also used for all sorts of household goods, such as cabinets, trunks, boxes, tubs, and the like. The branches and fallen wood serve for fuel. The common people also burn the nuts and leaves that fall from the trees; by gathering these daily, they keep the ground and roads neat and clean. For the sake of ornament, these trees are planted in rows along the roads and over the ridges of hills and mountains, which makes traveling very pleasant. The natives, as they improve every inch of ground, take care to plant them in sandy and barren places that are good for nothing else. No firs nor cypress-trees may be cut down without permission from the local Magistrate; and lest the felling of them should in time harm their growth, they must always plant young ones to replace those they cut down <note>An early example of sustainable forestry management practiced during the Edo period</note>.

Bambous.
</margin>

A particular sort of **Bamboo** <note>original: "Bambous"</note> grows in the Province of **Omi** <note>original: "Oomi"; the region surrounding Lake Biwa</note>, which the **Dutch** export by the name of **Rattan** <note>original: "Rottang"; a climbing palm used for wicker and canes</note>, and sell for walking-canes. I shall explain elsewhere, how they are fitted for sale. Both **Firs** and **Bamboo** are in great esteem among the Japanese, for their constant verdure; and the superstitious believe, that they have no small influence over the happy occurrences of human life. The Temple-walks, and other holy places, are adorned with them, chiefly upon their festivals and other solemn days: And they make frequent allusions to them in their emblematical and poetical writings, particularly in congratulatory Poems; for they are of opinion, that they will subsist a long while, that common **Bamboo** will stand several hundred years, and that the common **Pine tree**, which they call **Matsu-no-ki** <note>original: "Matznoki"; literally "the pine tree," a symbol of longevity in Japan</note>, will come to the age of a thousand, that then it will bend down its branches towards the ground, as not being able to support itself any longer. And lest the truth of this assertion should be called in question, they show up and down the Country some **Firs** and **Bamboo** of an uncommon size indeed, and pretended long standing. I have seen some extraordinary large ones myself.

<margin>Cypress-trees.</margin>
**Hinoki** <note>original: "Finoki"; *Chamaecyparis obtusa*, a high-quality cypress used in traditional shrine architecture</note>, and **Sugi** <note>original: "Suggi"; *Cryptomeria japonica*, or Japanese Cedar</note> are two sorts of Cypress-trees, yielding a beautiful light whitish wood, but nevertheless of a good substance, and remarkable for this singular quality, that it sucks in no water, and might well pass for **Cedar-wood**. It hath been sometimes forbidden by the Emperor to fell these trees for any use whatsoever. But little regard is had to orders of this kind, particularly in those provinces which are remote from Court, unless there be a very severe punishment put upon transgression thereof. 

<margin>Stinking Maki Tree. Oak. Iron-Tree.</margin>
**Kusa-maki** <note>original: "Ksamaki"; the "stinking maki" or *Podocarpus macrophyllus*</note>, that is a stinking **Maki-tree**, **Shiinoki** <note>original: "Ssinoki"; an evergreen stone oak</note> a sort of **Oak**, and **Yusunoki** <note>original: "Jusnoki"; the Japanese Ironwood or *Distylium racemosum*</note>, that is **Iron-tree**, so called from the uncommon hardness of its wood, are all very common trees. Most Houses are built of the wood of them. **Hachinoki** <note>original: "Fatznoki"; possibly a variety of ash or wood traditionally used for turning bowls</note>, a tree growing about the City of **Isesaki** <note>original: "Jeseri"; a regional center for timber trade</note>, and the root of the **Camphor tree** <note>original: "Camphire-tree"; *Cinnamomum camphora*</note>, afford the best and scarcest wood for cabinets, chests of drawers, and such sort of work, by reason of the curious running of its grain.

Japan I think may vie with most, if not all, known Countries, for a great variety of beautiful plants and flowers, wherewith kind nature hath most liberally and curiously adorned its fields, hills, woods and forests. Some of these they transplanted into gardens, and improved by assiduity and culture to the utmost, and indeed to a surprising degree of perfection. It is foreign to my present purpose to enumerate and to describe all those I met withal during my stay in the Country. I reserve this for another work <note>Kaempfer is referring to his landmark botanical work *Amoenitates Exoticae*, published in 1712</note>, and will here confine myself barely to mention some of the chief.

It hath many beautiful varieties, of which in the Japanese language, copious as it is, there are 900 names, if it be true what the natives report.

<margin>Observations concerning the State of Agriculture in Japan.</margin>
The Japanese are as excellent farmers <note>original: "Husbandmen"</note> as perhaps any people in the world. Indeed, it is not very surprising that they have made great improvements in agriculture, considering not only the extreme population of the Country, but chiefly that the Natives are denied all commerce and communication with Foreigners, and must necessarily support themselves by their own labor and industry. Hence, the Laws on this subject are very specific and strict. Not only the fields and flat country—which are seldom or never turned into meadows or pasture ground—but likewise the hills and mountains afford grain <note>original: "Corn"</note>, rice, peas, legumes <note>original: "Pulse"</note>, and countless edible plants. Every inch of ground is improved to the best advantage, and it was not without great admiration that we beheld, during our journeys to and from the Court, hills and mountains cultivated up to their very tops, including many so steep they are inaccessible to cattle, which would lie wholly neglected in other countries. They are very dexterous and skillful in manuring their ground, which they do in various ways and with many different substances, as I shall have occasion to show in several places of this History. Flat, low grounds are plowed with Oxen; steep and high ones are tilled by Men, and both are manured with human waste <note>original: "human dung"; historically referred to as "night soil," it was a vital fertilizer in Edo-period Japan</note>. As to Rice in particular, which is the main food of the Natives, whatever ground they can conveniently spare and which will allow for its culture is turned into rice-fields. This is particularly true of low, flat land which they can cut through with canals and where they have a command of water, which surprisingly quickens the growth of this plant, as it thrives in a wet, muddy soil. The Japanese Rice is accordingly esteemed the best in all *Asia*, particularly that which grows in the Northern Provinces; this variety will keep for many years, and for this reason they choose to fill their storehouses with it, having first washed it in muddy water and then dried it. All lands must be surveyed every year before they are sown by *Kenmi* <note>original: "Kemme"</note>, as they call them. These are sworn Surveyors who are very proud <note>original: "big"</note> of their skill in geometry and have the privilege of wearing two swords, a right otherwise allowed to none but the Nobility and Soldiers. When the harvest draws near, the lands are surveyed once more, at which time it is calculated what the entire crop is likely to amount to. They do this generally by estimation, but yet with a surprising accuracy, thereby preventing the tenants from cheating their landlords. If the harvest appears to be extraordinary good, they cause a square piece of ground to be cut and threshed, and from that result, they infer the yield for the whole. The Landlords claim *Rokubu* <note>original: "Rokubu," meaning six parts</note>, or six parts in ten, of all the produce of their land—whether rice, grain, wheat, peas, legumes, or other crops—and the tenant, for his trouble and maintenance, keeps *Shibu* <note>original: "Sijbu," meaning four parts</note>, or four parts in ten. Such as hold lands from the Crown give only four parts in ten to the Emperor's Stewards, and the remainder is for themselves. For encourage-

# Chap IX. The History of J A P A N. 121

For the sake of encouragement, those who cultivate untilled ground are allowed the entire crop for the first two or three years. The ground in general is divided into three categories: 1. <term>Sso</term> <note>Jō: the best quality</note>, 2. <term>Tsju</term> <note>Chū: middling quality</note>, and 3. <term>Ge</term> <note>the poorest quality</note>. However, they also allow for intermediate rankings such as <term>Dso no fio</term> <note>Jō-no-jō: superior quality</note>, <term>Dso no Tsju</term> <note>Chū-no-jō: upper-middle quality</note>, and <term>Dso no Ge</term> <note>Ge-no-jō: lower-middle quality</note>. Some consideration is given to the quality of the soil regarding the tax <note>original: "scot"</note>, which varies considerably across different provinces, but generally, the tax amounts to six parts out of ten <note>a 60% tax rate paid to the lord</note>. Among many excellent laws relating to agriculture, they have one stating that whoever does not cultivate his land for the term of one year forfeits his title and possession of it.

<margin>The Five Grains.</margin>
The primary produce of the fields, which contributes most to the sustenance of life, is categorized by the Japanese under the name <term>Gokokf</term> <note>Gokokf: the "Five Grains"</note>. It is by the success of these crops that they estimate the value of the land, the fruitfulness of the year, and the wealth of the owner. They constitute the main dishes at their meals and compensate for the lack of meat, which custom and religion forbid them to eat. The <term>Gokokf</term> are:

<margin>Rice. Sake Beer.</margin>
1. <term>Kome</term>, or Rice. There are several varieties of rice grown in the country. The best sort has no equal even in the East Indies. It is perfectly white, like snow, and so nourishing and substantial that foreigners who are not used to it can eat only a small amount at a time. Boiled to a firm consistency, they eat it at meals instead of bread. From the surplus of their yearly harvest, they brew a type of strong, rich beer called <term>Sacki</term> <note>Sake</note>, though they produce no more than they think their families will need. Foreigners are not permitted to export more rice or beer than the magistrate allows.

<margin>Barley.</margin>
2. <term>Oomuggi</term> <note>Ōmugi</note>, which means "great grain," is what we call barley. They feed their cattle and horses with it; some also use the flour for cooking and making cakes. There is a variety of barley in Japan with purple ears, which, when ripe, serves as a beautiful ornament to the fields.

<margin>Wheat.</margin>
3. <term>Koomuggi</term> <note>Komugi</note>, meaning "small grain," is what we call wheat. It is extremely cheap, and I know of no use for it other than making a particular kind of cake from the flour.

<margin>Soybeans.</margin>
4. <term>Daidfu</term> <note>Daizu</note>, or "great beans," are a type of bean about the size of Turkish peas, growing in the manner of lupins. They are second only to rice in use and importance. From the meal of these beans, they create what they call <term>Midsu</term> <note>Miso</note>, a mealy paste used in cooking much like we use butter. They also make <term>Soeju</term> <note>Shoyu, or soy sauce</note>, which is a type of savory condiment <note>original: "Embamma"</note> eaten at meals to sharpen the appetite. This <term>Soeju</term> is exported by the Dutch and brought even back to Holland. I have described the method of making it in my book <note>original: "Amoenitates Exoticae", Latin for "Exotic Pleasures" or "Foreign Delights"</note> on page 839, where the plant itself is illustrated and described.

<margin>Azuki Beans.</margin>
5. <term>Adfuki</term> <note>Azuki</note>, or <term>Sodfu</term>, which are small beans. These also grow like lupins and are black, not unlike

Lentils, or the Indian <term>Cajan</term> <note>original: "Cajan"; likely the pigeon pea</note>. The flour <note>original: "flower"</note> is baked with sugar into <term>Manju</term> <note>original: "Mansje"; a traditional Japanese steamed cake</note> and other cakes. Besides the several sorts of <term>Five Grains</term> <note>original: "Gokokf"</note> just mentioned, the following plants are included under the same name: <term>Foxtail Millet</term> <note>original: "Awa"; Latin: Panicum Indicum Tabern.</note>, which is a type of Indian corn; <term>Proso Millet</term> <note>original: "Kibi"; Latin: Milium vulgare nostras</note>, or our common millet; <term>Japanese Barnyard Millet</term> <note>original: "Fije"; Latin: Panicum vulgare juba minore semine nigricante, meaning "common panic-grass with a smaller mane and blackish seeds"</note>; and in general all sorts of grain, and <term>beans</term> <note>original: "Mami"</note>, which includes peas and legumes.

<margin>Turnips.</margin>
Turnips grow very plentifully in the country, and reach an exceedingly large size. Of all the produce of the fields, they perhaps contribute most to the nourishment of the locals. However, because the fields are fertilized with human waste <note>original: "dung"</note>, they smell so strong that foreigners, especially Europeans, cannot stand them. The locals eat them raw, boiled, or pickled. Horseradishes, carrots, gourds, melons, cucumbers, <term>eggplants</term> <note>original: "Mala insana", literally "mad apples"</note>, fennel, and some sorts of lettuce, which we cultivate in gardens, grow wild in Japan. The <term>Garden Parsnip</term> <note>original: "Pastinaca Hortensis"</note> is not to be found here. However, wild parsnips grow plentifully everywhere. Parsley, cumin, chicory <note>original: "Succory"</note>, and our common European lettuce are cultivated by the Dutch, as they were previously by the Portuguese, and they thrive remarkably well.

<margin>Great Variety of Plants in Japan.</margin>
Besides the plants I have mentioned so far, there are countless others that grow in the fields, on hills and mountains, in woods and forests, in marshy ground, in barren and uncultivated places, along the sea coasts, and in short, everywhere. Of all these, there are very few that do not provide roots, leaves, flowers, or fruits for the nourishment not only of the common people but even for the refined tables of the nobility. There is a great variety of mushrooms, most of which are eaten. Some indeed are poisonous, and unfortunate accidents happen frequently. The use of certain other plants often leads to similar dangerous consequences, as poisonous ones are sometimes mistaken for wholesome ones by the unlearned. Some, however, they know how to strip of their harmful and venomous qualities.

For instance, from the <term>Konjac</term> <note>original: "Konjakf"</note>, which is a poisonous kind of <term>Snake Lily</term> <note>original: "Dracunculus", or "little dragon"</note>, they prepare a sweet, floury porridge. In the same way, by pressing out the juice and by soaking and boiling the roots of the <term>Bracken</term> <note>original: "Warabi"</note> or fern, of the <term>Lotus</term> <note>original: "Ren"</note> or <term>Egyptian Bean</term> <note>original: "Faba Ægyptiaca"</note> (called by some the <term>Terate</term> flower), as well as what they call <term>Kuzu</term> <note>original: "Kafne"; likely kudzu or arrowroot starch</note>, they make a fine kind of flour. This is very useful in preparing their food, and they also eat it on its own, dissolved in water. Of all the soft submarine plants <note>seaweeds</note>, there is hardly one that the locals do not eat. Fishermen’s wives wash, sort, and sell them, and they are also very skilled at diving for them from the bottom of the sea at depths of twenty to forty fathoms.

# CHAP. X.

## Of the plenty of the Country, as to Beasts, Birds, Reptiles, and Insects.

<margin>Animals of Japan.</margin>
Regarding the Animals of this Country, some are merely Chimerical <note>imaginary or mythical</note>, not existing in nature, nor invented by the Japanese themselves, but borrowed from their Neighbors the Chinese. Of these it will not be improper to give some account, before I proceed to describe those which really exist.

<margin>Chimerical Animals. Kirin.</margin>
The <term>Kirin</term> <note>original: "Kirin"; a mythical hooved creature known in China as the Qilin, often called the "Chinese Unicorn"</note>, according to the description and figure which the Japanese give of it, is a winged Quadruped of incredible swiftness, with two soft horns standing before the breast and bent backwards, with the body of a Horse, and claws of a Deer, and a head which comes nearest to that of a Dragon. The good nature and holiness of this Animal are so great that they say it takes special care, even in walking, not to trample over any plant, however small, nor to injure even the most inconsiderable Worm or Insect that might by chance come under its feet. Its conception and birth require a particular constellation in Heaven, and the birth of a <term>Sesin</term> <note>original: "Sesin"; likely the Japanese word *Seijin*, meaning a sage or holy person of perfect virtue</note> upon earth. A <term>Sesin</term> is a Man endowed by nature with an incomparable understanding and a more than human penetration; a Man capable of diving into the Mysteries of divine and supernatural things, and moreover so full of love towards Mankind as to reveal his discoveries for their common benefit. Famous as such are the two Chinese Emperors <term>Gio</term> <note>original: "Gio"; Emperor Yao</note> and <term>Siun</term> <note>original: "Siun"; Emperor Shun</note>, the memory of whose excellent Government and the great discoveries they made in the knowledge and virtues of Plants will be always dear in that Empire; <term>Koofi</term> <note>original: "Koofi"; Confucius</note> and <term>Moosi</term> <note>original: "Moosi"; Mencius</note>, two Chinese Philosophers; <term>Siaka</term> <note>original: "Siaka"; Shakyamuni, the historical Buddha</note>, an Indian Philosopher and great discoverer of supernatural truths; <term>Darma</term> <note>original: "Darma"; Bodhidharma, the founder of Zen Buddhism</note> in China; and <term>Sotoktais</term> <note>original: "Sotoktais"; Prince Shōtoku Taishi</note> in Japan, both founders of particular Sects and Persons of an unspotted holy Life. (Table IX, Figure 1 is the Figure of this Creature according to the Chinese, and Figure 2 the same according to the Japanese.)

<margin>Suugu.</margin>
<margin>Kaitsu.</margin>
Besides the <term>Kirin</term>, there are two other Chimera's of the four-footed kind: One is called <term>Suugu</term>, represented in Table 9, Figure 3. It is not unlike a Leopard in its shape, but has two soft horns before the breast, bent backwards. The other is called <term>Kaitsu</term>, or <term>Kaifai</term>. This has something of the Fox in its shape, two horns before the breast, another horn in the forehead, and a row of prickles, like the Crocodile, along the back. (See Table IX, Figure 4.)

<margin>The Dragon.</margin>

The History of JAPAN. Book I.

Chronicles and histories of their Gods and Heroes are full of fabulous stories of this animal <note>the Dragon</note>. They believe that it dwells at the bottom of the sea, as its proper element. They represent it in their books as a huge, long, four-footed snake, scaly all over the body like the crocodile, with sharp prickles along the back; however, the head is monstrous and terrible beyond all the rest. The tail of the Japanese Dragon ends in something like a two-edged sword <note>See Plate 9, Figure 5</note>. Some of the Japanese Emperor’s clothing, his coats of arms, scimitars, knives, and the like—as well as the furniture and hangings of the Imperial Palace—are adorned with figures of this Dragon holding a round jewel or pearl in its right fore-claw. The Japanese Dragon has only three claws on each foot, which distinguishes it from the Chinese Imperial Dragon, which is represented with five.

<margin>
Tatsmaki.
Water-Dragon.
</margin>
The <term>Tatsmaki</term> <note>original: "Tatsmaki"; Japanese for "tornado" or "waterspout," here personified as a dragon</note> is another Dragon with a long, watery tail. It is believed that this also lives at the bottom of the sea; by flying up from there into the air, its violent turnings cause what we call a waterspout—a phenomenon very common on the Japanese seas and frequently observed to break toward the coasts <note>See Plate 9, Figure 6</note>.

<margin>Foo Bird of Paradise.</margin>
The <term>Foo</term> <note>original: "Foo"; refers to the Fenghuang, or Chinese Phoenix</note> is an imaginary but beautiful large bird of paradise, closely related to the Phoenix of the ancient Greeks and Romans. It dwells in the high regions of the air. It has this in common with the <term>Kirin</term>: the Japanese religiously believe that it never comes down to honor the Earth with its blessed presence except upon the birth of a <term>Sesin</term> <note>a sage or holy person</note>, or that of a great Emperor, or upon some other such extraordinary occasion. The <term>Foo</term> of the Chinese is represented in Plate 9, Figure 7, and that of the Japanese in Plate 9, Figure 8.

<margin>Animals of Japan.</margin>
So much for the mythical animals. I proceed now to give an account of those which really exist. Considering the size and extent of the Japanese Empire, it is but sparingly supplied with four-footed beasts, whether wild or tame. The former find few desert places where they could increase and multiply or follow their usual shy way of life. The latter are bred only for transport and agriculture. Because the doctrine of <term>Pythagoras</term> regarding the transmigration of the soul <note>The author is comparing Buddhist reincarnation to the beliefs of the Greek philosopher Pythagoras</note> is almost universally accepted, the natives eat no meat. Living as they do chiefly upon vegetables, they know how to use the ground to much better advantage than by turning it into meadows and pastures for breeding cattle.

<margin>Horses.</margin>
To begin with the tame beasts: there are horses in the country. They are generally small, but some of them are not inferior in shape, swiftness, and agility to the Persian breed. They serve for ceremony, for riding, for transport, and for plowing. The best horses come from the provinces of <term>Satzuma</term> <note>Satsuma</note> and <term>Osju</term> <note>Oshū, or Mutsu</note>. A certain breed of small horses from <term>Kai</term> <note>Kai Province</note> is also very highly esteemed.

<margin>Oxen and Cows.</margin>
Oxen and cows serve only for plowing and transport. Of milk and butter, the inhabitants know nothing <note>Dairy products were not part of the traditional Japanese diet during this period</note>.

<margin>Buffles.</margin>
They have a sort of large buffalo of a monstrous size, with humps on the back like camels, which serve only for the carriage and transport of goods,

# Chapter X. The History of JAPAN.

...in large cities. They know nothing of asses, mules, camels, and elephants.

<margin>Sheep and Goats</margin>
Sheep and goats were previously kept by the Dutch and Portuguese at *Firando* <note>original: "Firando"; modern-day Hirado</note>, where the species still survives. They could be bred in the country to great advantage if the natives were permitted to eat the meat or knew how to manage and manufacture the wool.

<margin>Swine</margin>
They have but few swine, which were brought over from China and are bred by the country people in *Fifen* <note>original: "Fifen"; likely Hizen province</note>—not, indeed, for their own use, which would be contrary to their superstitious beliefs, but to sell them to the Chinese. The Chinese come over for trade every year and are great admirers of pork, even though the doctrine of *Pythagoras* regarding the transmigration of souls <note>original: "transmigration of Souls"; the belief that souls move from one body to another after death, often across species</note> has also found a place in China.

<margin>Dogs</margin>
Since the currently reigning Emperor <note>Tokugawa Tsunayoshi, the fifth Shogun (reigned 1680–1709), famously known as the "Dog Shogun" for his extreme animal protection laws</note> came to the throne, more dogs have been bred in Japan than perhaps in any other country, and certainly more than there were before in this Empire. They have masters, but they lie about the streets and are very troublesome to passengers and travelers. By special command of the Emperor, every street must keep a certain number of these animals and provide them with food. There are huts built in every street where they are cared for when they fall sick. Those that die must be carried up to the tops of mountains and hills—the usual burying places—and very decently interred. Under severe penalties, nobody may insult or abuse them, and to kill them is a capital crime, regardless of whatever mischief they do. In such cases, notice of their misdeeds must be given to their keepers, who alone are empowered to discipline and punish them. 

This extraordinary care for the preservation of the dog-kind is the result of a superstitious whim of the currently reigning Emperor, who was born under the Sign of the Dog. (*The reader is asked to note that the Dog is one of the twelve celestial signs of the Japanese, as shall be shown later in Book II, Chapter 2.*) For this reason, he holds the animal in as high esteem as histories report the great Roman Emperor *Augustus Caesar* <note>original: "Augustus Cæsar"</note> held for rams. The natives tell a humorous story on this subject: A Japanese man, while carrying the dead carcass of a dog to the top of a mountain for burial, grew impatient and cursed the Emperor’s birthday and his whimsical commands. His companion, though sensing the justice of the complaints, told him to hold his tongue and be quiet. Instead of swearing and cursing, he told him to return thanks to the gods that the Emperor was not born under the Sign of the Horse—because in that case, the load would have been much heavier! Greyhounds and spaniels are missing here. They hunt very little, and only with common dogs, as this kind of diversion is not very suitable for such a populous country with so little game.

They have a particularly beautiful kind of cat, which is a domestic animal with them just as it is with us. They are of a whitish color with large yellow and black spots, and have very short tails, as if it had...

## The History of JAPAN. Book I.

It was a common misconception among early travelers that these cats' tails were docked, rather than being a natural genetic trait.</note>. They do not care for catching mice but love dearly to be carried about and caressed, mostly by women.

<margin>Four-footed wild beasts.</margin>
Regarding four-footed wild beasts, the country produces *deer*, *hares*, and *boars*, all of which the followers of certain sects are permitted to eat at certain times of the year.

<margin>Deer.</margin>
The island of *Mijofima* <note>original: "Mijofima"; modern-day Itsukushima, popularly known as Miyajima</note>, or *Akino Mijofima*, so named due to its proximity to the province of *Aki*, is famous for a particular breed of deer which are said to be very tame and familiar with the inhabitants. It is against the laws of the country to chase or kill them. The local people take great care to remove any dead carcasses from their houses and fields, because the Governor of the island is empowered by another law to sentence those before whose doors or upon whose ground such carcasses are found to several days of labor, either at the temples or for the public works.

<margin>Monkeys.</margin>
They have a few *monkeys* of a docile kind, with short tails and a brownish-dark color, having naked red faces and backs. A street performer showed one throughout the country which he claimed was 106 years old and which performed several clever tricks with great skill.

<margin>Bears.</margin>
They have a few *bears* in the northern provinces, though they are of a small variety.

<margin>Tanuki.</margin>
The *Tanuki* <note>original: "Tanuki"; the Japanese raccoon dog, a common figure in folklore</note> is a very singular kind of animal of a brownish-dark color, with a snout not unlike a fox’s and quite small. In other respects, it seems to be of the wolf species.

<margin>Wild Dogs.</margin>
They likewise have a sort of *wild dog* with large, gaping snouts.

<margin>Itutz.</margin>
The *Itutz* <note>original: "Itutz"; likely the *itachi* or Japanese weasel</note> is a small animal of a reddish color.

<margin>Tin.</margin>
Another larger variety of it is called the *Tin* <note>original: "Tin"; the *ten* or Japanese marten</note>. Both live in houses and lodge themselves under the roofs; they are so tame that they might be ranked among the domestic animals. They are very skilled at catching fowl, especially chickens, as well as fish.

<margin>Rats and Mice.</margin>
The whole country swarms with *rats* and *mice*. The rats are tamed by the natives and taught to perform several tricks. Rats trained in this way are a common diversion provided by some poor people. The best of their kind, which play with the most skill, are to be seen at *Osacca* <note>original: "Osacca"; modern-day Osaka</note>, as it is the place where street performers, jugglers, and peep-show operators gather from all parts of the Empire.

<margin>Foxes.</margin>
*Foxes* <note>original: "Foxes"; *kitsune* in Japanese</note> are also very common. The natives believe they are possessed by the Devil, and their historical and sacred writings are full of strange accounts of several odd accidents that happened involving foxes. The fox-hunters, however, are very expert in "conjuring" and stripping this "possessed devil," as the hair and fur are very much desired for making writing and painting brushes. They make the same distinction between the *Kis* <note>original: "Kis"; likely from *kitsune* (fox)</note> or *fox*, and the *Oni* <note>original: "Oni"; a demon or ogre</note> or *devil*, as they do in *Sweden* between *Faan* and *Dieblen* <note>original: "Faan, and Dieblen"; the Swedish terms 'Fan' and 'Djävulen' for the Devil</note>. *Japan* is entirely free of tigers, panthers, lions, and other such predatory animals.

### Chapter X. *The History of* JAPAN.

<margin>
White Ants.
</margin>
Among the insects, the one known all over the *East Indies* <note>Historically, this term referred to South and Southeast Asia, including India and the Malay Archipelago.</note> by the name of *white ants* <note>These are termites, which are not true ants but were often categorized as such by early naturalists due to their social behavior.</note> claims the first place. It is a small, slender worm, perfectly white like snow. They live together in a community, just as our *European* ants do, whom they do not much differ from in shape and size. Their head and breast are of a brownish dark color and hard to the touch. The *Japanese* call them *Do Toos* <note>original: "Do Toos"; likely referring to *dōtōshi*, meaning "borers" or "piercers."</note>, which is as much as to say, *Piercers*, a title which they very well deserve; for they pierce and bore through whatever they meet with, except for stones and metal ores. When they once get into a merchant’s warehouse, they are able within a very short time to ruin and destroy his best goods. Nothing has been found yet that will keep them off, except for salt laid under and spread about the goods. Our common *European* ants are their mortal enemies, and whatever place one group takes possession of, the others must necessarily leave. They are no more able than *moles* to endure the open air; whenever they go out on an expedition, they defend themselves by building arches or trenches all along their path, which they know how to secure firmly to the ground. These arches are made of much the same substance as *wasps' nests*. I was told surprising and melancholy stories of their quick and destructive marches. However, I will only relate what I was an eyewitness to myself. During my stay at *Coylang* <note>modern-day Quilon or Kollam, a port city in Kerala, India</note>, a Dutch fort upon the coasts of *Malabar*, I had an apartment assigned to me in the Governor’s own house. One night I did not go to bed until about midnight, having been very busy. The next morning, when I rose, I noticed the marks of such arches upon my table, which were about the thickness of my little finger. Upon a more careful inspection, I found that these animals had pierced a passage of that thickness up one leg of the table, then across the table (though, as good luck would have it, without any damage done to the papers and things I had left there) and then down again through the middle of the other leg into the floor. All of this was performed within a few hours. Some attribute the cause of such quick and surprising corrosion to the sharpness of their excrement, but wrongly, as I found upon examination; for I noticed that their snouts were armed with four sharp, crooked pincers, which in my opinion are instruments far more suited to do such quick execution than any excrement, no matter how sharp or corrosive it might be.

<margin>
Mukade
Forty-legs:
</margin>
The *Mukade* <note>original: "Mukadde"; the Japanese word for centipede.</note>, according to the common *Japanese* dialect, and *Goko* <note>original: "Goko"; likely the reading of the Chinese characters (wǔgōng) used for centipede in formal Japanese writing.</note> in their symbolic or character language, are not what we call *wood-lice* <note>original: "Aselli"; Latin for 'little asses,' a common historical term for wood-lice or pill bugs.</note>, but the *Indian millipedes*, *caterpillars*, or *forty-legs* <note>centipedes</note>. This is a worm of about two or three inches in length, slender, of a brown color, having a great number of legs on both sides, from which it has borrowed its name. These *Indian forty-legs* are very venomous, and their bites are reckoned more dangerous and painful than those of the *scorpion*. There are but few in *Japan*, and those are not very mischievous—

<margin>Lizards.</margin>
The **Lizards** of this country do not differ from our common *European* lizards.

<margin>Snakes. Fitakutz.</margin>
There are but few **Snakes** in the country. One of the most famous is called <term>Fitakutz</term> <note>Likely *hitakuchi*.</note>, and <term>Fibakari</term> <note>Literally "only for the day," referring to the belief that one dies within the day of being bitten.</note>. It is of a green color, with a flat head and sharp teeth. It has borrowed its name from the length of the day, or the time the sun stays upon the horizon, because people bitten by it are said to die before sunset. Soldiers are very fond of its flesh, which they eat, firmly believing that it has the virtue of making them bold and courageous. This snake, calcined <note>Reduced to a powder through heat.</note> in an earthen pot hermetically sealed, produces that powder which they call <term>Gawatsio</term>, and which is very famous for its virtues in curing several internal distempers <note>illnesses or ailments.</note>. This same powder, put under the gutters of a house, is said in a short time to produce young snakes of the same kind. I met with this sort of snake nowhere else but upon the coasts of <term>Malabar</term> <note>The southwestern coast of India.</note>, where I was shown some by the <term>Bramines</term> <note>Brahmins, the priestly caste of India.</note>.

<margin>Jamakagats.</margin>
Another sort of snake of a monstrous size, called <term>Jamakagats</term> <note>*Yamakagashi*, a species of venomous keelback snake.</note>, or according to the common dialect <term>Uwabami</term> <note>A term for a giant snake or python.</note>, and sometimes <term>Dsja</term> <gloss>Dragon</gloss>, is found in waters and upon mountains. It is very scarce, and when taken, is shown about for money. (*See Table X. Figure 2.*) From the reptiles I proceed to the birds.

<margin>Tame Fowl.</margin>
Of **tame fowl**, they keep chickens and sometimes ducks. However, being—as I noted above—imbued with the <note>Kaempfer uses "Pythagoras" as a Western shorthand for Buddhist beliefs in reincarnation and the sanctity of life.</note> superstitious notions of **Pythagoras**, the majority of people will not eat them. They are killed and sold to those who do venture to eat them only by persons of a mean extraction <note>People of low social status, often referring to the *Eta* or *Burakumin* classes who handled animal remains.</note>. When a man lies at the point of death, and also upon those days which are sacred to the memory of deceased persons, none of their relations and friends may kill any bird or beast whatever. In the mourning years for the death of an Emperor, and at any other time when the Emperor thinks fit to order it, no living creature whatever may be killed or brought to market in any part of his dominions.

<margin>The Cocks.</margin>
**The Cocks** often find pardon more than hens and are kept alive with great care because they are held in high esteem, chiefly among the religious orders, due to their measuring the time and foretelling future changes of the weather.

<margin>Wild Fowl. Crane.</margin>
**Wild fowl**, though naturally shy, have grown so familiar in this populous country that many kinds of them might be ranked among the tame. The <term>Tsuri</term> <gloss>Crane</gloss> is the chief of the wild birds of the country and has this particular **Imperial Privilege**: that nobody may shoot him without an express order from the Emperor, and only for the Emperor's own pleasure or use. In <term>Saikokf</term> <note>The island of Kyushu.</note>, however, and in other provinces remote from the Court, a less strict regard is had for such Imperial commands. The **Cranes** and **Tortoises** are reckoned very happy animals in themselves and are thought to portend good luck to others; this is because of their pretended long and fabulous life, of which there are several remarkable instances recorded...

### Chapter X. The History of JAPAN.

<margin>Cranes.</margin>
...in their historical writings. For this reason, the Imperial apartments, the walls of temples, and other auspicious places are commonly adorned with figures of them, alongside depictions of fir trees and bamboos for the same reason. I never heard the country people or carriers call this bird anything other than <term>O Tsurisama</term> <note>Original: "O Tsurisama"; an honorific title meaning "The Honorable Lord Crane."</note>, which translates to "My Great Lord Crane." There are two different kinds of them: one is as white as snow, and the other is grey or ash-colored. 

<margin>Herons.</margin>
There are several kinds of <term>Sagi</term> <note>Japanese for herons.</note>, or herons, which differ in color and size. The primary ones are the <term>Shiro Sagi</term> <note>White Heron.</note>, the <term>Goi Sagi</term> <note>Grey or Night Heron.</note>—both of which are very common—and the <term>Aoi Sagi</term> <note>Blue Heron.</note>, a bluish heron that is almost as large as a crane. 

<margin>Wild Geese.</margin>
There are two different types of wild geese, which each mate with their own kind. One sort is as white as snow, except for the tips of the wings which are black; the other is grey or ash-colored. Both are very common in this country, particularly the grey ones, and they are so familiar with humans that they might be mistaken for tame birds; they do not fly up or move out of the way when anyone approaches. They cause a great deal of damage in the fields, yet no one is permitted to disturb or kill them under penalty of death, except for those who have purchased the specific privilege to shoot them in certain areas of land. To keep them away, the country people surround their fields with nets, though this is largely ineffective as I have personally seen them fly over the nets to reach their food.

<margin>Ducks.</margin>
<margin>Kinmodsui, a beautiful Duck.</margin>
There are also several different kinds of ducks, and they are as tame as the geese. I cannot help but mention one kind in particular because of the surprising beauty of the male, called the <term>Kinmodsui</term> <note>Likely the Mandarin Duck (*Aix galericula*).</note>. Its beauty is so striking that when I was first shown a color illustration of it, I could hardly believe my own eyes until I saw the bird itself, as it is quite common. (*See Table X. Figure 3.*) Its feathers are wonderfully varied with the finest colors imaginable, particularly around the neck and breast, which are primarily red. The head is crowned with a most magnificent crest. The tail rises at an angle, and the wings stand up over the back in a very singular fashion, providing a sight as curious as it is uncommon.

<margin>Pheasants.</margin>
<margin>Woodcocks.</margin>
<margin>Wild Pigeons.</margin>
There are also pheasants of uncommon beauty. One kind in particular is remarkable for the varied colors and luster of its feathers and for the beauty of its tail, which is half the length of a man. In its curious variety and mixture of the finest colors—chiefly blue and gold—it is in no way inferior to a peacock. Woodcocks are a very common bird; they are eaten by the followers of certain religious sects, as are pheasants, geese, and ducks. There is also a type of wild pigeon with black and blue feathers, though they are otherwise not particularly beautiful. The natives will not allow them to nest in their houses because they have found through experience that their droppings, when moved, are very likely to catch fire; they say that many an unfortunate accident has happened because of this.

<margin>Storks.</margin>
Storks remain in the country all year round.

### The History of JAPAN. Book I.

<margin>Falcons.</margin>
The best falcons are caught in the northern provinces and are kept more for display and status than for actual sport.

<margin>Hawks.</margin>
<margin>Ravens.</margin>
Hawks are common here, as they are throughout the East Indies. They are very proud birds, as is a certain kind of raven of medium size. This raven was first brought over from China as a gift for the Emperor.

<margin>Korean Raven.</margin>
Another rare bird was sent over from <term>Korea</term> <note>Original: "Corea."</note> as a gift to the Emperor and is therefore called <term>Coreigaras</term> <note>Original: "Coreigaras"; likely from the Japanese *Kōrai-garasu*, meaning "Korean crow."</note>, which means "Korean Raven."

Our common European crows, as well as parrots and various other Indian birds, are not found in Japan.

<margin>Hototogisu, a night bird.</margin>
The <term>Hototogisu</term> <note>Original: "Foken" or "Fototenis"; the Lesser Cuckoo, a bird highly celebrated in Japanese poetry for its nocturnal song.</note> is a rare night bird with an excellent and delicious flavor. It is a dish reserved only for the tables of high-ranking nobility on extraordinary occasions. It is said that the calcined ashes of this bird, when added to old, sour <term>sake</term> <note>Original: "Sacki"; Japanese rice wine.</note>, can restore its original taste and quality. (*See Table X, Figure 4.*)

<margin>Osprey.</margin>
The <term>Misago</term> <note>Original: "Misago" or "Bisago"; the Osprey or sea hawk.</note> is a greedy sea bird of the hawk family that preys mainly on fish. It makes a hole in rocks along the coast to store its prey and supplies. It has been observed that this fish remains as well-preserved as if it were in <term>pickles</term> <note>Original: "Atjaar"; a term for pickled preserves used in the East Indies.</note>; for this reason, it is called <term>Misago-zushi</term> <note>Original: "Eisagonosusi"; literally "Osprey's sushi," referring to the naturally fermented fish found in their nests.</note>. It tastes very salty and is sold at a high price. Anyone who discovers such a cave can make a significant amount of money from it, provided they do not take too much at once. (*See Table X, Figure 5.*)

<margin>Gulls, etc.</margin>
Gulls, cormorants, snipes, oystercatchers, sparrows, swallows, and several other small birds are as common here as they are in Europe.

<margin>Larks.</margin>
Larks sing much better here than they do in Europe.

<margin>Nightingales.</margin>
Nightingales with particularly fine voices are sometimes sold to enthusiasts for as much as twenty <term>koban</term> <note>Original: "Cobangs"; large, oval gold coins.</note> each. This concludes my observations regarding the birds of this country.

<margin>Flying Insects. Bees.</margin>
Regarding flying insects, the country has bees, and consequently produces some honey and wax, though only in small quantities. Humble-bees, wasps, common flies, gnats, fireflies, several types of beetles and bugs, as well as locusts and a great variety of other insects of this type, are common here as in Europe. However, there are also some unique and remarkable varieties, the most important of which I will describe briefly.

<margin>Butterflies.</margin>
Among the butterflies, there is a very large variety called <term>Yama-cho</term> <note>Original: "Jamma Tsio"; literally "Mountain Butterfly."</note>. It is either entirely black or multicolored, beautifully patterned with white, black, and other spots, especially on its forked wings. The <term>Komori</term> <note>Original: "Komuri."</note> is a large, spotted, multicolored, hairy, and beautiful nocturnal moth. This same name is also given to bats.

<margin>Beetles.</margin>
They have several rare and beautiful kinds of beetles. One in particular is very large and shaped somewhat like a dung fly; it is a shining black with two crooked, branched horns, with the larger one positioned over—
