<margin>Cicadas, a kind of beetle-like insect.</margin>
A certain kind of brown beetle called <term>Sebi</term> <note>Original: *Sebi* or *Semi*; the Japanese name for the cicada.</note> affords several curious and remarkable things to the attentive eye of an inquisitive naturalist. They are of three different kinds. The largest is called <term>Kuma Sebi</term> <note>Original: *Kuma Sebi*, meaning "Bear Cicada."</note> (*Table X. Figure 6. A. B.*). It resembles in shape and size that sort of fly which we in Europe generally observe flying about in the evening, but it has no wings. In the spring, they creep out of the ground (where they have lain in winter quarters) during the night, and fasten themselves with their sharp, hairy legs to trees, branches, or leaves, or whatever they can lay hold of in their march. A little while after, they burst and split their backs length-wise to make room for another fly, not unlike a beetle, which was enclosed within it—though it is much bigger than the prison to which it was confined. Some hours later, this second fly flies away with a hurried noise. This curious little animal has been described by <note>Conrad Gessner (1516–1565), a Swiss physician and naturalist known as the father of modern zoology.</note> Gesner by the name <term>Cicada</term> <note>Original Latin: *Cicada*.</note>. Bursting open the shell in which it lay, and at the same time spreading out its four wings, it makes a sharp and loud noise, which they say—though it is almost incredible—may be heard very distinctly at a full English mile’s distance. Woods and mountains are full of the noise these little creatures make. They disappear gradually during the <term>Dog Days</term> <note>The hottest period of the summer, usually between July and August.</note>, and it is said that they creep into the ground again in order to undergo a new <term>metamorphosis</term> <note>Original: *Metamorphoſis*; a biological process of transformation from an immature form to an adult.</note> or change, and to re-appear in the same state the next year. How far this agrees with the truth, I am not able to determine for want of proper observations. The name *Semi* or *Sebi*, which they bear, is borrowed from their music, which begins slowly and on a low tune, then increases gradually in speed and loudness, and ends quite low again. This music, I thought, was not unlike the noise a button-maker's spindle makes while turning. They begin to sing with the rising sun and end about noon. The <term>cast-off shells</term> <note>Original Latin: *Exuviæ*.</note> called <term>Semi no Mukigara</term> <note>Original: *Semi no Mukigara*; literally "cicada's empty shell."</note> are preserved for medicinal uses and sold publicly in shops both in Japan and China. (*Table IX. Figure 6. C. D. E.*) Another smaller kind is, because of its size, called <term>Kosebi</term> <note>Original: *Koſebi*, meaning "Small Cicada."</note>, or the small *Sebi*. (*Table X. Figure 6. F. G. H. I.*) They appear later in the year, right around the time when the others disappear. They sing from noon to sunset and live until late in autumn. Their music is not nearly as loud as that of the first kind and is called <term>Tsuku Tsukuboo</term> <note>Original: *Tſuku Tſukuboo*; likely the *Meimuna opalifera*, known for its distinctive "tsuku-tsuku-boushi" call.</note> by the common people. The third kind differs from the second neither in shape nor size, only they sing from morning to night. The females of all three kinds are mute and have their breasts closed; in all other respects, they are like the males. (See *Table X. Figure 6. K. L.*)

<margin>Singular Night-fly.</margin>
But the finest of all the flying tribe of insects—and which, by reason of its incomparable beauty, is kept by the ladies among their curiosities—is a peculiar and scarce night-fly <note>Commonly identified as the *Tamamushi* or Jewel Beetle (*Chrysochroa fulgidissima*).</note>. It is about a finger long, slender, and round-bodied, with four wings. Two of these are transparent and hidden under a pair of outer wings which are shining, as if polished, and most curiously adorned with blue and golden lines and spots. The following fable owes its origin to the unparalleled beauty of this little creature: They say that all other night-flies fall in love with it, and to get rid of their importunities, it maliciously bids them (as a trial of their constancy) to go and fetch fire. These blind lovers do not hesitate to obey the command, and flying to the nearest fire or candle, they never fail to burn themselves to death. The female is not nearly so beautiful as the male, being grey or ash-colored and spotted.

## C H A P. XI.
### Of Fish and Shells.

<margin>Productions of the Sea.</margin>
The sea and its productions contribute just as much toward the sustenance of the natives as the crops grown on land, with the exception of rice. The sea all around *Japan* is plentifully stored with all sorts of underwater plants, fish, crabs, and shells. There are very few of these that were not eaten by their impoverished ancestors, and they continue to be eaten to this day. There are even many which, in these wealthy and refined ages, appear upon the sumptuous tables of people of the highest quality. Both fish, crabs, and shells are comprehended under one general name, <term>Kiokai</term> <note>original: "Kiokai"; a general term for marine animals.</note> or <term>Iwokai</term> <note>original: "Iwokai"; a collective term for fish and shellfish.</note>. In this present chapter—which may be looked upon as an introduction to a later one where I intend to treat of their dining customs and kitchens—I will set down as many of them as came to my knowledge, along with their true *Japanese* names. It must be observed in general, however, that several of them are also found in our European and other seas.

<margin>Whales.</margin>
Of all the animal productions of the *Japanese* seas, I know of none with such an extensive use for both the rich and the poor as the <term>Kudsuri</term> <note>original: "Kudsuri"; the modern Japanese term is *kujira*.</note>, or whale. It is caught frequently about *Japan*, but particularly in the Sea of <term>Khumano</term> <note>original: "Khumano"; the Kumano-nada sea area off the Kii Peninsula.</note>, which washes the southern coasts of the great island of <term>Nipon</term> <note>original: "Nipon"; referring to Honshu, the main island of Japan.</note>, as

also around the Islands of *Tsushima* and *Goto*, and along the coasts of *Omura* and *Nomo*. <margin>How they are caught.</margin> The common method of catching them is with darts or harpoons <note>original: "harping-irons"</note>, similar to the techniques used in the *Greenland* fishery. However, the *Japanese* boats seem better suited for this purpose than ours; they are small, narrow, and taper to a sharp point at one end. They are manned by ten men who use five oars to row with incredible speed. Around 1680, a wealthy fisherman in the province of *Omura* named *Gitaijo* developed a new method of catching whales using nets made of strong ropes approximately two inches thick. This method was later adopted with great success by a countryman in the *Goto* Islands named *Iwonomo*. They say that as soon as a whale finds its head entangled in a net, it cannot swim further without great difficulty and can then be easily killed with harpoons in the usual manner. The reason this new method—which seemed very promising—has not been universally adopted is that it requires a much larger and more expensive set of equipment <note>original: "Tackle"</note> than the average fisherman can afford. While the expense of whale fishing in the common manner seldom exceeds 20 chests of silver, this net method cannot even be attempted for a lesser sum.

<margin>Different sorts of Whales. Sebio.</margin> There are several types of whales, which differ in name, shape, and size. 1. The <term>Sebio</term> <note>Likely the North Pacific Right Whale (*Eubalaena japonica*).</note> is the most significant and indeed the largest of the whale kind. It yields the most whale oil <note>original: "Train-oyl"; oil rendered from whale blubber.</note>, and its flesh is considered very good and wholesome. In fact, fishermen and common people attribute their good health—despite constant exposure to the hazards of cold and weather—chiefly to eating this meat. 2. <margin>Awo Sangi.</margin> The <term>Awo Sangi</term>, commonly called <term>Kokadsura</term> (meaning a small whale), is gray or ash-colored and smaller than the *Sebio*, from which it also differs slightly in shape. 3. <margin>Nagass.</margin> The <term>Nagass</term> <note>Likely a Fin Whale or Blue Whale.</note> is commonly 20 to 30 fathoms <note>A fathom is approximately 6 feet (1.8 meters), making this whale 120 to 180 feet long, though this may be a historical exaggeration.</note> long. It is not a very large species, seldom exceeding ten fathoms in length. It is caught frequently around *Japan*, but its flesh is considered unwholesome; they say it is too "hot" for the body, causing coughs, fevers, skin eruptions, and sometimes smallpox. It is brought to market with other fish and sold as *Sebio* meat, but those who know better will never buy it. 5. <margin>Mako.</margin> The <term>Mako</term> <note>The Sperm Whale (*Physeter macrocephalus*).</note> never exceeds three or four fathoms in length. Indeed, I saw one myself on our journey to the Shogun's Court, between *Kaminoseki* and *Shimonoseki*, and I took it to be the fish which the Dutch call the *Noord Caper* <note>original: "Noord Caper"; a Dutch name for the North Pacific Right Whale.</note>. Of all these various kinds of whales, nothing is thrown away as useless, except for the large shoulder bone. The skin, which is black in most species; the flesh, which is red and looks like beef; and the intestines—which are called <term>Fiakfiro</term> <note>original: "Fiakfiro"; from the Japanese *hyakuhira*, meaning "one hundred fathoms," referring to their immense length</note>—are all eaten, whether pickled, boiled, roasted, or fried. Even the internal organs are consumed. The fat, or blubber, is boiled down into train oil <note>A common historical term for whale oil used in lamps and industry.</note>, and even the leftovers from the second boiling are eaten. The bones that have a cartilage-like substance are boiled while fresh and eaten, or otherwise scraped clean and dried for kitchen use. From the nervous and tendinous parts, both white and yellow, they manufacture cords and ropes used chiefly in cotton manufacturing and for the strings of their musical instruments. Not even the offal is thrown away, but is kept for various kitchen uses. Several small items are fashioned from the jawbones, fins, and other solid bones; notably, their fine steelyards <note>A type of portable balance scale.</note> for weighing gold and silver are made from them, and they have even borrowed their name from the whale.

<margin>*Satsifoko*</margin>
The <term>Satsifoko</term> <note>Likely referring to the *shachihoko*, which can represent a killer whale or a mythical creature with a tiger's head and fish's body.</note> is a fish two, three, and sometimes five to six fathoms long. It has two long teeth or tusks standing upward out of its mouth. These are sometimes used as ornaments on the roofs of castles, temples, and public buildings. I was informed by fishermen that this fish is a cunning and mortal enemy of whales, and that it kills them by creeping into the whale's mouth and devouring its tongue. As it creeps in, it has a way of positioning its head and teeth so that they do not hinder its movement.

<margin>*Iruku*</margin>
The <term>Iruku</term> <note>Japanese for dolphin (*iruka*).</note> is a well-known fish, called *Tenije* in the East Indies (Table XI. Figure 1).

<margin>*Furube*</margin>
The <term>Furube</term> <note>The pufferfish, known today in Japan as *fugu*.</note> is another fish, not very large (Table XI. Figure 2). The Dutch call it the *Blazer* <note>Dutch for "blower."</note>, because it can blow and swell itself up into the shape of a round ball. It is ranked among the poisonous fish, and if eaten whole, it is said to cause unavoidable death. There are three different sorts found in great plenty in the Japanese seas. The first sort, called <term>Susumebuka</term>, is small and rarely eaten. The second is called <term>Mabuku</term>, which means the "true puffer." The Japanese consider this a very delicate fish and are very fond of it. However, the head, guts, bones, and all the offal must be thrown away, and the flesh carefully washed and cleaned before it is fit to eat. Even so, many people die from it, allegedly due to a lack of thorough washing. People who are weary of life after long and tedious illnesses, or who are otherwise in miserable circumstances, frequently choose this poisonous fish as an alternative to a knife or a rope to end their lives. A neighbor of my servant in Nagasaki, who was so severely infected with the pox <note>A common historical term for syphilis.</note> that his nose was about to drop off, resolved to take this meal to rid himself of both his life and his disease at once. <margin>Sea-Horse.</margin>
The **Sea Horse**, or **Sea Dog**, and, as the Germans call him <term>Water-belly</term> <note>original: "Waſſer-bauch"</note>, is a very singular fish, much about the length of a Boy of ten years of age, without either scales or fins, with a large Head, mouth and breast, a large thin belly like a bag, which will hold a large quantity of water. He hath thin sharp teeth in the chops much like a snake. The inner parts are so minute, that they are scarce visible. He hath two flat cartilaginous feet with fingers, not unlike the hands of a child, under the belly, by the means of which, he creeps, in all likelihood or walks at the bottom of the Sea <note>This description likely refers to a type of Anglerfish or Monkfish, known for their "walking" pectoral fins and large, expandable stomachs.</note>. All his parts are eaten, none excepted. He is caught frequently in the Gulf of *Edo* <note>original: "Jedo"</note>, between *Kamakura* and that Capital, where I saw him brought to market.

<margin>Suzuki</margin> **Suzuki** <note>original: "Sufuki"; modern: Sea Bass</note> is what the Germans call a **baldhead** <note>original: "Kahlkopf"</note>. (*Table* XI. *Figure* 3.)

<margin>Funa</margin> **Funa** <note>Crucian Carp</note> is a fish similar to a carp, and much praised for its medicinal virtues, especially against intestinal worms.

<margin>Koi</margin> **Koi** is another sort of carp which sometimes grows to a length of one and a half <term>shaku</term> <note>A Japanese unit of length approximately equal to one foot; original: "Sacks" or "Saks"</note>. <margin>Masu</margin> **Masu** <note>original: "Maar"; Trout or Salmon</note>, the salmon, is taken in rivers and freshwater lakes.

<margin>Itoyori</margin> **Itoyori** is a "salmonet," or small salmon <note>Actually the Golden Threadfin Bream, but Kaempfer identifies it by its salmon-like appearance</note>.

<margin>Makutsu</margin> **Makutsu** is what the Dutch call a **mullet** <note>original: "Harder"</note>.

<margin>Sawara</margin> **Sawara** <note>Spanish Mackerel</note> is a "king's-fish."

<margin>Hiuwo</margin> **Hiuwo** <note>Icefish or "Thread-fish"</note> is what the Dutch call a **thread-fish** <note>original: "Draatvisch"</note>.

<margin>Ara</margin> **Ara** <note>Grouper; *Table* XI. *Figure* 5</note> is what the Dutch in the East Indies call a **Jacob Evertsen** <note>A name given by Dutch sailors to various species of grouper or snapper; original: "Jacobs Ewertz"</note>.

<margin>Kusuna</margin> **Kusuna**, a "short-nose." **Kamasu** <note>original: "Kamas"</note>, a **pike** <note>Barracuda</note>.

<margin>Suzuki</margin> **Suzuki** <note>original: "Sufuki"</note> is the **shear-fish** <note>original: "Schaarvisch"</note> of the Dutch, only a longer and narrower variety.

<margin>Aji</margin> **Aji** <note>original: "Adsi"</note> is the **horse mackerel** <note>original: "Maasbancker"</note> of the Dutch. There are several different kinds of this, the largest and most important of which is called **O-aji** <note>original: "Ooadsi"; literally "Big Aji"</note>. (*Table* XI. *Figure* 6.)

<margin>Taka</margin> **Taka** is what the Dutch call a **ray** <note>original: "Kaye"</note>.

<margin>Kame</margin> **Kame** and **Takafame** <note>original: "Takafame"; (*Table* XI. *Figure* 7.)</note> are **rays** or **skates**. <margin>Ei</margin> **Ei** <note>original: "Jeje"</note> is a broad, flat fish with a long tail. The Japanese believe that this sting, if taken from a live fish, is a certain remedy against snake bites if the wound is rubbed with it. For this reason, they keep it among their other household medicines.

<margin>Ei</margin> **Kome** <note>possibly a regional name for rays</note> or **Ei** <note>original: "Jei"</note> are **soles**.

<margin>Karei</margin> And **Karei** are **flounder** or **turbot** <note>original: "Bots" or "Bruts"</note>.

<margin>Bora</margin> **Bora** <note>Grey Mullet</note> is a fish much like a pike, with white and delicious flesh. Some call it the **New Year's fish** <note>original: "Songaats Fish"</note> because it is caught in **Shogatsu** <note>original: "Songaats"</note>, the first month of the Japanese year. They pickle and smoke them, just as pikes are prepared in **Bremen**.

<margin>Karasumi</margin> These and all pickled fish in general are called **Karasumi** <note>original: "Karafumi"; usually refers specifically to dried mullet roe</note>. They are exported from **Nagasaki** and **Nomo** <note>Coastal areas in Kyushu</note>, where they are frequently caught, and carried to **Edo** <note>modern-day Tokyo; original: "Jedo"</note> and other parts of the empire, tied to straw ropes with ten fish to a rope. They are also exported by the Dutch and Chinese. Other fish prepared as *Karasumi* are not highly valued by the locals.

<margin>Katsuo</margin> The best variety of the **Katsuo** fish <note>Skipjack Tuna; original: "Katfuwo"</note> is caught near the **Goto** Islands. They cut this fish into four pieces, which they dry slowly over the steam of boiling water. This is served at the table alongside liquors. The Dutch export it under the name **Comblomaas** <note>Kaempfer's name for *Katsuobushi* (dried bonito); original: "Comblomaas"</note>, though that is not its true name.

<margin>Managatsuo</margin> **Managatsuo** <note>Silver Pomfret; original: "Managatfuwo"</note> is a flat fish, similar to a **butt** <note>a flatfish like a turbot or halibut</note>, with one eye on each side of its head.

<margin>Sake</margin> **Sake** <note>Salmon</note>, perhaps a type of **cod** <note>original: "Cablian" from the Dutch "Kabeljauw"</note>, is a pickled fish not unlike cod. It is imported from the land of **Ezo** <note>modern-day Hokkaido; original: "Jeso"</note>.

<margin>Tortoises.</margin>
Of all the footed animal produce of the water, the **Ki**, or **Kame**, **Tortoises**, are most esteemed by the Japanese, being looked upon as peculiar Emblems of happiness, by reason of the long life which is ascribed to them.

<margin>Emblematical Tortoise.</margin>
That kind particularly, which hath a broad tail much like a large round beard, and which in their learned language <note>Referring to the Sino-Japanese or classical reading.</note> is called **Mooke** <note>original: "Mooke"; likely *Minogame* in scholarly context</note>, and by the common people **Minogame** <note>Literally "straw-raincoat turtle," referring to old turtles with long strands of algae growing on their shells, resembling a traditional Japanese raincoat.</note>, for all it doth not exist in nature, is yet frequently to be seen among other emblematical figures, wherewith they adorn the walls of their temples, the sides of their altars, and the apartments of the Emperor and Princes of the Empire. (*Table XIII. Figure 3. 4.*)

<margin>Sea Tortoise.</margin>

### Chapter XI. The History of JAPAN.

<margin>
Hermit Crab.
Horseshoe Crab.
</margin>
The shelled and crustacean animals found in these seas—and indeed throughout the Indian Ocean beyond the eastern shores of the Ganges—are observed to be meatier and fuller during the new moon, which is the opposite of what occurs in our European seas. **Gamina** <note>Plate 13, Figure 7</note>, otherwise called **Koona**, is a crab that lives in a beautiful shell decorated with various colors. <note>This is what is commonly known as the Soldier Crab or Hermit Crab, so named because they occupy the shells of other creatures.</note> **Kani**, which signifies "pocket crab," is our common European freshwater crab; it is the name used for the entire family of freshwater crabs. **Kabutogani** <note>Literally "helmet crab"; the horseshoe crab.</note>, or **Unkiu**, is a crab of a unique structure, featuring a sharp, long, jagged spike or spine protruding from its head and a rounded, smooth back <note>Plate 13, Figure 8</note>. **Gadsame** is no larger than a common crab, with an upper shell that tapers into a point on both sides. It has four claws: two large ones in the front and two smaller ones in the back <note>Plate 14, Figure 1</note>. **Simagani**, which means "striped pocket-crab," might also be called the "wart-crab" due to the many warts and prickles covering its shell, except for the back claws, which are smooth and nearly cylindrical <note>Plate 14, Figure 2</note>. They are frequently caught on the eastern coasts and in the Gulf of Suruga. Some of this species are incredibly large; I once bought one of the hind claws in a cook-shop in Suruga that was as long and as thick as a man's shinbone <note>Plate 14, Letter A, represents it at life size</note>.

<margin>
Oysters and Shells.
Abalone.
</margin>
All varieties of oysters, mussels, and shells—of which there is a great abundance and a surprising variety in the Japanese seas—are eaten without exception, whether raw, pickled, salted, boiled, or fried. They are gathered daily along the coasts at low tide. Divers plunge to considerable depths for them, while others catch them with nets. The following sorts are the most common and well-known: **Awabi** <note>The abalone</note>, which I mentioned previously regarding the country's pearls, is an open univalve <note>A mollusk with a single-piece shell.</note> about the size of a medium Persian pearl shell, but deeper <note>Plate 14, Figure 3</note>. These lie deep underwater, clinging tightly to rocks or the sea floor. They are harvested by the fishermen’s wives, who are the most skilled divers in the country. They descend armed with darts or long knives to defend themselves against sharks <note>original: "Kayes"</note> and porpoises. When they spot an **Awabi**, they must pull it off suddenly before the animal is aware; otherwise, it would fasten itself to the rock so strongly that no force could tear it away. This shell is filled with a large piece of flesh, yellowish or whitish in color, with a very tough consistency and no visible fibers. It is said that this was the primary food of their impoverished ancestors; in memory of this, when the Japanese host guests for dinner, they always provide a dish of it. It has also become a custom among both commoners and the nobility that when they send presents of money, cloth, fruit, or other goods, a string—or at least a small piece of the dried flesh of this shell—is sent along <meta>catchword: along</meta>

## The History of JAPAN. Book I.

...along with them, as a good omen and to remind them of the humble origins <note>original: "Indigency"</note> of their ancestors. <note>This refers to the Japanese tradition of "Noshi," where strips of dried abalone (awabi) are included with gifts to symbolize sincere intentions and respect for the simple life of their forefathers.</note> The flesh is cut into thin slices or strips, which are stretched on a board and dried. A large pearl is sometimes found in this shell, but it is of an unattractive yellowish color, misshapen, and of no value.

<margin>Tairagi.</margin>
The *Tairagi* <note>The Pen Shell or Fan Shell</note> is a flat, long, thin, and very large bivalve. It is almost transparent and roughly triangular in shape, tapering from a wide base to a point. The animal is firmly attached to both sides of the shell by a strong tendon. (*Plate 14, Figure 4.*) The best of this kind are found in the Gulf of Arima, where they occasionally produce pearls.

<margin>Akoja.</margin>
The *Akoja* <note>The Japanese Pearl Oyster</note> is a flat bivalve about a hand-breadth wide. It has a scaly, unattractive exterior, but the inside possesses an exquisite, shimmering mother-of-pearl luster. The finest of this species, which produce the highest quality pearls, are found in the Gulf of Omura.

<margin>Mirakai.</margin>
The *Mirakai* is the common black freshwater mussel, similar to those found <margin>Famaguri.</margin> in the rivers and lakes of Germany. The *Famaguri* <note>The Hard Clam or Hamaguri; Plate 14, Figure 5</note> are bivalves of a similar shape and size but are thicker, smooth and white on the inside, and brown or chestnut-colored on the outside. Various beautiful figures are painted on the inside of these shells, and they serve as an amusement for the Court of the *Dairi* <note>The hereditary Emperor in Kyoto, whom early European writers called the "Ecclesiastical" or "Spiritual" Emperor to distinguish him from the Shogun</note>. They play with them in the following manner: large heaps are thrown onto the ground, and after everyone in the group has taken their portion, the winner is the one who can show the most matching pairs. Every pair has specific hinges <note>original: "hooks"</note> by which they are easily identified and reunited, no matter how much they are mixed up. The best are gathered in great abundance on the coasts of Kuwana <note>original: "Quano"</note>.

<margin>Sidfimi. Katsi.</margin>
The *Sidfimi* <note>The Shijimi or Corbicula clam</note> is a small bivalve similar to the *Famaguri* but thinner; it is found buried in the mud. *Katsi*—or *Utsikaki*—are oysters. The oysters found around Japan are misshapen, rough, and stony, often growing together in clusters or onto rocks. There are mainly two types: one remarkably large and the other smaller. The best and largest are found in great numbers in the Gulf of Kamakura.

<margin>Kisa.</margin>
The *Kisa*, or *Akagai* <note>The Ark Shell</note>, is also a bivalve, white on the outside with deep parallel furrows and reddish on the inside. (*Plate 14, Figure 6.*) The Japanese attach a handle to this shell and use it in the <margin>Nakatagai.</margin> kitchen as a spoon or a scoop. The *Nakatagai* is a large, unattractive, roundish, and black shell with ridges. The *Asari* <note>The Manila Clam</note> is a small, thin shell of a grey or <margin>Te.</margin> ash color. The *Te* or *Matee* <note>The Razor Clam; Plate 14, Figure 7</note> is an oblong, thin bivalve that remains open at both ends. The creature living inside it is consid- <margin>Umi Take.</margin> ered a great delicacy. The *Umi Take* <note>Literally "Sea Bamboo"; a type of Pholad clam</note> is another bivalve of a similar kind, about a span long and so thick that one can barely grasp it between the thumb and forefinger. Its flesh is pickled and preserved for food. This shell is found only on the coasts of Chikugo <note>original: "Tsikungo"</note>, where, by the express order of the Prince of that province, fishing for them is forbidden until a sufficient quantity has been secured for the Emperor’s own table.

<margin>Takaragai. Cowries.</margin>
The *Takaragai*, called *Cowries* in the Indies, are brought from the Maldives and other islands and imported into Bengal, Bago <note>original: "Pegu"</note>, and Siam, where they are used as legal currency. Those found around Japan come in several different sorts.

<margin>Nisi.</margin>

<margin>Tannisi.</margin>
Common people use these shells as spittoons <note>original: "Pots to spit in"</note>. The *Tannisi* <note>Japanese River Snails or Mud Snails</note> are common black land snails gathered for food from the muddy rice fields. Their openings are closed with an oblong, almost stony lid.

<margin>Bai.</margin>
The *Bai* <note>Japanese Whelk, *Babylonia japonica*</note> is a snail with a common, oblong, spiral white shell.

<margin>Ras.</margin>
The *Ras*, also called the *Mina*, is another of the same kind, but it is black and smaller. Both are gathered along the shore during low tide.

<margin>Kabuto.</margin>
The *Kabuto* <note>Likely a Limpet; "Kabuto" means "helmet" in Japanese, reflecting the shell's shape</note> is a small, oval shell that is not spiral-shaped.

<margin>Sugai.</margin>
Another small, spiral-shaped shell is called the *Sugai*.

<margin>Sasai</margin>
The *Sabi* <note>Likely the *Sasai* or Turban Snail, *Turbo sazae*; see Plate 14, Figure 9</note> is a large, thick, and fragrant spiral-shaped shell <note>original: "turbinated univalve"</note>, white and covered in speckles. <margin>Nishi</margin>
There is another single-shelled creature of much the same shape but larger, though its meat is not of such good quality. Both of these can attach themselves very firmly to rocks and the seabed, much like *Limpets*. Common people often use these large shells as spittoons <note>original: "Pots to spit in"</note>.

<margin>Tanishi</margin>
The *Tsunai* <note>Likely *Tanishi*, the Japanese river or mud snail</note> are common black snails gathered for food from the muddy rice fields. They are found in both small and large varieties and have a nearly thorny lid <note>original: "operculum"</note>.

<margin>Bai</margin>
Another variety, found in a more common, oblong, spiral white shell, is the *Bai* <note>The Japanese whelk, *Babylonia japonica*</note>.

<margin>Kai or Naki</margin>
The *Kai* or *Naki* is another similar kind, but it is black and smaller. Both are gathered on the shore during low tide.

<margin>Mina & Sugai</margin>
The *Mina* is a small, oval, non-spiral shell. Another small spiral-shaped shell is called the *Sugai* <note>Likely *Lunella coreensis*</note>.

<margin>Eras of the Japanese.</margin>
To better understand the opinion of the Japanese regarding the original state of their country—which formerly they looked upon as the only inhabited part of the earth—and the succession of their Emperors and Monarchs down to this present time, I have thought it fit to divide the History and Chronology of this Empire into three eras: a fabulous, a doubtful, and a certain.

<margin>The first and legendary Era.</margin>
The first and legendary <term>epoch|A particular period of time in history or a person's life</term> of the Japanese Government reaches far beyond the time of the Creation, as fixed in Sacred writs <note>This refers to the Biblical chronology of the world, typically dating creation to around 4004 BCE in the 17th century</note>. Japan, they say, was during that period of time governed by a succession (or rather an evolution) of seven Celestial Spirits or Gods, which are by them called
<margin>Succession of Seven Spirits.</margin>
*Tenjin Shichidai* <note>original: "Ten Dsin Sitzi Dai"; literally "the seven generations of heavenly gods"</note>, that is, *the seven great Celestial Spirits*, each of which reigned for an immense, but undetermined number of years. The History of the Japanese Gods is full of strange, wonderful adventures and great bloody wars, which are said to have happened in this first Age of the Japanese World. The two Chronological Authors, whom I have followed

These figures succeeded the first gods in the government of Japan. Being five in number, they are called

<margin>The second succession of five Demi-Gods.</margin>

<margin>*Tenseo Dai Sin.*</margin>
1. **Ten Se O Dai Sin** <note>Also known as Amaterasu, the Sun Goddess and central deity of Shinto</note>, the eldest son and heir of *Isanagi Mikotto*. For his memory, and that of his brothers and descendants, the Japanese still maintain a most profound respect and veneration. He is said to have reigned for 250,000 years. During his reign, they say China was governed by *Ten Kwo Si*, to whom they also attribute a long and legendary rule, further mentioning that three descendants of his family successively ruled the Empire of China.

<margin>*Osiwo Ni.*</margin>
2. **Osiwo Ni no Mikotto** lived and reigned for a total of 300,000 years. During his reign, and during the reign of his successor up to the beginning of the fourth Japanese Terrestrial God, *Sat Teiki* governed the Empire of China.

<margin>*Ni ni ki.*</margin>
3. **Ni ni ki no Mikotto** reigned for 318,533 years. Throughout his entire reign, *Sat Teiki* remained the Emperor of China.

<margin>*Awase Dsu.*</margin>
5. The fifth and last of these demi-gods was **Fuki Awa se dsu no Mikotto**. He reigned for 836,042 years. Thus, the total span of time during which this race of god-men governed Japan amounts to 2,342,467 years. This is all the Japanese know of the ancient state and government of their empire—a tradition which some of the wiser people among them realize is subject to great doubt and uncertainty, if not entirely legendary and imaginary. However, all Japanese people, without exception, maintain a special veneration for *Isanagi* and his consort *Isanami*, viewing them as the ancestors of their nation—their own version of Adam and Eve. The right which the family of the <term>Ecclesiastical Hereditary Emperors|The Mikado or Tennō; the spiritual and theoretical head of Japan</term> claims to the crown and government of Japan—which they have enjoyed undisturbed through a succession of many ages—is based upon a direct descent from *Ten Seo Dai Sin*, the first-born son and heir of *Isanagi*. <margin>The second and uncertain Era of the Japanese.</margin>
I proceed now to the second and uncertain era <note>original: "Aera"</note>. Little is known about the state of these countries or the lifestyle of the inhabitants from the beginning of the Creation (when, according to the description of the great lawgiver Moses, the Supreme Being called this globe of our Earth out of nothing and formed it, by his infinite power, into a state entirely suited to his divine goodness and wisdom) until the time of their first monarch Jimmu <note>original: "Sin Mu Ten Oo"; Jimmu Tennō, the legendary first Emperor of Japan</note>, whose reign begins quite late, within 660 years of the birth of our Savior. It is highly probable that in those early times, the people lived scattered throughout the country in nomadic groups <note>original: "hoords"</note>—much like the Scythian <note>ancient nomadic people of central Eurasia</note> inhabitants of Great Tartary <note>a historical term used by Europeans for North and Central Asia</note> do to this day. They were separated from the rest of the world by a rocky and tempestuous sea that surrounds their islands, living in a state of nature and freedom, without a settled form of government and lacking in arts and sciences. The neighboring Empire of China was already very powerful at that time; arts and sciences flourished there and were eventually brought over into Japan by the Chinese. It was due to this influence that the Japanese in time became polite and civilized. It is not unlikely that, in imitation of their neighbors—who provided them with the concept of a monarchical government—they submitted more cheerfully when Jimmu began to reign over them, especially since this Prince was descended from a family so beloved and held so sacred among them. Meanwhile, so that such a significant span of time would not remain empty in their chronological records, they have filled the vacancy with the names of the most eminent monarchs who sat on the throne of China after the death of Katsurakuki <note>likely referring to a legendary Chinese figure or dynasty branch</note> and the five descendants of his family.

<margin>Emperors of China before Jimmu. Fohi.</margin>
The first Chinese Emperor mentioned in this second era is Fuki, and by his full title *Tai Ko Fuki* <note>The Chinese pronounce it Fohi, also known as Fuxi, a culture hero in Chinese mythology</note>. According to some, this Prince had the body of a serpent, or according to others, the head of one, combined with a most sublime understanding. He discovered the motions of the heavens and the twelve celestial signs <note>the zodiac</note>, and divided time into years and months. He invented many other useful arts and sciences besides, and shared them with the world for the common benefit of mankind. The Chinese consider him their first Emperor and the founder of their monarchy. Many among them claim that from his reign down to the present age, they can show an accurate history of their Empire and a true chronological succession of their Emperors—records which, before his time, had been very doubtful and mythical. However, according to one of my Japanese historians, he began to reign 20,446 years before Jimmu <note>original: "Synmu"</note>, or 21,106 years before Christ—which is many thousand years before the

<margin>Shennong <note>original: "Sin Noo"</note></margin>
The second Chinese Emperor was *Shennong* <note>original: "Sin Noo"</note>, (the Chinese pronounce it *Xin Num*, or *Sijnnum*,) and with his full title *Yandi Shennongshi* <note>original: "Jen Tei Sin Noo Si"; meaning Flame Emperor of the Shennong clan</note>. This illustrious Prince, like another Egyptian *Serapis* <note>a Greco-Egyptian deity of the sun and fertility, often associated with the grain supply</note>, taught mankind agriculture, and those arts which relate to the support of our Life. For this reason he is by some represented with the head of an Ox, by others only with two horns placed on his forehead. He also discovered the virtues of several Plants, and communicated them to the world in a treatise he wrote on this subject, which was doubtless the first Herbal <note>a book containing the names and descriptions of plants with their properties</note> that ever was written. His Picture is held in high esteem among the Chinese. The Physicians particularly have it hung up in one of the best apartments of their houses, with a plant or leaf in his mouth, on which he smells. He reigned 140 years, and was succeeded by seven descendants of his family, who reigned 380 years; so that the Empire continued in this family 520 years.

After the demise of the last Emperor of the family of *Shennong*, *Huangdi* <note>original: "Kuo Tei" or "Hoam Ti"; the Yellow Emperor</note>, and with his full title *Huangdi Youxiongshi* <note>original: "Hon Tei Juu Hin Si"; referring to his lineage from the Youxiong clan</note>, came to the Crown. The Chinese Historians unanimously agree, that this Prince reigned in China. Those who call the existence of the preceding reigns in question, begin the History and Chronology of the Chinese Empire with the reign of *Huangdi*. He began to reign in the year before *Jimmu* 2029, before Christ 2689, or according to Father *Couplet*, whom Dr. *Mentzelius* <note>Christian Mentzel (1622–1701), a German physician and botanist who studied Chinese language and medicine</note> accurately follows, 2697. He was but eleven years old when he came to the Crown. During his minority the Empire was governed by wise and prudent Councilors, who took great care to give the young Monarch an education becoming so great a Prince, and to instruct him in all the useful arts and sciences then known. The Chinese stand indebted to this Emperor for the art of feeling the pulse, which he learned himself from his Tutors, and afterwards commanded that it should be published to the World. # Chapter I. The History of JAPAN.

<margin>*Tei Gio* <note>Emperor Yao (traditionally r. 2356–2255 BCE), one of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors of ancient China.</note></margin>
Of the five Princes who succeeded *Hoam Ti* <note>Huangdi, the Yellow Emperor</note>, *Tei Gio*—or *Ti Jao* according to the *Chinese* pronunciation—was the most illustrious. He was a great *Sefin* <note>Likely a corruption of the Japanese *Sennin* or Chinese *Zhenren*, meaning an enlightened sage or immortal</note>, which is to say, a man incomparably well-versed in the occult arts and sciences. He was also a very virtuous Prince and a true "Father of his Country." His death was universally lamented by all his subjects, who went into mourning for three years. He ascended to the throne in the year 1697 before *Synmu* <note>Jimmu Tennō, the legendary first Emperor of Japan; his reign is the benchmark for the Japanese "Kōki" calendar</note>, which corresponds to 2357 BCE. He reigned for 72 years and died during the reign of his successor at the age of 118. Although he had twelve children—ten sons and two daughters—he instead delivered the Crown and the government of the Empire to an honest and wise farmer, to whom he had married his two daughters.

<margin>*Tei Sjun* <note>Emperor Shun, the successor to Yao, famous for his filial piety.</note></margin>
*Tei Sjun* (also called *Gu*, or according to the *Chinese*, *Ju Ti Sjun* or *Ju Ti Xun*) was the son-in-law and successor of *Ti Jao*. He reigned for twenty-eight years alongside *Ti Jao*, and thirty-three years alone, totaling sixty-one years. My source places the beginning of his reign in the year 1634 before *Synmu*, which is 2294 BCE. During his reign, a great Deluge occurred in *China*, which overflowed many provinces and drowned a great number of inhabitants. Parts of the country remained underwater for several years afterward.

<margin>*Uu* <note>Yu the Great, the legendary founder of the Xia Dynasty.</note></margin>
*Uu*, known by his full title as *Katewu*—meaning Emperor *Uu* of the *Ka* family (or as the *Chinese* pronounce it, *Ju* of the *Hia* <note>The Xia Dynasty</note> family)—reigned for seventeen years with Emperor *Tei Sjun* and ten years after his death, totaling twenty-seven years. He was crowned in the year 1573 before *Synmu*, or 2233 BCE. This Emperor ordered canals and sluices to be cut to drain the waters that had overflowed a great part of *China* during the reign of his predecessor and lead them down to the sea. Through these efforts, deep rivers were formed, and the country was freed from the floods. He lived for one hundred years and was succeeded by eleven descendants of his family, who reigned for 431 years; thus, the crown remained with this family for 458 years. The last ruler of this family was famous for his extraordinary physical strength, but he grew to be a great tyrant to his subjects. He lived with such extravagance that he ordered two thousand men to dig a lake and fill it with *Chinese* Beer <note>likely referring to *huangjiu* or rice wine</note>. It is also said that he built a tower of gold and precious stones for one of his mistresses. He was eventually deposed and banished in the 52nd year of his age.

<margin>*Sioo Sei Too* <note>Tang of Shang, the founder of the Shang Dynasty.</note></margin>
*Sioo Sei Too*, which is to say King *Too* of the *Sioo* family (or as the *Chinese* pronounce it, King *Tam* of the *Ksjam* <note>The Shang Dynasty</note> family), came to the throne in the year 1106 before *Synmu*, or 1766 BCE, at the age of eighty-seven. He reigned for thirteen years and died in his hundredth year. During his reign, there was a great famine in *China* that lasted seven years, much like the famous *Egyptian* famine mentioned in Holy Scripture. He was succeeded by twenty-seven princes of his family, who reigned for a total of 631 years; therefore, the Empire remained with this family for 644 years. The last Emperor of this family was a great tyrant,

## C H A P. II.

->*Of the Ecclesiastical Hereditary Emperors of* Japan *in general, of their Succession, Residence, and Court; as also of the Chronology of the Japanese.*<-

<margin>Third Era of the Japanese <note>original: "Third Aera of the Japaneſe"</note></margin>
THE third and last Era <note>original: "Epocha"</note> of the Japanese Monarchy, which is that of their *Great Divine Lineage of Kings* <note>original: "Oo Dai Sin Oo"</note>, or Ecclesiastical Hereditary Emperors, begins with the year 660 before Christ. This was the seventeenth year of the reign of the Chinese Emperor *Hui* <note>original: "Kaiwo" or "Huivam"</note>, who was the seventeenth Emperor of the *Zhou* <note>original: "Sjeu"</note> family. From that time to the year of Christ 1693, one hundred and fourteen Emperors, all of the same family, sat successively on the Throne of Japan.

<margin>The ancestry of the Japanese Emperors <note>original: "Japaneſe Emperors, whose Offspring"</note></margin>
They value themselves extremely upon being the eldest branch of the family of the *Great Divinity who Illuminates the Heavens* <note>original: "Tensio Dai Sin"; the sun goddess Amaterasu</note>, that most sacred founder of the Japanese Nation, and the lineal issue of her first-born son, and so down. Uncommon respect, and a more than human veneration, is on this account paid them by their subjects and countrymen. # Chap. II. The History of JAPAN.

...some preliminary account of their sacred Persons and Court, as also of the Chronology of this Empire, whereby the succession of the Emperors must be calculated.

---

<margin>
Titles of the Ecclesiastical Emperors of Japan.
</margin>
And here it must be observed in the first place, that these <term>Ecclesiastical hereditary Monarchs <note>Early European visitors, like Kaempfer, used "Ecclesiastical" to describe the Emperor (Tenno) because his role was primarily ritual and sacred, while the Shogun held political power.</note></term>, though they are heirs to the throne and government of their divine predecessors, have not inherited the title of *Mikotto* <note>original: "Mikotto"; modern: *Mikoto*</note>. This title is reserved only for the divine and semi-divine beings of the first and second successions <note>This refers to the legendary "Age of the Gods" in Shinto mythology.</note>. Instead, they are called *Mikaddo* <note>original: "Mikaddo"; modern: *Mikado* (御門), literally "The Honorable Gate"</note>, which is a lesser version of *Mikotto*. They are also known as *Dai*, *Oo*, *Kwo*, and *Tai* <note>These are different readings for titles such as "Great," "King," "Emperor," and "Imperial."</note>, all of which signify an Emperor, a Prince, or a great Lord. They are likewise called *Tensin* <note>original: "Tensin"; modern: *Tenshin*, meaning "Sons of Heaven"</note>, and many more titles of a similar nature have been given to them. In common conversation, they are frequently called *Dairi* <note>original: "Dairi"; literally the "Inner Palace," used here to refer to the Emperor himself</note>, a name which properly refers to their entire Court; for this reason, he is also sometimes called *Kintsiusama* <note>modern: *Kinshū-sama* (禁中様), the "Lord of the Forbidden Center"</note>. When the Emperor speaks of himself, he assumes the title of *Tsin* <note>original: "Tsin"; modern: *Chin* (朕), the royal "We"</note>, and when he signs his name, he uses *Maro* <note>original: "Maro"; an archaic first-person pronoun used by the nobility.</note>.

<margin>
Their right to the Throne.
</margin>
But to come closer to our purpose: it was about the time mentioned previously that the Japanese—who had until then lived without any settled form of government, following a way of life similar to the Patriarchs where families lived under the authority of their fathers or the wisest among them—agreed to submit to the government of a single Prince. It is not improbable that the Chinese who arrived in Japan from time to time, having been raised under a monarchy themselves, played a significant role in persuading the Japanese to adopt the same system. In this state of affairs, no one had a better claim to supreme power than a Prince descended directly from the first-born line of the family of *Tensio Dai Sin* <note>modern: *Amaterasu-Omikami*, the Sun Goddess</note>. By the law of primogeniture, he seemed naturally entitled to the sovereignty attributed to that founder of their nation, whose holiness and virtues he also inherited.

<margin>
Respect shown them.
</margin>
Even to this day, the Princes descended from this family, especially those who sit on the throne, are looked upon as persons most holy in themselves, and as Popes by birth.

To preserve these reverent beliefs in the minds of their subjects, the Emperors are obliged to take extraordinary care of their sacred persons and to perform rituals that might seem ridiculous or trivial when judged by the customs of other nations. It is worth giving a few examples. He believes it would be deeply harmful to his dignity and holiness to touch the ground with his feet; for this reason, whenever he wishes to go anywhere, he must be carried on the shoulders of men. Much less will they allow his sacred person to be exposed to the open air, and the Sun is [not...]

# The History of JAPAN. Book II.

...not thought worthy to shine on his Head. <note>It was a long-standing tradition that the sun should never shine directly upon the Emperor, as his own divine radiance was considered equal to it.</note> There is such a Holiness ascribed to all the parts of his Body, that he dares not cut off, neither his Hair, nor his Beard, nor his nails. However lest he should grow too dirty, they may clean him in the Night, when he is asleep, because they say, that what is taken from his Body at that time, hath been stolen from him, and that such a theft doth not prejudice his Holiness or Dignity. 

In ancient times he was obliged to sit on the Throne for some hours every morning, with the Imperial Crown on his Head, but to sit altogether like a Statue, without stirring either Hands or Feet, Head or Eyes, nor indeed any part of his Body, because by this means it was thought that he could preserve peace and tranquility in his Empire; for if unfortunately he turned himself on one side or the other, or if he looked a good while towards any part of his Dominions, it was apprehended that War, Famine, Fire, or some other great Misfortune was near at hand to desolate the Country. But it having been afterwards discovered, that the Imperial Crown was the <term>Palladium <note>A "Palladium" refers to an object of antiquity upon which the safety of a city or nation is believed to depend, named after the statue of Pallas Athena in Troy.</note></term>, which by its immobility could preserve peace in the Empire, it was thought expedient to deliver his Imperial Person, consecrated only to idleness and pleasures, from this burdensome duty, and therefore the Crown is at present placed on the Throne for some hours every morning. 

His Victuals must be dressed every time in new pots, and served at table in new dishes: Both are very clean and neat, but made only of common clay, that without any considerable expense they may be laid aside, or broke, after they have served once. They are generally broke, for fear they should come into the hands of <term>Laymen <note>In this context, "Laymen" refers to anyone who is not part of the sacred imperial bloodline or the high-ranking court priesthood.</note></term>, for they believe religiously, that if any Layman should presume to eat his food out of these sacred dishes, it would swell and inflame his mouth and throat. The like ill effect is dreaded from the *Dairi’s* sacred habits <note>Sacred clothing or vestments.</note>, for they believe that if a Layman should wear them, without the Emperor’s express leave, or command, they would occasion swellings and pains in all parts of his body.

Their Succession.
</margin>
As soon as by the demise of a *Mikaddo* <note>modern: *Mikado*</note> the Throne becomes vacant, he is by the Ministry of this <term>Ecclesiastical Court <note>The *Kuge*, the hereditary court nobility who surrounded the Emperor in Kyoto.</note></term> put into the deceased’s place, whom they think the nearest Heir, without regard had to Age or Sex. Hence it is, that often Princes under age, or young unmarried Princesses ascend the Throne, and there are also instances, that the deceased Emperor’s <term>Relict <note>A widow.</note></term> succeeded her Husband. If there be several Pretenders to the Crown, and it doth not appear plainly, who it is that hath the nearest Title, the Difference is adjusted in an amicable way, according to equity, and the supreme power delivered successively, to each of them for some years, in proportion to the degree of kindred, they bore to the deceased *Mikaddo*. Sometimes the Father resigns the Crown successively to one or more of his Children, that he, and their Mothers, whilst yet alive, may have the pleasure to see them upon the Throne, of which perhaps after their demise, they would...

# Chap. II. The History of JAPAN.

...would be excluded. All of this is handled at Court with as little trouble as possible; a **Mikado** <note>The spiritual Emperor of Japan.</note> may die, or resign, and another may be put in his place without anyone outside of the Court knowing of it until the affair is concluded. However, it has happened at times that members of the Imperial family who believed they were entitled to the succession, but were excluded, maintained their rights by force of arms. They attempted to remove the **Dairi** <note>A title used for the Emperor, referring to the "Great Interior" or the court itself.</note> whom they considered to be an unlawful possessor of the Throne. From this arose wars and dissensions that were very damaging to the Empire. The Princes of the Empire took different sides, and these quarrels seldom ended without the total destruction of one of the competing parties, followed by the cruel execution of entire families.

<margin>Their Court.</margin>
The entire Court of the **Dairi** belongs to the family of **Tensho Daijin** <note>original: "Tensio Dai dsin"; the Sun Goddess Amaterasu, the divine ancestor of the Japanese Imperial line.</note>. It is because of a birth so eminent and noble that they consider themselves entitled to a far greater degree of respect and submission than any commoner <note>original: "Laymen"</note> could claim. Although they are all descended from a single family, they have gradually branched out into different lines and currently number many thousands. A few are provided for with positions in the abbeys and priories of wealthy monasteries founded throughout the Empire. However, the majority of them remain at Court, religiously devoted to the **Dairi’s** most holy person, upon whom they must entirely depend for their support and maintenance, according to the office or rank they hold.

<margin>Provision made for their maintenance.</margin>
At present, the **Secular Emperor** <note>The Shogun, the military ruler who held actual political power in Japan while the Mikado remained a symbolic figurehead.</note> grants the necessary funds for the maintenance of the **Dairi** and his **Ecclesiastical Court**. For this purpose, he has assigned to him the entire revenue of the **City of Kyoto** <note>original: "Miaco"; the traditional capital where the Emperor resided.</note> and all its lands. However, because these funds fall far short of covering his expenses, it has been agreed that any shortfall should be made up from the Secular Emperor’s Treasury. But these allowances are so small, and furthermore so unreliably paid, that the Court can hardly survive on them. At the very least, they cannot maintain the same status they once did when the **Dairi** was himself the master of the Empire and had all the revenues at his own disposal. Nevertheless, they still maintain their former grandeur and magnificence; it can truly be said of this Court that it is remarkable for a "splendid poverty." The high-ranking officials run themselves into debt, and the lower officers and servants, whose allowances are far from sufficient to support them, must work for a living. Consequently, they make and sell straw baskets <note>See Chapter I of Book V for more on these crafts.</note>, tables, shoes for men and horses, and other humble items of this nature. The **Mikado**, although his revenues are small compared to former times, still manages them himself. He ensures that he first takes care of his own needs, providing what is necessary to keep up his former splendor and to satisfy his luxury and <meta>catchword: profuseness.</meta>

# The History of JAPAN. Book II.

...extravagance. He is the better able to do this, as one very significant right of the Crown and supreme authority—which he once held in full—has been left to him by the **Secular Monarch** <note>The Shogun, the military leader who held actual political power in Japan.</note>. This is the power of granting titles of Honor to the great Men of the Empire, their children, and relations, which brings vast treasures into his **Exchequer** <note>The royal treasury or financial office.</note>. He follows the custom of his ancestors by keeping twelve wives, one of whom—being the mother of the heir, whether a Prince or Princess—holds the title of Empress. It would be too long a story to relate all the splendid and pompous ceremonies observed for his marriage, the birth of a child to the Empress, or the choosing of a nurse and the education for the Heir to the Crown. It is enough to say that these events are magnificent beyond expression; indeed, if the entire happiness and welfare of the Empire depended solely upon the birth of this Prince, the celebrations could not be greater.

<margin>Ranks and Titles of the Courtiers.</margin>
There are several eminent dignities belonging to this Ecclesiastical Court, and its Nobility is composed of persons of different ranks and quality. The **Mikado** <note>The spiritual Emperor.</note> himself is the fountain of honor. While there are certain duties attached to specific Titles, other honors are merely titular. These are frequently granted by the **Mikado** to secular individuals, the Princes of the Empire, and men of note. This is done either at the recommendation of the **Secular Monarch** <note>The Shogun.</note> or at their own request, provided they pay a large sum of money. All honors and titles are divided into six **I** <note>original: "I"; the *rank* or *grade* system (known as *位, i* in Japanese).</note>, as they call them—that is, ranks or classes. 

The Title of the first class is ***Dai Seo Dai Sin*** <note>The *Dajō-daijin*, or Chancellor of the Realm.</note>. The person honored with this Title is esteemed so great and sacred that it is believed his soul becomes a ***Cami*** <note>A *Kami*, or Shinto deity.</note>, or God, the very moment it leaves the body. For this reason, the **Mikado** usually keeps this title for himself and seldom grants it to anyone else. The dignity of ***Quanbuku*** <note>The *Kanpaku*, or Imperial Regent.</note> also belongs to this first class. The ***Quanbuku*** is the second-highest person of the Ecclesiastical Court and the **Dairi’s** <note>The Emperor’s</note> Vicegerent and Prime Minister in all affairs relating to the Empire. (*This Title is assumed by the secular Monarch, or given to the presumptive heir of the Crown, and is the same as that of **Quabacondono** <note>Lord Regent (Kanpaku-dono).</note>, which is so frequently mentioned in the letters of the **Jesuits** <note>Catholic missionaries who provided many early European accounts of Japan.</note>.*) 

The following three Titles belong to the second **I**, or rank: ***Sa Dai Sin*** <note>Minister of the Left.</note>, ***U Dai Sin*** <note>Minister of the Right.</note>, and ***Nai Dai Sin*** <note>Inner Minister.</note>. These are never granted to more than three people at Court at one time. The ***Dai Nagon*** <note>Major Counselor.</note> and ***Tsunagon*** <note>Middle Counselor (Chūnagon).</note> make up the third rank. These two Titles are always attached to specific official duties. The titles belonging to the fourth and fifth **I**, rank or class, are ***Seonagon*** <note>Lesser Counselor (Shōnagon).</note>, ***Tsunagon***, ***Tsuseo*** <note>Chūjō, or middle captain.</note>, ***Seosjo*** <note>Shōshō, or minor captain.</note>, and ***Sidsu*** <note>Jijū, or chamberlain.</note>. Both these classes are very large and are further subdivided into several different ranks. The people of these classes are also called ***Tensio bito*** <note>Tenjōbito, literally "heavenly people" or those permitted to enter the Emperor's private quarters.</note>, and the entire Ecclesiastical Court in general takes the title of ***Kuge*** <note>The court nobility.</note>, which signifies...

### Chap. II. The History of JAPAN. 153

...as Ecclesiastical Lords, and they use this title to distinguish themselves from the *Gege* <note>original: "Gege"; a term for commoners or those outside the high-ranking courtly circles</note>, a name they use to describe all the laity and common people who are not of such holy and honorable descent. The titles of the sixth and lowest class are *Tai U*, *Goi*, and many others of lesser importance. 

All titles and degrees of honor, of any kind, are conferred, as I have already noted, by the *Mikado* <note>The spiritual Emperor of Japan, believed to be of divine descent.</note>, and by him alone. When the Secular Monarchs <note>The Shoguns, who held the actual military and political power in Japan.</note> took the government of the Empire into their own hands, the *Dairi* <note>The Emperor and his court.</note> reserved for himself—along with his supreme authority—this significant branch of the Imperial rights. Consequently, whatever titles the Secular Emperors wish to bestow upon their favorites and Prime Ministers must be obtained from the *Mikado*. 

There are primarily two titles which the Secular Emperor, with the consent of the *Dairi*, can confer upon his chief ministers and the Princes of the Empire: *Maquandairo* <note>Likely a variation of "Matsudaira," a prestigious surname and title granted to high-ranking lords.</note> and *Cami*. The first was formerly hereditary and signifies a rank similar to a Duke or Earl. The second denotes a *Knight*. 

It should be observed here that the character representing a deified soul is also pronounced *Cami* <note>Kami (神), meaning a god, spirit, or divine being.</note>, but it is of an entirely different nature from the character that expresses the title and honor of knighthood. All the gods and idols of the country generally share the name and character of *Cami*.

<margin>Their Clothing.</margin>
The members of this Ecclesiastical Court, among other marks of distinction, dress in a particular fashion unique to themselves. This style differs widely from the clothing of secular people, whom they look down upon as being of a common and unholy origin. There is so much variety even among their own garments that their specific rank or their office at court can be easily identified by their dress alone. 

They wear long, wide trousers and a large gown over them, which is very broad and fashioned in a singular way—especially around the shoulders—and features a long train that they trail behind them on the floor. They cover their heads with a black lacquered cap. By the different shapes and figures of these caps, one can tell, among other distinctions, their rank or their position at court. Some have a broad band of black crepe or silk stitched to their caps, which is either tied up or hangs down behind their shoulders. Others have a type of flap, shaped like a fan, positioned in front of their eyes. Some wear a sort of scarf or a broad band that hangs forward from their shoulders. The length of this scarf varies according to each person's rank or dignity; it is the custom of this court that no one bows lower than is necessary for the end of their scarf to touch the floor. 

The women's dress at the Court of the *Dairi* is also very distinctive and different from that of secular women. Most notably, the *Dairi's* twelve wives wear twelve sumptuous, unlined gowns, interwoven with gold and silver flowers. These are so large and wide that it is very difficult for them to walk when they are fully dressed in this manner.

### The History of JAPAN. Book II.

<margin>
Their Pastimes.
</margin>

Academic studies and learning are the primary pastimes of this religious court. Not only the <term>Kuge<note>The ancient hereditary nobility of the Imperial Court in Kyoto, distinct from the Daimyo or military lords.</note></term>, or courtiers, but even many noblewomen have acquired great reputations for their poetical, historical, and other writings. In former times, all the official almanacs were produced at court; however, they are now compiled by a learned citizen in <term>Miaco<note>The historical name for Kyoto, the capital where the Emperor resided.</note></term>. Nevertheless, these calendars must still be examined and approved at court by officials commissioned for the task, who ensure they are sent to <term>Isje<note>Ise, the site of the most sacred Shinto shrines, where the almanacs were printed under religious authority.</note></term> as a holy place to be printed there. The courtiers are great lovers of music, and the women in particular play all types of musical instruments with great skill. Young noblemen divert themselves with riding, racing, dancing, fighting, playing tennis, and other exercises suited to their social rank. I did not specifically ask whether they perform comedies and tragedies at court. But as the Japanese people in general are very fond of plays and will spend a great deal of money on them, I am inclined to believe that these religious figures—despite their gravity and holiness—would not willingly deprive themselves of such an agreeable, entertaining, and innocent diversion.

<margin>
The Dairi's Residence.
</margin>

In ancient times, when the <term>Dairi<note>A term used here to refer to the Emperor himself or the Imperial Court enclosure.</note></term> was the sole master of the country, he resided with his court wherever he pleased. He honored various towns or provinces of his empire with his sacred presence, and it seldom happened that two succeeding Emperors chose the same place to live. In recent times, however, their residence has been more or less fixed to Kyoto. They occupy the north-east part of this large capital, which deserves to be called a separate town. This is not only because of its vast size and the number of streets, palaces, and houses built within its borders, but also because it is physically separated from the rest of Kyoto. It is defended against the sudden approach of an unexpected enemy by ditches, walls, ramparts, and gates. 

The <term>Mikaddo<note>The Emperor, seen as a divine figurehead.</note></term> himself lives near the center of this area in a large and spacious palace, distinguished from others by the height and magnificence of its tower. His Imperial Consort lives with him in the same palace, while the palaces of his other wives stand nearby. A short distance away are the houses of the Lords of the Bedchamber and other officials whose duties require constant and immediate attendance upon his sacred person. If a Mikado resigns, a separate palace is assigned to him, his family, and his court; another is provided for the hereditary prince and his own retinue. The remaining streets and houses are divided among the officers of this court according to their rank and dignity. The Secular Monarch <note>The Shogun, the military dictator who held actual political power in Japan.</note> constantly maintains a strong guard of <term>Bugjos<note>Bugyō; high-ranking officials or magistrates appointed by the Shogun.</note></term> and soldiers at the Imperial Court. This is done ostensibly out of tenderness and care for the safety of the Emperor's sacred person and family, but in reality, it is to ensure he never has the power to attempt to recover the throne and the supreme authority that was taken from him.

Thus much of the <term>Dairi</term>, his court, and his government in general. It now remains, before I proceed to the history and succession of the...

### Chap II. The History of JAPAN. 155

...regarding the Ecclesiastical Emperors, I will lay down some general observations tending to explain the chronology made use of in the same.

<margin>Eras of the Japanese.</margin>
The Japanese have two principal eras, or epochs. The first, and also the more common, begins with the reign of their first Emperor, <term>Jimmu<note>Original: "Synmu." Jimmu Tenno is the legendary first Emperor of Japan, traditionally said to have ascended the throne in 660 BCE.</note></term>, in the year 660 before Christ. Consequently, the year of Christ 1693, which was the sixth year of the <term>Genroku<note>Original: "Genrokf." This era (1688–1704) is remembered as a golden age of Japanese culture, known for its vibrant arts and literature.</note></term> era, was the year 2353 from Jimmu.

<margin>Nin O.</margin>
This epoch is by them called <term>Nin O<note>Literally "Human King," used to distinguish the historical lineage of emperors from the preceding "Age of the Gods."</note></term>, which properly speaking signifies a *great and powerful Lord*, or *Monarch*, and in a more sublime sense, *the very first*.

<margin>Nengo.</margin>
The second epoch made use of in Japan is called <term>Nengo<note>The era name system, where a specific name is chosen for a period of time to mark a reign or a significant omen.</note></term>. It was invented by the Chinese for greater certainty in chronology than they thought their common epochs would admit of, and it was not introduced in Japan until the reign of the thirty-sixth Emperor. It takes in a period only of a few years, commonly less than twenty, and seldom beyond this number. The beginning, as also the proper figure to express it, are determined by the Emperor; this is done commonly in memory of some remarkable accident, or of some considerable alteration in church or state. As the Emperor has the sole power of instituting them, so he can continue them as long as he pleases. 

The Japanese character expressing the <term>Nengo</term> then current when I was in Japan—the sixth year of which falls in with the year of Christ 1693—was pronounced <term>Genroku</term>, which signifies the *Happiness of Nature and Art*. By this name, the then-reigning <term>Mikado<note>The spiritual Emperor residing in Kyoto.</note></term> alluded to the desirable happiness and tranquility of a private life, which the late Emperor, his father, resolved to lead after his resignation of the Crown. This epoch is used in their almanacs, orders, proclamations, journals, letters, and writings. In their printed books, chiefly those that relate to history and chronology, the current year of the <term>Nin O</term> epoch is added to it. 

It must be observed that a new <term>Nengo</term> always begins with a new year, even though it was ordered and instituted several months before. Sometimes it also happens that although a new <term>Nengo</term> has already begun, the years of the preceding <term>Nengo</term> are continued on the title pages of their books, letters, journals, and so on. This I take to be owing either to the people’s not liking the character expressing the new <term>Nengo</term>, or to it not being as yet known, which is not impossible in an empire of so great an extent. 

Thus, for instance, the almanacs of the first and second year of the <term>Genroku</term> era were printed with the fifth and sixth year of the preceding era, <term>Jokyo<note>Original: "Dfiokio." The era immediately preceding Genroku, lasting from 1684 to 1688.</note></term>, though it had already expired. In this case, however, care is taken that no error or confusion should be caused in their chronology by such an inadvertency. For this reason, in the next almanac (which was that of the year of Christ 1690), the third year of the then-current <term>Genroku</term> era was set down accordingly, without any mention made of the first two. The character of a <term>Nengo</term> is composed of two, seldom more, figures, which are and must be taken out of a particular table composed for this purpose.

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 155 regarding the Japanese systems of timekeeping. Having already introduced the Imperial era (Nin O) and the era names (Nengo), the author now explains the third system: the sixty-year cycle borrowed from China.</meta>

### The History of JAPAN. Book II.

<margin>Periods of 60 Years.</margin>
There remains still a third <term>Epoch<note>A starting point in time used to calculate years.</note></term>, which is likewise used in the chronology of the Japanese. This consists of <term>cycles<note>Original: "Cycli." Reoccurring periods of time.</note></term> or periods of sixty years, and the Japanese are indebted for it to the Chinese, just as they are for their *Nengo* <note>The era names system explained on the previous page.</note>. These sixty years arise from a combination of the *Fetta* <note>Known today as the "Twelve Earthly Branches" or the signs of the Japanese zodiac.</note>, which are the names of the twelve Celestial signs, with the ten names of their elements <note>Known as the "Ten Heavenly Stems."</note>. The characters of the Celestial signs being combined with those of the ten elements five different times—or these six times with the former—there arise sixty compound figures or characters, each of which is taken for a year. When the sixty years have expired, a new cycle is begun, which runs again through all these several combinations. 

The Japanese use this period of 60 years to better establish the most remarkable occurrences in church and state, which are recorded in their histories; these are referred to under the current year of the cycle, as well as those of the two other epochs, *Nin O* and *Nengo*. By this means, they also maintain a perpetual harmony between their own history and chronology and that of the Chinese. There is one difference, however: while the Chinese in their historical writings mention not only the year but also the number of the cycle in which something happened, the Japanese, on the contrary, set down only the year. The cycles of the Japanese are not numbered at all. The reason for this appears plainly if we consider the natural pride of this nation; they would fall far short, in this particular, of their neighbors the Chinese, who can show a succession of cycles for many centuries before the very foundation of the Japanese Monarchy. In the following history, which I propose to give of the succession of the Japanese Monarchs, I shall avoid troubling the reader with all these different epochs, though I thought it necessary to give some preliminary account of them.

<margin>Their Celestial Signs.</margin>
The *Fetta*, or twelve Celestial Signs of the Japanese, are:

| | |
|---|---|
| 1. Ne, the Mouse. | 7. Uma, the Horse. |
| 2. Us, the Ox or Cow. | 8. Hitsuji, the Sheep. <note>Original: "Tſitſuſe."</note> |
| 3. Tora, the Tiger. <note>Original: "Torra."</note> | 9. Saru, the Monkey. <note>Original: "Sar."</note> |
| 4. U, the Hare. <note>Original: "Ow."</note> | 10. Tori, the Cock or Hen. <note>Original: "Torri."</note> |
| 5. Tatsu, the Dragon. <note>Original: "Tats."</note> | 11. Inu, the Dog. <note>Original: "In."</note> |
| 6. Mi, the Serpent. | 12. I, the Boar. |

<margin>Their Hours.</margin>
The same names are given, and in the same order, to the twelve hours of the natural day, and to the twelve parts into which every hour is divided. By this means, they are able to mention in their histories with great accuracy not only what day the most remarkable occurrences happened, but also what hour, and what part of the hour. It must be observed, however, that what they call *Day* is the interval of time between sunrise and sunset; this is divided into six equal parts or hours, as is the Night, from sunset to sunrise, which is divided into six others. <note>Because the length of the day and night changes with the seasons, these "hours" varied in length throughout the year.</note>

### Chap. II. The History of JAPAN.

Hence it is, that their hours differ in length every day, so that in the Summer the hours of the day are much longer than those of the night, and shorter, on the contrary, in the Winter. <note>The Japanese used a system of "seasonal hours," where the periods of daylight and darkness were each divided into six equal units. Consequently, an "hour" in summer was physically longer than an "hour" in winter.</note>

<margin>Their Elements.</margin>
As to their Elements, there are properly speaking but five; it is only by giving two different names and characters to each of them that they have raised the number to ten. This was absolutely necessary because, by combining them with the twelve Celestial Signs <note>The twelve signs of the Zodiac, represented by animals such as the Dragon, Horse, and Rat.</note> repeated five times, they were able to obtain the <term>Cycle<note>Original: "Cyclus." A recurring period of time.</note></term> of sixty years. The names of their ten elements are:

| | | | |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Kino Je | Wood | 2. Kino To | Wood |
| 3. Fino Je | Fire | 4. Fino To | Fire |
| 5. Tsutsno Je | Earth | 6. Tsutsno To | Earth |
| 7. Kanno Je | Metal <note>Original: "Oar." This refers to the element of Metal in the Eastern five-element system.</note> | 8. Kanno To | Metal |
| 9. Midsno Je | Water | 10. Midsno To | Water |

In *Table XV* annexed to this work, I have represented the characters of the twelve Celestial Signs, those of the ten Elements, and those of the whole period of sixty years as they arise from a combination of the former.

<margin>Beginning of the Japanese Year.</margin>
The beginning of the Japanese year falls between the Winter Solstice and Spring Equinox, about the fifth of *February*. But as the Japanese are extremely superstitious in celebrating the day of the New Moon, they commonly begin it with the New Moon which immediately precedes or follows the fifth of *February*. 

Thus the first year of the <term>Nengo<note>The era name designated by the Emperor.</note></term> *Genroku* <note>Original: "Genrokf." An era of Japanese history spanning 1688–1704, known as a golden age for culture.</note>, which in the Cycle is called *Tsutsno Je Tats* <note>The Year of the Earth Dragon.</note>, being the year of Christ 1688, began on the second of *February*. The second year of *Genroku*, in the Cycle *Tsutsnoto Mi* <note>The Year of the Earth Snake.</note> (the year of Christ 1689), began on the twenty-first of *January*. The third of *Genroku*, in the Cycle *Kano Je Uma* <note>The Year of the Metal Horse.</note> (the year of Christ 1690), began on the ninth of *February*. The fourth of *Genroku*, in the Cycle *Kanoto Hitsuji* <note>Original: "Fitsuse." The Year of the Metal Goat.</note> (the year of Christ 1691), began on the twenty-first of *January*. The fifth of *Genroku*, in the Cycle *Midsno Je Saru* <note>Original: "Sar." The Year of the Water Monkey.</note> (the year of Christ 1692), began on the seventeenth of *February*. And the sixth of *Genroku* (the year of Christ 1693) began on the fifth of *February*. The Japanese have a Leap-year every other or third year, or seven Leap-years in nineteen common years. <note>To keep the lunar months in line with the solar seasons, the Japanese inserted an entire "intercalary" month periodically, rather than a single leap day.</note>
