### C H A P. III.

->*Of the Ecclesiastical Hereditary Emperors in particular, and first of those, who governed from the beginning of the Japanese Monarchy until the Birth of Christ.*<-
<note>Original: "Saviour's Nativity." This refers to the start of the Common Era (A.D.).</note>

<margin>How the beginning of new reigns is mentioned in their histories.</margin>
I am now come to the history and succession of the ecclesiastical hereditary monarchs <note>These are the *Tennō* or Emperors of Japan, who were historically regarded as semi-divine, spiritual leaders.</note> of Japan. But before I begin this account, I must not omit to mention that in their historical and chronological books, a new reign always begins with a new year. Although a new Emperor frequently takes possession of the throne—whether by the death or resignation of his predecessor—several months before the year has expired, the remaining part of that year is still credited to the reign of the previous ruler. This is done, as they claim, to avoid any confusion in their chronological tables; however, in their historical remarks, they constantly record the specific month and day that every *Mikado* <note>The title for the Emperor of Japan.</note> took possession of the throne.

<margin>The Japanese authors from which this history was taken.</margin>
In writing this history of the Japanese monarchy, I consulted two chronicles written and published in Japan. These works say very little regarding the personal lives of the Emperors, their virtues and vices, or the political aspects of their government. Instead, they focus with great accuracy on their names, their descent and birth, their succession, the duration of their reign, and the names of the *Nengos* <term>Nengo<note>Era names used in Japan to identify specific periods within a reign.</note></term> instituted by them (including how many years those era names lasted). They also record the location of the imperial residence and other remarkable occurrences that happened under each reign. These include, for instance: the building and consecrating of significant *Shinto* <note>Original: "Sintos." Referring to the indigenous spirituality of Japan.</note> or Buddhist <note>Original: "Budsdo." An archaic term for Buddhist.</note> temples; the birth and death of great heroes, eminent priests, and other illustrious persons; the rise and fall of great ministers at court; and various rebellions, wars, and fires. They also record celestial and natural phenomena, such as the appearance of comets, new stars, and strange meteors, as well as earthquakes, famines, plagues, and other epidemic diseases. Furthermore, they note the arrival of new idols, priests, people, or objects from foreign countries; the publication of noteworthy books; and the institution of festival days in honor of their gods, saints, and heroes. They even record the time when some of their idols were carved or moved from one temple to another, along with the names of the craftsmen; the appearances of their gods and spirits; the discovery of idols; prophecies; and miracles. Finally, they include the most remarkable events which happened from time to time in *China*. From all these details mentioned by these two Japanese authors, I have extracted only what was necessary for my cur-

<margin>Emperor I. JIMMU</margin>
**JIMMU** <note>original: "SYN MU"</note>, and with his full Title Emperor Jimmu <note>original: "Syn Mu ten Oo"; the title "Tennō" translates to "Heavenly Sovereign"</note>, founded the Japanese Monarchy in the 58th year of the 35th Chinese Cycle <note>The sexagenary cycle is a 60-year system used in East Asian calendars to track time</note>, when Emperor Teikwo <note>original: "Teikwo"</note>—or according to the Chinese pronunciation, Ku-ho <note>original: "Hoyuam"</note>—had already entered the eighth year of his Reign, in the year 660 before Christ, and the 78th year of his Age.

Before that time, he was called Iwa-biko <note>original: "Jwa Fikono Mikotto"; a legendary prince's name</note>. He was the fourth and youngest of his Brothers who preceded him in the Government, but they lived for such a short and insignificant time, and reigned in such an obscure manner, that the Foundation of the Empire, with the Title of Human Sovereign <note>original: "Nin O"; meaning "Human King," distinguishing him from the preceding era of "Divine" rulers</note>—that is, the Supreme of all Men—is by all Japanese Writers unanimously attributed to him, as to their Julius Caesar <note>A comparison to the Roman leader to illustrate Jimmu's role as the state's great founder and reformer</note>.

He civilized the Inhabitants of Japan—which was then called Akitsushima <note>original: "Akitsuffima"; an ancient poetic name for Japan meaning "Dragonfly Island"</note>—introduced Chronology among them by dividing Time into Years, Months and Days, and made a thorough Reformation in the Laws and Government of the Country.

In the 59th Year of his Reign, which was 601 years before Christ and 346 Years after the Death of the Buddha <note>original: "Siaka"; the Japanese name for Shakyamuni Buddha</note>, on the 14th Day of the ninth Month, the great Philosopher Laozi <note>original: "Roosi"</note> was born in China, in the Province of Chu-kuo <note>original: "Sokokf"</note>. He was already eighty-one years old and grey-haired when his Mother was brought to bed of him, for which reason he was called Laozi <note>original: "Roo-si"</note>, which signifies an *Old Child* <note>original: "Roo" (Old) and "Si" (Child)</note>. The Soul of Kasyapa <note>original: "Kassobofats"</note>, the Buddha's Companion and chief Disciple, is believed to have dwelt in him through Transmigration; and yet his Doctrine is entirely different from that of Kasyapa. The Buddha taught his Followers the Immortality of our Souls, the reward of our actions in a future Life, and how necessary the Practice of Virtue in this Life is to all who aim at a State of Bliss in the next. Laozi, on the contrary, absolutely denied these important Truths and maintained that all our Happiness consists in living long and well. In pursuit of these notions, he endeavored to find through Alchemy an universal Medicine <note>An "elixir of life" intended to grant longevity</note> which could prolong his Life, if not render him immortal. The same attempt was made afterwards by his Disciples and the followers of his Sect, with as much success as our European Philosophers can boast to have had in their searches after the Philosopher’s Stone. He lived 84 Years.

About this Time, in the Year 600 before Christ, foreign Idols <note>Early statues of deities, possibly indicating the first arrival of foreign religious influences</note> were first brought into Japan and worshiped in Kumano <note>original: "Khumano"</note>.

Jimmu reigned 79 Years, and having secured the Throne for his Posterity, he died in the 157th Year of his Age. With his Reign begins the Japanese Era of the Human Sovereigns <note>original: "Nin O"</note>.

<margin>Emperor II. SUISEI</margin>
**SUISEI**, Jimmu’s third Son, succeeded his Father in the 80th Year of his Reign, in the 580th year before Christ, and the 51st year of his Age.

<margin>Birth of Confucius</margin>
In the 30th Year of his Reign <note>Referring to the second Emperor, Suizei</note>, 399 years after the death of Shakyamuni Buddha <note>original: "Siaká"</note>, and 551 years before the birth of our Savior, on the fourth day of the eleventh month, the illustrious philosopher **Confucius** <note>original: "KOOSI"</note> was born in China, in the Province of Lu <note>original: "Rokokf"</note>. According to the Chinese, he is called Kong Fuzi <note>original: "Cumfusu"</note>, whom our European writers call *Confutius*. Chinese historians record that at the time of his birth, heavenly music was heard, stars descended closer to the earth, and two dragons attended him while the child was washed. They also note that nature had marked his forehead with a small prominence or mole, similar to that of the legendary Emperor Shun <note>original: "Siun"</note>, and that his face resembled that of the Emperor Yao <note>original: "Gio"</note>. In short, he possessed all the signs of a future <term>Sefin</term> <note>From the Japanese "Seijin," meaning a Sage or a person of incomparable understanding and profound learning</note>. When he came of age, his stature was majestic and noble, for he stood 9 <term>Shaku</term> and 6 <term>Sun</term> tall <note>Roughly 9 feet 6 inches in traditional measurements; such extreme height is a common legendary attribute for ancient sages</note>. His writings, particularly those regarding moral philosophy, are not unknown in Europe. Through his works, in which he displayed all his learning for the universal benefit of mankind, his virtuous and exemplary life, and his great number of disciples (who never numbered fewer than 3,000), he achieved such a high degree of fame and reputation among his own countrymen, as well as in Japan, that after his death temples were erected to his memory. To this day, he is honored with profound reverence and almost divine worship. He died in the 74th year of his age.

**Sui Sei** <note>The 2nd Emperor, Suizei</note> reigned thirty-three years and lived to be eighty-four.

<margin>Generation II. ANNEI.</margin>
<note>Historically, Annei is the 3rd Emperor; the "II" in the margin is likely a printer's error</note>
His son **ANNEI** succeeded him in the 113th year of the Jimmu Era <note>original: "Synmu"; the Japanese calendar system</note>, 548 BC, and in the twentieth year of his age.

In the thirty-second year of his reign (516 BC), Yan Hui <note>original: "Ganquai"</note> was born in the Chinese Province of Lu. He was a very learned man and a distinguished disciple of Confucius. It is remarked as something extraordinary that in the eighteenth year of his age his hair turned perfectly grey, giving him the appearance of an old man. He lived only thirty-two years. It is believed that the soul of <term>Kashyapa</term> <note>original: "Quosofobatz"; likely referring to Mahakasyapa, one of the primary disciples of the Buddha</note> dwelt within him through the transmigration of souls.

**Annei** reigned thirty-eight years and lived a full fifty-seven years.

<margin>Generation IV. I TOKU.</margin>
His second son **I TOKU** succeeded him in the 151st year of the Jimmu Era, 511 BC, and in the forty-fourth year of his age.

In the fourth year of his reign, he moved his Court and residence to Karu <note>original: "Keitz"; referring to the palace at Karu-no-magari-no-oka</note> where he died, after a reign of thirty-five years, in the seventy-seventh year of his age.

<margin>Generation V. KOSIO.</margin>
His son **KOSIO** succeeded him in the 186th year of the Jimmu Era, 476 BC, and in the thirty-third year of his age.

In the fifth year of his reign, a war arose between the Chinese provinces of Yue <note>original: "Jetz"</note> and Wu <note>original: "Go"</note>, which is the first war mentioned in the Japanese histories.

He reigned for nearly eighty-three years and died in the one hundred and fifteenth year of his age.

<margin>The 6th Emperor <note>original: "Dai VI"</note> **KOAN**</margin>
His second son **Koan** succeeded him in the 269th year of the <term>Jimmu</term> era <note>original: "Synmu"; referring to the years since the reign of the first Emperor, Jimmu</note>, in the year 392 BC, at the age of thirty-six.

He moved his residence to Muro in the province of Harima <note>original: "Farima"</note>, and some years later to Kuroda <note>original: "Khuroda"</note>.

Under his reign, a comet appeared in China, and there was an eclipse of the sun in Japan so complete that the day, according to the records, was suddenly transformed into a dark night.

He reigned for one hundred and one years and lived to be one hundred and thirty-seven.

<margin>The 7th Emperor <note>original: "Dai VII"</note> **KOREI**</margin>
His eldest son **Korei**, also called **Kosi**, succeeded him in the 371st year of the Jimmu era, in the year 290 BC, at the age of fifty-three.

In the sixth year of his reign (284 BC), the lake and river of **Omi** <note>Referring to Lake Biwa and the Seta River</note> in the province of the same name emerged suddenly in a single night.

In the thirty-third year of his reign (257 BC), the great tyrant **Qin Shi Huang** <note>original: "Sinofikwo"; the first emperor of a unified China</note> was born in China.

In the forty-sixth year of his reign (244 BC), the Empire of Japan was first divided into thirty-six provinces.

He reigned for 76 years and lived to be 128 years old.

<margin>The 8th Emperor <note>original: "Dai VIII"</note> **KOOKIN**</margin>
His son **Kookin** <note>Known modernly as Emperor Kōgen</note> succeeded him in the 447th year of the Jimmu era, in the year 214 BC, at the age of sixty.

He moved his court and residence to Karutsu <note>original: "Karutz"</note>.

About this time, the Emperor **Shi Huangdi** <note>original: "Sikwo" or "Sino Siko"</note> of the **Qin** <note>original: "Cin"</note> dynasty reigned in China. He is a prince no less famous in Chinese and Japanese histories for his extravagance and magnificence than he was feared by his subjects for his unparalleled cruelty and tyrannical government. He ascended the throne of China in 246 BC and died after a reign of thirty-seven years, at the age of fifty. Of the many instances of his lavishness and tyranny recorded by my Japanese authors, I will mention only a few. He once ordered a massive lake to be excavated and filled with Chinese rice-beer <note>Sake</note>; once this was done, he sailed across it in boats with his mistresses, who were unclothed. He built the famous **Great Wall of China**, which is 300 <term>German Miles</term> long <note>A historical unit; 300 German miles is roughly 1,400 English miles or 2,250 kilometers</note>, to protect his empire against the raids of the Tartars. He sent 300 young men and 300 young women across the sea under the command of one of his physicians, who had convinced him to do so. Their mission was to find and bring back the plants and other ingredients necessary to prepare a "Universal Medicine" <note>An elixir of immortality</note> which he desperately desired. This physician traveled with his youthful colony to Japan and settled there, never intending to return to China. He built the famous **Epang Palace** <note>original: "Kanjoku"</note>, a name meaning a "Great House Resembling Heaven." The floors were covered with gold and silver, and the entire palace was so costly, vast, and magnificent that its name later became a proverb for luxury. It was set on fire and destroyed in 205 BC by the order of **Xiang Yu** <note>original: "Kool"</note>, who rose up against the Qin dynasty, and after putting to death the Emperor **Ziying** <note>original: "Syse"</note>,

header: Chap III. The History of JAPAN.

In the fortieth year of his reign <note>referring to the 10th Emperor, Sujin</note>, on a clear and serene day, there arose of a sudden in *China* a violent storm of thunder and lightning: Comets, **Fiery-Dragons** <note>a common historical term for large, bright meteors or bolides</note> and uncommon Meteors appear'd in the Air, and it rain'd fire from Heaven.

In the sixtieth year of his reign they begun to make Fish-ponds in *Japan*, to cultivate Rice-fields, and to inclose the same with ditches.

In the sixty-fifth year of his reign, in the seventh month, many People were kill'd in *China* by lightning and hail. This storm was follow'd by so dreadful a famine, that People kill'd and eat one another.

In the eighty-eighth year of his reign an extraordinary swift Horse was brought over from the Indies into *Japan*. He could run a thousand miles a day. (A race between this Horse and the famous Horse of *Ali* <note>Ali ibn Abi Talib, a central figure in Islam; his horse, often called Duldul, was legendary for its speed and stamina</note>, would have been a very diverting sight.)

In the ninety-fifth year of his reign, *Bupo* <note>a corruption of "Buddha" or "Butsu-po," meaning the law of Buddha</note>, otherwise call'd *Kobotus*, came over from the Indies into *Japan*, and brought over with him, on a **white Horse**, the *Kio* <note>meaning *Kyo* or Sutra</note> or Book of his Religion and Doctrine. A temple was afterwards erected to him, which is still call'd *Fakubasi*, or the **Temple of the White Horse** <note>likely referring to the *Hokke-ji* or perhaps the legendary *Hakuma-ji*</note>. Ever since that time, the foreign Pagan worship of the Chinese and other Nations begun to spread in *Japan*, and the number of temples and religious houses was from time to time considerably increas'd.

The reign of this Emperor is the longest of any that sat upon the throne of *Japan*, for he reign'd 98 years, and liv'd 139.

I must not forget, before I close this Chapter, to take Notice: *That in the 29th year of the reign of this Emperor, which was the 661 year of <term>Synmu</term> <note>Jimmu, the legendary first Emperor of Japan; years were often counted from the start of his reign in 660 BC</note>, the sixth and last year of the Chinese Emperor* **A I**, *by the Chinese call'd* **HIAO N GAI TI** <note>Emperor Ai of Han</note>, (*who was then already expir'd and succeeded by the Emperor* **HIAO PIM TI** <note>Emperor Ping of Han</note>) *and the second year of his last <term>Nengo</term> <note>era name</note>, was born* **CHRIST**, *the Saviour of the World, and that in the 66th year of the reign of* **SY NIN** <note>Emperor Suinin, the 11th Emperor</note>, *which was the ninth year of the reign of the Chinese Emperor* **KWOO BU** <note>Emperor Guangwu of Han</note>, *he was crucify'd, buried, and rose again from the dead, supposing that his death happen'd in the 33d year of his Age.*

### CHAP. IV.

#### Of the **Ecclesiastical Hereditary Emperors** <note>Kaempfer uses the term "Ecclesiastical" to describe the *Tenno* (Emperors), whom he viewed as divine or priestly sovereigns, as opposed to the "Secular" *Shoguns* who held military and political power</note>, who lived and governed with an unlimited Authority from the Birth of our Saviour to Joritomo <note>Minamoto no Yoritomo, the founder of the Kamakura Shogunate</note>, the first **Secular Monarch**.

<margin>The 12th Emperor: KEIKŌ</margin>
KEIKŌ, Suinin’s third son, succeeded his father in the year of Synmu 731 <note>This refers to the *Jinmu* era, a traditional Japanese calendar counting from the reign of the first legendary emperor</note>, the 71st after our Saviour’s Nativity, and the 84th of his Age.

In the twenty-third year of his reign a new Island rose up near *Japan*, from the bottom of the Sea. It was called *Tsikubasima* <note>Chikubushima, a small island in Lake Biwa</note>, and consecrated to *Nebis* <note>Ebisu, the Japanese god of luck and the sea, whom Kaempfer identifies with the Roman god Neptune</note>, who is the **Neptune** of the *Japanese*. Three years after a *Mia* <note>A Shinto shrine (*miya*)</note>, or Temple, called *Takajanomia*, was built upon the said Island in honour of *Nebis*, and a sufficient number of **Bonze’s** <note>A term used by early travelers for Buddhist or Shinto priests</note> or Priests appointed to attend it. This Temple, in succeeding ages, became very famous and rich, and the Island itself is said to have been always free from Earthquakes.

He reigned sixty years, and lived one hundred and forty-three.

<margin>The 13th Emperor: SEIMU</margin>
SEIMU, his fourth Son succeeded him in the year of Synmu 791, of Christ 131, and the forty-ninth of his age.

He removed his Court and Residence to *Sigga* <note>Shiga</note> in the Province *Oomi* <note>Ōmi Province</note>.

In the sixth year of his reign he settled the confines of all the Provinces of his Empire.

He reigned 60 years, and lived one hundred and eight.

<margin>The 14th Emperor: CHŪAI</margin>
CHŪAI, the second Son of *Sei Mu’s* Sister (who was married to *Jamatta Dakino Mikotto* <note>Yamato Takeru, a legendary prince and hero of the Yamato dynasty</note>), and *Keiko’s* Grandson, succeeded him, in the year of *Synmu* 852, of Christ 192 and the forty-fourth of his age.

He made his way to the Throne by the murder of *Kumasi Usomu Kuno Mikotto* <note>A reference to the suppression of the Kumaso, a people who lived in southern Kyushu and resisted the Yamato expansion</note>.

He reigned but nine years, and died fifty-two years old.

<margin>The 15th Emperor: JINGŪ</margin>
SINGUKOGU, or *Jingū Kōgō*, succeeded him in the year of *Synmu* 861, of Christ 201, and the thirtieth of her age.

She was the deceased Emperor's relict <note>An archaic term for a widow</note>, and besides entitled to the Succession, by the relation she bore, in the fifth degree, to the Emperor *Keikoo*.

She carried on war against the **Coreans** <note>Koreans</note>, and at the very beginning of her reign went over with a numerous Army, which she commanded in person, but finding herself with child in a foreign Country, she hastened back to *Japan*, and was brought to bed (in *Tsikusen* <note>Chikuzen</note>, in the Province *Mikassa*, where she then resided) of a Son,

ŌJIN, or *Woojin*, her only Son, succeeded her in the year of Jinmu 930 <note>This refers to the Japanese era dating from the first Emperor, Jinmu</note>, the year of Christ 270, and the seventy-first year of his age.

He reigned eighty-seven years, and lived to be 110. In the province of Settsu, where there is a Temple built to his memory, they call him *Naniwa Takatsu-no-miya Koreshira-no-Daimyōjin*.

### The History of J A P A N. Book II.

<margin>21st Mikado: ANKOO</margin>
ANKOO <note>Emperor Ankō, traditionally reigned 453–456 AD</note>, the second son of *Inkioo*, succeeded his father in the year of *Synmu* 1114 <note>The "Year of Synmu" refers to the traditional Japanese calendar dating from the first Emperor, Jinmu</note>, which corresponds to the year of Christ 454, and the fifty-fourth year of his age.

He resided in *Jamatto* <note>Yamato Province, the heartland of early Japanese civilization</note>.

His reign was but short, for in the third year after his accession to the throne, *Maijuwa* <note>Prince Mayowa</note>, a near relation of his, rebelled against him, conquered and killed him, in the fifty-sixth year of his age.

<margin>22nd Mikado: JUU RIAKU</margin>
JUU RIAKU <note>Emperor Yūryaku, traditionally reigned 456–479 AD</note>, *Ankoo*’s younger brother and *Inkioo*’s fifth son, succeeded him in the year of *Synmu* 1117, the year of Christ 457.

It is said of this Emperor that he was born grey-haired. Hence it is perhaps that some authors put his accession to the throne in the seventy-first year of his age, which does not agree with the chronology and the age of the Emperors who preceded him.

He revenged the death of his brother upon *Maijuwa*, or, as some call him, *Maijuwano o sin*, whom he put to death.

In the seventh year of his reign, he married the Princess *Wakaki*, declared her Empress, and at the same time made a law, which still subsists, importing that the children of that wife of the *Dairis* <note>Dairi is a term for the Emperor or the Imperial Court</note> who was declared Empress should be acknowledged as the only lawful heirs of the Crown.

In the ninth year of his reign, the first *Putjes* <note>Small copper or iron coins, often called "cash"</note> were coined in *Japan* by one *Sinka*.

He reigned twenty-three years. How long he lived is uncertain.

<margin>23rd Mikado: SE NEI</margin>
His second son SE NE <note>Emperor Seinei, traditionally reigned 480–484 AD</note> succeeded him in the year of *Synmu* 1140, the year of Christ 480, and the 37th year of his age.

He reigned but five years and lived to be forty-two.

<margin>24th Mikado: GEN SOO</margin>
GEN SOO <note>Emperor Kenzō, traditionally reigned 485–487 AD</note>, the Emperor *Ritsius*’s grandson, succeeded *Se Ne* in the year of *Synmu* 1145, the year of Christ 485, and the 46th year of his age.

He reigned three years and resigned. He lived 85 years.

<margin>25th Mikado: NINKEN</margin>
His brother NINKEN succeeded him in the year of *Synmu* 1148, the year of Christ 488, and the 41st year of his age.

He reigned eleven years and lived to be fifty-one.

<margin>26th Mikado: BURETZ</margin>
His son BURETZ <note>Emperor Buretsu, traditionally reigned 498–506 AD</note> succeeded him in the year of *Synmu* 1159, the year of Christ 499.

He was a cruel and barbarous Prince. He took great delight in cutting off people’s heads unawares. He ripped open, with his own barbarous hands, the bellies of pregnant women, on which occasion it is said that fire fell from Heaven; the Emperor, to guard himself against it, caused a room to be built entirely of stone. He gave many other instances of his unparalleled cruelty. He plucked off people’s nails from their hands and feet, from which my *Japanese* author says he ordered spades to be made for digging up roots. He tortured others by plucking the hair out of all parts of their bodies. Others he commanded to climb up high trees, and when they had reached the top, he would shoot at them with arrows, or order the trees to be sawed or shaken until they tumbled down, which...

About the same time the Doctrine of Amitabha, the Great Tathagata <note>original: "Jambadan Gonno Niorai"; refers to Amida Buddha, the "Nyorai" or Tathagata of the Pure Land</note> (that is, **Amida**, the great God and Patron of departed Souls) was brought over into China, or Baekje <note>original: "Fakkufai"; an ancient kingdom in Korea from which Buddhism actually reached Japan</note>, and spread into the neighbouring Countries. This Doctrine, continues he, did now manifest itself also in Japan <note>original: "Tsinokuni"</note>, at a place called **Naniwa** <note>modern-day Osaka</note>, where the Idol of **Amida** appeared at the entry of a Pond, environed with golden Rays, no body knowing how it was conveyed thither. The pious Emperor in memory of this miraculous event, instituted the first era name <note>term: "Nengo"; a system of naming periods of time based on an Emperor's reign or significant events</note> in Japan, and called it **Konquo**. The Idol itself was by Honda Yoshimitsu <note>original: "Tenda Josijmitz"; the legendary founder of Zenkō-ji</note>, a Prince of great Courage and Piety, carried into the Country of **Shinano**, and placed in the Temple of **Zenkō-ji** <note>original: "Sinquofi"</note>, where it afterwards by the name of **Zenkō-ji Nyorai** <note>original: "Sinquofi Norai"; meaning the Buddha of Zenkō-ji</note> wrought many great Miracles, which made that Temple famous all over the Empire. Thus far my Japanese Author. **Kimmei** reigned thirty-two and lived sixty-three years.

<margin>31st Mikado: BIDATSU <note>original: "Dai XXXI. FITATZU"</note></margin>
He was succeeded by his second Son **BIDATSU** <note>original: "FITATZU, or FINTATZ"</note>, in the year of Jinmu <note>original: "Synmn"; the Japanese calendar dating from the legendary first Emperor</note> 1232, of Christ 572.

My Author makes no mention of his Age, but sets down the following remarkable events, which happened during his reign.

In the third year of his reign, on the first day of the first month, was born, at the Emperor's court, **Prince Shōtoku** <note>original: "Sotoktais"; Shōtoku Taishi, the influential regent who promoted Buddhism</note>, the great Apostle of the Japanese. His birth was preceded and attended with several remarkable circumstances. His Mother one night in a dream saw herself environed with Celestial Rays, as bright as the Sun, and heard the following Words addressed to her:

> *I the holy Bodhisattva of Compassion <note>original: "Gusobofatz"; referring to Guze Kannon</note> must be born again to teach the world, and therefore I descend to enter into thy Womb:*

Upon which she awaked and found herself with child. Eight months after she heard the child speak distinctly in her womb, and in the twelfth month she was, not only without any pain, but with great delight and pleasure delivered of a Son, who was then named **Hachishi** <note>original: "Fatsisino"</note>, and after his death called **Taishi** and **Shōtoku Taishi**. The child very early gave tokens of his future greatness and piety. Devotion and prayers were his greatest delight in his tenderest years: When but four years old, and once in fervent prayers, the bones and relics of the burnt body of the great Shakyamuni <note>original: "Siaka"</note> were in a miraculous manner delivered into his hands.

The Idol Worship in general increased greatly in Japan during this Emperor's reign. Abundance of Idols, and Idol-carvers, and Priests, came over from several Countries beyond Sea.

In the sixth year of his reign an Edict was made public, importing, that on six several days of each month all living creatures whatsoever should be set at liberty, and that those of his subjects, who had none, would do well to buy some on purpose, that they should not want opportunities on those days to give public proofs of their merciful disposition towards these Creatures.

### Chap IV. The History of JAPAN

In the eighth year of his reign <note>referring to Emperor Bidatsu, the 31st Emperor</note>, the first Image of <term>Shakyamuni<note>original: "Siaka"; the historical Buddha</note></term> was brought over from across the sea and carried to Nara, into the Temple of <term>Kōfuku-ji<note>original: "Kobusi"; one of the powerful "Seven Great Temples" of Nara</note></term>, where it is still kept with great reverence, occupying the chief and most distinguished place in that temple.

In the fourteenth year of his reign, a man named <term>Moriya<note>Mononobe no Moriya, a high-ranking official who led the resistance against the introduction of Buddhism</note></term>, a great antagonist and declared enemy of <term>Prince Shōtoku<note>original: "Sotoktais"; the prince-regent credited with establishing Buddhism and centralized government in Japan</note></term>, caused great troubles and religious strife in the Empire. He held a deadly hatred for all the <term>Buddhas<note>original: "Fotoge"; likely a rendering of 'Hotoke', referring to Buddhist statues or deities</note></term>, or idols of the country, which he took out of the temples and burned wherever he could find them. But within two years, his enemies gained the upper hand; he was defeated and paid with his life for his bold undertaking. It is added that after he had thrown the ashes of the burned idols into a lake, there suddenly arose a most terrifying storm of thunder, lightning, and rain.

He reigned fourteen years. It is not known how long he lived.

<margin>The 32nd Emperor: JOMEI.</margin>
He was succeeded by **JOMEI**, his fourth son, in the year 1246 from the era of <term>Jimmu<note>original: "Synmu"; the legendary first Emperor and founder of the imperial line</note></term>, and the year of Christ 586.

My author is entirely silent about the age of this Emperor and that of several of his successors.

Under his reign, Moriya was defeated and killed, and the Temple <term>Sakatarina</term> was built in the small province of <term>Tamatsukuri</term> to commemorate this event.

He reigned only two years.

<margin>The 33rd Emperor: SUSHUN.</margin>
**SUSHUN**, his brother, succeeded him in the year 1248 from Jimmu, and the year of Christ 588.

In the third year of his reign, in the seventh month, the Empire of Japan was first divided into seven large regions called <term>Goki Shichidō<note>original: "Goki Sitzi Do"; meaning "Five Provinces and Seven Circuits", a system of administrative geography</note></term>. This division (of which I have provided a more detailed account in the fifth chapter of the first book) still exists and is to be observed in all their maps.

He reigned five years and died.

<margin>The 34th Empress: SUIKO.</margin>
**SUIKO** (also called *Syko*), the second daughter of Emperor Kimmei and the widow of Emperor <term>Bidatsu<note>original: "Fitatz"</note></term>, succeeded Sushun on the throne in the year 1253 from Jimmu, and the year of Christ 593.

In the fifth year of her reign, a foreign prince from <term>Baekje<note>original: "Fakuſai"; an ancient kingdom in southwestern Korea</note></term> came over to her court, solely to pay his respects to Prince Shōtoku.

In the sixth year of her reign, a crow and a peacock were brought over from across the sea as a present to the Empress. Both species still survive there, and the crows in particular have multiplied to such a degree that they currently do a great deal of damage.

In the seventh year of her reign, all of Japan was shaken by earthquakes in a terrifying manner, and vast numbers of buildings were collapsed and swallowed up.

The following year, fire fell from the sky, followed by such a quantity of rain that many towns were flooded.

In the tenth year of her reign, a religious book called <term>Rekkoto-so<note>likely referring to the 'Rekidō', books on the calendar and divination brought from Korea</note></term> was brought over from Baekje.

### The History of JAPAN. Book II.

In the twelfth year, the Empress caused a statue of <term>Shakyamuni<note>original: "Siaka"; the historical Buddha</note></term> to be cast in brass. This statue was afterwards melted down to coin money, and another made of plaster, or stucco, was put in its place. The same year, gold was first brought over into Japan from Korea.

In the twenty-first year of her reign, <term>Bodhidharma<note>original: "Darma"; the semi-legendary monk credited with bringing Zen Buddhism to China</note></term> is said to have appeared to <term>Prince Shōtoku<note>original: "Sotoktais"; the influential regent and scholar-prince</note></term>, in the province of <term>Yamato<note>original: "Jamatta"</note></term>, on Mount <term>Kataoka<note>original: "Katta Joka"</note></term>; and it is added, that they composed verses spontaneously for one another.

In the twenty-eighth year of her reign, on the twenty-second day of the second month, <term>Prince Shōtoku</term> died in the forty-ninth year of his age.

In the thirty-fifth year of her reign, a swarm of strange flies was observed in the country, which made a great humming noise and did much mischief.

**Suiko** died after a reign of thirty-six years.

<margin>
The 35th Emperor:
JOMEI.
</margin>
**JOMEI**, the grandson of Emperor <term>Bidatsu<note>original: "Fitatz"</note></term>, succeeded her in the year 1289 of the <term>Jimmu<note>original: "Synmu"; the legendary first Emperor</note></term> epoch, and the year of Christ 629.

He resided in **Yamato**.

In the third year of his reign, on the first day of the first month, the great devotee <term>En no Gyōja<note>original: "Gienno Giosa"</note></term> was born in Japan. He was the founder of the religious order of Japanese hermits, or <term>Yamabushi<note>original: "Jammabos"; literally "mountain-warriors," these were ascetic practitioners of Shugendō</note></term>, as they are called—that is, mountain priests or religious persons living in the mountains, woods, and deserts. The same year, a comet appeared. (*A full account of this order is given in the fifth chapter of the third book of this history.*)

In the twelfth year of his reign, on the seventh day of the second month, a star was observed in the moon.

He reigned twelve years.

<margin>
The 36th Sovereign:
KŌGYOKU.
</margin>
**KŌGYOKU**, his imperial consort and the daughter of Emperor Bidatsu by adoption, succeeded him in the year 1302 of the Jimmu epoch, and the year of Christ 642.

In the second year of her reign, five different colors were observed in the sky. The same year, in the fourth month, a great deal of hail fell.

She reigned three years.

<margin>
The 37th Emperor:
KŌTOKU.
</margin>
**KŌTOKU**, her younger brother, succeeded her in the year 1305 of the Jimmu epoch, and the year of Christ 645.

He removed his <term>Miyako<note>original: "Miaco"; the capital city and imperial residence</note></term> to **Naniwa Nagara-toyosaki**.

He was the first to honor his ministers and other officers of his court with titles and marks of distinction according to their several ranks and stations. He also regulated the manner in which due respect should be paid to secular persons not belonging to his court but placed in civil employments.

The years having been computed until then only by the <term>Ninnō Epoch<note>original: "Nin O Epocha"; the era of the human sovereigns, dating from the start of Jimmu's reign</note></term>, or from the beginning of the reign of Jimmu, the founder of the Japanese monarchy, he introduced shorter periods, called <term>Nengō<note>original: "Nengo's"</note></term>, into use, and ordered them to be observed throughout his empire. These era names, however, were not of his own invention, but were introduced by him in imitation of the Chinese,

### Chapter IV. The History of JAPAN.

The <term>Nengō<note>Japanese era names used to track time based on an Emperor's reign or significant events</note></term> system was adopted from the **Chinese**, where it had been in use for several centuries, having been established by the **Chinese** Emperor **Guangwu** <note>original: "Koo Bu"</note> soon after his accession to the throne, about 140 years before the birth of Christ. These era names are composed, as I have shown above, of two characters and are commonly dated from some remarkable event. As it is entirely up to the Emperor’s will and pleasure to begin and name them, he can allow them to continue as long as he pleases, or until some significant change in the religious or political state of the country gives rise to a new one. In their letters, account books, almanacs, and in daily conversation, these **Nengō** are commonly used, as it is a much easier and shorter way of calculating dates. In their annals, histories, and other printed books, the year of the <term>Jimmu<note>original: "Synmu" or "Nino"; the chronological era dating back to the first legendary Emperor, Jimmu, in 660 BCE</note></term> epoch is also added. The first **Nengō** was <term>Hakuchi<note>original: "Fakutsij"; meaning "White Pheasant"</note></term>, which began in the sixth year of the reign of this Emperor <note>Emperor Kōtoku</note>, which was the year 1310 of the **Jimmu** era, and 650 AD. It continued for twenty-two years, specifically until the first year of the reign of Emperor **Tenmu**.

He reigned ten years.

<margin>
The 38th Sovereign:
SAIMEI
</margin>
**SAIMEI** <note>original: "Si Me"</note>, the daughter of Empress **Kōgyoku**, an unmarried Princess, succeeded her uncle in the year 1315 of the **Jimmu** era (645 AD).

She soon moved her court and residence to **Hunga** in the province of <term>Yamato<note>original: "Jamatto"</note></term>, and in the last year of her reign, she moved to **Asakura**.

She reigned seven years, during which time her uncle’s first **Nengo** was continued.

<margin>
The 39th Sovereign:
TENJI
</margin>
**TENJI** <note>original: "Tentsii"</note>, the son of Emperor **Jomei** and the <term>itoko<note>original: "itoku"; the Japanese word for cousin</note></term> of Empress **Kōgyoku**, succeeded **Saimei** in the year 1322 of the **Jimmu** era (662 AD). (**Itoko** refers to cousins, such as the son of a father’s or mother’s brother or sister.)

In the fourth year of his reign, the famous temple <term>Seigan-ji<note>original: "See Guanfi"</note></term> was built, and its primary idol was carved by the famous master **Kasuga** <note>original: "Kassiga"</note>, who was sainted after his death for his incomparable skill in this sort of craftsmanship.

In the sixth year of his reign, he moved his court and residence to **Shiga**, in the province of **Otsu**.

In the tenth year of his reign, a monstrous stag with eight legs was displayed in the province of **Chikugo**.

He reigned ten years.

<margin>
The 40th Sovereign:
TENMU
</margin>
**TENMU**, his younger brother, succeeded him in the year 1332 of the **Jimmu** era (672 AD).

It was not without great trouble and difficulty that this Emperor gained possession of the throne, as it was contested by his younger brother <term>Prince Ōtomo<note>original: "Oto Mo No Oosi"; later recognized as Emperor Kōbun</note></term>, who resolved to maintain his claim to the crown by force of arms at the head of a numerous army. However, this unhappy pretender was entirely defeated within five months, at which point, out of despair, he <term>committed ritual suicide<note>original: "ript open his own belly"; a reference to seppuku</note></term>. His body was honorably interred in the temple of **Okamoto**, located in the province of **Yamato**, in the ninth month of his brother’s reign.

# The History of JAPAN. Book II.

---

In memory of this victory, **Tenmu** established the <term>Nengō Hakuhō<note>original: "Nengo Fakwo"; an era name meaning "White Phoenix," typically chosen to mark a joyous or auspicious event</note></term>, which lasted fourteen years, until the beginning of the third era, <term>Shuchō<note>original: "Siuwu"</note></term>.

In the second year of his reign, the famous Temple **Mii-dera** <note>A significant Buddhist temple of the Tendai sect near Lake Biwa</note> was built. That same year, the holy book <term>Issaikyō<note>original: "Iffaikio"; the complete collection of Buddhist scriptures</note></term>, which is a type of prayer book, was brought over from **China**.

In the third year of his reign, silver was brought over from **Tsushima**, where they had begun to mine and process it. <note>This marks a significant milestone in Japanese mineralogy and currency history.</note>

In the fourth year of his reign, on the fourth day of the fourth month, the first **Matsuri** was celebrated at **Nara** and **Tatsuta**, an example that was afterwards followed by several other places in the Empire. A **Matsuri** is a great festival day, celebrated in honor of the God who is acknowledged as the particular patron and protector of a place; it is celebrated with all the pomp and splendor imaginable, with solemn processions, grand plays, dances, musical concerts, and other entertainment.

In the seventh year of his reign, in the sixth month, hail fell as large as peaches.

In the eighth year, they had ripe peaches at **Ikedamura** in the first month, which corresponds with our **February**. <note>In traditional historiography, such unusual seasonal occurrences were often recorded as celestial omens or signs of the Emperor's influence.</note>

That same year, on the third day of the eleventh month, the sky appeared very luminous to the east, looking as if it were all in flames.

In the ninth year, the use of silver money was forbidden, and in its place brass <term>Zeni<note>original: "Sennis"; small copper or brass coins with a hole in the middle</note></term> were minted, which are called <term>Pitis<note>original: "Puties"; a term likely derived from the Javanese "pitis," used by European traders to describe low-value Asian coinage</note></term> by foreigners.

Around this time, the Empire of **Japan** was divided into sixty-six provinces. (The islands of **Iki** and **Tsushima**, which formerly belonged to the Kingdom of **Korea**, having been conquered and annexed to the Empire of **Japan** in the preceding century, mean there are now sixty-eight provinces in all.)

In the thirteenth year of his reign, on the fourteenth day of the tenth month, a violent earthquake occurred.

In the fourteenth year of his reign, a new **Nengō** called **Shuchō** <note>original: "Suiwu"</note> was established, which lasted only one year.

That same year, the Emperor died on the ninth day of the ninth month. His death caused fresh troubles at the <term>Imperial Court<note>referred to here as the "Ecclesiastical Court" due to the sacred nature of the Japanese Emperor's office</note></term>, raised by **Prince Ōtsu** <note>original: "Ootzno Ofi"</note> regarding the succession.

<margin>The 41st Sovereign: JITŌ</margin>
**JITŌ**, the Emperor **Tenmu's** Imperial Consort and also his niece, succeeded her husband and uncle despite the claims of **Prince Ōtsu**, in the year 1347 of the <term>Jimmu era<note>The traditional Japanese chronological system dating from the first Emperor, Jimmu</note></term> (687 AD).

She resided at **Fujiwara** in **Yamato**.

In the sixth year of her reign, the first <term>Sake<note>original: "Sakki"; Japanese rice wine</note></term> was brewed in **Hekishinokori** in the province of **Ōmi**.

She reigned ten years.

<margin>The 42nd Sovereign: MONMU</margin>
She was succeeded by **MONMU**, **Tenmu's** grandson, in the year 1357 of the **Jimmu era** (697 AD).

### Chap. IV. The History of J A P A N.

Soon after his accession to the Throne he begun a new <term>Nengo<note>An era name or "reign name" used for dating years</note></term>, call'd *Gen* <note>original: "Gen"; likely referring to the Keiun era (704–708)</note>, which continu'd four years, and was follow'd by the *Nengos*, *Tenpo* <note>likely the Taihō era</note> of three years, and *Keewuun* <note>Keiun</note> of four years, but little us'd.

He was the first that granted <term>Tsiaps<note>original: "Tsiaps"; refers to "mon" or heraldic coats of arms</note></term>, or particular Coats of Arms, to each Province, which was done in the eighth year of his reign.

In the ninth year he caus'd a square measure, (by the *Japanese* call'd <term>Seo<note>shō</note></term> and <term>Maas<note>masu</note></term>, by the *Dutch* <term>Ganten<note>original: "Ganten"; from the Malay/Dutch "gantang," a unit of volume</note></term>, three of which contain exactly four pound of Rice, *Dutch* weight) to be made of wood, and to be sent as a Pattern into all the Provinces of his Empire, with strict orders that thenceforward it should be a standard for measuring of Rice, Corn, and other Grain.

He reign'd eleven years.

<margin>
43rd Sovereign.
GENMEI.
</margin>
**GENMEI**, the Emperor **Tentsij’s** <note>Tenji</note> Daughter succeeded him by virtue of her hereditary right, in the year of <term>Synmu<note>The traditional Japanese calendar counting from the legendary first Emperor, Jinmu</note></term> 1368, of Christ 708.

She resided at **Nara**.

She instituted a new *Nengo*, *Wat To* <note>Wadō era (708–715)</note>, which continu'd seven years, till the *Nengo Reiki*.

In the first year of her reign, she order'd Money to be coin'd in Gold and Silver, but the latter was again prohibited the next year. The same first year was born **Abenokamar** <note>likely referring to the scholar Abe no Nakamaro</note>, a Prince of the Imperial blood, very famous in *Japanese* Histories.

In the third year of her reign was built the famous Temple **Koobokusi** <note>Kōfuku-ji in Nara</note>, where there is an Idol of <term>Siaka<note>Shaka or Shakyamuni, the historical Buddha</note></term>, cast in a mixt metal of brass and gold, by the great Master **Taifoquan**.

In the sixth year of her reign she settled the Names of all the Provinces, Cities and Villages throughout the Empire, and order'd that they should be enter'd into the publick Records.

She reign'd seven years, and died.

<margin>
44th Sovereign.
GENSIO.
</margin>
She was succeeded by **GENSIOO** <note>Genshō</note>, the Emperor **Tenmu's** Grand-daughter by his Son, in the year of *Synmu* 1375, of Christ 715, in the ninth month.

This Empress instituted the *Nengos Reiki* of two, and *Jooro* <note>Yōrō</note> of seven years.

Her reign is particularly famous for the miraculous appearance of the Gods, <term>Khumano Gongin<note>Kumano Gongen</note></term>, **Amida**, **Jakusi** <note>Yakushi Nyorai, the Medicine Buddha</note>, <term>Senfiu Quanwon<note>Senju Kannon, the Thousand-Armed Goddess of Mercy</note></term>, and <term>Bissam-monten<note>Bishamonten, one of the Seven Lucky Gods and protector of Buddhism</note></term>, in several parts of the Empire.

In the fifth year of her reign she made new regulations concerning the dress of women.

She reign'd nine years, and resign'd the Crown to **Sioomu** <note>Shōmu</note> her Brother's Son. She liv'd twenty five years after her resignation, and died in the forty eighth year of her age, and the year of *Synmu* 1408 in the fourth month.

<margin>
45th Sovereign.
SIOOMU.
</margin>
**SIOOMU** came to the Crown, by his Aunt's resignation, in the year of *Synmu* 1384, of Christ 724.

### The History of JAPAN. Book II.

He <note>Emperor Shōmu</note> first resided at **Nara**, from whence he removed to **Naniwa** <note>modern-day Osaka</note>, four years before his death.

He instituted the <term>Nengo Sinki<note>The Jinki era (724–729)</note></term> in the first year of his reign, which lasted five years, and was followed by the <term>Nengo Tempe<note>The Tenpyō era (729–749)</note></term>, which continued twenty.

In the eighth year of his reign, the Japanese Histories mention that the Sea upon the Coasts of **Kij** <note>Kii Province</note> looked red, like blood, for five days successively, and that the ensuing year followed dreadful storms, a great drought, and a sterile crop, particularly in the **Gokoks** <note>The "Five Grains" or the core agricultural provinces</note>, which occasioned a great famine.

In the thirteenth year, the Smallpox was very mortal in all parts of the Empire. (The Japanese Physicians distinguish between three sorts of the Smallpox. What we properly call the Smallpox, is by them called <term>Fooso<note>Hōsō</note></term>; another sort is called <term>Fasika<note>Hashika</note></term>, these are the Measles. The third kind is called <term>Kare<note>Likely mizuhōsoro or "watery pustules"</note></term>, which is as much as to say, Watery Pustules. They think it very material, in the cure of the Smallpox, to wrap up the patient in red cloth. When one of the Emperor's Children falls sick of this Distemper, not only the room and bed are furnished with red, but all persons that come near the Patient must be clad in gowns of the same colour. The Great Pox <note>Syphilis</note> is not unknown in *Japan*, and they call it <term>Nambankassa<note>Literally "The Southern Barbarian Sore," as it was believed to have been introduced by the Portuguese</note></term>, that is, the *Portuguese* Disease.)

In the sixteenth year of his reign, they began to build Nunneries in *Japan*.

In the twentieth year was built the great Temple of <term>Daibods<note>Daibutsu, the "Great Buddha" at Nara</note></term>.

**Sioomu** <note>Shōmu</note> reigned in all twenty-five years.

<margin>
46th Sovereign.
KOOKEN.
</margin>
He was succeeded by his Daughter **KOOKEN**, in the year of <term>Synmu<note>The traditional Japanese calendar counting from the legendary first Emperor, Jinmu</note></term> 1409, of *Christ* 749, on the second day of the seventh month.

Whether or no she was married, is not mentioned in my Authors <note>As was tradition for reigning Empresses of this era, Kōken remained an unmarried vestal</note>.

With her reign began the <term>Nengo Tempe Seofo<note>Tenpyō-shōhō</note></term>, or <term>Foosi<note>Hōji</note></term>, which continued eight years till the <term>Nengo Tempe Singo<note>Tenpyō-jingo</note></term>.

In the first year of her reign, Gold was first dug up in **Osio** <note>Ōshū, in Northern Japan</note>, and presented to the Empress. This Metal had been till then imported from *China*.

In the fourth year of her reign she built the Temple **Toodaisi** <note>Tōdai-ji</note>, pursuant to a Vow made by the late Emperor her Father, who was by his death prevented to accomplish it. Upon the consecration of this Temple, one **Giogij** <note>Gyōki, a famous monk</note> in his prayers desired the assistance of <term>Barramoas<note>Baramon Sōjō, an Indian Buddhist monk also known as Bodhisena</note></term>, an eminent God <note>The author uses "God" for a holy man or Buddhist figure</note> in the western parts of the *Indies* (with regard to *Japan*) who accordingly came over in a miraculous manner, and appeared to him that very instant.

About the same time was built **Isia Jamma** <note>Ishiyama-dera</note>.

### Chap IV. The History of J A P A N.

She <note>Empress Kōken</note> reign’d ten years.

47th Sovereign:
**FAI TAI**
<note>Emperor Junnin, r. 758–764</note>

Nothing remarkable happen’d during his reign, but that in the third year he remov’d his court and residence to **Fora** in **Oomi** <note>Hora-no-miya in Ōmi Province</note>, in the fourth to **Tairanokio** <note>Heijō-kyō, or Nara</note>, and in the sixth to **Fairo** in the Province of **Awadsi** <note>Awaji</note>.

**SEO TOKU**, the Empress **Kooken’s** eldest daughter, succeeded him in the year of **Synmu** 1425, and the year of Christ 765.

She begun with her reign a new <term>Nengo<note>An era name used for dating</note></term>, which she call’d **Sinkake Un** <note>Jingō-keiun era</note>, and which continued two years, till the <term>Nengo</term> **Fooke** <note>Hōki era</note>, which continued three years.

During her reign was born **Kiamar** <note>Kibi no Makibi, a scholar and courtier</note>, who afterwards became a very eminent <term>Kuge<note>A member of the aristocratic court nobility</note></term>, or a great Man at Court.

<margin>
49th Sovereign:
**KOONIN**
<note>Emperor Kōnin, r. 770–781</note>
</margin>
**KOONIN**, **Ten Tsij’s** <note>Emperor Tenji</note> Grandson, succeeded her in the year of **Synmu** 1430, and the year of Christ 770.

With his reign began the <term>Nengo</term>, call’d **Fooki** <note>Hōki era</note>, which subsisted eleven years.

In the second year of his reign, there happen’d a storm of thunder and lightning, dreadful beyond Expression. It rain’d fire from Heaven, like stars, and the air was fill’d with a frightful noise. The Emperor for this reason order’d <term>Matsuri’s<note>Shinto festivals or solemn rituals</note></term>, or solemn festivals and processions, to be celebrated in all parts of the Empire, to honour and to appease the angry **Jakusi**, or the evil Spirits, who have the command of the air and fields. <note>The author identifies "Jakusi" as evil spirits, though the name usually refers to Yakushi Nyorai, the Medicine Buddha, often invoked for protection against disasters.</note>

In the fifth year of his reign was born **Kobotais** <note>Kōbō-Daishi, also known as Kūkai</note>, an eminent Priest and great Saint among the Japanese.

In the eighth year the River **Fuju Usingava** <note>Likely the Uji River</note> dried quite up.

In the tenth year died in **China**, **Abeno Nakemar** <note>Abe no Nakamaro</note>, a Man very famous in Japanese Histories. <note>Nakamaro was a Japanese scholar-poet who served in the Chinese Tang court.</note>

In the same tenth year a dreadful fire broke out at **Miaco** <note>Kyoto</note>, which destroy’d all the Temples of that City.

In the eleventh year he appointed a new <term>Nengo</term>, which he call’d **Tenwo** <note>Ten’ō era</note>, and which subsisted but one year.

He reign’d in all but twelve years.

50th Sovereign:
**KWAN MU**
<note>Emperor Kanmu, r. 781–806</note>
</margin>
He was succeeded by his son **KWAN MU**, in the year of **Synmu** 1442, of Christ 782, and the forty-sixth of his age.

Soon after his accession to the Throne he begun a new <term>Nengo</term> call’d **Fenriaku** <note>Enryaku era</note>, which subsisted twenty-four years.

In the third year of his reign he remov’d his court and residence to **Nagajoka** in **Jamasijro** <note>Nagaoka-kyō in Yamashiro Province</note>, and eleven years after to **Fejankio** <note>Heian-kyō, the site of modern-day Kyoto</note>.

In the sixth year of his reign a foreign people, who were not Chinese, but natives of some further distant Country, came over to invade **Japan** in a hostile manner. The Japanese did what they could to get rid of them,

Nine years after they arrived, **Tamamar** <note>Sakanoue no Tamuramaro (758–811), a famous general and the first to be granted the title of Shogun</note>, a renowned and brave General, was sent against them with great success; he reduced their numbers significantly and killed their **Troji** <note>likely a corruption of *Taishō*, meaning Commander-in-chief</note>. However, they continued to resist for some time, and were not entirely defeated until the year of **Synmu** <note>the traditional Japanese era dating from the first Emperor, Jinmu, beginning in 660 BCE</note> 1466 [806 AD], eighteen years after their first arrival.

**Quanmu** <note>Emperor Kanmu, r. 781–806</note> reigned for 24 years and died at 70 years of age.

51st Sovereign:
**FEI DSIO**
<note>Emperor Heizei, r. 806–809</note>

He was succeeded by his eldest son **FEI DSIO**, in the year of **Synmu** 1496 <note>original: "1496", though chronologically this should be 1466 to match the date 806 AD</note>, and in the year of Christ 806 <note>original: "206", a likely printing error for 806</note>.

Nothing remarkable happened during his reign, except that a new <term>Nengo<note>An era name used for dating</note></term> began with it, which was called **Taito** <note>Daidō era</note>, and lasted four years.

He reigned four years and died.

<margin>
52nd Sovereign:
**SA GA**
<note>Emperor Saga, r. 809–823</note>
</margin>
He was succeeded by his younger brother **SA GA**, the Emperor **Quanmu**'s second son, in the year of **Synmu** 1470, and in the year of Christ 810.

Soon after his accession to the throne, he began the <term>Nengo</term> **Koonin** <note>Kōnin era</note>, which continued until his death, for a space of fourteen years. During this time, nothing remarkable happened, except that several stately **Sjin** or **Mija** <note>Shinto shrines, dedicated to the native spirits</note>, and **Budsussi** or **Tira** <note>Buddhist temples</note>—that is, Temples of the local Gods and of foreign Idols—were erected in several parts of the Empire.

He reigned in all fourteen years.

<margin>
53rd Sovereign:
**SIUN WA**
<note>Emperor Junna, r. 823–833</note>
</margin>
He was succeeded by his younger brother **SIUN WA**, who was the Emperor **Quanmu**'s third son, in the year of **Synmu** 1484, and in the year of Christ 824.

He followed the customs of his predecessors by appointing a new <term>Nengo</term> soon after his accession to the throne, which was called **Ten Tsio** <note>Tenchō era</note> and lasted ten years.

In the second year of his reign, my Author observes that **Urasima** <note>Urashima Tarō, a famous figure in Japanese folklore</note> returned from **Foreisan** <note>Mount Hōrai, the mythical land of eternal youth</note> to Japan in the 348th year of his age. He had lived all the while under water with the **Water-Gods**, where it is believed that people do not grow old.

**Siunwa** reigned ten years.

**NINMIO**
<note>Emperor Ninmyō, r. 833–850</note>
</margin>
**NINMIO** succeeded him in the year of **Synmu** 1494, and in the year of Christ 834.

This Emperor was **Saga**'s second son and **Siunwa**'s **Oi** <note>nephew</note> by his brother.

In the first year of his reign, he appointed the <term>Nengo</term> **Sioa** <note>Jōwa era</note>, which continued fourteen years, and was followed by the <term>Nengo</term> **Kassoo** <note>Kashō era</note>, which lasted three years.

He reigned seventeen years.

**MONTOKU**
<note>Emperor Montoku, r. 850–858</note>
</margin>
**MONTOKU**, or **Bontoku**, his first-born son, succeeded him in the year of **Synmu** 1511, and in the year of Christ 851.

After his accession to the throne, he appointed the <term>Nengo</term> **Ninsiu** <note>Ninju era</note>, which continued three years, and was followed by the <term>Nengo</term>s **Saije** <note>Saikō era</note> and **Tenjan** <note>Ten'an era</note>, the first lasting three years and the second two years.

### Chapter IV. The History of JAPAN

In the fourth year of his reign, several violent Earthquakes happened in Japan, by one of which, on the fifth day of the fifth month, the head of the great **Daibuts** <note>Daibutsu, or "Great Buddha," a massive bronze statue</note>, or Idol of **Siaka** <note>Shakyamuni, the historical Buddha</note>, was thrown down to the ground in his Temple at **Miaco** <note>Kyoto, the imperial capital</note>.

**Montoku** <note>Emperor Montoku, r. 850–858</note> reigned eight years.

<margin>56th Sovereign: **SEIWA** <note>r. 858–876</note></margin>
He was succeeded by his fourth Son **SEIWA**, in the year of **Synmu** <note>the traditional Japanese era dating from the first Emperor, Jinmu</note> 1519 [859 AD].

He followed his Predecessors in appointing a new <term>Nengo<note>An era name used for dating and identifying periods of a reign</note></term> after his accession to the throne, which was called **Toquam** <note>Jōgan era</note>, and subsisted eighteen years.

In the fifth year of this Emperor's reign, the Books of the illustrious Chinese Philosopher **Confutius** <note>Confucius</note> were first brought to Court, read and well liked.

In the ninth year of his reign, was born in **Jamatto** <note>Yamato Province</note>, **Isje** <note>Lady Ise, a famous poet and high-ranking lady of the court</note>, a daughter of **Tfike Kugu** <note>Fujiwara no Tsugukage</note>, a Prince of the Imperial Blood. This Lady became afterwards very famous for her uncommon Learning, of which she gave a proof to the world by writing a Book, which is highly esteemed in Japan to this day.

**Seiwa** reigned eighteen years, and resigned the crown to his son.

He died four years after his abdication, on the 8th day of the fifth month.

<margin>57th Sovereign: **JO SEI** <note>Emperor Yōzei, r. 876–884</note></margin>
**JO SEI**, **Sewa**'s eldest Son, was but nine years old, when his Father resigned the crown to him in the year of **Synmu** 1537 [877 AD].

With his reign a new <term>Nengo</term> was begun, which subsisted eight years, and was called **Genjwa** <note>Gangyō era</note>.

In the third year of his reign, two Suns appeared in China <note>a celestial omen recorded in East Asian chronicles, often interpreted as a sign of political upheaval</note>.

The crown was so great a burden to this Emperor, that in a short time he lost his senses. For this reason the **Quanbuku** <note>Kanpaku, the Chief Advisor or Regent to the Emperor</note>, as he is called, or Prime Minister, who is the first person after the Emperor, thought it necessary to depose him, which was done accordingly, after he had reigned eight years. And

<margin>58th Sovereign: **KOOKO** <note>Emperor Kōkō, r. 884–887</note></margin>
**KOOKO**, the Emperor **Nimio**'s <note>Emperor Ninmyō</note> second Son, and **Montoku**'s younger Brother, was put into his place, in the year of **Synmu** 1545 [885 AD].

In the first year of his reign, in the seventh month, it rained Sand and Stones, which destroyed almost the whole crop of rice.

With his reign began the <term>Nengo</term> **Ninwa** <note>Ninna era</note>, which lasted four years.

He reigned but three years.

<margin>59th Sovereign: **UDA** <note>Emperor Uda, r. 887–897</note></margin>
He was succeeded by his third Son **UDA**, in the year of **Synmu** 1548 [888 AD].

This Emperor in the second year of his reign, appointed a new <term>Nengo</term> called **Quanpe** <note>Kanpyō era</note>, which continued nine years.

<margin>60th Sovereign: DAIGO</margin>
His eldest Son **DAI GO** <note>Emperor Daigo, r. 897–930 AD</note>, succeeded him in the year of **Synmu** <note>The traditional Japanese calendar starting from the first Emperor, Jinmu</note> 1558 [898 AD].

The <term>Nengo’s<note>Era names used to divide an Emperor's reign into smaller chronological periods</note></term> appointed by this Emperor were, **Sootai** <note>Shōtai era, 898–901</note> of three years, at the beginning of his reign, **Jengi** <note>Engi era, 901–923</note> of two and twenty years, and **Jentsjo** <note>Enchō era, 923–931</note> of eight.

In the second year, died **Somme Donno** <note>Fujiwara no Onshi, also known as Somedono</note>, who was declared **Kissaki** <note>Kisaki</note>, that is, the supreme Woman, which is the title given to that of the **Dairi’s** <note>The Emperor's</note> Women, whom he declares Empress, and who is the mother of the presumptive Heir of the Crown.

In the sixteenth year, on the second day of the fifth month, a fire broke out at **Miaco** <note>Kyoto, then the imperial capital</note>, the Emperor’s residence, which consumed 617 Houses.

In the twenty-sixth year a Hare with eight legs was sent to court out of the Province **Jamatto** <note>Yamato Province</note>. <note>In historical chronicles, such mutations were often recorded as significant omens.</note>

He reigned in all thirty-three years.

<margin>61st Sovereign: SUZAKU</margin>

In the second year of his reign **Massakaddo** <note>Taira no Masakado</note>, a Prince of the Imperial Blood, and one of the chief men at Court, revolted against him. This rebellion could not be suppressed till seven years after, when **Massakaddo** was defeated and killed. <note>Masakado is famous for leading one of the most significant early provincial rebellions against the central government.</note>

In the third year of his reign on the twenty seventh day of the seventh month happened a violent Earthquake, and another in the seventh year, on the fifteenth day of the fourth month. During his reign, **Japan** was much troubled with Storms of thunder and lightning, which fell upon several Temples and religious Houses, and laid them in ashes. Particularly in the thirteenth year of his reign, the storms were almost universal in all the Provinces of the Empire.

He reigned sixteen years.

### Chap IV. The History of JAPAN.

The <term>Nengo's<note>Era names used in Japan to divide an Emperor's reign into smaller chronological periods</note></term> of this period were **Tentoku** <note>957–961 AD</note> for four years, **Oowa** <note>Ōwa, 961–964 AD</note> for three, and **Koofu** <note>Kōhō, 964–968 AD</note> for four years.

In the fourteenth year of his reign, a kind of Synod, or Council, was held at Court in the great hall **Seiro deen** <note>The Seiryō-den, or 'Serene Cool Hall,' a primary hall in the Imperial Palace used for ceremonies and research</note> regarding matters of religion. The heads of the several sects then existing were present.

<margin>
63rd Sovereign:
**RENSEI**
</margin>
He reigned twenty-one years.

He was succeeded by **RENSEI** <note>Emperor Reizei, r. 967–969 AD</note>, or according to another author, *Rei Sen*, his second son. He came to the crown in the sixty-first year of his age <note>Historical records suggest he was actually 17 when he ascended; the original text may reflect a different tradition or a transcription error</note>, which was the year of **Synmu** <note>The traditional Japanese calendar beginning from the reign of the first Emperor, Jimmu</note> 1628, or 968 AD.

He reigned only two years, during which time the *Nengo* **Anwa** <note>Anna era, 968–970 AD</note> continued, having begun with his reign.

64th Sovereign:
**JENWO**
</margin>
**JENWO** <note>Emperor En'yū, r. 969–984 AD</note>, or as others pronounce it, *Jen Jo*, his younger brother and the Emperor *Murakami's* fifth son, succeeded him in the year of **Synmu** 1630, or 970 AD.

The *Nengo's* of his reign were **Tenrok** <note>Tenroku, 970–973 AD</note> for three years, begun with his accession to the throne; **Teijen** <note>Ten'en, 973–976 AD</note> likewise of three years; **Teiquan** <note>Jōgen, 976–978 AD</note> for two years; **Tengen** <note>978–983 AD</note> for five years; and lastly **Jeiquan** <note>Eikan, 983–985 AD</note> for two years.

<margin>
65th Sovereign:
**KWASSAN**
</margin>
He reigned in all fifteen years.

**QUASSAN** <note>Emperor Kazan, r. 984–986 AD</note>, or *Kwassan*, the Emperor *Rensei's* first son and *Jenwo's* nephew, succeeded him in the year of **Synmu** 1645, or 985 AD, in the seventeenth year of his age.

He established a new *Nengo* after he came to the crown, which was called **Genwa** <note>Kanna era, 985–987 AD</note> and continued only two years.

In the second year of his reign, which was the second of the said *Nengo*, he was suddenly overcome with such a desire for retirement and a religious life that he left his palace privately in the night time. He retired into the monastery of **Quansi** <note>Kazan-ji, a temple in Kyoto</note>, where he had himself shaved like the rest of the monks and took the religious name **Nigugaks Foogu** <note>Nyūgaku Hongō</note>. In this monastery he lived twenty-two years, and was forty-one years old when he died.

**ITSI DSIO**
</margin>
**ITSI DSIO** <note>Emperor Ichijō, r. 986–1011 AD</note>, the Emperor *Jenwo's* son and the late Emperor’s cousin, succeeded him after his retirement into a convent in the year of **Synmu** 1647, or 987 AD.

The *Nengo's* appointed during his reign were **Jejen** <note>Eien, 987–989 AD</note> for two, **Jengen** <note>Eisō, 989–990 AD</note> for one, **Soorak** <note>Shōryaku, 990–995 AD</note> for five, **Tsio Toku** <note>Chōtoku, 995–999 AD</note> for four, **Tsioofo** <note>Chōhō, 999–1004 AD</note> for five, and **Quanko** <note>Kankō, 1004–1012 AD</note> for eight years.

In the eighth year of his reign, there was a great mortality <note>Likely a reference to the devastating smallpox or measles epidemics of the late 10th century</note> all over **Japan**.

His reign was famous for several eminent and learned men who then flourished at Court.

# The History of JAPAN. Book II.

He appointed the <term>Nengo<note>An era name used in Japan to divide an Emperor's reign into smaller chronological periods</note></term> **Chōwa** <note>original: "Dsio A"; 1012–1017 AD</note>, which lasted for five years.

In the third year of his reign, his residence burned down, as did a great part of the city a year later.

He reigned five years and died at 51 years of age.

<margin>
68th Sovereign:
**GO-ICHIJŌ**
</margin>
He was succeeded by **GO-ICHIJŌ** <note>r. 1016–1036 AD</note>, that is, Ichijō the Second, who was the second son of Ichijō the First. He ascended to the Crown in the year of <term>Synmu<note>The traditional Japanese calendar counting from the reign of the first Emperor, Jimmu</note></term> 1677 (1017 AD), in the ninth year of his age.

The era names appointed by this Emperor were **Kannin** <note>original: "Quanin"</note>, lasting four years and beginning with his accession to the throne; **Jian** <note>original: "Tsijan"</note> for three years; **Manju** <note>original: "Mansju"</note> for four years; and **Chōgen** <note>original: "Tsiooquan"</note> for nine years.

In the fifth year of his reign, **Saisen** <note>original: "Sai Sin"; likely referring to the influential statesman Fujiwara no Michinaga</note> first obtained permission from the Emperor to be carried about in a <term>Kuruma<note>A traditional heavy wooden carriage or covered chariot</note></term> drawn by two oxen. This was so well liked that the whole Ecclesiastical Court <note>The Kuge, or high-ranking court nobility</note> soon followed his example.

That same year, on the 22nd day of the 7th month, there was a violent storm which caused a great deal of damage. In the same month, two moons were reportedly seen in China.

In the sixth year of his reign, the <term>Jeki<note>The plague or a similar fatal epidemic</note></term> was very deadly throughout the Empire.

In the 12th year of his reign, in the fourth month (which corresponds to our June), a great quantity of snow fell, covering the ground to the height of four <term>Shaku<note>A Japanese unit of length roughly equal to a foot</note></term> and five <term>Sun<note>A Japanese unit roughly equal to an inch</note></term>—that is, about four and a half feet deep.

In the nineteenth year of his reign, on the ninth day of the eighth month, there was again a very violent storm.

He reigned in total for twenty years.

<margin>
69th Sovereign:
**GO-SUZAKU**
</margin>
**GO-SUZAKU** <note>r. 1036–1045 AD</note>, meaning Suzaku the Second, who was his younger brother, succeeded him in the year of Synmu 1697 (1037 AD), at the age of 28.

The era names he appointed were **Chōryaku** <note>original: "Tsioraku"</note> for three years, **Chōkyū** <note>original: "Tsiokiu"</note> for four years, and **Kantoku** <note>original: "Quantoku"</note> for two years.

In the fifth year of his reign, on the first day of the first month, a violent earthquake occurred.

He reigned nine years and died at the age of thirty-seven.

<margin>
70th Sovereign:
**GO-REIZEI**
</margin>
He was succeeded by his eldest son **GO-REIZEI** <note>r. 1045–1068 AD</note>, or Reizei the Second, in the year of Synmu 1706 (1046 AD), in the seventeenth year of his age.

The era names appointed during his reign were **Eishō** <note>original: "Jeiso"</note> for seven years, **Tenki** for five, **Heigo** <note>original: "Feiko"</note> for seven, and **Jōkyū** <note>original: "Tsioku"</note> for four years.

In the 13th year of his reign, **Abe no Yoritoki** <note>original: "Foori Ije"; the leader of the Abe clan</note> rebelled against the Emperor in the province of **Ōshū** <note>The northernmost part of the main island of Honshu</note>. The rebels held their ground for five years until **Minamoto no Yoriyoshi** <note>original: "Jori-Josj"</note>, the Crown General and Commander-in-Chief of all the Imperial troops, defeated them. He killed their two brave generals, **Abe no Sadatō** <note>original: "Abino Sadato"</note> and **Fujiwara no Munetō** <note>original: "Takano Munto"</note>. This rebellion is described at length in a book called **Ōshū Gassen** <note>original: "Osju Gassen"; literally "The Wars in Ōshū," referring to the Zenkunen War</note>.

**TOBA**
</margin>

This Emperor’s era names were **Tennin** of two, **Ten'ei** <note>original: "Tenjei"</note> of three, **Eikyū** <note>original: "Jeikju"</note> of five, **Gen'ei** <note>original: "Guanje"</note> of two, and **Hōan** <note>original: "Foan"</note> of four years.

In the first year of his reign, a strange noise was heard in the air, as if drums had been beating, which continued for several days together.

In the second year of the era Hōan, which was the fourteenth of his reign, was born **Kiyomori** <note>Taira no Kiyomori, 1118–1181 AD</note>, a Prince of the Blood, very famous in Japanese histories. He assumed the title of <term>Dairi<note>A term for the Emperor or the Imperial Court</note></term>, or Emperor, and made himself a court of his adherents after the manner of the Dairi’s own Court; but not being able to maintain his title and dignity, he was forced to fly to the famous convent **Mii-dera** <note>original: "Midira"</note>, on the mountain **Hiei-zan** <note>original: "Jeesan"</note>, where the monks protected him against the Imperial Court and his enemies headed by the **Heike** <note>original: "Feki"; Note: the author here confuses Kiyomori’s biography, as Kiyomori was actually the leader of the Heike/Taira clan</note>. Soon after, he caused himself to be shaved in order to turn monk, and took the name **Shōkai** <note>original: "Siookai"</note>. He lived fourteen years in this convent and died in the 60th year of his age, which was the year of Synmu 1841 <note>1181 AD</note>, on the fourth day of the second month, of a malignant burning fever which made him look red, as if he had been all on fire—a just punishment, as my Japanese author observes, of his presumptuous revolt against his lawful Sovereign.

Toba reigned 16 years.

<margin>
75th Sovereign:
**SUTOKU**
</margin>
He was succeeded by his eldest son **SUTOKU** <note>original: "SINTOKU"; r. 1123–1142 AD</note> in the year of Synmu 1784 (1124 AD).

->### The History of JAPAN. Book II. 182<-

The <term>Nengo<note>Era names used in the traditional Japanese calendar to measure time within a reign</note></term> appointed by this Emperor were **Tenji** <note>original: "Tentfi"</note> of seven years, **Tenshō** <note>original: "Tenfio"</note> of one, **Chōshō** <note>original: "Tfioofo"</note> of three, **Hōen** <note>original: "Fojen"</note> of six years, and **Heiji** <note>original: "Feeitfi"</note> of one.

He reigned eighteen years. Under his reign was built the Town of **Kamakura**.

<margin>
76th Sovereign:
**KONOE**
</margin>
He was succeeded by his youngest Brother **KONOE** <note>r. 1142–1155 AD</note>, the Emperor **Toba**’s eighth Son, in the year of <term>Jimmu<note>original: "Synmu"; the traditional counting of years from the founding of Japan by the legendary first Emperor</note></term> 1802, and of Christ 1142.

The era names appointed during his reign were **Kōji** <note>original: "Kootfi"</note> of two, **Ten’yō** <note>original: "Tenjo"</note> of one, **Kyūan** <note>original: "Kiuan"</note> of six, **Ninpei** <note>original: "Nimpe"</note> of three, and **Kyūju** <note>original: "Kijfu"</note> of two years.

Under this Emperor lived **Yorimasa** <note>Minamoto no Yorimasa, 1106–1180</note>, a Prince of the Imperial Blood, and another Japanese *Hercules*. By the assistance of **Hachiman** <note>original: "Fatzman"</note>, who is the Mars <note>The Roman god of war</note> of the Japanese, he killed, with his arrows, the infernal Dragon **Nue** <note>original: "Nuge"</note>, who had the head of a Monkey, the tail of a Serpent, and the body and claws of a Tiger. This monstrous Beast inhabited the **Mikado**’s <note>The Emperor</note> own Palace, and was very troublesome both to his sacred Person and to all his Court, particularly in the night time, frightening them and disturbing them out of their sleep. This **Yorimasa** was twenty-seven years after, in the civil wars carried on between the four most powerful families of the Empire, particularly the **Taira** <note>original: "Feki"</note> and **Minamoto** <note>original: "Gendfij"</note>, overcome by his enemies, and extirpated with his whole family. This long and bloody War, which desolated the Empire for many years, till the entire suppression of the **Taira** party, and the death of the Prince, who was at their head, and whom the **Minamoto** killed with all his family, is at large and fully described in a Book entitled, **Heike Monogatari** <note>original: "Fekinowonogatari"</note> that is, *an account of what happened in the War with the Taira family*.

In the sixth year of his reign, on the 22nd day of the seventh month, appeared a Comet.

In the tenth year of his reign, which was the fourth year of the era **Kyūan**, was born at Court **Yoritomo** <note>Minamoto no Yoritomo, 1147–1199</note>, the first great **Shogun** <note>original: "Seogun"</note>, or Crown General. The ensuing civil wars, which desolated the Japanese Empire, and were likely to have torn it to pieces, gave him an opportunity of increasing his power and authority to that degree, that he is unanimously mentioned by the Japanese Historians, as the first of the now reigning secular Monarchs. It was about that time the supreme and unlimited authority of the **Dairi**’s, or Ecclesiastical Hereditary Emperors, which they had fully enjoyed till then, began to decline. The Princes of the Empire, governed by ambition, jealousy and envy, abandoned by degrees the duty and allegiance they owed to their Sovereign, assumed an absolute power in the government of their Dominions and Principalities, entered into alliances for their own defence, and carried on war one against another, to revenge what injuries they did, or fancied to have received. In this disposition of affairs **Yoritomo** was sent by the Emperor, at the head of a numerous army, and with an absolute power to adjust the differences, and to terminate the wars between the Princes of the Empire.
