->### The History of JAPAN. Book II. 183<-

...supported by the experience of all ages, that men entrusted with power seldom care to part with it. This was the case of **Yoritomo** <note>Minamoto no Yoritomo, 1147–1199, the founder of the first shogunate</note>, who gladly embracing so favorable an opportunity as was put into his hands, espoused the interest of that of the contending parties which he thought the most likely to support his own. By this means, he increased his power to such a degree as not only to arrogate to himself an absolute authority in the decision of all the secular <note>Non-religious or political</note> affairs of the Empire, but to leave to his Successors a plausible pretext to claim the same. Thus the Power of the **Ecclesiastical Hereditary Emperors** <note>The Mikados, who were considered divine descendants of the sun goddess</note> received at first a fatal shock by the disobedience and quarrels of the Princes of the Empire, and was at last entirely taken from them by the usurpation of their **Crown Generals** <note>The Shoguns</note>, though without prejudice to their supreme Dignity, Rank, Holiness, and some other Rights and Prerogatives, which do not properly relate to the government of the secular affairs of the Empire, as will appear more fully in the following Chapter. **Konoe** <note>original: "Kon Je"</note> reigned fourteen years.

### CHAP. V.
#### Regarding the *Ecclesiastical Hereditary Emperors*, who lived after *Yoritomo*, to the present time.

<margin>
77th Sovereign:
**GOSHIRAKAWA**
</margin>
**Konoe** was succeeded by his elder Brother **GOSHIRAKAWA** <note>r. 1155–1158 AD</note>, or **Shirakawa the second**, the Emperor **Toba**’s fourth Son, in the year of **Jimmu** <note>original: "Synmu"</note> 1816, and of Christ 1156. After his accession to the Throne, he appointed the <term>Nengo<note>Era name</note></term> **Hōgen** <note>original: "Foogien"</note>, which subsisted three years.

In the first year of his reign, on the eleventh day of the seventh month, **Sutoku-in** <note>original: "Ssi In"; the retired Emperor Sutoku</note> revolted against the Emperor. This Rebellion occasioned a bloody and pernicious War, which from the time of its beginning is called **Hōgen no Midare** <note>original: "Foogienno midarri"</note>, that is, the *turmoil of the Hōgen era*, and is by this name described at length in their Histories.

In the third year of his reign, in the eighth month, there happened a violent Earthquake.

After a short reign of three years, he resigned the Crown to his Son. Twelve years later, he entered into religious Orders, caused himself to be shaved, and took the name of **Gyōshin** <note>original: "Joossin"</note>. He died in the forty-third year of his age.

<margin>
78th Sovereign:
**NIJŌ**
</margin>
**NIJŌ** <note>original: "Nidsioo"</note>, the eldest son of **Goshirakawa**, was sixteen years old when his father resigned the crown to him in the year 1819 of the **Jimmu** era <note>Traditional Japanese calendar dating from the first Emperor, Jimmu; 1159 AD</note>, which corresponds to the year of Christ 1159.

The **Era names** (<term>Nengo</term> <note>Title given to a specific period of an Emperor's reign for record-keeping</note>) appointed during his reign were **Heiji** for one year, **Heiryaku** for one year, **Ōhō** for two, **Chōkan** for two, and **Eiman** for one year.

In the first year of his reign, the two great generals **Nobuyori** and **Yoshitomo** (the father of **Yoritomo**), both of whom were princes of the blood, rebelled against the Emperor. This rebellion and the war it caused are named in history books after the time they began: the **Heiji Rebellion** <note>original: "Feitsi no midarri," literally "The Desolation of the Heiji Era"</note>. Two years later, **Yoshitomo** was killed in **Owari** Province, and his son **Yoritomo** was subsequently banished to **Izu**.

In the fifth year of his reign, during the first year of the **Chōkan** era, a poor woman gave birth to three children, each of whom reportedly had two heads and four feet <note>Such reports of unusual births were often recorded as omens in historical chronicles</note>.

He reigned for seven years and died at twenty-three years of age.

79th Sovereign:
**ROKUJŌ**

He appointed the **Nin’an** era, which lasted for three years.

He reigned for only three years and died at the age of thirteen.

He was married to a daughter of **Kiyomori** <note>Taira no Kiyomori, the powerful military leader mentioned previously</note>, who was noted above during the reign of Emperor **Toba**.

He appointed the following era names: **Kaō** for two years, **Shōan** for four, **Angen** for two, and **Jishō** for four years.

In the third year of his reign, his father, the former Emperor, had his head shaved and became a monk, taking the religious name **Gyōshin** <note>original: "Joossin"</note>.

In the fourth year of his reign, on the twenty-third day of the first month, a great part of the capital city and the Emperor’s residence was destroyed by fire.

In the seventh year, a fatal **smallpox** epidemic spread across the entire Empire.

In the eleventh year, the Emperor moved his court and residence to **Fukuhara** <note>original: "Kuwara"</note>.

In the twelfth year of his reign, and the last of the **Jishō** era, the enemies of **Yoritomo** were defeated in the Province of **Izu**, and **Yorimasa** <note>Minamoto no Yorimasa, a poet and warrior</note> was killed along with his entire family.

He reigned for twelve years and died at twenty-one years of age.

->### Chapter V: The History of JAPAN.<-

In that year, **Kiyomori** <note>original: "Kijomori," referring to Taira no Kiyomori, the head of the Taira clan</note>, the Emperor’s grandfather, died in the manner described previously. In the same year, General **Kajiwara** <note>original: "Kadsuwara," likely Kajiwara Kagetoki</note> left the **Heike** <note>original: "Feki," the Taira clan</note> party and went over to **Yoritomo** <note>Minamoto no Yoritomo, the first Shogun</note>, who was then called **Hyōe-no-suke** <note>original: "Tiojenoski," a junior military title Yoritomo held</note>. This **Kajiwara** was of very humble origins, but through his courage and heroic actions, he raised himself to be one of the most prominent princes of the empire. That same year saw the birth of **Yoriie**, **Yoritomo's** son and his successor in the command of the armies and the government of secular affairs <note>The author uses "secular affairs" to describe the military government of the Shogun, as opposed to the spiritual/ritual role of the Emperor</note>.

After a short reign of three years, **Antoku** was forced to resign the crown.

<margin>
82nd Sovereign:
**GO-TOBA**
</margin>
He was succeeded by **GO-TOBA**, or **Toba the Second**, the fourth son of Emperor **Takakura**, in the year 1844 of the **Jimmu** era <note>The traditional Japanese calendar; this corresponds to 1184 AD</note>.

He appointed the era names (<term>Nengo</term>) of **Genryaku** <note>original: "Genriaku"</note> for one year, **Bunji** <note>original: "Buanitz"</note> for five, and **Kenkyū** <note>original: "Kenkiu"</note> for nine years.

In the first year of his reign, **Yoshinaka** <note>original: "Joofnaga," referring to Minamoto no Yoshinaka</note> died; he was a great general whose heroic actions are frequently mentioned in the history of the wars against the **Heike**.

In the third year of his reign, his predecessor **Antoku**, being pursued by his enemies, was unhappily drowned in the Western Seas <note>This occurred at the Battle of Dan-no-ura</note>. After his death, he was called **Antoku-tennō** <note>original: "Antokuten O," meaning Emperor Antoku</note>, having taken the name **Sentei** <note>original: "Sen Tei," meaning "The Former Emperor"</note> after his resignation.

About that time, **Yoshinaka** <note>original: "Jofinaga"</note>, **Yoritomo's** son-in-law, died.

In the sixth year of his reign, **Yoshitsune** <note>original: "Jofitzne," the famous warrior Minamoto no Yoshitsune</note>, another very eminent commander, was killed. His death was followed by that of **Hidehira** <note>Fujiwara no Hidehira</note>, his Lieutenant-General, and the total destruction of his whole family.

In the eleventh year, **Yoritomo** went to court to pay his respects to the **Mikado** <note>The Emperor</note>, by whom he was honored with the title of **Seii Taishōgun** <note>original: "Sei Seogun," meaning "Barbarian-Subduing Generalissimo"</note>, which has been ever since given to the crown-generals and secular monarchs <note>Shoguns</note>.

In the fourteenth year of his reign, a horse with nine feet was sent to court from the island of **Awaji** <note>original: "Awadsi"</note> as a present to the Emperor.

He reigned fifteen years and resigned the crown to his eldest son. He died at sixty years of age.

<margin>
83rd Sovereign:
**TSUCHIMIKADO**
</margin>
**TSUCHIMIKADO** (where **Mikado** is here used as the Emperor's name) was but three years old when he came to the crown by his father's resignation, in the year 1859 of the **Jimmu** era <note>1199 AD</note>.

The era names (<term>Nengo</term>) appointed during his reign were **Shōji** <note>original: "Seotzi"</note> for two years, **Kennin** for three, **Genkyū** <note>original: "Genkiu"</note> for two, **Ken’ei** <note>original: "Kenje"</note> for one, and **Shōgen** <note>original: "Soojen"</note> for four years.

In the first year of his reign, **Yoritomo**, the crown-general and the first secular monarch <note>Shogun</note>, died. His son **Yoriie** succeeded him in the command of the armies and, five years after his father's death, was honored by the **Dairi** <note>The Imperial Court</note> with the title of **Seii Taishōgun**. He was killed two years later.

**Tsuchimikado** reigned twelve years and resigned the crown to his younger brother. He lived 37 years.

The era names (<term>Nengo</term> <note>Nengō are era names used to divide time into manageable periods, often named for auspicious omens or major events</note>) appointed during his reign were **Kenryaku** <note>original: "Genriaku"</note> for two years, **Kempō** <note>original: "Genpo"</note> for six, and **Jōkyū** <note>original: "Seokin"</note> for three years.

He endeavored to maintain himself in the succession of his father’s and brother’s offices by force of arms.

In the ninth year of his reign, on the twenty-second day of the second month, the two stately temples **Kiyomizu** <note>original: "Kiomidz"</note> and **Gion** <note>original: "Giwon"</note> were destroyed by fire.

In the first year of his reign, and the first of the **Jōō** era, on the first day of the second month, **Nichiren** <note>original: "Nitjsjren"</note> was born in the province of **Awa**. He was a famous Buddhist <note>original: "Pagan," reflecting the 18th-century European perspective of the author</note> teacher and the founder of a specific sect <note>The Nichiren sect, known for its focus on the Lotus Sutra</note>.

In the eleventh year of his reign, on the twenty-third day of the second month, a violent earthquake occurred.

He resigned the crown after a reign of thirteen years and lived to the age of sixty.

### Chap. V. The History of JAPAN

<margin>
89th Sovereign:
**KAMEYAMA**
<note>original: "KAME JAMMA"</note>
</margin>
**KAMEYAMA**, the late Emperor’s younger brother, came to the Crown by his Resignation, in the year 1920 of the **Jimmu** era <note>The traditional Japanese calendar starting from the first Emperor</note>, or 1260 AD.

The <term>Nengo</term> <note>Era names used to track time during an Emperor's reign</note> appointed during his reign were: **Bun’ō** <note>original: "Bunwo"</note> for one year, **Kōchō** <note>original: "Kotfio"</note> for three, and **Bun'ei** <note>original: "Bunje"</note> for eleven years.

In the fifth year of his reign, on the 21st day of the eleventh month, died **Shinran** <note>original: "Sinran"</note>, the leader of the **Ikkō-shū** <note>original: "Ikofiu," now known as Jōdo Shinshū or "True Pure Land" Buddhism</note> sect. He was formerly a disciple of **Hōnen Shōnin** <note>original: "Foonin Seonin"</note>, who was the founder of the **Jōdo-shū** <note>original: "Seodofiu"</note> sect.

In the seventh year of his reign, a great comet appeared, which was also seen in **China**.

In the ninth year, on the eighth day of the fifth month, two Suns were seen; and in the tenth year, on the eleventh day of the second month, three Moons appeared <note>Atmospheric phenomena like parhelia (sun dogs) were historically recorded as significant omens for the state</note>.

In the fifteenth and last year of his reign, **Prince Munetaka** <note>original: "Mune Taka"</note>, who was then the **Shogun** <note>original: "Crown General"</note> and in charge of secular affairs, took up his residence in the city of **Kamakura**.

He reigned fifteen years and resigned the crown to his eldest son. He lived thirty-two years after his resignation and died in the fifty-seventh year of his age, during the fifth year of the reign of Emperor **Go-Nijō** <note>original: "Gonidfi"</note>.

<margin>
90th Sovereign:
**GO-UDA**
<note>original: "GOUDA"</note>
</margin>
**GO-UDA** succeeded his father in the year 1935 of the **Jimmu** era, or 1275 AD.

The era names (<term>Nengo</term>) appointed during his reign were **Kenji** <note>original: "Gentfi"</note> for two years, **Kōan** <note>original: "Kooan"</note> for four, and **Shōō** <note>original: "Sioo"</note> for three years. Some authors mention only two eras: **Kenji** for three years and **Kōan** for ten years.

In the ninth year of his reign, on the twenty-first day of the fifth month, the Mongol <note>original: "Tartar"</note> army <note>original: "General Mooko" - Mōko is the Japanese term for Mongol</note> appeared upon the coasts of **Japan** with a fleet of 4,000 sail and 240,000 men. The then reigning Mongol Emperor **Kublai Khan** <note>original: "Sijfu," likely a reference to his posthumous name Shizu</note>, after he had conquered the Empire of **China** around 1270 AD, sent this force to also subdue the Empire of **Japan**. But this expedition proved unsuccessful. The <term>Kami</term> <note>original: "Cami" - the indigenous Shinto deities of Japan</note>, being the gods of the country and protectors of the Japanese Empire, were so incensed at the insult offered them by the Mongols that on the first day of the seventh month, they excited a violent and dreadful storm, which destroyed all of this supposedly invincible Armada. The leader <note>original: "Mooko"</note> himself perished in the waves, and but few of his men escaped. *(This expedition, of which more is said in the Translator’s Preface, is mentioned by **Marco Polo** <note>original: "Marcus Paulus"</note>, a noble Venetian who was then himself in China at the court of the Mongol Emperor.)*

In the tenth year of his reign, on the thirteenth day of the tenth month, **Nichiren** <note>original: "Nitfirin"</note> died in the province of **Musashi**. The followers of the **Hokke-shū** <note>original: "Fokefiu" - the Lotus Sect</note> still celebrate a yearly festival to commemorate the day of his death.

# The History of JAPAN. Book II.

**Go-Uda** <note>original: "Gouda"</note> reigned for thirteen years and lived to be fifty-eight.

<margin>91st Sovereign: **FUSHIMI**</margin> He was succeeded by **Fushimi**, the second son of **Go-Fukakusa** and cousin to the previous emperor, in the year 1948 of the **Jimmu** era <note>The traditional Japanese calendar; this year corresponds to 1288 AD</note>.

The <term>Nengo</term> <note>Era names used to track time during a reign</note> appointed during his reign were **Shōō** <note>original: "Soowo"</note> for five years, and **Einin** <note>original: "Jenin"</note> for six years.

In the first year of his reign, on the third day of the third month, his son and successor was born, to whom he resigned the throne after a reign of eleven years.

He lived to be fifty-three years old.

<margin>92nd Sovereign: **GO-FUSHIMI**</margin> **Go-Fushimi**, or **Fushimi the Second**, succeeded his father in the year 1959 of the **Jimmu** era (1299 AD) at the age of twelve.

He appointed a new era name called **Shōan** <note>original: "Seoan"</note>, which continued for three years until he resigned the throne.

He lived for thirty-five years after his resignation and died at the age of forty-eight, in the year 1997 of the **Jimmu** era (1337 AD).

<margin>93rd Sovereign: **GO-NIJŌ**</margin> He resigned the crown to **Go-Nijō**, or **Nijō the Second**, the eldest son of Emperor **Go-Uda**, in the year 1962 of the **Jimmu** era (1302 AD).

This Emperor appointed the era names **Kagen** for four years and **Tokuji** <note>original: "Tokuds"</note> for two years.

In the fifth year of his reign, in the eighth month, a violent earthquake occurred. This same year is notable for the death of the former Emperor **Kameyama** <note>original: "Kame Jamma"</note> and the birth of **Takauji** <note>Ashikaga Takauji, 1305–1358 AD</note>, who later became the <term>Shogun</term> <note>original: "Crown-General"</note> and secular ruler of Japan.

He reigned for six years and resigned the crown to:

<margin>94th Sovereign: **HANAZONO**</margin> **Hanazono** <note>original: "FANNA-SONNO"</note>, the younger brother of Emperor **Go-Fushimi** and second son of **Fushimi**, in the year 1968 of the **Jimmu** era (1308 AD).

The era names appointed during this Emperor’s reign were **Enkyō** <note>original: "Jenke"</note> for three years, **Ōchō** <note>original: "Outsjo"</note> for one year, **Shōwa** <note>original: "Sood"</note> for two years, and **Bunpō** <note>original: "Bun O"</note> for five years.

He reigned for eleven years and resigned the crown to **Go-Daigo**, the younger brother of **Go-Nijō** and second son of **Go-Uda**.

<margin>95th Sovereign: **GO-DAIGO**</margin> **Go-Daigo**, or **Daigo the Second**, came to the throne in the year 1979 of the **Jimmu** era (1319 AD).

He appointed the era names **Gen’ō** <note>original: "Genwo"</note> for two years, **Genkō** for three, **Shōchū** <note>original: "Seotsju"</note> for two, **Karyaku** <note>original: "Karaku"</note> for three, **Gentoku** for two, and **Genkō** for one year.

In the final year of his reign, much blood was shed in the civil wars that desolated the Empire; these events are described in the book titled ***Taiheiki*** <note>original: "Teifeki"; a famous historical epic meaning "The Chronicle of Great Peace"</note>.

He reigned for thirteen years and resigned the crown to **Kōgon** <note>original: "Kwo Gien"</note>, the eldest son of **Go-Fushimi**.

<margin>96th Sovereign: **KŌGON**</margin> **Kōgon** <note>original: "KWO GIEN or Koo Gien"</note> came to the throne in the year 1992 of the **Jimmu** era (1332 AD).

He appointed the era name **Shōkyō** <note>original: "Seoke"</note>, which lasted for two years.

### Chap. V. The History of JAPAN.

In the second year of his reign, **Takauji** <note>original: "Takadsi"; referring to Ashikaga Takauji, the founder of the Ashikaga Shogunate</note>, who was then the Crown General and Secular Monarch <note>The Shogun</note>, came to the imperial court to pay his respects to the **Mikado**. The same year, **Takakoku**, a noted General, ended his own life by ritual suicide <note>original: "ripping open his belly," a reference to seppuku</note>.

**Kōgon** <note>original: "Kwoo Gien"</note>, after a short reign of two years, resigned the crown to his predecessor. He lived thirty-two years after and died in the year 2026 of the **Jimmu** era <note>The traditional Japanese calendar; this corresponds to 1364 AD</note>.

**GO-DAIGO** therefore resumed the Crown in the year 1994 of the **Jimmu** era (1334 AD).

He then appointed the <term>Nengo</term> <note>Era names used to track time</note> **Kenmu** and **Engen** <note>original: "Kemmu" and "Jenken"</note>, each lasting two years.

In the third year of his second reign, the late Emperor **Go-Fushimi** died, as did **Kusunoki Masashige** <note>original: "Kusnokimaka Sugge"</note>, a famous General. The same year, in the eighth month, Japan was shaken by violent Earthquakes.

He reigned this second time for only three years.

<margin>97th Sovereign: **KŌMYŌ**</margin>
He was succeeded by **KŌMYŌ**, the younger brother of **Kōgon** and the fourth son of Emperor **Go-Fushimi**, in the year 1997 of the **Jimmu** era (1337 AD).

The era name **Engen**, which had been appointed by his predecessor, was continued during the first year of his reign and was followed by the era name **Ryakuō** <note>original: "Riakuwo"</note>, which lasted four years.

In the second year of his reign, the Crown General **Takauji** was honored by him with the illustrious title of **Sei-i Taishōgun** <note>original: "Sei Dai Seogun"; the highest military title, often translated as "Barbarian-Subduing Generalissimo"</note>.

My two Japanese historians differ about the length of this Emperor's reign. One claims that he reigned for only twelve years, but the other insists that after a short reign of two years he was succeeded by:

**GO-MURAKAMI**, or **Murakami the Second**, the seventh child of Emperor **Go-Daigo**, in the year 1999 of the **Jimmu** era (1339 AD). This Emperor, however, has no number assigned to him in the list of the **Mikados** <note>This refers to the split between the Northern and Southern imperial lines; Kaempfer’s source here prioritizes the Northern Court's numbering</note>.

The era name **Ryakuō** was continued during the first three years of his reign, assuming that he possessed the throne of Japan, and it was followed by the era names **Kōei** <note>original: "Kooje"</note> for three years, and **Jōwa** <note>original: "Tewa"</note> for four years.

Whoever it was that governed Japan during the time of these several era names, both my authors agree that after the **Jōwa** era expired, **Sukō** <note>original: "Siukwo"</note> came to the crown.

<margin>98th Sovereign: **SUKŌ**</margin>
**SUKŌ**, who was the eldest son of Emperor **Kōgon**, began to reign in the year 2009 of the **Jimmu** era (1349 AD).

During the first year of his reign, I find there was no specific era name appointed, for the era **Kannō** <note>original: "Quano"</note> began with the second year and was continued for two years.

In the first year of his reign, an end was put to the **Shijō-nawate** War <note>original: "Sidšio Nawatto"; a major battle where the Southern Court forces were defeated</note>.

He reigned for three years.

<margin>99th Sovereign: **GO-KŌGON**</margin>
He was succeeded by **GO-KŌGON**, or **Kōgon the Second**, his younger brother, in the year 2012 of the **Jimmu** era (1352 AD).

The era names <term>Nengo</term> <note>distinctive names used to identify periods of time during an Emperor's reign</note> appointed during this Emperor's reign were: **Bun'ya** <note>original: "Bunjwa"</note> for four years, **Enbun** <note>original: "Jenbun"</note> for five, **Kōan** <note>original: "Kooan"</note> for one, **Jōji** <note>original: "Teeidſi"</note> for six, and **Ōan** <note>original: "Ooan"</note> for seven years. This last era name was continued during the first three years of the reign of his successor.

In the third year of his reign, **Yoshiakira** <note>original: "Joſiſaki"; referring to Ashikaga Yoshiakira</note>, the third son of the Crown General **Takauji** <note>original: "Takaudſi"</note>, came to the imperial court.

In the fourth year of his reign, **Takauji** himself was sent by the Emperor into the Province of **Ōmi** <note>original: "Oomi"</note> to settle certain disputes which had arisen in those parts of the Empire.

In the eighth year of his reign, **Takauji** died on the 29th day of the fourth month. His son **Yoshiakira** succeeded him in his duties, and in the same year obtained from the Emperor the title of **Great Barbarian-Subduing General** <term>Sei-i Taishōgun</term> <note>original: "Sei Dai Seogun"; the supreme military commander and de facto secular ruler</note>.

In the eleventh year of his reign, the new Crown General **Yoshiakira** was sent to command the Imperial army in **Ōmi**.

In the eighteenth year of his reign, **Yoshimitsu** <note>original: "Joſimitz"</note>, the son of **Yoshiakira**, was made Crown General and honored with the title of **Great General** <term>Sei-i Taishōgun</term>.

**Go-Kōgon** <note>original: "Gokwoo Gen"</note> reigned for twenty years.

<margin>99th Sovereign: **GO-EN'YŪ**</margin>
He was succeeded by **GO-EN'YŪ** <note>original: "GO JENJU"</note>, his eldest son, in the year 2032 of the **Jimmu** era <note>original: "Synmu"; the traditional Japanese calendar dating from its legendary first Emperor</note>, or 1372 AD.

The last of his father's era names was continued during the first three years of his reign. In the fourth, he appointed the era name **Kōryaku** <note>original: "Kooraku"</note>, which lasted four years and was followed by the era names **Eitoku** <note>original: "Sei Toku"</note> for two years and **Kōwa** <note>original: "Koowa"</note> for three years; this last one continued during the first year of his successor's reign.

In the eighth year of his reign, there was a great famine in Japan. In the same year, a comet appeared.

He reigned for eleven years.

<margin>100th Sovereign: **GO-KOMATSU**</margin>
He was succeeded by his eldest son **GO-KOMATSU** <note>original: "GOKOMATZ"</note> in the year 2043 of the **Jimmu** era, or 1383 AD, during the third year of the **Kōwa** era.

The era names appointed during his reign were: **Shitoku** <note>original: "Sitoku"</note> for three years (begun in the second year of his reign), **Kakei** for two, **Kōō** <note>original: "Ikoo O"</note> for one, **Meitoku** <note>original: "Meetoku"</note> for four, and **Ōei** <note>original: "Oo Jei"</note> for thirty-four years.

In the ninth year of his reign, there was a war in the district of **Uji** <note>original: "Udſi"</note>.

In the fourteenth year, on the seventeenth day of the eleventh month, the famous temple **Kennin-ji** <note>original: "Kenninſi"</note> was burned to the ground.

In the twentieth year, a comet appeared in the Spring. It was observed that there was a great drought and lack of water during the following Summer and Autumn, and many violent earthquakes occurred the next Winter.

In the twenty-second year, a mountain at **Nasuno** <note>original: "Naſno"</note>, in the Province of **Shimotsuke** <note>original: "Simotski"</note>, began to burn and to erupt stones and ashes. However, the flames ceased soon after.

### Chap. V. The History of JAPAN.

In the twenty-fifth year, the autumn was very wet, which caused floods in several parts of the Empire. This was followed by stormy weather and earthquakes.

He reigned thirty years.

<margin>102nd Emperor: **Shōkō** <note>original: "SEOKWO"</note></margin>
He was succeeded by his son **Shōkō**, in the 2073rd year since **Jimmu** <term>Synmu</term> <note>the legendary first Emperor of Japan, used as a starting point for the traditional Japanese calendar</note>, in the year of Christ 1413, and the twentieth year of the **Ōei** era <term>Nengo</term> <note>specific era names used to track time within a reign</note>.

The **Ōei** era <note>original: "Oojei"</note> was continued during the first fifteen years of his reign, after which he appointed a new one called **Shōchō** <note>original: "Seootfjo"</note>, which lasted only one year.

In the fourth year of his reign, **Uesugi Ujinori** <note>original: "Uje Suggi," referring to the head of the Uesugi family</note> rebelled against the Emperor.

In the ninth year, on the twelfth day of the tenth month, two suns appeared in the sky.

In the sixteenth year, on the eighteenth day of the first month, **Ashikaga Yoshimochi** <note>original: "Josimotz"</note>, then the Crown General, died; he was succeeded in his title and duties by **Ashikaga Yoshinori** <note>original: "Josijnobu"</note>.

That same year, on the twenty-seventh day of the seventh month, the Emperor himself died after a reign of sixteen years.

<margin>103rd Emperor: **Go-Hanazono** <note>original: "GOFUNNA SO"</note></margin>
He was succeeded by his son **Go-Hanazono**, in the 2089th year since Jimmu, in the year of Christ 1429.

The era names <term>Nengo</term> appointed during his reign were: **Eikyō** <note>original: "Jeiko"</note> for twelve years, **Kakitsu** <note>original: "Kakitz"</note> for three, **Bun'an** <note>original: "Bunjan"</note> for five, **Hōtoku** <note>original: "Fotoku"</note> for five, **Kōshō** <note>original: "Kosio"</note> for two, **Chōroku** <note>original: "Tsioorok"</note> for three, and **Kanshō** <note>original: "Quanjsio"</note> for six years.

In the first year of his reign, on the fifth day of the eighth month, a very large and terrifying comet appeared, and another followed in the third month of the eleventh year.

In the sixteenth year, **Ashikaga Yoshimasa** <note>original: "Josimassa"</note> was honored by the Emperor with the title of **Shogun** <term>Sei Seogun</term> <note>the supreme military commander</note>.

In the eighteenth year, the Emperor’s Palace was burned to the ground.

During the last seven years of his reign, Japanese historians mention many strange and wonderful appearances in the heavens, which were followed by famine, plague, and a great number of deaths throughout the Empire.

He reigned thirty-six years.

<margin>104th Emperor: **Go-Tsuchimikado** <note>original: "GO TSUTSI MIKADDO"</note></margin>
He was succeeded by his son **Go-Tsuchimikado** (or Tsuchimikado the second), in the 2125th year since Jimmu, in the year of Christ 1465.

The era names appointed by this Emperor were: **Bunshō** <note>original: "Bunfio"</note> for one year (begun in the second year of his reign), **Ōnin** <note>original: "Onin"</note> for two, **Bunmei** <note>original: "Fumjo"</note> for eighteen, **Chōkyō** <note>original: "Tsiooko"</note> for two, **Entoku** <note>original: "Jentoku"</note> for three, and **Meiō** <note>original: "Me O"</note> for nine years.

In the first year of his reign, in the second month, a comet appeared with a tail that seemed to be three fathoms long.

In the second year, several earthquakes occurred, particularly on the twenty-ninth day of the twelfth month. That same year, there was such a severe famine in China that people killed and ate one another.

The third year was very fatal to *Japan*, which was filled with troubles and civil wars <note>This refers to the beginning of the Ōnin War (1467–1477), a decade-long conflict that initiated the "Sengoku" or Warring States period</note>. This great desolation began on the sixth day of the fifth month.

In the fifth year, on the tenth day of the ninth month, another comet appeared with a tail over one fathom <note>about six feet</note> long.

In the seventh year, there was a great mortality <note>a widespread plague or epidemic</note> all over the Empire.

The same year, on the first day of the twelfth month, another comet appeared, larger than any observed so far, with a tail—according to my author—as long as a street.

In the ninth year, **Hosokawa Katsumoto** <note>original: "Foffokawa Katfmotto"</note> died; he was a great General, very famous for his courage and military exploits. After his death, he was honored with the title of **Ryuan** <note>original: "Riu Ans"</note>, and the title of **Shogun** <term>Sei Seogun</term> <note>the military dictator of Japan</note> was given to **Ashikaga Yoshihisa** <note>original: "Joofnavo"</note>.

In the eleventh year, on the sixth day of the eighth month, there were very hard winds. The waters around **Amagasaki** in the Province of **Settsu** <note>original: "Setz"</note> swelled to such a height that a great part of that country was overflowed, and many inhabitants drowned.

In the twenty-fifth year, on the twenty-sixth day of the third month, **Yoshihisa** <note>original: "Jofijnavo"</note> died. He was the son of the Shogun **Ashikaga Yoshimasa** <note>original: "Jofijmaffa"</note>; besides the title of **Shogun** <term>Sei Seogun</term>, he shared the command of the armies and the administration of the secular affairs of the Empire with his father.

The next year, which was the year of Christ 1490, **Yoshimasa** himself died and was very much regretted.

In the twenty-ninth year, **Ashikaga Yoshizumi** <note>original: "Jofijfummy"</note> was honored with the title of **Great Shogun** <term>Sei Dai Seogun</term>. Soon after, he went to command the army in **Yamashiro** <note>original: "Jafijro", a province near Kyoto</note>.

In the thirtieth year, on the seventh day of the eighth month, another violent earthquake occurred.

He <note>Emperor Go-Tsuchimikado</note> reigned for a total of thirty-six years and lived for fifty-nine.

105th Emperor:
**Go-Kashiwabara**
<note>original: "KASIUWABARA"</note>

He was succeeded by his son **Go-Kashiwabara**, in the 2161st year since **Jimmu** <term>Synmu</term> <note>the legendary first Emperor of Japan</note>, in the year of Christ 1501.

The era names <term>Nengo</term> appointed during his reign were **Bunki**, lasting three years; **Eishō** <note>original: "Feeseo"</note>, lasting seventeen years; and **Daei** <note>original: "Teije"</note>, lasting seven years, the last of which continued through the first year of his successor's reign.

In the fourth year of his reign, there was a great famine in *Japan*, and another in the sixteenth year.

In the sixth year, in the seventh month, a comet appeared.

In the eighth year, the title of **Shogun** <term>Sei Seogun</term> and the command of the army were given to **Ashikaga Yoshitane** <note>original: "Jofitanne"</note>.

The tenth year was fatal to *Japan* due to both war and earthquakes.

In the twelfth year, in the fifth month, **Yoshitane** went to court to pay his respects to the Emperor.

**Go-Kashiwabara** reigned twenty-six years.

### Chapter V. The History of JAPAN.

<margin>106. GO-NARA</margin>
He was succeeded by his son **Go-Nara** <note>original: "GONARA"; reigned 1526–1557</note>, in the year 2187 from the reign of Jimmu <note>original: "Synmu", the legendary first Emperor of Japan</note>, or the year of Christ 1527.

The last of his father’s <term>Nengo</term> <note>Era names used for dating</note> was continued during the first year of his reign, after which he appointed the eras of **Kyōroku** <note>original: "Koraku"</note> for four years, **Tenbun** <note>original: "Tembun"</note> for twenty-three, and **Kōji** <note>original: "Koodſi"</note> for three years.

Soon after his accession to the throne, an end was put to the war between **Hosokawa** <note>original: "Foſſokawa"</note> and **Katsuragawa** <note>original: "Kadſuragawa"</note>. The former of these two Princes made away with himself two years after, ripping open his belly <note>The ritual suicide known as *seppuku*</note> with that courage and resolution which is so much admired by these heathens.

During this Emperor's reign, the Japanese Empire was afflicted twice with pestilence and a great mortality; thrice with extraordinary wet and rainy seasons, whereby the waters increased to such a degree that they overflowed a great part of the country; and once with such a violent and universal storm that many stately buildings, and part of the Emperor's own Palace, were blown down.

In the fifth year, on the twenty-ninth day of the sixth month, a comet appeared; and another again in the twelfth month of the twelfth year.

In the seventh year, on the eighth day of the tenth month, an eclipse of the moon was observed.

In the twenty-first year, on the seventeenth day of the second month, **Yoshiteru** <note>original: "Joſi Tir"</note> received from the Emperor the title of <term>Sei-i Taishōgun</term> <note>original: "Sei Dai Seogun"; the supreme military commander</note>, with the command of the armies. Eighteen years after this, Yoshiteru made away with himself by cutting his belly.

In the twenty-fourth year, on the fourth day of the fifth month, died the Crown General and Secular Monarch <note>The author uses "Secular Monarch" to refer to the Shogun</note> **Yoshiharu** <note>original: "Joſij Far"</note>.

Go-Nara reigned thirty-one years.

<margin>107. ŌGIMACHI</margin>
He was succeeded by his son **Ōgimachi** <note>original: "OOKIMATZ"; reigned 1557–1586</note>, in the year of Jimmu 2218, or the year of Christ 1558.

The era names appointed during his reign were **Eiroku** <note>original: "Jeekoku"</note> for twelve years, **Genki** for three, and **Tenshō** <note>original: "Jenfoo"</note> for nineteen years; this last one continued during the first five years of the reign of his successor.

In the very first year of his reign, there was a great famine in Japan, preceded by an exceedingly dry summer.

In the eighth year of his reign, **Yoshiteru**, then Crown General and Secular Monarch, made away with himself, as mentioned above.

In the eleventh year, **Yoshiaki** <note>original: "Joſij Tira", likely referring to Ashikaga Yoshiaki</note> was appointed Crown General and honored by the Emperor with the title of **Shogun** <term>Sei Seogun</term>.

In the sixteenth year, it is mentioned as something remarkable that a tortoise with two heads was caught in the spring. The same year, on the third day of the fourth month, some arsonists set fire to **Kamigyō** <note>original: "Kamio"</note>, which is the upper part of the city of **Kyoto** <note>original: "Miaco"</note> (the lower part is called **Shimogyō** <note>original: "Si Mio"</note>), where the Emperor himself then resided; by this fire, the greatest part of the city was laid in ashes.

## The History of JAPAN. Book II.

In the twentieth year, on the twenty-ninth day of the ninth month, a great comet appeared, which did not vanish until the following year.

The twenty-first year was very wet, and a great portion of the country was flooded on the twelfth day of the fifth month.

In the twenty-third year, sickness and death were widespread across the Empire.

In the twenty-fifth year, on the second day of the sixth month, the Commander-in-Chief and Secular Monarch **Nobunaga** <note>Oda Nobunaga, the first great unifier of Japan; he was assassinated at Honnō-ji temple</note>, and his eldest son, were killed at **Kyoto** <note>original: "Miaco"</note>.

In the twenty-sixth year, ambassadors from the **Ryukyu Islands** <note>original: "Riuku"</note> arrived at the Court.

In the twenty-eighth year, which was the year of Christ 1585, in the seventh month, **Hideyoshi** <note>original: "Fide Jos"; Toyotomi Hideyoshi</note>—who later took the name **Taiko** <note>original: "Taikofama"; a title given to a retired Regent</note>—was honored by the Emperor with the title of **Kanpaku** <note>original: "Quanbuku"; the Emperor's chief advisor or regent</note>. He was entrusted with the command of the armies and the government of the secular affairs of the Empire. The <term>Kanpaku</term> is the highest-ranking person after the <term>Dairi</term> <note>The Emperor</note>, and by virtue of this title, serves as his supreme Lieutenant and Vice-regent in the government. This **Taiko** was of very humble origins and raised himself to this eminent post purely through his courage and merit. He was, strictly speaking, the first absolute secular monarch of Japan; that is, the first who took for himself the absolute government of the Empire, over which the Ecclesiastical Hereditary Emperors had, until then, maintained some share of power. Ever since that time, the Secular Monarchs <note>The Shoguns and Regents</note> have remained independent of the Ecclesiastical Emperors, to whom nothing was left but a mere shadow of their former authority, along with a few insignificant privileges regarding their rank and holiness, and the titles of honor which must be conferred by them.

In that same 28th year, on the 29th of the 11th month, a violent earthquake occurred, which continued with repeated, though smaller shocks, for almost an entire year.

In the 29th year of his reign, the Emperor resigned the crown to his grandson and died seven years later.

In the fifth year, the title of **Kanpaku** <note>original: "Quanbuku"; the high office of Imperial Regent</note> was given to the aforementioned **Hidetsugu** <note>Toyotomi Hidetsugu, the nephew and ill-fated heir of Hideyoshi</note>.

In the sixth year, which was the year of Christ 1592, the **Taiko** <note>Toyotomi Hideyoshi</note> declared war against the **Koreans** and sent over a numerous army. He did this under the pretext of using the conquest of this peninsula as a path to the conquest of the **Empire of China** itself. This war lasted seven years.

In the seventh year, **Ogimachi** <note>original: "Ookimatz"; Emperor Ōgimachi, who had abdicated in favor of his grandson</note>, the Emperor's grandfather and predecessor, died.

In the eleventh year, **Ieyasu** <note>original: "Fejias"; Tokugawa Ieyasu, who would later become the first Tokugawa Shogun</note>, a great favorite of the **Taiko** and his first minister of state, was honored by the Emperor with the title of **Naidaijin** <note>original: "Nai Dai Sin"; the "Inner Minister," one of the highest ranks in the Imperial Court</note>.

That same year, on the twelfth day of the seventh month, several violent earthquakes occurred, and the tremors continued intermittently for a whole month. Around that time, it rained hair, four to five inches long, in several parts of the Empire. This phenomenon is often mentioned in Japanese histories <note>Atmospheric anomalies and earthquakes were frequently recorded in Japanese chronicles as omens of political change</note>.

In the twelfth year—which was the year 2258 of the **Jinmu** era <note>original: "Synmu"; the traditional Japanese calendar dating from the legendary first Emperor Jinmu</note>, and 1598 of Christ—on the eighteenth day of the eighth month, **Hideyoshi** <note>original: "Fide Josi"</note> took the name **Taiko**, which signifies a **Great Lord**. This great monarch died the same year (on the sixteenth of December, New Style) early in the morning, leaving the secular government to his only son **Hideyori** <note>original: "Fide Jori"</note>, whom he committed to the care and tutelage of **Ieyasu**.

In the fourteenth year, **Ishida Mitsunari** <note>original: "Josijda Tfibbu"; a high-ranking official and rival to Ieyasu</note>, who held a position at **Hideyori's** court, rebelled against the ruler. The rebels were soon defeated, and their leader, along with his entire family, was exterminated.

In the seventeenth year, the title of **Sei-i Taishōgun** <note>original: "Sei Dai Seogun"; the "Commander-in-Chief," the title of the secular military dictator</note>, which belongs to the Crown General, was given to **Ieyasu**, the tutor of the hereditary Prince **Hideyori**, the **Taiko's** only son. The same year, **Hideyori** himself was honored with the title of **Naidaijin**.

In the nineteenth year, the title of **Sei-i Taishōgun** was given to **Hidetada** <note>Tokugawa Hidetada, Ieyasu’s son</note>, the son of the Crown General **Ieyasu**.

The same year, a very extraordinary accident happened on the fifteenth day of the twelfth month: a mountain arose out of the sea in a single night near the rocky island of **Hachijō-jima** <note>original: "Fatfisio"</note>, where the high officials of the secular monarch’s court are usually exiled when they are out of favor.

In the twenty-first year, which was the year of Christ 1608, an ambassador arrived at **Suruga** <note>The seat of the retired Shogun Ieyasu</note>, sent by the Chinese Emperor to compliment the secular monarch of **Japan**.

109th Emperor.
**Go-Mizunoo**
</margin>
**Go-Yōzei** <note>original: "Go Josei"</note> reigned for twenty-five years in total.

He was succeeded by his son **Emperor Go-Mizunoo** <note>original: "DAISEOKWO TEI"</note>, in the year 2272 of the Japanese calendar <note>calculated from the legendary founding of Japan by Emperor Jimmu</note>, which corresponds to the year of Christ 1612.

In the fourth year of his reign, he established the era name <term>Nengo</term> <note>A system of naming periods of time based on significant events or imperial transitions</note> **Genwa** <note>original: "Geniwa"</note>, which lasted nine years. This was followed by the era **Kan'ei** <note>original: "Quan Je"</note>, which continued for twenty years through the remainder of his reign and the entire reign of the Empress who succeeded him.

In the second year of his reign, it was again observed that hair fell from the sky in several parts of the Empire, primarily in autumn <note>Such atmospheric anomalies were traditionally recorded as omens of major political shifts</note>.

In the third year, on the twenty-fifth day of the tenth month, a very violent earthquake occurred. That same year, **Toyotomi Hideyori** <note>original: "Fide Juri"</note>—the only son and heir of the late secular Emperor **Hideyoshi** <note>the "Taiko"</note>—was besieged in the **Castle of Osaka** by **Ieyasu**, who had been his guardian and father-in-law. The castle was surrendered in the fourth year, on the seventh day of the fifth month. However, the Prince caused the palace, where he had retreated with his most faithful followers, to be set on fire, choosing rather to perish in the flames than to fall into the hands of a victorious enemy, even though they were so closely related.

In the fifth year, on the seventeenth day of the fourth month, **Ieyasu** himself died, in full and quiet possession of the secular throne, which he had seized from his ward and left to his son. This Ieyasu was the first Emperor <note>Early European authors often referred to the Shogun as the "Secular Emperor"</note> of the currently reigning family. He was buried at **Nikko** <note>original: "Nicquo"</note> and, according to custom, was ranked among the gods by the name **Gongensama** <note>The deified title "Tōshō Daigongen," or Great Incarnation who Illuminates the East</note>.

In the eighth year, which was the year of Christ 1619, a very remarkable comet appeared.

In the tenth year, the **Ecclesiastical Emperor** <note>The Mikado or spiritual sovereign</note> was married with great pomp and solemnity to the daughter of the secular monarch, **Tokugawa Hidetada** <note>original: "Fide Tada"; the bride was Tokugawa Masako</note>.

In the twelfth year, **Iemitsu** <note>original: "Jemitz"</note>, the son of Hidetada, traveled to **Kyoto** <note>original: "Miaco"</note> to pay his respects to the Emperor, from whom he obtained the title of <term>Sei-i Taishōgun</term> <note>original: "Sei Dai Seogun"; the highest military rank, often shortened to Shogun</note>.

In the eighteenth year, he <note>Emperor Go-Mizunoo</note> resigned the crown to his daughter. He lived for fifty years after his resignation and died at the age of ninety, in the eighth year of the **Tenna** era <note>original: "Tempo"; likely referring to the late 17th-century era names</note>, on the eighth day of the eighth month, or late in autumn, when, as my Japanese author poetically expresses it, the trees had already been stripped of their leaves.

The last of her father’s <term>Nengo</term> <note>These are era names used to track time in Japan, often chosen to mark a significant event or a new reign</note> was continued throughout her entire reign.

In the third year of her reign, on the twenty-fourth day of the first month, the secular Monarch **Hidetada** <note>Tokugawa Hidetada, the second Shogun of the Tokugawa dynasty</note> died. After his death, he was deified according to custom and given the name **Teitoku-in**.

In the ninth year, in the second month—specifically on April 12, 1638—37,000 Christians were put to death in a single day. This act of cruelty immediately ended the rebellion and served as the final blow in the total abolition of the Christian religion in Japan.

In the twelfth year, the year of Christ 1641, on the fifth day of the eighth month, **Ietsuna** <note>Tokugawa Ietsuna, who would become the fourth shogun</note> was born. He was the father of the currently reigning secular Monarch. That same year, there was a great famine and a high mortality rate throughout Japan, lasting from the beginning of spring until the following harvest.

This Empress <note>Empress Meishō, who reigned from 1629 to 1643</note> reigned for fourteen years and then resigned the crown to her younger brother.

In the fourth year, in the fourth month, the Emperor order’d the **Jūshufuse** <note>original: "Jusja Fuse"; a "no-give, no-receive" sub-sect of Nichiren Buddhism that refused to interact with non-believers or the government</note>, a branch of the **Hokke** <note>original: "Fokesu"</note> Sect, to be abolish’d, forbidding all his subjects, ever hereafter, to adhere thereto. In the seventh year, there being a great famine in *Japan*, occasion’d by an excessive drought the year before, the Emperor order’d that from the twentieth day of the first month, for one hundred days successively, boil’d rice should be distributed to the poor, at his own expence, in all parts of the Empire.

In the eighth year, they had very violent storms at **Osaka** <note>original: "Ofacca"</note>, and in several other maritime Provinces, follow’d by Inundations, and a great mortality among men and beasts.

In the ninth year, in the fourth month, as they were cleaning the river, which runs by **Otsu** <note>original: "Ofaua"; likely referring to the area near Lake Biwa or the Yodo river system</note>, they took up great quantities of gold and silver, which, in all probability, were sunk there during the late Civil Wars.

In the eleventh year, on the ninth day of the fifth month, a fire broke out at the **Imperial Court** <note>original: "Dairi’s court"</note>, which burnt with such fury, that great part of the city of **Kyoto** <note>original: "Miaco"</note> itself was laid in ashes, and because it unluckily happen’d, that among other buildings several publick granaries were destroy’d by the fire, the Emperor, for the ease and comfort of his Subjects, order’d, that three <term>Kokus</term> <note>A unit of volume for rice, approximately 180 liters, theoretically enough to feed one person for a year</note> of rice should be given, or lent to any family, that stood in need of it, as is done frequently in time of famine.

In the eighteenth year, which was the eighth year of the <term>Enpō era</term> <note>original: "Nengo Jenpo"; the era spanning 1673–1681</note>, on the eighth day of the fifth month (June 24, 1680), the secular Monarch <term>Ietsuna</term> <note>original: "Ijetsna"; the 4th Tokugawa Shogun</note> died. Following his death, he was, according to custom, ranked among the gods and given the posthumous name <term>Gen-yū-in</term> <note>original: "Gen Ju in den"</note>.

In the nineteenth year, in the fifth month, the grand title of <term>Commander-in-Chief and Senior Minister</term> <note>original: "Sei Dai Seogun Nai Dai Sin Sioni i ukonjeno Taiso"; This represents a series of high court ranks and titles: Sei-i Taishōgun (Great Barbarian-Subduing General), Naidaijin (Minister of the Inner), Shō-ni-i (Senior Second Rank), and Ukon'e-no-Taishō (Captain of the Right Inner Palace Guards).</note> was conferred by the Emperor upon the now-reigning secular Monarch <term>Tsunayoshi</term> <note>original: "Tsinajos"; the 5th Tokugawa Shogun</note>. He was a younger brother of Gen-yū-in and the third son of <term>Iemitsu</term> <note>original: "Ijetiru, or Daijoin"</note>.

In the twentieth year, and the second of the <term>Tenwa era</term> <note>original: "Nengo Tenwa"; 1681–1684</note> (the year of Christ 1682), there was again a great famine and high mortality in Japan, particularly in and around <term>Kyoto</term> <note>original: "Miaco"</note>.

In the twelfth month of the same year, on the 28th day, a fire broke out at <term>Edo</term> <note>original: "Jedo"; modern-day Tokyo</note>, which reduced the best part of that great city to ashes.

In the twenty-first year, which was the third of the Tenwa era, <term>Tokumatsu</term> <note>original: "Tokumatz"</note> died. He was the only son and hereditary prince of the currently reigning Shogun. Because of his death, the Empire entered a period of general mourning; no musical instrument was to be played, nor were any kind of festivities to be held for three years.

That same year, on the fifth day of the twelfth month, the city of Edo suffered from fire once again.

This Emperor reigned twenty-four years and then resigned the crown to his son.

# The History of JAPAN. Book II.

XXIX. **TOYOTOMI HIDEYOSHI** <note>original: "Taicosama"</note> declared himself to be the military ruler of Japan. He reduced all the provinces of Japan—which were then still divided and governed by independent princes—under his power and sovereignty, becoming the first absolute secular monarch. After his death, according to the custom of the country, he was ranked among the gods and honored by the <term>Dairi</term> <note>The "Dairi" refers to the Titular or Spiritual Emperor of Japan, who resided in Kyoto.</note> with the divine title *Toyokuni Daimyōjin* <note>original: "Toyokuni Daimiosin"</note>. His temple, where his funeral urn is kept, stands at Kyoto <note>original: "Miaco"</note>, but it is currently almost in ruins, as the secular empire has since passed to another family.

XXX. **TOYOTOMI HIDETSUGU** <note>original: "FIDE TSUGU"</note>, also known as the Regent <note>original: "Quabacundono," a corruption of Kanpaku-dono</note>, who was the son of *Jōin Ishiro* <note>referring to Miyoshi Yoshifusa</note> and Hideyoshi's nephew, reigned under his uncle, though only for a short time.

XXXI. **TOYOTOMI HIDEYORI** <note>original: "FIDE JORI"</note>, Hideyoshi’s son, was a minor when his father died. He was committed to the care and guardianship of **Lord Ieyasu** <note>original: "Ijejas Sama"</note>, one of his father’s favorites and state counselors. Ieyasu bound himself by a solemn oath, signed with his own blood, that as soon as the young prince reached adulthood, he would resign the regency and hand the Empire over to him. On this condition, Ieyasu’s daughter was married to the hereditary prince, who held the title of Emperor <note>meaning Shogun</note> under his tutor and father-in-law for fourteen years.

XXXII. **TOKUGAWA IEYASU** <note>original: "I E J A S S A M A"</note>, otherwise known as the Retired Shogun <note>original: "Ongosio" or Ogosho</note> and *Daifusama*, usurped the throne from his son-in-law Hideyori. He granted the Dutch East India Company free trade in Japan in the year 1611. After his death, he was deified according to custom and called *Gongensama* <note>Tōshō Daigongen</note>. He lies buried at Nikko <note>original: "Niko"</note>, near Kyoto, which is the burial place of this family. He reigned for a total of fourteen years, including some of his regency. However, some authors claim he reigned for only four or five years, assuming he was already seventy years old when he took the throne.

XXXIII. **TOKUGAWA HIDETADA** <note>original: "FIDE TADA"</note>, Ieyasu’s third son, who was posthumously called *Taitoku-in* <note>original: "Taitokonni" or "Taitokuinsama"</note>, renewed the privileges his father had granted to the Dutch in 1616 or 1617. He reigned for eighteen years.

XXXIV. **TOKUGAWA IEMITSU** <note>original: "I J E T I R U K O"</note>, also known as *Ijemitzko*, the son of Hidetada, was posthumously called *Taiyū-in* <note>original: "Daijoinsama" or "Taijoinfama"</note>. He reigned for twenty-one years.

XXXV. **TOKUGAWA IETSUNA** <note>original: "I J E T Z N A K O"</note>, his son, who was posthumously called *Genyū-in* <note>original: "Ginjoinsama" or "Genjuinsama"</note>, reigned for thirty years and died on the fourth of June, 1680.

XXXVI. **TOKUGAWA TSUNAYOSHI** <note>original: "T S I N A J O S I K O"</note>, also called *Tsinasofama*, or by his full title which he recently received from the Emperor: **Great Barbarian-Subduing General, Inner Minister of the Second Rank, and General of the Right Imperial Guard** <note>original: "SEI DAI SEOGUN, NAI DAI SINI UKON JENO TAI SO"</note>. This is the currently reigning monarch, who succeeded his brother. He was in the 43rd year of his age when I was in Japan (in 1692) and had been on the throne for 12 or 13 years.

*Of the Religions of this Empire in general, and of the* Shinto <note>original: "Sintos"</note> *Religion in particular.*

<margin>The Religions of Japan.</margin>
<image-desc>A large ornamental drop cap 'L' within a square frame, decorated with intricate floral scrollwork.</image-desc> LIBERTY of Conscience, so far as it does not interfere with the interests of the secular Government, or affect the peace and tranquility of the Empire, has been at all times allowed in *Japan*, as it is in most other countries of *Asia*. Hence it is that foreign religions were introduced with ease and spread with success, to the great prejudice of that religion which was established in the country from the most remote antiquity. In these last hundred years, there were chiefly four religions notable for the number of their adherents, namely:

<margin>Shinto <note>original: "Sinto"</note></margin>
1. *Shinto* <note>original: "Sinto," meaning "The Way of the Gods"</note>, the old religion, or worship of local spirits <note>original: "Idol-worship"</note>, of the *Japanese*.

<margin>Buddhism <note>original: "Budsdo"</note></margin>
2. *Buddhism* <note>original: "Budsdo," from 'Butsudo' or 'the way of the Buddha'</note>, the worship of foreign idols which were brought over into *Japan* from the Kingdom of *Siam* <note>Modern-day Thailand</note> and the Empire of *China*.

<margin>Confucianism <note>original: "Siuto"</note></margin>
3. *Confucianism* <note>original: "Siuto," referring to 'Shuto' or the 'Way of the Scholars'</note>, the doctrine of their moralists and philosophers.

<margin>Christianity <note>original: "Deivus"</note></margin>
4. *Deus* <note>original: "Deivus," a Japanese corruption of the Latin word for God</note>, or *Christianity* <note>original: "Kiristando"</note>, is as much as to say, the way of God and Christ, by which must be understood the Christian religion.

The History of J A P A N. Book III.

<margin>The fate of the Christian Religion in Japan</margin>
It was due to the commendable zeal and the tireless efforts of the Spanish and Portuguese Missionaries—particularly the Jesuits <note>The Society of Jesus, a Catholic religious order</note>—that the Christian Religion was first introduced into *Japan*. It was spread with a success that far exceeded their expectations; from the first arrival of the Fathers of the Society in the Province of *Bungo* <note>original: "Bongo"</note> around the year 1549 (roughly six years after the first European discovery of *Japan*), until the year 1625 or nearly 1630, it spread through most provinces of the Empire. Even many of the Princes and Lords openly embraced the faith. Considering the vast progress it had made until that time, even amidst the many storms and difficulties it faced, there was good reason to hope that within a short time the entire Empire would have been converted to the faith of our Savior. This might have happened had not the ambitious goals and impatient efforts of these Fathers to reap temporal <note>worldly or political</note> as well as spiritual fruits from their labor so provoked the supreme Majesty of the Empire. Their actions sparked a persecution against themselves and their converts which has no equal in History, by which the Religion they preached, and all those who professed it, were entirely exterminated within a few years.

<margin>The Shinto <note>original: "Sintos"</note> Religion</margin>
Of the three chief Religions which now flourish and are tolerated in *Japan*, 

->### S H I N T O <note>original: "S I N T O S"</note><-

must be considered first, more for its antiquity and long standing than for the current number of its followers.

*Shinto* <note>original: "Sinto"</note>, which is also called *Shinshu* <note>original: "Sinsju"</note> and *Kami-no-michi* <note>original: "Kamimitsi"</note>, is the worship of spirits <note>original: "Idol-worship"</note> as established in the Country since ancient times. *Shin* <note>original: "Sin"</note> and *Kami* denote the spirits or deities which are the objects of this worship. *Yo* <note>original: "Jo"</note> and *Michi* <note>original: "Mitfi"</note> translates to the "way" or "method" of worshiping these deities. *Shu* <note>original: "Siu"</note> signifies Faith or Religion. *Shinja* <note>original: "Sinsja"</note>, and in the plural *Shinshu* <note>original: "Sinsju"</note>, are the persons who adhere to this Religion.

<margin>Beliefs of the Shintoists.</margin>
The most immediate goal which the followers of this Religion set for themselves is a state of happiness in this World. They do indeed have some notions, though obscure and imperfect, regarding the Immortality of our Souls and a future state of bliss or misery. And yet, as little mindful as they are of what will become of them in that future state, great is their care and attention to worship those Gods whom they believe to have a particular share in the government and management of this world. They believe these gods have a direct influence, each according to his specific function, over the events and necessities of human life. And although they acknowledge a Supreme Being who, they believe, dwells in the highest part of Heaven, and though they likewise admit some inferior Gods whom they place among the

If it is in any way probable that the first Japanese are descended from the Babylonians <note>The author refers to a then-common theory that all civilizations originated from the migration of people following the fall of the Tower of Babel</note>, and that, while at Babel, they acquired some notions of the true religion, of the creation of the world, and its state before that time, as they are delivered to us in sacred scripture, we may upon as good grounds suppose that by the alteration of their language, and by the troubles and fatigues of so long and tedious a journey, the same were almost entirely worn out of their minds. Upon their arrival in this extremity of the East, they deservedly bore a most profound respect to their leader, who had happily conducted them through so many dangers and difficulties; after his death they deified him. In succeeding ages, other great men who had well deserved of their Country—either by their prudence and wisdom, or by their courage and heroic actions—were likewise ranked among their *Kami* <note>Divine spirits or deities</note>, that is, among the Immortal Spirits worthy to have divine honors paid them; and to perpetuate their memory, *Mias* <note>Shrines</note>, or Temples, were in time erected to them. (*Mia*, properly speaking, signifies the House, or dwelling-place of a living Soul.) The respect due to these great men became in succession of time so universal that ever since it is thought to be a duty incumbent on every sincere lover of his Country, whatever sect otherwise he adheres to, to give public proofs of his veneration and grateful remembrance of their virtues and signal services by visiting their Temples and bowing to their Images, either on such days as are more particularly consecrated to their memory, or on any other proper occasion, provided they be not in a state of impurity and unfit to approach these holy places. Thus, what was at first intended as a simple act of respect and gratitude turned by degrees into adoration and worship. He possesses the sole power of canonization.

This Japanese Pope <note>The author uses this term to help 17th-century European readers understand the Emperor's role as a supreme spiritual leader</note> assumes also to himself, the sole power and authority of deifying and canonizing others, if it appears to him that they deserve it, either by the apparitions of their Souls after their death, or by some miracles wrought by them. In this case the Emperor confers an eminent title upon the new God, or Saint, and orders a *Mia* <term>Miya: A Shinto shrine or temple</term>, or Temple, to be built to his memory, which is done either at his own expence, or by the charitable contributions of pious, well-dispos’d Persons. If afterwards it so happens, that those, who worship in this Temple, and more particularly devote themselves to the new God, prosper in their undertakings, but much more if some extraordinary miracle hath been wrought, seemingly by his power and assistance, it will encourage other people to implore his protection, and by this means the number of his temples and worshippers will quickly increase. Thus the number of divinities is augmented every age. But besides all the illustrious men, who from time to time, for their heroic actions or singular piety, have been by the Spiritual Emperors related among the Divinities of the Country, they have another Series of Gods, of a more ancient date.

### CHAP II.
### Of the *Shinto* Temples, Belief and Worship.

<margin>Names of the Shinto Temples.</margin>
THE **Shintoists**, that is, the adherents of the **Shinto** Religion, call their Temples, or Churches, **Miya**, which word, as I have observed, signifies dwelling places of immortal Souls. They come nearest to the *shrines* <note>original: "Fana," the Latin term for a sanctuary or consecrated space.</note> of the ancient Romans, as they are gene-
<margin>And Gods</margin>rally speaking so many lasting monuments erected to the memory of great men. They call them also **Yashiro**, and **Sha**, or **Shinsha**, which last takes in the whole Court of the **Miya**, with all other buildings and dependencies belonging to the same. The Gods, who are the subject of their worship, they call **Shin** and **Kami**, which signifies Souls or Spirits. Sometimes also they honor them with the epithet of **Myojin**, sublime, illustrious, holy; and **Gongen**, just, severe, jealous. The adherents of other religions call the convents of their religious
<margin>Description of their Shrines</margin>men, and the places of their worship, **Tera**, that is, temples, and the Gods themselves, which they adore, **Hotoke** <note>original: "Foge," a likely transcription of Hotoke, the Japanese word for a Buddha or an enlightened being.</note>. All other foreign Idols, the worship of whom was brought into **Japan** from beyond the Sea, are comprehended under one general name of **Bodhisattvas**, or **Buddhas**. The **Miya**, as indeed all convents and religious houses in general, as well of this, as of their other sects, are seated in the pleasantest parts of the Country, on the best spots of ground, and commonly within, or near great cities, towns, villages and other inhabited places. I will confine myself in this chapter only to the **Miya** of the Shintoists. A broad and spacious walk planted with rows of fine cy-
press trees, which grow in the country, and are a tall fine tree, leads straight to the **Miya**, or else to the Temple-court, on which there are sometimes several **Miya** standing together, and in this case the walk aforesaid leads directly to that, which is reckoned the chief. The **Miya** are, generally speaking, seated in a pleasant wood, or in the ascent of a fine green hill, and have neat stone staircases leading up to them. Next to the highway, at the entry of the walk, which leads to the temple, stands, for distinction's sake from common roads, a particular
<margin>Temple Gates.</margin>fashioned gate, called **Torii**, and built either of stone or wood. The structure of these gates is but very mean and simple, they consisting of two perpendicular posts or pillars, with two beams laid across, the uppermost of which is, for ornament's sake, depressed in the middle, the two extremities standing upwards. Not far from the <term>Miya</term> is a basin, commonly of stone, and full of water for those who go to worship to wash themselves. <note>This is the *chozuya*, used for ritual purification of the hands and mouth before approaching the deity.</note> Close to the <term>Miya</term> stands a great wooden alms-chest. <note>Known as a *saisenbako*, where visitors drop coins as offerings.</note> The <term>Miya</term> itself is neither a splendid nor a magnificent building, but very mean and simple, commonly quadrangular, and built of wood, the beams being strong and neat. It seldom exceeds twice or thrice a man's height, and two or three fathoms in breadth. It is raised about a yard, or upwards, from the ground, being supported by short wooden posts. There is a small walk, or gallery, to go round it, and a few steps lead up to this walk. 

The frontispiece of the <term>Miya</term> is as simple as the rest, consisting only of one, or two, grated windows, for those that come to worship to look through, and to bow towards the chief place within. It is shut at all times, and often without anybody to take care of it. Other <term>Miyas</term> are somewhat larger, sometimes with an anti-chamber, and two side-rooms, wherein the keepers of the <term>Miya</term> sit, in honor of the <term>Kami</term> <note>original: "Cami"; the Shinto deities or spirits</note>, richly clad in their fine ecclesiastical gowns. All these several rooms have grated windows and doors, and the floor is covered with curious mats. Generally speaking, three sides of the temple are shut with deal-boards <note>Planks of fir or pine wood.</note>, there being no opening left but in the front. 

The roof is covered with tiles of stone, or shavings of wood, and juts out on all sides to a considerable distance, to cover the walk which goes round the temple. It differs from other buildings by its being curiously bent, and composed of several layers of fine wooden beams, which jutting out underneath make it look very singular. At the top of the roof there is sometimes a strong wooden beam, bigger than the rest, laid lengthways, at the extremities of which, two other beams stand up, crossing each other, sometimes a third one is laid athwart behind them. <note>This describes the *chigi* (forked roof finials) and *katsuogi* (decorative logs), hallmarks of Shinto architecture.</note> This structure is in imitation, as well as in memory, of the first <term>Ise Temple</term> <note>original: "Isje Temple"; the Grand Shrine of Ise, the ancestral shrine of the Imperial Family.</note>, which though simple, was yet very ingeniously and almost inimitably contrived so, that the weight and connection of these several beams was to keep the whole building standing. 

Over the Temple-door hangs sometimes a wide flat bell, and a strong, long, knotted rope, wherewith those that come to worship strike the bell as it were, to give notice to the Gods of their presence. This custom however is not very ancient, nor did it originally belong to the <term>Shinto</term> <note>original: "Sintos"</note> Religion, for it was borrowed from the <term>Budso</term> <note>original: "Budſo"; Buddhism (the way of the Buddha).</note>, or foreign idol-worship. Within the temple is hung up white paper, cut into small bits, the intent of which is to make people sensible of the purity of the place. <note>These paper streamers are called *shide*, often attached to a wand called a *gohei*.</note> Sometimes a large <term>Looking-glass</term> <note>The *kagami* (mirror) is one of the most sacred objects in Shinto, representing the honesty and purity of the heart.</note> is placed in the middle, for the worshippers to behold themselves, and withal to consider, that as distinctly as the spots of their face appear in the <term>Looking-glass</term>, so...

### The History of JAPAN. Book III.

...conspicuous are the secret spots and frauds of their hearts in the eyes of the Immortal Gods. These temples are very often without any Idols, or Images of the <term>Kami</term> <note>original: "Cami"; the spirits or deities of the Shinto religion.</note>, to whom they are consecrated. Nor indeed do they keep any Images at all in their temples, unless they deserve it on a particular account, either for the reputation and holiness of the carver, or because of some extraordinary miracles wrought by them. In this case a particular box is contrived at the chief and upper end of the temple, opposite to its grated front, and it is called <term>Hongo</term> <note>original: "Fongu"; literally the "real" or "true" temple, referring to the inner sanctuary.</note>, which is as much as to say, the real, true Temple. In this box, which the worshippers bow to, the Idol is locked up, and never taken out, but upon the great festival day of the <term>Kami</term>, whom it represents, which is celebrated but once in a hundred years. In the same shrine are likewise locked up, what relics they have, of the bones, habits <note>clothing</note>, swords, or handy-works of the same God.

<margin>Mikoshi, what they are.</margin>
The chief <term>Miya</term> <note>Shinto shrine</note> of every place hath one or more <term>Mikoshi</term> <note>original: "Mikosi"; portable shrines used to transport the deity during festivals.</note>, as they call them, belonging to it, being square, or six, or eight-cornered small shrines <note>original Latin: "Sacella"</note>, or smaller Temples, curiously lacquered, adorned without with gilt cornices, within with looking-glasses, cut white paper and other ornaments, and hanging on two poles in order to be carried about upon proper occasions, which is done with great pomp and solemnity, when upon the <term>Sennichi</term> <note>original: "Sennitz"; likely referring to a "thousand-day" festival or a primary feast day.</note>, that is, the chief festival-day of the God, to whom the <term>Miya</term> itself is consecrated, the <term>Kannushi</term> <note>original: "Canusi"; Shinto priests, literally "deity-master."</note> or Officers of the Temple celebrate the <term>Matsuri</term> <note>A Shinto festival.</note>, of which more in another place. Sometimes the Idol of the <term>Kami</term>, to whom the <term>Miya</term> is dedicated, or such of his relics, as are there kept, are carried about in these <term>Mikoshi</term> upon the same solemn occasion. The chief of the <term>Kannushi</term> takes them out of the shrine of the Temple, where they are kept in curious white boxes, carries them upon his back to the <term>Mikoshi</term>, and places them backwards into the same, the people in the mean time retiring out of the way, as being too impure and unworthy a race to behold these sacred things.

<margin>Ema, or Ornaments of the Temple.</margin>
The outside of the <term>Miya</term>, or the Anti-chamber, and other rooms built close to it, are commonly hung with divers ornaments, Scimitars <note>curved swords</note> curiously carved, Models of Ships, Images of different sorts, or other uncommon curiosities, affording an agreeable amusement for the idle spectators, who come to view and to worship in these Temples upon their holidays. These several ornaments are called <term>Ema</term> <note>original: "Jemma"; votive tablets or offerings given to the shrine.</note>, and are generally speaking free gifts to the Temple, given by the adherents of this religion, pursuant to vows, which they made, either for themselves, or for their relations and friends, when taken ill of some violent sickness, or laboring under some other misfortunes, and which they afterwards very scrupulously put in execution, both to show the power of the Gods, whose assistance they implored, and their own deep sense of gratitude for the blessings received from them. The same custom is likewise observed by the adherents of the <term>Bodhisattvas</term> <note>original: "Bosatz"; enlightened beings in Buddhism.</note>, or <term>Buddhism</term> <note>original: "Budsdo-Religion"; Butsudo, "the way of the Buddha."</note>. ### Chapter II. The History of JAPAN 211

<margin>Shrines, and those who serve them.</margin>
These *Miya*, or Shinto Temples, are not attended by monks or spiritual recluses, but by secular married men who are called <term>Negi</term>, <term>Kannushi</term> <note>literally "shrine-keepers" or "masters of the deity"</note>, and <term>Sannin</term>. They are supported either by the legacies left by the founder of the shrine, by subsidies granted to them by the <term>Mikado</term> <note>The Emperor of Japan</note>, or by the charitable contributions of pious worshippers. The word *Mikado*, according to its literal sense, signifies the "Sublime Port" <note>An 18th-century comparison to the "Sublime Porte," the central government of the Ottoman Empire</note>, with *Mi* being the same as *On*, *Go*, *O*, or *Gyo*—meaning high, mighty, illustrious, supreme, or sublime—and *Kado* signifying a port, gate, or door. These *Kannushi*, or secular priests, wear large gowns for distinction when they go out in public. These are commonly white, though sometimes yellow or other colors, and are styled after the fashion of the Emperor’s Court. However, they wear their ordinary secular clothes beneath these gowns. They shave their beards but allow their hair to grow. They wear a stiff, oblong, lacquered cap shaped somewhat like a ship, which stands out over the forehead and is tied under the chin with twisted silk strings. From these strings hang fringed knots, which are longer or shorter depending on the office or rank of the wearer. These officials are not required to bow deeply to those of superior rank; instead, they simply make the ends of these knots touch the floor. Their superiors have their hair twisted up under black gauze or crape in a very specific style, and their ears are covered by a particular kind of lap or flap—about a span and a half long and two or three inches broad—which stands out by their cheeks or hangs down according to the titles and honors conferred upon them by the Emperor.

<margin>By whom they are governed.</margin>
In spiritual matters, they fall under the absolute jurisdiction of the Emperor. However, in worldly or "temporal" affairs, they—and all other ecclesiastical persons in the Empire—are under the command of two <term>Jisha-bugyō</term> <note>original: "Dsi Sin Bugios"; Imperial Magistrates or Judges of Temples and Shrines</note>, who are appointed by the secular Monarch <note>The Shogun</note>.

<margin>Their Character.</margin>
They are incredibly haughty and proud, imagining themselves to be of a much better make and nobler ancestry than common people. When they appear in secular dress, they wear two swords <note>original: "Scimiters"</note> after the fashion of the nobility. Though they are secular persons themselves, they believe it is their duty to religiously abstain from all intimacy with the common people. Indeed, some carry these scrupulous ideas about their own purity and holiness so far that they avoid conversation even with other religious persons of different sects, fearing it might damage their reputation. Regarding this behavior, I must admit that something can be said in their defense: this uncommon carriage and religious avoidance of others seems to be the best way to hide their great ignorance and the inconsistencies of their theological system. Their divinity would likely be mocked if it ever became the subject of casual conversation, for the entire Shinto religion is so simple and basic—
