### The History of JAPAN. Book III. 212

The religion is so simple that, beyond a collection of mythological and fanciful stories about their gods, demi-gods, and heroes—which often seem to defy reason and common sense—their theologians have nothing in their sacred books or oral traditions to satisfy the curiosity of those seeking the true nature and essence of the gods. They lack clear teachings on the gods' power, their governance of the world, or the future state of the soul—essential points about which other pagan systems of divinity are rarely silent. For this reason, when the foreign religion of <term>Buddhism</term> <note>original: *Budsdo*-Religion</note> was introduced to Japan, it not only spread rapidly and with surprising success, but it soon caused a rift even among those who remained loyal to the religion of their ancestors. This led to the birth of two distinct sects into which the Shintoists are now divided.

<margin>
Two Sects of the Shintoists.
The Yuiitsu.
</margin>
The first of these sects is called <term>Yuiitsu</term> <note>original: *Juitz*; referring to Yuiitsu Shinto, which claimed to be the "one and only" original tradition</note>. The orthodox followers of this group remained so steadfast in the religion and customs of their ancestors that they would not yield on even the smallest or most insignificant point. However, they are so few in number that the <term>Kannushi</term> <note>original: *Canusi’s*; Shinto shrine priests</note> themselves make up the majority of the sect.

<margin>The Ryōbu.</margin>
The other sect is that of the <term>Ryōbu</term> <note>original: *Riobu’s*; meaning "Dual Shinto," a syncretic blend of Shinto and Buddhist beliefs</note>. These are a type of "syncretists" <note>people who attempt to merge different beliefs or schools of thought</note> who, seeking a more extensive knowledge of religious matters—particularly regarding the afterlife—attempted to reconcile the foreign religion with that of their ancestors. To achieve this, they proposed that the soul of <term>Amida</term> <note>The Buddha of Infinite Light, central to Pure Land Buddhism</note>, whom the Buddhists worship as their Savior, lived through reincarnation within the greatest of the Shinto gods, <term>Amaterasu</term> <note>original: *Ten Sio Dai Sin*; the Sun Goddess and primary deity of Shinto</note>, whom they call the essence of light and the sun. Most Shintoists identify with this sect. Even the <term>Dairi</term> <note>The Imperial Court</note>—perhaps aware of the inconsistencies in their own religion and how weak the arguments are for the divine status their master claims for himself—seem to favor this syncretism. Indeed, they recently showed they are not enemies to foreign worship by appointing Princes of the Imperial Blood to lead the three highest bishoprics of the <term>Ikkō-shū</term> <note>original: *Ikossu*; a powerful and wealthy Buddhist sect</note>.

<margin>Religion of the Secular Monarch.</margin>
The Secular Monarch <note>The Shogun, the military ruler of Japan as opposed to the spiritual Emperor</note> follows the religion of his forefathers and pays his respects once a year to the <term>Mikado</term> <note>The Emperor</note>. Today, this is done through a formal embassy and expensive gifts rather than in person. He personally visits the tombs of his imperial predecessors and frequents the major temples and religious houses where they are worshipped. When I was in Japan, the Secular Monarch ordered the construction of two magnificent temples in honor of the Chinese philosopher <term>Confucius</term> <note>original: *Koosju*</note>, whose philosophy they believe was communicated to him directly from Heaven,

<meta>The text ends here on a catchword "which," preparing for the next page's description of Confucian influence.</meta>

<margin>Shinto beliefs regarding the afterlife.</margin>
This is the same opinion that the Greeks formerly held concerning the philosophy of Socrates. <note>The author suggests that like Socrates, who focused on ethics rather than metaphysical speculation, Shinto is viewed as a practical rather than a complex theological system.</note> One thing remains worth observing: many, and perhaps the majority of those who during their lives constantly profess the <term>Shinto</term> <note>original: *Sintos*</note> religion—and even some of the <term>moralists</term> <note>original: *Siutosjus*; referring to scholars of the "Way of the Scholar" or Confucian-influenced Shintoists</note>—recommend their souls on their deathbeds to the care of the <term>Buddhist</term> <note>original: *Budsdo*</note> clergy. They request that the <term>Namu Amida Butsu</term> <note>original: *Namanda*; a sacred Buddhist invocation to the Amida Buddha for salvation</note> be sung for them, and that their bodies be cremated and buried according to <term>Buddhist</term> <note>original: *Budsdoists*</note> customs. The followers of Shinto do not believe in the <term>transmigration of souls</term> <note>original: "Pythagorean Doctrine"; the ancient Greek belief that souls are reborn into new bodies</note>, although this is almost universally accepted by other Eastern nations. However, they do abstain from killing and eating those animals that are useful to mankind, regarding it as an act of cruelty and ingratitude. They believe that after souls depart from their bodies, they migrate to a place of happiness located just beneath the thirty-three heavens and the dwellings of their gods. For this reason, they call this place <term>Takamagahara</term> <note>original: *Takamanofarra*; meaning the "High Plain of Heaven"</note>, which signifies the "high and subcelestial fields." They believe the souls of those who have led a good life in this world are admitted there without delay, but the souls of the wicked and impious are denied entrance and condemned to wander for a time sufficient to atone for their crimes. This is the extent of their knowledge regarding a future state of bliss. Beyond these "Elysian fields" <note>a reference to the paradise of Greek mythology</note> and stations of happiness, they recognize no hell, no places of torment, no <term>absolute darkness</term> <note>original: "Cimmerian darkness"; a classical reference to the mythical Cimmerians who lived in perpetual mist and gloom</note>, nor any unfortunate state awaiting the soul in the world to come. Furthermore, they know of no other Devil except that which they believe possesses the Fox—a very mischievous animal in this country. The fox is so dreaded that some believe the wicked are transformed into foxes after death, which their priests call <term>Ma</term> <note>original: *Ma*; a term for an evil spirit or demon</note>.

<margin>Essential points of the Shinto religion.</margin>
The chief points of the Shinto religion are the observances that followers believe make them pleasing to the Gods and worthy of receiving divine mercy—either through immediate admission into the stations of happiness after death or, as is more commonly desired, a series of temporal blessings in this life. These points are: 1. The inward purity of the heart. 2. A religious abstinence from whatever makes a person impure. 3. Diligent observance of solemn festivals and holy days. 4. Pilgrimages to the holy places at <term>Ise</term> <note>original: *Isie*; the location of the Grand Shrine of Ise, dedicated to the sun goddess Amaterasu</note>. To these, some very religious people add a fifth: 5. Chastising and mortifying their bodies. I shall now proceed to treat each of these individually.

<margin>The inward purity of the heart.</margin>
To begin with the inward purity of the heart: this consists of performing or avoiding those things which one is ordered to do or shun, whether by the laws of nature and the dictates of reason, or by the more immediate and special commands of civil magistrates. The law of external purity—of which more will be said later—is the only one whose observance is strictly recommended to the followers of this religion. They have no other laws given to them, by either Divine or Ecclesiastical authority, to direct and regulate them in their...

### The History of JAPAN. Book III. 214

...outward behavior. Hence, it might seem natural to think that they would give themselves over to all kinds of luxury and sinful pleasures, allowing themselves, without restraint, whatever could gratify their wishes and desires. One might expect them to be free from the fear of acting against the will of the Gods and little concerned about the effects of divine anger or displeasure. This might indeed be the miserable state of a nation in such a condition, were it not for a more powerful ruler within their hearts: natural reason. This reason exerts itself with full force here and is quite capable of restraining people from indulging in vice and winning them over to the side of virtue, provided they listen to its dictates. Furthermore, the government officials have taken sufficient care to provide what is lacking in this area; by their authority, very severe laws are currently in force against all sorts of crimes and misdemeanors. Certainly, the Japanese nation, when considered as a whole, makes it clear that the dictates of natural reason and the laws of civil magistrates are reliable enough guides for those who wish to lead a good and virtuous life and keep their hearts in a state of purity.

<margin>
Laws of external purity.
</margin>
But regarding **external purity**—the observance of which is less important in itself, yet more strictly commanded—it consists of abstaining from blood, from eating meat, and from contact with dead bodies. Those who have rendered themselves impure by any of these things are forbidden from entering temples, visiting holy places, and generally from appearing in the presence of the Gods. Anyone stained with their own or another’s blood is <term>ritually impure</term> <note>original: *Fusio*; referring to the Shinto concept of *kegare* or ritual pollution</note> for seven days, meaning they are unfit to approach holy places. If, during the construction of a <term>shrine</term> <note>original: *Mia*; a Shinto temple</note>, one of the workmen should happen to be injured so that he bleeds, it is considered a very great misfortune. Such an accident makes him entirely incapable of working on that sacred building in the future. If the same accident occurs during the building or repairing of any of the temples of <term>Amaterasu</term> <note>original: *Tensio Daï Sin*; the Sun Goddess and supreme deity of Shinto</note> at <term>Ise</term> <note>original: *Isje*; the site of the most sacred Shinto shrines</note>, the misfortune does not affect the workman alone; the temple itself must be pulled down and rebuilt from scratch. 

No woman may come to the temple while she is having her menstrual cycle. It is commonly believed that during holy pilgrimages to Ise, these cycles cease entirely for that time. If this is true, it must be due either to the exhaustion of a long and tedious journey or to the great pains women take to conceal it, fearing their labor and expenses might otherwise be wasted. Anyone who eats the flesh of any four-footed beast (deer being the only exception) is <term>ritually impure</term> for thirty days. In contrast, anyone who eats a bird—whether wild or tame—is impure for only one "Japanese hour" (which is equal to two of our hours), though water birds, pheasants, and cranes are exceptions. Anyone who kills an animal, is present at an execution, attends to a dying person, or enters a house where a corpse lies, is impure for that entire day. But of all the things that make a person impure, none is reckoned—

# Chapter III. The History of JAPAN.

<margin>The closer your relationship to the deceased, the greater the impurity.</margin>
<margin>The symbol of the three monkeys.</margin>
<margin>A <term>Fujo</term><note>Japanese: *Fujo* (不浄), meaning "unclean" or "impure."</note>.</margin>
...people are considered so contagious as when they are near the death of parents and close relatives. The closer your relationship to the deceased, the greater the **impurity** is considered to be. All the ceremonies to be observed on these occasions—such as the length of the mourning period and similar requirements—are determined by this rule. By failing to follow these precepts, people make themselves guilty of an "external impurity" which is hated by the Gods, and they become unfit to approach the temples. Overly cautious people, who wish to be seen as great saints, take these matters even further; they imagine that even the impurities of others can infect them in three different ways: through the **eyes** which see impure things, the **mouth** which speaks of them, and the **ears** which hear them. These three paths to sin and impurity are represented by the emblem of **three monkeys** sitting at the feet of *Jizō* <note>original: "Dsisjo"; refers to Ksitigarbha, a popular Bodhisattva in Japan associated with the protection of travelers and children.</note>. One monkey covers both his eyes with his paws, the second covers his mouth, and the third covers his ears. This symbol can be seen in most temples of the *Buddhists* <note>original: "Budsdoists," Kaempfer's term for practitioners of Buddhism.</note>, from whom it was borrowed. We also found it in several places along the highway. An acquaintance of mine in Nagasaki was so incredibly fussy and cautious on this point that if he received a visit from someone he suspected of being <term>impure</term> <note>original: "Fusjo"</note>, he would have his entire house washed and scrubbed with water and salt from top to bottom. Yet, despite all this superstitious care, the wiser of his countrymen look upon him as a complete hypocrite.

# CHAPTER III
## Concerning the *Shinto Festivals*, that is, *their lucky days and holidays, and how they are celebrated.*

<margin>The celebration of festivals.</margin>
The celebration of solemn festivals and holidays, which is the third essential part of the *Shinto* <note>original: "Sintos"</note> religion, consists of what they call *Mairu* <note>original: "Majiru," meaning to go or to visit a shrine.</note>—that is, going to the *Miya* <note>original: "Mias," refers to Shinto shrines.</note> or temples of the Gods and deceased great men. This may be done at any time, but it should never be neglected on those days specifically consecrated for worship—unless the believer is in a state of impurity and therefore not properly qualified to appear before the immortal Gods, who detest all uncleanness. Scrupulous worshipers go even further, believing it is inappropriate to appear before the Gods even when the thoughts or memory of their own misfortunes occupy their minds. For, since these immortal beings live in a state of constant bliss and happiness, it is thought that such sad objects would be offensive and unpleasant to them, just like the prayers and pleas of people...

### The History of JAPAN. Book III.

<margin>How the Japanese perform their devotions.</margin>...people, whose hearts—the very inmost parts of which are laid open to the [Gods'] penetrating sight—labor under deep sorrow and affliction. They perform their devotions at the temples in the following manner: The worshippers, having first washed and cleaned themselves, put on the very best clothes they have, including a ***Kamishimo*** <note>original: "Kamisijno"; a formal ceremonial garment worn by samurai and officials during the Edo period.</note>, as they call it, or a garment of ceremony, each according to his ability. 

Thus dressed, they walk with a composed and grave countenance to the temple court. First, they go to the water basin to wash their hands, if necessary; for this purpose, a pail is hung by its side. Then, casting down their eyes, they move on with great reverence and submission toward the ***Miya*** <note>original: "Mia"; a Shinto shrine.</note> itself. Having ascended the few steps that lead to the walkway around the temple, they place themselves opposite the grated windows of the shrine and the looking-glass <note>A mirror, or *Shinkyo*, which represents the purity of the deity and reflects the soul of the worshipper.</note> within.

They fall down upon their knees and bow their heads quite to the ground, slowly and with great humility. Then, lifting their heads again while still kneeling and turning their eyes toward the mirror, they offer a short prayer in which they reveal to the Gods their desires and necessities, or recite a <term>Takamano Farokami Fodomari</term> <note>original: "Takamano Farokami Fodomari"; likely a phonetic transcription of a Shinto purification prayer (*Harae*) invoking the gods of *Takamagahara*, the High Celestial Plain.</note>. They then throw some ***monies*** <note>original: "Putjes"; referring to small copper coins used as offerings.</note>, or small pieces of money, as an offering to the Gods and as charity to the priests, either through the grates onto the floor of the shrine or into the alms-box which stands close by. 

All this being done, they strike the bell thrice—which is hung up over the door of the shrine—for the diversion of the Gods, whom they believe to be highly delighted with the sound of musical instruments. They then retire to enjoy themselves for the remaining part of the day with walking, exercises, eating or drinking, and treating one another in the very best manner they can. 

This plain and simple act of devotion, which may be repeated at any time even when they are not dressed in their best clothes, is performed on solemn festivals by all Shinto worshippers at the temples of one or more Gods in whom they particularly trust—either because those Gods are the patrons of their profession or because they believe the Gods have the power to assist and forward their private undertakings. 

They have no settled rites or church ceremonies, no prayer beads, nor any fixed forms of prayers. Everyone is at liberty to express his needs to the Gods in whatever words and in whatever manner he pleases. Indeed, there are some among them who think it unnecessary to speak at all, assuming that the very inmost of their hearts—all their thoughts, wishes, and desires—are as fully known to the immortal Gods as their faces are seen in the mirror. Nor is it in the least required that they should prepare themselves through any particular mortification of their bodies or other acts of devotion to worthily celebrate their festival days (ordinary or extraordinary) or the days of commemoration for their deceased parents or nearest relations. Even on those days, which are more particularly consecrated to commemorate...

It is observable in general, that their Festivals and Holidays are days sacred rather to mutual compliments and civilities, than to acts of holiness and devotion, for which reason also they call them *Rebi’s* <note>original: "Rebi’s"; likely a transcription of *Ennichi* or *Reibi*, referring to festive or commemorative days.</note>, which implies as much as *Visiting-days*. ’Tis true indeed, that they think it a duty incumbent on them on those days, to go to the Temple of *Tensio Daifin* <note>Amaterasu-Omikami, the Sun Goddess and principal deity of the Shinto faith.</note>, the first and principal object of their worship, and the Temples of their other Gods and deceased great men. And although they are scrupulous enough in the observance of this duty, yet the best part of their time is spent with visiting and complimenting their superiors, friends and relations. Their feasts, weddings, audiences, great entertainments, and in general all manner of publick and private Rejoicings are made on these days preferably to others, not only because they are then more at leisure, but chiefly because they fancy, that their Gods themselves are very much delighted, when men allow themselves reasonable pleasures and diversions. All their *Rebi’s* or Holidays in general, are unmovable, and fix’d to certain days. Some are monthly, others yearly, both which I proceed now more particularly to enumerate.

<margin>Monthly Holidays. Day of the New Moon.</margin>
The Monthly Holidays are three in number. The first is call’d *Tsi-tatz* <note>original: "Tsi-tatz"; *Tsuitachi*, the first day of the lunar month.</note>, and is the first day of each month. It deserves rather to be call’d a Day of Compliments and mutual Civilities, than a Church or Sunday. The Japanese on this day rise early in the morning, and pass their time going from house to house to see their superiors, friends and relations, to pay their respects and compliments to them, and to wish them *Medito* <note>original: "Medito"; from *Omedetou*, meaning "Congratulations" or "Joy to you."</note>, or Joy on the happy return of the New Moon. The remainder of the day is spent about the Temples and in other pleasant Places, where there is agreeable walking. Some divert themselves with drinking of *Soccana* <note>original: "Soccana"; likely referring to *Sakana*, which usually denotes snacks eaten with alcohol, though the author identifies it here as the liquor itself.</note>, a sort of liquor peculiar to this Country. Others pass the afternoon in company with Women. In short, every one follows that day, what pleasures and diversion he likes best. And this custom is grown so universal, that not only the *Sintoists* <note>Followers of Shinto, the indigenous spirituality of Japan.</note>, but the Japanese in general, of all ranks and religions, observe it as a custom, derived down to them from their ancestors, and worthy, were it but on this sole account, that some regard should be paid to it.

<margin>Day of the Full Moon.</margin>
The second Monthly Holiday, is the fifteenth of each month, being the day of the Full-Moon. The Gods of the Country have a greater share in the visits, the Japanese make on this day, than their Friends and Relations.

<margin>Their third Monthly Holiday.</margin>
Their third Monthly holiday, is the twenty-eighth of each month, being the day before the New Moon, or the last day of the decreasing Moon. Not near so much regard is had to this, than there is to either of the two former, and the *Sintos* Temples are very little crowded on it. There is a greater concourse of People on this day at the Budsdos <note>original: "Budsdos"; referring to Buddhist temples or shrines (from *Butsudo*, the way of the Buddha).</note>

<margin>Yearly Festivals.</margin>
They have five great yearly *Rebi*, or *Sekkū* <note>original: "Sekf"; the five seasonal festivals</note>, that is, Festivals or holidays, which from their number are called *Gosekku* <note>original: "Gosekf"</note>, that is, the five solemn festivals. They are purposely laid upon those days, which by reason of their odd numbers <note>original: "Imparity"</note> are judged to be the most unfortunate, and they have also borrowed their names from thence. They are, 1. *Shōgatsu* <note>original: "Soguatz"</note>, or the New Year's day. 2. *Sangatsu Sannichi* <note>original: "Sanguatz Sannitz"</note>, the third day of the third month. 3. *Gogatsu Gonichi* <note>original: "Goguatz Gonitz"</note>, the fifth day of the fifth month. 4. *Shichigatsu Nanuka* <note>original: "Sitfiguatz Fanuka"</note>, the seventh day of the seventh month, and 5. *Kugatsu Kunichi* <note>original: "Kuguatz Kunitz"</note>, the ninth day of the ninth month.

These five great yearly festivals are again little else but **Public Festivals** <note>original: "Festa Politica"</note>, days of universal rejoicings. It hath been already observed, that they were by their Ancestors purposely and prudently appointed to be celebrated on those days, which were judged by their odd numbers to be the most unfortunate; this was done in order to divert their *Kami* <note>original: "Cami's"; Shinto deities</note> or Gods by their universal mirth, and by their wishing of Joy and happiness to each other to decline, and to avoid, all unhappy accidents that might otherwise befall them: on this account also, and because of their being days sacred not so much to the worship of their Gods, as to joy and pleasure, they are celebrated indifferently, not only by the Shintoists <note>original: "Sintoists"</note>, but by the generality of the Japanese, whatever sect or religion they otherwise adhere to.

<margin>New-Year's-Day.</margin>
But to take them into a more particular consideration, I will begin with the *Shōgatsu* <note>original: "Songuatz"</note>, or *New-Year's-Day*, which is celebrated in *Japan* with the utmost solemnity, preferably to all other Holidays. The main business of the day consists in visiting and complimenting each other on the happy beginning of the New Year, in eating and drinking, and going to the Temples, which some do to worship, but far the greater part for pleasure and diversion. Whoever is able to stir, gets up early <note>original: "betimes"</note> in the morning, puts on his best clothes, and repairs to the houses of his patrons, friends and relations, to whom he makes, with a low bow, his *Medetō* <note>original: "Medito"; a congratulatory greeting</note>, as they call it, or compliment suitable to the occasion, and at the same time presents them with a box, wherein are contained two or three fans, with a piece of the dried flesh of the *Awabi*, or **Sea Ear** <note>original: "Auris Marina"; a type of abalone</note>, tied to them, and his name written upon the box, for the information of the person to whom the present is made, in case he should not be at home, or not at leisure to receive Company. The piece of the *Awabi* flesh in particular, is intended to remind them of the frugality, as well as the poverty of their Ancestors, who lived chiefly upon the flesh of this shell-fish, and to make them sensible of their present happiness and plenty. In houses of people of quality, where the number of visitors on such days must needs be very considerable, they keep a Man on purpose, waiting at the entry of the house, or in one of the lowermost apartments, to receive both the

<margin>Second Yearly Festival.</margin>
The second *Sekku* <note>original: "Seks"; one of the five seasonal festivals.</note>, or great yearly Festival, is called *Sangatsu Sannichi* <note>original: "Sanguatz Sannitz"</note>, because it is celebrated on the third day of the third month. On this day also, after the usual compliments and visits that friends and relations pay to one another, and inferiors to their superiors, everyone diverts himself in the best manner he can. The season of the year—the beginning of spring—and the trees—chiefly Plum, Cherry, and Apricot trees, which are then in full blossom and loaded with numberless white and pink <note>original: "incarnate"</note> flowers, both single and double—invite everybody to take the diversion of the Country. The trees are no less remarkable for their size and abundance than for their singular beauty, and they beckon all to behold nature in her new and inimitable dress. But this same festival is, besides, a day of pleasure and diversion for young girls, for whose sake a great entertainment is commonly prepared by their parents, to which they invite their nearest relations and friends. A large and spacious apartment is curiously adorned with puppets of considerable value, which represent the Court of the *Dairi* <note>The Imperial Court of the Emperor in Kyoto.</note>, or Ecclesiastical Hereditary Emperor, along with the person of *Hina-kugyō* <note>original: "Finakuge"; doll-sized representations of court nobles.</note>. A table with Japanese victuals is placed before each puppet, and among other things, cakes made of rice and the leaves of young mugwort <note>Known as kusa-mochi, these are still traditional for the Spring festival.</note>. These victuals, and a dish of *Sake* <note>original: "Saki"; Japanese rice wine.</note>, are presented to the guests by the girls for whose diversion the entertainment is intended—or by their parents, if the children are too young.

Soon after, she found herself pregnant and gave birth to 500 eggs. The poor woman, extremely surprised by this extraordinary occurrence and filled with fear that the eggs, if hatched, might produce monstrous animals, packed them all into a box and threw them into the *Ryūfagawa* <note>original: "Riufagawa"; likely referring to the Tatsunokawa or "Dragon-fold River".</note> River. However, she took the precaution of writing the word *Hōjō* <note>original: "Fosjoroo"; likely referring to the Buddhist concept of *Hōjō*, the ritual release of captive animals to earn merit.</note> upon the box.

Some time later, an old fisherman who lived a good way down the river found this box floating. He picked it up and, finding it full of eggs, carried them home to show them to his wife. She was of the opinion that there could not be anything ordinary about them and that they had certainly been cast into the water for a significant reason; therefore, she advised him to carry them back to where he found them. But the old man replied, "My dear, we are both old and just on the brink of the grave. It will be a matter of very little consequence to us, whatever comes out of the eggs; therefore, I have a mind to hatch them and see what they produce."

Accordingly, he hatched them in an oven, using hot sand and cushions, as is the custom in the *Indies* <note>A historical reference to South or Southeast Asia, where artificial incubation of eggs was a known practice to Europeans.</note>. Having afterwards opened them, they found a child in every one. To support such a number of children proved to be a very heavy burden for this old couple. However, they managed and raised them on minced mugwort leaves and boiled rice. 

In time, they grew so big that the old man and his wife could no longer maintain them. They were necessitated to shift for themselves as well as they could and took to highway robbery. Among other projects, it was proposed to them to go up the river to the house of a rich man who was very famous for his great wealth in that part of the country.

As good luck would have it, this house proved to be that of their mother. Upon application made at the door, one of the servants asked what their names were. To this they answered that they had no names, that they were a brood of 500 eggs, and that mere want and necessity had obliged them to call; they promised to go about their business if the household would be so charitable as to give them some food. 

The servant, having brought the message to his lady, she sent him back to inquire whether there had not been something written upon the box in which the eggs had been found. Being answered that the word *Hōjō* <note>original: "Fosjoroo"</note> was found written upon it, she could then no longer doubt but that they were all her children. Accordingly, she acknowledged and received them as such and held a great entertainment. At this feast, every one of the guests was presented with a dish of *sakana* <term>Sakana: Traditionally side dishes or snacks served with drinks; in a festive context, these are ceremonial offerings.</term>, cakes of mugwort and rice, and a branch of the apricot tree <note>While the text says "Apricock" (Apricot), this festival (the 3rd day of the 3rd month) is the Peach Festival, or *Momo no Sekku*, and usually features peach blossoms.</note>. 

This is the reason they give for why, on this festival, branches of apricot trees are laid over the kettle, and cakes are made of mugwort and rice, which they call *Kusamochi* <term>Kusamochi: Literally "grass cake," a traditional green rice cake flavored with Japanese mugwort (yomogi).</term> (original: *Futfumotzi*), and prepare in the following manner: the mugwort leaves are soaked in water overnight, then pressed, dried, and reduced to powder...

<margin>The third yearly Festival.</margin>
The third *Sekku* <note>original: "Seku"; a seasonal festival.</note>, or yearly Festival, is *Gogatsu Gofun-nichi* <note>original: "Goguatz-Gonitz"; the fifth day of the fifth month.</note>, or the fifth day of the fifth month. It is also called *Tango no Sekku*, and is much of the same nature with the last, with this difference only, that it is intended chiefly for the diversion of young boys, who in this, as well as in other countries, neglect no opportunity to make a holiday, and to play about. The inhabitants of *Nagasaki* divert themselves on the water on this and some following days, rowing up and down in their boats, which are for this purpose curiously adorned, and crying, according to the custom of the Chinese, *Peiron*, *Peiron* <note>original: "Peiruun"; the Dragon Boat races, a tradition imported from China.</note>. Mugwort leaves are put upon the roofs and over the doors of their houses. It is commonly believed that the Mugwort gathered about this time of the year, and particularly on these holidays, makes the best and strongest <term>Moxa<gloss>A traditional medical practice involving the burning of dried mugwort on the skin to stimulate healing.</gloss></term>, when three or four years old. This Festival owes its origin to the history of *Peiron*, a King of the Island *Maurigasima*, <margin>History of Peiruun.</margin> of whom, and the tragical destruction of this once rich and flourishing Island, I have given a large account in my <note>original: "Amœnitates Exoticæ"; translated as *Exotic Pleasures*, Kaempfer’s scientific and ethnographic work.</note> *Exotic Pleasures*, Volume 3. Section 13. whereto I refer the Reader. (See the History of the Tea in the Appendix.) It began to be celebrated at *Nagasaki*, by the *Fukien* <note>original: "Fokisui"; likely referring to Chinese immigrants from the Fujian province.</note> people, who introduced it at first among the young boys, and kept it for some time, before elderly and grave people would conform themselves to the custom. It is said, that at the place, where the Island stood, some remains of it do still appear in low water. The very best earth for porcelain ware is found at the same place, and sometimes entire vessels of a fine, thin, greenish, old china are taken up by the Divers, which the Japanese have a very great value for, both for their antiquity and for the good quality, which it is said they have, not only to preserve Tea a long while, but even to restore old Tea, which begins to decay, to its former strength and goodness.

<margin>Fourth yearly Festival.</margin>
The fourth great yearly Festival is called *Shichigatsu Nanuka* <note>original: "Sisfiguatz Nanuka"; the seventh day of the seventh month.</note>, because of its being celebrated on the seventh day of the seventh month. They give it also the name of *Shisseki Tanabata*, which implies as much, and *Tanomu no Sekku*, which is as much as to say, an Auxiliary Festival. The usual pleasures and diversions consisting in visiting one another, in eating and drinking, are followed on this day with the same freedom, as on other solemn days. The School-boys in particular, among various sorts of plays, erect poles or posts of Bamboos, and tie verses of their own making to them, to show their application and progress at School.

# The History of JAPAN. Book III. #

<margin>Fifth yearly Festival.</margin>
The fifth and last of the great yearly Festivals is *Kunitz* <note>original: "Kunitz"; likely referring to *Kunichi* or the *Kiku no Sekku* (Chrysanthemum Festival)</note>, or *Kugatsu Kokonoka* <note>original: "Kuguätz Kokonoka"; the ninth day of the ninth month</note>, so called because it is celebrated on the ninth day of the ninth month. Drinking is the favorite diversion during this Festival, though without neglecting their other usual rejoicings. No expense is spared to provide plenty of food and good liquors, each person according to their means. The joy and mirth are universal. Neighbours take turns hosting one another on that day and those that follow. Not even strangers or unknown persons are allowed to pass by without being invited to make merry with the company. In short, one would imagine that the <term>Bacchanals<gloss>Ancient Roman festivals for Bacchus, the god of wine, famous for wild and drunken celebrations.</gloss></term> of the Romans had been brought over into Japan and established there. At Nagasaki, the solemnity is even greater, as the festival of *Suwa* <note>original: "Suwa"; a Shinto deity</note>—formerly a renowned Hunter and now the God and Protector of hunting—luckily happens to fall upon this same day. All sorts of diversions and public shows, such as dancing, plays, and processions (which they call *Matsuri* <note>original: "Matsuri"; meaning a festival or an offering</note>, or *Matsuru* <note>original: "Matsuru"; the act of making an offering or worshiping</note>) so greatly entertain the people that many choose to skip their dinner rather than stop wandering and staring about the streets until late at night.

<margin>Other Festivals.</margin>
But besides these five great yearly Festivals, there are many more holidays observed in Japan. These are of less note and are sacred to particular Gods and Idols in whose honor they are celebrated, either universally throughout the Empire or only in specific places that acknowledge their favor and protection in a more personal way. It would be unnecessary and almost endless to mention them all; however, to satisfy the reader, I will limit myself to some of the most prominent. But before I proceed, I must observe that for the most part, these are not as ancient as the five great festivals mentioned above. Instead, they are of a later date, established at different times to honor the memory of certain Emperors and other great men. These individuals either performed signal services for their country during their lifetimes, or, through apparitions and extraordinary miracles after their deaths, convinced their countrymen that they had been transported into the regions of immortal spirits. By providing powerful assistance in private undertakings, they proved they held a significant share in the government of this world and were worthy of divine worship.

<margin>Festival of Tensho Daijin</margin>
*Tensho Daijin* <note>original: "Tenfio Dai Sin"; the Sun Goddess Amaterasu, the supreme deity in Shinto</note> is the supreme of all the Japanese Gods and is acknowledged as the Patron and Protector of the whole Empire. His <note>Kaempfer identifies the deity as male here, though Amaterasu is traditionally female.</note> annual Festival falls upon the sixteenth day of the ninth month and is celebrated in all cities and villages throughout the Empire. Among other things, it is marked by solemn *Matsuri’s*, as they call them, involving processions and public shows in honor of—and often in the presence of—his idol and priests. Two such <term>Matsuris<gloss>Traditional Japanese festivals or rituals held to honor Shinto deities (kami).</gloss></term> are celebrated every year with great pomp and solemnity in honor of that God, to whose more particular care and protection the people have devoted themselves. As for **Tensio Dai Sin** <note>original: "Tensio Dai Sin"; known today as Amaterasu Omikami, the Sun Goddess and the supreme deity of Shinto.</note>, besides his great yearly festival—which falls on the sixteenth day of the ninth month—the sixteenth, twenty-first, and twenty-sixth days of every month are likewise sacred to him, though they are not celebrated with any great solemnity.

<margin>Festival of *Suwa*.</margin>
The ninth day (though the common people also add the nineteenth and twenty-ninth) of every month is sacred to **Suwa** <note>original: "Suwa"; refers to Suwa Myojin, a deity of wind, water, and hunting.</note>. All lovers of hunting, and those persons who recommend themselves to Suwa’s more immediate protection, never fail on these days to pay their duty and worship to him at his temples. His annual festival is celebrated with more than ordinary pomp and solemnity on the ninth day of the sixth month. On this day, the <term>Kannushi<gloss>Shinto priests responsible for the maintenance of shrines and leading worship.</gloss></term> require all those who come to worship at Suwa’s temples to creep through a circle or hoop made of bamboo and wound about with linen; this is done in memory of a certain accident which is said to have happened to the Saint during his lifetime. However, the greatest of his yearly festivals is celebrated at **Nagasaki** on the ninth day of the ninth month. This city holds a particular veneration for Suwa, and the Matsuris and other public and private rejoicings made on this occasion last for three successive days.

<margin>Festivals of *Tenfin*.</margin>
**Tenfin** <note>original: "Tenfin"; Tenjin, the deified spirit of the scholar Sugawara no Michizane, revered as the god of learning and scholarship.</note> has two yearly festivals: one on the twenty-fifth day of the second month, and the other on the twenty-fifth day of the eighth month, the latter of which is celebrated with much greater solemnity than the first. His chief temple is at **Saif** <note>original: "Saif"; Dazaifu in Fukuoka, the site of Michizane's exile.</note>, the place of his banishment. He has another temple at **Miaco** <note>original: "Miaco"; the historical name for Kyoto, the imperial capital.</note>, where he manifested himself through many miracles. His worshippers travel in pilgrimage to these two places from all parts of the Empire, chiefly on the twenty-fifth day of the eighth month. He also has a private monthly holiday on every twenty-fifth day of the month.

<margin>Festivals of *Fatzman*.</margin>
The Festival of **Fatzman** <note>original: "Fatzman"; Hachiman, the syncretic god of war and protector of the Japanese people.</note>, a brother of Tensio Dai Sin <note>In Shinto mythology, Hachiman is the deified Emperor Ōjin, not literally the brother of the Sun Goddess Amaterasu; the author may be relaying a local or misunderstood tradition.</note>, is likewise celebrated on the 25th day of the eighth month. He was known in his lifetime as **Oofin** <note>original: "Oofin"; Emperor Ōjin.</note> and was the 16th Emperor of Japan.

The Festival of **Mori Saki Dai Gongen** is on the 11th day of the third month.

**Simios Dai Miosin** <note>original: "Simios Dai Miosin"; Sumiyoshi Daimyōjin, deities of the sea and sailing.</note>.

His monthly holiday is the same as Hachiman’s, but it is little regarded.

<margin>Gods of the Merchants.</margin>
Merchants worship and devote themselves in a more particular manner to the four following gods, whom they regard as the gods of fortune and prosperity:

<margin>Ebisu.</margin>
1. **Ebisu** <note>original: "Jebisu".</note> was the brother of **Amaterasu** <note>original: "Tensio Daisin".</note>, but was disgraced by her and banished to an uninhabited island. It is said of him that he could live two or three days under water. He is, as it were, the Neptune of this country and the protector of fishermen and seafaring people. They represent him sitting on a rock with a fishing rod in one hand, or the celebrated **Tai** <note>original: "Tai" or "Steenbrassem"; a red sea bream, considered a symbol of luck.</note> in the other.

<margin>Daikoku.</margin>
2. **Daikoku** is said to have the power that whenever he knocks with his hammer, he can bring forth anything he wants, such as rice, food, cloth, money, and so forth. He is commonly represented sitting on a bale of rice, holding his fortunate hammer in his right hand and a bag slung nearby to hold what he produces.

<margin>Toshitoku.</margin>
3. **Toshitoku**, also called **Kurokushi** <note>original: "Kurokusi"; likely referring to the deity Fukurokuju or Jurojin, who are often conflated in early Western accounts.</note> by some. The Japanese worship him at the beginning of the New Year to obtain his assistance for success and prosperity in their endeavors. He is represented standing, dressed in a large gown with long sleeves, having a long beard, a huge, unusually high forehead, large ears, and a fan in his right hand. The pictures of these three gods can be seen among the other illustrations on Plate VIII, the large map of Japan.

<margin>Hotei.</margin>
4. **Hotei**, called **Miroku** <note>original: "Miroku"; the name of the future Buddha, though Hotei is considered an incarnation of him.</note> by some, is represented with a very large belly. His worshippers expect from his kind assistance, among other blessings, health, riches, and children.

These are the greatest of their gods and the festival days sacred to them. ## CHAPTER IV.

### Concerning the *Sanga* or Pilgrimage to *Ise*

<margin>Pilgrimages of the Japanese.</margin>
The Japanese are very much devoted to pilgrimages. They make several, and to different places. The first and most important goes to Ise <note>original: "Isje"; site of the Inner Shrine dedicated to the Sun Goddess Amaterasu.</note>; the second to the thirty-three chief Kannon Temples <note>original: "Quanwon"; the Bodhisattva of Mercy</note> of the Empire; the third to some of the most eminent Shinto <note>original: "Sin, or Cami"</note> or Buddhist <note>original: "Fotoge or Buds"</note> Temples, famous for the great miracles performed there and the help and benefit pilgrims found by going to worship there. Such places are, for instance, Nikkō <note>original: "Nikotira"; meaning the Temple of the Splendor of the Sun</note> in the Province of Ōshū, some temples of Hachiman <note>original: "Fatzman"; the god of war</note>, some temples of the great teacher Yakushi <note>original: "Jakusi"; the Medicine Buddha</note>, and several others, of which every person is at liberty to choose which they like best, or which best suits their convenience to visit. A true Orthodox Shintoist visits no other Temples on pilgrimage but those of his own Gods, and the Temple of Dazaifu <note>original: "Saif"</note> in Chikuzen, where Tenjin <note>original: "Tensin"; the deified scholar Sugawara no Michizane</note> died. It may be helpful to observe in general that of the three different types of pilgrimages mentioned above, the last are made indifferently by Shintoists as well as Buddhists <note>original: "Budsdoists"</note>, with the difference, however, that everyone goes only to those Temples and worships only those Gods whom his religion commands him to worship. The second, which is the pilgrimage to the thirty-three Kannon Temples, is peculiar to neither of these two religions but is made indifferently by the adherents of both; it is looked upon by the generality of the Japanese as a sure means to obtain happiness in this world and bliss in the one to come. But the first of all, which is made to Ise, I propose to take into a more particular consideration in this Chapter.

<margin>Pilgrimage to Ise.</margin>
<margin>Its Names.</margin>
*Sanga* <note>original: "Sanga"; likely referring to Sangū, meaning "visiting the shrine"</note>, in the literal sense of the word, means the "Ascent," or going up to the Temple, and must be understood only of this most eminent Temple of **Amaterasu Ōmikami** <note>original: "Tensio Dai Sin, or Tensio ko Dai Sin"</note>, that is, according to the literal meaning of these words, *The Great Heaven-Shining Deity.*

hereditary Imperial God of the Celestial Generation. This <term>Tenshō Daijin <note>original: "Tensio Dai Sin"; the Sun Goddess Amaterasu-ōmikami, the supreme deity in Shinto and mythical ancestor of the Imperial House.</note></term>, is the greatest of all the Gods of the Japanese, and the first and chief object of the Shinto <note>original: "Sintos"</note> Worship, on which account also his Temple is called <term>Daijingū <note>original: "Dai Singu"</note></term>, that is, the *Temple of the great God*, for *Dai* signifies great, *Shin* and *Kami* <note>original: "Sin and Cami"</note>, a God, a Spirit, or Immortal Soul, and *Gū* <note>original: "Gu"</note> in conjunction with these words, a *Miya* <note>original: "Mia"</note>, that is, a *Temple*, or holy building erected in honor and memory of a God, or Immortal Spirit. The common people call it <term>Ise-Miya <note>original: "Isje Mia"</note></term>, or the Temple of Ise, from a Province of that name, wherein it stands. A particular and extraordinary holiness is ascribed to this Province, because <term>Amaterasu <note>original: "Tensio Dai Sin"</note></term> was born, lived and died there, whence also they derive the name Ise.

<margin>Temple at Ise.</margin>
This Temple, according to the account of those that have been to see it, is seated in a large plain, and is a humble, low building of wood, covered with a low, flattish, thatched roof. Particular care is taken to preserve it exactly as it was built originally, so that it should be a standing monument of the extreme poverty and simplicity of their ancestors and founders of the Temple, or the "first men" as they call them. In the middle of the Temple is nothing else but a mirror cast of metal and polished, according to the fashion of the Country, and some cut-paper is hung round the walls; the mirror <note>original: "looking-glass"</note> is placed there as an Emblem of the All-seeing Eye of this great God, and the knowledge he has of what passes in the inmost heart of his worshippers; the cut white paper <note>This refers to *shide* or *gohei*, ritual paper offerings used in Shinto to mark a sacred space.</note> is to represent the purity of the place, and to remind his adorers that they ought not to appear before him except with a pure, unspotted heart and clean body. This principal Temple is surrounded with near an hundred small Chapels, built in honor of other inferior Gods, which have little else of a temple but the mere shape, being for the greatest part so low and small that a man can scarce stand upright in them. Each of these Chapels is attended by a <term>Kannushi <note>original: "Canusi"</note></term>, or Secular Priest of the Shinto Religion. Next to the Temples and Chapels live multitudes of <term>Negi <note>original: "Nege"</note></term>, Lords or Officers of the Temple, and <term>Oshi <note>original: "Taije"; these were low-ranking priests or guides who distributed amulets and organized pilgrimages.</note></term>, as they also style themselves, that is, *Evangelists* or *Messengers of the Gods*, who keep houses and lodgings to accommodate Travelers and Pilgrims. Not far off lies a Town, or rather a large Borough, which bears the same name as the Temple, and is inhabited by Inn-keepers, Printers, Paper-makers, Book-binders, Cabinet-makers, Joiners and such other workmen, whose business and profession are in any way related to the holy trade carried on at this place.

<margin>Pilgrimage to Ise, by whom made, and how often.</margin>
Orthodox Shintoists go in Pilgrimage to Ise <note>original: "Isje"</note> once a year, or at least once in their life. Nay, it is thought a duty incumbent on every true Patriot, whatever sect or religion he otherwise adheres to, and a public mark of respect and gratitude, which every one ought to pay to <term>Amaterasu <note>original: "Tensio Dai Sin"</note></term>, if not as the God and Protector of the Nation, at least as its founder and first parent. To keep up the superstitious vulgar in these advantageous notions, every Pilgrim is presented by the <term>Kannushi <note>original: "Canusi's"; Shinto shrine priests who perform rituals and manage the sanctuary.</note></term>, for a small consideration, with an <term>O-harai <note>original: "Ofarai"; a "great purification" ritual or, as described here, a paper talisman or amulet believed to provide spiritual protection and forgiveness of sins.</note></term>, as they call it, that is, *a great purification*, being, as it were, a publick and undoubted Instrument of the absolution and remission of their sins, insured to themselves by this holy act. But as many people are not able to fetch them at Ise <note>original: "Isje"</note> in person, by reason either of sickness, and old age, or because of their employments, attendance upon their Prince, or for some other weighty cause, care is taken not to let them want so great and singular a benefit, but to provide them at home. Many of the <term>Buddhists <note>original: "Budsdoists"; Kaempfer’s term for practitioners of Buddhism, which he calls "Budsdo."</note></term> resort in Pilgrimage to this place, at least once, if not oftner, in their life, were it but in order to get the reputation of a true Patriot amongst their Countrymen. But still there are very many who stay at home, and think it sufficient for the ease and quietness of their conscience, besides the yearly indulgences of their own Priests, to purchase the *O-harai*, from Ise, great quantities whereof are sent yearly to all parts of the Empire.

<margin>The pilgrimage is made at all Times of the Year.</margin>
This Pilgrimage is made at all times of the year, but the greatest concourse of people is in the three first months (*March, April and May*,) when the season of the year, and the good weather, make the journey very agreeable and pleasant. Persons of all ranks and qualities, rich and poor, old and young, men and women, resort thither, the Lords only of the highest quality, and the most potent Princes of the Empire excepted, who seldom appear there in person. An Embassy from the Emperor is sent there once every year, in the first month, at which time also another with rich presents goes to <term>Kyoto <note>original: "Miaco"; the historical capital and residence of the Emperor.</note></term>, to the Ecclesiastical Hereditary Monarch <note>The Emperor, or Mikado, who was considered a divine figure in Shinto.</note>. Most of the Princes of the Empire follow the Emperor's Example.

<margin>Pilgrim's dress</margin>
As to the Pilgrims, who go there in Person, every one is at liberty to make the Journey in what manner he pleases. Able people do it at their own expence in litters, or on horseback, with a retinue suitable to their quality. Poor people go a foot, living upon charity which they beg along the road. They carry their bed along with them upon their back, being a Straw-mat roll'd up, and have a Pilgrim's staff in their hands, and a pail hung by their girdle, out of which they drink, and wherein they receive people's charity, pulling off their hats much after the European manner. Their hats are very large, twisted of split reeds. Generally speaking their names, birth, and the place from whence they come, are writ upon their hats and pails, that in case sudden death, or any other accident, should befall them upon the road, it might be known, who they are, and to whom they belong. <margin>Effects of Impurity on the Pilgrim.</margin>
After the Pilgrim is set out on his Journey to <term>Ise</term>, a rope with a bit of white paper twisted round it <note>This describes a *shimenawa* and *gohei*, traditional Shinto markers of sacred space used to ward off spiritual pollution.</note>, is hung up over the door of his house, as a mark for all such as labour under an <term>Imimi <note>original: "Ima"; ritual impurity or "mourning," specifically related to the pollution of death.</note></term>, as they call it, that is under a considerable degree of impurity, occasioned chiefly by the death of their parents or near relations, to avoid entering the same, it having been observed, that when by chance, or through inadvertency, such an impure person came into a Pilgrim's house, the Pilgrim at the same time found himself very much troubled with strange uneasy dreams, or exposed to some misfortunes. The like marks of purity are also hung up over the walks which lead to the <term>Miya <note>original: "Mias"; Shinto shrines.</note></term>, or Temples.

<margin>Laws of purity to be observed by him.</margin>
But it is required besides, that the Pilgrim himself, when he is about, or hath already undertaken this holy journey, should abstain religiously, from what will make a man impure, as amongst other things from whoring, nay, lying with his own wife, not that otherwise it be thought an act of unholiness, and unpleasing to the Gods, to comply with the duties of married persons, but because they are apprehensive that doing it at a time, when their minds should be wholly taken up with the holy action, they are about to perform, would prove prejudicial to them. The <term>Yamabushi <note>original: "Jammabos"; mountain-dwelling ascetics who practice Shugendō, a mix of Shinto and Buddhist traditions.</note></term>, that is, *Mountain Priests*, (a certain religious order affecting a very austere life) in order to keep up these ridiculous notions in the minds of the superstitious, never fail to report about, and to make people believe strange stories of persons in this case, who were so firmly and closely joined one to another, that nothing but the power of their charms, and magical ceremonies could bring them asunder. <note>Kaempfer is referring to the folk belief in *penis captivus* as a form of divine punishment for violating sexual taboos during sacred times.</note> Should a <term>Fujo <note>original: "Fusio"; a person in a state of ritual defilement.</note></term>, a person that labours under any degree of impurity, presume to undertake this holy journey, before he hath sufficiently purified himself, he would undoubtedly draw upon him, and his family, the <term>Shinbatsu <note>original: "Sinbatz"; the wrath or punishment of the gods.</note></term>, that is the displeasure and vengeance of the just and pure Gods. The <term>Shukke <note>original: "Siukkie"; Buddhist monks who have "left the home" to enter the priesthood.</note></term>, or Priests of the <term>Butsudo <note>original: "Budsdo"; Buddhism, literally "the way of the Buddha."</note></term> Religion, stand excluded for ever from these holy places, because they follow an impure profession and are obliged to attend sick people, and to bury the dead.

<margin>Pilgrims; how they are to behave at <term>Ise <note>original: "Isje"; the site of the most sacred Shinto shrines dedicated to the Sun Goddess Amaterasu.</note></term>.</margin>
When the pilgrim has arrived at <term>Ise</term>, the desired end of his journey—which is visited daily by great numbers, and upon certain special days by several thousands—he immediately goes to one of the <term>Kannushi <note>original: "Canusi"; Shinto priests who serve as guides and spiritual intermediaries at the shrines.</note></term> with whom he is acquainted, or to whom he has been recommended, or from whom he has previously received <term>O-harai <note>original: "Ofarrais"; purification talismans or amulets.</note></term>. He approaches the priest in a polite and humble manner, bowing his forehead all the way to the ground according to the custom of the country. Upon this, the <term>Kannushi</term> either conducts the pilgrim himself, along with others who have applied for the same purpose, or commands his servant to accompany them to show them the various temples and tell them the names of the gods for whom they were built. Once this is finished, the priest himself leads them before the chief temple of <term>Tensho Daijin <note>original: "Tensio Dai Sin"; the Sun Goddess Amaterasu, the supreme deity in the Shinto pantheon.</note></term>, where they prostrate themselves flat on the ground with great humility. In this lowly posture, they offer their supplications to this powerful God, describing their needs and hardships, and praying for happiness, wealth, health, long life, and similar blessings. In this manner, they fulfill their duty toward <term>Tensho Daijin</term> and complete the purpose of their pilgrimage. Afterward, they are entertained for the duration of their stay at <term>Ise</term> by the <term>Kannushi</term>, who lodges them at his own house if they cannot afford the expense of a public inn. The pilgrims, however, are generally so grateful that they give the <term>Kannushi</term> a handsome gift in return for his hospitality, even if it must come from what they have gathered by begging; the priest is courteous enough not to refuse it.

<margin><term>O-harai</term>, or Amulet Box.</margin>
Having performed all the acts of devotion required by this pilgrimage, the pilgrim is presented by the <term>Kannushi</term> with an <term>O-harai</term>, or "Indulgence." <note>The author uses the European term "Indulgence" to explain the spiritual merit associated with the talisman.</note> This <term>O-harai</term> is a small, oblong, square box, about a span and a half long, two inches broad, and an inch and a half thick. It is made of small thin boards and is filled with thin sticks, some of which are wrapped in bits of white paper to remind the pilgrim to remain pure and humble—these two virtues being the most pleasing to the gods. The name of the temple, <term>Daijingu <note>original: "Dai Singu"; literally "the Great Shrine of the God."</note></term>, printed in large characters, is pasted to the front of the box. The name of the <term>Kannushi</term> who provided the box is pasted to the opposite side in smaller characters, for there are many who conduct this trade. This is accompanied by the noble title of <term>Taiyu <note>original: "Taiju"; a high-ranking priestly title.</note></term>, which means "Messengers of the Gods," a title assumed by all the officers of the <term>miya <note>original: "Mias"; Shinto shrines.</note></term>.

<margin>How received and kept by the pilgrim.</margin>
The pilgrims receive this <term>O-harai</term> with great signs of respect and humility and immediately tie it under their hats to protect it from the rain. They wear it right against their forehead and balance it with another box, or a bundle of straw of similar weight, fastened to the opposite side of the hat. care for the preservation of this <term>O-harai <note>original: "Ofarrai"; a sacred purification talisman or amulet, usually consisting of a small box containing a wand with paper streamers.</note></term>, as being a relic of very great moment and consequence to them. And although the effects and virtues of it are limited only to a year, yet after this term has expired, they allow it a very honorable place in one of the chief apartments of their houses, on a shelf made for this purpose and raised above a man's height. In some places, the custom is to keep the old <term>O-harai</term> over the doors of their houses, underneath a small roof. Poor people, for want of a better place, keep them in hollow trees behind their houses. In like manner, the <term>O-harai</term> of deceased people, and those that are dropped upon the road, when found, are put up carefully in the nearest hollow tree.

<margin>They are sent to all parts of the Empire.</margin>
Large quantities of these <term>O-harai</term> are sent by the <term>Kannushi <note>original: "Canusi's"; Shinto priests who serve the shrines.</note></term> every year into all parts of the Empire to supply those who cannot conveniently, or are not willing to, come and fetch them at <term>Ise <note>original: "Isje"; the site of the most sacred Shinto shrines in Japan.</note></term>. These <term>O-harai</term> merchants make it their business to resort to the principal and most populous towns towards the <term>Sangatsu <note>original: "Sanguatz"; referring here to the third month, though the text associates it with the New Year celebrations.</note></term>, as they call it, or New Year's Day, this being one of their most solemn festivals and a day of great purification, and certainly the time when they are most likely to dispose of their merchandise quickly and to their advantage. They sell at the same time new almanacs, which are made by the command of the <term>Mikado <note>original: "Mikaddo"; the Emperor, residing in Kyoto as the ecclesiastical head of the state.</note></term>, or Ecclesiastical Hereditary Emperor, and cannot be printed anywhere else but at <term>Ise</term>. One may buy an <term>O-harai</term> and an almanac together for one <term>mace <note>original: "Maas"; a unit of silver currency.</note></term> or one <term>ichibu <note>original: "Itzebo"; a small rectangular silver coin.</note></term>. People of means will give more by way of charity. Those who buy them once are sure to be called upon the next year and to be presented with three things: namely, a receipt from the <term>Kannushi</term> (or rather a compliment of thanks to the buyer), a new <term>O-harai</term>, and a new almanac. Such as pay handsomely, and more than is due—which common people seldom do—receive moreover a <term>sakazuki <note>original: "Sakkant"; a traditional lacquered wooden cup used for drinking sake.</note></term>, as a small return for their generosity.

<margin>Account of Ise, taken from a Japanese author.</margin>
The following account of the present state and situation of the Temples at <term>Ise</term> is taken from <term>Ichinobe <note>original: "Itznobe"; a Japanese author or chronicler cited by Kaempfer.</note></term>, a Japanese author. There are two temples at <term>Ise</term>, about the length of twelve streets distant from each other, both relatively low structures. The ground whereon they stand is no more than six mats in circumference, including the place where the <term>Kannushi</term> sit in honor of <term>Tensho Daijin <note>original: "Tensio Dai Sin"; the Sun Goddess Amaterasu, the supreme deity of Shinto.</note></term>. They are both covered with a thatched roof, and both were built—which is very remarkable—without any one of the workmen receiving the least hurt to any part of his body. Behind these two temples, on a small eminence, stands the small but true temple of <term>Tensho Daijin</term>, which is called <term>Hongu <note>original: "Fongu"; meaning "main shrine" or "original building."</note></term>, that is, the true temple, and which has been purposely built higher than the others, in the same manner as the temple of <term>Suwa</term> is at Nagasaki. Within this temple (a view of which, taken from a Japanese drawing, is represented in Table XVIII) there is nothing to be seen but a looking-glass and bits of white paper.

The first of the Temples mentioned above is called the <term>Geku <note>The Outer Shrine of the Ise Grand Shrine complex, traditionally dedicated to Toyouke, the deity of food, clothing, and housing.</note></term>. It has several <term>Kannushi <note>original: "Canusi's"; Shinto priests who serve as "shrine masters."</note></term> to attend it, and about eighty <term>Massha <note>original: "Maffia"; small branch or "sub-shrines" located within the grounds of a larger shrine.</note></term> or smaller Temples around it, built in honor of Inferior Gods. Each is about four <term>mats <note>Refers to tatami mats, used here as a measurement of floor space (roughly 72 square feet).</note></term> large and guarded by a <term>Kannushi</term> sitting within to receive the people's charity, which serves as his payment for his attendance.

The second <term>Miya <note>A Shinto shrine or "holy palace."</note></term> is called the <term>Naiku <note>The Inner Shrine of Ise, the most sacred site in Shinto, dedicated to Amaterasu, the Sun Goddess.</note></term>, and it stands about the length of twelve streets further away. It likewise has great numbers of <term>Kannushi</term> and forty <term>Massha</term> or smaller Temples around it, each with a <term>Kannushi</term> as described before. The <term>Kannushi</term> of these smaller Temples have a very singular title, being called <term>Miya Suzume <note>original: "Mia Dfufume"; literally "Shrine Sparrows," likely a nickname for these low-ranking attendants who lived off the "crumbs" of the main temple's offerings.</note></term>, which signifies *Temple-Sparrows*.

<margin>Rules to be observed in seeing what is remarkable at Ise.</margin>
Those who wish to see these Temples and the remarkable sights in and around them without being led by a <term>Kannushi</term> or his servants must observe the following rules. First, they go to the <term>Miyagawa <note>original: "Mijangawa"</note></term> River, which runs by the village of <term>Ise <note>original: "Isje"</note></term> opposite to the Temples, to wash and clean themselves. From there, they walk toward the houses of the <term>Kannushi</term> and other merchants, located about three or four streets' distance from the river banks. Passing these houses, they reach a broad gravelly walk that leads them straight to the <term>Geku</term> Shrine. Here they worship first, then go around to view the inferior Temples, beginning on the right side and continuing until they return to the main Temple. From there, they proceed straight forward to the second Temple, called the <term>Naiku</term>, where they worship as before and see the <term>Massha</term> around it.

From this second Temple, they proceed further up a neighboring hill near the coast. After walking about fifteen streets' length, they come to a small cavern called <term>Ama-no-Iwato <note>original: "Awano Matta"; likely a corruption of "Ama-no-Iwato," meaning the "Heavenly Rock Cave."</note></term>, which signifies *the Coast of Heaven*, located no more than twenty <term>Ikken <note>original: "Ikins"; a unit of length approximately equal to six feet.</note></term> from the Sea. It was in this cavern that the great <term>Amaterasu <note>original: "Tensio Dai Sin"; referring to Tensho Daijin or Amaterasu Omikami, the Sun Goddess.</note></term> hid himself, thereby depriving the world, sun, and stars of their light to show that he alone is the Lord and Fountain of Light and the supreme of all the Gods. <note>While the Sun Goddess is female in Japanese mythology, 17th and 18th-century European accounts often used male pronouns for Japanese deities.</note> This Cavern is about a mat and a half large, with a small Temple or Chapel where they keep a <term>Kami <note>original: "Cami"; a deity or spirit.</note></term> or Idol sitting on a Cow, called <term>Dainichi Nyorai <note>original: "Dainitz no rai"; the "Great Sun Buddha" of Esoteric Buddhism, who was syncretically identified with the Sun Goddess Amaterasu during this period.</note></term>, that is, *the great Representation of the Sun*.

Nearby live some <term>Kannushi</term> in two houses built upon the coast, which is very steep and rocky here. The Pilgrim performs his devotions at this Cavern and Temple and then presents the <term>Kannushi</term> with a few <term>Putjes <note>Small copper coins of low value.</note></term>, asking them to plant a <term>Sugi <note>A Japanese cedar tree.</note></term> plant in memory of his visit. From the top of this hill, a large Island can be seen in the distance, about a mile and a half off the coast, which they say rose out of the ocean in the time of the Sun Goddess. These are the most remarkable things to be seen at <term>Ise</term>. Curious Pilgrims, before returning, go a couple of miles further to see a stately Buddhist Temple called <term>Asamadake <note>original: "Asamadaki"; referring to the Kongosho-ji temple on Mount Asama near Ise.</note></term>, where they worship a <term>Kannon <note>original: "Quanwon"; the Bodhisattva of Compassion.</note></term> called <term>Kokuzo-bosatsu <note>original: "Kokuso-fatz"; the Bodhisattva of Wisdom and Memory.</note></term>.

# C H A P. V.

->Of the Yamabushi, or Mountain-Priests, and other Religious Orders.<-

<margin>The Japanese inclination toward religious vows.</margin>
The superstitious Japanese are no less inclined to make religious vows than they are to visit holy places on pilgrimage. Many among them—particularly those who aim for a quick, unhindered passage into their <term>Elysian Fields <note>A reference to the Buddhist "Pure Land" or paradise, described here using a term from Greek mythology familiar to 18th-century European readers.</note></term>, or a more eminent place in those stations of happiness—devote themselves to a certain religious order of hermits called <term>Yamabushi <note>original: "Jammabos"; practitioners of Shugendō, a tradition of mountain asceticism.</note></term> in the country’s language. Others, who suffer under some worldly misfortune or are about to undertake an affair of great consequence, frequently make a vow that, in case of delivery from present danger or success in their undertakings, they will (out of respect and gratitude to the Gods) worship at certain Temples, keep a rigorous fast on certain days, build Temples, make valuable presents to the Priests, give extensive charities to the poor, and the like.

<margin>What the Yamabushi are.</margin>
*Yamabushi* properly signifies a "Mountain Soldier." <note>The author notes a discrepancy here; while the term "Yamabushi" literally means "one who lies down in the mountains," the author likely associates them with "bushi" or warriors due to their historical role as protectors of shrines.</note> The characters, indeed, by which this word is expressed do not altogether answer to this meaning, which depends more upon the rules of their order and their original establishment, whereby all the individual members of this society are obliged, in case of need, to fight for the Gods and the religion of the country. They are a sort of hermits who pretend to abandon the temporal for the sake of the spiritual and eternal; to exchange an easy and comfortable way of life for an austere and rigorous one, and pleasures for mortifications. They spend most of their time going up and down holy mountains and frequently washing themselves in cold water, even in the midst of winter. The richer among them, who live more at their ease, reside in their own houses. The poorer go strolling and begging about the country, particularly in the Province of <term>Suruga <note>original: "Syriga"</note></term>, in the neighborhood of the high mountain <term>Mount Fuji <note>original: "Fusi Jamma"</note></term>, to the top of which they are obliged by the rules of their order to climb every year in the sixth month. Some few have *Miya* (Temples), but generally speaking, these are so poorly provided for that the priests can scarcely earn a livelihood from them.

<margin>The founder of the Yamabushi order.</margin>
The founder of this order was one <term>En no Gyōja <note>original: "Gienno Giossa"; a 7th-century mystic and the legendary father of Shugendō.</note></term>, who lived about 1,100 years ago. They can give no account of his birth, parents, or relations, nor did he have any children. He was the first who chose this solitary way of life for the mortification of his body. He spent all his time wandering through desert, wild, and

By this means, he found new, easier, and shorter roads between locations, to the great advantage of travelers. In the course of time, his followers split into two differing orders. One is called <term>Tofansa <note>Tōhanyatō, a lineage of the Yamabushi.</note></term>. This is a very high mountain in the Province of <term>Busen <note>Buzen Province.</note></term>, upon the borders of <term>Tsikusen <note>Chikuzen Province.</note></term>. Even more daunting is the belief that the mountain possesses a singular quality: all those who dare to ascend it while <term>Fusio <note>original: "Fusio's"; likely from "fujō," meaning ritual impurity or pollution.</note></term>—that is, laboring under any degree of impurity—are punished for their impious rashness by being possessed by a Fox (others would say the Devil) and turning completely mad.

<margin>Fonfansa.</margin>
The second order is called <term>Fonfansa <note>Honhanyatō, another lineage of the Yamabushi.</note></term>. Those who enter into this order must make a pilgrimage once a year to the grave of their founder at the top of a high mountain in the Province of <term>Jostsino <note>Yoshino, in Nara Prefecture.</note></term>. Because of its height, this mountain is called <term>Omine <note>Mount Ōmine; "Omine" translates to "Great Peak."</note></term>, meaning the top of the high mountain. It is said to be excessively cold at the summit. The steepness and precipices make the ascent no less dangerous than that of the other mountain mentioned above. Should anyone presume to undertake this journey without having first duly purified and prepared himself, he would run the hazard of being thrown down the horrid precipices and dashed to pieces. At the very least, he might pay for his folly and his contempt for the gods' just anger with a lingering sickness or some other significant misfortune. And yet, despite all these dangers and difficulties, every person who enters either of these two orders must undertake this journey once a year. To qualify themselves, they undergo a previous <term>mortification <note>In this context, rigorous ascetic discipline and self-denial.</note></term>. By virtue of this, they must for some time abstain from lying with their wives, from "impure" food <note>Likely referring to meat or certain pungent vegetables forbidden in Buddhist practice.</note>, and from other things that might cause even the smallest degree of impurity. They also frequently bathe and wash themselves in cold water. While on the journey, they must live only on the roots and plants they find on the mountain.

<margin>Ranks and Titles of the Yamabushi.</margin>
If they return safely home from this hazardous pilgrimage, they repair immediately to the general of their order, who resides at <term>Miaco <note>The old name for Kyoto, meaning "The Capital."</note></term>. They present him with a small gift of money—which, if they are poor, they must obtain by begging—and receive from him a more honorable title and higher dignity. This promotion causes an alteration in their dress and increases the respect shown to them by their brethren of the same order.
