<margin>The current state of this order.</margin>
These Shinto <note>original: "Sintos"</note> hermits have now significantly strayed from the strict discipline of their predecessors. Those ancestors, following the example and rules of their founder, lived from the moment they entered the order on nothing but plants and roots. They subjected themselves to constant and harsh trials and penances: fasting, washing in ice-cold water, and wandering through woods, forests, and desolate, uninhabited places. In the same way, the modern members have wandered far from the simplicity of the religion they once practiced. They have admitted the worship of foreign idols <note>referring to Buddhist deities integrated into Shinto practice</note> which they believe hold great power over the events of human life. They have expanded their theological system and increased the number of superstitious ceremonies. Among other things, they have taken up a type of trade that proves very profitable for them. To deceive the common people, they claim to be specially skilled in the magical arts and sciences. They pretend that by using certain ceremonies, mystical words, and charms, they can command all the gods worshiped in the country—both the native Shinto deities and the Buddhist ones brought from overseas. They claim to conjure and drive out evil spirits, perform feats beyond the power of nature, uncover secrets and mysteries, recover stolen goods, identify thieves, predict the future, interpret dreams, cure desperate illnesses, and determine the guilt or innocence of those accused of crimes, among other things.

<margin>Their methods for curing illnesses.</margin>
I trust the reader will be pleased to learn more about how they proceed in these matters. To begin with the cure of illnesses: the patient must give the <term>Yamabushi <note>original: "Jammabos"; mountain-dwelling ascetic monks known for their spiritual and physical endurance.</note></term> as detailed an account as possible of their sickness and condition. After a full hearing, the Yamabushi writes certain characters on a scrap of paper; he claims these characters have a specific connection to the patient's physical makeup and the nature of the disease. Once this is done, he places the paper on an altar before his idols and performs many superstitious ceremonies intended, as he claims, to grant the paper healing powers. He then rolls the paper into pills, which the patient must take every morning with a large drink of water. This water must be drawn from a specific spring or river and from a specific direction—such as a particular cardinal point—as directed by the Yamabushi. These pills made of written characters are called <term>Gofu <note>original: "Goof"; sacred talismans or charms, often consisting of paper with ink inscriptions or stamps, used for protection or healing.</note></term>. It must be noted, however, that the Yamabushi rarely administer this mysterious cure, and patients even more rarely resolve to undergo it, until they are almost past all hope of re-

covery. In less desperate cases, people turn to more natural remedies.

<margin>Methods for determining guilt or innocence.</margin>
Their trials to determine the guilt or innocence of persons accused of crimes and misdemeanors are conducted in the presence of an idol called *Frido* <note>original: "Frido," referring to Fudō Myō-ō, the "Immovable One," a fierce protective deity in Japanese Buddhism often depicted surrounded by flames</note>, who is shown sitting amidst fire and flames. These trials are not held in a public or judicial manner—like those of the *Brahmines* <note>Brahmins of India</note>, *Siamites* <note>people of Siam, modern-day Thailand</note>, and other non-Christian peoples—nor do they involve the use of torture as is often seen in Europe, especially in witchcraft cases. Instead, they are held privately in the house where the crime occurred, in the presence of the household servants. The process involves either a simple conjuration—the chanting of specific words—a trial by fire, or the drinking of *Khumano Goo* <note>original: "Khumano Goo," or Kumano Go-o hōin, a sacred talisman or "bull-tablet" from the shrines of Kumano</note>. 

If the first method, a simple conjuration, proves ineffective, they turn to the second: a trial by fire. This is performed by making the suspected persons walk three times over a bed of glowing coals about six feet <note>original: "fathom," a unit of roughly six feet</note> long. If they can do this without burning the soles of their feet, they are acquitted. Others are brought to confession by drinking *Khumano Goo*. This *Goo* is a piece of paper filled with characters and pictures of black birds, such as ravens, and marked with the seals of the *Jammabos* <note>original: "Jammabos," or Yamabushi, the mountain ascetics</note>. These papers are pasted to the doors of houses to ward off evil spirits and are used for several other superstitious purposes. While they are made by all *Jammabos* generally, the most effective ones come from Kumano, which gives them their name. The accused person must swallow a small piece of this paper mixed in a drink of water; it is said that if he is guilty, the charm will churn and trouble his insides most cruelly until he confesses. 

The ascetics boast loudly of the surprising and wonderful virtues of their charms and conjurations. They claim to be able to handle burning coals and red-hot iron without receiving any injury, to suddenly extinguish fires, to make cold water boiling hot and hot water ice-cold in an instant, and to keep people's swords and scimitars so tightly locked in their sheaths that no force can draw them out. They also claim to protect themselves from being hurt by these or other weapons and to perform many more such uncommon and surprising feats. If these were examined more closely, however, they would likely be found to be little more than jugglers' tricks and the effects of natural causes. They call these techniques *Jamassu* <note>possibly a corruption of "Yamabushi-jutsu" or "kuji-kiri"</note>, which translates to "conjuring strokes." These mighty strokes are actually specific motions of their hands and fingers, through which they pretend to represent crocodiles, tigers, and other monstrous animals while uttering obscure sounds. By doing this and frequently changing their hand positions and vocal pitch, they claim to "strike" through all obstacles and hindrances until they reach their desired magical goal.

<margin>Their greatest charm.</margin>
One of their most important and mysterious *Sin* <note>possibly from "shirushi" (sign/seal) or "shingon" (mantra)</note>, or charms, is performed by holding up both hands and interlacing the fingers to represent the *Si Tensio* <note>original: "Si Tensio," likely referring to the Shitenno, or the Four Heavenly Kings who guard the cardinal directions</note>,

...that is, the four most powerful Gods of the thirty-third and last Heaven <note>This refers to the Trāyastriṃśa heaven in Buddhist cosmology, located at the peak of Mount Meru</note>. The position in which they place their fingers is as follows. They hold up the two middle fingers against each other almost perpendicularly, and cross the two adjacent fingers on each side in such a way that they point toward four different corners of the world. This represents these four Gods, whom they call *Tammonden* <note>Bishamonten, guardian of the North</note>, *Tsigokten* <note>Jikokuten, guardian of the East</note>, *Sosioten* <note>Zōjōten, guardian of the South</note>, and *Kamokten* <note>Kōmokuten, guardian of the West</note>. The two middle fingers, held up as I observed almost perpendicularly, serve them—as they claim—as a type of spyglass. Through this, they spy out spirits and diseases, seeing the *Kitz* <note>Kitsune, or fox-spirit; in Japanese folklore, foxes were believed to be powerful shapeshifters capable of possessing humans</note> or Fox, and the *Ma* <note>Mara, or evil spirit</note>, lodged in people’s bodies. This allows them to find out precisely what sort they are, in order to then tailor their charms and superstitious ceremonies to more effectively drive them out. 

But this same position of the middle fingers relative to the rest also represents *Fudo mio wo* <note>Fudō Myō-ō, the "Immovable Wisdom King," a fierce deity who protects the faithful and burns away impediments to enlightenment</note>, that is, the holy great *Fudo*. He was formerly a *Giofia* <note>Gyoja, a wandering ascetic or practitioner of Shugendō</note>, a mighty devotee of their order, who—among other extraordinary mortifications—sat down daily in the middle of a large fire without receiving any harm. Because of this, they believe they can use his powerful assistance not only to destroy the burning quality of fire whenever they please, but also to command it to serve whatever purposes they think fit. A lamp filled with oil made from a certain black venomous water lizard called *Mari* <note>likely the *imori*, or Japanese fire-bellied newt</note> is kept continually burning before the idol of *Fudo*.

<margin>The trial of their novices.</margin>
The *Jammabos* <note>Yamabushi</note> keep these charms and mysterious arts a great secret. However, for a handsome reward, they will teach them to others, provided they keep the secret. The account I have given in this chapter regarding this singular order was primarily obtained from a young Japanese man well-versed in the affairs of his country. During my stay in Japan, I taught him medicine <term>Physick: an archaic term for the study and practice of medicine</term> and surgery, and he had been one of their students himself. He further told me that before they would let him into the secret, they made him undergo a very harsh novitiate <note>a period of training and probation for a new member of a religious order</note>. 

First, he had to abstain from anything that had once had life in it, subsisting only on rice and herbs for six days. Next, they commanded him to wash himself seven times a day in cold water. While kneeling on the ground with his buttocks to his heels and clapping his hands over his head, he had to lift himself up seven hundred and eighty times every day. He found this last part of his trial the most brutal; after getting up and down two or three hundred times, he was drenched in sweat and grew so weary that he was often on the verge of running away from his masters. However, being a strong young fellow, shame rather than curiosity motivated him to endure it to the end.

### The History of JAPAN. Book III. 238

Thus much of the <term>Yamabushi</term> <note>original: "Jammabos"; mountain-dwelling practitioners of the Shugendō religion</note>. There are still many more religious orders and societies established in this country, a particular account of which would swell this Chapter to an unbecoming length. The superstitious veneration of the common people for their Clergy, and the ease and pleasures of a religious life—great as they are—make it no wonder that the number of costly temples, rich monasteries, and convents has grown to a barely credible excess. Within these, under the cloak of retirement and divine worship, the Monks give themselves up to an uninterrupted pursuit of wantonness and luxury. But there are also some particular societies that are not purely religious, nor confined to the Clergy alone, but rather of a mixed nature, with a touch of the secular.

<margin>Societies of Blind People.</margin>
Among these many groups, the society of the blind is not unworthy of consideration. It is a singular, but very ancient and numerous body, composed of persons of all ranks and professions. Originally they made up but one society, but in the course of time they split into two separate bodies: one of which is called <term>Heike-zato</term> <note>original: "Feekisado"; literally the "guild of the Heike-blind"</note>, or the Blind <term>Heike</term>, the other <term>Bussatsu-zato</term> <note>original: "Buffetz Sato"</note>, or the Blind <term>Bussatsu</term>. It will not be amiss to enquire into the origin and rules of both.

<margin>That of the Bussatsu.</margin>
The <term>Bussatsu-zato</term> must be considered first, as being of a more ancient standing. At present this society is composed only of religious persons, whose rules and customs are not very different from those of the <term>Yamabushi</term>.

<margin>By whom founded.</margin>
Their Founder was <term>Semimaru</term> <note>original: "Senmimar"; a legendary poet and musician</note>, the third (and according to some authors, the fourth) son of the Emperor <term>Ninmyō</term> <note>original: "Jengino Mikaddo"; Emperor Ninmyō reigned from 833 to 850 AD</note>. The occasion of their founding is recorded in Japanese Histories to have been as follows. Semimaru was a youth of incomparable beauty, and exceedingly beloved by all who came near him. It happened that a Princess of the Imperial Blood fell desperately in love with him: Her beauty and virtues proved charms as irresistible to the young Prince as his graceful person and princely qualities had been to her. For some time the happy lovers enjoyed all the satisfaction and mutual returns of passion and friendship, when the death of the Princess intervened. Semimaru took it so much to heart that not long after, through grief and sorrow, he lost his sight. Upon this, to perpetuate the memory of his dearly beloved, and to make known to posterity what an unfortunate effect his unfeigned concern and sorrow for her loss had had upon himself, he resolved—with his father’s leave and under an Imperial Charter—to erect a society into which none should be admitted but such as had the misfortune to be blind by birth or accident. His design was put into execution accordingly. The newly erected society prospered exceedingly, flourished, and attained great reputation at Court and in the Empire.

<margin>Society of the Heike Blind.</margin>
For some centuries they continued united in one body, until a new society of the <term>Heike</term> Blind <note>original: "Feki Blind"; blind storytellers who chanted the "Tale of the Heike"</note>, as they are now called, sprung up. In a short time, this group got so far the better of the former—many great men in the Empire who were blind voluntarily entering into it—that by degrees the older group lost much of its reputa-

# Chap. V. The History of JAPAN.

...reduced very low in number, none being left at last but ecclesiastical persons, to whom the order remains now confined. Ever since their first institution, the <term>Heike</term> <note>original: "Feki"; referring to the Taira clan</note> blind continued in an uninterrupted possession of all the esteem and authority that the <term>Bussatsu</term> <note>original: "Bussetz"; the older guild of blind musicians</note> had once enjoyed. Indeed, being still more numerous, they are also much more highly regarded in proportion.

<margin>The reason for their founding.</margin>
They owe their origin to the civil wars between the Heike and the <term>Genji</term> <note>original: "Gendzi"; the Minamoto clan</note>, both of whom were contending for the Empire. Whole volumes have been written about the long and bloody dissensions between these two once considerable and powerful parties, and the manifold calamities which consequently befell the Empire. The cause of the Heike and his adherents appeared more just to the then-reigning <term>Dairi</term> <note>The Emperor</note> than that of the Genji; he therefore thought himself bound in conscience to support it. This he did so effectively that the Genji and his party were defeated and almost totally destroyed. The victorious Heike—as success is often followed by pride and ambition—soon forgot the obligations he lay under to the Dairi, and behaved himself with so much insolence and ungratefulness toward him that the Emperor resolved to support the interest (though it was almost totally sunk) of the Genji and his adherents. He promised them all manner of encouragement and assistance if they would once more gather all their strength together and take up arms against the Heike and his party. Affairs upon this soon took another turn; victory in a decisive battle favored the Genji. The Heike leader himself was slain near <term>Shimonoseki</term> <note>original: "Simonoseki"; site of the naval battle of Dan-no-ura in 1185, which ended the Genpei War</note>, and his whole army defeated, with but few escaping.

<margin>The history of Kagekiyo, their founder.</margin>
Among those who escaped with their lives was <term>Kagekiyo</term> <note>original: "Kakekigo"; Taira no Kagekiyo, a legendary warrior often celebrated in Noh and Kabuki theatre</note>, a general very much renowned for his valor and supernatural strength, which it was believed he obtained from <term>Kannon</term> <note>original: "Quanwon"; the Bodhisattva of Mercy</note> as a reward for his constant devotion to that deity. This general fled in a small boat. <term>Yoritomo</term> <note>original: "Joritomo"; Minamoto no Yoritomo, who became the first Shogun of the Kamakura period</note>, general of the Genji and himself a very resolute soldier, knew of what consequence it was to secure the person of Kagekiyo; thinking his victory incomplete until then, he caused him to be pursued and taken. However, when the prisoner was brought before him, Yoritomo treated him kindly and with all the respect due to a person of his rank and character. He confined him so little that Kagekiyo found means several times to make his escape, but he was as often retaken. The generous Yoritomo had no thoughts of putting him to death, though he was his enemy and his prisoner. Nay, far from it—he put such a value upon the friendship and affection of a person of his note that he thought it worth his while to purchase it at any price. One day, when he was pressing him very close to enter into his service upon whatever terms he pleased, the captive general returned him the following resolute answer:

> "I was once," said he, "a faithful servant to a kind master. Now he is dead, no other shall boast of my faith and friendship. I own that you have laid me under great obligations. I owe even my life to your clemency. And yet such is my misfortune that I cannot set my eyes on you but with a design, in revenge of him and me, to cut off your head."

Having said this, he plucked out both his eyes and presented them to <term>Yoritomo</term> <note>original: "Joritomo"; Minamoto no Yoritomo (1147–1199), the founder and first shogun of the Kamakura Shogunate</note> on a plate. He remained undaunted, much like that bold Roman <note>referring to Gaius Mucius Scaevola, who famously thrust his right hand into a fire to prove his resolve to the Etruscan king Porsenna</note> who, in the sight of <term>Porsenna</term>, burnt his right hand on the altar. Yoritomo, astonished by such magnanimity and resolution, immediately set the captive General at liberty. The General then retired to the Province of <term>Hyuga</term> <note>original: "Fiuga"; a province on the eastern coast of Kyushu</note>, where he learned to play the <term>Biwa</term> <note>original: "Bywa"; a traditional Japanese short-necked lute</note>, a specific musical instrument used in Japan. Thus, he gave birth to this Society of the <term>Heike</term> <note>original: "Feki"; the Taira clan, whose defeat is the subject of many epic blind-monk recitations</note> blind, of which he himself was the first <term>Kengyo</term> <note>original: "Kengio"; the highest rank of the official guild for the blind</note>, or Head.

<margin>Present state of this Society.</margin>
This is the account Japanese histories give regarding the original institution of this Society, which has since grown very numerous, being composed of persons of all ranks and professions. They shave their heads, as do the <term>Bussatsu-zato</term> <note>original: "Buffetz sato"; the older, ecclesiastical guild of blind men mentioned on the previous page</note>, or ecclesiastical blind. Otherwise, being secular persons, they also wear secular clothing—though it is different from the common dress of the Japanese, and varies among themselves according to their rank and dignity. They do not live on charity; instead, they manage to earn a livelihood for themselves and provide for the maintenance of their community by following various professions not altogether inconsistent with their unhappy condition. Many of them apply themselves to music, in which capacity they are employed at the courts of princes and great men, as well as during public solemnities, festivals, processions, weddings, and similar events. 

Whoever is once admitted as a member of this Society must remain so for life. They are dispersed throughout the Empire, but their General resides at <term>Kyoto</term> <note>original: "Miaco"; the historical imperial capital</note>, where the company's treasury is kept. He is called the <term>Oshoku</term> <note>original: "Osiokf"; likely referring to the Grand Master or 'Oshoku' rank</note>, and he is allowed 4,300 <term>Taels</term> <note>original: "Thails"; a unit of currency or weight in silver</note> a year for his maintenance by the <term>Dairi</term> <note>The Emperor</note>. He governs the commonwealth, assisted by ten counselors called <term>Shuro</term> <note>original: "Siu Ro"; meaning 'Elders'</note>, of which the General himself is the eldest. They reside at Kyoto and, jointly with the General, have the power of life and death—with the restriction, however, that no person can be executed unless the sentence is approved and the death warrant signed by the Lord Chief Justice of Kyoto. 

The Council of Ten appoints their inferior officers, who reside in the several Provinces. Some of these are called <term>Kengyo</term>, acting as "Father Provincials," each being in his province what the General is to the whole Society. The founder himself took only the title of Kengyo. However, as the society became very numerous over time, it was thought necessary to alter the government and appoint a court superior to the Kengyos. Every Kengyo has his <term>Koto</term> <note>original: "Kotos"; the second-highest rank in the guild</note>, as they are called, to assist and advise him. The Kotos sometimes govern particular districts by themselves. At <term>Nagasaki</term>, there is one Kengyo and two Kotos, under whose command stand all the blind people of that town and the adjacent country. The Kengyos and Kotos have many other inferior officers...

They differ from the general membership of the blind by being permitted to wear long breeches. These members do not wear breeches and are divided into four ranks or classes. Those of the fourth and lowest class are eligible to be promoted to <term>Shibun</term>, from which office they can gradually rise to the dignity of <term>Koto</term> <note>the second-highest rank in the guild</note>, <term>Kengyo</term>, and so on. Sometimes, through money or personal favor, they rise through these ranks very suddenly.

## CHAPTER VI.

### Of <term>Buddhism</term> <note>original: "Budsdo"; literally "The Way of the Buddha"</note>, or *Foreign Religious Worship*, and its *Founder*.

<margin>Foreign Religious Worship.</margin>
Foreign deities—to distinguish them from the <term>Kami</term> or <term>Shin</term> <note>the indigenous spirits or gods of Shinto</note>, who were worshipped in the country since ancient times—are called <term>Butsu</term> <note>original: "Buds"</note> and <term>Hotoke</term> <note>original: "Fotoke"</note>. The written characters used to express these two words also differ from those used for the native <term>Shin</term> and <term>Kami</term>. <term>Butsudo</term>, in the literal sense, signifies *the Way of Foreign Deities*—that is, the practice of worshipping deities from abroad.

<margin>Its Origin.</margin>
The origin of this religion, which quickly spread through most Asian countries to the very extremities of the East (not unlike the Indian Fig-tree, which propagates itself and spreads far around by sending down new roots from the ends of its branches), must be looked for among the <term>Brahmins</term> <note>the priestly class of India</note>.

<margin>Buddha, its Founder.</margin>
I have strong reasons to believe, both from the similarity of the name and the very nature of this religion, that its author and founder is the very same person whom the Brahmins call <term>Buddha</term> <note>original: "Budha"</note>. They believe him to be an essential part of <term>Vishnu</term> <note>original: "Wisthnu"</note>, or their Deity, who made his ninth appearance in the world under this name and in the shape of this man. The Chinese and Japanese call him <term>Butsu</term> and <term>Shaka</term> <note>original: "Buds and Siaka"; Shaka is the Japanese name for Shakyamuni, the historical Buddha</note>. These two names indeed became, in the course of time, a common epithet for all gods and idols in general whose worship was brought over from other countries; sometimes they were also given to the saints and great men who preached these new doctrines. The common people in <term>Thailand</term> <note>original: "Siam"</note> call him <term>Phra Phuttha Chao</term> <note>original: "Prah Pudi Dsau"; Thai for "Holy Lord Buddha"</note>, meaning *the Holy Lord*, and the learned among them, in their <term>Pali</term> or holy language, call him <term>Shramana Gautama</term> <note>original: "Sammona Khodum"</note>. The people of <term>Pegu</term> <note>a region in modern-day Myanmar</note> call him <term>Sammana Khutama</term>. (*See Book I. Chapter II.*)

# The History of J A P A N. Book III,

<margin>His Native Country.</margin>
His native country, according to the Japanese (with regard to whom he is chiefly considered in this place) is <term>Magadha</term> <note>original: "Magattakokf"; the ancient kingdom in India where the Buddha lived and taught</note>, or the Province of *Magatta* in the Country of <term>Tenjiku</term> <note>original: "Tenfik"; the traditional Japanese name for India</note>. *Tenjiku*, in the literal sense, signifies a *Heavenly Country*, or a *Country of Heavens*. The Japanese comprehend under this name the Island of *Ceylon* <note>modern Sri Lanka</note>, the Coasts of *Malabar* and *Coromandel* <note>regions of the Indian peninsula</note>, and in general all the Countries of *South Asia*, the continent as well as the neighboring Islands, which are inhabited by people of dark complexion, such as the Peninsula of *Malacca*, the Islands of *Sumatra*, *Java*, the Kingdoms of *Siam* <note>Thailand</note>, *Pegu* <note>modern Myanmar</note>, and others.

<margin>His Birth.</margin>
He was born in the twenty-sixth year of the reign of the Chinese Emperor *Soowo*, who was the fourth successor of the famous *Suno Buo*, on the eighth day of the fourth month. This was, according to some, the year 1029 before the birth of Christ, and according to others 1027. (When I was in *Siam* in 1690, the inhabitants of Siam then counted 2232 years from the time of their *Buddha*; if he be the same as the *Siaka* <note>Shakyamuni Buddha</note> of the Japanese, his birth would be no earlier than 542 years before Christ). His father was King of *Magadha*, a powerful Kingdom in the Country of *Tenjiku*. I conjecture this to be the Island of *Ceylon*. Indeed, the Kingdom of *Siam* is called by this name to this day by the common people in *Japan*.

<margin>His Life.</margin>
*Siaka*, when he reached nineteen years of age, quitted his Palace, leaving his wife and an only son behind him. Voluntarily, and by his own choice, he became a disciple of <term>Alara Kalama</term> <note>original: "Arara Sennin"; one of the Buddha's first spiritual teachers, described here as a mountain hermit</note>, then a Hermit of great repute who lived at the top of a mountain called *Dandoku*. Under the inspection of this holy man, he betook himself to a very austere life, wholly taken up with an almost uninterrupted contemplation of heavenly and divine things. He practiced a posture very singular in itself, but reckoned very proper for this sublime way of thinking: specifically, sitting cross-legged, with his hands placed in his lap so that the tips of both thumbs touched one another. This posture is thought to engage one’s mind in so profound a meditation, and to wrap it up so entirely within itself, that the body lies for a while as if senseless, unattentive, and unmoved by any external objects whatsoever. This profound state of spiritual focus is called <term>Zazen</term> <note>original: "Safen"; a meditative discipline typically performed seated</note>, and the divine truths revealed to such persons are called <term>Satori</term> <note>spiritual awakening or enlightenment</note>. As for *Siaka* himself, the force of his spiritual focus was so great that through it he penetrated into the most secret and important points of religion. He discovered the existence and state of Heaven and Hell as places of reward and punishment, the state of our souls in a life to come, the <term>transmigration</term> <note>the passing of a soul into a new body after death; reincarnation</note> thereof, the way to eternal happiness, the divine power of the Gods in the government of this world, and many more things beyond the reach of human understanding. These he afterwards freely communicated to the numerous crowds of his disciples, who followed him in flocks for the sake of his doctrine and instructions,

<margin>His Death.</margin>
He lived seventy-nine years, and died on the fifteenth day of the second month, in the year 950 BC <note>Historical dates for the Buddha's death vary significantly across traditions; modern scholarship generally places it between 480 and 400 BC.</note>.

<margin>His Doctrine</margin>
The most essential points of his doctrine are as follows: 
The souls of men and animals are immortal. Both are made of the same substance, and differ only according to the different bodies they are placed in, whether human or animal.

The souls of men, after their departure from their bodies, are rewarded in a place of happiness or punished in a place of misery, according to their behavior in this life.

<margin>Place of Happiness.</margin>
The place of happiness is called <term>Gokuraku</term> <note>original: "Gokurakf"; the Pure Land or Western Paradise in Buddhist cosmology</note>, that is, a *place of eternal pleasures*. Just as the Gods differ in their nature, and the souls of men differ in the merit of their past actions, so too do the degrees of pleasure and happiness in these <term>Elysian Fields</term> <note>The author uses this Greek mythological term for the dwelling of the blessed to explain the concept of a Buddhist paradise to European readers</note>, so that everyone may be rewarded as they deserve. However, the entire place is so thoroughly filled with bliss and pleasure that every happy inhabitant thinks their own portion is the best; far from envying the happier state of others, they wish only to enjoy their own forever.

<margin>Amida.</margin>
<term>Amida</term> <note>Amitabha, the Buddha of Infinite Light, who presides over the Western Paradise</note> is the sovereign Commander of these heavenly stations. (The author notes that all of this doctrine was not introduced by the <term>Brahmins</term> <note>The priestly caste of India</note> until after the era of the Christian resurrection). He is looked upon as the general Patron and Protector of human souls, but more particularly as the God and Father of those who happily transmigrate <note>reincarnate</note> into these places of bliss. Through his mediation alone, men are to obtain absolution for their sins and a portion of happiness in the future life.

Leading a virtuous life, and doing nothing that is contrary to the Commandments of the Law of <term>Siaka</term> <note>Shakyamuni, the historical Buddha</note>, is the only way to become pleasing to <term>Amida</term> and worthy of eternal happiness.

<margin>Five Commandments of Siaka.</margin>
The five Commandments of the Doctrine of <term>Siaka</term>, which are the standing rule for the life and behavior of all his faithful adherents, are called <term>Gokai</term> <note>The Five Precepts</note>, which signifies the *five cautions* or *warnings*. They are:
*Sesshō* <note>original: "Se Seo"</note>, the Law not to kill anything that has life in it.
*Chūtō* <note>original: "Tfu To"</note>, the Law not to steal.
*Jayin* <note>original: "Sijain"</note>, the Law not to commit adultery or engage in "whoring."
*Mago*, the Law not to lie.
*Onshu* <note>original: "Onfiu"</note>, the Law not to drink strong liquors; a law which <term>Siaka</term> most earnestly recommended to his disciples to be strictly observed.

<margin>Their Division and Sub-division in Sikkai.</margin>
Next to these five chief and general Commandments, which contain the substance of the entire Law of <term>Siaka</term>, follow the ten <term>Jikkai</term> <note>original: "Sikkai"; the Ten Precepts</note>, as they call them. These are counsels or admonitions, being nothing else but the first five laws branched out and applied to more specific actions,

# The History of JAPAN. Book III.

...and tending to a stricter observance of *Virtue*. For the sake of the learned, and those who aim for a state of *Virtue* and *Perfection* beyond the ordinary even in this world, a further subdivision has been devised into the <term>Five Hundred Precepts</term> <note>original: "Go Fiakkai," or *Go-hyaku-kai*; a detailed set of monastic rules in Mahayana Buddhism</note>, wherein are specified and determined with the utmost exactness and particularity whatever actions have—according to their notions—the least tendency toward virtue or vice, and thus ought to be performed or omitted.

<margin>
And the Five Hundred Precepts.
</margin>
The number of these <term>Five Hundred Precepts</term> is so very extensive that it is no wonder that those who will commit themselves to a strict observance of them are few in proportion. This is especially true since the rules lead to such a thorough mortification of their bodies, even measuring and prescribing the smallest details of their diet and allowing barely enough food to keep them from starving. Nothing but the ambition of acquiring a great reputation for *Perfection* and *Sanctity* in this world, and the desire to be raised to a more eminent station of happiness in the next, can prompt anyone to undergo such a harsh and severe discipline as is prescribed by the <term>Five Hundred Precepts</term>. Indeed, there are few even among the best part of their *Clergy* who, for the sake of a greater portion of happiness in a future world, would willingly renounce even the smallest pleasures of this one.

<margin>
Place of Torment.
</margin>
All people, whether secular or ecclesiastical, who by their sinful lives and vicious actions have rendered themselves unworthy of the pleasures prepared for the virtuous, are sent after their death to a place of misery called <term>Hell</term> <note>original: "Dsigokf," or *Jigoku*</note>. There they are confined and tormented, not indeed forever, but only during a certain undetermined time. Just as the pleasures of the <term>Elysian Fields</term> <note>The author uses this Greek mythological term for the dwelling of the blessed to explain the concept of the Buddhist Pure Land to his European readers</note> differ in degree, so too do the torments in these infernal places. Justice requires that everyone should be punished according to the nature and number of his crimes, the number of years he lived in the world, the station he lived in, and the opportunities he had to be virtuous and good. <term>King Enma</term> <note>original: "Jemma," or "Jemma O"; the Buddhist judge of the dead, known in Sanskrit as Yama</note>—by which name he is also known to the <term>Hindus</term> <note>original: "Brahmines"</note>, <term>Thais</term> <note>original: "Siamites"</note>, and **Chinese**—is the severe judge and sovereign commander of this place of darkness and misery. All the vicious actions of mankind appear to him in all their horror and wickedness by means of a large looking-glass placed before him called the <term>Mirror of Knowledge</term> <note>original: "Ssofarino Kagami," or *Joshō-no-kagami*; a miraculous mirror in the underworld that reflects the past deeds of the deceased</note>. The miseries of the poor, unhappy souls confined to these prisons of darkness are not so absolute or lasting that great relief may not be expected from the virtuous lives and good actions of the family, friends, and relations they left behind. But nothing is so helpful toward this desirable end as the prayers and offerings of the priests to the great and good <term>Amida</term> <note>The Buddha Amitābha, the central figure of Pure Land Buddhism, revered for his infinite compassion and his vow to save all sentient beings</note>, who by his powerful intercession can prevail upon the almost inexorable judge of this infernal place to reduce the severity of his sentence,

# Chapter VI. The History of JAPAN.

...sentence, to treat the unhappy imprisoned souls with kindness—at least as far as is consistent with his justice and the punishment their crimes deserve—and last of all, to send them back into the world again as soon as possible.

<margin>The return of wicked souls into the world.</margin>
When the miserable souls have been confined in these prisons of darkness for a time sufficient to atone for their crimes, they are, by virtue of the sentence of <term>Enma-ō</term> <note>original: "Jemma O"; the Buddhist King of Hell who judges the dead</note>, sent back into the world. They return to animate not the bodies of men, but those of vile creatures whose nature and properties are closely related to their former sinful inclinations—such as, for instance, serpents, toads, insects, birds, fish, four-legged animals, and the like. From the lowliest of these, transmigrating by degrees into higher and nobler animals, they are finally permitted to enter human bodies again. By this means, it is placed in their power either to lead a good and virtuous life and render themselves worthy of a future state of uninterrupted happiness, or to follow a new course of vice and expose themselves once more to the miseries of confinement in a place of torment, followed by another unhappy reincarnation.

Thus far are the most essential points of the doctrine of the <term>Buddha</term> <note>original: "Siaka," referring to Shakyamuni</note>.

<margin>The Buddha’s disciples.</margin>
Among the disciples of the Buddha arose several eminent men who contributed greatly to the propagation of his doctrine. They were succeeded by others equally learned and zealous, so that we need not wonder that his religion spread to the very extremities of the East within a very short period of time, despite all the difficulties they had to struggle against.

<margin>Ananda and Kassapa.</margin>
The most eminent of his disciples were <term>Ananda</term> and <term>Kassapa</term> <note>original: "Annan" and "Kasia"</note>, or by their full titles, <term>Ananda Sonja</term> and <term>Kassapa Sonja</term> <note>the title "Sonja" refers to a Buddhist saint or "venerable one"</note>. They collected his wise sayings and the writings found after his death—written by his own hand on the leaves of trees—into a book. Because of its peculiar excellence, this book is called <term>Hokke-kyō</term> <note>original: "Fokekio"</note>, which means the *Book of the Flower of the Good Law* (in comparison with the holy <term>Lotus Flower</term> <note>original: "Tarate-Flower"</note>). It is also sometimes called, by way of pre-eminence, <term>Kyō</term> <note>original: "Kio"</note>, or *The Book*, as it is the most perfect performance of its kind and the Bible of all Eastern nations beyond the Ganges who embraced the Buddha's doctrine. The two compilers, for their care and pains, were numbered among the saints and are now worshipped alongside the Buddha; in his temples and upon his altars, they are placed one to his right and the other to his left.

<margin>The ancient religion of the Japanese and Chinese.</margin>
Before the doctrine of the Buddha was brought over into China, and from there through Korea into Japan, the ancient <term>Shinto</term> <note>original: "Sintos"</note> or <term>Kami</term> worship, simple as it was, was the only religion flourishing in this Empire. They had few temples and few holidays, and the yearly pilgrimage to the Temple of <term>Amaterasu</term> <note>original: "Tensio Dai Sin," the Sun Goddess</note> at <term>Ise</term> <note>original: "Isje"</note> was thought to be the best and surest way to happiness. It is true that, over time, the number of gods and saints increased, their system of divinity was embellished with new fables, and arts and sciences were improved—

### The History of JAPAN. Book III.

...chiefly since the time of <term>Jimmu Tennō</term> <note>original: "Synmu Ten O"; the legendary first Emperor and founder of Japan</note> their first Monarch. But still a certain simplicity prevailed, and people, following the dictates of reason, aimed at nothing so much as to live morally well. The Chinese also, before that time, followed the illustrious examples and moral precepts of their two great Emperors <term>Yao</term> <note>original: "Tee Gio"</note>, that is the Emperor Gio, who according to their chronological computation lived 2359 years before Christ, and his successor <term>Shun</term> <note>original: "Tee Siun"</note>, or the Emperor Siun, who though a peasant, was yet for his prudence and honesty made by Yao first his co-partner in the government, and afterwards his successor, though in prejudice to Yao’s twelve children, namely ten sons and two daughters. These two illustrious princes were the two first <term>Sesins</term> <note>original: "Sesin"; derived from the Chinese *Sheng-ren*, meaning a "sage" or "holy man" of perfect wisdom</note>. A **Sesin** is a philosopher able to find out truth and wisdom merely by the force of his own understanding, and without being taught by others. By mistake, this same name has been sometimes given to some of their most eminent divines.

<margin>Doctrine of Lao-tzu.</margin>
Some hundred years after the reign of these princes, the pagan doctrine of <term>Lao-tzu</term> <note>original: "Roos"; the founder of Taoism</note> arose in China. This man was born in <term>Chu</term> <note>original: "Sokokf," meaning the Province of So</note>, on the fourth day of the ninth month, 346 years after the death of the <term>Buddha</term> <note>original: "Siaka," referring to Shakyamuni</note>, or 604 years before our Saviour’s Nativity. They say that his mother had been pregnant with him for 81 years, for which reason, when she was brought to bed, they called him *Lao-tzu* <note>original: "Roos"</note>, which implies as much as *Old Son*, or *Old Child*. They further add, that the soul of <term>Mahakashyapa</term> <note>original: "Kassobosatz," or the holy Kasso</note>, the eldest disciple of the Buddha, dwelt in him through transmigration, which made it easy for him to attain to such a high pitch of knowledge about the nature of Gods and Spirits, the immortality of our souls, a future state, and such other important points as are highly conducive to the instruction of those who are desirous of learning, and which fill the credulous common people with admiration. He lived eighty-four years.

<margin>Doctrine of Confucius.</margin>
Meanwhile, as the doctrine and philosophy of Lao-tzu gained ground in China, another incomparable *Sesin* appeared upon the philosophical stage of that Empire. 
<margin>His Birth.</margin> 
This was <term>Confucius</term> <note>original: "Koosi"</note>, born in the Province of <term>Lu</term> <note>original: "Kok"</note>, on the fourth day of the eleventh month, 399 years after the death of the Buddha, and 53 years after the birth of Lao-tzu, who was then still alive. His birth was in a manner miraculous, attended with clear signs of a future *Sesin*. He had some natural marks on his head, like those of the Emperor Yao, and his forehead was of the same shape as that of the Emperor Shun. At the time of his birth, music was heard in Heaven, and two dragons were observed to attend when the child was washed. His stature, when grown up, was very noble and majestic, measuring nine <term>shaku</term> and nine <term>sun</term> <note>original: "Saku" and "Suns"; traditional units of measurement roughly equivalent to feet and inches</note>, proportionate to the greatness of his genius.

### Chap. VI. The History of JAPAN.

the East ever produced. <margin>His Philosophy.</margin> His writings and philosophy have maintained a constant and uninterrupted reputation for what is now upwards of two hundred years <note>The text says "two hundred," though Confucius lived over two thousand years before this account was written; the author correctly identifies the "two thousand year" span later in the paragraph.</note>, and are thought in China to have been brought down from Heaven, just as the philosophy of **Socrates** was formerly regarded in **Greece**. A profound respect is shown to his memory both in **China** and **Japan**, by public officials as well as private individuals. Very lately, the Emperor of Japan <note>The author refers to the Shogun, likely Tokugawa Tsunayoshi (reigned 1680–1709), who was a dedicated patron of Neo-Confucianism.</note> caused two temples to be built to him in his capital, **Edo** <note>original: "Jedo"</note>, where he went in person as soon as they were finished. On this occasion, he delivered a handsome speech to his courtiers, setting forth the merits of this great man and the singular excellence of the maxims of government he established. His portrait is given the most honorable place in the houses of philosophers, and all those who apply themselves to study and learning never mention his name without specific signs of respect. 

It is no wonder, then, that the fanciful and—in several respects—incomprehensible doctrine of **Laozi** <note>original: "Roosi"</note> was unable to hold its ground against the reasonable and pleasing morality of **Confucius** <note>original: "Confutius"</note>. Instead, it was effectively smothered in its infancy and gradually decreased as the followers of Confucius increased, who gathered from all parts of the Empire in numbers almost beyond imagination. He died in the seventy-third year of his age, leaving behind many capable men who spread his doctrine and philosophy. They did this not only by teaching others but by gathering all his wise sayings and moral maxims, which he shared with them during his lifetime, into a book called the **Shidō** <note>original: "Siudo"; refers to the "Way of the Scholar" or the Confucian Path</note>, which means the *Philosophical Way of Life* or the *Way of Life agreeable to Philosophy*. 

For over two thousand years now, this work has been looked upon as an incomparable achievement in its field and an excellent model for a good and virtuous life. It is a book extolled not only by the admirers of Confucius but is admired for its moral and political maxims even by the followers of **Buddhism** <note>original: "Budsdo"</note> and other religions. In the very same way, the writings of the ancient Greek and Roman philosophers, which have escaped the common shipwreck of time, deservedly stand as the admiration of all Europe and a lasting monument to the excellent genius of their great authors.

<margin>The doctrine of Shaka, when introduced into Japan.</margin> While the doctrine and pleasing philosophy of Confucius began to flourish in China and spread to the neighboring Empire of Japan, the doctrine and religion of **Shaka** <note>original: "Siaka"; the historical Buddha, Shakyamuni</note>—which had already penetrated the kingdoms of **Siam** <note>Modern-day Thailand</note> and **Laos**—was not likely to find a favorable reception in this farthest part of the East. If we believe the Japanese historians, the first people to teach this religion in China arrived there around the year 63 AD. They obtained permission to build a temple, which is still called **Baima-si** <note>original: "Fakubasi"; the White Horse Temple in Luoyang</note>, or the *Temple of the White Horse*, because the **Kyo** <note>original: "Kio"; a Sutra or scripture</note>, or holy book of Shaka, was brought over on a white horse. The greatest difficulty the preachers of this new doctrine had to struggle with was the—

### The History of JAPAN. Book III.

The philosophy of <term>Confucius</term> <note>original: "Confutius"</note> was then shining at its peak and was universally approved. Indeed, it appears that for several hundred years, the religion of <term>Shakyamuni</term> <note>original: "Siaka"; the historical Buddha</note> made very slow and insignificant progress, until about the year of Christ 518. At that time, <term>Bodhidharma</term> <note>original: "Darma"</note>, a great saint and the thirty-third successor to the holy seat of Shakyamuni, came over into **China** from <term>India</term> <note>original: "Seitenfiku"; a term used in Japan to denote the Indian subcontinent, literally "Western Heaven"</note>, as the **Japanese** writers explain it—that is, from that part of the world which lies westward with regard to **Japan**. He properly laid the first sure foundations of <term>Buddhism</term> <note>original: "Budsdoism"; from the Japanese 'Butsudō', the Way of the Buddha</note> in that mighty empire. 

The fame of his dignity and holiness, the austerity of his life, and his ardent, uninterrupted devotion—which was so strong that in the height of his zeal he did not hesitate to cut off his own eyelids because they had once drawn him out of his deep meditations into sleep—soon brought a crowd of admirers about him. But the most effectual and persuasive arguments he used to induce people to worship the gods were the doctrine of the immortality of our souls and the promises of a reward in a future life. He taught that they would not fail to obtain these rewards if they would only worship the gods as his doctrine, religion, and example directed. 

This new worship, having once gained ground in **China**, soon spread into <term>Baekje</term> <note>original: "Fakkusai"; an ancient kingdom in the southwestern Korean Peninsula</note>, which was then the name given to the peninsula of **Korea** (and is now the name of one of its three provinces). There, the first statue or idol of Shakyamuni was erected and worshiped in the year of Christ 543. 

**Japan**, whose inhabitants were then divided between the old religion of the country <note>Shinto</note> and the philosophical doctrines brought to them from **China**, could now hold out no longer. They soon admitted the religion of Shakyamuni, following the example of neighboring countries as they had done in many other matters. The first <term>Buddhist scriptures</term> <note>original: "Bukkio"; likely referring to 'Bukkyō', the teachings of Buddha</note> were brought over into **Japan** about the year of Christ 550. 

About eighteen years later, according to **Japanese** writers, a curious carved idol of <term>Amida</term> <note>original: "Amida"; the Buddha of Infinite Light</note>—which had been brought over from **India** into **Baekje** some years before—appeared in a miraculous manner in the province of <term>Chinu-no-kami</term> <note>original: "Tsino Cami"</note>, surrounded by sparkling rays. Because of this, a temple was built in **Shinano** in memory of this remarkable event. This temple was called <term>Zenkō-ji</term> <note>original: "Sanquosi"</note> and is still the chief and largest temple of that province. 

About that time, <term>Emperor Kinmei</term> <note>original: "Kimmei"</note> ruled over **Japan**. He was no enemy to this religion and quietly allowed its introduction and spread. This was the same Emperor who divided time into <term>Era Names</term> <note>original: "Nengo's"</note> in imitation of the **Chinese**. The Era Name then in use when this temple was built was called <term>Zenkō</term> <note>original: "Cengo"</note>.

# CHAPTER VII.

## Of the <term>Ju-do</term> <note>original: "SIUTO"; derived from the Japanese 'Ju-dō', the Way of the Scholars</note>, *that is, the Doctrine and Way of Life of their Moralists and Philosophers.*

<margin>*Doctrine of the <term>Confucianists</term> <note>original: "Siudosja"</note>, or Philosophers.*</margin>
The Way of the Scholars, in the literal sense, signifies the way or method of the Philosophers. The Confucian scholars <note>original: "Siudosja", or in the plural "Siudosju"</note> are the Philosophers who follow this method. These people have, properly speaking, no religion at all—that is, they conform themselves to none of those forms of worshipping the Gods which are established in the Country. They say that the greatest perfection and the supreme good men are able to acquire consist in that pleasure and delight which our minds find in a good and virtuous life. They admit of none but temporal rewards or punishments, and only such as are the necessary consequences of the practice of virtue or vice. They say that we are obliged to be virtuous because nature hath endowed us with reason on purpose that, living according to the dictates of reason, we should show our difference and superiority over irrational brutes. **Confucius** <note>original: "Koosi"</note>, born in **China** 2243 years ago (computing from the 5th year of the <term>Genroku era</term> <note>original: "Genrokf"; this corresponds to the year 1692</note>), was the first who taught that the supreme good consists in the practice of virtue, and must consequently be looked upon as the founder of this Philosophical Sect. It hath been observed above how prejudicial the <term>Elementary Learning</term> <note>original: "Sioogakf"; refers to the 'Xiao Xue', a foundational text of Confucian ethics</note>, or the Book wherein are contained his precepts and morals, proved to the then flourishing doctrine of **Laozi** <note>original: "Roosi"; the founder of Taoism</note>. **Mencius** <note>original: "Moosi"</note>, one of **Confucius's** disciples, was very instrumental in establishing and propagating this Philosophy, which he published in the <term>Four Books</term> <note>original: "Sisio"; the 'Sishu', which are the canonical scriptures of Confucianism</note>, which are still held in great esteem and read in all Countries where the learned language <note>Classical Chinese</note> wherein they were written is understood.

<margin>*Its five chief Points.*</margin>
This Philosophy, so far as it relates to the practice of virtue and good morals, may be reduced to the following five points, which they call **Benevolence**, **Righteousness**, **Propriety**, **Wisdom**, and **Sincerity** <note>original: "Dsin, Gi, Re, Tsi and Sin"</note>. **Benevolence** <note>original: "Dsin"</note> teaches them to live virtuously (hence a <term>virtuous man</term> <note>original: "Dfinsja"</note>); **Righteousness** <note>original: "Gi"</note> to do right and justice to every body; **Propriety** <note>original: "Re"</note> to be civil and polite; **Wisdom** <note>original: "Tsi"</note> sets forth the maxims of a good and prudent Government; and **Sincerity** <note>original: "Sin"</note> treats of a free conscience and uprightness of heart. They admit no transmigration of Souls, but believe in a <term>World-soul</term> <note>original: "Animam mundi"</note>—an universal Soul, Spirit, or power diffused throughout the whole world which animates all things, and which re-assumes the departing Souls (as the Sea doth all rivers and waters that flow into it from all parts of the Globe) as

This universal spirit they confound with the supreme Being, attributing to one the same divine qualities, which only belong to the other. They often make use of the word <term>Ten</term> <note>The Japanese word for "Heaven" or the celestial order</note>, Heaven or Nature, in things, which more immediately concern our life and actions. They make the world eternal and suppose men and animals to have been produced by *In* and *Jo*, the heaven and five terrestrial elements. Admitting no Gods, they have no temples, no forms of worship. Thus far however they conform themselves to the general custom of the Country, in that they celebrate the memory of their deceased parents and relations, which is done by putting all sorts of victuals, raw and dressed, on a <term>Biosju</term> <note>Likely referring to a memorial tablet or a home altar (butsudan), though the scholars avoided Buddhist ritual</note>, as they call it, or table purposely made with this view, by burning candles before them, by bowing down to the ground as if they were yet alive, by monthly or anniversary dinners, whereto are invited the deceased’s family and friends, who appear all in the best cloth, and wash and clean themselves by way of preparation for three days before, during which time they abstain from lying with their wives, and from all impure things, and by many other tokens of respect and gratitude. As to the burial of their dead, they do not burn them <note>The author contrasts this with the Buddhist practice of cremation, which was common in Japan at the time</note>, but keep the corpse three days, and then lay it on the back into a coffin, after the European manner, with the head raised. Sometimes the coffin is filled with spices and sweet scented herbs, to preserve the body from corruption, and when every thing is ready, they accompany it to the grave, and bury it without any further ceremony.

Their way of Life.

The practice of virtue, a free conscience, and a good and honest life, is all what they aim at. Formerly this sect was very numerous. Arts and sciences were cultivated and improved among them, and the most educated part of the nation belonged to it. But that unparalleled persecution of the Christian religion weakened it very much, and it has lost ground ever since; the extreme rigor of the imperial edicts makes people cautious even regarding the reading of their books, which formerly were the delight and admiration of the nation, held in as great an esteem as the writings of Plato, Socrates, and other heathen philosophers are in Europe.

<margin>History of the Prince of Hizen.</margin>
About thirty years ago, the Prince of **Hizen** <note>original: "Sifen"</note> and **Inaba**, a great **Confucian scholar** <note>original: "Siudosia"</note> and patron of learned men, endeavored to revive this philosophy, then almost extinct, in his dominions. In order to do this, he founded a university, endowed it with great privileges, and settled handsome pensions upon able learned men, whom he sent for from all parts of the Empire. The design of this undertaking was to open the eyes of his subjects, and to teach them, if possible, to make use of their reason. No sooner did they do this, than they began to see through the impertinent and ridiculous fables of their priests; discovering their deceptions, they refused to grant them any further financial support. Consequently, this numerous crew of monks, which until then lived only upon the charity of gullible people, was reduced to a starving condition. 

Heavy complaints regarding such a dangerous innovation were made to both Emperors <note>Refers to the Shogun in Edo and the Mikado in Kyoto</note>; and the unhappy Prince was likely to be sacrificed for his good intentions, had he not, by a voluntary resignation of his dominions to his son, prevented the fatal blow of imperial disgrace that was ready to fall upon him and his family. His son, though of a more prudent and reserved behavior, nonetheless leaves no room to doubt through his life and conduct that his principles are nearly the same as those of his father. An instance of this, though secondary to my present purpose, will not be improper to close this chapter and book.

On the **New Year's Day** <note>original: "Songuats"</note>, one of their greatest festivals, there was a large gathering at court of gentlemen and ladies, who came there in their richest apparel to compliment the Prince on the occasion of the day, and were entertained by him at dinner. Among other presents made to him that day, there happened to be a peacock and a hen. Everyone was delighted and struck with admiration by the uncommon beauty of these rare, foreign birds, which gave the Prince the opportunity to ask their opinion on which of the—

### Chapter I: The History of Japan

The journey into the harbor could be easily completed in about two hours, were it not for the many sandbanks, shoals, and cliffs that make the narrow passage both difficult and dangerous. To avoid these hazards, ships must steer westward, keeping the mainland to their right, and pass between several small islands to reach the open sea. <margin>The Harbor Guards</margin> Several bastions <note>fortified structures</note> are built along the harbor as if for defense, but they are not equipped with cannons. About half a mile from the town are two Imperial guards stationed opposite one another and surrounded by palisades <note>wooden stake fences</note>. Each station consists of about 700 men who perform duty in guard-boats; these boats are positioned in the harbor both for defense and to monitor foreign ships riding at anchor. Near the Papenberg <note>original: "Papenberg" – Dutch for 'Priests' Mountain,' known in Japanese as Takaboko-jima. It was a site where Christians were famously executed by being thrown from the cliffs</note>, where the harbor truly begins, is a small island where the last Portuguese ship sent from Macao to Japan was burned along with all its cargo around the year 1642. Ever since then, they have called it "the burning place of hostile ships," having designated it as the permanent site for similar executions in the future.

<margin>Number of ships and boats</margin>
There are seldom fewer than fifty Japanese ships and boats in this harbor, in addition to several hundred fishing boats and other small craft. As for foreign vessels, there are rarely fewer than thirty present—except for a few months during the winter—and most of these are Chinese junks <term>Yonks<gloss>an archaic spelling of junks, the traditional sailing ships of China and Southeast Asia</gloss></term>. The Dutch ships never stay longer than three months in the autumn; indeed, they rarely stay that long, for around that time the south or west seasonal winds, or <term>Monsoon<gloss>seasonal winds in South and East Asia that dictated the sailing schedules for all merchant trade</gloss></term>, which brought them to Japan, shift. Once the north or northeast monsoon sets in, they must take advantage of it to return to Batavia <note>modern-day Jakarta, Indonesia, which served as the headquarters for the Dutch East India Company</note> or their other intended destinations. The anchorage is located at the end of the bay within reach of the Imperial guards, about a musket shot's distance from the town. There, ships ride at anchor on a bed of soft clay in about six fathoms <note>about 36 feet</note> of water at high tide, and four and a half fathoms <note>about 27 feet</note> at low tide.

The town of Nagasaki, its harbor, and part of the surrounding countryside are shown in Table 19, which was copied on a small scale from a very large map made by the Japanese themselves.

<margin>Location of the town of Nagasaki</margin>
Nagasaki is located at 32° 36' North latitude and 151 degrees longitude <note>This longitude reflects an older meridian system, likely measured from the Canary Islands, rather than the modern Greenwich meridian</note>. It sits at the end of the harbor where the water is broadest and where the shoreline turns north to form a nearly semicircular shape. The town itself is shaped like a half-moon, somewhat resembling a triangle. It is built along the shore in a narrow valley that runs eastward, formed by an opening in the neighboring mountains. The town is about three-quarters of a mile long and nearly as wide, with its main and widest streets extending almost that far up the valley. The mountains surrounding the city are not very high but are quite steep; they are otherwise green to their summits and offer a very pleasant and agreeable view. Just behind the city, as one ascends the mountains, many stately temples are built, beautifully adorned with fine gardens and terraced walks according to the local custom. Higher up, there are innumerable burial places...

<margin>Remarkable places in the neighborhood of Nagasaki</margin>
The most remarkable places in the neighborhood of *Nagasaki* are: *Fukafori*, a pleasant village situated to the southwest, about five Japanese water leagues <note>approximately 12 miles or 20 kilometers</note>,
<margin>Fukafori</margin>
or two small German miles <note>approximately 9 miles or 15 kilometers</note> from the town. It has a small fort or castle, the residence of a *Bugyo* <term>Governor<gloss>original: "Bugjo"; a high-ranking administrative official or magistrate</gloss></term>, who governs the whole district for the Prince of *Fisen* <note>original: "Fisen" – the Hizen Province</note> as the proprietor. It produces a great quantity of firewood, and its yearly revenue amounts to nearly three *Mangokf* <term>ten thousand koku<gloss>original: "Mangokf"; a "koku" was a unit of rice equaling about 180 liters, used to measure the wealth of a domain</gloss></term>, though in the general list of the empire's revenues, it is recorded as only one.

<margin>Remarkable Pond</margin>
Not far from this village is a great lake or pond, which is said to have this particular quality: that, though surrounded with trees, there is never a leaf nor any dirty thing to be seen upon it. This they attribute to the great cleanliness and purity of the spirit under whose protection the pond stands. For this reason, they have such a high veneration for it that it is forbidden, under severe penalties, to fish in it. To the north of *Nagasaki* lies the princely town and
<margin>Omura</margin>
residence *Omura*, situated on a gulf and in the district of the same name.
<margin>Isafai</margin>
A few miles further eastwards lies the city *Isafai* <note>modern Isahaya</note>, belonging to the Prince of *Fisen*, upon an arm of the gulf of *Simabara* <note>modern Shimabara</note>.

<margin>Description of the Town of Nagasaki</margin>
The town of *Nagasaki* itself is open, as most other towns in *Japan*, without either castle, walls, fortifications, or indeed any other defense. The streets are neither straight nor broad, running uphill and ending near the temples. Three freshwater rivers run through the town, which come down from the neighboring mountains. The middlemost and largest crosses the valley from east to west. For the greatest part of the year, they have scarcely enough water to irrigate some rice fields and to drive a few mills, though in rainy weather they are prone to increase so much as to wash away whole houses.

<margin>Its state in ancient times</margin>
*Nagasaki* obtained its name from its former lords who held it in possession, along with its whole district of 3,000 *Kokf* <note>koku; units of rice</note> in yearly revenue, from *Nagasaki Kotari*, the first of this name, through a succession of twelve of his lineal descendants to *Nagasaki Sijn Seijemon* <note>Nagasaki Jinzaemon</note>. The ruins of their former residence are still shown at the top of a hill behind the town. The last Lord of *Nagasaki*—the aforementioned *Nagasaki Sijn Seijemon*—died without issue about 200 years ago, and the town fell, with its whole district, to the Prince of *Omura*. The place where the town now stands was then nothing but a poor, miserable hamlet, the abode of a few fishermen, and was called *Fukaje* or *Irije* <note>original: "Fukaje" or "Irije" – meaning "Deep Bay" or "Inlet"</note>, that is, the *long Bay*, due to the length of the harbor, as well as to distinguish it from another village situated not far off on the same harbor called *Fukafori*, which is to say the *long Pond*, a name it still retains. The new Lord of *Fukaje* then saw fit to change the name of this hamlet to *Nagasaki*.

<margin>During the time of the Portuguese</margin>
Things continued in this way until some time after the first arrival of the Portuguese in *Japan*. For a period, this nation enjoyed free commerce on the same terms as the Chinese, who were also trading with these islands at that time. They were not restricted to any specific harbor, but were at liberty to dock wherever they pleased or found most convenient. Accordingly, they established several settlements on the island of **Saikoku** <term>Saikoku<gloss>literally "Western Provinces," referring to the island of Kyushu</gloss></term>, primarily in the provinces of **Bungo** and **Fifen** <note>original: "Fifen"; the Hizen Province</note>. Their first settlement in the province of **Fifen** was at a village called **Fakuda**, located on the island of **Firando** <note>modern Hirado</note>, not far from the entrance to the harbor of **Nagasaki**, about six Japanese sea leagues <note>approximately 15 miles or 24 kilometers</note> or two long German miles from this town. This place was under the jurisdiction of the Prince of **Omura**. Their next settlement was in the village of **Fukafori**, mentioned previously. At these locations, and all others where they settled, they made two things the primary focus of their attention: one was to conduct their trade and commerce, and the other was to spread the Christian religion and raise the standard of our Savior in this remote empire. They succeeded in both beyond their highest hopes. Their trade prospered more than expected, and through their conduct—which at first was humble and accommodating—they won the hearts not only of the common people but even of the nobility, especially as there was a natural similarity between the minds and temperaments of both nations. Around that time, the Prince of **Omura** himself openly supported the interests of the Christian religion and invited the Portuguese to come and settle at **Nagasaki**. By then, the place had already grown into a substantial village of about twenty-three streets, which now constitute the part of the town called **Utsimatz** <term>Uchimachi<gloss>the "inner town" or original central districts of Nagasaki</gloss></term>, which today contains twenty-six streets. In this state, it was handed over by the said Prince into the possession of the Portuguese, both for the purpose of trade and for the spreading of the Gospel. Whether he did this with a sincere desire to advance the Christian religion, or rather with the intent to increase his own revenue and enrich his subjects by making this place a center of foreign commerce, I will not attempt to decide. Regardless, it is certain that this new establishment soon proved advantageous to the town in many ways. The convenient and secure location of its harbor, along with several other benefits, also invited the Chinese to bring their ships and goods there. The Japanese, attracted by the prospect of profit, came to settle there in such numbers that the old town was no longer large enough to contain them. Therefore, new streets were built and named after the various provinces, towns, or boroughs from which their first inhabitants came—for example, **Bungomatz**, **Jedomatz**, **Kabasima-** <note>These names refer to Bungo-machi, Edo-machi, and Kabashima-machi; "machi" (transcribed here as "matz") means street or town district.</note>

<margin>Nagasaki is taken from the Prince of Omura, and why.</margin>
The flourishing condition and increasing wealth of the town of *Nagasaki*, while in the possession of the *Portuguese*, soon became a source of jealousy and discontent for the Imperial Court. **Taico** <term>Taico<gloss>The Taikō, a title referring to the regent Toyotomi Hideyoshi, who ruled Japan in the late 16th century</gloss></term>, the then-reigning Secular Monarch <note>The author uses this term to distinguish the military ruler from the spiritual Emperor (Mikado)</note>, reprimanded the Prince of *Omura* very severely for imprudently parting with a place of such importance in favor of a foreign nation. Furthermore, he told the Prince that since he was no longer fit to keep and govern it, the Emperor would annex it to his own dominions. 

The haughty conduct of the *Portuguese* contributed significantly to this resolution. Puffed up with pride and success, they "pulled off the mask" too soon; they began to think it beneath the honor and gravity of their nation to pay the same deference and respect to the great men of the Empire as they had previously condescended to do. 

I was told by an old *Japanese* man that the following incident, along with many others of a similar nature, greatly incensed the Emperor and hastened his decision to let the proud *Portuguese* feel the effects of his Imperial displeasure. **Taico**, wanting to be closer at hand to support his military expedition into *Korea* <note>The Japanese invasions of Korea, 1592–1598</note>, established his Court and residence for some time at **Facatta** <note>modern Hakata, part of Fukuoka</note>. One day, a *Portuguese* Priest met one of the principal Counselors of State on the road to court. The priest caused himself to be carried past without stopping or alighting from his chair—as is the custom in the country—and indeed, without showing the Counselor even the most common marks of respect and civility. 

It is easy to imagine how much such a haughty and contemptuous act provoked a man of his high rank. Consequently, he resolved that as soon as he reached the court, he would acquaint the Emperor with what had passed. He did so with great resentment, painting a most hateful picture of the pride and arrogance of the *Portuguese* nation in general. He also suggested how inconsistent it was with the Emperor’s plans, and how dangerous it might prove, to continue allowing these foreigners to exert their interest and influence over his subjects, given they had already gained too much power. 

In short, whether the Emperor was truly displeased at the disrespect shown to his Minister, or whether he viewed the increasing prosperity of the *Portuguese* and the spread of the **Christian Religion** in general as detrimental to the peace and tranquility of the Empire, the indiscreet behavior of this priest furnished him with a plausible pretext. He moved to let these foreigners experience the first proofs of his displeasure by taking their town away from them and their patron, the Prince of *Omura*, and besides, to de-

Thus much of the Town of Nagasaki in general; I proceed now to a more particular survey of it.

<margin>Division of Nagasaki.</margin>
Nagasaki (or as it is sometimes pronounced, though not written, *Nangasacki* <note>the 'n' reflects a nasalized pronunciation common in certain Japanese dialects</note>) is divided into two parts: One is called *Uchimachi* <note>original: "Utsimatz"</note>, or the inner town, consisting of 26 *Chō* <note>original: "Tsjoo"; a street or ward</note>, or Streets, all very irregular, as they had been built during the infancy of that town. The other is called *Sotomachi* <note>original: "Sottomatz"</note>, which is as much as to say, the outward city, or as it might be otherwise expressed, the suburbs. This contains 61 streets, so that there are 87 in all.

<margin>Its Public Buildings.</margin>
The most remarkable public buildings in and about Nagasaki are:

<margin>Boat Storehouses.</margin>
Some *Funagura* <note>original: "Janagura"</note>, as they call them, belonging to the Emperor, being five large houses built of wood on the North side of the town, on low ground not far from the shore. Here they keep three large Imperial Junks <note>original: "Yonks"</note>, or Men-of-war, with all their tackle, ready to be launched at command.

<margin>Powder Magazine.</margin>
*Enshō-gura* <note>original: "Jen Siogura"</note>, or the Powder Magazine, stands on the shore opposite to the town. For greater security and to prevent accidents, they have built a large vault in a neighboring hill where they keep the gunpowder.

<margin>Palaces of the Governors.</margin>
The Palaces of the two residing Governors. They occupy a large plot of ground, standing somewhat higher than the rest of the streets. The houses are very neat and handsome, all uniform and of equal height. Strong gates, well-guarded, lead into the court. The third Governor lodges at *Tateyama* <note>original: "Tattejama"</note> in a Temple, until his predecessor, by his departure for Edo <note>original: "Jedo"; the capital and seat of the Shogun</note>, makes room for him in the Palace.

<margin>Houses of the Princes and Lords of the Empire.</margin>
Besides the Governor’s Palaces, there are about twenty other houses and plots of ground belonging to all the <term>Daimyō<gloss>Lords of the first rank, or Princes of the Empire</gloss></term> and some of the most eminent <term>Shōmyō<gloss>all other Lords of an inferior rank</gloss></term> of the Island of Kyushu <note>original: "Kiusju"</note>, or as it is otherwise called *Saigoku* <note>original: "Saikokf"</note>, that is, the Western Country, wherein the town of Nagasaki lies. Some of their noblemen constantly reside there to take care of the affairs and interests of their Principals upon all occasions, being answerable upon their return for what happens. If the *Daimyōs* or *Shōmyōs* come to Nagasaki themselves, these houses serve to lodge them and their retinue.

<margin>Accommodation of Foreigners.</margin>
The Foreigners live outside the town in separate places, where they are very narrowly watched and guarded, like persons suspected of ill practices. The Dutch live on a small island situated in the harbor, close by the town, called Dejima <note>original: "De Sima"</note>, that is, the "Island De." The Chinese and neighboring nations, who profess the same religion and trade under the same name, live behind the town at the Southern extremity...

The Girls are purchas'd from their Parents, when very young.
