They are very conveniently lodged in handsome apartments, and great care is taken to teach them to dance, sing, play upon musical instruments, to write letters, and in all other respects to qualify them for the way of life they are obliged to lead. The older women, being more skillful and expert, instruct the younger ones, and these in their turn serve them as their mistresses. Those who make considerable improvements in what they are taught, and who are often sent for due to their beauty and agreeable behavior, are also better accommodated by their masters with clothes and lodging—all at the expense of their lovers, who must pay so much the dearer for their favors.

The price paid to their landlord is from one <term>Maas</term> <note>original: "Maas"; a unit of silver weight, approximately 3.7 grams, used as currency</note> to two <term>Itzebi</term> <note>original: "Itzebi" (Ichibu); a rectangular silver or gold coin</note> for a night, beyond which they are forbidden to ask under severe penalties. One of the poorest, and almost worn out by too much use, must watch the house overnight in a small room adjoining the door, where any passerby may have to do with her, paying but one <term>Maas</term>. Others are sentenced to keep the watch as a punishment for their misbehavior. 

After having served their time, if they are married, they pass among the common people as honest women; the guilt of their past life is by no means laid to their charge, but to that of their parents and relations, who sold them into such a scandalous way of earning a livelihood in their infancy, before they were able to choose a more honest one. Besides, as they are generally well-bred, this makes it less difficult for them to find husbands. 

The brothel-keepers <note>original: "Bawds"</note>, on the contrary, though possessed of even the most plentiful estate, are forever denied admittance into honest company. They call them by the scandalous name of <term>Katsuwa</term>, which signifies the very worst sort of rabble, and put them on the same footing as the <term>Jetta</term> <note>original: "Jetta" (Eta); an outcast class in feudal Japan associated with "unclean" professions</note>, or leather-tanners. These are the most infamous sort of people in their opinion, who are obliged in this country to perform the office of public executioners and to live outside of the town in a separate village, not far from the place of execution. The brothel-keepers are also obliged to send their own servants to assist the <term>Jetta</term> at all public executions, or to hire other people to do it.

<margin>The current state of Christianity in Japan.</margin>
These poor people are very ignorant of the Christian religion, knowing little more than the names of our Savior and his blessed Mother. Yet, they are so zealously attached to it that they choose to die miserably in jail rather than renounce their faith to gain their liberty, even though they are frequently pressured to do so.

It first happened in September 1692 that three of the prisoners sent money to the temples of *Amida* <term>Amida</term> <note>Amitābha, the principal Buddha in Pure Land Buddhism</note> to pray for the souls of their deceased relatives. The priests would not accept the money without first asking the Governor’s advice and permission. The Governor, in turn, refused to decide on such a delicate case until he had received instructions from the Imperial Court. However, these Christians are not executed immediately without mercy as they once were. This leniency is due both to their great simplicity and the fact that there is little need for such severity nowadays. Instead, they are condemned to end their miserable lives in this "Temporal Hell," from which they are never allowed to leave, except when they are taken to the Governor’s Palace. This occurs once every two months, where they are examined—more as a matter of formality than with any real rigor—and pressured to reveal other Christians.

The only recreation these poor wretches are allowed is being taken out of their dungeons twice a year to be treated with *Moxa* <term>Moxa</term> <note>original: "Moxa"; a traditional medical practice (moxibustion) where dried mugwort is burned on specific points of the body</note> according to the custom of the country, washing themselves six times a year in the prison’s *Tange*, and walking six times a year in a large, spacious house built for this purpose within the prison walls.

The rest of their miserable time is spent spinning hemp yarn to hem mats. They sew their clothes with needles made of *Bambu* <term>Bamboo</term>, as they are denied iron tools. Some know how to make socks and other small items. Any money they earn through their labor is their own, and they may use it to buy refreshments, which they share freely and without reserve with their wives and children, who are kept as prisoners in the same jail.

From the remainder of the portion of rice which is allowed them for their daily sustenance, they prepare—by letting it ferment overnight—a particular liquor called *Ama Saki* <term>Ama Saki</term> <note>original: "Ama Saki"; a sweet, low-alcohol or non-alcoholic fermented rice drink</note>, or the "pleasant sake," which, for its agreeable sweetness, is one of their greatest comforts. The Governors give them a mat to lie on every year. <margin>Bridges.</margin>
Among the public buildings of Nagasaki, the bridges must not be forgotten. There are thirty-five in all, great and small, twenty of which are built of stone and fifteen of wood. There is nothing remarkable in their structure, which is very simple, as they are made more for strength than for show.

<margin>Streets.</margin>
The streets, in the main, are neither straight nor large, but irregular, dirty, and narrow, leading some uphill and others downhill because of the uneven ground upon which the town is built. Staircases of stone are built along some of the steepest parts for a more convenient ascent and descent. They are fully stocked with inhabitants, as many as they will ever hold. The streets are separated from each other by two wooden gates, one at each end, which are shut at night and often during the day whenever there is the slightest occasion for it. There is, besides, in every street a *Kashi-dōgu* <term>Kashi-dōgu</term> <note>original: "Qua Si Doogu"; literally "fire utensils," referring to firefighting equipment</note>, as they call it; that is, a place where they keep what is required in case of fire, which does a great deal of damage in this country where all the buildings are made of wood. These include, for instance, a well full of water, a pail or bucket, a fire-hook, and so on. The ladder is at the disposal of the commanding officer of the street and is kept in his house. It must be observed that the streets of Nagasaki and other towns in Japan never run to an excessive length. However, they are not all exactly the length of a Japanese *Chō* <term>Chō</term> <note>original: "Tſio"; a traditional unit of measurement</note>, which is a measure of 60 *Ken* <term>Ken</term> <note>original: "Kins"; a unit of length equal to about six feet</note>, although they have borrowed their name from it; rather, they are built so that they may be conveniently shut with gates at each end. Thus, for instance, a street may reach the full length of a *Chō* and include a few more houses, all of which are under the command of one officer. As to the number of houses, there are seldom more than sixty or fewer than thirty in a street.

<margin>Houses.</margin>
The houses of the common people are very humble, sorry buildings—small, low, and seldom more than one story high. If there are two stories, the uppermost is so low that it scarcely deserves the name. The roof is covered with shavings of fir-wood, which are fastened only by other pieces of wood laid across them. The houses are built of

# The History of JAPAN. Book IV.

The buildings are made of wood, as are all other structures throughout the Empire. The interior walls are paneled with wood and covered with painted and variously colored paper. The floors are covered with thick, woven mats <note>likely tatami</note>, which the residents take great care to keep exceedingly clean and neat. The rooms are divided from one another by sliding paper windows and screens <note>shoji and fusuma</note>. They have no seats or chairs, and possess only a few household goods, primarily those absolutely necessary for daily use in the kitchen. Behind every house is a back yard for private facilities; though these yards are often quite small, they always contain curious and beautiful plants to delight the eyes, which are maintained with great care. The houses of prominent merchants, both foreign and native, and of other wealthy people, are of a much better construction, commonly two stories high and built in the Chinese style, with a large courtyard in front and a garden behind.

<margin>Inhabitants of Nagasaki.</margin>
Nagasaki is inhabited chiefly by merchants, shopkeepers, tradesmen, craftsmen, artisans, and brewers, in addition to the numerous retinue of the town's Governors and the people employed in the Dutch and Chinese trade. <margin>Beggars.</margin> There are more poor people and beggars here, and more persistent ones, than anywhere else. Among the beggars are many mendicant monks <term>Kanshin-bo</term> <note>original: "Quansin Bos"</note> and mendicant nuns <term>Kanshin-bikuni</term> <note>original: "Quansin Bikuni"</note>. One single street, which is called Yahata-machi <note>original: "Jawatta Matz"</note> and sometimes Hachiman-machi <note>original: "Fatsmanmatz"</note>, contains over a hundred of them. They are poor people who make a vow to lead a devout, chaste, and disciplined life like the priests; to this end, they have their heads shaved and dress in black like other members of the clergy to more easily obtain charity. In this dress, with a rosary or beads in their hands, and carrying images, small bells, and other signs of unusual devotion, they go begging through the town. Some of these devotees are shaved publicly in one of the temples and consecrated to this peculiar way of life with great solemnity, while the priests murmur certain prayers and obscure words. However, this is only done when wealthy old people resolve to enter this order to spend the remainder of their days in their houses in a devout and retired way of life. The monks of the Chinese and other Zen <note>original: "Sensju"</note> monasteries also send some of their brothers to go begging six times a month. They do this more to follow the vow they make upon entering the order—to follow the example of their great founder and patron Shaka <note>original: "Siaka"; the historical Buddha</note>—than out of any actual want or necessity.

<margin>Dogs.</margin>
The dogs also deserve to be mentioned among the inhabitants of Nagasaki, as they are maintained and cared for just as well as, or even better than, many of the human residents. Although the Imperial orders <note>A reference to the "Edicts on Compassion for Living Things" issued by Shogun Tokugawa Tsunayoshi, who was known as the "Dog Shogun"</note> on this subject are not followed as strictly in Nagasaki as they must be in other parts of the Empire closer to the court, the streets are still full of these animals. They lead a most easy and quiet life, giving way neither to

If they happen to hurt any body, or otherwise to do mischief, so as to deserve punishment or death, no body dares presume to touch them, but the publick Executioner, and not even he, without a direct order from the Governors. Huts are built in every street to keep such as grow old and infirm, and when they die, they must be carried up to the tops of the mountains in order to be buried. This uncommon care and regard for the preservation of the Dog-kind, is the effect of a superstitious whim of the now reigning Emperor <note>This refers to Shogun Tokugawa Tsunayoshi, famously known as the "Dog Shogun" for his "Edicts on Compassion for Living Things."</note>, who being born in the Sign of the Dog, hath no less an esteem for this animal, than the great Roman Emperor *Augustus Caesar* is mention'd in History to have had for Rams <note>Augustus was famously associated with the zodiac sign Capricorn, often represented as a sea-goat or ram</note>. I have elsewhere related the comical conversation of two *Japanese*, who were carrying up a dead dog to the top of a mountain, in order to his burial.

<margin>Manufactur. s.</margin>
Manufactures, in the main, are not so good at *Nagasaki*, as they are in other parts of the Empire, and yet every thing is sold dearer, chiefly to foreigners. However, what is wrought in Gold, Silver and <term>Sawaas</term> <note>original: "Sawaas"; likely refers to *shakudo*, a traditional Japanese alloy of copper with gold and silver, often patinated to a dark blue-black</note>, being not so proper a commodity for the inland trade, as it is for the foreign, is made here with a much better taste, and of a far more curious workmanship, than I believe any where else.

<margin>Nagasaki how it is supplied with victuals.</margin>
As to victuals and drink, the country about *Nagasaki* doth not produce rice enough, which is the common food all over *Asia*, for the sustenance of its Inhabitants, so that the necessary provisions must be imported from the neighbouring Provinces of Hizen <note>original: "Fifen"</note>, Higo <note>original: "Figo"</note>, and Chikugo <note>original: "Tsikungo"</note>, and from the Islands *Amakusa* and *Gotho*, which lie to the North of this Town. The gardens in and about this City, the neighbouring mountains and villages abundantly furnish it with all sorts of fruits, plants and roots, with firewood, as also with some venison and poultry. The harbour and neighbouring shores yield plenty of fish and crabs. The rivers, which run through the town, provide it with clear and sweet water, very fit for daily drink. The <term>Saki</term>, or rice beer, as it is brew'd in *Japan*, being too strong, and that in particular which is brew'd at *Nagasaki*, of a disagreeable taste. Another light and clear water springs forth on the neighbouring mountain *Tatta*. The ships in the harbour take in their store of water from a clear spring, not far from the town to the East of it. The water, tho' it is very good and clear, (as indeed the water is in all parts of the Empire) yet it hath been observ'd to give people the cholick, or belly-ach, a distemper which the Inhabitants themselves are very much subject to, chiefly when they drink their *Saki* cold, and in too large a quantity.

<margin>Is very noisy.</margin>
This Town is never without a great deal of noise. In the day time victuals, and other merchandize, are cried up and down the streets. Day labourers encourage one another to work with a certain sound. The Seamen in the harbour measure the progress of their work according to another loud tune. In the night time, the watchmen and

Yet all this is minor compared to the loud cries and chanting of the priests and the family members of those who are dying or have recently passed. Whether in the home where the body rests, or on specific days dedicated to the memory of the dead, they loudly sing a *Namanda* while ringing bells to seek relief for the soul of the deceased. *Namanda* is a short prayer contracted from the phrase *Namu Amida Budsu* <note>original: "Namu Amida Budsu"; the phrase *Namu Amida Butsu* means "I take refuge in Amitabha Buddha"</note>, directed to their god *Amida*, whom they ask to intercede with the supreme Judge of the Infernal Court <note>referring to Enma-O, the Buddhist king and judge of the afterlife</note> on behalf of the poor, condemned soul. A similar practice is observed by the *Nembuds Koo* <term>Nembutsu-kō</term> <note>devotional lay-confraternities or neighborhood societies</note>, who are groups of pious neighbors or relatives. They take turns meeting in each other's homes every morning or evening to sing the *Namanda* as a form of spiritual insurance for the future relief of their own souls.

# CHAPTER II.

## Concerning the Government of NAGASAKI.

<margin>Government of the Imperial Cities.</margin>
<margin>Of Nagasaki.</margin>
Every Imperial City is commanded by two Governors (or Lords Lieutenants), who are addressed by their subjects as *Tono Sama*, which means "Supreme Lord" or "Prince." They command in rotation; while one is present at his post of government, the other resides at *Jedo* <note>Edo, modern-day Tokyo</note> at the Emperor’s Court <note>referring to the Shogun's court</note>, until he receives orders to return and relieve his predecessor, who then travels to the Court himself. 

*Nagasaki* alone is commanded by three Governors. Since the year 1688, it has been deemed necessary for the security of such an important location—and to maintain a more watchful eye over the behavior of the foreign nations permitted to trade there—to add a third official. This ensures that there are always two residing on-site while the third remains at Court. The two Governors present in *Nagasaki* command jointly, though they take turns presiding every two months. When a two-year term expires, the senior of the two is relieved by the third official, who is appointed by the Council of State to succeed him. As soon as the new Governor arrives in *Nagasaki*, the official he is replacing relinquishes his power and his residence in the palace, and

Moreover, so long as he stays in the capital city of *Jedo*, he makes it his business to court and to visit the chief ministers and great men at court, who are most in favor with the Emperor <note>historical: The author uses "Emperor" to refer to the Shogun, the military ruler of Japan</note>, to whom he makes rich presents, according to his ability, both as an acknowledgment for their last favors, and which is more material, to secure to himself the continuation of their good offices for the future. He stays at *Jedo* about six months, during which time he is at liberty to live with his family; for, as soon as he hath received orders from the Council of State to depart for his last or any other government, and hath taken his leave of its several members, he must set out forthwith, leaving his wife and children at *Jedo* till his return, in a manner as hostages of his fidelity <note>This refers to the *Sankin-kōtai* system, which used family hostages to ensure the loyalty of regional officials and lords</note>. Nay, all the time he is upon his government, no woman is to be admitted within his residence and apartments, under pain of incurring the Imperial displeasure, the fatal consequences whereof are no less than death by his own hands <note>referring to *seppuku*, or ritual suicide</note>, or else perpetual banishment, or imprisonment, with the unavoidable entire ruin of his family, it being thought beneath the majesty of the Emperor to inflict a less punishment upon any the least disregard shown to the Imperial Commands.

<margin>Conduct of the three present Governors.</margin> The conduct of the three present Governors, in managing the affairs of their government and regulating the foreign trade, hath been such as turned very much to the satisfaction of the Emperor and the Council of State, the rather since the inhabitants of *Nagasaki* reaped thereby considerable advantages, to the great prejudice, as may be easily imagined, of the foreign nations trading here. For this reason, and in consideration of their faithful services, the Emperor was pleased, not only to continue them in their governments, but to confer upon them the honor of knighthood, with the title of *Cami* <note>original: "Cami"; the title *Kami*, often translated as "Lord" or "Governor," was an honorary suffix for high-ranking officials</note>, which two of them have already received in their last journeys to court, and the third expects to be honored with upon his next going thither. *Cami*, in the Japanese language, signifies several things: as for instance, a great and powerful Spirit, worthy of divine worship; a sublime and immortal Soul; a deceased Emperor or great Man, whom the *Mikaddo* <note>original: "Mikaddo"; referring to the Emperor of Japan in Kyoto, whom Kaempfer viewed as a spiritual or ecclesiastical sovereign</note> hath deified and commanded to be worshipped amongst the Gods of the Country; and lastly, in the lowest sense, a Knight. Those persons who are honored with it as the title of Knighthood, commonly add to it, to give it more weight and authority, the name of some Province, or part of a Province. But to return to our three Governors, it will not be improper, before I proceed any further, to mention their names, and in a few words to give their character.

# The History of JAPAN. Book IV.

<margin>Tsino Kami <note>original: "Tfino cami"</note></margin>
The first is **Kawagutsu Genseiemon**, or according to his present title (wherein he has retained the name of his family), **Kawagutsu Tsino Kami** <note>likely Kawaguchi Settsu-no-kami, a Governor of Nagasaki</note>. The yearly revenue of his own estate amounts to 4,700 *Koku* <note>a *koku* is a traditional Japanese unit of volume, used to measure rice, roughly equivalent to five bushels; it was the standard measure of wealth and rank</note>. He is a handsome, well-shaped person, about 50 years of age—a cunning but malicious man, a great enemy to the Dutch, an unjust and severe judge, but an agreeable, liberal, and happy courtier.

<margin>Tsushima no Kami <note>original: "Tfuffimano Cami"</note></margin>
The second is **Yamaoka Shubiōie**, or according to his present title, **Yamaoka Tsushima no Kami**. He was formerly the High Constable <note>likely the *Machi-bugyō*, or City Commissioner/Chief of Police</note>, and was appointed by the Emperor <note>historical: the author refers to the Shogun, the military ruler of Japan, as the "Emperor"</note> to clear the Imperial Capital, **Edo** <note>modern: Tokyo</note>, of thieves and pickpockets. With the troops ordered for this expedition, he exterminated upwards of a thousand of them in a short time and was afterwards rewarded with this government position. The revenue of his own estate is 2,000 *Koku* a year. He is about 60 years of age, short-sized, sincere, humble, and liberal—chiefly to the poorer people in his government, to whom he made a present of all his perquisites <note>extra income or tips beyond his official salary</note> when he last went up to court. These were so considerable that some of the inhabitants received upwards of a hundred *Taels* <note>a silver currency unit used in East Asia</note> per head. Now, whether this liberality was truly owing to his generous disposition, or whether he endeavored thereby to rival, if not outdo, his partner in the government, I will not take it upon myself to determine. This much is true: despite his generosity and other good qualities, the habits of his former profession still stick so close to him that he often orders his domestic servants to be put to death without mercy, no matter how trifling their faults and misdemeanors.

<margin>Miyaki Tonomo</margin>
The third is **Miyaki Tonomo**, a nobleman of great generosity, endowed with many excellent qualities. He is much the same age as **Yamaoka Tsushima no Kami** and has 4,000 *Koku* in yearly revenues from his own estate, but as of yet, he has no official title.

<margin>Their Salary</margin>
Their salary is quite small for an employment of this importance, for it does not exceed 1,500 or 2,000 *Koku* of rice. In money, this may amount—since the price of this commodity is very variable—to between 7,000 and about 10,000 *Taels*. However, the perquisites are so considerable that they might acquire vast estates in a few years, if the presents which must be made to the Emperor and the Grandees of his court did not consume the best part of their profits.

<margin>Their Court</margin>
Out of this small allowance, however, they must maintain all the state, grandeur, and magnificence thought becoming to the dignity of their office and the majesty of their master. Their court consists of ten **Yoriki** <note>high-ranking police and administrative officials who served under the governors</note>, who are both military and civil officers and all noblemen of good families, and thirty **Dōshin** <note>original: "Doosju"; lower-ranking police officers or "constables" who handled the day-to-day enforcement of the law</note>, who are likewise military and civil officers, but inferior to the former in their office and status. Their business is to assist the governor with their advice, if needed, and to execute his commands. At least, it was with this design that they were first appointed by the Emperor,

# Chapter II. The History of JAPAN.

...on whom they formerly depended and were paid by the Imperial Treasury. But recently, since the year 1688, the Governors of **Nagasaki** <note>original: "Nagafacki"</note>, at their urgent request, obtained permission to choose these officers themselves and to pay them out of their own salaries. This was because these officers frequently took it into their heads to oppose the Governors simply to display their own authority as **Direct Imperial Vassals** <note>original: "Fattamatto," referring to the *Hatamoto*, or "bannermen," who were high-ranking samurai in direct service to the Shogun</note>. These independent Imperial officers often caused great confusion and hindered the Governors in carrying out many worthwhile plans.

For this reason—and to distinguish them from those noblemen who serve the Governors of other Imperial cities or the provincial Lords on the original terms (meaning they depend on no one but the Emperor <note>historical: the author refers to the Shogun, the military ruler of Japan, as the "Emperor"</note> himself)—their titles were also changed. They are now called the **High-Ranking Retainers** <note>original: "Kiu Ninſiu" (Kyu-nin-shu)</note> and the **Lower-Level Officials** <note>original: "Sita Jaku" (Shita-yaku)</note>. The titles of **Assistant Magistrates** <note>original: "Joriki" (Yoriki)</note> and **Police Assistants** <note>original: "Dooſju" (Doshin)</note> are now used only by the uneducated commoners. These commoners also sometimes mistakenly honor the **Assistant Magistrates** with the title of **High Commissioner** <note>original: "Bugjo" (Bugyō)</note>. That title properly belongs only to those who, during their commission, enjoy the privilege of having a Governor's pike carried before them as a badge of the power and authority granted to them by their master. In the official language of the court, the title of **High Commissioner** is given only to such Imperial commissioners and other military or civil officers who receive their commission directly from the Emperor himself and are answerable for their conduct to him alone.

<margin>**Assistant Magistrates** <note>original: "Joriki's"</note></margin>
But to return to the **Assistant Magistrates**, or as they are now called, the **High-Ranking Retainers**: it is their duty and office here, in other governments, and at all the courts of the provincial Lords where they are established, to assist their master with advice to the best of their ability. They must faithfully execute whatever commands he gives them, whether as military officers in times of war or as magistrates in civil affairs, such as judicial inquiries, trials, judgments, and executions. They are likewise employed in embassies, important messages, and all other affairs where it is required that their master's authority be represented. On these and similar occasions, they are attended by several **Police Assistants** <note>original: "Dooſen"</note> and other inferior officers and servants whose aid or assistance they might need in the execution of their duties.

Besides what has been mentioned so far, they are employed at **Nagasaki** for several other menial tasks which they consider very unbecoming of their character and rank as noblemen. These include keeping a watchful eye over foreigners, their trade, and their conduct; attending the buying and selling of goods; and overseeing the loading and unloading of ships. For this reason, few noblemen from prestigious families care to enter the service of the Governors of **Nagasaki**, especially since they must depend entirely on the Governor's favor—as he has the power to discharge them whenever he pleases—and because they are paid out of...

# The History of JAPAN. Book IV.

...out of the Governor’s own pocket, who, as one might easily imagine, allows them as little as he possibly can. They have some distinctions among themselves regarding their rank, based on the various offices they serve. The most important of those at **Nagasaki** <note>original: "Nagasacki"</note> is the **Inquisitor General of the Christian Religion** <note>original: "Kiristan Bugjoo"; this official was responsible for identifying and suppressing any remnants of Christianity in Japan</note>, who has the oversight of all affairs related to the further abolition and suppression of that faith. The allowance of the **Assistant Magistrates** <note>original: "Joriki’s"</note> at **Nagasaki** is so small—being no more than 100 **Taels** <note>a unit of currency based on a weight of silver</note> a year, in addition to their meals and a new suit—that they are hardly able to keep the necessary servants required of their rank. For instance, an **Assistant Magistrate** <note>original: "Joriki"</note> is expected to have a pike-bearer, a keeper of their great sword, and a shoe or slipper-bearer, yet they can barely afford to maintain a family. For this reason, servants frequently quit their master’s service, which forces the master to employ his other household staff to do their business.

<margin>**Police Assistants** <note>original: "Doosin" (Dōshin)</note></margin>
The **Police Assistants** <note>original: "Doosin"</note> are a type of helper or assistant to the **Assistant Magistrates** <note>original: "Joriki’s"</note>, and are employed by them, or by the Governors, for several lowlier tasks. For example, they serve in the guards, perform duty on board ships, junks <note>traditional Chinese or Japanese sailing vessels</note>, convoy-ships, and particularly the previously mentioned guard-boats, where watch must be kept overnight for the security of the town and harbor. On these and similar occasions, they serve either as commanding officers or as common soldiers; in the event of an attack, they are usually placed at the head of the troops because of their reputation for courage and bravery. Sometimes they perform the office of bailiffs or constables and put people under arrest, for which purpose they always carry a rope with them. Their yearly allowance, besides their meals, does not exceed 50 **Taels**, out of which money they must each maintain a servant.

<margin>**Stewards of the Household** <note>original: "Karoo" (Karō)</note></margin>
The **Stewards**, **Major-domos**, or **Stewards of the Household** <note>original: "Karoo"</note>, are superior to the **Assistant Magistrates** in rank and status. There are usually two, and sometimes three, and they have the supreme management of the Governor’s Court. All domestic affairs are examined and determined by them, either alone or—if the matter is of great consequence—with the advice of some of the **Assistant Magistrates**, whom they call in to help. They do this to avoid creating jealousy or mistrust in their masters by appearing to take on too much power. If they behave themselves well, they are assured a great share of their master’s confidence; they are often employed as Secretaries or Privy Counselors, and sometimes as Deputies in important matters. They are chosen by their masters from among their oldest, ablest, and most faithful servants, or from the nearest relatives of a deceased Steward if there is one capable of succeeding him. Sons often succeed their fathers in this employment.

The inhabitants imagine, that these persons make it their business to take care of their interest, liberties and necessities, at the Governor's court, and for this reason they share the expences and trouble of this office, hiring people to discharge it, or doing duty themselves, if call'd upon.

The History of J A P A N. Book IV. 272

<margin>
The Governor's retinue.
</margin>

The Governor’s retinue and attendance, when he goes out in public, consists of a spare horse led by hand, a **Norimon** <term>a palanquin or sedan chair used by the elite</term> in which he is carried, four **Kats** <term>original: "Kats" (Kachi); footmen or grooms</term> walking before the palanquin, four of his chief **Chamberlains** <note>original: "Tsugosjo's" (Tsukaisban or Tsugosho); gentlemen of the bedchamber</note> walking on each side of the palanquin, and two **Pike-bearers** <note>original: "Jarimots" (Yarimochi)</note> following behind. Finally, there is a numerous train of **Elders** <note>original: "Karo's" (Karō); high-ranking retainers</note>, **Military Assistants** <note>original: "Joriki's" (Yoriki)</note>, and **Police Assistants** <note>original: "Doosen" (Dōshin)</note>, accompanied by their own servants and attendants. His retinue is even larger and much more magnificent during his journey to **Edo** <note>original: "Jedo"; the capital of the Shogunate, modern-day Tokyo</note>, though during his stay in that capital he reduces it to a single pike-bearer and a few domestic servants.

<margin>
Their power and authority.
</margin>

The power of the Governors of **Nagasaki** <note>original: "Nangasaki"</note> extends not only over the Japanese inhabitants of this town, but also over the foreigners established here. These foreigners, like the natives, are subject to the laws of the Empire and liable to the same penalties for breaking them. Any moderation or forgiveness for these penalties depends entirely on the care and favor of the Governor; furthermore, on all occasions—whether his orders and proclamations benefit or disadvantage them—they must express their satisfaction and gratitude for the efforts he makes on their behalf. Among these foreigners are included the **Dutch** (those belonging to the **Dutch Factory** <term>the trading post on the man-made island of Dejima</term> and employed by the **Dutch East India Company** in Japan) and the **Chinese** (including neighbors who trade under their name, such as those from **Tonkin** <note>original: "Tunquineese"; northern Vietnam</note>, **Cambodia**, **Siam** <note>modern Thailand</note>, and others, as well as Chinese people settled in various parts of the East Indies). 

Besides an almost absolute power over the lives and fortunes of the inhabitants of this place—both foreign and native—the Governors also direct foreign trade. They have the power to judicially examine and punish smugglers and **Christians** <note>Christianity was strictly prohibited in Japan at this time</note>. They manage regulations for foreign ships entering the harbor, as well as ships and crews forced onto the Japanese coast by storms or distress. All such cases, including any followers of the Christian religion discovered anywhere on this Western Island <note>Kyushu</note>, must be brought to Nagasaki. Moreover, they are responsible for overseeing all foreigners in the city, watching their conduct closely, and, finally, providing for the security of the harbor.

<margin>
Restraints placed upon the Governors.
</margin>

However, to ensure that so many important affairs are not left entirely to the management and honesty of the Governors—which would be inconsistent with the suspicious nature of the Japanese government—the Imperial Court has made ample provision to watch their actions narrowly. This is done by a person residing at Nagasaki in the capacity of a **Daikan** <note>original: "Daiquan"; an Imperial Deputy or Factor</note>. And lest he should also be

For this purpose, orders have been sent to all the **Lords** <note>Daimyo; the powerful territorial lords of Japan</note> of the various provinces in **Kyushu** <note>original: "Kiusju"</note> to command their representatives at **Nagasaki** to immediately inform the Shogunal court of any remarkable occurrences. In the event of an invasion or an uprising, these Princes must march their troops toward the city with all possible speed. Such extensive precautions make it impossible for either the Governors or anyone else to attempt any action without the court being immediately informed through one channel or another.

<margin>Interpreters.</margin>
For the sake of trade and communication with foreign nations, the **Emperor** <note>Here referring to the Shogun, the military ruler in Edo</note> maintains a sufficient number of **Interpreters** with annual salaries. These officials cover the **Dutch**, **Portuguese**, **Tonkinese** <note>from northern Vietnam</note>, **Siamese** <note>from modern-day Thailand</note>, three dialects of **Chinese**, and several other languages. However, the knowledge and skill of these people is generally quite limited; it is often little more than a simple and mediocre stringing together of broken words from those languages. They arrange these words according to the grammar and idiom of their own native Japanese, without regard for the actual nature or spirit of the language they are translating. They do this in such a strange manner that, frequently, other interpreters would be needed just to explain what they are trying to say.

<margin>Provision made for the Security of the Harbour.</margin>
To secure the harbor against any foreign invasion and to prevent the foreigners living here from attempting anything against the public peace and tranquility, four different types of guards have been established. These are organized in such a way that they secure both the town and the harbor while also serving to watch one another. I will now provide a brief account of these guards.

<margin>Great Imperial Guard.</margin>
The first is the **Great Imperial Guard**. This unit is independent of the Governor's authority and is kept in the Emperor's name. The expense for this guard is paid by the Princes of **Hizen** <note>original: "Fizen"</note> and **Chikuzen** <note>original: "Tshikusen"</note> on an alternating basis, each for one year. It is called **Gobansho** <term>original: "Gobansio"; a guard house or government office</term>, **Goban**, or **Goban Tokoro**, meaning the "chief guard," "head guard," or "Imperial guard," because it does not report to the local Governor. 

It is stationed about half a **German mile** <note>A geographical mile, roughly equal to 4.6 English miles or 7.4 kilometers</note> from the town on two hills facing each other. The hill on the left as one sails out of the harbor is called **Tomachi** <note>original: "Tomatsi"</note>, and the one on the right is **Nishidomari** <note>original: "Nisidomari"</note>. There are no walls, ramparts, or ditches surrounding them, nor are they equipped with cannons for defense. Upon the arrival or departure of our ships, these stations are draped in red cloth for decoration, and it is the custom for our ships to salute each station with a discharge of our onboard guns. There are about 700 men on duty across both stations, though if they were at full strength, there should be no fewer than a thousand. They live in wooden huts and are commanded by a **Gobangashira** <term>original: "Gobangasijra"; a Captain of the Imperial Guard</term>. A few of these men are **Yoriki** <term>original: "Joriki's"; high-ranking military assistants</term>, others are **Doshin** <term>original: "Doosen"; lower-level police assistants</term>, and the rest are **Bushi** <term>original: "Bus"; common soldiers or samurai</term>.

# The History of JAPAN. Book IV. #

They <note>referring to the mountain guards mentioned on the previous page</note> have a fine open view over the whole harbour, and a great boat, or barge, at their disposal, which lies ready somewhat below the town, in order to carry them with all speed, where their presence is wanted.

<margin>Ship-guard.</margin>
The second Guard is the **Funaban**, or Ship-guard <note>original: "Funaban"; a maritime security station</note>. This is composed of eighteen **Bus**, or common Soldiers <note>Bushi; the warrior or samurai class</note>, who have a competent number of Guard-ships, with the necessary hands on board. They are to watch all the foreign ships lying at anchor near the town, and to go round the harbour in the night. As soon as a foreign ship enters the harbour, two of these boats, each with a **Dosin** <note>Dōshin; a lower-ranking samurai official serving as a policeman or guard</note>, as commanding officer, are posted on the sides of her. They are relieved every three hours by two others. This continues so long as she stays in the harbour. Upon her departure they keep her company, till she is got out of the harbour to the main Sea. These Guard-ships are kept at the expense of the inhabitants of the **Water-streets**, as they call them, or the streets which are built along the water-side, who are also to take care, to furnish the necessary number of water-men. And that they should have no reason to complain, of any extraordinary hardships put upon them, another burden of the like kind hath been laid upon the inhabitants of the upper part of the town, towards the mountains, or of the **land-streets**, as they call them, who must send six, and, if needful more **Kulis** <note>Coolies; unskilled laborers or porters</note>, every day to the Governor's court, to be by them employed in the dispatch of necessary business. No house nor street is exempted from this duty, which all the inhabitants must discharge in their turn. The **Funaban**, or common Ship-guard, is assisted and enforced by a third one, called

<margin>Third Guard.</margin>
**Mi Okuri Bune**, that is to say, the **Convoying Inspectors** <note>original: "Mi Okuri Bune"; literally "seeing-off boats"</note>, who make up the third of the chief guards appointed for the security of the harbour. Their business is to convoy the outward-bound ships so far out of the harbour into the Ocean, as seems necessary to put it out of their power to return upon any pretence, or for any reason whatsoever. For the same purpose, but chiefly to hinder the Chinese from landing their **junks** <note>original: "yonks"; traditional Chinese sailing vessels</note> any where else, but at **Nagasaki**, as the only harbour they are allowed to go to, and likewise to discover the Japanese Smugglers, who are often caught, several other Japanese boats, rowed each by eight watermen, are continually cruising along the Coasts. The main business of these people is the Whale-fishing. They stand all under the command of a general officer, who hath a yearly allowance of 300 **Taels** <note>original: "Tails"; a unit of silver currency used in East Asia</note>, and takes care of the Whale-fishing, as well as to hinder ships from putting in any where but at **Nagasaki**, and to chase Smugglers. In this view they choose for the Whale-fishing, what time and upon what coasts they think it most likely to meet with them.

# Chapter II. The History of JAPAN. #

<margin>Spy-guard <note>original: "Tomi Ban"</note></margin>
The fourth and final of the primary guards of the harbor is the **Spy-guard** <note>original: "Tomiban," from the Japanese *to-mi* (distant look) and *ban* (guard)</note>, which literally means the lookout or far-seeing guard. It consists of more than twenty **warrior-soldiers** <note>original: "Bus" or *Bushi*</note>, known as the **Guard of Ten** <note>original: "Siu Ninsi"</note> because their number originally did not exceed ten. They reside with their families at the southern end of the town, near the coast on a hill. From this vantage point, they have a clear view over the residences of the **Chinese**—who are their closest neighbors—and the **Dutch**. Their duty is to keep watch from the **lookout peaks** <note>original: "Tomi Dake"</note>, which are small huts built atop the mountains surrounding the harbor. Using spy-glasses to scan the open sea, they immediately notify the Governor when a ship is spotted steering toward the harbor. They provide regular updates on the vessel's progress using fast dispatch boats kept specifically for this purpose. 

A similar watch is maintained from the summit of a mountain called **Jewel-flower Mountain** <note>original: "Fooqua San," likely Mount Hoko</note>, located near the town. There, they always keep a supply of combustible materials ready to be ignited. This beacon is lit if a fleet of ten or more European ships is seen approaching, if there is confirmed news of **Portuguese** ships arriving—as they are strictly and forever banned from entering the Empire—or in the event of a sudden uprising anywhere on this western island of **Kyushu** <note>original: "Kiusju"</note>. This alarm fire, which cannot be lit without the Governors' express permission, serves to alert the entire country of an impending disaster requiring urgent assistance. The fire can be seen as far away as a high mountain in the province of **Amakusa**, where a second fire is lit, which in turn is visible from **Higo** <note>original: "Figo"</note>. By successively lighting signal fires on various mountains along the southern coasts of **Japan**, a warning can reach the Imperial court at **Edo** <note>original: "Jedo," modern-day Tokyo</note> within twenty-four hours.

<margin>Mayors of Nagasaki</margin>
The town of **Nagasaki** and its residents are under the supreme authority of the Imperial Governors, but are managed by four **Mayors** <note>original: "Burghermasters"</note> and their deputies. They serve in this office for one year at a time, and during their term, they are called the **Yearly Warden** <note>original: "Ninban"</note>, which literally means the "annual watchman" or the mayor in command. His duty is to inform the presiding Governor of his daily activities. He must report significant matters in person and, in cases of legal difficulty or disputes between the mayors, present the case before the **Imperial Court of Justice** <note>original: "Emperor's Bench"</note>. With the court's consent, he may also refer the matter to the Governors for a final decision.

All civil matters are brought before this Imperial Court. The parties involved and their witnesses are examined by the court, and after a formal hearing where both sides present their arguments, judgment is given accord-

...ing to the laws of the Empire, their printed reports, the imperial orders and proclamations, or the opinion of persons learned in the Law. Once a sentence has been handed down in this Court, there is no appeal to any other. However, those individuals who have received a sentence of death cannot be executed without a warrant signed by the Council of State at **Edo** <note>original: "Jedo," the administrative capital of the Shogunate, modern-day Tokyo</note>. This Council must also be consulted on all matters of great importance that more directly affect the public welfare of the Empire, provided these matters are not of such a nature that they would be harmed by the delays required for the sending and return of a messenger.

<margin>City Elders <note>original: "Tofij Jori," referring to the *Toshiyori*</note></margin>
The four Mayors, or **Burgomasters** <note>original: "Burghermafters," a Dutch-derived term for city officials</note>, are otherwise called the **Assembly of Elders** <note>original: "To Sij Jori Sju" (*Toshiyori-shū*)</note>. This title, according to the literal meaning of the characters used to write it, signifies the *Seniors* or *Elder Men* (*Aldermen*), so named because they were formerly chosen from among the oldest and most prudent inhabitants. However, in recent times, this office has become effectively hereditary. Out of respect for a father's merit, his son is sometimes allowed to succeed him in his position, provided the Governors of the town give their consent and the candidate is approved by the Emperor's Council of State. The candidate must then express his gratitude in person for this singular mark of favor. At this very time, **Takaku Goparo**, a child of eleven years, has inherited the title and dignity of his father, **Takaku Shirobei** <note>original: "Takaku Sijro Bioje"</note>, who died about a year ago; when he reaches adulthood, he will be entrusted with the office itself. Another of the current Mayors, **Takaku Saemon** <note>original: "Takaku Sajemon"</note>, who was previously called **Takaku Genso**, inherited his father's title and dignity five years ago upon his death, even though he is currently only twenty-two years old. In fact, there are three close relatives of the **Takaku** family currently holding the office of Mayor, and a fourth member of the same family has command over the surrounding countryside. 

The Mayors or Burgomasters of **Nagasaki** formerly depended directly upon the Emperor's Council of State, from whom they also received their commissions. At that time, they enjoyed the privilege of wearing **two swords** <note>original: "two Scymeters," the *daishō* carried by the samurai class</note> like the noblemen of the kingdom, and of having a pike carried before them as a public sign of their authority. However, since the Governors of this city were granted greater power and authority by the Emperor in the year 1683, the grandeur and power of the Burgomasters here and in other Imperial Cities has been reduced to a smaller scope. Among the many privileges and exemptions they were forced to surrender to the Governors were the right to hold elections and the power to levy taxes on the inhabitants. In short, they have little left of their former status and greatness, except that after completing their yearly duties, they must—according to the custom of the country—travel to the Court to pay their respects to the Emperor and to present...

<margin>Deputies of the Mayors.</margin>
The **Permanent Officers** <note>original: "Dsiojosi," likely *Jo-yoshi*, meaning "continual heads"</note>—so called because their positions are held for life—are next to the **City Elders** <note>original: "Tosijori," or *Toshiyori*</note> in rank and authority. They serve as their lieutenants or deputies in matters concerning the management of the **Outer Town**, while the Mayors themselves, together with their **Ward Heads** <note>original: "Ottona," or *Otona*</note>, have the immediate government of the **Inner Town** <note>original: "Utsimatz," or *Uchimachi*, the oldest part of the city</note>. (The **Ward Head** <note>original: "Ottona"</note> is another specific magistrate who acts as a sort of Justice of the Peace for the street in which he lives, as I shall explain in greater detail in the next chapter.) It is one branch of the office of these **Permanent Officers** to settle and resolve, in company with the Ward Heads, minor disputes arising in that part of the town committed to their care. They are chosen from the ranks of the Ward Heads by the presiding Mayor, with the consent of the Governor, and are generally selected from among the oldest members of that group. Like the Mayors, they receive a small salary assigned to them by the Emperor, along with some perquisites from the foreign trade in which they are involved; yet, as the common people judge the importance of an office by the appearance of the official, they strive to maintain their dignity, living always in a state of **splendid poverty** <note>An evocative phrase meaning they maintain high social status and formal appearance despite limited actual wealth</note>.

<margin>Annual Officers.</margin>
Next to the Permanent Officers follow four **Annual Officers** <note>original: "Nengiosi," or *Nengyōji*</note>. The character expressing this word signifies "annual heads or officers," which they truly are, as they remain in their employment for only one year. They are four in number: two for the Inner Town and two for the **Outer Town** <note>original: "Sotomatz"</note>. They are appointed by the Mayors to provide a faithful report to the Governors regarding the daily transactions in the execution of their office. They serve, at the same time, as representatives for the people, whose interests they must look after at the Governor’s court. For both these purposes, they are assigned a small room in the Governor’s Palace, next to the **Great Guard** <note>original: "Genquaban," likely *Genkan-ban* or entrance guard</note> of the **Police Officials** <note>original: "Joriki," or *Yoriki*, high-ranking samurai assistants to the governors</note>. There they wait all day long until the Governor is at leisure to receive the messages they deliver in the name of the Mayors, or the petitions they present to him on behalf of private individuals. They also wait to learn, either directly or through one of the Governor's **Stewards** <note>original: "Karoo," or *Karō*, the high-ranking household elders of a lord</note>, what commands he wishes to lay upon the **City Elders**, the **Ward Heads**, or the interpreters of the foreign nations established here, as well as to be informed of whatever other business he...

...he expects should be done by the inhabitants, either at his own house, or elsewhere. It is a very delicate and demanding office, and it requires all the prudence and attention they are capable of, if they wish to maintain themselves in the Governor’s favor. They are chosen, like the **Permanent Officers** <note>original: "Dsiojosi," likely *Jo-yoshi*, meaning "continual heads"</note>, from among the most capable **Ward Heads** <note>original: "Ottona’s," or *Otona*, the local neighborhood administrators</note> of both parts of the town.

These are the chief magistrates and commanding officers of the town of Nagasaki. They have no Town Hall, nor any other public place of assembly. When they meet for business, it is at the house of the presiding Mayor.

I proceed now to give a short account of some other lower-ranking officers, by whose means and assistance policy and good order are maintained in this town.

<margin>Company of Town Messengers.</margin>
The **Town Messengers** <note>original: "Tsioosino Mono," likely *Chōshin-mono*</note> are a company of officials who serve also as constables and bailiffs. They were formerly under the command of the Mayors, but since the Mayors' power and authority have been reduced and the Governor’s authority raised upon their ruin, they are now employed chiefly in the service of the latter. This company consists of about thirty families living together in one street, which is called **Messenger Street** <note>original: "Tsioofimatz," or *Chōshimmachi*</note> for that reason, and has been in their possession for almost as long as anyone can remember. Their number increases in proportion to the strict and thorough regulations to which the inhabitants are held; very recently, a new street began to be built for them, which is to be called **New Messenger Street** <note>original: "Sintsioofimatz," or *Shin-chōshimmachi*</note>. Their name is more honorable than their profession, which consists chiefly of pursuing and arresting criminals. They are also now and then employed at public executions, primarily beheadings. They are all skilled wrestlers and have their particular ways to quickly catch and disable an opponent, no matter how much they are on their guard. For the execution of their office, they always carry a rope <note>original: "halter," referring to the ropes used in *hojōjutsu*, the martial art of restraining prisoners</note> with them. Their office, though low and contemptible in practice, is regarded by law as military and noble. For this reason, they wear two swords <note>original: "Scimiters," referring to the *daishō* or pair of swords that was the status symbol of the samurai class</note> like the noblemen. Some of their company are of less note and are called **Assistants** <note>original: "Sadsi," likely *Sashi*</note>. These wear only one sword. The sons follow their father’s profession and either succeed them upon their death or are admitted into the company before that time.

<margin>Tanners and public Executioners.</margin>
But no profession is so much despised by the Japanese as that of the **Tanners** <note>original: "Jetta," or *Eta*, a historical outcaste group in Japan who dealt with "unclean" tasks</note>, whose business it is to skin dead cattle and to dress and tan leather for shoes, slippers, and the like. These people are obliged to perform the office of public executioners, to put prisoners to the rack, and to execute them—whether they are to be beheaded, crucified, or put to any other death whatsoever. They live by themselves in a separate village out of town, not far from the place of execution, which here, and everywhere else...

<margin>The Bellman.</margin>
The last of the public officers is the **Bellman**, whose business it is to measure the time and to indicate the hours by striking a bell. For convenience, this bell is hung on the side of a mountain, not far from the Temple of **Daikoosi** <note>likely the Daion-ji temple in Nagasaki</note>. The great bell of that temple is rung only at sunrise and sunset; if they ring it at other times, it is to summon people to the temple to hear an explanation of some moral precept or a text taken from one of their religious books.

## CHAPTER III.

### Concerning the Administration and Regulation of the Streets of Nagasaki; also the Government of the Surrounding Country.

In the preceding chapter, I treated the government of Nagasaki in general very extensively. I proceed next to take into more particular consideration the **administration** <note>original: "policy," referring here to local management and policing</note> and regulations of every street. The main goal of these is to keep a watchful eye over the conduct of the inhabitants and to assist the Governors, Mayors, and other chief officers in the discharge of their duties. To this end, it has been found necessary to appoint the following officers for every street.

<margin>**Ottona** <note>The *Otona* was the headman or ward chief of a neighborhood</note></margin>
The first and most important person is the **Ottona**. He is the head and chief magistrate of his street. He gives the necessary orders in case of fire; he takes care that a good and regular watch is kept at night and that the orders of the Governors and Mayors are punctually complied with. He keeps books and registers where he enters which persons are born in the street, how many die, or marry, or go traveling, or leave the street altogether, as well as which new inhabitants move in—recording their names, birthplaces, religion, trade, and so on. In the case of small disputes arising between the inhabitants of his street, he summons the parties before him to settle the matter and set them right, if possible. He punishes minor crimes by putting the criminals under arrest or laying them in irons. He commands criminals within his district to be taken up by his own people and confines them until further orders from superior magistrates, before whom he lays all criminal affairs and all cases of importance. In short, he is answerable for whatever accidents happen within the compass of the street of which he is the head and chief commanding officer. He is chosen

Every inhabitant writes the name of the person whom he would wish to see elevated to this dignity upon a slip of paper, which he then signs and seals. Once all the votes are collected, the papers are opened, and the names of those who received the most votes are presented by the <term>Nengiosi<gloss>annual municipal officers who acted as intermediaries</gloss></term> to the Governor. They accompany this with a humble petition from the inhabitants, requesting that he be pleased to nominate and appoint one of them as the <term>Ottona<gloss>the headman or chief magistrate of a street or ward</gloss></term>. His salary consists of a tenfold portion drawn from the public treasury of the street—or, what amounts to the same thing, from the profits of foreign trade which are set aside for the joint benefit of all the town's inhabitants.

<margin>His Deputies.</margin>
Every **Ottona** has three deputies, called <term>Oogumi<gloss>literally "great group"</gloss></term>, **Oja**, or **Oogumigasira**, which translates to "Chiefs or Heads of the great company or Corporation." They serve as the **Ottona's** lieutenants, assisting him with their advice and support to ensure the better execution of his office and the speedier handling of affairs relating to the management of the street.

<margin>Companies of five.</margin>
The inhabitants of every street are divided into <term>Goningumi<gloss>five-man groups</gloss></term>, which are small corporations of five men. There are typically ten or fifteen of these groups, more or less, in every street. Each is composed of five—and sometimes a few more—immediate neighbors, but only those who are the owners of the ground and houses they live in. The rest of the residents, who do not own their own houses, are not admitted into these corporations even though they live in the same street. Instead, they are looked upon as tenants and, consequently, as dependents of their landlords who own the houses. Sometimes as many as fifteen or more families of tenants may belong to a single **Goningumi**. These tenants are exempted from taxes and other public burdens laid upon their landlords, with the sole exception of the <term>Monban<gloss>night watch</gloss></term>; they are obliged either to perform the night watch and rounds themselves or ensure it is done, as it is a general duty that all inhabitants must observe in their turn. However, this apparent advantage of tax exemption comes with significant disadvantages: tenants have no voice in the election of street officers and no claim to any share of the public trade profits. Furthermore, the rents they pay to their landlords are very high, especially considering how small and poor the houses are. Rents are paid monthly, calculated by the number of <term>mats<gloss>tatami floor coverings</gloss></term> used to cover the floors, charging five <term>Condors<gloss>Kandarin, a unit of silver currency</gloss></term> per mat in the poorest houses and ten in the best.

<margin>Head of the Corporation.</margin>
Every corporation of five has a <term>Kogomi Oja<gloss>head of the small group</gloss></term> or **Kogomi Gasijra**, who acts as the head of the corporation or Elder. He is responsible for inspecting the conduct of his four companions and is held answerable for their actions. If they commit any act contrary to the law, he shares in

<margin>Public Notary.</margin>
The <term>Fifia<gloss>secretary or public notary</gloss></term> is another of the street's officers. His duties include writing and publishing the orders of the <term>Ottona<gloss>the street headman</gloss></term> to the inhabitants, as well as issuing passports, testimonials, and letters of dismissal. He maintains the headman's records and journals, such as the census of all houses and residents in the street—including their names, ages, occupations, and religions—as well as a book recording everyone who dies in the street, including the time and cause of death and evidence regarding the religion they practiced on their deathbed. He also keeps a register of all passports issued by his office, the names of the recipients, their business abroad, and the dates of their departure and return; finally, he keeps a journal of daily events within the neighborhood.

<margin>Treasurer.</margin>
<term>Takura Kaku<gloss>literally "jewel-keeper"</gloss></term> is the Street Treasurer. He manages the public funds and provides regular accounts to his fellow inhabitants, detailing all money received and spent. The public treasury mainly consists of funds that the town magistrates set aside from the profits of foreign trade for the collective benefit of the residents. This money is distributed among the streets to help the people pay the additional taxes levied upon them. The inhabitants take turns serving in this office for one year each.

<margin>Messenger.</margin>
The <term>Nitzi Josi<gloss>literally "daily messenger"</gloss></term> is the person responsible for the daily delivery of messages. He informs the senior officers when a resident dies or moves away, or when anything else occurs that requires their attention. He also delivers petitions from the inhabitants and the testimonials they receive from their <term>Kogomi Oja<gloss>heads of the small neighborhood corporations</gloss></term>. He collects the <term>Fassaks<gloss>contributions for gifts</gloss></term>—money gathered at specific times to be presented to the Governors and high magistrates. Furthermore, he communicates the magistrates' orders to the heads of the corporations and publishes them throughout the street.

<margin>Guards.</margin>
For the security of the streets at night, two types of watches are kept.

<margin>Head Guard of the Street.</margin>
The first is the primary guard, where the inhabitants themselves serve on rotation, three at a time. For this reason, it is called the <term>Dsisinban<gloss>the personal or local ward watch</gloss></term>. They are assigned a room or house near the center of the street or at the corner of a cross-street. On important festival days, or at any other time the magistrates deem it necessary, it

The watch must be kept all day long. It must be doubled when the authorities are fearful of danger; in such cases, the <term>Ottona<gloss>the street headman</gloss></term> assists in person along with one of his deputies for a good part of the night, until the largest crowds or the greatest dangers have passed. If any misfortune should happen that could be blamed on their carelessness or neglect, the officials and the entire street would be held responsible and severely punished. So much respect must be given to this watch that it is considered a capital crime to oppose or insult it.

The second type of watch is the **Monban**, or the "gate and round guard," which is appointed to watch for accidents involving fire or thieves and to give notice at the slightest suspicion. It consists of two laboring men, or others of the poorer class among the street's inhabitants, who sit in a <term>sentry box<gloss>a small hut for a guard</gloss></term> built for that purpose at each gate. They walk from one gate to the other all night long, indicating that they are awake and signaling the hours of the night—just as all other watchmen do on land and on their ships—by striking two wooden sticks against one another. They are maintained at the expense of the inhabitants of the street, some of whom perform the duty themselves in their turn. In some towns, a small hut is built at the top or side of a house near the middle of the street, specifically for a man to watch for signs of fire.

<margin>The current condition of Nagasaki's inhabitants regarding civil affairs.</margin>
Due to so many strict regulations and the many demanding offices that must be served in person, it cannot be denied that the inhabitants of **Nagasaki** are kept in a state of great slavery and submission, which is indeed almost without parallel. On the other hand, they have the significant advantage of not being overburdened with taxes, unlike the subjects of most European Princes. Furthermore, they are even assisted in paying the few taxes and contributions that are required of them by the sums of money which the town magistrates set aside from the profits of foreign goods. This money is later distributed equally among the residents—an advantage unique to **Nagasaki**, as it is the only one of the Imperial Cities where trade with foreigners is permitted. Regarding these three things—the rigorous submission of the inhabitants, the small taxes levied upon them, and the care taken by the magistrates to help them pay—I shall now proceed to describe them briefly, assuring the reader that I will state nothing but what I know to be true.

<margin>The burdens and charges they live under.</margin>
No crimes are punished in **Japan** by fines or <term>pecuniary mulcts<gloss>monetary penalties</gloss></term>. The Japanese argue that if punishments could be bought off with money, the rich would have the power to commit whatever crimes they pleased—a concept which, in their opinion and by its very nature, is absurd and inconsistent with reason and justice. This is why they recognize only corporal punishments, death, and imprison-

[punish]ment, banishment, loss of estates, preferments <note>original: "preferments," referring to social standing or professional appointments</note>, and the like. They have variety of torments to torture their criminals, and to bring them to confession, but when convicted and cast for their life, they are either beheaded, or laid on the cross <note>Crucifixion was a common execution method in Edo-period Japan for serious crimes such as arson or treason.</note>, according to the nature and heinousness of the crime, for which they are to be executed. Other punishments, and these often inflicted for crimes and misdemeanors of others, tho sometimes never so trifling, are, imprisonment for life, banishment from the town, or country, with the loss of estate and places. These and the like no body ever lives secure from, forasmuch as they are afflicted even for the crimes of others, and may befal one unawares. Thus the Street-officers must suffer for the crimes of the House-keepers <note>Property owners or heads of households were legally responsible for everyone living under their roof.</note>, who live within the district committed to their trust, the House-keepers for the crimes of their domesticks and lodgers, the masters for those of their servants, children for those of their parents; a corporation for those of its individual members, and lastly, neighbours for the crimes of each other. In inflicting these punishments however, great regard is had to the nature of the crime, the condition of the person who committed it, and the share of guilt to be laid in reason, to the charge of his superiors, relations, or neighbours.

Besides the burden of so many different watches, which must be kept within and without the town, and in the harbour, and so many troublesome offices which must be serv'd personally, or by deputy's, another considerable disadvantage, the inhabitants of *Nagasaki* labour under, is, that every now and then the streets are for some time entirely shut up, and no body suffer'd to go in or out. This is done, when they are apprehensive of some danger, mutiny, or insurrection, or in case of search after criminals, and in many other inquiries, tho' as it often happens, after very trifling things. But there is never so much caution and strictness used, as upon the departure of foreign ships and <term>yonks<gloss>junks; traditional Chinese sailing vessels</gloss></term>, in order to prevent the inhabitants from following them, to smuggle goods, which is a crime forbid under pain of death. When the outward-bound ships set sail, till they are got out of sight of the harbour, strict search is made in all the streets, to see, whether there be none of the inhabitants wanting, that could be suspected to be out upon some such occasion or other. This search is made at uncertain times, but thrice every night, as for instance, sometime in the evening, about midnight, and the next morning, in presence of the <term>Ottona<gloss>the street headman</gloss></term>, if he be at leisure, of an <term>Ogumigashira<gloss>a head of a "great group" or neighborhood deputy</gloss></term>, or the *Ottona*'s deputy, of two <term>Koogumi Oja<gloss>heads of the "small groups" or local trade associations</gloss></term>, and the <term>Nitzi Josi<gloss>the street’s daily messenger</gloss></term>. Every body must be present at these searches, to answer when call'd by his name. The Street's-messenger reads the names of all the domesticks out of the Register-book. For dispatches sake he sometimes satisfies himself with comparing the number of heads present, with the number of people mention'd in his book, without asking for every one in particular.

During the time of such searches, and when the street gates are shut, as well as at other times when they are apprehensive of some trouble—even if the gates are not shut—no one is allowed to pass through from one street into another without a <term>wooden pass-token<note>original: *Forifuda*; a small stick of wood marked by the presiding official or burgomaster.</note></term>. Upon showing this specific kind of passport, the traveler is accompanied from one end of the street to the other by the <term>watchman<note>original: *Monban*; the round-watch or street guard.</note></term> of every street, and then delivered up to the watchman of the next street, and so on, until he reaches his intended destination.

If an inhabitant intends to leave the street and house where he lives to move to another, he must first of all apply to the <term>ward headman<note>original: *Ottona*; the magistrate or presiding official of a street.</note></term> of the other street with a petition, expressing his desire to be admitted among the inhabitants of that street. When he delivers the petition, he simultaneously presents the ward headman with a gift of fish. The headman then informs himself of the petitioner's life, character, and conduct, and sends the <term>street messenger<note>original: *Nitzi Joši*; an official who handles communications within the ward.</note></term> to every inhabitant, asking them to let him know whether or not they consent to admit the petitioner as a neighbor. 

If even one inhabitant opposes his admission and has any charge to bring against him—for instance, that he is prone to drunkenness, has a quarrelsome nature, or is inclined to any other crime for which the neighbor refuses to be held responsible—it is sufficient to exclude him. But if the petitioner obtains the consent of all the inhabitants, he applies to the <term>public notary<note>original: *Fifia*</note></term> of his former street for a certificate of his behavior and a letter of dismissal, both signed by the ward headman. These two documents are carried by the street messenger to the ward headman of the street the petitioner intends to move into, who then receives him under his protection and incorporates him among the inhabitants of his street. 

In the meantime, the new headman is not responsible for the petitioner’s behavior before the delivery of these two documents; if the petitioner should be found guilty of any crimes committed before that time, the blame would fall upon the street where he formerly lived. For this reason, the headman of the previous street protests in his letter of dismissal that, from the time of the resident's departure, he will no longer answer for his conduct, which makes it necessary for the petitioner to ensure that these documents are delivered to his new ward headman as quickly as possible. After the petitioner has been admitted among the inhabitants of the new street and his name has been entered into the registry books, he celebrates his entry with a formal dinner, which he gives either to his own <term>neighborhood group<note>original: *Kumigašira*; a small association or 'corporation' of households that share collective responsibility.</note></term> or, if he wishes, to all the groups of the street. After all this trouble, the greatest difficulty still remains: the selling of his old house. This, again, cannot be done without the collective consent of all the inhabitants of the street.

Once all obstacles are finally removed and the house is sold, the buyer must pay a fee into the public treasury of the street for the common benefit of its inhabitants. This fee is 8 percent of the agreed price in the <term>Outer Town<note>original: *Sotomatz* (Sotomachi), the newer sections of Nagasaki.</note></term> and slightly over 12 percent in the <term>Inner Town<note>original: *Utsimatz* (Uchimachi), the original urban core of the city.</note></term>. This money is called the <term>Eighth Part<note>original: *Fatsijbun* (Hachibun).</note></term>. Of this sum, five parts are distributed equally among the street’s inhabitants as compensation for the effort of vetting the new neighbor; the remaining three parts are intended for a public dinner, though this is rarely actually held. 

As soon as the new inhabitant has taken possession of his house, all his neighbors in the street come to congratulate him, offer their services, and assure him of their friendship and neighborly help.

When a resident of any street in <term>Nagasaki</term> intends to travel abroad—whether to go on a pilgrimage to a holy site or for any other business—the <term>Group Chief<note>original: *Kogomi Oja* (Kogumi Oya), the head of a neighborhood unit.</note></term> and the other members of the corporation he belongs to must provide him with a certificate addressed to the town magistrates. In this document, they testify that he is traveling for an honest and good purpose, and they act as bail for his return and appearance within a set timeframe. For this process, they use a specific ledger called the <term>Passport Signing Book<note>original: *Kitte no sita Gaki* (Kitte no shitagaki), literally a draft or notebook for permits.</note></term>. On these occasions, by order of the <term>Ward Elder<note>original: *Ottona* (Otona), the headman of the street.</note></term>, the inhabitants write their names under the certificate and, for even greater security, apply their personal seals. 

Once the certificate and the legal obligation are entered into the book, the <term>Ward Elder</term> orders the street messenger to take it to the house of the <term>Presiding Town Mayor<note>original: *Ninban Tosij Jori* (Ninban Toshiyori).</note></term>, where it is delivered to the <term>Entrance Guard<note>original: *Genquaban* (Genkanban).</note></term>. The guard presents it to the Mayor, who then instructs his <term>Secretary<note>original: *Jusitz* (Yūshitsu)</note></term> to write a passport for the petitioner and seal it with his great seal, which he uses only during his term as mayor. This seal is kept by the secretary; it is about the size of a crown coin and features the characters of the Mayor’s own <term>Formal Name<note>original: *Nanori*, a dignified name used by the samurai and official classes.</note></term>. 

This passport is then brought to the <term>Annual Commissioner<note>original: *Nengiosj* (Nengyōji)</note></term>, who also adds his name and seal. If the petitioner lives in the <term>Outer Town</term>, it may instead be signed by the <term>Permanent Official<note>original: *Dsio Josi* (Jōyoshi)</note></term>. No fees are charged for this administrative labor, except for three <term>small coins<note>original: *Condors* (Kondori), a unit of currency.</note></term> paid to the <term>Daily Messenger<note>original: *Nitzi Josi* (Nichiyoshi)</note></term> for the sheet of strong, thick paper he provides, which is one of the perks of his office.
