# The History of JAPAN. Book IV. #

<margin>Proceedings in Criminal Affairs.</margin>
If a resident of a street is accused of any crime or minor offense, his case is first presented to the **Street Council**. This is an assembly of the street's chief officers, consisting of the <term>Headman<note>original: *Ottona*</note></term>, his three <term>Deputies<note>original: *Kumi Gafijra*</note></term>, and all the <term>Heads of the Corporations<note>original: *Kogomi Oja*</note></term>. If, after examining the case, they find it too difficult to resolve among themselves, or if it is too complex and beyond their authority, they bring it before the common council of the town. If the members of the town council meet the same difficulties, the <term>Yearly Commissioners<note>original: *Nengioſi*</note></term> are requested to consult with some of the Governor’s <term>High Stewards<note>original: *Karoo’s* (Karō)</note></term>. If they deem it necessary, they then communicate the matter to the Governors themselves. This same hierarchy is followed when delivering the Governor's orders to the people. He informs the *Yearly Commissioners*, either in person or through his *High Stewards*. The *Commissioners* pass these orders to the Mayors of the town, who pass them to the *Headmen*. The *Headmen* then publish the orders in their respective streets, either in person or through the <term>Street Messengers<note>original: *Nitzi Joſi’s*</note></term>. Occasionally, the Governor issues his commands through written proclamations; these are regarded by all residents as sacred Laws and inviolable Imperial Orders.

---

<margin>Decision of their Quarrels.</margin>
If a quarrel or dispute breaks out in a street—whether between residents or strangers—the nearest neighbors are required to break up the fight immediately. This is because if anyone is killed, even if they were the aggressor, the survivor must inevitably be put to death. In Japanese law, pleas of <term>self-defense<note>original: *se defendendo*</note></term> or the legal argument of <term>justifiable force for protection<note>original: *moderamen inculpatæ tutelæ*</note></term> do not excuse the act. To avoid the shame of a public execution, the only option for such an unfortunate person is to <term>commit ritual suicide<note>original: "ripping open his belly" (Seppuku)</note></term>. 

Even the death of this person is not considered enough to satisfy the law and atone for the blood of the deceased. The three families living closest to the site of the incident are locked inside their houses for three, four, or even more months. Rough wooden boards are nailed across their doors and windows, after they have been given time to prepare for this imprisonment by gathering necessary food and supplies. The rest of the residents of that street also share in the punishment, being sentenced to several days or months of hard labor on public works, or required to serve the magistrates for a time, which causes great damage to their own businesses. These penalties are imposed in proportion to how much guilt each person carries for failing to do their utmost to prevent the fatal outcome of the quarrel. An even higher penalty is inflicted on the <term>Group Chiefs<note>original: *Kumi Gafijra*</note></term> of the street where the crime occurred. Their guilt is significantly worsened, and the punishment increased, if it is discovered they knew beforehand that the offenders had a "quarrelsome nature" or—as applies in other criminal cases—were prone to the specific crime for which they are being punished. The landlords and masters of the offenders are also held responsible...

<meta>catchword: ...held responsible</meta>

### Chap. III. The History of JAPAN. ###

Those who house or employ lawbreakers share in the punishment for their lodgers’ or servants’ crimes. This harsh Japanese practice seems to be based on the same principle found in the Church Law <term>He who Acts<note>original: *Facientis*</note></term>, section 86: *He who neglects to correct what he can amend, doubtless shares the guilt of the one who commits the fault.* <note>original: *Facientis culpam procul dubio habet, qui quod potest corrigere, negligit emendare.*</note>

Anyone who draws his sword—even if he does not touch or harm his enemy—is sentenced to death if he is accused and the act is fully proven before the magistrate.

If an inhabitant flees from justice, the <term>Head of the Corporation<note>original: *Kumigafira*</note></term> is required to hand him over to the civil magistrate. He must pursue the fugitive himself or hire others to do so until the person is found, under threat of physical punishment. This punishment is decided based on the circumstances and the severity of the fugitive’s crime.

<margin>The Census <note>original: *Fito Aratame*</note></margin>
In the final month of the year, the <term>Street Messenger<note>original: *Nitzio Giosj*</note></term> of every street conducts the <term>Census<note>original: *Fito Aratame*, literally "People Examination"</note></term>. During this, he records the names of every resident in every house—both old and young—along with their date and place of birth, and the <term>Sect<note>original: *Sinu* (Shū)</note></term> or religion of the landlords. It sometimes happens that devout people, especially followers of the <term>Pure Land Sect<note>original: *Siodo* (Jōdo-shū)</note></term>, are not satisfied with the Messenger only recording the landlord's religion, but insist that he record their own as well. Women are also counted in this investigation, and the total number of women is added to the list.

<margin>The act of trampling over the images of our Savior and the Virgin Mary.</margin>
Once the list of every street's inhabitants (male and female, young and old) is completed—usually toward the end of the year—another ceremony, which they consider solemn and important, is performed at the start of the new year. This is the <term>Image-trampling<note>original: *Jesumi* (fumi-e)</note></term>. In the strictest sense, this means "figure-treading," because they trample over an image of our Blessed Savior stretched upon the cross, as well as images of his holy Mother or other Saints. This is done as a convincing and unquestionable proof that they renounce Christ and his religion forever. This grim ceremony begins on the second day of the first month. They start in two different locations simultaneously and move from street to street and house to house, covering four, five, or more streets a day until the entire task is finished, which takes at least six days. The street officials who must be present for this act are the <term>Headman<note>original: *Ottona*</note></term>, his three <term>Deputies<note>original: *Oogumi Oja*</note></term>, the <term>Secretary<note>original: *Fiziu*</note></term>, and the <term>Street Messenger<note>original: *Nitzi Josj*</note></term>, along with two <term>Watchmen<note>original: *Monban*</note></term> who carry the images. The images are about a foot long, cast in brass, and kept in a special box made for this purpose. The ceremony itself is performed in the following order: After the inquisitors have seated themselves on a mat, the landlord, his family, all his servants (male and female, old and young), and whoever else lodges in the

### The History of JAPAN. Book IV. ###

Residents of the same house, and occasionally those from neighboring houses if the first is too small for the ceremony, are gathered into a room where the previously mentioned images are placed on the bare floor. Then, the <term>Secretary of the Inquisition<note>original: *Jefumi Tsio* (E-fumi-chō)</note></term> takes the list of inhabitants and reads their names one by one. Each person is compelled to appear as they are called and walk over the images. Young children who are not yet able to walk are carried in their mothers' arms and held down so that their feet touch the images. Once this is finished, the landlord applies his seal to the list as a certificate for the Governor, proving that the inquisition was performed in his house. After they have proceeded through all the streets and houses of the town in this manner, the inquisitors themselves trample over the images, followed last of all by the <term>Neighborhood Headman<note>original: *Ottona*</note></term>. They serve as witnesses for one another and confirm their own certificates with their seals. This inquisition is performed only in Nagasaki, in the district of Omura, and the province of Bungo—places where the Christian religion had formerly established its strongest presence.

<margin>Procedures in Case of Death.</margin>
When anyone dies, the landlord (or if the landlord himself dies, his family) must request that the <term>Corporation Members<note>original: *Kogomi* (Goningumi), members of the local five-household collective responsibility group</note></term> to which the house belongs act as witnesses to the death. They must certify both that the death was natural and that it was "un-Christian." These witnesses sit with the body and examine it closely to see if there are any external signs of violence or marks of the Christian religion. If they find nothing suspicious, they provide a certificate signed with their hands and seals, which is then presented to the presiding Mayor by the <term>Street Messenger<note>original: *Nitzi Giosi*</note></term>.

Very few taxes are raised from the inhabitants of Nagasaki, and they apply only to those who own land within the town, whether through inheritance or purchase. The rest of the inhabitants, who are not regarded as true citizens or freemen, are exempt from land taxes and other charges, even though they make up the vast majority of the population. The taxes levied on the landowners are as follows:

<margin>Land-Tax.</margin>
The <term>Land Tax<note>original: *Dsisi Gin* (Jishi-gin), a ground-rent paid in silver</note></term> is properly the ground-rent raised in the Emperor’s name during the eighth month. It is collected from all persons who own houses or plots of land within the town. The ground is not measured by its total square area, but only by its length—specifically, the front of the house facing the street. Owners must pay four <term>Maas<note>original: *Maas* (mace), a unit of silver currency</note></term> in the "Outer Town" and six *Maas* in the "Inner Town" for every <term>Kin<note>original: *Kin* (ken), a unit of length roughly equal to six feet or one fathom</note></term> of frontage they possess. It does not matter how far back the houses extend, unless the depth exceeds fifteen *Kin*. <margin>Tax for the August Festival (*Fassaku Gin*)</margin>
<margin>Flower Money (*Fannagin*)</margin>

*Fassaku Gin* <note>original: "Fassaku Money"</note> is another tax laid upon the inhabitants of Nagasaki—if it even deserves that name, as it is more of a voluntary contribution given as a gift to the Governors by all those who possess hereditary lands or houses within the town, or by lower-ranking officers to their superiors. This gift is usually presented on the first day of the eighth month, which is a festival day called *Fassaku* <note>The *Hassaku* festival, marking the first day of the eighth lunar month on the traditional Japanese calendar</note>. It has thus earned the name *Fassaku Gin*, or *Fassaku* silver. 

Those who hold public office and help manage the town provide a specific gift according to their own wishes or wealth, in addition to the general contribution. These gifts go to the town's Governors, the Treasurer and Surveyor of the Imperial Lands and Rents living in Nagasaki, and the Mayors. Even the sons of the <term>Interpreters<note>The professional class of Japanese officials who mediated all communication with the Dutch and Chinese</note></term>—specifically those training in foreign languages in hopes of succeeding their fathers—present the Governors with 25 <term>Maas<note>A unit of currency based on a weight of silver; ten *maas* equal one *tael*.</note></term> and give proportional amounts to the other high-ranking officers mentioned above. 

This contribution money is not collected from the common people until after the festival. It is gathered in every street and then delivered to the Governors. The amount is based on the size of the land where the houses stand, charging for the <term>Kasjo<note>original: *kasho*; a standardized unit of urban land measurement used for tax purposes</note></term> of each house. In the <term>Outer Town<note>original: *Sotomatz* (Sotomachi)</note></term>, they pay 6 *Maas*, and in the <term>Inner Town<note>original: *Utsimatz* (Uchimachi)</note></term>, they pay 9 to 10 *Maas*. This totals 4,350 *Kasjo*, or 2,630 <term>Tails<note>Taels of silver; a larger currency unit worth 10 *maas*.</note></term>, calculating 50 *Kasjo* for each street. 

A *Kasjo* is a square plot as measured during the original division of the land before the streets were built; these measurements are recorded in the town’s official land registry. Over time, several *Kasjo* plots were combined into single large buildings, while others were split into two smaller houses. This specific tax on the *Kasjo* of houses is unique to Nagasaki. To help the residents pay these extra charges more easily, the authorities created the *Fannagin*. 

*Fannagin* <note>literally "flower money"</note> (which I will explain further later) is money that the Governors withhold from the sale price of foreign goods. This money is used for the collective benefit of the inhabitants and is later divided among them proportionally. In all other towns across the Empire—whether they are part of the Emperor's personal lands, crown lands, or the domains of provincial Lords—no tax is levied on residents other than the ground rent mentioned previously. The city of <term>Miaco<note>Kyoto, the historic capital and residence of the spiritual Emperor.</note></term> was granted a special privilege by the <term>Emperor Taiko<note>Toyotomi Hideyoshi (1537–1598), the second "Great Unifier" of Japan.</note></term> exempting it from both, and it remains exempt to this day.

Besides these two taxes, there are other minor expenses that must be paid by those Nagasaki residents who own land within the town. Most of these individuals are em-

This money is employed in honor of the God *Suwa*, who is the patron and protector of the town. For instance, 800 <term>Siumome<note>A unit of silver weight, likely referring to the *momme* (approximately 3.75 grams).</note></term> are allocated for the maintenance of his temple and the staff who attend to it, as well as for comedies to be acted for his diversion in his temple, and lastly for the repairs of the building. The festival day of this Saint is another considerable event, being celebrated with great pomp and solemnity, with processions, dramas, plays, dancing, and all manner of public diversions. But notwithstanding this is done once every year, the inhabitants of the town are not all obliged to contribute yearly toward it; the necessary sums are raised only from ten or eleven streets at a time, so that they pay only once every seven or eight years when their turn falls upon them. This regulation was made to make the payment easy for them. However, that quarter of the town where the public stews <note>The legal red-light district, known as Maruyama.</note> stand is not indulged in this particular, for they must contribute their quota every year. This festival being always celebrated with the utmost pomp and magnificence—with new plays, processions, songs, dances, and so on, all the actors appearing in new dresses and every thing being paid for at a very high price—it is no wonder that expenses run high, so much so that from three to four hundred *Siumome* must be raised from every street.

<margin>Advantages of the Town of Nagasaki arising from the foreign trade.</margin>
The situation of this populous town, upon the extremity of the Province *Fisen* <note>The province of Hizen, covering parts of modern-day Nagasaki and Saga prefectures.</note>, between the sea and high mountains at the end of a secure and convenient harbor, is very advantageous for trade and commerce with such foreigners as are tolerated by this jealous nation. Yet, on the other hand, it is attended with this considerable disadvantage: the produce of the adjacent country is by no means sufficient to maintain the inhabitants, much less to enable them to pay the necessary taxes and contributions. Besides, as the very trade for which the town is so conveniently located puts the inhabitants to a great deal of extra trouble, costs, discontents, and vexations, reason and the nature of things have taught them that maxim of <term>Justinian<note>The 6th-century Roman Emperor known for his codification of law, the *Corpus Juris Civilis*.</note></term>: *It is according to nature that the advantages of any thing should follow the person who also bears the disadvantages* <note>original: "Secundum naturam esse, commoda cujus cunque rei eum sequi, quem sequuntur incommoda"</note>. Therefore, as soon as the supreme direction of the foreign trade was put into the hands of the Governors, proper ways and means were found to make the same advantageous and profitable to their subjects. Indeed, one might wish that they had not gone even further, under the pretext of a maxim just and reasonable in itself, to unjustly defraud foreigners of a reasonable and lawful gain, for—

There is no other reason for this system but to enable the local inhabitants to pay their required taxes and to make it easier for them to support themselves. The money raised this way is called <term>Fanna Gin<note>Original Japanese: *Hana-gin*, literally "Flower Money."</note></term>, which means "Flower Money." This name perhaps comes from their hope that even greater benefits than those already secured will "flower" out of foreign trade, or perhaps because they compare this money to flowers and the merchants' actual profits to the fruit. 

This fund consists of what the Governors of the town and their subordinate officers—through various clever methods—deduct from the price and profit of all foreign goods sold here. To be fair to the Governors, it must be noted that they do not take a personal share of this money. However, their subordinates, the town magistrates, and generally everyone involved with the foreign trading nations, take a portion for themselves as legal fees for the work they perform. 

The remaining money is sent to the <term>Kanna Sa<note>Original Japanese: *Kanazashi*, the street treasury.</note></term>, or the treasury of every street. This final portion is left to the management of the <term>Ottona<note>The headman or chief of a local street or ward.</note></term>, who divides it equally among the residents based on the number of <term>Kafio<note>Original Japanese: *Kaho*, a unit of measurement for a house plot or property frontage used to calculate tax and dividends.</note></term> they own. He always keeps a reserve for necessary repairs to the street, its gates, fountains, and public buildings, and for firefighting equipment. He also uses it for public works ordered by the Town Governors. The *Ottona* accounts for these expenses every year, sending his records to every resident of his street for their review. 

The dividend is distributed by order of the Governors two, three, or four times a year, or more, depending on the number of <term>Camban<note>Original Japanese: *Kanban*, referring to the scheduled public sales or auctions of foreign commodities.</note></term> (trade sales) allowed. If someone chooses not to take a share of this public money, they are also exempt from the common burdens of the street—such as serving in difficult offices, keeping the night watch, and similar duties. Such a person would only be required to pay the imperial ground-rent and the <term>Fassaku Gin<note>Original Japanese: *Hassaku-gin*, a contribution for gifts given on the first day of the eighth month.</note></term>, which is money for a gift to the Governors. Despite this being a significant advantage, I know of very few people—even among the wealthiest inhabitants—who are willing to trade their share of this "Flower Money" for such an exemption.

The account I have given so far may serve as a model for the government established in all other towns, boroughs, and villages throughout the Empire. <margin>Government of the adjacent Country.</margin>
Before the close of this chapter, it will not be improper to add a few words concerning the government of the neighboring villages and adjacent country, which extend some few miles from the town up towards the mountains. This area is in the hands of an Imperial Steward, who in his Master's name gathers the yearly <term>Nengu<note>The annual land tax paid in kind, usually rice.</note></term>, as they call it, or tax of rice, corn, and all the produce of cultivated fields. For such spots of ground as are planted with fruit trees or garden vegetables, a sum of money must be paid each year which, according to a reasonable calculation, would equal the tax itself if the land were turned into rice or corn fields. The tax on rice or corn amounts to somewhat more than half the crop, which the farmer must bring to the <term>Okura<note>A storehouse or granary.</note></term>, or <term>Komegura<note>Specifically a rice granary.</note></term> (Imperial Magazines, which stand near <term>Mangome</term>, or the North suburb) cleaned and ready threshed at his own expense. This is done according to an estimate made by official surveyors who, before the harvest begins, go out to survey the fields and make their calculations accordingly—either by estimation or, if the harvest looks to be very good, by ordering a <term>Tsubo<note>A standard unit of area, roughly 3.3 square meters.</note></term> (or a square spot of ground of a <term>Kin<note>A Japanese fathom or unit of length.</note></term> or fathom) to be cut and threshed, and inferring from that what the whole crop will amount to. Woods and forests pay a small <term>Dsisi Gin<note>Original Japanese: *Jishigin*, or ground rent.</note></term>, or ground-rent, which varies according to the number of *Tsubo* units and the quality and fruitfulness of the soil. 

The revenue of the land around Nagasaki, totaled according to the custom of the country, makes in all 3,000 <term>Koku<note>A unit of volume used to measure rice, roughly 180 liters; it was the standard measure of wealth and land value.</note></term>. In money, this amounts to 15,000 <term>Siumome<note>Likely *silver momme*, a unit of currency by weight.</note></term>—though the price of this commodity varies from year to year—with each *Koku* reckoned at five *Siumome*. The management and inspection of these lands has been for a considerable time hereditary in the illustrious family of **Sije Tsugu Feso** <note>Suetsugu Heizo, a powerful merchant and administrator family in Nagasaki.</note> and his male heirs. They governed in the capacity of <term>Daiquans<note>Original Japanese: *Daikan*, or local deputy governors acting on behalf of the Shogun.</note></term>, or Independent Imperial Commissioners, with a state suitable to the majesty of their master and becoming the dignity of their office. Furthermore, they maintained themselves in such high credit and favor at court that even the Governors of Nagasaki, despite their high rank and authority, showed great regard for them and often consulted them on important affairs relating to the town's government. 

But a fatal incident, which happened in the year 1676, at once put an end to the grandeur of this family and to the dignity of this hereditary employment. Upon the discovery of some swords and other arms hidden in a mat, which were to be sent privately to <term>Corea<note>Korea.</note></term> by the direction of his <term>Fedai<note>A high-ranking steward or personal vassal.</note></term>, or Steward, this unfortunate wretch and his accomplice were condemned to the cross. # CHAP. IV.

## Of the Temples and Clergy of this City

<margin>
Temples and Clergy of Nagasaki.
</margin>
To complete the description of *Nagasaki*, it remains to give an account of its Temples and Clergy. The Clergy is divided into different Sects and Religions. Those of every particular Sect have their Head, General, or Chief, residing at *Miaco* <note>The old name for Kyoto, the imperial capital.</note>, the centre of religion, devotion and holiness, where is kept the court of the Ecclesiastical hereditary Emperor <note>Kaempfer's term for the Tennō, or Emperor, whom he distinguished from the Shogun, the "Secular" Emperor.</note>. Thence they send out their deputies—or as one would call them in the style of Europe, Provincials, Superiors, Abbots and Priors—into every Province for the direction and government of its Clergy, Convents and Temples. At *Nagasaki*, and in the neighbourhood of this Town, although there be several Temples and religious Houses belonging to one Sect, or Religion, as for instance, the *Budsdos* <note>Buddhist</note> Religion, yet they have no particular Head, or Bishop of the Diocese, as one might call him, set over them, but stand under the immediate command of their General at *Miaco*.

<margin>
Suwa, Protector of Nagasaki.
</margin>
Amongst the *Sin* or *Cami* <note>original: *Sin* or *Cami*, meaning the Shinto deities or *Kami*</note>, that is, the national Gods, I must mention in the first place, the <term>Udsigami<note>From *Ujigami*, a guardian deity of a particular place or family.</note></term> of this Town. *Udsigami* is the chief God, Saint and Protector of a Province, City, or Village. The Inhabitants of *Nagasaki* acknowledge, and worship as such, <term>Suwa Dai Miojin<note>The 'Great Bright Deity Suwa.' This refers to the Shinto deity enshrined at the Suwa Shrine, the most important shrine in Nagasaki.</note></term>, that is, the *great holy Idol Suwa*. His Temple stands not far from the Town upon the mountain *Tatta*. A fine staircase of stone of two hundred steps leads up to the <term>Mia<note>From *Miya*, a term for a Shinto shrine.</note></term>, before which he is worshipped, and which is the highest building of his Temple, for *Suwa* having had very lately a more illustrious Title conferred on him by the <term>Dairi<note>The Imperial Court in Kyoto.</note></term>, or the Court of the Ecclesiastical hereditary Emperor, his *Mia* also was to be built higher than it stood before. The Temple-court stands somewhat lower than the *Mia* itself, upon the declivity of the mountain aforesaid. At the entry of the Court, next to the gate, is a long open room, or gallery, where Plays are acted for the diversion both of *Suwa* and his worshippers. This room is curiously adorned with many fine Pictures and carved Images, being the usual presents and gifts, which the adherents of this religion, upon occasion, vow to give to the <term>Sinsja<note>From *Jinja*, meaning a Shinto shrine.</note></term>, or Temples of the national Gods. Further off stand some small Chapels, or Temples, built of wood, clean and neat, but without any other ornaments. In the same Court stand the Temples of *Murasaki Dai Gongen*, that is, the *great and just Murasaki*, and *Symios Dai Miojin* <note>Sumiyoshi Daimyōjin, the great deity of the Sumiyoshi shrines, traditionally protectors of sailors and travelers.</note>, that is, *the great and holy Symios*; each of these two Gods hath also his <term>Mikosi<note>A portable Shinto shrine or divine palanquin used to carry the deity during festivals.</note></term>, or small eight-angular shrine, curiously adorned and hanging in beautiful poles, wherein their images or relics are carried about upon solemn

I also noticed another small, specific chapel, or temple, built in honor of the **God and Lord of a Thousand Legs** <note>This likely refers to a folk shrine where travelers or those with leg ailments offered *waraji* (straw sandals) to a protective deity.</note>, which was hung with many items from his followers—specifically, legs of all sorts and sizes, given by his worshipers to decorate it. There are several festival days sacred to **Suwa**; the most important of these, and one of the great annual holidays, is the ninth day of the ninth month, known by the name ***Kunitz*** <note>original: "Kunitz"; modern: *Kunchi*, the famous autumn festival of Nagasaki.</note>, or ***Kuguatz Kokonoka*** <note>original: "Kuguatz Kokonoka"; Japanese: *Kugatsu Kokonoka*, meaning the ninth day of the ninth month.</note>. 

As this is his birthday, it is celebrated with universal rejoicing throughout the Empire, but more particularly here in Nagasaki, as he is the patron and protector of this place. It is celebrated with great pomp and magnificence, and a solemn ***Matsuri*** <note>original: "Matsuri"; a Shinto festival involving processions and performances.</note>—that is, public spectacles, plays, dramas, processions, and similar events. The solemnity begins as early as the seventh day of the month. On the eighth day, which immediately precedes the holiday itself, the God is entertained at the expense of wealthy and devout people in his temple with a special kind of musical ensemble performed by boys beating on drums and bells. 

This music is the very same used to appease the supreme ***Cami*** <note>original: "Cami"; Kami, the Shinto deities.</note>, or God of the Country, ***Tensio Dai Sin*** <note>original: "Tensio Dai Sin"; *Amaterasu Ōmikami*, the Sun Goddess and ancestral deity of the Imperial line.</note>, when she hid herself in a cavern out of disdain and anger, thereby depriving the world of light and the sun. The 12th day of the ninth month (Suwa’s birth month) is also sacred to him and is celebrated chiefly with public plays and spectacles. 

The persons attending the service of Suwa’s temples are called ***Nege*** <note>original: "Nege"; *Negi*, a rank of Shinto priest.</note>, though they are sometimes—incorrectly—called ***Kuge***; this title belongs only to the holy court of the Ecclesiastical Hereditary Emperor <note>The *Kuge* were the high-ranking court nobility in Kyoto who served the Emperor.</note>. They are like all other ***Sinsio*** <note>original: "Sinsio"; *Shinshō*, a general term for Shinto shrine officials.</note>, or ministers of the temples of the ***Sin*** <note>original: "Sin"; Shinto, the "Way of the Gods."</note>—the national gods of the country. They are not monks, but secular, married persons; however, because of their honorable employment, they claim for themselves a much higher degree of holiness and respect than they believe the common mass of laypeople deserve. They live with their families in houses built for them on the slope of the mountain mentioned earlier, not far from the temple courtyard. 

Their way of life, as well as their everyday clothing at home and abroad, is no different from that of other inhabitants, except that they do not shave their heads. Instead, they let their hair grow and tie it together behind their heads. When they go to the temple, they dress in priestly robes with various head-dresses according to each person's office and rank. They support themselves through the alms and offerings given to them by the inhabitants during their appearance in the solemn procession of the ***Matsuri*** (which I will describe later) and at other times when people come to worship at the temple. Wealthy people give them specific presents the day before the great festival of Suwa—the eighth day of the ninth month—to pay for an extraordinary musical performance for the idol’s diversion. From each district of the town, officials are chosen for this employment, for which they receive a salary from the public treasury. They are assisted by two other members of their company, who attend them by turns for one year each, though these assistants are not paid. Their business is to keep the temple and its buildings in repair, to oversee the maintenance of the *Negi* <note>original: "Nege"; a rank of Shinto priest responsible for shrine rituals.</note>, and to ensure that the *Matsuri* <note>original: "Matfuri"; Shinto festivals involving processions and performances.</note>, plays, and other public entertainments in honor of this Idol are performed with the pomp and magnificence thought becoming of his greatness. 

The processions of this Secular Clergy <note>This refers to Shinto priests who, unlike Buddhist monks, were often integrated into civic life and sometimes allowed to marry.</note>—for such they are in fact—made in honor of this great Protector of Nagasaki, are performed with the following pomp and order:

1.  **Two Led-horses**, half-starved and every bit as lean as the horse that the Patriarch of Moscow <note>A reference to the Russian Orthodox tradition where the Patriarch rode a horse (representing a donkey) through Moscow on Palm Sunday.</note> mounts on Palm Sundays when he rides to his Cathedral.
2.  **Several Ecclesiastical Ensigns** and badges of honor, such as were used by their ancestors and remain in use to this day at the Ecclesiastical Court at Kyoto <note>original: "Miaco"; the traditional capital where the Emperor resided.</note>. These include, for instance, a short broad lance gilded all over; a pair of shoes remarkable for their great size and coarse workmanship; and a large bunch of white paper <note>This is a *gohei*, a ritual wand decorated with folded paper streamers used in Shinto ceremonies.</note> tied to the end of a short staff as a badge of ecclesiastical authority.
3.  **Hollow benches** on which to place the *Mikoshi* <note>original: "Mikofi"; portable shrines used to carry the essence of a deity during a festival.</note>. These are carried about inverted so that the people may throw in their charity; for this purpose, two laborers are also hired to carry a large, sturdy alms-chest.
4.  **The *Mikoshi* themselves**, which are eight-sided shrines, almost too large to be carried by one man. They are lacquered and expertly adorned with gilded cornices and finely polished metal mirrors; among other ornaments, a gilded crane sits at the top.
5.  **Two small wooden chairs**, or palanquins, somewhat different in shape from a *Norimono* <note>original: "Norimon"; a high-status sedan chair.</note>, and similar to those used at the court of the Ecclesiastical Hereditary Emperor <note>The Mikado, or Emperor of Japan.</note>. In these are carried the two Superiors of the temple.
6.  **Two other Led-horses** with their full gear, belonging to the said superiors, and just as lean and handsome as the two at the head of the procession.
7.  **The clergy in a body**, walking on foot in good order and with great decency.
8.  **The inhabitants and common people of Nagasaki**, closing the cavalcade in their usual confusion.

After the clergy have arrived at the temple court along with the *Mikoshi*, shrines, and other ornaments, and have taken their assigned places, the deputies of the Governors make their appearance with their usual retinue. Additionally, because of the solemnity of the day, they carry twenty long pikes of state. To the ends of these are tied bunches of wood shavings, lacquered and painted to represent the feathers of an Indian Cock <note>Likely referring to a peacock or a colorful pheasant, commonly used to decorate ceremonial pikes.</note>. Four of the chief officials, having first washed their hands in the basin standing before the temple, walk toward it. With the humility that becomes the holiness of the place, they pay—in their masters' names and their own—the usual compliments to the two Superiors of the temple, who, to decently receive the same,

Once this is done, one of the *negi* <note>original: "Nege"; a rank of Shinto priest responsible for rituals.</note> fills a large golden spoon with a certain sweet liquor called *amazake* <note>original: "Amasaki"; a traditional sweet, low-alcohol drink made from fermented rice.</note> and pours it into a small, unglazed earthen dish as a way to commemorate the poverty of their ancestors. He then presents this to the deputies of the Governors. *Amazake* is a particular sort of beer brewed from boiled rice by letting it ferment overnight. They usually brew it before their major holidays to drink on those occasions, thereby commemorating the frugal lifestyle of their ancestors, who knew of no other brewing method but this easy, simple one. 

Upon the first of the holidays sacred to *Suwa* <note>The Suwa Shrine is the main Shinto shrine in Nagasaki, famous for the "Kunchi" festival.</note>, the two aforementioned bodies—that is, the clergy and the deputies of the Governors—do not make their appearance until the ritual act of the day is almost over. However, upon the third and great holiday, which is the Idol’s birthday and one of the great yearly festivals, they appear early in the morning to assist at the ensuing *matsuri* <note>original: "Matsuri"; a Shinto festival.</note>. *Matsuri* signifies, properly speaking and in a general sense, an offering made to a *kami* <note>original: "Cami"; the spirits or deities of the Shinto faith.</note>. In the sense it must be taken here, to fulfill the purpose of such a great holiday, it denotes a solemn jubilee to be celebrated with unusual rejoicings, processions, dancing, plays, and other public spectacles, held in honor and for the diversion of that God or Idol who is acknowledged and worshiped as the *ujigami* <note>original: "Udsigami"; a tutelary or guardian deity of a specific community.</note>, or protector of a place, upon his birthday.

The *matsuri* being one of the most magnificent solemnities that can be seen in this or any other town, I flatter myself that the reader will not be displeased to find a more detailed description of one which I saw myself at Nagasaki, and which may serve as a pattern for others as they are celebrated elsewhere.

<margin>Detailed description of a *matsuri*.</margin>
The *matsuri*, as I noted above, is celebrated at Nagasaki in honor of *Suwa* on the ninth day of the ninth month, that being *Suwa*’s birthday. It does not consist of preaching, worshiping, or going to the temples, but of specific processions through the principal streets of the town and elegant public spectacles performed upon a large marketplace built for this purpose. Because of the visits this place receives on this day from the idols of *Suwa* and his companion, who are carried there in procession, it is called *O-tabisho* <note>original: "Oo Tabi Tokora"; literally "the place of the great journey," referring to the temporary resting place of the deity's shrine during a festival.</note>. 

On this site, for the solemnity of the day, a temple of bamboo is built with wings on each side; the front is left open toward the square, and the roof is covered with straw, ending in a gable made of *sugi* <note>original: "Tsugi"; Japanese cedar branches.</note> branches. This entire building hardly deserves to be compared even to one of our barns, it is so humble and simple; for it must be built this way on purpose to match the meager architecture of their poor ancestors. A tall fir tree stands on each side of the front of this temple. Three sides of the square are built around with benches and lodges for the convenience of the spectators.

### The History of JAPAN. Book IV.

With everything prepared, the Shinto <note>original: "Sintos"</note> clergy appear as a group, accompanied by a magnificent retinue. They carry the *mikoshi* <note>original: "Mikosi"; portable shrines used to transport the spirit of a deity during festivals.</note> of their great deity Suwa in a formal procession, along with that of Sumiyoshi <note>original: "Symios"; a Shinto deity associated with the sea and protection.</note> to keep him company. Murasaki <note>A third deity associated with the shrine; the author notes he is left behind because he was not known for traveling.</note> is left at home because there is no instance in the history of his life and actions from which it could be inferred that he delighted in walking and traveling. Upon this occasion, the Shinto clergy style themselves *Otomo* <note>original: "Ootomi"</note>, which means the "great retinue." Despite this pompous title, one of the principal items they carry in the procession is an alms chest. This serves a very good purpose, for the crowds of superstitious spectators throw such a multitude of offerings at them that it is as if they intended to stone them out of mere charity. When they reach the aforementioned place, the ecclesiastics seat themselves in good order according to their rank upon three benches built for them in front of the temple. This rank is clearly shown by their dress. The two superiors of the temple occupy the highest bench, dressed in black with a unique head ornament and a short staff as a badge of their authority. Four others, next in rank, sit upon the second bench, dressed in white ecclesiastical gowns with black lacquered caps, slightly different from those worn by their superiors. The main body of the clergy takes possession of the third and lowest bench, sitting together and all clad in white gowns with black lacquered caps, somewhat resembling those worn by the Jesuits. The servants and porters appointed to carry the holy utensils of the temple, along with others involved in the solemnity, stand next to the ecclesiastics with their heads uncovered.

On the other side of the square, opposite the ecclesiastics, the deputies of the governors sit under a tent upon fine mats raised somewhat from the ground. For the sake of magnificence and out of respect for this holy act, they have twenty ceremonial pikes planted in the ground before them. They order the crowding spectators to be kept back with staffs and take care that no accidents happen and that no disorder is committed by the mob. For this purpose, some of the *yoriki* <note>original: "Foriki's"; low-ranking samurai officials who served as assistants to the governors and performed police duties.</note> are constantly going to and fro between the site and the Governor's Court to report what is happening and to inquire what commands the governors have for their deputies.

<margin>Plays and Spectacles.</margin>
The public spectacles shown on this occasion are a sort of play, or rather dramas, acted by eight, twelve, or more persons. The subject matter is taken from the history of their gods and heroes. Their remarkable adventures, heroic actions, and sometimes their romantic intrigues are put into verse and sung by dancing-actors, while others play upon all sorts of musical instruments. If the subject is thought to be too grave or moving, a comical actor will occasionally jump out unexpectedly upon the stage, using gestures and merry discourse in prose to divert the people. # Chapter IV. *The History of* JAPAN.

The performances consist only of ballets, or dances, like those of the **Mimic Actors** <note>In ancient Rome, mimic actors performed silent, gestural dramas; here Kaempfer compares Japanese theater—likely *Noh* or early *Kabuki* styles—to this classical tradition.</note> upon the *Roman Stage*. For the dancers do not speak, but endeavor to express the contents of the story they are about to represent as naturally as possible, both by their dress and by their gestures and actions, which are regulated according to the sound of musical instruments. The chief subjects of the play—such as fountains, bridges, gates, houses, gardens, trees, mountains, animals, and the like—are likewise represented. Some are as large as life, and all are generally constructed so that they may be removed at command and taken to pieces, much like the scenes in our *European Plays*.

The actors are commonly young girls, taken out of the **bawdy-houses** <note>A term for brothels; in this period, many performers were courtesans or entertainers associated with the pleasure districts.</note>, as well as young boys and children from the very streets at whose expense the solemnity is performed. They are all magnificently clad in various colored silken gowns suitable to the characters which they are to represent. It must be owned, in justice to them, that generally speaking, they act their parts with such assurance and becoming dexterity that they are not to be exceeded—indeed, they are scarcely to be paralleled—by the best *European Actors*. 

The streets which bear the expense of the solemnity make their appearance in the following order: First of all is carried a rich canopy, or else an umbrella <note>original: "umbrello"</note> made of silk, which serves as the **palladium** <note>A term for a sacred object or safeguard that protects a city or group.</note> of the street. Over it, in the middle, is placed a shield upon which is written in large characters the name of the street. Next to the canopy follow the musicians, masked and wearing proper uniforms. The music is both vocal and instrumental. The instruments are chiefly flutes of different sorts and small drums; now and then a large drum, cymbals, and bells are brought in among the rest. 

This instrumental music is so poor and lamentable that it seems much easier to satisfy their Gods than to please a musical ear. Nor is the vocal part much preferable to the instrumental; for although they keep to the time tolerably well and sing according to specific notes, they do it in such a very slow manner that the music seems rather calculated to regulate their actions and the motions of their bodies in their ballets and dances. In these, I must admit, they are very ingenious and dexterous, and little inferior to our *European dancers*, except only that they seem to lack a little more action and swiftness in their feet. 

But to return to the procession: The musicians are followed by the necessary machines and the whole apparatus for the ensuing representations. The largest pieces are carried by laboring people; the lesser items—such as benches, staffs, flowers, and the like—are carried by the children of the inhabitants, who are neatly clad. Next follow the actors themselves, and after them all the inhabitants of the street in a body, wearing their "holiday" clothes (that is, their finest garments) and their formal ceremonial robes. To make the appearance even grander, the procession is closed by a considerable number

The dances and shows of a street commonly last about three quarters of an hour, and once over, the company marches off in the same order they appeared in, to make way for the appearance and shows of another street, which is again followed by another, and so on. All the streets strive to outdo one another in magnificent retinues and surprising scenes. The processions and shows begin early in the morning, and the whole event ends about noon. The shows and scenes are nearly the same on the seventh day of this month as they are on the ninth—which is *Suwa’s* <note>Suwa-no-Kami is the patron deity of Nagasaki; this festival, the Nagasaki Kunchi, is still held today at the Suwa Shrine.</note> birth-day—with some small difference in the dresses of the actors and their dances, as also in the order and march of the processions, as they return on one day the same way they came in on the other. 

When everything is over, the two Superiors of the clergy, having now discharged the duties of their office, leave their benches and walk towards the tent where the deputies of the governors sat. They return thanks to the deputies for their gracious presence at this holy act, performing this with nearly the same marks of deference and submission which the representatives showed to them in the morning. The spectacles, machines, songs, and dances must be new every year; it would be thought beneath the dignity and majesty of that great God if, when repeating the same story on occasion, they did not at least dress it up in a new fashion.

For the reader’s further satisfaction, I have not hesitated to insert a more ample and particular description of the several representations, scenes, machines, and so on, of a recent *Matsuri* <term>Matsuri: A Japanese festival or holiday, often involving Shinto rituals and local processions.</term>, which was performed during my stay in *Japan*, and at which I was present myself.

<margin>Scenes of a *Matsuri* at *Nagasaki*.</margin>

1. **Scene.** Eight young girls, clad in colored gowns interwoven with large white flowers, wearing broad hats as if to defend them from the heat of the sun, with fans and flowers in their hands, dancing by turns. They were from time to time relieved by a couple of old women dancing in a different dress.

2. **Scene.** A garden with fine flowers appearing on each side of the performance area, with a thatched house in the middle. Out of this house jumped eight young girls, dressed in white and red, dancing with fans, canes, and flower-baskets. They were relieved by a very good actress, who danced by herself.

3. **Scene.** Eight triumphal chariots <note>original: "triumphal chariots"; these are likely *dashi* or *kasaboko*, the massive, ornate floats pulled through the streets during Japanese festivals.</note>, with oxen of different colors before them—the whole very naturally represented and drawn by well-clad young boys. Upon these chariots stood a *Tsubaki* <gloss>Camellia</gloss> tree in flower; a mountain covered with trees; a forest of bamboos with a tiger lurking; a load of straw with an entire tree, including its roots and branches; and a whale under a rock, half-covered with water. Last of all, another mountain appeared with a live young boy, magnificently clad, who stood at the top under an apricot tree <note>original: "Apricock-tree"</note> in full blossom. This mountain was also drawn by boys.

Then two giants masked, with prodigious large heads, representing some <term>Fotoge</term><note>The author is transliterating *Hotoke*, a Japanese term for a Buddha or an enlightened being; early European visitors often categorized these broadly as "Indian Deities."</note>, or Indian Deities, began a dance. He was followed by seven Chinese jumping out of the same mountain, though to all appearance never so small, and dancing about in company with the giants. After some time spent in dancing, the great monstrous giant beat the cask to pieces, out of which came a young boy very handsomely clad, who after a fine long speech, which he delivered in a very graceful manner, danced with the giant alone. Meanwhile three monkeys as big as life, with roe's heads <note>The heads of roe deer.</note>, crept out of the fountain, and jumping upon the walk round it, performed a dance, mimicking that of the giant and boy. This done, every one retired to his place, and so this scene ended.

11. *Scene.* A handsome, well-shaped young acrobat <note>original: "jumper"</note>, before whom was placed a table, a sort of scaffold or stage, with eight steps leading up on one side and as many going down on the other. A hollow bamboo was laid across the scaffold, along with a door featuring a round hole at the upper end, which was no more than two and a half spans <note>A span is approximately 9 inches; the hole was roughly 22 inches in diameter.</note> in diameter. This fellow performed several very surprising tricks, some of which—and in my opinion not the least of them—were as follows: He lay down flat upon the table, either upon his belly or back, and jumped onto his legs with surprising dexterity in a moment. He walked upon stilts up one staircase of the scaffold, then over the hollow bamboo, and, changing the stilts, proceeded down the other staircase. He jumped from a distance of about three fathoms <note>About 18 feet.</note> through the hole in the door mentioned above, despite its smallness and the large size of the hat he was then wearing, which was considerably broader than the diameter of the hole.

12. *Scene.* Several huge floats <note>original: "machines"</note>, accurately resembling both in size and color the things they were meant to represent, but made of a thin substance so that one man could easily carry one upon his back. But besides this load on the back, every one of these men had a very large drum hanging before him, which others played upon with bells. In this manner they crossed the stage dancing, though they did not jump very high because of their load. Although the objects were made only of very light and thin material, they were nevertheless so heavy that the men were obliged to rest on stools placed for them before they entered the square, just as they had done in several other places during their procession through the streets.

The objects which they carried across the stage were:
*   A well, with all the equipment for extinguishing fires.
*   A large church bell with its supporting timber-work, featuring a dragon wound around it for ornament.
*   A mountain covered with snow, shaped like the head of a dragon, with an eagle sitting at the top.
*   A brass gun <note>A cannon.</note>, weighing twenty-four pounds, with all the tackle belonging to it.
*   A heavy load of travelers' trunks packed into twelve straw bales <note>original: "straw balls"; these are *tawara*, traditional Japanese straw containers.</note>, according to the country’s fashion.
*   A whale in a dish.
*   Several shellfish and fruits, as large as life, each carried by one person.

...national Gods, which are worshiped by the followers of the Shinto <note>original: "Sintos"; the indigenous spiritual tradition of Japan</note> religion, as established in the country since ancient times. Among several, there is one temple built to the Great Sun Goddess <note>original: "Tensio Dai Sin"; Amaterasu Omikami</note>, and another to her brother, the Heavenly Deity <note>original: "Ten Sin"; likely referring to Susanoo-no-Mikoto or the deified scholar Tenjin</note>. There are likewise some Chapels, hardly deserving to be called Temples, erected to other Idols of less note. These are not served by the <term>Negi</term> <note>original: "Nege"; secular Shinto priests</note> of the <term>Kami</term> <note>original: "Cami"; divine spirits or gods</note> Temples, but either by the <term>Yamabushi</term> <note>original: "Jammabos"</note>, that is, *Mountain-Soldiers*—a type of hermit who may marry if they wish, and who, in their religion and worship, largely conform to the foreign Buddhist <note>original: "Budsdo"</note> doctrine—or by the <term>Tendai</term>, otherwise called <term>Shingon</term> <note>original: "Singon"</note>, another sort of Priests. These priests similarly endeavor to reconcile the foreign Buddhist worship with the national religion as anciently established in the country. These last may be looked upon as followers of the Sect of <term>Laozi</term> <note>original: "Lanzu"; the founder of Taoism</note>, as the Chinese call it, or according to the Japanese, <term>Rōshi</term> <note>original: "Noosi"</note>. This philosophy began in *China* during the time of the great Philosopher <term>Confucius</term> <note>original: "Koosi"; called *Confutius* by Europeans</note>, and was afterwards received in *Japan*, being compatible with both of these two religions. The Shogun <term>Tokugawa Ieyasu</term> <note>original: "Gongen"; the posthumous divine title of the first Tokugawa Shogun</note> adhered to this sect; for this reason there is at the <term>Anzen-ji Temple</term> <note>original: "Anfensu"; likely Anzen-ji, a temple in Nagasaki</note>, one of the *Tendai* Temples, a Spirit Tablet <note>original: "Isai"; an ancestral tablet known as an *ihai*</note> erected to his memory, before which the Priests say their prayers every day for the happiness and welfare of his soul.

<margin>The <term>Negi</term> <note>secular Shinto priests</note>, and who governs them.</margin>
All the *Negi*, that is, the secular Priests of the Shinto shrines <note>original: "Mia"</note> or *Kami* Temples, recognize the Imperial Court <note>original: "Dairi"</note>—that is, the court of the <term>Mikado</term>, the Ecclesiastical Hereditary Emperor—as their superiors. Accordingly, by order and authority of this Ecclesiastical Court, <term>Lord Yoshida</term> <note>original: "Fosijda Donno"; referring to the Yoshida family, who held hereditary authority over Shinto affairs</note>, a man of the highest quality at that court, has been appointed Superior or General of all the *Negi* clergy. He was consecrated as such by the *Mikado* himself, who at the same time invested him with the power to confer greater honors and titles, not only upon the *Negi*, but likewise upon their Idols and upon the souls of deceased great men, though this was never done without the *Mikado’s* consent and approval.

The *Yamabushi* have a Head or General of their own, who resides at Kyoto <note>original: "Miaco"</note>. (See Book III. Chap. VI.)

<margin>The Buddhist <note>original: "Budsdo"</note> Temples.</margin>
So much for the Shinto <note>original: "Sintos"</note> Temples. I proceed now to the Buddhist <note>original: "Budsdo" or "Bupo"; the "Way of the Buddha"</note> worship—the foreign religion that was originally brought over from *India* into *Japan*. Many stately convents and temples have been built at *Nagasaki* by the four chief sects of this religion; a few of these lie within the Town, but by far the greatest part lie outside it, on the slopes of the neighboring hills and mountains. They have beautiful stone staircases leading up to them, and several small chapels or temples built within the same courtyard. These are not so much to be commended for their size or splendor as for their pleasant and agreeable locations; they are, moreover, adorned within with fine raised altars, gilded Images as large as life, lacquered columns, gates, and pillars... <note>The text ends here, continued by the catchword "lars"</note>

...pillars, the whole very neat and pretty, rather than magnificent. All these <term>Buddhist</term> <note>original: "Budsdo"</note> Temples are attended by Priests of the same religion, and every particular Temple by Priests of that very Sect to which it belongs. All the temples belonging to the same sect are distinguished into <term>Hon-ji</term> <note>original: "Tonsi"; the "head" or "main" temple</note>, and <term>末寺 Matsuji</term> <note>original: "Matsusi"; literally "branch temples"</note>, which signifies filial or dependent temples, or convents, because they are dependent on the former and stand under the direction of the same Superiors.

<margin>Kōtaiji <note>original: "Kataisi"</note></margin>
**Kōtaiji** is the chief convent and temple of the <term>Zen</term> <note>original: "Sensju" or "Senzhu"</note> Sect, which is of the order (or rather Schism) of the **Sōtō** <note>original: "Sotosa" or "Sotosju"</note> school. At the side of this temple, within its court, stands another temple or chapel, which is open on all sides, with the Image of **Shaka** <note>original: "Siaka"; Shakyamuni, the historical Buddha</note>, the founder of this religion, gilded, of an extraordinary size, and sitting on a gilded **Lotus-Flower** <note>original: "Tarate-Flower"; known in Latin as *Faba Ægyptiaca* or the Egyptian bean</note>. Several *Matsuji*, or inferior temples, are dependent on this, wherein are maintained very many Ecclesiastical Persons, or Monks, both old and young.

<margin>Shuntokuji <note>original: "Siuntokusi"</note></margin>
**Shuntokuji** is another of the chief temples of the **Zen** Sect, specifically of the **Rinzai** <note>original: "Rinsaisa"</note> order. The Superior likewise has several branch temples under his direction, wherein are maintained as many Monks as in those mentioned above.

<margin>Zenryūji <note>original: "Senriusi"</note></margin>
**Zenryūji** is another temple of this last mentioned order. The Superior of this has no branch temples under him, though otherwise he stands, as well as the two Superiors of the temples aforesaid, under the sole and immediate dependence of their General at **Kyoto** <note>original: "Miaco"; the imperial capital</note>.

These **Zen** Temples are frequented by most of the inhabitants of this town. The Ecclesiastics thereof travel much, and are often changed and sent to other convents, which makes their number very uncertain, though there are seldom less than 300.

<margin>Daionji <note>original: "Daiwonsi"</note></margin>
**Daionji** is the chief temple of the **Jōdo** <note>original: "Siodosju"; the Pure Land sect</note> sect. Several branch temples stand under the direction of its Superior. In all the temples of this sect there are tables, or monuments, erected to the memory of the deceased Emperors of the now reigning family <note>The Tokugawa Shogunate</note>, who professed themselves of it. The Monks say their prayers daily before these memorial monuments for the souls of the deceased Emperors, and upon certain days one of their number offers some eatables. The number of Ecclesiastics attending the temples of this sect is nearly the same as the former.

<margin>Hōrinji <note>original: "Forinsi"</note></margin>
**Hōrinji** is the chief temple of the **Hokke** <note>original: "Fokke Siu"; the Nichiren sect</note> sect. **Chōshōji** <note>original: "Tsosiosi"</note> and some few other branch temples stand under the direction of its Superior. The Ecclesiastics are not nearly so numerous as in the two former Sects, there being but few people who adhere to it.

<margin>Daikōji <note>original: "Daikoosi"</note></margin>
**Daikōji** is the chief temple of the sect and order of **Omote no Ikkō-shū** <note>original: "Omotteno Ikosju"</note>, that is, of the "furthermost" **Ikkō** sect, so called from the residence of its General at **Kyoto**.

<margin>**Kōyen-ji** <note>original: "Koojenfi"</note>:</margin>
***Kōyen-ji*** is the chief temple of the second order of the said **Ikkō Sect** <note>original: "Iko Sect"; a major branch of Japanese Pure Land Buddhism</note>, called ***Ura-no-Ikkō-shū*** <note>original: "Aurano Ikosju"</note>, that is, the hindmost **Ikkō Sect**, which is again so called from the place of residence of their general, and the situation thereof with regard to the former.

<margin>**Ikkō** Monks.</margin>
The Monks of these two orders of the **Ikkō Sect** are permitted to marry, though there are but few that take this liberty, and those only the chief among them. Those who are married, have leave to educate their male issue in the convent, for which reason the number of young Ecclesiastics is sometimes so increased, that the revenues of the convent will scarce suffice to maintain them. Under these circumstances those, who are not married, either retire to live in the **Ikkō** Convents of other provinces, or else, under pretext of conversion, go over to other sects, in order to be admitted, if possible, into their monasteries. The Superiors of the two **Ikkō** Temples mentioned above, have no <term>**Matsuji**</term> <note>original: "Matsusi"; branch or dependent temples</note> under them, nor are there more than twenty full grown Monks, with the families of some in each convent. Their temples are most frequented by the common, and almost all the country people, because they affect a great devotion and simplicity in their conversation, preaching and writings, the latter of which are published in the vulgar characters, called <term>**Kana**</term> <note>original: "Kanno"; the phonetic Japanese script accessible to those not trained in complex Chinese characters</note>, on purpose to make them understood by the common people.

<margin>**Kanshin-ji** <note>original: "Quansiensi"</note></margin>
There is besides another small temple, or chapel, belonging to this same **Ikkō Sect**, called ***Kanshin-ji***, whose <term>**Danna**</term> <note>original: "Danna"; parishioners or patrons who support a temple</note>, that is, the persons who go to worship there, contributed of late, some ten, others an hundred <term>**Momme**</term> <note>original: "Siumome"; a unit of silver weight</note> for rebuilding and enlarging the same. For this purpose they sent last year the <term>**Oshō**</term> <note>original: "Osje"; a high-ranking Buddhist priest or abbot</note>, or Superior of the temple, with the collected money to <term>**Kyoto**</term> <note>original: "Miaco"; the historical capital of Japan</note>, to offer it to the disposal of their general. But he, instead of going to **Kyoto**, stayed at **Osaka** <note>original: "Ofacca"</note>, where it is said, he spent almost all the money. He left his wife and children at **Nagasaki** <note>original: "Nagafaki"</note>. The **Danna** having heard no news of him for some time, resolved in the mean time, that in case he did not return quickly, they would drop this undertaking, and incorporate themselves amongst the **Danna**, or parishioners of another **Ikkō** Church, or Temple.

The Ecclesiastics of all the above-mentioned sects of the <term>**Buddhist**</term> <note>original: "Budsdo"</note> Religion have no processions, nor other public spectacles like the <term>**Shinto**</term> <note>original: "Sintos"</note> Clergy. They always keep within the district of their convent, where besides a due care for their support and maintenance, they mind little else but their prayers in the temple at certain stated hours. Their maintenance arises from what fees are given them for prayers to be said in their temples for the relief of departed souls, as also from the voluntary and charitable contributions of their **Danna**, or parishioners. It appears, by what hath been said above, that every convent stands under the direction of a Prior, or Superior, whom they call <term>**Junji**</term> <note>original: "Dsjunfi"</note>, or **Oshō**, and to whom all the Monks of the convent

### The History of **JAPAN**. Book IV.

The monks of the convent are obliged to pay due respect and obedience to their leaders. The Superiors themselves stand under the command of the General, or <term>**Oshō**</term> <note>original: "Osjo"; a high-ranking Buddhist priest</note> in chief of their sect, who resides at **Kyoto** <note>original: "Miaco"</note>. The Superiors of the **Ikkō-shū** <note>original: "Ikosju"</note> convents, belonging to both orders of this sect, are called <term>**Shōnin**</term> <note>original: "Sioonin"; a title for a high-ranking priest or "holy man"</note>. The generals of this order, who reside at **Kyoto**, assume the pompous title of <term>**Monzeki**</term> <note>original: "Monseki"</note>, or ***Gomonzeki***, which in the literal sense signifies "the place of the sublime gate abandoned." This is because they were of the family and blood of the **Mikado** <note>The Emperor of Japan</note>, which they left to join this sect and embrace this high dignity. On this account, they still consider themselves to be nearest in rank to the court of the **Mikado**—by which is understood the Ecclesiastical Hereditary Emperor. The word **Mikado**, taken in a literal sense, signifies "the sublime gate." <note>Kaempfer compares the Japanese term for the Emperor's court to the "Sublime Porte" of the Ottoman Empire.</note>

<margin>Temples of the Chinese.</margin>
There are three temples at **Nagasaki** which belong to the Chinese. They are all equally remarkable for their handsome structure and the number of monks maintained within them. They belong properly to the **Zen** sect <note>original: "Sect Sen"</note>, though they are adorned inside with life-sized idols and images of several Chinese Emperors and Saints. Fine triumphal arches and many more strange ornaments are to be seen in the temple courts. The Chinese, and those from neighboring nations who trade with **Japan** under the same name despite speaking different languages, founded these temples after the total eradication of the Christian religion. They did this for the free exercise of their worship and the reception of their ship-idols. As soon as their ships enter the harbor of **Nagasaki**, these idols <note>Likely images of Mazu, the Taoist goddess of the sea, often enshrined by Chinese sailors</note> are carried ashore and placed into certain chapels built for them near the great temple. This is done with uncommon respect and particular ceremonies, involving the playing of cymbals and the beating of drums. These same ceremonies are repeated when the idols are carried back on board their **junks** <note>original: "yonks"</note> upon departure. These convents and temples bear the names of the country or province of their founders, along with another epithet borrowed from their wealth. They are:

<margin>**Nankin-dera** <note>original: "Nankindira"</note>.</margin>
1. ***Nankin-dera***, that is, the temple of the city of **Nanjing** and the neighboring country. It is the first temple built in **Japan** by foreigners, specifically by the people of **Nanjing** and their neighbors who speak the same language. They have also given it the name ***Kōfuku-ji*** <note>original: "Koofukusi"</note>, which means "the temple of settled riches."

<margin>**Shōshū-dera** <note>original: "Tsiaksjudira"</note>.</margin>
2. ***Shōshū-dera*** <note>original: "Tsiaksjudira" or "Tsiansjudira"</note>, that is, the temple of the country of **Amoy** <note>original: "Aimos"; modern Xiamen</note>, by which must be understood the southern provinces of the Empire of **China**. The Chinese who inhabit the island of **Taiwan** <note>original: "Formosa"</note> and are settled in other countries distant from **China** also belong to this temple. There is a <term>**Matsuji**</term> <note>original: "Matsusi"; a branch or dependent temple</note> under the direction of its Superior. It is one of the largest temples and is well-stocked with monks. Its other name is ***Fukusai-ji*** <note>original: "Fukusi"</note>, that is, the temple of riches.

### Chapter IV. The History of **JAPAN**.

<margin>**Hokushū-ji** <note>original: "Foksiudira"; likely referring to the Fukusai-ji, a major Chinese Zen temple in Nagasaki</note></margin>
3. **Hokushū-ji**, which means the "Temple of the Northern Countries," was founded and is frequented by those **Chinese** who come from the northern parts of **China**. Its other name is **Fukusai-ji** <note>original: "Fuku Saisi"</note>, which means the "Temple of Riches and Offerings."

<margin>Maintenance of the Monks.</margin>
These convents were formerly attended by **Chinese** priests only and were maintained at the sole expense of that nation. However, since the closing of the Empire and the new, strict regulations regarding foreign trade, they now permit only two Chinese-born monks to live in each of them. Their maintenance, as well as that of other temples belonging to this foreign <term>**Buddhist**</term> <note>original: "Budsdo"</note> worship, is provided by the voluntary charitable contributions of their countrymen, as well as from fees given to them for prayers and offerings made for the relief of departed souls. If the money gained by these means is not sufficient to maintain them, a supply is expected from the Imperial bounty. The Superiors of these three convents are under the immediate authority of a particular General of their own, who resides near **Kyoto** <note>original: "Miaco"</note> on Mount **Ōbaku** <note>The headquarters of the Ōbaku school of Zen</note>. He claims to be the third successor to the high religious seat of **Ingen**, and is consequently the head of all the clergy of this foreign religion. To better understand this, it will be necessary to insert the history of this **Ingen**.

<margin>History of **Ingen**.</margin>
**Ingen** <note>Ingen Ryūki (1592–1673), a Chinese Zen master</note> was a native of **China**, where he succeeded to the holy seat of <term>**Bodhidharma**</term> <note>original: "Darma"; the semi-legendary founder of Zen Buddhism</note>, the first Chinese "Pope" <note>Kaempfer uses Western ecclesiastical terms like "Pope" and "Archiepiscopal" to explain Buddhist hierarchies to his readers</note>, and was himself the twenty-eighth successor of <term>**Shakyamuni**</term> <note>original: "Siaka"; the historical Buddha</note>, who was the founder and is still acknowledged as the protector of this religion. 

The love for his countrymen—who lived in the three convents mentioned above without a settled leader—and a strong zeal and desire to propagate the <term>**Buddha-dharma**</term> <note>original: "Bupo"; the teachings of the Buddha</note> or Buddhist doctrine in the Empire of **Japan**, as well as to secure its establishment against the **Mukurrokoku** <note>A derogatory term used at the time to refer to Christians or "the country of corpses"; Kaempfer notes it refers to all antagonists of Buddhism</note>, motivated him to act. Though the Christians had already been sufficiently silenced by the famous and unparalleled persecution that arose in this Empire, these reasons prevailed upon him to give up the high dignity and power he held in favor of his successor and come over to **Japan**. There, he intended to establish a sort of religious headship or Archiepiscopal See for this doctrine. 

He arrived in **Japan** in the year of Christ 1653 and was received with all imaginable respect. The Princes and Lords of several provinces came to pay their respects to him, dressed in their <term>**Kamishimo**</term> <note>original: "Camisimo"; formal samurai attire consisting of a pleated skirt and a wing-shouldered vest</note> or ceremonial garments. The Emperor offered him a residence on a mountain in the neighborhood of the holy city of **Kyoto**, which he named **Ōbaku** after the name of his former residence in **China**. 

An incident that happened soon after his arrival contributed greatly to his designs and raised an uncommon respect for his person and a high opinion of his holiness among several inhabitants of this Empire. After a very great drought, the local country people—his neighbors—asked him to perform a <term>**Kitō**</term> <note>original: "Kitoo"; a ritual prayer for a specific benefit, in this case, rain</note>, or an extraordinary solemn prayer, in order to

His companions, who came over with him from **China**, had likewise very great respect paid them, as more immediate partakers, of his glory, insomuch, that even a cook, who came over with this learned and sanctified company, was rais'd to the dignity of Superior of **Fukusai-ji** <note>original: "Faksudira"; one of the three "Chinese temples" in Nagasaki</note>, one of the three convents at **Nagasaki**, where by his sublime understanding and reputed great knowledge in divine mysteries he obtain'd, and still keeps, the name and repute of a **Godo** <note>likely *godo*, "enlightened one" or "man of the Way"</note>, that is, a person bless'd with a divine and most accute understanding, whom they suppose to be able to find out by his **Satori** <note>The experience of Zen enlightenment or awakening</note>, or Enthusiastic Speculations, such misterious truths, as are far beyond the reach of common knowledge. He sits with a wonderful grave countenance, and without stirring or uttering any the least sound, as if he was entirely life, or speechless, only to express his gratitude to the people for these extraordinary marks of honour, he is pleas'd now and then to favour them with a small scarce perceptible wink. ### Chap IV. *The History of JAPAN.*

...and show it to his neighbors, who would otherwise be held responsible for this neglect if, upon investigation, none were found. Despite **Ingen’s** <note>Ingen Ryūki (1592–1673), a Chinese Chan master who founded the Ōbaku school of Zen in Japan</note> eminent position and his extraordinary learning, he could not fully persuade the clergy of this Empire—who were then, as they still are, divided into several sects—to accept his protection or acknowledge him as their supreme head, not even those of his own religion. He was succeeded by a man named **Okussi** <note>Likely Mu'an Chenghui (known in Japan as Mokuan Shōtō), Ingen's successor</note>, a man of lesser talent, learning, and authority. After his death, a native of **Japan** was placed in his position and declared the Superior of the monastery on **Mount Ōbaku** <note>The head temple of the Ōbaku school, Manpuku-ji, located in Uji</note>, and General of the three **Chinese Temples** and monasteries at **Nagasaki**.

<margin>Generals of the various religious orders.</margin>
<margin>Jisha-bugyō, or Temple Judges.</margin>
The clergy of all sects and orders in **Nagasaki**, and throughout the Empire, have their General residing in **Kyoto** <note>original: "Miaco"</note>. Through the quiet permission and protection of the Emperor <note>Here, the author refers to the Shogun’s administration</note>, these Generals have absolute command and almost sovereign authority over the members of their respective sects. They make it their priority to remain in the favor of the civil magistrates with great humility, primarily so that they might rely on their assistance and protection when needed. The Superiors of the monasteries, who are appointed by these Generals, have the power to grant the monks of their houses the necessary passports for their travels. Aside from this, they have very little involvement in civil affairs and are, like other secular persons, subject to the Emperor, who governs them through two <term>**Jisha-bugyō**</term> <note>original: "Dsisja Bugjo"; the Commissioners of Temples and Shrines</note>, as they are called, or by the more formal title, <term>**Jisha-go-bugyō**</term>. These are the Imperial Commissioners who act as inspectors, protectors, and judges for all temples and the monks belonging to them. This office is one of the highest in the Empire, second only to the Emperor’s Council of State, and those appointed to it are very highly regarded at court. They hold their court in **Edo** <note>original: "Jedo"; the seat of the Shogunate, modern-day Tokyo</note>. Every day, a great number of civil matters relating to the clergy—such as lawsuits, disputes over land boundaries or revenues, and prosecutions for wrongs or damages received—are brought to this court for a decision. Furthermore, all criminal cases, such as rebellion, disregard for Imperial proclamations and commands, and generally all capital crimes committed by the clergy, are tried before them. In cases of conviction, they are punished with death, though these clerics are treated with much more indulgence than other people; they cannot be executed without the consent and a warrant signed by their General in **Kyoto**. Another branch of the <term>**Jisha-bugyō's**</term> business is to oversee the financial support of the clergy, to keep the temples in repair, and to assist them on any occasion where secular power and authority are required.
