## C H A P. V.

### Of the arrival and reception of the *Portuguese* and *Castilians* in *Japan*; of their Trade, and how they were banish'd the Empire.

<margin>Discovery of the East-Indies by the Portuguese.</margin>
THE Portuguese were the first of all European nations to venture upon the Indian Ocean. In the year 1497, four ships were equipped by order of King Manuel <note>Original text: "Emanuel"</note> of Portugal, under the command of Admiral Vasco da Gama. They traveled as far as Calicut <note>A major trading port in Kerala, India</note>, where a peace and commerce agreement was made with the Zamorin <note>The hereditary title of the Hindu monarch of the Kingdom of Calicut</note>, or King of that country. The conquest of Goa by Afonso de Albuquerque <note>Original: "Alonso de Albuquerque"</note> in the year 1510 was the foundation of their future power and the first firm settlement they made in the Indies. From that time, they vigorously pursued their discoveries and conquests among the defenseless Indians and expanded their trade all over the East, reaching as far as the remote Empire of China.

<margin>Discovery of Japan.</margin>
In 1542, one of their ships, bound for China, was forced by a storm upon the then still unknown islands of Japan. After enduring many hardships, she came to an anchor in a harbor of the province of Bungo <note>A historical province in eastern Kyushu</note>, one of the nine provinces of the island of Kyushu <note>original: "Kiusju"</note>. Japanese histories mention that the first European ship seen upon their coasts came to anchor before Awa, opposite the island of Shikoku <note>original: "Tfikokf"</note>. Be that as it will, the honor of the first discovery of Japan by way of the Indies is unquestionably due to the Portuguese, though it happened accidentally. Afterward, one of their ships laden with commodities was sent every other year to the same province of Bungo.

<margin>First Establishment of the Portuguese.</margin>
In 1549, a young Japanese man who had fled to Goa and was baptized there gave some hints to the Portuguese merchants regarding the great gain our European commodities would likely produce in his country. At the same time, he spoke with the Fathers of the Society of Jesus <note>The Jesuits</note> about the possibility of converting his countrymen to the faith of Christ. Both of these considerations led the Portuguese to think of making a better establishment and erecting a factory <note>In this era, a "factory" was a merchant's trading post or warehouse in a foreign country</note> in Japan. In order to do this, the young Japanese man was sent back to his native country on board a Portuguese ship, and several Jesuits went along with him, including the Reverend Father Francis Xavier <note>St. Francis Xavier (1506–1552), a co-founder of the Jesuit Order and influential missionary</note>. At that time, the Empire of Japan was not yet shut up <note>A reference to "Sakoku," the period of national isolation that began in the 1630s</note>, nor were the princes or petty kings <note>The *daimyo*</note> kept to such strict obedience and submission to their Emperor <note>Here referring to the Shogun’s central administration</note> as they are now. The Japanese were at liberty to travel within their own country and abroad,

...abroad, wherever they pleased, or were called by their business or commerce. Foreign nations could then frequent the Empire in whatever manner they pleased, and put into whichever harbors they thought most convenient. This was the case for the Portuguese, who not only had the freedom to go to any part of the Empire they saw fit, but were also warmly welcomed by the Princes of the Island **Kyushu** <note>original: "Kiusju," the southernmost of Japan's four main islands</note> and invited to settle in their territories. Indeed, the potential profits for their subjects from trade with the Portuguese created no small jealousy among these lords. Each one used his most persistent efforts to persuade these foreigners to use his harbors instead of others. In this way, they sold their goods freely and widely throughout the Empire. The Japanese, being naturally curious, competed to be the first to own these foreign rarities; being unfamiliar with their actual value, they willingly paid whatever price was asked. 

The reverend fathers of the <term>Society of Jesus<gloss>The Jesuits, a Catholic religious order known for missionary and educational work</term>, who accompanied this first Portuguese colony into Japan, were equally intent on spreading the Gospel among these people <note>original: "Infidels"</note>. It was quite easy for the Portuguese to make their trade flourish while simultaneously supporting the conversion of the Japanese to the faith of our Savior. Their nearby base at **Macau** in China, which they already controlled, could supply them with a ready stock of European and Indian goods as well as a sufficient number of priests. Their countrymen, the Spaniards—who were then established in the city of **Manila** <note>original: "Manilhas"</note> in the Philippine Islands, not far from Japan—were also close by to assist if needed. Even the city of **Goa** itself, known as the "Indian Rome" <note>Goa was the center of Catholic administration and mission work in Asia, earning it this nickname</note> and the capital of all Portuguese territories in the East, could easily send reinforcements of <term>ecclesiastics<gloss>priests and religious officials</gloss></term> without hardship to its own people, despite the distance. It is therefore no surprise that the Portuguese reached the height of their fortune in a short time.

<margin>The flourishing state of their trade and their success in spreading the Gospel.</margin>

In exchange for European and Indian goods—such as raw silk, fine fabrics, drugs, wines, medicines, and a wide variety of other natural and man-made curiosities—the merchants gained immense treasures, the very "golden marrow" <note>A metaphor for the country's most valuable resources, specifically the massive amounts of Japanese gold and silver exported by the Portuguese</note> of the country. For their part, the Jesuit fathers won the hearts of the people, who were always eager for novelty, through the gentle and comforting doctrine of the Gospel—which was entirely new and unknown to the Japanese at that time. They were also impressed by the priests' modest and virtuous lifestyle, their charitable and selfless care for the sick and poor, and the grand splendor of their religious services, which the Japanese found exceptionally delightful. Beyond these advantages, there was a natural similarity between the temperaments and inclinations of the Japanese and the Portuguese, both being born nearly...

On one side, this contributed significantly to the advancement and flourishing condition of the Portuguese trade; on the other, it filled the *Jesuits* with just grounds to hope for success in converting these people <note>original: "Heathens"</note> to the faith of Christ. 

It is true that at first—as beginnings are always difficult—they did not find the Japanese to be as receptive as they had expected. In fact, even that great Apostle of the Indies, *St. Francis Xavier*, was initially unwilling to stay any longer to so little purpose. He resolved to leave the country and retire to where he thought his presence could be more useful. But these early difficulties they struggled with are easily explained: the fathers were not yet acquainted with the customs, manners, language, and politics of the Japanese. They were obliged to have their sermons and other proposals translated into Japanese by unskilled interpreters, with the Japanese words written out in Latin characters. When this was done, they read from their papers what they did not understand themselves, in a manner that—as can be easily imagined—exposed them to the laughter of an audience that was otherwise serious and attentive. 

However, in the course of time, when they became familiar with the natives—learning their language and studying their religion, customs, and inclinations—they met with success infinitely beyond their expectations. The number of converts, especially on the Island of **Kyushu** <note>original: "Kiusju," the southernmost of Japan's four main islands</note> where they first settled, was almost inconceivable. This was largely because the Princes of **Bungo**, **Arima**, and **Omura** did not only openly support the interests of the Christian religion, but were converted and baptized themselves. In the year 1582, they sent some of their nearest relations, bearing letters and presents, to pay homage to the then **Pope Gregory XIII** and to assure his Holiness of their filial submission to the Church. An account of this most celebrated embassy has been recorded in the works of that incomparable historian *Thuanus* <note>Jacques Auguste de Thou (1553–1617), a French historian and statesman</note> and by many other Roman Catholic writers. 

The illustrious and pious example of these Princes was quickly followed, not only by their own subjects but also by the subjects of neighboring Princes, with such zeal and forwardness that it may be justly said of them: "they forced themselves into the kingdom of heaven." The gospel was thus propagated in Japan—slowly in some places, but with incomparable success in others. Fresh recruits of "workmen" for such a good, though unexpected, harvest were sent over from **Manila** <note>original: "Manilhas"</note>, **Macau**, and **Goa**. In the meantime, some of the Japanese natives were educated by the *Jesuits* and later admitted into their order. ### Chap. V. The History of JAPAN.

...incredible, considering the inconsistency of their religion and their worship of idols. Considering this, there was good reason to hope that the conversion of the entire Empire of **Japan** would be achieved in time, when suddenly and unexpectedly, affairs took quite a different turn. 

This new religion, and the great number of people from all ranks and social standing who were converted to it, caused significant changes in the church <note>Referring here to the religious landscape of Japan</note> that were extremely harmful to the heathen <note>The author uses "heathen" to refer to the Buddhist and Shinto clergy</note> clergy. It was feared that this might lead to fatal consequences even for the state. For this, and several other reasons to be mentioned later, the **Secular Emperor** <note>The Shogun, who held the actual political and military power in Japan, as opposed to the Mikado or spiritual Emperor</note> thought it necessary to put a stop to this growing evil and to forbid all his subjects, under penalty of death, from embracing a religion that seemed likely to prove so damaging. 

To this end, proclamations were issued in 1586. The persecution began that same year, and several people were executed for disobeying the Imperial commands. However, this unexpected turn was not able to stop the progress of Christianity. The common people continued to openly embrace and profess it, while many people of high quality <note>People of high social rank or nobility</note> did the same in private out of fear and caution. Not even the raging flames of a persecution—the most dreadful mentioned in any history—seemed at first to have the effect the non-Christian government expected. For although according to the letters of the **Jesuits**, 20,570 people suffered death for the faith of Christ in the year 1590 alone, yet in 1591 and 1592, when all the churches were actually shut down, they made 12,000 new converts. 

The Japanese writers themselves do not deny that the young ruler **Fide Jori** <note>Toyotomi Hideyori (1593–1615), the son and successor of the unifier Toyotomi Hideyoshi</note>, who in the year 1616 <note>Historical records usually date the fall of Osaka Castle and Hideyori's death to 1615</note> was put to death by his tutor **Ijejas** <note>Tokugawa Ieyasu, the founder of the Tokugawa Shogunate</note>, who usurped the throne from him, was suspected of being a Christian, and that the greatest part of his court, soldiers, and military officers professed the same religion. The cheerfulness with which the new converts suffered all imaginable torments and the most cruel deaths, rather than renounce their Savior, excited the curiosity of many people to know what doctrine it was that could make its followers so joyful even in the pangs of death; and as soon as they were instructed in it, it appeared so clearly full of truth and comfort that many resolved to embrace it.

The merchants married the daughters of the wealthiest inhabitants and sold their goods to the best advantage. The gold of the country was exchanged for European and Indian curiosities, medicines, fabrics, and other similar things. Upwards of 300 tons of this precious metal were exported every year, for at that time they had full liberty to import and to export,

At the height of their prosperity, they imported their goods in large ships; however, as their trade began to decline, they arrived only with *Galliots* <note>original: "Galliots"; small, fast merchant ships used by the Portuguese</note>, or smaller vessels. They first arrived at the harbours of **Bungo** and **Firando** <note>modern-day Oita and Hirado</note>, but later they came only to **Nagasaki**. It is believed that had the **Portuguese** enjoyed the trade with Japan for just twenty years longer, on the same terms as they did for a time, such riches would have been transported out of this *Ophir* <note>A biblical reference to a land of legendary wealth, comparing Japan to the source of King Solomon's gold</note> to **Macao**, that there would have been such a plenty and flow of gold and silver in that town as the sacred scriptures mention was in **Jerusalem** during the time of **Solomon**. It is unnecessary to detail every particular of their trade here; I believe it is enough to mention that even in the final years of their presence in **Japan**, when their trade was at its lowest point—specifically in 1636—four ships carried 2,350 chests of silver, or 2,350,000 <term>Taels<note>A "Thail" or Tael was a unit of weight used for silver currency in East Asia</note></term>, from **Nagasaki** to **Macao**, along with 287 **Portuguese** and their families. In 1637, they imported goods and exported money to the value of 2,142,365 <term>Taels</term> <note>The fractional numbers 4 and 1 likely refer to "mace" and "candareens," sub-units of the tael</note> on board six ships. In 1638, the value was 1,259,023 <term>Taels</term> with only two *Galliots*. I even found records mentioning that a few years earlier, they sent away over 100 tons of gold on a single small ship.

<margin>The Fall of the Portuguese.</margin>
Now, regarding the fall of the **Portuguese**, I have often heard it confirmed by reliable sources among the **Japanese** themselves that pride and greed were the primary causes. Specifically, pride among the high-ranking officials and greed among those of lower status made the entire nation hated. Even the newly converted **Japanese Christians** were shocked and grew impatient when they saw that their "Spiritual Fathers" <note>The Jesuit and Franciscan missionaries</note> sought not only the salvation of their souls but also had their eyes on their money and lands. Furthermore, the merchants sold their goods in a greedy and unreasonable manner. Their growing wealth and the unexpected success in spreading the Gospel made both the clergy and the laypeople arrogant. Those leading the clergy thought it was beneath their dignity to walk on foot anymore, as **Christ** and his **Apostles** had done. Nothing would satisfy them but to be carried about in magnificent chairs, imitating the grand displays of the **Pope** and his **Cardinals** in **Rome**. They not only treated themselves as equals to the highest officials of the Empire but, filled with religious pride, imagined that even a superior rank was their rightful due. It happened one day that a **Portuguese** Bishop met one of the State Counselors on the road while the official was traveling to court. This arrogant prelate refused to order his chair to be stopped or to step out to pay his respects to this great man, as is the custom of the country, but instead passed by without...

This great man, exasperated at so signal an affront, thenceforward bore a mortal hatred to the Portuguese, and in the height of his just resentment, made his complaints to the Emperor himself, with such an odious picture of the insolence, pride and vanity of this nation, as he expected could not but raise the Emperor’s utmost indignation. This happen’d in 1596. The next year the persecution against the Christians began a-new, and twenty-six persons <note>A reference to the Twenty-six Martyrs of Japan, who were crucified in Nagasaki on February 5, 1597</note>, of the number whereof were two foreign Jesuits, and several Fathers of the Franciscan Order, were executed on the cross. The inconsistency of the Christian doctrine with the religion and idol-worship, as it was then establish’d in the country, was another of the essential causes of that cruel persecution rais’d against the adherents thereof. The new converted Christians told their countrymen, that so long as they continu’d <term>Heathens<note>The term used by European writers of the time to describe followers of non-Abrahamic religions</note></term>, they had nothing to expect but eternal damnation; and not only this, but they carried their zeal for their newly embrac’d doctrine, and their hatred against the Pagan worship, and its <term>Bonzes<note>A term historically used by Europeans to refer to Buddhist monks or priests in East Asia</note></term> or Priests, so far, as to pull down their Temples and Idols. And it was to be fear’d, that both church and state would be thereby thrown into a still greater confusion, were not the growing evil timely remedied. The union and harmony which was observ’d to reign among the Christians, and their joint endeavours to abolish the Pagan Religions of the country, and upon the ruins thereof to raise their own, afforded matter of jealousy and speculation to the prudent Emperor *Taico* <note>Known historically as Toyotomi Hideyoshi, the second "Great Unifier" of Japan</note>, and his successor *Ijejas* <note>Known historically as Tokugawa Ieyasu, the founder of the Tokugawa Shogunate</note>, the former of whom ow’d the crown, and his greatness, entirely to his courage and conduct, the latter to treachery and indirect practices. *Ijejas* indeed had so much the more reason to be apprehensive, that the increase of the Christian Religion might prove prejudicial to his interests, as his pupil *Fidejori* <note>Toyotomi Hideyori, the son and intended heir of Hideyoshi, whom Ieyasu eventually overthrew</note>, (*Taico*’s only son, upon whom he usurp’d the throne,) and the greater part of his court and party had been either Christians themselves, or at least very favourably inclin’d to this religion. Both *Taico* and his successor *Ijejas*, as they had no hereditary right to the throne they were possess’d of, made it their endeavour, for their own security, to remove all obstacles, that could possibly tend to make the possession thereof troublesome to them, and amongst others, to put an entire stop to the further propagation of a religion so inconsistent with all the others, then existing in the country, and so like to beget enmities and jealousies between their subjects.

### The History of JAPAN. Book IV.

First of all, therefore, an Imperial Proclamation was issued, forbidding the "doctrine of the Fathers"—as the *Japanese* then termed the *Roman Catholic Religion*—to be taught and propagated any further. After this, the Governors, Princes, and Lords of the several Provinces were desired, by persuasion or force, to oblige their subjects to renounce the faith of our Savior and to return to their old religion. The directors of the *Portuguese* trade also received strict orders not to bring over any more ecclesiastics <note>A general term for priests, monks, and other church officials.</note> on board their ships, and finally, the monks and priests then in the country were ordered to depart immediately. 

However, little regard was had at first for these Imperial orders. The Princes and Governors of several Provinces indeed left no stone unturned to make their subjects renounce their belief in Christ and return to the worship of their idols. But the *Portuguese* and *Castilians* <note>Referring to the Spaniards, who were then ruled by the Crown of Castile.</note> did not stop bringing over fresh recruits of ecclesiastics on board their ships, albeit in private. Nor could the *Jesuits*, who were then well-established in the country, be brought by any means to comply with the Imperial commands; they refused to quit the *Empire* and lose at once what they had spent so many years laboring to achieve. Much about the same time, another unlucky accident happened.

Some *Franciscan Friars*, whom the Governor of *Manila* in the *Philippine Islands* had sent as his ambassadors to the Emperor of *Japan*, preached openly in the public streets of *Miaco* <note>Modern-day Kyoto, then the capital and residence of the Emperor.</note> during the whole time of their stay. In that city, where they resided, they built a church of their own accord, contrary to the Imperial commands and against the advice and earnest solicitations of the *Jesuits*. They had nothing to allege for such an imprudent and untimely proceeding except an ardent longing for the crown of martyrdom and the command of the Apostle, *that God ought to be obeyed preferably to men* <note>original: "Oportet obedire Deo magis quam hominibus" (Acts 5:29)</note>. This was despite the fact that it was evident to all that such an open disregard for the Emperor’s commands and so notorious a breach of the laws of the *Empire* would prove, in the end, not only fatal to themselves but highly prejudicial to the advancement of Christianity and the good of the church. 

And indeed, the persecution which was afterwards raised against the Christians has no equal in history. At last, after a cruel butchery of many thousands of its adherents which lasted for forty whole years, it ended with the total extirpation of the faith, the loss of that profitable trade which the *Portuguese* and *Castilians* had carried on for nearly a hundred years, and the permanent banishment of these nations. The intent of the Court, as appears by several instances, was not at first to vent its full resentment upon the whole *Portuguese* nation. <term>Taiko</term> <note>Toyotomi Hideyoshi (1537–1598), the second "Great Unifier" of Japan, who held the title of Taikō (retired regent).</note>, once provoked by false information, flew into a sudden passion against the fathers of the Society <note>The Jesuits, or Society of Jesus.</note> and commanded them to depart the *Empire* within twenty days; but soon after, he not only mitigated this decree but gave them leave to build a church near *Miaco*, though at the same time he ordered them never to preach—

# The History of JAPAN. Book IV.

## 320

In this manner, and for the several reasons already discussed, the **Portuguese** lost their profitable trade and commerce with **Japan**. They were totally expelled from the country before the end of the year 1639.

<margin>The Portuguese make vain attempts to revive their trade.</margin>
The **Portuguese** were not discouraged by the many hardships and great losses they had already suffered. Before they would completely abandon hope of continuing or reviving this lucrative branch of their trade, they resolved to try one final step. In the year 1640, the year after their total expulsion, the Government of **Macao** sent two Ambassadors to the Emperor <note>While the text says "Emperor," it refers to the Tokugawa Shogun, the military ruler of Japan who held actual power.</note>, accompanied by a large retinue totaling seventy-three people. As soon as these Ambassadors arrived in the harbor of **Nagasaki**, they were immediately arrested along with their entire retinue, in accordance with the standing Imperial orders. Their ship was also seized, even though they carried no trade goods—proving they did not come for commerce. When news of their arrival and imprisonment reached the Court, the Emperor, violating the international laws of diplomacy, sentenced them all to be beheaded. Only twelve men of the lowest rank were spared and sent back to **Macao** to bring their countrymen the news of this tragic failure. They carried a proud and threatening message from the Emperor, stating in essence that even if the King of **Portugal** himself—or even the God of the Christians—dared to enter his dominions, he would treat them in the same way. The fate of these twelve men remains unknown, as they never reached **Macao**; it is highly probable that, lacking the skill to manage their ship, they perished at sea. The remaining prisoners were executed according to the custom of the country, with an executioner standing by each man. At a given signal, all their heads were struck off in an instant.

This occurred shortly before the execution of the ambassadors and involved a large **Spanish** ship that came to **Japan** from the **Philippine Islands**. The ship was sunk with all its cargo, and the entire crew was butchered in the harbor of **Nagasaki**. About a year later, a three-decked Spanish ship, sailing from the Philippine Islands to Japan, came to an anchor in the harbor of **Nagasaki**. The Governors of the town immediately sent swift word of this to the court. Upon receiving this news, the Emperor ordered the **Prince of Arima** <note>Arima Naozumi, a daimyo who had been a Christian but became a loyal enforcer for the Shogunate.</note> to destroy and burn the ship, along with all its cargo and everyone on board.

About three days before this order arrived, the Spaniards were warned by some sympathetic locals and friends in **Nagasaki** that a storm was about to break over their heads. They were advised to flee quickly to escape this looming danger. However, greed at first—and eventually unfavorable winds—prevented them from taking such good advice. They busied themselves day and night, loading the ship with gold, silver, and precious Japanese goods, packing in as much wealth as the ship could possibly hold, while preparing to defend themselves in case of an attack.

Meanwhile, the **Prince of Arima**, who had been appointed to carry out the Imperial orders, arrived in the harbor with a sufficient number of soldiers and a great many boats. The Spanish ship was surrounded immediately. This, combined with the contrary winds, made it impossible for the ship to break out and escape. In this desperate situation, the Spaniards unanimously resolved to sell their lives dearly. The Japanese soon found that capturing and burning the ship was not as easy as they had imagined.

The Prince, for his part, did everything possible to encourage his soldiers to launch a vigorous attack, using both his presence and promises of great rewards. However, finding that no one wanted to be the first to board, he jumped onto the Spanish vessel himself. He was followed in an instant by such a large number of his soldiers that they covered the entire deck. At this, the Spaniards retreated below deck, shutting the hatches behind them. The Prince, suspecting that this was a trap, jumped back onto his own ship under the pretense of fetching more men. A moment later, the Spaniards ignited several barrels of gunpowder they had placed under the deck, blowing it up along with all the Japanese soldiers standing upon it.

Once the first explosion was over, the Prince commanded fresh troops to board the enemy a second time. Again, the Spaniards retreated under the second deck and blew it up in the same manner. They did the same a third time after the Japanese made another attempt, with the Spaniards finally retreating to the very bottom of the ship. Because of these repeated explosions, the harbor was covered with dead, wounded, and mangled <note>original: "bruis’d"</note> Japanese soldiers before they could even reach the Spaniards. The crew defended themselves with the utmost bravery for several hours, refusing to surrender until every last man was killed. <margin>Watch-guards at the mountain peaks.</margin>
Once the Japanese had finally cleared the country of all Portuguese (with the exception of a few priests who remained hidden throughout the land), the court at **Edo** <note>original: "Jedo"; The seat of the Tokugawa Shogunate, modern-day Tokyo.</note> received reports that the Portuguese had been very well received in China and held great influence at the court of the Chinese Emperor. This news forced the Japanese to stay on their guard. To this end, guard-houses or signal beacons (which still exist today) were built on the peaks of high mountains. The soldiers stationed there were ordered to immediately light signal fires if they spotted a fleet of ten or more European ships sailing toward Japan. They always keep dry, combustible materials ready at hand for this purpose. When these fires are spotted and answered by other beacons on distant mountains, the court at **Edo** can be alerted within twenty-four hours. Consequently, they can issue the necessary orders for the defense of the country without delay. Because of these excellent regulations, as soon as the fires are lit, every man knows exactly which post he must occupy and what role he must play in the defense of his country.

### CHAP. VI.

## Concerning the Dutch Trade in Japan in General.

<margin>The first Dutch settlements in Japan.</margin>
The Dutch, drawn by the profitable trade of the Portuguese, decided to establish their own settlements in Japan shortly after the founding of their East India Company. In the very early years of their voyages to the East Indies, at the start of the last century <note>The early 1600s.</note>, they sought to provide a base for the ships and goods they intended to send there annually. Their first factory <note>A "factory" in this context refers to a fortified trading post and warehouse, not a manufacturing plant.</note> and residence was built on a small island near the town of **Hirado** <note>original: "Firando"; A port in Nagasaki Prefecture.</note>, which was connected to the town by a bridge. They were welcomed all the more warmly because they were the sworn enemies of the Portuguese—the very people whom the supreme authorities had already resolved to expel from the Empire. The Portuguese indeed used every effort and all the influence they still held with powerful men in the Empire to crush the Dutch establishment at its start and keep the trade for themselves, but their efforts were in vain. The reigning Emperor **Ieyasu** <note>original: "Ijejas"; Tokugawa Ieyasu, the founder of the Tokugawa Shogunate.</note>, who was known after his death by the title **Gongen** <note>A divine title meaning "Avatar."</note>, granted the Dutch a permit for free trade throughout all his dominions in the year 1611 <note>The OCR text says 1601, but the historical date for the formal trade pass was 1609/1611.</note> by an express **vermilion seal letter** <note>original: "Gosjunim"; referring to a *Goshuinjo*, a trade permit bearing the Shogun's red seal which granted the Dutch legal status and protection.</note>.

<summary>This page describes Japan's early warning beacon system for detecting European fleets and the arrival of the Dutch, who were granted trading privileges by Tokugawa Ieyasu to replace the expelled Portuguese.</summary>

### Chapter VI. The History of JAPAN.

...as they call it, which literally translates as a **"red-seal" mark** <note>The *Goshuin*, or "red-seal" letter, was a permit issued by the Shogunate to authorize trade.</note>, and refers to the Imperial letters patent signed by all the State Councilors and stamped with the red Imperial seal. This entire document takes its name from that seal. By virtue of these Imperial letters patent, the Dutch were granted permission to import and sell their goods throughout all parts of the Emperor’s <note>In this context, Kaempfer refers to the Shogun as the Emperor.</note> dominions. This permission was backed by a strong recommendation to all his subjects to assist and support the Dutch as much as possible, written in very significant and favorable terms. 

After the death of **Ieyasu** <note>original: "Ijejas"; Tokugawa Ieyasu, the founder of the Tokugawa Shogunate.</note>, the Dutch applied for a renewal of their privileges. This was an imprudent move, as it went entirely against the customs of the Japanese nation, which holds great respect for—and keeps inviolable—the laws and promises made by their ancestors. Their request was indeed granted and their privileges renewed on similar terms, but the wording was changed to less favorable characters. 

Meanwhile, as the prosperity of the Portuguese was daily declining toward its fatal end, the Dutch spared no effort to build the foundation of their own establishment upon the ruins of their rivals. No trouble or expense was spared to please the Shogun, upon whom alone the success or failure of their trade depended. They did everything possible to win over the State Councilors—particularly the **Prince of Hirado** <note>original: "Firando"; referring to the *daimyo* (lord) of the Hirado domain.</note>—and other powerful men who could promote or hinder their reputation and interests at court. 

The most exquisite curiosities of nature and art were purchased and brought over as annual presents. They even bought the rarest and strangest animals from the most distant kingdoms of Europe, Persia, and the Indies to satisfy the Shogun's demands—demands that were often ridiculous and fanciful. They frequently asked for animals so strange in nature, color, and shape that they perhaps never existed in reality, even though the Japanese provided drawings to help the Dutch find them.

<margin>Their behavior toward the Imperial court</margin>
In short, the interests of the Dutch and the massive profits the East India Company expected from such a lucrative trade branch forced them into a position of absolute, passive obedience. They felt they had to blindly follow whatever commands were laid upon them, no matter how harsh or unreasonable. This becomes clear through the following examples: 

In the year 1638, the Shogun commanded them to demolish their newly built factory and warehouse on the island of **Hirado** <note>original: "Firando"</note> and to level it to the ground. This order was so sudden it seemed as if they were his greatest enemies. The only reason given was that the buildings were made of hewn stone—handsomer than the local buildings—and that the year of our **Lord's birth** <note>original: "Saviour's nativity"; referring to the Christian date (1638) carved into the stonework.</note> was engraved on the front. Even though this order was entirely unreasonable, they were forced to comply immediately, not only with-

...without showing the least mark of dislike, but even with seeming satisfaction. Not long after, and within that very same year, the Court did not hesitate to make them undergo a still severer trial, and to exact most convincing proofs of which was greater: their regard for the Imperial orders, or their love for their fellow Christians. 

The case was this: About 40,000 Christians—reduced to desperate measures by the many unparalleled cruelties and torments which many thousands of their brethren had already suffered, and which they themselves had narrowly escaped—rose up and retired into an old fortified place <note>This was Hara Castle, located on the Shimabara Peninsula.</note> in the neighborhood of **Shimabara** <note>original: "Simabara"</note>, with a firm resolution to defend their lives to the utmost of their power. 

The Dutch, as friends and allies of the Emperor <note>Kaempfer consistently refers to the Shogun as the "Emperor."</note>, were requested to assist the Japanese in the siege of this place and the impending total destruction of the besieged Christians. **Mr. Koeckebacker** <note>original: "Mr. Kockebecker"; Nicolaes Koeckebacker was the Chief of the Dutch trading post at the time.</note>, who was then the director of the Dutch trade and nation at **Hirado** <note>original: "Firando"; a small island and port in Nagasaki Prefecture.</note>, having received the Emperor's order to this purpose, repaired there without delay. He arrived on board a Dutch ship lying at anchor in the harbor of Hirado. All the other Dutch ships had set sail only the day before, perhaps having received some hint that such a request was likely to be made to them from the court. 

Within a fortnight's time, Koeckebacker battered the town with 426 cannonballs, fired both from his ship and from a battery which was raised on shore and planted with the Dutch's own guns. This compliance of the Dutch, and their conduct during the siege, was entirely to the satisfaction of the Japanese. Although the besieged seemed in no way ready to surrender, their numbers had been greatly reduced and their strength broken by this cannonading. 

**Mr. Koeckebacker** was finally given leave to depart with his ship, but only after they had obliged him to leave six more guns for the use of the Japanese, in addition to those already on shore. They did not consider that the ship was thereby made very defenceless for such an insecure voyage as the passage from **Japan** to **Batavia** <note>Modern-day Jakarta, Indonesia, which was then the headquarters of the Dutch East India Company.</note> was at that time. 

By this submissive readiness to assist the Emperor in the execution of his designs regarding the final destruction of Christianity in his dominions, it is true that we held our ground enough to maintain ourselves in the country and were permitted to carry on our trade—even though the court was then considering a total exclusion of all foreigners whatsoever. However, many generous and noble persons at court and throughout the Empire judged our conduct quite differently, and not very favorably for the reputation we had tried to gain. It seemed to them inconsistent with reason that the Dutch should ever be expected to be sincerely faithful to a foreign Monarch—and one whom they looked upon as a Heathen Prince—while they showed such eagerness to assist him in the destruction of a people with whom they otherwise agreed in the most essential...

In short, our humble, complaisant, and obliging conduct notwithstanding, we were so far from bringing this proud and jealous nation to any greater confidence, or more intimate friendship, that on the contrary their jealousy and mistrust seemed to increase, in proportion to the many convincing proofs of sincerity and faithfulness we gave them. The better we deserved of them, the more they seemed to hate and despise us, till at last in the year 1641, soon after the total expulsion of the Portuguese, orders were sent us to quit our old factory at **Hirado** <note>original: "Firando"</note>, to exchange the protection of a good and indulgent Prince, for the severe and strict government of **Nagasaki**, and under a very narrow inspection to confine ourselves within that small Island—I should rather say, Prison—which was built for the Portuguese. So great was the covetousness of the Dutch, and so great the alluring power of the Japanese gold, that rather than to quit the prospect of a trade, indeed most advantageous, they willingly underwent an almost perpetual imprisonment (for such in fact is our stay at **Dejima** <note>original: "Desima"</note>), and chose to suffer many hardships in a foreign and heathen country. They chose to be remiss in performing divine service on Sundays and solemn festivals, to leave off praying and singing of psalms in public, entirely to avoid the sign of the cross, the calling upon Christ in presence of the natives, and all the outward marks of Christianity. Lastly, they chose patiently and submissively to bear the abusive and injurious behavior of these proud Infidels towards us, than which nothing can be offered more shocking to a generous and noble mind.

...are soldiers constantly upon duty. On the North side of the Island are two strong gates, which they call the water-gates, which are never opened except for the loading and unloading of our ships, and only when certain Commissioners appointed by the Governors are present. The whole Island is enclosed with quite high fir planks <note>original: "deal-boards"</note>, covered with small roofs. Along the top of these is planted a double row of pikes, similar to a spiked defensive barrier <note>original: "Cheval de Frize"; a medieval defensive structure used to stop cavalry or intruders</note>. The entire enclosure is, in truth, very flimsy and unable to hold out against any real force in case of need.

A few paces away from the Island, standing in the water, are thirteen very high posts placed at specific distances. At the top of these are small wooden signs upon which are written, in large Japanese characters, an order from the Governors. This order strictly forbids all boats or vessels from coming within these rails or approaching the Island, under threat of severe penalties. Just before the bridge leading toward the town is a place built of square stones where they display the Imperial Mandates, Proclamations, and the orders of the Governors. Two specific orders from the Governors are always visible there, written on multiple boards. One of these orders relates to the regulation of the guard, while the other is directed to the street-officers of **Dejima** <note>original: "Desima"</note> and to all persons who have business there and are required to enter or exit. 

In addition to this, the *Ottona* <term>Ottona: the Japanese headman or chief officer of a specific street or district</term>, to demonstrate both his vigilance and the authority he holds—especially during the sale of our goods—causes another order of his own to be posted. This is much like the Governors' orders and is placed on the other side of the bridge, right at the entrance to our Island. I intend to discuss all these various orders and proclamations in a specific chapter (See Chapter 10 of this Book).

The square surface area of our Island is commonly supposed to be equal to a Greek furlong <note>original: "Stadium"; an ancient unit of length approximately 600 feet</note>, being 600 feet in length and 240 feet in breadth. By my own measurement, I found the breadth to be 82 common paces and the main length to be 236 paces. I say the "main length" because, as shown in the attached diagram, the island is narrower toward the town and wider toward the harbor. 

A broad street runs across the entire Island. There is also a small path for walking along the wooden planks that enclose it; this walk can be closed off at any time if necessary. The gutters all drain into the sea through crooked, narrow pipes. These were made intentionally winding so that nothing could be smuggled out of the Island through them, which the Japanese believe could easily happen if the pipes were straight. 

Only the street that runs across the length of the Island has houses built on both sides. These houses, and indeed the entire Island, were built at the expense of several inhabitants of **Nagasaki**. We still pay a yearly rent to them or their heirs, based on the original agreement, of 6,500 silver pieces <note>original: "Siumome"; likely referring to silver monme, a Japanese currency unit</note>. This price is far beyond the actual value of the property. All the houses are built of wood, primarily fir, and are quite paltry and poor, looking more like simple cottages. Behind the main street, the Dutch East India Company paid for a convenient house to be built for the sale of our goods, as well as two warehouses strong enough to withstand fire. Very recently, several people were executed at this same spot for smuggling; on this occasion, the Governors informed us that unless proper care is taken in the future, the Dutch will be punished for this crime just as the natives are.

### The History of JAPAN. Book IV. ###

They remain there as long as they stay in the harbor, usually two or three months. After the ships have left the harbor, the Director of our trade remains on the island with a small number of people—about seven or more, if he thinks it necessary. In former times, when our trade was free and more extensive, there were seldom fewer than twenty who stayed there. Now, considering that there are so very few Dutchmen left on the island, one would imagine that the Japanese had no reason in the world to be uneasy or in any way apprehensive of our conduct. 

Surely such a small number of people, deprived of arms and ammunition (the very first thing which the Japanese take into their custody upon the arrival of our ships), would never think to make any attempt against the peace and tranquility of the Empire. As for smuggling, they have prevented any attempts of that kind on our side by not only taking an exact inventory of all our goods and commodities, but by locking them up under their own locks and seals. Even the cloth and fabrics brought over for our own use must be delivered into the custody of the *Ottona* <term>Ottona: The Japanese official or "ward head" responsible for managing the Dutch residents on Dejima.</term>, until one of their own tailors, sworn for this purpose, cuts them, allowing each of us just enough to make a proper suit. 

But what they have even less reason to be apprehensive of is the subversion of their pagan doctrine and religion, so little conspicuous are the principles of Christianity in our lives and actions. <note>The author, Engelbert Kaempfer, is making a dry, satirical observation here; the Dutch merchants were required to strictly hide their religion—even refraining from outward prayer—to avoid the same fate as the Portuguese, who were expelled for missionary activities.</note> Nevertheless, so many guards, corporations, and societies, with their numerous attendants—all bound by oath and themselves jealous and mistrustful of one another—are set to guard and narrowly watch us. They treat us as if we were the greatest criminals, traitors, or spies—in a word, the worst and most dangerous set of people. To use a very significant expression of the Japanese, they treat us as if we were, and I think we really are, *Fitozitz* <term>Hitojichi: A hostage or a person held as security for an agreement.</term>, that is, the Emperor’s Hostages. This leads me to give an account of these several guards and watches under whose inspection we stand.

<margin>Gate Guard.</margin>The first and chief of our guards is the *Monban*, or *Gate-Guard*, which guards the gate leading toward the town. This is the only passage left for people to go in or out, and for goods to be carried in or out. It is staffed daily by five persons, not counting their servants. At the time when our goods are sold, there are never fewer than ten, but sometimes twelve or more; their number at that time is very uncertain. At the same time, there are constantly two men of the *Funaban* <term>Funaban: The ship and harbor guard.</term>, two of the *Siuninſi* <term>Shuninsu: Spy guards or inspectors.</term>, a servant of the *Ninban Toſij Jori* <term>Ninban Toshiyori: The presiding mayor or town elder currently on duty.</term>, and a servant of the *Dſioſoſj* <term>Joshi: The deputy mayor or assistant official.</term>, as the chief officers of the *Sottomatz* <term>Shitamachi: The "lower town" or the district of Nagasaki nearest the harbor.</term> do duty there. One of the two last mentioned keeps the journals of the guard, wherein is entered what passes from hour to hour, which persons go in or out, and what things are carried in or out, for the instruction of the governors of the town.

<margin>*Mawariban*, or the Round.</margin>
The second guard, or rather watch, is the *Mawariban* <term>Mawariban: Literally the "rotating watch" or "round," a night patrol system.</term>. During the periods when our goods are being sold, the **Ottona** (the head of our street), our landlords, and the officials of our exchequer perform this duty themselves—as they are held responsible for any accidents—or else they send their most trusted servants.

They go around knocking at every door to ask whether there are any Japanese people hidden in the house and to remind the inhabitants to be careful with fire. The **Ottona** <term>Ottona: The Japanese head official of the ward or island, responsible for order and administration.</term> must be present himself at least once a night; according to the custom of the country, his iron fire-staff, hung with iron rings as a badge of his authority, is carried rattling behind him. <note>This staff, known as a *kanabō* or *hikizue*, signaled the watchman's approach to deter criminals and alert residents.</note> At the same time, the Dutch keep another watch of their own, using their own people to go on rounds across the island all night long to ensure their masters are not robbed by their Japanese guards.

<margin>Funaban: Ship or Harbor Guard</margin>
Besides all these various guards I have mentioned so far, there are others appointed to have general oversight of all foreigners (meaning the Dutch, as well as the Chinese and those Eastern nations who trade with Japan under their name). The chief of these is the **Funaban** <term>Funaban: The harbor police or maritime guard responsible for monitoring ships and water security.</term>, or ship and harbor guard, which patrols the harbor all night, particularly around our island. <margin>Officers of our Island</margin>
I proceed therefore to our officers—the people involved in the government of our island and the carrying out of our trade, whether they are appointed by the Governors of **Nagasaki** or hired by us and paid out of the money yearly withheld from the price of our goods. Although all these people maintain themselves and their families entirely on what they earn from us and our service, one would take them for our sworn enemies based on their conduct. They seem always intent on doing us whatever mischief they can, and they are all the more to be feared because their hatred and enmity are hidden under the plausible mask of friendship, deference, and goodwill.

<margin>The Ottona</margin>
The chief of our officers, who ought to be mentioned first, is **Fofijkawa Gibujemon** <note>Original: "Fofijkawa Gibujemon," likely the Japanese official Yoshikawa Gibuemon.</note>, our current **Ottona**. In addition to the command he has over one of the streets of the town, he is also entrusted with the command of our island, **Deshima**. He ranks next after our chief interpreter, who is the president of the whole group of interpreters (which does not fall under the Ottona’s control). The business of his office is as follows: He must take care of whatever relates to us, our island, and its government. He inspects our trade and the yearly sale of our goods, alongside and with the assistance of the group of interpreters. He keeps a particular list of our goods that belong to private individuals, keeps them in his custody, and gives orders on when and how they are to be sold. He ensures that our streets, houses, and other buildings are kept in good repair, and also, as much as lies in his power, that they are not harmed by thieves, fire, or other accidents. He protects our servants, cooks, kitchen masters, or daily laborers, and all persons within the reach of his jurisdiction. He settles any disputes arising between them. He admits

He admits and swears them into their respective employments, and dismisses them as he pleases. He must keep us in strict obedience to the Imperial orders, though he is very cautious in laying any commands upon us of his own accord and sole authority, knowing that we would refuse to obey them in such a case. 

However, he has so much power over us that in case any considerable crime is committed, or any disregard shown to the Imperial orders by any one of us, he can arrest him and lay him in irons, of which there are many and almost daily instances. Our present **Ottona** <term>Ottona: The Japanese official serving as the head of a city ward or the Dutch trade island.</term>, while on one hand he worked himself into no small esteem and favor with the government through his great severity in the execution of his office—and chiefly by having betrayed us and our interests in a late affair—is on the other hand much hated by us. I will not take it upon myself to examine what reasons he might allege for his conduct in that affair, though I have been credibly informed he had very good ones. 

Thus far I must do justice to his character and own that he shows a great deal of prudence in his conduct; he is in no way given to greed or falsehood, and is also an enemy to ignorance and brutality. He is so well versed in the moral doctrine of **Koosi** (or **Confucius**) <note>Confucianism was the state ideology of the Tokugawa Shogunate, emphasizing social order and hierarchy.</note> and in the history, laws, and religion of his country, that he has been requested to write the history of the Province of **Hizen**.

*   A **Nichi-yoshi** <term>Nichi-yoshi: A daily messenger or inspector who reported on the physical state of the island.</term>, or Messenger, whose business it is to daily examine the condition and safety of the locks at the water-gates, the state of our warehouses, and other buildings, and to give his master notice of what he finds out of repair.
*   Several **Hissha** <term>Hissha: Clerks or scribes responsible for record-keeping and inventory.</term>, or Clerks, who are to make lists of all the moveable goods belonging to private persons which may be disposed of, to seal them up in the **Ottona's** name, and to take them into safe custody.

I will not mention at present several other inferior officers who are at all times in readiness to put his orders into execution. He is allowed the same salary by the **Dutch East India Company** <note>Also known as the VOC (Vereenigde Oost-Indische Compagnie).</note> as the chief interpreter, and receives the same share of the money detained by order of the government from the price of our goods. <margin>Proprietors of our Island.</margin>
Next to the **Ottona** <term>Ottona: The Japanese official serving as the head of a city ward or the Dutch trade island.</term> are the **Desima Tsijuonin** <term>Desima Tsijuonin: Literally "Island Landlords"; the 24 owners of the properties on Dejima.</term>, that is, our twenty-four landlords, or proprietors of our Island. They visit us but seldom, except during the time of our sales, when they make their appearance daily to look after the condition of our houses, to be present and lend a helping hand in making a list of all our commodities, household goods, and other items, and—what is more—to keep a watchful eye over us, their tenants, and to examine our behavior and conduct. By virtue of the laws and customs of the country, they are answerable for us; in case of accidents or misdemeanors, they are sentenced to share in either the financial loss or the punishment.

<margin>Company of Interpreters.</margin>
The chief and most extensive company, or guild, of the officers of our island is that of the **Hollanda Tsjuunsi** <term>Hollanda Tsjuunsi: The official guild of Dutch-Japanese interpreters.</term>, or Dutch Interpreters, a very numerous body generally consisting of about 150 persons. During my stay in **Japan** their number was not complete, there being then no more than 123. The government took care to provide such a large number of interpreters on purpose to make it unnecessary for us to learn the language of the country. By this means, they keep us—as much as lies in their power—ignorant of its present state and condition, its customs, laws, commerce, history, and other things which might be worthy of our knowledge and inquiry. <note>Kaempfer highlights the deliberate policy of isolation (Sakoku), where the high ratio of handlers to foreigners served as a barrier to cultural exchange.</note> Formerly there were not nearly so many, but it has since been thought proper to increase their number, chiefly for two reasons: first, so that many more of the inhabitants of **Nagasaki** should be enabled by this means to earn an honest livelihood; and secondly, so that we should be more narrowly watched during our sales. A more particular account of this corporation, its management, laws, and customs, which may serve as a pattern for other similar guilds established in this country, would be too large a subject to enlarge upon at present; I shall therefore defer it to the next chapter. For the same reasons, I shall also now refrain from giving an account of the **Desima Fisia** <term>Desima Fisia: Secretaries of the island who served as deputies to the interpreters.</term>, or Secretaries of our island, who are deputies of the interpreters; the **Desima Tsietzi** <term>Desima Tsietzi: Inspectors overseeing the porters and daily laborers.</term>, or the inspectors of our porters and daily laborers; and the **Cannabana Kama** <term>Cannabana Kama: Directors and officers of the treasury.</term>, or the directors and other officers of our Treasury. All these various offices and companies have a more particular relation to our trade and commerce, which will be the subject of the following chapter.

<margin>Commissioners for Victualling.</margin>
Next to the several corporations and offices mentioned above, that of the **Kaimono Tskai** <term>Kaimono Tskai: Officials in charge of purchasing supplies; literally "shopping messengers."</term> must be considered, or—as they are otherwise called with a word half-derived from **Portuguese**—the **Compranakama** <term>Compranakama: From the Portuguese "comprar" (to buy) and Japanese "nakama" (guild/group); the provisioners' guild.</term>, which is to say, Commissioners for Victualling <note>Victualling: The process of providing food, drink, and daily necessities.</note>. It is composed at present of about seventeen housekeepers of **Nagasaki**, along with their families. Their business is to provide our island with victuals, drink, household goods, and whatever else...

### Chapter VI. The History of JAPAN. ###

->333<-

...anything else we require, or are permitted to buy of this nature. No one else, except for the members of this guild, is allowed to sell us any food or goods, though they overcharge us so significantly that they make us pay at least twice or thrice the market price. They also take responsibility for providing our men, upon request, with prostitutes; and truly, our young sailors—who are usually unacquainted with the virtue of moderation—are not ashamed to spend five **Rixdollars** <note>A common European silver trade coin.</note> for a single night’s pleasure. This is for the company of women whom a native of **Nagasaki** could have for about two or three **Maas** <note>A 'mace', a Japanese unit of silver weight and currency.</note>, as they are by no means the best or most beautiful. Furthermore, the **Bawd** <note>A woman who manages a brothel or prostitutes.</note> receives no more than one **Siumome** <note>original: "Siumome"; refers to a 'momme', a unit of silver weight approximately equal to 3.75 grams.</note>, which is about one-third of the fee. The remainder is placed into the treasury of this company for their own private use and, as they claim, to pay for the proper servants needed to escort the young women over to our island.

<margin>Officers of the Kitchen.</margin>
Next are the **Daidokoro Nomono** <term>Daidokoro Nomono: Literally 'kitchen people'; the official guild of cooks and staff assigned to the Dutch.</term>, that is, the officers of the kitchen. This company consists of three cooks who serve in rotation, each for one month (for which service they are each paid twenty-four **Siumome**), two kitchen assistants, an apprentice or two—who are generally the cooks' own sons and likely to eventually succeed their fathers—and finally some laborers to carry water. Occasionally, the servants of the commissioners for victualling <note>The officials in charge of supplying food and provisions.</note> assist them. This is why our table is so very expensive, as for the greater part of the year—with the exception of the trading season—there are actually more cooks than there are people to cook for. Despite this, we have strict orders from the governors of the city not to reduce this number in the slightest, nor are we allowed to have our food prepared by our own people. Formerly, the head cook was paid six, the second four, and the third three **thails** <note>Taels; a unit of silver currency where 10 mace equals 1 tael.</note> per month. However, since 1674, we have been forced by an order from the governors to pay 150 taels a year to the first, 130 to the second, and 100 to the third, which is nearly double their previous wages. There are also other individuals who occasionally perform minor services in and for our kitchen, such as a gardener or a man to look after our livestock. (Though we have very few animals, and they are of little use to us, as the males are often secretly poisoned or have their legs broken during the night to prevent them from breeding too much; this, it is feared, would harm the profits of the victualling commissioners.) There are also other menial servants. Because this work is viewed by the lower classes in **Nagasaki** as a small benefit or perquisite that everyone wishes to share in, these servants are rotated once a month. New ones are sent from every street in **Nagasaki** to take their place. However, the primary reason they rotate them so frequently is that the authorities fear a longer stay would make them too familiar with us, and perhaps too sympathetic to our interests.

# The History of JAPAN. Book IV. #

->334<-

<margin>
Servants of the Dutch.
</margin>
The Dutch, by a special favor, are permitted to have several young boys to wait upon them during the day. These boys are entered into the **Ottona’s** <term>Ottona: The Japanese ward headman or chief official responsible for the oversight of the Dutch island of Dejima.</term> register in the capacity of messengers. They are commonly the sons of the inferior interpreters and other officers of our island, who use this opportunity to learn the Dutch language and thereby qualify themselves in time to succeed their fathers. However, care is taken that they do not remain in our service any longer than they are considered simple and ignorant of the state and interests of their country; or otherwise, they stay only as long as the **Ottona** pleases to grant them leave. This is never done without sufficient security given upon oath by an honest inhabitant of **Nagasaki**, who binds himself to be answerable for their misbehavior. In justice to these young boys, it must be admitted that a greater readiness to do what they are commanded, and a greater fidelity in guarding the goods entrusted to them by their masters, is hardly to be found in any other nation.

<margin>
Tradesmen.
</margin>
Lastly, there are also some tradesmen and artisans from several guilds in **Nagasaki** who are permitted to come over to our island when sent for, provided they have permission from the Governors, which must be obtained every time they are needed. They divide their profits with the rest of their guild. Furthermore, to remain in favor with the **Ottona** and our interpreters—who act as the chief managers of our business—they provide them with a present once a year.

These are the various officers concerned with the management of our island and trade. They are permitted, on this account, to come over to us and to converse with us, though never without some plausible pretext. Even so, no sincere friendship, good understanding, or familiarity can be expected from them by any means. For before they are admitted into our service, they must bind themselves by a solemn oath to deny us all forms of communication, credit, or friendship that might in any way tend to support or promote our interests. This obligation must be frequently renewed by them as long as they continue in our service.

<margin>
Oath.
</margin>
The oath, as it is taken in **Nagasaki** and everywhere else in the Empire, is a solemn obligation to perform certain tasks, made according to a fixed form as contained in the laws and statutes of the Empire. The person who takes this oath prays for the vengeance of the supreme gods of the heavens and the chief magistrates of his country to fall upon him, his family, his household, his friends, and his near relations, in case he does not sincerely fulfill and satisfy every article as it is read and specified to him. After the form of the oath, he must sign his name and seal it with his seal dipped in black ink. For a still stronger confirmation, he pours some drops of his own blood upon it, which he draws by pricking one of his fingers behind the nail. ...even the slightest violation of it is a crime that cannot be atoned for except by shedding the very same blood with which the oath was confirmed.

<margin>
*Articles sworn to.*
</margin>
The articles signed and solemnly sworn to in this manner differ in both number and importance, depending on the person taking the oath, the nature of their office, and the extent of the power entrusted to them. Generally, these oaths can be divided into three types.

The first type, which is the most significant and carries the most severe punishments for any violation, is signed and sworn by the *Ottoná* <term>Ottona: The Japanese headman or chief official responsible for managing the Dutch enclave of Dejima.</term>, the chief interpreter, his deputy, and their apprentices (who are the designated successors to these roles). This oath is only renewed upon the arrival of a new Governor, who administers it in person at his own palace. This is not done by having the participants repeat words after him, hold up three fingers, or lay their hands upon a sacred book—as is customary in European countries—but by having them sign the articles read to them with their own seals and blood, in the manner described previously.

The second type of articles, which are of less weight and consequence, are signed and sworn to in the same manner by the main body of our interpreters, our cooks, the treasury officers, the secretaries and clerks of our island, the *Kuli* Masters <term>Kuli Masters: Overseers of the manual laborers or "coolies" who worked on the island.</term> (the inspectors of our workmen), and the commissioners for victualing <note>Those responsible for providing food and supplies.</note>. The oath is administered to them by the *Ottoná* and the chief interpreter in the *Ansenji* temple <note>original: "Ansenfi"; likely the Anzen-ji temple, belonging to the Tendai sect.</note> of the *Tendai* sect <term>Tendai: A major school of Japanese Buddhism.</term>, which is the usual place for their meetings.

The third type of articles, which are of the least significance, are sworn to by all our menial servants and lower officers, the young men permitted to wait upon us, and the workmen and tradesmen who have any business with us. They take this oath only in the presence of the *Ottoná* and within his own house. Because this last oath is taken by low-ranking, young, and insignificant people, it is not considered sufficient on its own. For this reason, every one of them must find a respectable house-owner in town to act as a guarantor for their good behavior and to be held answerable for any of their misconduct. The commissioners for victualing, who are likewise responsible for the behavior of the servants in their office, require a particular oath from them; however, they only require the servants to apply their seals and do not demand they use their blood.

<margin>
*How often the oath is repeated.*
</margin>
The wary and suspicious magistrates are not satisfied with having our officers and servants of the second and third ranks take the oath only once a year. It must be repeated at least twice. The first time is near the beginning of the year, during the solemn ceremony where they perform the act of trampling over the image of our blessed Savior on the Cross, the Virgin Mary, and other holy figures <note>This ceremony is known as *fumi-e*. It was a loyalty test used by the Tokugawa shogunate to identify Christians or ensure their total renunciation of the faith.</note>. This serves as a public and undeniable proof that they renounce the Christian religion forever. The oath is administered a second time after the arrival of our ships in the harbor; this is done to remind them of their solemn obligations and to renew their hostility toward us. Those who are chosen to accompany us on our journey to court...

<margin>Orders of the *Ottoná*, etc.</margin>
In addition to all the articles mentioned above, which are so solemnly sworn to, several specific orders are created and published by the *Ottoná* <term>Ottoná: The Japanese headman or chief official responsible for managing the Dutch enclave of Dejima.</term>, and posted in various parts of our island. The primary purpose of these is to instruct those permitted to communicate with us on how to behave regarding our affairs and the dispatch of our business during their stay at Dejima. Five of these orders are posted at the time of our public sale at the entrance of the *Ottoná*’s house, where he resides during the summer. The most important relates to the inspection of our imported and exported goods. The appointed inspectors receive necessary instructions from the *Ottoná*, along with a list of all contraband goods to guide their work. A proclamation from the Governors concerning the conduct of individuals entering or leaving our island during the sale is posted at every street corner. Proper orders regarding the regulation and management of our treasury are displayed in that office, and those concerning our interpreters are kept in the house where they meet.

<margin>Merchants.</margin>
Beyond those sworn into the various offices managing our island and trade, others are permitted to visit us, though only during the time of our sale and on other specified days. Among these are the merchants who come to buy imported goods, and the copper merchants (or their agents and deputies) who come primarily from *Miaco* <note>original: "Miaco"; referring to Kyoto, then the imperial capital of Japan.</note> and other parts of the Empire. When our sale concludes, various local manufactures—such as lacquerware and various copper items, which the Japanese craft with extraordinary skill, as well as other domestic goods—are offered for sale in a specially constructed area. None of the people mentioned so far may pass through our gates without undergoing a search and producing a valid permit, which is typically required upon their departure. However, the commissioners or deputies of the Governors—who have a pike carried before them as a sign of their authority—and their attendants who wear two swords, are exempt from being searched. Also exempt are the *Ottoná*, eight of our senior interpreters, and their sons or apprentices who are privileged to learn our language to qualify as future successors. This special favor is granted to the *Ottoná* as the commissioned inspectors of our behavior, and to the others as our avowed enemies, both by virtue of their oath and for the sake of their own interests <note>The author highlights the paradoxical role of interpreters: they were essential for communication but were sworn to remain suspicious and distant from the Dutch.</note>.

<margin>Pass-board.</margin>
The pass-board is a small wooden board about three inches long and two inches wide. It features the common or family name of the *Ottoná* <term>Ottoná: The Japanese official or headman responsible for a specific street or ward; in this case, the overseer of the Dutch enclave.</term> of the street where the bearer lives, with his seal stamped below in black ink, a limitation on how long the pass remains valid, and the name of the bearer. On the other side is an impression of the larger mark of our *Ottoná*, made with a hot iron, with his title *Dejima Ottoná* <note>Original: "Deſima Ottona"</note> added to it. When our ships are expected shortly in the harbor, he sends a sufficient quantity of these marked boards to all the *Ottonás* of the town for the use of the inhabitants of their streets, or for strangers who travel there from all parts of the Empire at that time for the sake of our trade.

<margin>Orders of the Japanese to the Dutch.</margin>
The orders of the Japanese Government to the Dutch are communicated in two ways: partly read to the director of our trade in the Imperial palace at Edo <note>Original: "Jedo", the seat of the Shogunate, modern-day Tokyo.</note> in the presence of some of the Privy Councilors, and partly communicated to us by the Governors of Nagasaki, either by word of mouth or through their *Bugjōs* <term>Bugjō: A high-ranking magistrate or deputy acting on behalf of the Governor.</term> and our interpreters. Upon the arrival of our ships, our interpreters take special care to remind us to strictly obey these orders. These mandates primarily aim to prevent smuggling of any kind, as the rules are precisely detailed for the instruction of newcomers. They also require us to avoid all outward marks of Christianity <note>Following the suppression of the Shimabara Rebellion, the Japanese government strictly prohibited Christian symbols and practices; the Dutch were only allowed to stay if they remained entirely secular in public.</note> in the presence of the natives and to live in harmony with our own officers, servants, and the other inhabitants of Nagasaki. Otherwise, they do not need to remind us to remain within the bounds of self-restraint, because there are so many guards and watches placed upon us in every corner of our island that one would think it more than sufficient to prevent any opportunity for loose or extravagant behavior.

<margin>Pleasures allowed them.</margin>
Thus, we live all year round little better than prisoners, confined within the limits of a small island under the perpetual and narrow inspection of our keepers. It is true that we are occasionally allowed a small "escape" or indulgence. However, without flattering ourselves, we cannot suppose this to be an act of love or friendship, as it is never granted unless it is to pay our respects to great men or for some other business necessary for us and advantageous for the natives. Furthermore, leaving the island on these occasions gives us no more liberty than we enjoy at home; this is evident by the great expenses of our journeys and visits, the number of guards and inspectors who constantly attend us as if we were traitors and declared enemies of the Empire, and by the specific opportunities that call us abroad, which are as follows.

<margin>Journey to Court.</margin>
After the departure of our ships, the director of our trade (the resident of the Dutch East India Company) sets out with a large retinue on his journey to the court to pay his respects to the Emperor <note>Referring to the Shogun, the military ruler of Japan, who held actual political power.</note> and to provide the usual yearly presents. be made once a year, not only by the Dutch, but even by all the Princes and Lords of the Empire, as being the Emperor's <note>Kaempfer refers to the Shogun—the military ruler in Edo—as the "Emperor," though the titular Emperor resided in Kyoto.</note> vassals, and our own embassy is looked upon at court, as an homage paid by the Dutch Nation to the Emperor of Japan, as their sovereign Lord. As soon as we come to an Inn, we are without delay carried upstairs, if possible, or into the back apartments, which have no other view but into the yard, which for a still greater security, and to prevent any thoughts of an escape, is immediately shut and nailed up. All these people, though never so needless, must be maintained at the company's expense.

<margin>Visits to the Governors.</margin>
Before our departure for Edo, and again upon our return from thence, our Captain as he is called by the Japanese, or the Director of our Factory, with one of his company, goes to make a visit to the Governors of Nagasaki at their Palace, to return them thanks for their favors, and to entreat the continuation of their protection. Now, not even this visit can be made without a numerous train of guards, soldiers and bailiffs, carrying halters <note>Original: "halters"; these were ropes carried by officials to bind and arrest individuals at a moment's notice.</note> in their pockets. The **Ottona**, <term>Ottona: A Japanese official or headman responsible for the Dutch enclave at Dejima.</term> some of our chief Interpreters, and some few of our servants, are also of the party. The whole company is often obliged to stay a good while at the **Genquaban**, <term>Genkan-ban: Guards stationed at the entrance or "great house-guard" of an official residence.</term> or great House-guard, before they are admitted to audience.

Another visit, and with the like numerous attendance, is made to the Governors, by the director of our factory, upon the **Hassiaku**, <term>Hassaku: The first day of the eighth month of the lunar calendar, a day traditionally used for formal visits and gift-giving.</term> that is, the first day of the eighth month, when it is usual to make them a present.

<margin>Some more regulations concerning the Dutch.</margin>
If the Governors want to speak with any of the Dutch, upon any particular occasion, either to communicate new orders to them, or else to get some information from them, the same means and inspections are made use of to bring them over to their palace, and they must take it as a singular favor, if they are admitted into the Governors' presence, who often send only some of their officers to let them know what they were sent for.
