# Chapter VI. The History of JAPAN. #

->339<-

The few Dutchmen who remain at *Deshima* after our ships have departed are permitted once or twice a year to take a walk into the adjacent countryside, and in particular to view the temples around *Nagasaki*. This liberty is granted more often to physicians and surgeons, under the pretense of searching for medicinal plants. However, this pleasure walk turns out to be very expensive for us, for it must be made in the company of the *Ottona* <term>Ottona: A local ward headman or Japanese official acting as a supervisor of the Dutch.</term>, our regular interpreters, and other officers in our service. We are expected to treat all of them to a handsome dinner at one of the temples of the *Ikosju Sect* <term>Ikosju: The Ikkō-shū, a powerful branch of Pure Land Buddhism (Jōdo Shinshū).</term>. On these occasions, we must—even while appearing satisfied—watch our purses be "strongly squeezed" for the most basic civilities shown to us by the priests of that temple.

Another day is set apart for viewing five large boats, which must be constantly maintained at the expense of the Dutch East India Company for the loading and unloading of our ships. This excursion is again conducted with the same numerous retinue of officials, whom we must afterwards entertain at dinner at one of the neighboring temples.

The festival of *Suwa* <note>This refers to the Nagasaki Kunchi festival, held at the Suwa Shrine to honor the city's patron deity.</note>, the patron and protector of *Nagasaki*, occurs just at the time when our ships are lying in the harbor. Our people are permitted to view this solemnity from a scaffold built at our own expense. Our presence is not only thought to be honorable to their Saint, but—what they value even more—is advantageous to many of his worshippers who profit from us. It can easily be imagined that our train of guards and attendants is not reduced for such an occasion. On the contrary, we are examined and searched four times before we reach the place where the ceremony is performed. We are then counted several times with the utmost accuracy as we go up and down from the scaffold, as if it were possible for one of us to slip through their fingers. Our slaves are also admitted to this ceremony, referred to as "black Dutchmen" <note>Original: "black Dutchmen." This term refers to the enslaved people or servants brought by the Dutch from their colonies in Southeast Asia, such as Batavia (modern-day Jakarta).</note>.

When one of our ships is discovered steering toward the harbor, some of the Dutchmen left at *Deshima* are sent to meet her. This is done to get preliminary information about her cargo and condition, both for our own instruction and for the governors. For this purpose, the Company constantly keeps two barges in readiness, large enough to carry our usual numerous attendance. These officials, along with the *Compra Nakama* <term>Compra Nakama: A guild of licensed Japanese victuallers or suppliers who provided the Dutch with food and provisions.</term> (the commissioners for victualling) who attend in their own barge with a good supply of food and refreshments, must all be treated to a meal on the nearby small island of *Iwara Gasima* <note>Likely Iō-jima, an island near the entrance to Nagasaki harbor.</note>. The entire cost is, once again, born by the Company.

There are likewise standing orders in case of fire in or near *Deshima* to carry us and our belongings away into safe custody in another location. These and several other regulations can be seen in detail in the last chapter of this book.

# The History of JAPAN. Book IV. #

->340<-

<margin>Civility of the Japanese:</margin>
These are the days allowed to us for our recreation—if it can even be called recreation to be led about like prisoners under the narrow inspection of so many watchful eyes. However, in justice to the natives, I cannot help but admit that even amidst all the troubles and hardships we are exposed to in this country, we have at least this comfort: we are treated by our numerous guardians and overseers with apparent civility, with kindness, compliments, gifts of food, and other marks of respect, so long as it is not inconsistent with their national policy. But this polite and reasonable behavior toward us is due more to the custom of the country and the innate civility and good manners of the natives than to any particular respect they have for us or any favor they wish to show us.

<margin>Their Injustice.</margin>
In fact, quite the opposite is evident from their conduct toward us in many instances, which is not only unreasonable but, in the highest degree, dishonest. It will not be out of place to mention a few details which I know to be facts, either from my own experience or from their own confessions in private conversation. It would be endless to list all the roguish tricks and cheats our Interpreters have played on us at all times, all the unjust demands laid upon us (chiefly during the time of our sales), and the unreasonable requests made even of our "Captains"—as they call them—the directors of our <term>factory: A "factory" in this period was not a manufacturing plant, but a fortified trading post or warehouse where "factors" (merchants) resided and conducted business.</term>, despite their official status as public ambassadors to the Emperor.

<margin>Instances thereof.</margin>
Generally, any Japanese person who appears to have any regard or friendship for the Dutch is not looked upon as an honest man or a true lover of his country. This maxim is grounded upon the following principle: that it is absolutely contrary to the interest of the country, against the pleasure of their sovereign, and even—by virtue of the oaths they have taken—against the supreme will of the Gods and the dictates of their conscience to show any favor to foreigners. They carry this false reasoning even further and pretend that a friend of foreigners must necessarily be an enemy to his country and a rebel to his sovereign. For they say that if the country should happen to be attacked or invaded by these foreigners, the ties of friendship would oblige such a person to stand by them, and consequently to become a traitor to his own country and ruler.

For this reason, to overcharge a Dutchman, to ask extravagant prices of him, and to cheat and defraud him—as far as they think will not damage their own reputations, which they regard very carefully—are seen as acceptable. To limit our liberties and advantages, or to propose new projects to make our servitude and condition even worse, are looked upon as good, honorable, and lawful things in themselves, and as unquestionable proof of a good Patriot.

# Chapter VI. The History of JAPAN. #

->341<-

If anyone steals anything from the Dutch and is caught with it—an act at which the *Kuli*, or porters, we employ during our sales are very skilled—there is rarely any punishment beyond returning the stolen goods and receiving a few lashes from the soldiers on duty at our gate. Sometimes the thief is banished from the island for a short time, or from the town if the crime is particularly notorious, though this happens rarely. However, the penalty for <term>smuggling: In this context, smuggling referred to "private trade" by Dutch or Japanese individuals attempting to bypass the official monopoly of the VOC and the Shogunate.</term> is nothing less than certain death, either by beheading or by the cross, depending on the nature of the crime and the level of guilt.

The loading and unloading of our ships, and all other business of this kind, must not be performed by our own crew, but by the natives. These locals are well-paid for their work, while our own men must stand idle with nothing to do but watch them. But this is not the only grievance we have reason to complain of in this regard: they always hire at least twice as many people as are necessary, and even if they work for only one hour, we must nevertheless pay them for a full day’s wages.

All the people who have anything to do for or with us—no matter how numerous or unnecessary they may be—must be supported by us. This is done either directly through fixed salaries or indirectly through the money which the Governors of the town deduct from the price of our commodities, in the manner previously described.

No Dutchman can send a letter out of the country unless the contents are first recorded in a Register-book kept for this purpose, and a copy of it is left with the Governors. To accomplish this, two identical copies must always be delivered to the proper officer: one remains on file, and the other is sent aboard the outward-bound ships. As for letters sent from abroad, all official ones must be sent directly to the Governors before they are opened. However, regarding private letters, there are secret ways and means to deliver them to us, which the government ignores even though it is technically against the law.

No Japanese person is permitted to send any letters or presents to their relatives abroad <note>This refers to the Japanese wives and children of Dutch men who were exiled to Batavia (modern-day Jakarta) when the exclusion laws were tightened in the 1630s.</note> or to receive any from them, unless the items are first brought to the Governors to be opened and left entirely to their disposal.

Formerly, when a Dutchman died at *Nagasaki*, his body was considered unworthy of Japanese soil and was thrown into the sea somewhere outside the harbor. More recently, however, a vacant spot of waste ground on the mountain *Inassa* was assigned to us, and permission was given to decently bury our dead there. Even so, a Japanese guard is appointed to watch the place, a task which is generally performed with such great care that

# The History of JAPAN. Book IV. #

...a few days after the burial, it would be nearly impossible to find out where the body was interred.

It is a simple matter for anyone, whether a native or a foreigner, to make a claim against the Dutch; however, we find it very difficult to obtain justice from others. In the first case, the Government is always willing to grant damages to the complaining party without so much as considering whether the claim is against the company as a whole or against specific officers and servants, or whether it is just to make the former suffer for the wrongdoings of the latter. In the second case, if we have a complaint to make, we generally meet with so many difficulties and tedious delays that it would deter anyone from pursuing even the most righteous cause. 

One instance out of many will be sufficient to make the reader realize the truth of this claim. The famous Chinese Pirate **Coxeng** <note>The Dutch name for Zheng Chenggong, better known as Koxinga (1624–1662), a Ming loyalist who expelled the Dutch from Taiwan.</note>, having made himself master of the island of **Formosa** <note>The historical name for Taiwan.</note> and our fort **Tayovan** (or Zelandia) on that island, gave us cause for retaliation. Around the year 1660, by way of reprisals, we attacked a large junk of his bound for the said island with about 300 men on board. We disabled her with our fire so effectively that, although she drifted for about thirteen days after the attack, no more than nine of the entire company survived. Upon this, heavy complaints were made by the Chinese to the Government of Nagasaki, and with such good effect that in the same year, 27,000 *Siumome* <term>Siumome: A Dutch rendering of "silver momme," a Japanese unit of currency weight (approx. 3.75 grams).</term> in damages were assigned to them from our treasury. 

Sometime later, around the year 1672, one of our ships called the *Kuylenburg* was unfortunately stranded upon the coasts of **Formosa**. The ship's company was barbarously murdered, and the whole cargo was taken into possession by the Chinese subjects of **Coxeng**. We then made our complaints before the very same court against this act of hostility, but with so little success that, far from having any damages assigned to us, we could not even obtain the restitution of a single farthing.

# Chap. VII. The History of JAPAN. #

...particular in my account of this corporation, its unworthiness notwithstanding, and to lay down the rules and maxims it is governed by, so far as they came within the reach of my own knowledge. I do this because it may serve as a pattern to show how other corporations are governed, and what strict regulations the policy of this country is subject to.

<margin>Their division</margin>
**Tsjuunsj**, or *Tsjuunsi Sju* <note>Original Japanese: *Tsūji-shū*. The author interprets this as "through-mouth people."</note>, in the literal sense of the characters this word is expressed by, is as much as to say, a *through-mouth*, or a *through-mouth people*, by which must be understood persons through whose mouths things must be dispatched <note>Meaning interpreters or intermediaries.</note>. They differ in rank and dignity, and may be divided into two orders. Those of the first order, who are our interpreters in ordinary, have leave to come to our island whenever and upon what occasion they please. Those of the second order are admitted only during the time of our sale, and even then, not so much to serve us as Interpreters, as to be useful to the Government by having a watchful eye over our conduct.

<margin>First order of Interpreters.</margin>
The first order of our Interpreters consists of eight persons, called **Fon Tsjuusi**, or *Fon Tsjuunsj* <note>Original Japanese: *Hon-tsūji*, meaning "True" or "Full" Interpreters.</note>, which signifies the *true Interpreters*. By virtue of their office they are obliged to assist and attend us whenever there is occasion; and so far indeed they execute their duty with great preciseness that we can scarce ever for one moment get rid of their importunate presence. As they are made answerable for our conduct, they spare no pains nor trouble to keep a watchful eye over us.

<margin>Chief Interpreters.</margin>
Four of these are **O Tsjuusi** <note>Original Japanese: *Ō-tsūji*.</note>, that is *High*, or *chief Interpreters*, one of whom is **Ninban** <note>Original Japanese: *Nenban*, a term for an official serving a one-year rotation.</note>, which signifies, in the literal sense of the word, a *yearly Guardian*, as also a person who is to make his reports to another. This office is only annual: our petitions, complaints, and whatever else relates to us and to our commerce, must be delivered to him, and by him—with the consent of his brethren—to the commanding Governor or his deputy. He has the greatest share in the management of our island, in the direction of our trade, and in all our affairs in general. As *Ninban*, he presides in the college of the eight chief Interpreters. 

The four other Interpreters, though of the same order, are called **Ko Tsjuusi** <note>Original Japanese: *Ko-tsūji*.</note>, that is, *inferior Interpreters*. They have not nearly the power and authority with which the former are invested, whom they are to assist in the execution of their office. They have a *Ninban*, or President of their own, who is a sort of deputy to the chief *Ninban*, and has the first vote in the <term>Quadrumvirate</term> <note>A Latin term for a group of four men in a position of authority.</note>, or College of four, of which he is president. Both *Ninbans* attend us in our journey to court, and upon our return from there to **Nagasaki**, they quit their stations as presidents of these two colleges. If anything that relates to our commerce, or persons, is to be laid before the college of the eight chief Interpreters for a determination, it must be done in the presence of the **Ottona** <note>A Japanese official title for a ward headman or community leader.</note> of our island, who claims his place next to the first and chief...

<margin>Their salaries and perquisites</margin>
The *Tsijo* <note>Japanese: *Chijō*, meaning income or revenue.</note>, that is, the yearly salaries and perquisites of our chief Interpreters amount to a very considerable sum, and are as follows. A *Jakukio* <note>Japanese: *Yakuryō*, an official salary or allowance attached to a specific office.</note>, or Salary, which since the confinement of our persons and trade to the Island *Desima* <note>Dejima, the fan-shaped artificial island in Nagasaki harbor where the Dutch were restricted.</note>, hath been assigned them by the Emperor in proportion to every one's office and the rank he hath in the company. It was formerly a certain determined sum of money: For the present it consists in a certain quantity of silk, which as I have been informed, they are permitted to buy of us, and which if sold in the Country, yields about so much money clear gain, as their former salary amounted to. Besides this the company allows them some raw silk every year, by way of a present, or reward for their trouble, to wit, a bale, or 141 and 3 quarters *Catti* <note>A <term>Catti</term> (catty) is a traditional unit of weight in East Asia, equal to approximately 1.3 pounds or 600 grams.</note> for every chief Interpreter, which we buy for about 400 *Thails* <note>The <term>Thail</term> (tael) was a unit of currency based on a weight of silver.</note>, and is worth in *Japan* 850. Half this quantity is allowed to every inferior Interpreter. Another yearly gratuity is given to them by the company of copper merchants, as it were to reward them for their trouble, but in fact, to buy them over to their interest, and to engage them to turn the sale of copper to the best advantage. This puts us under an obligation to act the part of the best bidder for their favor, and to countermine the intentions of the copper merchants by a larger gratuity of 300, 600, or 800 *Thails*, more or less, in proportion to the quantity and goodness of the copper bought by us. Mr. *Camphuysen* <note>Andreas Cleyer or perhaps Cornelis van Outhoorn? Likely a reference to a specific Dutch Director, possibly Joannes Camphuys.</note>, when he was director of our trade, having bought 22,466 *Pickels* <note>A <term>Pickel</term> (picul) is a weight unit equivalent to about 133 pounds.</note> of refined copper, at twelve *Thails* and a half the *pickel*, and 102 *pickels* of coarse copper, made the company of Interpreters a present of 1,360 *Thails*, besides a pack instead of a pickel, which he gave to every chief Interpreter, and half a pack to every Inferior Interpreter. The *Kosen* <note>Japanese: *Kōsen*, meaning a commission or brokerage fee.</note>, that is, the tax, or duty which is laid upon foreign commodities belonging to private persons, not exceeding the value of 40,000 *Thails*, light, as they call it, or gold-money, must be paid by the buyer, at so much per cent. This makes out a sum far beyond 20,000 *Thails*, which is assigned for the joint benefit of the Governors, presiding mayor, *Ottona* <note>Japanese: *Otona*, the headman or ranking official of the local district or ward.</note>, and the whole body of Interpreters. This tax, though it be paid by the buyer, is yet in fact indirectly exacted from us, insomuch as the buyers generally take care to make up their losses, by giving us a less price for our goods. Another very advantageous perquisite both of the Interpreters and of the *Ottona*, is the selling of some goods of private persons, which remain over and above the allowed yearly sum of 40,000 *Thailes*, and are bought for them at a very cheap rate. Add to this 150 *Cubangs* <note>The <term>Cubang</term> (koban) was an oval-shaped Japanese gold coin.</note>, which the company allow them for boarding during the time of our sale, because at that time they must be constantly attending. ### Chapter VII. The History of JAPAN. ###

I will not even go into all the tricks and deceptions—some quite obvious, others more subtle—that they constantly use against us. I almost forgot to mention another significant source of their extra income: the wages for the <term>Coolies</term> <note>original: "Culis"; laborers used for heavy lifting.</note>, or the people employed in loading and unloading our ships. The interpreters keep a large portion of this money for themselves. They charge us six <term>Taels</term> <note>original: "Thails"; a unit of silver currency used in trade.</note> per person, but they only pay the workers four, and they also hire many more laborers than are actually needed. The profits made by the two interpreters chosen to accompany us to the imperial court, just from this one journey, are estimated to be around 1,200 Taels. The following examples prove this is true: there is an official requirement for twenty horses to carry us and our luggage by land from **Osaka** <note>original: "Osacca".</note> to **Edo** <note>original: "Jedo"; the modern-day city of Tokyo.</note>, and another twenty to bring us back from **Edo** to **Kyoto** <note>original: "Miaco".</note>. However, they consistently hire at least twenty extra horses and list them in the accounts at fifteen Taels each, even though they never pay more than eight.

They use the same tactics regarding the people employed to load and unload our baggage and look after our horses. In this way, they manage to charge us twice for the 186 <term>Koban</term> <note>original: "Cubangs"; oval gold coins used in the Edo period.</note> allocated for our horses and porters. They also profit from the barge used to carry our baggage from **Nagasaki** to **Osaka**; they use this trip as an opportunity to transport goods for local private merchants and always pocket the freight fees for themselves. At **Edo**, they receive tips or "gratuities" from all the high-ranking officials at court to whom we traditionally give presents in the Company’s name. Consequently, the total annual income of a chief interpreter can reach 3,000 Taels or more, and even a lower-ranking interpreter rarely earns less than 1,500. Despite this high income, they live very modestly because they must support large families and often poor relatives; due to the natural pride of the Japanese people, they will not allow their kin to appear needy. A portion of their earnings is also spent on gifts for the Governors of **Nagasaki** and their <term>Karo</term> <note>The high-ranking samurai officials who served as executive councils or deputies.</note>.

The guild of Interpreters is not only the largest group involved in managing our island and trade, but also the most expensive and the most damaging to our reputation, freedom, and well-being. They operate based on two main principles: first, to do everything in their power to gradually increase the yearly expenses of the Dutch for the benefit of their own countrymen (acting, as they see it, like true patriots); and second, to hide as many of their tricks and frauds as possible so the local population does not find out. They try to achieve both goals by restricting our movements more and more. They see this confinement as the most effective way to keep us from learning the Japanese language and to prevent any friendly conversation or familiarity with the local people. If any of our people—

### The History of JAPAN. Book IV. ###

anyone who has made any considerable progress in the Japanese language, they are sure to find some excuse to obtain an order from the Governors to expel him from the country. The only way the "Captains," as they are called here, or the directors of our trade—a role the Japanese allow them very little involvement in—can be useful to the company and show their dedication to their master’s service, is to act against these Japanese tactics. They must find polite ways to refuse the new requests that are made to them from time to time. For if even one of their demands is granted once, or any new charge, no matter how small, is allowed to be placed upon us, they turn it into a permanent precedent. In this regard, they specifically try to deceive new directors who have not been in the country before and whom they assume are not fully aware of their ways of proceeding. For this reason, they will often help a director to a very profitable trade in his first year, knowing that if their future demands are not granted, they can balance it out the next year with a much more expensive and less profitable trade.

<margin>Junior Interpreters and Apprentices.</margin>
Next to the chief interpreters, the <term>learning interpreters</term> <note>original: "Keekotjjusi"; from the Japanese *keiko-tsūji*.</note>, or apprentices, must be mentioned. There are never fewer than eight, but sometimes more, and all are the biological or adopted sons of the chief interpreters. They come to visit us every day to learn the Dutch and Portuguese languages, as well as the "art and mystery" of dealing with foreigners. They are employed as spies on several occasions, and are also tasked with inspecting the loading and unloading of our ships. They search the sailors and any persons going on board or coming from the ships to examine the imported and exported goods. For their trouble in these various tasks, the company allows them a salary of forty <term>Taels</term> <note>original: "Thails"; a currency unit based on a weight of silver.</note> a year. They also receive a share of the food allowances and several other perks.

<margin>Private Interpreters.</margin>
After the apprentice interpreters come the <term>house interpreters</term> <note>original: "Naitsjusi"; from the Japanese *nai-tsūji*, literally "inner interpreters."</note>, a name used because they are employed by individual Dutchmen within their own houses. They have no duties on our island except during the time of our yearly fair or sale. At that time, after taking a solemn oath to avoid all personal communication, intimacy, and familiarity with us, they are admitted into our service by the <term>ward official</term> <note>original: "Ottona"; the headman of the Dejima district.</note> and are each presented with one of his "Pass-boards" <note>Permits or identity tags allowing them entry to the Dutch compound.</note>. Between two and six of these people are assigned to every Dutchman for the duration of the fair, acting as interpreters in name, but in reality, they serve as spies to watch his actions. In truth, barely one in ten understands a single word of Dutch, except for a few who were formerly servants to the Dutch.

There are more than a hundred of these house interpreters, who all serve under the command of the chief interpreters, and specifically the <term>Presiding Official</term> <note>original: "Ninban"; a rotating administrative role.</note> for the time being. They, as well as the mem-

They divide this among themselves according to their rank and office. It is computed that the twelve chiefs among them receive at most two hundred Taels each, while the rest must make do with half that amount, or sometimes even less.

<margin>Clerks of the Island.</margin>

Nay, they themselves, being not always willing to dispatch their business in person, keep also their deputies. The company allows a constant salary only to two, and these are to attend us in our journey to court. The rest are rewarded by handsome gratuities at the time of our sale.

<margin>Inspectors of our Workmen.</margin>
Amongst the officers of our Island, I must not forget to mention the <term>Dejima Inspectors</term> <note>original: "Desima Tsijetzkni"</note>, or Inspectors of our <term>laborers</term> <note>original: "Kuli"; often referred to in colonial contexts as 'coolies'</note>, or Workmen. This honourable company consists of fifteen persons, who keep a list of our workmen, in order to divide the work among them, and to assign every one his task. One of these 15 is **Quarter-master**, who must be present in person, to encourage and look after them, when there is any work to be done. The whole company is to take care, that we be not robb'd by these laborers, they being very dextrous at it, whenever a favourable opportunity offers. For this reason our East-India company allows them a constant salary. The laborers, who are employ'd in lading and unlading of our ships, are people unknown to us, and taken out of the town. All we know of them is, that we must pay them well for their trouble. In order to make it beneficial to the whole town, every <term>Ward Magistrate</term> <note>original: "Ottona"; the headman of a Nagasaki neighborhood</note> is to keep a list of what people in his street are willing, or able, to serve as laborers, that in their turn they may be sent over to Dejima.

Besides the business of these people as officers of our treasury, they must also be present at the examination of all goods, imported or exported, which belong to private persons.

### Some more Particulars concerning the Dutch Trade in JAPAN. ###

<margin>Proceedings upon the arrival of our Ships.</margin>
THE Dutch ships are expected in the harbor sometime in September, toward the latter end of the Southwest **Monsoon** <note>The seasonal wind used for sailing</note>, that being the only one proper for this navigation. As soon as the spy-guards with their telescopes discover a ship steering toward the harbor and send notice of her approach to the Governors of **Nagasaki**, three persons from our **factory** <note>The Dutch trading post and residence at Dejima</note> are sent with the usual attendance to meet her about two miles outside the harbor. They deliver to our captain the necessary instructions from the director of our trade regarding his behavior, which are delivered sealed. The Interpreter and the deputies of the Governors immediately demand the list of the cargo and crew, as well as the letters on board; these are carried to **Nagasaki**, where the governors first examine them and then deliver them to our director. The ship follows as soon as possible and, having entered the harbor, salutes every **Imperial guard** <note>The military outposts protecting the bay</note> with all her guns, then

... casts anchor opposite to the town about a musket-shot from our Island <note>Dejima</note>. If the wind be contrary, rowing boats (kept for this purpose by the common people of the town) are sent at our expense, but not at our desire, to tow her in by force. In still weather they send about ten of these boats; if it be stormy, and the wind contrary, they increase the number to fifty, and sometimes to a hundred—as many as they think necessary, which is at least twice the number there is occasion for. When the ship has entered the harbour, two guard-boats with a good number of soldiers are positioned, one on each side of her, and remain there, being mounted with fresh troops every day, until she has left the harbour and reached the open sea. 

As soon as the ship has dropped anchor, a great number of officers come on board to demand all our guns, cutlasses, swords, and other arms, as also the gunpowder packed up in barrels; these are taken into their custody and kept in a storehouse built for this purpose until the ship’s departure. They also attempted in former times to remove the rudder, but having found it impractical, they now leave it in place. 

The next day after her arrival, the commissioners of the Governors come on board with their usual attendance of soldiers, interpreters, and subordinate officers, to make an exact review—in the presence of our director—of all the people on board, according to the list which has been given them. This list contains every person's name, age, birthplace, residence, and office, and the officers examine them from head to toe. Many questions are asked concerning those who died during the voyage, as well as when and of what disease they died. Even now and then a dead monkey or parrot may occasion a strict inquiry into the cause and manner of its death; they are so fastidious that they will not give their verdict without performing an inquest <note>original: "sitting upon the body itself"; a formal legal inquiry or examination of the remains</note> and carefully examining it. 

Upon this, the orders of our resident, and likewise of the Governors of Nagasaki, relating to our behaviour toward the natives, are read in Dutch <note>original: "Low Dutch"; the language of the Netherlands</note>, and afterwards, for everyone's instruction, posted in several places on board the ship and at Dejima. The same rules are observed with the rest of our ships, of which there are two, three, or four sent from Batavia <note>modern-day Jakarta, the headquarters of the Dutch East India Company</note> to Japan every year, according to the quantity of copper they require. Formerly, when the Dutch still enjoyed free trade, they sent seldom less than six or seven ships, and sometimes more, in proportion to the quantity of goods they were likely to sell.

### Chap. VIII. The History of JAPAN. ###

...being determined, the water gates of our Island <note>Dejima, the fan-shaped artificial island in Nagasaki harbor where the Dutch were confined.</note>, through which the cargo is to be brought in, are opened in the presence of the **Karoo** <note>original: *Karoo*; likely from the Japanese *karō*, meaning 'elder' or high-ranking official serving the local governor.</note>, that is, high commissioners of the Governors, and their retinue. So long as the gates are kept open, the **Karoo’s**, with their deputies and other assistants, stay in a room built for this purpose not far off. The whole body of Interpreters, as also our landlords, clerks and other officers of our Island give their attendance, as well as necessary assistance, at that time. Then they fall to work with 300 or more **Kuli’s** <note>unskilled laborers or "coolies."</note>, or workmen, always at least twice the number there is occasion for. The unloading of every ship ought to be performed within two days' time, but notwithstanding the great number of workmen they employ, they generally make a three days' work of it, in order to make it so much the more beneficial to the town. The goods are brought over from on board the ship in small boats, called **Prauen** <note>Prahus; small, flat-bottomed vessels.</note>, and kept only for this purpose at the company's expense, and within the water gates laid before the commissioners, who set them down in writing, count them, compare them with the list that has been given in, opening a bale, or two, of each sort picked out from among the rest, and then order that they should be locked up, under their seal, in the company's warehouses until the time of our sale.

The trunks belonging to private persons are set down at the entry of the Island, and there opened and examined. If the owner does not forthwith appear with his key, they proceed without any further ceremony to open them with axes. All vendible goods are taken out, and locked up under their seals. Some other things also which they do not approve of, as for instance, arms, stuff, and cloth wrought with gold and silver, as also all contraband goods, are taken into custody by the **Ottona** <note>From the Japanese *otona*, the ward headman or official responsible for the oversight of the Dutch on Dejima.</note>, who returns them to the owner upon his departure.

<margin>Contraband Goods.</margin>
No European, nor any other foreign money, and in general nothing that has the figure of a cross, saint, or beads upon it, is suffered to pass. If any such thing should be found upon any of our people, it would occasion such a confusion and fright among the Japanese, as if the whole Empire had been betrayed <note>The Tokugawa Shogunate maintained a strict ban on Christianity; any religious iconography was viewed as a threat to national security.</note>. I took notice above, in the journal of our voyage, that upon our drawing near the harbor every one was obliged, pursuant to orders, to deliver his prayer-books, and other books of divinity, as also all European money he had about him, to the captain who packed them all up in an old cask, and hid them from the natives.

<margin>Orders about Searching.</margin>
Those who are newly arrived, in going in or coming out of our Island, must suffer themselves to be searched, whether or not they have any contraband goods about them, chiefly amber and corals, which they might exchange for gold, the natives being very fond of these commodities. Even one of our directors (who was afterwards raised to the eminent post of Director-general) had it practiced upon himself, upon his first arrival in *Japan*. However this is done but seldom.

### The History of JAPAN. Book IV. ###

<margin>Pass-boards.</margin> Everyone who wishes to go on board a ship, whether for their own private business or in the service of the Company <note>The Dutch East India Company, or VOC.</note>, is obliged to take out a pass-board from the commissioners at the water-gates to show to the officials on the ship; likewise, when he returns to shore, he must obtain another from the ship’s officials. By this method, the authorities know at all times exactly how many people are on board the ship or on the shore.

<margin>Their Proceedings on board in the Night-time.</margin> At night, when the commissioners sent on board the ship return with their retinue to *Nagasaki*, the cabin is sealed up in their presence, and all the Dutchmen are accurately counted to ensure that no one is missing, which would cause a very great confusion. During my stay in *Japan*, it happened that a common sailor unfortunately drowned himself in the night without anyone noticing him falling into the water. At the review made the next morning (for these inspections are conducted every morning and night) the man was missed. This unlucky accident suddenly stopped all proceedings. The fear that it might be a Roman Catholic Priest <note>Christianity was strictly forbidden in Japan at this time, and the authorities were terrified of missionaries smuggling themselves into the country.</note> who had escaped into the countryside caused such a consternation among the Japanese that all the officers ran about scratching their heads, behaving as if they had lost their senses. Some of the soldiers in the guard-ships were already preparing to rip open their bellies <note>The practice of *seppuku*, or ritual suicide, performed to avoid the shame of failing in one's duty.</note> before superior orders could compel them to answer for their carelessness and neglect of duty. This state of panic continued until the unhappy sailor's body was finally recovered from the bottom of the sea, putting an end to their fears and further inquiries.

<margin>Water-gates shut.</margin> At all other times, except for those designated for the loading and unloading of our ships, the water-gates are kept shut. By this means, all communication is cut off between those who stay on board and those who remain on shore, both being equally confined within their proper bounds. Once the entire cargo of the ship has been brought into the warehouses in this manner, the goods lie there until the authorities decide to sell them during the two or three days of sale, which they call **Cambangs** <term>Cambang; from the Malay *kambing*, referring to the regulated trade sessions or auctions where the Dutch were allowed to sell their goods.</term>. Whatever remains unsold is carried back to the warehouses and kept there until the next year’s sale.

<margin>Goods imported by us.</margin> The following goods are imported by us: Raw silk from *China*, *Tonkin*, *Bengal*, and *Persia*; all sorts of silk, woolen, and other fabrics from the aforementioned and some other countries (provided they are not embroidered with gold or silver), such as **Taffaceel** <term>a striped or checked cotton cloth</term> from *Bengal* and the coast of *Coromandel*; large white **Pelangs** <term>a type of Chinese silk</term> rolled up, white **Gilangs** <term>a silk fabric</term>, **Armosins** <term>a thin taffeta silk</term>, **Sumongis** <term>a Japanese-style silk made abroad</term>, and **florette-yarn** <term>high-quality spun silk</term>; several sorts of half-silk Indian **Chits** <term>Chintz; printed or painted cotton cloth</term>, and coarse cotton fabrics without floral patterns and not painted; white **Gunnies** <term>coarse jute or hemp fabric</term>, **Salempuris** <term>a blue cotton cloth from India</term>, and **Paraceels**; woolen cloth from Europe, besides some other silk and woolen fabrics, chiefly serges and English serges; **Sappanwood** <note>original: *Tsiampan*</note> or dye-wood (known in Europe as **Brazilwood**), buffalo and deer hides, ray skins, wax, and buffalo horns from *Siam* <note>modern Thailand</note> and *Cambodia*; **Cordovans** <term>fine Spanish leather</term> and tanned hides from *Persia*, *Bengal*, and other places.

...places, and specifically not from *Spain* or *Manila* <note>Originally "Manhilhas." At this time, Japan strictly forbade trade with the Spanish due to their association with Catholic missionaries.</note>, under pain of incurring the Japanese authorities' utmost displeasure and facing harsh treatment. The imports include: pepper and sugar (both powdered and candied) from various parts of the **East Indies**; cloves and nutmegs from the **Spice Islands**, *Ambon*, and *Banda*; (cinnamon is currently not in demand); white sandalwood from *Timor*; **Baros Camphor**, gathered on the islands of *Borneo* and *Sumatra*; quicksilver, cinnabar, and saffron from *Bengal*; lead, saltpeter, borax, and alum from *Bengal* and *Siam* <note>Modern-day Thailand.</note>; musk from *Tonkin* <note>Northern Vietnam.</note>; benzoin resin from *Aceh*; gum lacca <note>A resin used for lacquer and dyes.</note> from *Siam*; *liquid storax* <note>A fragrant resin used in perfumes and medicine, referred to in the text as "Rosmal."</note> and *catechu* (commonly called *Japan Earth*) from *Mocha* in **Arabia Felix** <note>Originally "happy Arabia," a literal translation of the Latin *Arabia Felix*, referring to the fertile southern region of the Arabian Peninsula, modern-day Yemen.</note>; the root of *costus amara* <note>An aromatic root used in incense and medicine, here called "Futsjuk."</note> from *Surat* and *Siam*; corals, amber, and genuine antimony (which they use to color their porcelain and for making mirrors from *Europe*). The Japanese often break these imported mirrors to repurpose the glass into spyglasses, magnifying glasses, and spectacles. 

Other items of lesser note include *cow stones* <note>Bezoars or stones found in the gallbladders of cattle, highly prized as medicine; here called "Masang de Vaca."</note> from *Mozambique*; snakewood; *atjar* <note>Pickled vegetables or fruits, originally "Atsiaer."</note> made from bamboo; mangos and other unripe East Indian fruits pickled with Turkish pepper, garlic, and vinegar; black lead and red pencils for writing; mercury sublimate (though no calomel); fine files, needles, spectacles, large high-quality drinking glasses, counterfeit corals, exotic birds, and other foreign curiosities, both natural and man-made. Some of these items are often sold privately by sailors and individuals without being officially listed at the **trade fair** <note>Originally the "Cambang," the official market where Dutch goods were auctioned.</note>; in these private sales, the Dutch have no hesitation in charging as much as they possibly can above the items' real value.

<margin>Most profitable commodities.</margin>
Of all the imported goods, **raw silk** is the most sought after, although it yields the smallest profit margin. Because of this, the *Portuguese* referred to the sale of this specific commodity as the ***Pancado*** <note>A system where the Japanese authorities set a fixed price for the entire silk cargo, rather than allowing free-market bidding.</note>, a name that has become common in the country and is still used by the locals. All types of fabrics and cloth yield a reliable and significant profit; no matter how much is imported, the demand in such a populous country always remains higher. *Brazilwood* <note>A wood used for producing red dye, here called "Tsiampan."</note> and animal hides are also sold to great advantage. 

The most profitable commodities are sugar, *catechu*, *liquid storax*, *patsju* <note>Likely patchouli or a similar aromatic herb.</note>, and **Borneo Camphor** (which the Japanese value far above all other types of camphor), mirrors, and various other luxury goods. However, these are only highly profitable when there is a specific need for them or when the *Chinese* traders have failed to import them in large quantities. Corals and amber are two of the most valuable items in these Eastern regions, but *Japan* has been so thoroughly supplied by smugglers that there is currently barely a fifty percent profit to be made on them. In the past, we could sell them for ten or even a hundred times their original cost. The price of these items, and of all natural and artificial curiosities, fluctuates greatly depending on the number and mood of the buyers—who are themselves certain to make at least a one hundred percent profit regardless of the price they pay. # The History of JAPAN. Book IV. #

...formerly, when we still enjoyed full liberty in our trade and commerce, we sent no fewer than seven ships a year laden with the goods mentioned above. At present, we never send more than three or four; one of these goes first to **Siam** <note>Modern-day Thailand.</note> to complete her cargo with the commodities of that country. Any goods that remain unsold are stored in our warehouses until the next year's sale.

<margin>The Dutch Trade in Japan considered in its several Periods.</margin>
The state of our trade and commerce in this country, since our first arrival, has been subject to various changes and setbacks. These fluctuations relate to which commodities were forbidden for import or export over time, the gradual restriction of our liberties and privileges, the diminishing of our profits, and the manner in which we were treated by the natives. Since our first establishment, I find four remarkable periods, which I will now consider individually to give the reader a true and complete account of this significant branch of Dutch trade in the **East Indies**.

<margin>Its first Period.</margin>
The first period spans upwards of thirty years, from our first settlement in the town and island of **Hirado** <note>Originally "Firando." This was the Dutch base before they were moved to Dejima.</note> and the privilege of free trade and commerce (which was granted to us by the Emperor in 1611), until the year 1641, when we received orders from the Emperor to remove our factory <note>In the 17th century, a "factory" was a merchant's trading post or base of operations.</note> to **Nagasaki**. The trade of the **Spanish** <note>Originally "Castilians."</note> and **Portuguese**, who had a large and flourishing settlement at **Nagasaki**, was then at its greatest height. They held one considerable advantage over us: they could furnish **Japan** with raw silk and silk fabrics, commodities for which there was, and still is, a vast demand in this populous Empire. At that time, we did not yet have any settled establishment in **China** or the neighboring kingdoms where the finest silk is produced. The Empire of **China** itself was still governed by its native Monarchs, before the late **Manchu Conquest** <note>Originally "Tartarian Conquest." This refers to the fall of the Ming Dynasty and the rise of the Qing Dynasty.</note>, and was closed off from all commerce with foreign nations. The **Chinese**, forbidden from leaving their country or exporting native goods, could only provide us with a small quantity of silk—and even that had to be smuggled, as we did not dare to fetch it from their own coasts.

The **Portuguese**, on the contrary, having a settlement at **Macao** (a small island on the coast of **China** which still belongs to that Empire), had more frequent opportunities to procure this valuable and highly profitable commodity. Furthermore, we had no commerce with **Tonkin** <note>Northern Vietnam.</note> until about the year 1637, nor any settled establishments in the kingdoms of **Bengal** and **Persia**. But when fortune and our own good conduct finally opened a way into these silk-rich countries, and after we had established firm settlements there, we were then able to furnish the **Japanese** with silk and other coveted commodities just as well as the **Portuguese** and **Spanish**. At that time, we still sold our silk and other goods freely and without restraint to the highest bidder, and exported yearly a sum of roughly 60 **tons of gold** <note>A "ton of gold" (*ton gouds*) was a Dutch unit of currency representing 100,000 guilders, rather than a physical weight of metal.</note>, more or less (according to the Dutch...

<margin>Reasons for our removal and confinement at Dejima.</margin>
Many reasons contributed to make us suspected and hated at court, and occasioned at last the fatal change we underwent at this time; but the profession we make of the **Christian** religion was one of the chief reasons, the whole court being exasperated against it to the highest degree as a public nuisance and the only cause of the ruin and destruction of so many thousands of the Emperor’s subjects. Perhaps it would not have been possible for us to maintain ourselves in the country and the possession of our trade, had we not made it our business to give the court convincing proofs that we were **Christians** indeed, but quite of another sect, and professed enemies of the **Romish Priests** <note>Meaning Catholic clergy, particularly the Jesuits and Franciscans who had been active in Japan.</note>, whose dangerous conspiracies against the Emperor and the Empire we had discovered ourselves. This, with the deference and readiness we showed in assisting the Japanese at the **Siege of Shimabara** <note>The 1637–1638 uprising of mostly Christian peasants; the Dutch provided naval artillery to help the Shogunate suppress the rebellion to prove they were different from the "rebellious" Catholics.</note>, saved us so far that we were suffered to stay in the country and to continue our trade, though under so strict a guard and so narrow an inspection that ever since there has been scarce any opportunity left us to converse with the natives.

As things now stand, the main endeavor of the Japanese Government is to keep us ignorant of what passes in the country and at court, and to prevent any attempt we could make to bring over the natives to the faith of our **Saviour**, which might probably occasion new troubles and disturbances in the Empire. They are so much the more upon their guard because, taking it for granted that the **Spaniards** and **Portuguese** would miss no opportunities to revenge the affront and insulting usage they had met with, they apprehend that in order to bring this about they might one time or other combine with the **Dutch**.

We happened just at that time to build a new warehouse at **Hirado** <note>Original: "Firando."</note>, which greatly increased the jealousy and suspicion the Japanese had already conceived of us, and contributed not a little to forward our removal from there to **Nagasaki**. For it was, contrary to the custom of the country, built too high and all of stone, so that it looked more like a castle than a warehouse. It had besides—which made the case still worse—the year of our blessed **Saviour’s** nativity engraved on a stone in the front <note>The Dutch had inscribed the date "Anno Domini 1639," which the Shogunate took as a forbidden Christian symbol.</note>. # The History of JAPAN. Book IV. 358

...[In this] position, this man being asked whether or not he was a Christian, he answered—to save his and his companion's life—"What Christians? Christians? We are Dutchmen." The Inquisitors <note>Refers to the religious magistrates or *Shūmon-arata-yaku* tasked with identifying and suppressing Christians.</note> seemed satisfied with this confession at the time.

<margin>Second Period of the Dutch Trade.</margin>
I now come to the second period of our trade in this country, which dates from the time we left **Hirado** <note>Original: "Firando."</note> and moved to **Nagasaki**. No sooner had we entered the harbor than they immediately secured us on the island of **Dejima** <note>Original: "Desima," the artificial island to which the Dutch were restricted.</note> and deprived us at once of all the liberties and privileges we had enjoyed until then. Surrounded by numerous guards and watches, both inside and outside the island, we were denied any kind of conversation with the locals—except for those in our service, who were forced to take a solemn and terrifying oath, signed with their own blood, never to become familiar with us or communicate anything to us regarding the state and affairs of the country. 

Our ships, as soon as they dropped anchor in the harbor, were taken into their possession. Guard ships were placed on every side; the gunpowder, cannonballs, swords, cutlasses, and all other weapons were brought ashore and kept in safe custody until our departure. Even the heaviest cannons and the rudder itself were removed and brought ashore back then, though now they have stopped putting themselves to such great and unnecessary trouble. A review was conducted of everyone on board based on the provided list, and an exact record was taken of each person's age, name, and role. Those permitted to go ashore, whether on their own or the Company's business, were thoroughly searched. Their swords and firearms, as well as any goods for sale, were taken into custody by the **Ottona** <term>Ottona: The Japanese ward head or official responsible for the administration and oversight of the Dutch on Dejima.</term>. 

Even though the place where ships anchor is no more than 300 paces from **Dejima**, no one was allowed to go ashore or return to the ship without a passport from the proper officers. Our ships were unloaded and the cargo brought ashore by their own people, then locked in our warehouses under their seals. In short, we were treated then, and have been ever since, like traitors and declared enemies of the country. 

However, despite this sudden and disastrous change in our affairs—and the perfect opportunity the **Japanese** had to reduce our privileges and profits as much as they liked—the populous town of **Nagasaki** and its government (having recently lost the profitable trade with the **Portuguese**) could not survive without foreign commerce. Thus, we continued for some time to send no fewer than six or seven ships a year and sold our cargo at a very good profit. That very year, 1641—so notable for the disastrous turn in our affairs—was actually one of our most profitable. We sold goods worth eighty tons of gold <note>A "ton of gold" was a Dutch unit of account representing 100,000 florins or guilders.</note>, or 8,000,000 florins (over £700,000 sterling), and exported no less than 1,400 chests of silver.

Sometime after, we petition’d the court for leave to take, as we had done formerly, copper in exchange and part of payment for our foreign commodities, the exportation of this metal having been forbid ever since 1637. # The History of JAPAN. Book IV.

The gift was included among the presents intended for the Emperor himself that year, in the hopes of winning his favor. This occurred in 1666. **Mino** <note>Inaba Mino-no-kami Masanori, a powerful member of the Shogun's council.</note>, disappointed in his expectations, felt insulted to the highest degree. From that moment, he conceived such a hatred for the entire **Dutch** nation that he sought a total revenge—one which, according to the local customs, would be carried on by his descendants and relatives even after his death. The **Japanese** in general, once they have taken a dislike to someone, are experts at concealing it for a long time, waiting for a favorable opportunity to take revenge for the insults or slights they have—or imagine they have—received.

In this same way, **Mino** watched for his opportunity to carry out the revenge he planned against us. As soon as the chance appeared, he embraced it gladly and punished us most severely. He managed to obtain the Government of **Nagasaki** for **Ushigome Chūzaemon** <note>Original: "Usjingomi Tsusejemon," a relative of Mino appointed as Governor/Magistrate.</note>, one of his near relations. When this new Governor arrived to take possession of his post in 1672 (**Mr. Camphuysen** <note>Johannes Camphuys, who later became the Governor-General of the Dutch East India Company in Batavia, was then the director of trade in Japan.</note> was our director of trade at the time), he reduced our commerce to the following miserable condition:

He demanded samples and patterns of all the goods we imported for sale so he could show them to people who had knowledge of their quality and value, allowing them to tax and estimate the goods. Meanwhile, merchants gathered at his palace to view the items. After they decided which goods they wanted to buy and in what quantity, the Governor—without permitting us to be present—negotiated and sold the goods himself.

As one might easily imagine, the agreement was made for a price far below what we usually sold them for. He then informed us of the deal, though he indulged us just enough to give us a choice: we could either part with the goods at the price he had set, or export them out of the country again. By this unheard-of proceeding and unreasonable taxation, the very foundation of the privileges graciously granted to us by the late illustrious Emperors **Ieyasu** <note>Original: "Gongen," the posthumous title of the first Tokugawa Shogun.</note> and **Hidetada** <note>Original: "Teitokuni," the posthumous title of the second Tokugawa Shogun.</note> was ruined and overturned at once. The price set upon our commodities in this manner was reduced every year, and we were forced to sell them for a small profit rather than export them at a loss. To make matters worse, they forced us to accept the **Koban** <note>An oval gold coin.</note> as payment for our goods. ### Chapter VIII. The History of JAPAN. 361

...for the use and common benefit of the town of *Nagasaki*. In this condition it would have been impossible for us to stay in the country, and the continuation of this proceeding would infallibly have forced us to leave our trade there. We resolved therefore to try what ways and means we could to restore our commerce to the condition it had been in before. Nothing could be thought of that was likely to have a better effect than to represent our grievances, in an humble petition, to the Emperor <note>The Shogun, Tokugawa Tsunayoshi.</note>, as he was beyond doubt ignorant of this notorious breach of the sacred privileges granted us by the Emperors his predecessors. The consequence of an order at first view so favorable for our commerce was, in fact, more fatal to it than any we had as yet received, and brought it from the third to the last and "iron period," wherein it has continued ever since.

<margin>Gains of the Japanese during the third Period of our Trade.</margin>
The Governors of *Nagasaki* were exceedingly dissatisfied with this new order, not only because it had not been obtained by their favor and intercession (which would have been purchased with large presents), but because they, and other *Japanese* managers of our trade, were by it deprived of considerable sums which they gained by taxing and setting a price of their own making upon our commodities. Our *Ottoná* <note>A local ward headman or official responsible for overseeing the Dutch community.</note> once confessed to me that, for his own share, he lost by this order a yearly profit of 3,600 *Thails* <note>Taels, a unit of currency based on silver weight.</note>. *Minofama* <note>Inaba Mino-no-kami Masanori, the official mentioned on the previous page who held a grudge against the Dutch.</note>, having not yet forgotten the above-mentioned vexatious disappointment, did not lie quiet upon this occasion; and though he had been put out of his offices four years earlier—upon the demise of the Emperor his master and the accession of *Tsinajos* <note>Tokugawa Tsunayoshi, the fifth Tokugawa Shogun (reigned 1680–1709).</note> to the throne—and was consequently out of power to hurt us himself, he still urged the restriction of our privileges at court through his son-in-law, *Kangofama* <note>Likely a reference to a high-ranking counselor or daimyo related to the Inaba family.</note>, then one of the prime ministers and a privy Councilor. He likewise prevailed upon his nephew *Genfejemon* <note>Genseimon, a local official.</note>, Governor of *Nagasaki*, to do us what mischief he could. The latter in particular, and in conjunction with his colleagues, represented to the court how prejudicial this renewal of our privileges was to the natives, and what vast profits it brought in to us foreigners. This they did with so much success that, even though by virtue of this late order we had obtained leave to sell our goods freely and to the best bidder, it was now resolved that <margin>Fourth period of our trade.</margin> the said order should subsist in full force, and that we should have leave to import what goods and in what quantity we pleased, but that we should be so far restrained in the sale as not to exceed the

And thus, this "restored liberty" proved more fatal to us than the taxation itself had been, even though we had previously considered that tax an insufferable hardship. We found it was much more profitable to sell large cargoes for a small gain than to sell small cargoes for a higher profit. 

In the meantime, so that it would not appear as if this fatal reduction had been decided upon merely to spite the Dutch nation—but rather as a political maxim agreeable to the Emperor <note>The Shogun, Tokugawa Tsunayoshi.</note> and advantageous to the Empire—the commerce of the Chinese and other Eastern nations who trade to Japan under their name was likewise reduced to a yearly sum of 600,000 **Thails**. The Emperor was so well pleased with the discovery of this tactic, by which our commerce was regulated and our profit reduced low enough without violating the liberty granted by his late Imperial orders (nor forcing us to leave the country, which the court was somewhat worried about), that he later conferred upon the Governors of Nagasaki the honorable and illustrious title of **Cami** <term>Cami: Or Kami, an honorary title indicating a lord or high-ranking official.</term>.

<margin>State of our Trade in 1685</margin>

The Dutch had not yet received any notice of this new regulation when, in the autumn of 1685, their ships arrived in the harbor very richly laden. The joy over their safe arrival was great, as the merchants once again promised themselves "mountains of gold" and held well-grounded hopes to see the first and happiest period of their commerce revive. But we had scarcely begun to unload them, and had just brought the cargo of one ship ashore, when to our unspeakable grief, new orders were sent from the court to limit the liberty restored to us (and to the Chinese) to a specific, determined sum, beyond which nothing could be sold. To prevent smuggling, an exact account was to be taken of the entire cargo, which was narrowly examined and afterwards locked up in our warehouses. Though secured under our own locks, the Japanese also applied their own seals to them. Since that time, we are never allowed the liberty of entering the warehouses to care for our goods unless we have their permission and are in their presence.

The yearly sum for which the Dutch are permitted to sell imported goods is exactly half the sum allowed to the Chinese. This amounts in Dutch money to ten and a half "tons of gold," which is 1,050,000 guilders (nearly £100,000 sterling), and in Japanese money to 300 chests or boxes of silver. ### Chapter VIII. The History of J A P A N.

The Japanese government arranged matters so that the Company was forced to accept an exchange rate of sixty-eight <note>This refers to the number of silver units per gold coin, an exchange rate manipulated to favor the Japanese.</note>, yet they were paid entirely in gold. In this way, while the Company nominally sells 300,000 **Thails** <term>Thail: Also known as a Tael, a weight of silver (approx. 37 grams) used as a currency unit across East Asia.</term> worth of goods each year, they actually receive no more than 260,000 **Thails** in real silver value. 

Through this scheme, the government of **Nagasaki** found a way to compensate the Dutch Directors and other officers for their trouble and harsh treatment. They did this by granting these officials certain private profits, independent of the Company’s accounts. They were permitted to sell their own private goods—which they previously sold in any quantity they liked—up to a value of 40,000 **Thails**, or 5,888 **Cobangs** <term>Cobang: Or Koban, an oval-shaped Japanese gold coin.</term>. Together with the 260,000 **Thails** mentioned earlier, this makes up the total yearly sum limited by the latest Imperial orders. The Company does not have the power to change this regulation because the Japanese government has seen fit to order it this way; nor can the Company interfere with its own officers or prevent them from selling their private goods. 

These 40,000 **Thails** are divided among the various officers involved in the Japanese trade in the following way: 
* The **Captain** (as he is called here), who is the chief director and Ambassador to the Shogun’s court <note>The author uses "Emperor," but refers to the Shogun in Edo.</note>, is assigned 10,000 **Thails**. 
* The new director, who has recently arrived to replace him, receives 7,000 **Thails**. 
* His Deputy, the second-in-command, receives 6,000 **Thails**. 
* The ship captains, merchants, clerks, and others who arrived on the most recent ships receive shares in proportion to their standing with the managers. 

The Japanese interpreters are responsible for dividing this sum and ensuring that no one sells more than their assigned share.

<margin>Director of the Dutch trade</margin>
The reader should note that the Company keeps a permanent Director in Japan, whom the Japanese call the "Captain of the Dutch." He has command over all the people in our factory <note>In this context, a "factory" is a merchant trading post, not a manufacturing plant.</note> and oversees our trade. This same person must lead the embassy sent to the Shogun’s court once every year. According to the custom of the country, he must be replaced after his year is up. The ships from **Batavia** <term>Batavia: The administrative capital of the Dutch East Indies, modern-day Jakarta.</term> bring his successor, along with a deputy and a few merchants and clerks to assist him during the trading season. When the sale is over and the ships are ready to sail, he boards the ship to return to **Batavia**, leaving the post to his successor, who will be replaced the following year in the same manner.

<margin>Sale of our goods.</margin>
The sale of our goods is conducted as follows: When the day of the **Combang** <term>Combang: A term derived from the Dutch word "kompanie," referring to the official regulated auctions or sales of the Dutch Company's goods.</term> (as they call our sale) draws near—a date that must be set by the court—a list of all available goods is posted on the gates outside our island. It is written in very large characters so that anyone can read it from a distance. Meanwhile, the government notifies the various **Ottonas** <term>Ottona: Neighborhood or ward headmen in Nagasaki responsible for local administration and overseeing merchants.</term> of the town, and these in turn notify the merchants...

# The History of JAPAN. Book IV.

The merchants, who have come to the city from various parts of the Empire and are staying within the local district, consider what duties must be paid *per Cent* <note>original: "per Cent." This refers to a percentage-based tax or customs fee.</note> for the benefit of the inhabitants of **Nagasaki** on several of our goods. This allows them to decide what price they can afford to pay for our merchandise. It is a clever trick indeed; they tax our goods indirectly and mock us by claiming they are restoring our "liberty and privileges." 

They tell us—and it is true—"When we taxed your goods directly, you arrived with no fewer than seven ships and sold massive cargoes. Now you can only send three or four ships and sell very little. Would it not have been better for you to remain as you were, rather than applying for a renewal of your privileges only to make your condition worse?" 

The day before the **Combang** <term>Combang: A Dutch adaptation of the Japanese word "kōban," here referring to the public auction or trade negotiations.</term>, notices are posted at all the street gates to invite merchants to appear the next morning at **Desima** <note>Dejima: The fan-shaped artificial island in Nagasaki harbor where the Dutch were confined.</note>. For their further information, they find a list of the goods stored in every warehouse posted at the doors. 

Because the direction of our trade is entirely in the hands of the **Nagasaki** government, the **Combang** cannot be held except in the presence of two stewards of the Governors. These men act as deputies, authorized to oversee the proceedings. The chief officers of our Island must also be present. The first Interpreter presides and directs everything, while our own "triumvirs"—the two directors (the old and the new) and the deputy director—have little to no say in the matter. 

Once everyone required for the sale has met, our directors order samples of all our tradable goods to be displayed. They then give a signal with a **Gum Gum** <note>A "Gum Gum" is a type of flat bronze gong or bell, likely a "gane."</note> for the merchants to enter. 

The house where the sale is held is a very neat building, constructed at the Company’s expense. By removing the shutters, the building is opened toward the street so people can look in. There is a small gallery around it, and the interior is divided into several partitions, conveniently designed for this process. 

The sale itself is performed in the following manner: Only one type of goods is put up at a time. Those who wish to buy them submit several tickets, signed with sham names, indicating how many **Quan, Me, Momi, Burin, Re,** and **Futz** <term>These represent subdivisions of Japanese silver currency: Kwan (Quan), Momme (Me/Momi), Fun (Futz), Rin (Burin/Re), and Mo.</term> they intend to give for a piece or a **Catti** <term>Catti: A "Catty," a unit of weight equal to about 1.3 pounds or 600 grams.</term> of the goods. All wholesale goods are sold by these quantities. 

I noticed that every merchant submits several tickets. This is done to see how the bidding is going; it allows them to stick to a lower price if they regret a higher bid, which is why they sign with fake names. Because of the great number of sub-divisions in the small currency, it rarely happens that two tickets exactly match one another. After all the bidders have submitted their tickets, our directors open them and separate the high bids from the low. They are then delivered to the presiding chief Interpreter, who reads them aloud—

### Chap. VIII. The History of JAPAN.

The tickets are read aloud one after another, beginning with the highest bid. They call for the bidder three times, and if no answer is made, the official lays that ticket aside and takes up the next one. He continues this process, always moving to a lower bid, until a bidder cries out, "Here I am!" That person then draws near to sign the note, putting his true name to it with the black ink which the Japanese always carry with them for such purposes. 

Once the goods put up for auction are sold, they proceed to others, which are sold in the same manner. They continue until the total sum determined by the Emperor has been raised, which is commonly achieved in two or three—and seldom more than four—**Combangs** <term>Combangs: Trading sessions or auction days, derived from the Japanese "kōban."</term>, or days of sale. The day after each **Combang**, the goods are delivered to the buyer and carried away from our island <note>Dejima, the fan-shaped artificial island where the Dutch were confined.</note>. 

A guild of merchants from the five Imperial Cities <note>These cities were Kyoto, Edo (Tokyo), Osaka, Sakai, and Nagasaki.</note> has obtained a monopoly for the buying and selling of raw silk through imperial patents. This commodity is sold first, much to their great advantage and our significant disadvantage <note>original: "prejudice"</note>; they would even like to force us to make raw silk at least one-third of our total cargo. 

The **Quanmotz** <term>Quanmotz: From the Japanese "kanmotsu," referring to official duties or customs taxes.</term>, a duty or custom laid upon goods, is little used elsewhere in **Japan**. It was introduced at **Nagasaki** purely with the intent to take a portion of the vast profits that foreigners made on their commodities and assign those funds for the use and maintenance of the town's poorer inhabitants. It was formerly moderate enough, but the late taxation—which proved so beneficial to the Governors and other magistrates of the town—having been abolished, the Governors have seen fit to raise this duty. They do this specifically to encourage Japanese merchants to buy our goods at a lower rate, proportional to the duty laid upon them. 

When this **Quanmotz** is levied, it is called by the Japanese **Koosen** or **Kosen Gin** <term>Kosen Gin: Commission or "reward money" for one’s trouble.</term>. In its distribution, they call it **Fannagin**, or **Flower-money** <term>Fannagin: Literally "flower money" (hanagin), a form of rebate or dividend given to the citizens.</term>, to signify that it "flowers" out of the foreign trade for the benefit and advantage of the poorer inhabitants of **Nagasaki**. 

It is distributed among them in proportion to the labor they must perform for the public offices they serve by turns, which vary according to the street they live in. It also serves as a form of compensation for many other troubles and hardships they complain of—especially since the barrenness of the land around **Nagasaki** and other disadvantages caused by foreign commerce might otherwise tempt them to flee to other parts of the Empire where they could live at less expense and with more ease. They commonly receive between three and fifteen **Thails** <term>Thails: Taels, a unit of currency based on a weight of silver.</term> each in this distribution. 

The duty itself laid upon the goods belonging to the Dutch East India Company is fifteen percent, which, from the total sum of 300,000 **Thails**, produces a duty of 45,000 **Thails**. The goods belonging to private individuals, which are commonly sold at the end of the **Combang**, pay much more: no less than 65 percent for all fabrics and goods sold by the piece. # The History of JAPAN. Book IV.

13,000 **Thails** <term>Thails: Also known as Taels, a unit of weight and currency used in East Asian trade, typically representing a specific weight of silver.</term> custom duty. Goods sold by weight pay a duty of 70 **Thails** per cent, which upon 20,000 **Thails** makes 14,000 duty. The reason they give for this great difference in the duty laid upon the company’s goods versus private goods is that private goods are brought over on board the company’s ships at the company's own risk and expense, and consequently the private traders deserve less profit. The **Chinese**, for a similar reason—that is, because they do not bear the expense of such long and hazardous voyages as the **Dutch**, being located nearer at hand—pay a duty of 60 per cent for all their goods. Based on the 600,000 **Thails** worth of goods they are permitted to sell every year, this brings in a sum of 360,000 **Thails** in duty. If to this we add the yearly rents for our houses and factory <note>The "factory" refers to the Dutch trading post on the island of Dejima.</note>, which is 5,580 **Thails**, and that of the **Chinese** factory, which is 16,000 **Thails** a year, it makes up, in all, a sum of 453,580 **Thails** which foreign commerce produces annually for the **Magistrates** and inhabitants of **Nagasaki**.

<margin>Profits upon the Dutch Goods.</margin>
As to the profits the Company earns upon the commodities we import, they differ greatly and vary every year, as the same goods are not constantly sold in equal quantities, nor at the same rate. The whole depends upon the price each sort of goods commands at **Miaco** <term>Miaco: The historic name for Kyoto, which served as the center of Japanese commerce and the Imperial capital.</term>, and this is commonly regulated by the consumption and the demand for them in the country. The profits our goods produce may be computed to amount, one year with another, to 60 per cent. However, if all the charges and expenses of our sale are taken into consideration, we cannot easily earn more than 40 or 45 per cent clear gain. Thus, the goods we sell in **Japan** to the value of ten tons of gold and a half <note>A "ton of gold" was a common Dutch idiom in trade representing 100,000 guilders; thus 1,050,000 guilders.</note>, or 1,050,000 **Gilders** <term>Gilders: Also called Guilders or Florins, the currency of the Netherlands.</term>, yield no more than four tons, or four and a half—that is, 400,000 or 450,000 **Gilders** clear profit. This is indeed a very inconsiderable profit for so great a Company, which must constantly keep at least 18,000 men in its pay at an expense of upwards of 260,000 **Gilders** (near £24,000 sterling) a month in wages alone, besides the vast number of ships, factories, and forts they must maintain and oversee all over the **East-Indies**. Considering such a small profit, it would be scarcely worth the company’s while to continue this branch of our trade any longer, were it not that the goods we export from there—and particularly the refined copper—yield much the same profit, so that the total profit may be computed to amount to 80 or 90 per cent.

<margin>Our Charges.</margin>
The charges and expenses we must bear are not the same every year. They are greater if anything requires building or repairing, if there are more presents to be made <note>These "presents" were the obligatory tributes and bribes given to the Shogun and officials during the annual Dutch embassy to the capital at Edo.</note>, or if any extraordinary event occurs. For the satisfaction of the reader, I will here set down the expenses of two years as they stood in the last and fourth period of our commerce: namely, in 1686, when Mr. **Licentiate Cleyer** <note>Andreas Cleyer (1634–1698), a German physician and botanist who served as the VOC Chief (Opperhoofd) at Dejima.</note> was Director and the expenses were much higher than usual; and in 1688, when Mr. **Butenheimb** was Director and the expenses were as small as could possibly be expected.
