### The History of JAPAN. Book IV.

<margin>Profits upon the Goods of private Persons.</margin>
Before I close this subject and proceed to send our four ships back to **Batavia** <note>The administrative capital of the Dutch East India Company in the East Indies, modern-day Jakarta, Indonesia.</note> with their profits and fresh cargoes, it is worth discussing the profits earned on goods belonging to private individuals. In particular, we should examine what the three chief Directors of our trade can earn from their positions. Since private goods are brought over and sold without any shipping expenses to the owner, they produce pure profit. Despite the high duties placed upon them, this profit is in no way inferior to that of the Company, even though the Company pays a smaller duty. 

The two chief Directors (who, by order of the Japanese court, cannot hold office for more than three years, and even then not consecutively) have the greatest share of this. After serving one year, they are obliged to return to **Batavia** with the departing ships, from where they are sent back again either with the next year’s ships or two years later. These Directors are permitted to sell their own goods upon arrival to the value of 7,000 **Taels** <term>Tael: A unit of silver weight used as currency in East Asia, often called a *momme* by the Japanese.</term>. Furthermore, during their own directorship, when they are preparing to return to **Batavia**, they may sell goods to the value of 10,000 **Taels**, totaling 17,000 **Taels** in a single year. The deputy Director is permitted to sell 12,000 **Taels** worth of his own goods. 

If the Directors are on good terms with the chief Interpreter and have found ways to secure his favor by giving him large presents *de alienis* <note>Latin: "from the property of others." This implies the Directors used the Company’s resources or funds to bribe the official for their own personal gain.</note>, he can arrange things so that some of their private goods are included and sold during the first or second **Combang** <note>From the Japanese *kamban*, referring to the official public auctions or "signboard" sales where the Dutch trade was conducted.</note> alongside the Company’s inventory. Because of the smaller duty applied to Company goods, this will produce a profit of at least 65 to 70 percent. This can be done without any apparent harm to the Company, for when the sums are tallied to meet the official 300,000 **Tael** trade limit, these private articles are simply overlooked. 

If they possess goods beyond their legal allowance—especially red coral, amber, and similar luxuries—it is easy to dispose of them privately with the help of the Japanese officers on our island, who will generally purchase the items themselves. The **Ottona** <note>The Japanese headman or "street commissioner" responsible for the administration of the Dutch island of Dejima.</note> himself is very often involved in such deals, as they are highly profitable. In former times, we could sell such goods through a deputy to the foreign merchants who came to our island during the **Combang** auctions, which was far more profitable for us. However, in 1686, one of our Directors handled these matters so clumsily that ten Japanese men were beheaded for smuggling, and he himself was banished from the country forever. 

The resident Director, who also serves as the Ambassador to the Emperor’s court, has another significant advantage. If the Governors of **Nagasaki** <note>The port city where the Dutch were confined; it served as the gateway for all foreign influence in Japan.</note> desire specific presents for the Emperor that are not currently in the Company’s warehouses and would otherwise need to be bought from the **Chinese** traders, the Director can provide them from his own private stock. If he happens to have the required items, he keeps all the profit for himself without technically harming the Company. Indeed, they might possibly go even further...

### Chap. VIII. The History of J A P A N.

...rs, <note>Completing the word "Interpreters" from the previous page.</note> in pursuit of their own private advantages, were it not that they endeavour to pass for men of conscience and honour, or at least aim to appear fearful, lest they should be thought too notoriously to injure both the confidence and interest of their masters. I do not pretend hereby to charge them with any indirect practices, as to the annual expenses, though perhaps even these are sometimes run up to an unnecessary height: Nor is it in the least my intention to detract from the reputation and character of probity of so many worthy Gentlemen who have filled this station with honour and discharged their duty with the utmost faithfulness to their masters. 

However, to support what I have here asserted, and to show that if the Directors had not the common interest of the Company more at heart than their own private advantages, they could enrich themselves by defrauding their principals, I cannot forbear mentioning one instance. The instructions from the government of **Batavia** <note>The headquarters of the Dutch East India Company in Asia, now Jakarta.</note>, with regard to the refined copper, are not to buy it for less than twelve **Taels** <term>Tael: A weight of silver used as currency; approximately 37 grams.</term>, or twelve and a half, a **Picul** <term>Picul: A traditional Asian unit of weight, roughly 133 lbs or 60 kg, defined as the amount a man can carry on a shoulder pole.</term>. This they do to keep the refiners in good humour, and not to discourage them by allowing them too inconsiderable a profit. Nevertheless, the Interpreters may sometimes get it for a **Mace** <term>Mace: A unit of currency equal to one-tenth of a Tael.</term> cheaper, which upon 12,000 **Piculs**, the quantity commonly bought, makes a sum of 600 **Taels**, which they may, if they please, put in their pockets, because it is contrary to their instructions in their account to charge the copper for so much less. Now, whether or not they actually do this, I will not take upon me to assert. 

Thus much I can say, without exaggeration, that the Directorship of the Dutch trade in **Japan** is a place which the possessor would not easily part with for 30,000 **Guilders** (about 3,000 pounds sterling <note>A massive fortune in the 17th century, equivalent to several hundred thousand pounds today.</note>). It is true, it would be a great disadvantage to the Director, and considerably lessen his profits, if he has not a good cash in hand to provide himself, before his departure, with a sufficient quantity of goods, but must take them upon credit, and upon his return share the profits with his creditors. For besides, he must not presume to leave **Batavia**, much less to return there, without valuable considerations <note>A polite 17th-century term for bribes or strategic gifts.</note> to his benefactors, unless he intends to be excused for the future from the honour of any such employment. 

The goods he brings back to **Batavia** are: Silk gowns, which he received as presents from the Emperor and his Ministers, and whereof he makes presents again to his friends and patrons; victuals, china-ware, lacquered or "japanned" things, and other manufactures of the country, which he can dispose of at **Batavia** at 50 per cent <note>original: "per cent"</note> profit; and besides some **Koban** in gold. But since we have been obliged to take them at a higher rate, they yield a much less, and in the main very inconsiderable profit. But it is time at last, to send our ships on their return. # Chap. VIII. The History of JAPAN.

...tobacco, tea, and marmalades; besides several thousand **Koban** <term>Koban: Large, oval-shaped Japanese gold coins (referred to here as "Cobangs").</term> of gold in the form of physical currency <note>original: "specie"</note>.

<margin>Procedures for departure.</margin>
Our ships cannot be loaded, nor can they set sail from the harbor, until special permission has been granted and the day of their departure is determined by the court. Once they are loaded, all of our private goods and anything else we intend to bring on board must be strictly searched once again. For this purpose, two of our landlords, two apprentice interpreters, and two clerks—either from the **Otona** <term>Otona: The Japanese official serving as the head of the Dutch island of Dejima.</term> or from the treasury office—along with several **laborers** <term>Kulis: Manual workers or porters.</term>, visit everyone in their rooms about two or three days before departure. This applies to those staying at **Dejima** <note>The small, artificial island in Nagasaki harbor where the Dutch were confined.</note> as well as those returning home who had been staying in our vacant houses during the trade season. These people inspect every corner and examine all our belongings piece by piece, taking an exact inventory of what they find. They then bind the items together with straw ropes and apply their seals, along with a list of the contents for the gate guards, who would otherwise open them again. 

All contraband goods are seized during this search. These include, for example: anything with the image of a local idol; a **Kuge** <term>Kuge: The ancient class of hereditary court nobles who served the Emperor.</term> or an ecclesiastical person of the **Dairi’s** <note>The "Dairi" refers to the Imperial Court in Kyoto, centered around the Emperor.</note> Court in their official dress; all printed books and papers; metal mirrors or other metal objects with Japanese characters on them; silver money; and fabrics woven within the country. Most strictly forbidden are weapons and anything that could be classified as such, including figures of soldiers, saddles, ships or boats, armor, bows and arrows, swords, and scimitars. Should any of these be found in the possession of any Dutchman, the owner would be banished from the country for life at the very least. Furthermore, the interpreters and servants appointed to manage his affairs, along with any other suspicious persons, would be put to the rack <note>A device used for torture to extract confessions.</note> until the seller and all accomplices are discovered—a crime that can only be atoned for by their blood. 

We recently saw an example of this involving the Imperial Steward’s own secretary. Having attempted to send some scimitar blades over to China, he was executed along with his only son, an innocent child no more than eight years old. Upon my own departure, although my things (for good reasons) were only lightly inspected over a bottle of wine, they still seized an old Japanese razor and a few small sticks tied to some dolls <note>original: "babies"</note> instead of sabers, simply because they happened to see them.

<margin>Regulations regarding smuggling</margin>
All gold belonging to private individuals must be exported openly and shown to the Commissioners before leaving **Dejima** to verify if it passed through their hands. They know this by a mark they stamp onto all **Koban** at the Exchequer office. By this method, they can determine if the gold was obtained through smuggling. However, they cannot be extremely thorough in this regard because of the great rush of other business that must be finished upon our departure. All these strict Japanese orders and regulations were created primarily to prevent smuggling, a crime that is severely punished.

### The History of JAPAN. Book IV.

Smuggling is forbidden by the Emperor—and for good reason—as it not only makes goods more common and cheaper, but it also reduces the **Kosen** <term>Kosen: A percentage-based commission or duty paid on goods, which provided a significant portion of the income for the residents of Nagasaki.</term>. This loss of duty is very damaging to the town of **Nagasaki**, as the inhabitants rely on it for a large part of their livelihood. The penalty for this crime is death, without any hope of a reprieve. However, this penalty extends only to the person convicted and their accomplices; it does not affect their families, unlike the punishments for other crimes.

Yet, the Japanese are so prone to this crime that, by current estimates, no fewer than 300 people have been executed in a span of six or seven years just for smuggling with the Chinese. These smugglers follow the departing **junks** <note>original: "yonks", referring to traditional Chinese sailing vessels.</note> out to the open sea and buy the goods that the Chinese were unable to sell at the official auctions in Nagasaki. There are not many instances of people being executed for smuggling with the Dutch. During my stay in Japan, which lasted just over two years, more than fifty smugglers lost their lives. Some of those who were caught committed suicide, others were publicly executed, and some were executed privately in prison. As recently as 1691, two Japanese men were executed on our island for smuggling one pound of **Baros Camphor** <term>Camphire of Baros: A highly valuable, high-quality camphor from Sumatra, used for medicine and incense.</term> from a Dutchman; the camphor was found on the buyer just as he was trying to carry it off the island.

I will first describe the departure of our ships, and then close this long chapter with the history of that execution. As the day set for our ships' departure approaches, they begin to load their cargoes one after another. Finally, the weapons and gunpowder are brought on board, followed by the ship’s crew. The crew must once again undergo a review according to the list provided when the ship first arrived. Once a ship is ready to set sail, she must weigh anchor immediately and move about six miles <note>original: "two leagues"</note> away from the town toward the harbor entrance. There she waits until the other ships are loaded in the same manner.

When all the ships bound for home are joined together, they proceed on their voyage. Once they reach the open sea, at a significant distance from the harbor, the Japanese **Ship-guard**—which has never left them from the moment of their arrival—finally departs and returns home. If the wind is against the ships as they try to leave, a large number of Japanese rowing boats are fastened to a rope and tow them out by force, one after another. The Emperor's orders must be carried out regardless of the wind or weather, even if it means the ships might later risk being wrecked.

<margin>Execution of two Japanese Smugglers.</margin>
I come now to the account of the execution mentioned above, with which I intended to close this long chapter. On the 10th of December, early in the morning, the presiding Governor—formerly called **Ginzaemon**, now **Tshima-no-kami** <note>original: "Ginsejemon" and "Tsino Cami"; these are the titles of the Nagasaki Bugyō or governors.</note>—sent notice through the **Ottona** <term>Ottona: The Japanese official who served as the headman and supervisor of the Dutch on Dejima.</term> of our island to our Director. He was told to keep himself and the rest of the Dutchmen ready to witness the criminals' execution. About an hour later

He had nothing in return for his kind invitation but a sharp reprimand, with an admonition, to take care of his people, that no more such accidents should happen for the future. This was the first time criminal blood was shed upon our Island.

## C H A P. IX.

### Of the way of Life, Trade and Privileges of the Chinese in JAPAN.

<margin>
Ancient State of the Chinese Trade.
</margin>
THE Chinese from remotest antiquity, exported the growth and commodities of their country, chiefly raw silk, wherein it abounds, all over the East. It is from thence they were by the Greeks and Romans called *Seres* <note>original: "Seres". A Latin and Greek term meaning "the people of silk," referring to the inhabitants of North China.</note>. They traded particularly to the Kingdoms and Islands situated beyond **Sumatra** and **Malacca** to the East. Since the late Tartarian conquest <note>This refers to the Manchu conquest of China (the transition from the Ming to the Qing Dynasty) in 1644.</note> many of them, unwilling to conform to the orders issued by their Conqueror, to shave their heads after the manner of the Tartars <note>The "queue" hairstyle—shaving the front of the head and wearing a long braid—was forced upon Han Chinese by the Manchu Qing rulers as a sign of submission.</note>, left their native country, and settled in the same Kingdoms and Islands, which till then they had frequented only as traders. They had also, from times almost immemorial, carried on a commerce with **Japan**, though but small, and with a few **junks** <term>junks: translated from "yonks," these are traditional Chinese sailing vessels used for long-distance trade</term>.

### Chap. IX. *The History of* JAPAN.

junks. <term>junks: traditional Chinese sailing vessels, referred to in the original text as "yonks."</term> For under the reigns of some former Emperors, *China* was, as *Japan* now is, shut up and kept from all commerce with foreign nations, and the Inhabitants strictly forbid under severe penalties, to export the growth of the country, or to have any communication with their neighbours. Nevertheless, those who lived along the Sea coasts, and in the neighbouring Islands, found means, tho’ with some difficulty and in private, to fit out a small number of junks, and now and then to pass over to the Kingdoms, and Islands, which lay nearest, whereof *Japan* was one. Things stood upon this foot, when the late *Tartarian* <note>The "Tartarian Conqueror" refers to the Manchu leaders who established the Qing Dynasty in 1644, overthrowing the Ming Dynasty.</note> Conqueror of *China*, and his Successor the now reigning Monarch of that mighty Empire, thinking that it would very much conduce to the honour of his subjects, and to the advantage of his dominions, for the future to permit a free and undisturb’d commerce, resolv’d to suffer his subjects to trade abroad, and to give foreigners a free access to his dominions.

The *Chinese* ever since exported the produce and commodities of their country to a much greater quantity, than before, and enlarg’d their trade and commerce, as with most Eastern Nations, so particularly with their neighbours the *Japanese*, by whom they had been all along receiv’d as welcome guests, and tolerated, because of the affinity there is between the religion, customs, books, learned languages, arts and sciences of both nations. Formerly they frequented the harbour of *Osacca* <note>Modern-day Osaka.</note>, and others less secure, because of the frequent cliffs, rocks and shoals, which make the whole navigation that way exceedingly difficult and dangerous, and wholly impracticable for ships of any bulk. The *Portuguese* some time after shew’d them the way to that of *Nagasaki*, which is not only more secure, but was in many other respects much more advantageous. The resort of merchants to this place, who came from all parts of the Empire to trade with the *Portuguese*, was too great, not to engage the *Chinese* to put in there preferably to other places. At last orders from court, importing, that the harbour of *Nagasaki* should be for the future the only one open to foreigners, in all the *Japanese* dominions, fix’d them there. 

Ever since, the *Chinese*, as well those who live in *China*, as others who were by the late *Tartarian* conquest dispers’d into the neighbouring Countries and Islands beyond the *Ganges* to the East <note>A geographical term then used to describe Southeast Asia and the East Indies.</note>, traded to *Nagasaki*, either upon their own account, or that of their principals, for sometime with all the liberty they could possibly desire. They came over when, and with what numbers of people, junks and goods they pleas’d. So extensive and advantageous a liberty could not but be very pleasing to them, and put them upon thoughts of a surer establishment, in order to which, and for the free exercise of their religion, they built three temples, according to the three chief languages spoke by them, each to be attended by priests of their own Nation sent over from *China*. ### The History of J A P A N. Book IV.

them. To mention only some recent examples, there came over to Nagasaki in the years 1683 and 1684 at least two hundred Chinese junks <term>junks: traditional Chinese sailing vessels, referred to in the original text as "yonks"</term> a year, each one with no less than fifty people on board (at present, they are not permitted to have more than thirty hands on board each junk). Consequently, no less than ten thousand people came over from China to Nagasaki every year. Some of the largest junks, besides the necessary crew, brought over numbers of passengers and other private individuals who came to trade on their own account; several of these ships had from fifty to eighty, and sometimes a hundred men on board.

Prostitution <note>original: "Whoring"</note>, which is strictly forbidden in *China*, being openly permitted in *Japan*, many young, wealthy persons came over to *Japan* purely for their pleasure, to spend their money on Japanese courtesans <note>original: "wenches"</note>, which proved very profitable for this town. Not long ago, a Manchu official <term>Mandarin: a high-ranking official of the Chinese imperial government; "Tartarian" refers to the Manchu/Qing Dynasty</term> came over with a very numerous retinue in the role of Admiral of a small fleet of six junks, but he was obliged to return to *China* immediately. The Japanese informed him that their country would not tolerate any other commanders or officials except for those who were natives of Japan.

The liberty which the Chinese enjoyed in this country for some time was too great to continue long without change, and it quickly came to a disastrous end. The Japanese received word that the Jesuits—their mortal enemies, who had been banished from *Japan* forever—were being treated favorably at the court of the then-reigning Manchu Emperor of *China*, who had granted them the freedom to preach and spread the Gospel throughout his vast dominions. Some books relating to the Roman Catholic religion, which the Jesuit fathers had found ways to print in *China* in the Chinese language, were brought over to *Japan* among other Chinese books and sold privately. This made the Japanese fearful that by this means the Christian religion, which had been eradicated with so much trouble and the loss of so many thousand lives, might be revived again in the country.

Some suspicion of Christianity was even cast upon the importers of these books; if they were not viewed as actual converts, they were thought, at least, to be favorably inclined toward the Roman Catholic religion. For these several reasons, which were of great importance to such a jealous and apprehensive nation, it was proposed at court to restrict the extensive liberty of the Chinese and to place them on much the same footing as the Dutch, both regarding their trade and their way of life. The court's intentions, which aimed first to alter the state of Chinese trade and later to confine the merchants (just as they had done to the Dutch at *Dejima* <term>Desima: a small, artificial island in Nagasaki harbor where foreign traders were restricted</term>) and make their settlement subject to the same rigorous regulations and narrow inspection that our own trade suffers under, were strongly supported by the arrival of the aforementioned official and the daily increase of Chinese and Manchus suspected of Christianity,

And as to the first, I mean the regulations concerning their trade, that same year 1685, in which the Dutch had been reduced to the sum of 300,000 <term>Thails: taels, a weight of silver used as currency throughout East Asia</term>, or 300 chests of silver per year <note>original: "per annum"</note>, the Court thought fit to limit also the Chinese to a certain sum, beyond which none of their goods should be sold. This sum is not to exceed 600 chests of silver, that is 600,000 <term>Siumome: momme, a Japanese unit of weight for silver</term>, or *Taels*, and according to the Dutch way of computing 21 tuns of gold <note>A "tun of gold" was a Dutch unit of account equal to 100,000 guilders</note>, that is 2,100,000 guilders (about 200,000 pounds sterling). It was ordered at the same time, that the goods which might be reasonably supposed to yield 600,000 *Taels* should be brought over on board seventy junks <term>junks: traditional Chinese sailing vessels, written as "yonks" in the original text</term> at farthest, and this according to the following division made by the Japanese themselves:

seventeen junks from the province *Hokshu* <note>Fuzhou</note>, or *Foktshu*, or *Fukutshu*, sixteen from *Nanking*, five from the city and Province *Cantoo*, or *Canton*, five from *Nefa*, four from *Sintsheu* <note>likely Quanzhou</note>, four from the Island *Aymo*, or *Hainan*, and the coasts of the neighbouring continent of *China*, three from *Kootz*, or *Kootsha* <note>likely Kochi/Cochin</note>, three from the Kingdom of *Siam*, two from the Kingdom of *Tonquin* <note>northern Vietnam</note>, two from *Cammon*, two from the Kingdom of *Cambodia*, two from *Takkasagga*, otherwise *Taiwan* <note>original: "Tafwaan"</note> upon the Island *Formosa*, one from *Fudasan* <note>Mount Putuo, a famous Buddhist island</note>, situate below *Raktshu*, where there is a famous *Quanwon* <note>Guanyin, the Bodhisattva of Mercy</note> Temple, one from *Cochin-China* <note>original: "Kootshj"</note>, and one from *Tani*, which is one of the most considerable of the *Ryukyu* <note>original: "Kiuku"</note> Islands, besides some others, which I could not learn.

After this manner the Japanese have thought fit to divide the allowed number of junks among the Chinese settled in the several Kingdoms and Islands above mentioned. They admit also one from *Batavia* <note>modern-day Jakarta, original: "Siakkatarra"</note>, and one from *Peking*, which two last should be either added to the foregoing to make up the number of seventy, or else admitted in lieu of such as stayed too late, or were cast away in their voyage.

And yet, despite the great accuracy and nice circumspection of the Japanese, the Chinese will frequently impose upon them. Thus, for instance, some of the junks which came to *Nagasaki* early in the year, after they have disposed of their cargoes, return to clean and to be new painted and varnished; then they take in another cargo and other hands on board, and so make the voyage twice the same year, without the Japanese being able to discover their cheat. Others go to the province *Satsuma* early in the year, as if they had been cast thither by chance, or stress of weather, dispose of what goods they can, then haste back to take in a new cargo, and so go up to *Nagasaki*. If in going to *Satsuma* they are met by the Japanese Coast Guard <note>original: "Guard de coasts"</note>, which by order of the Government cruise in those seas to hinder the natives from carrying on a smuggling trade, they will then alter their course, as if they had been against their inclination cast out of it, and proceed directly on their voyage to *Nagasaki*, as the only harbour foreigners are permitted to put into.

# The History of JAPAN. Book IV.

E a

<margin>
The confinement of the Chinese.
</margin>
As for the second of the two points mentioned above, which the court intended for the Chinese nation—namely, to shut them up just as they had done with the Dutch at *Desima* <note>Dejima, the artificial island in Nagasaki harbor</note>—that plan was not put into effect until three years later. Until the year 1688, they still enjoyed significant freedom. At that time, the fine garden of *Sije Tsugu Feso* <note>Suetsugu Heizo, a high-ranking official who was executed or disgraced</note>, the late Steward of the Imperial Lands and Tenements around *Nagasaki* (whose tragic downfall I have related previously), was designated as their residence. This garden was pleasantly situated almost at the end of the harbor, not far from the shore and the town. It had been maintained at great expense as the Emperor’s own property and was elegantly decorated with a vast number of beautiful plants, both native and foreign, as the owner himself had been a great lover of botany.

Upon this plot of ground, several rows of small houses were built to house the Chinese. Each row was covered by a single common roof, and the whole area was surrounded by ditches, palisades, and strong, well-guarded double gates. All this was completed with such speed that the same location, which at the beginning of *February* was one of the most pleasant gardens, had by the end of *May* taken on the grim appearance of a high-security prison. To make matters worse, the Chinese were forced to pay an annual rent of 1,600 <term>Thails: taels, a weight of silver used as currency</term> for it. Whenever they come to *Nagasaki*, they must live here; and so great is their greed and love of profit that they allow themselves to be so closely watched and so poorly accommodated—if not worse than I have described the Dutch to be at *Desima*. 

However, there are some notable differences to observe regarding the treatment of the Dutch and the Chinese:

1. The Chinese are not granted the favor of being admitted into the presence of the Emperor, as the Dutch are once a year. However, in exchange for this, they are spared the trouble and expense of a three-month journey and the many gifts that must be given to his Imperial Majesty and his ministers.

2. They have food and supplies brought to them and offered for sale at the very gates of their factory, whereas we Dutch must bear the expense of maintaining an entire company of Japanese "Commissioners for Victualling."

3. Because they are viewed as private merchants—and because they reinforce the low opinion the Japanese have of them through frequent arguments and fights—they are not treated with as much civility as we are. Their inspectors, guards, and interpreters think nothing of hitting them with canes as punishment for minor offenses.

4. They do not have a Director of their trade residing there constantly like the Dutch do. Instead, when the sale of their goods is finished, they all depart on their <term>yonks: junks, traditional Chinese sailing vessels</term>, leaving their houses empty in the meantime.

# Chapter VIII. The History of JAPAN.

<margin>Goods imported by the Chinese.</margin>
They hold three sales every year, occurring at three different times: one in the Spring, when they dispose of the cargoes of twenty <term>yonks: junks, the traditional sailing vessels of China and Southeast Asia</term>; another in the Summer for thirty others; and another in Autumn for twenty more. Any other junks that arrive beyond this number, or after a sale is concluded, must return home without even being allowed to unload. Their cargoes consist of raw silk from *China* and *Tonkin* <note>Northern Vietnam</note>, and all sorts of silk and woollen fabrics, which are also imported by the Dutch and were named in the preceding chapter. They also import Sugar from several parts of the East Indies; Calamine Stone from *Tonkin* for the manufacture of brass and brazier’s wares; Turpentine (extracted from wild pistachio trees); Gums, myrrh, Agate, and Calambak wood <note>also known as aloeswood or agarwood, highly prized for its scent</note> from *Champa* <note>part of modern Vietnam</note>, *Cambodia*, and neighboring countries; the precious Camphor of *Baros* from *Borneo*; the valuable Chinese root *Nisin*, or *Ginseng* <note>original: "Ninseng"</note> (wild sugar-root) from *Korea*; and several other drugs and medicines, both simple and compound, from *China*, in addition to various Philosophical and Theological Books printed in *China*. 

Regarding these Books, it happened—as I have noted above—that some works relating to the Christian Religion, which were composed and printed by the Jesuits in *China*, slipped in among the rest. When this was first discovered by the Japanese, they forced the owner of the books to testify in the most solemn manner that he was not a Christian himself and that he did not bring these books over intentionally, knowing what they were. Then, to make him more cautious for the future, they sent him back with his junk and his entire cargo, without permitting him to sell any part of it. Following this incident, it was ordered that for the future, all books whatsoever imported by the Chinese should be first examined, and one of each kind read and censored before they are granted permission to sell them. This office of Censors, provided with a sufficient yearly allowance, has been given to two learned men of this town. One of these is the Father Prior of the monastery *Shotoku-ji* <note>original: "Siutokus"</note>, who is to read and censor all the Ecclesiastical <note>religious</note> Books; the other is a Shinto philosopher <note>original: "Sjutos"</note> and Physician to the *Dairi* <note>the Imperial Court in Kyoto</note>, as he calls himself, who is to read and censor all the Philosophical, Historical, and other Books. This latter gentleman resides at *Tateyama* <note>original: "Tattajamma"</note> and wears his hair long, which he ties together behind his head, as is the custom among the philosophers, physicians, and surgeons of the country.

<margin>Proceedings at their Sales.</margin>
The procedures at the sale of the goods imported by the Chinese are nearly the same as our own <note>the Dutch</note>; therefore, I do not need to add anything to the description I provided in the preceding chapter.

<margin>Taxes laid upon them.</margin>
It must only be observed that, as the voyage of the Chinese is shorter than ours, and not exposed to as many dangers nor subject to such great expense, the government has, in consideration of this, placed a much higher duty upon all their commodities. Specifically, a tax of 60 percent is to be paid by the buyer for the benefit of the various officers concerned in the management of the Chinese trade, and for other inhabitants of *Nagasaki*, among whom this money is later di-

As soon as a <term>yonk: a junk, or traditional Chinese sailing vessel</term> has disposed of the portion of her cargo assigned to her in the distribution, the <term>Funaban: guard ships</term> (which were 

<margin>Worship of their ship Idol</margin>
posted on both sides of her as soon as she entered the harbor) escort her out of the port until she reaches the open sea. The day before her departure, the Chinese "Neptunus," or sea-idol, called *Pusse* or *Bossa* <note>original: "Pusse" or "Bossa," likely referring to a Bodhisattva or the sea goddess Mazu</note>, is retrieved from the temple where he was kept since the vessel's arrival. With great pomp and ceremony, accompanied by the sound of timbrels and other musical instruments, he is carried back on board. This *Bossa* is an idol unknown in *Japan* and is not worshipped by the Japanese people. Chinese sailors carry him with them on all their voyages and make solemn vows to him when they are in danger. Every evening, a piece of gilded paper is lit before him and thrown into the sea as an offering, accompanied by the ringing of bells and the playing of music. If they have had a successful voyage, and particularly if they have escaped some great danger, they perform <term>Weijangs: theatrical plays or comedies, likely derived from the Malay "Wayang"</term> at night in the open streets for his amusement. They are also said to sacrifice pigs and other animals to him, though they eat the meat afterward. They never sacrifice cows to him, however, as they hold a great veneration for this animal and religiously abstain from eating its flesh.

<margin>Smugglers.</margin>
Because Chinese merchants often return with a large quantity of unsold goods on board, they are frequently followed by Japanese smugglers, who buy the remainder of the cargo at a low price. However, these unfortunate wretches are almost as frequently caught by the Japanese coast guard and delivered to the authorities at *Nagasaki*, who are invariably severe and unmerciful toward them. Not long after my arrival in *Japan*, namely on November 20, 1690, eleven persons were caught in a single boat and brought to prison in *Nagasaki*, where they were executed a few days later. To say nothing of other instances, twenty-three people suffered death for smuggling on December 28, 1691; ten of them were beheaded, and the others were placed upon the cross <note>a reference to *haritsuke*, the Japanese form of public crucifixion</note>. Among the latter group were five who, upon being captured, took their own lives to avoid the shame of a public execution; nevertheless, their bodies were preserved in salt so that they could still be displayed upon the cross.

<margin>Trade of the Ryukyu Islands to Japan.</margin>
Before I close this chapter, it is appropriate to briefly mention another group of merchants from the *Riuku*, or *Liquejo* Islands <note>the Ryukyu Islands, modern-day Okinawa</note>, who are permitted to carry on a specific trade with the province of *Satzuma* <note>Satsuma, a powerful domain in southern Kyushu</note>.

### Chap. IX. The History of JAPAN.

<sig>D d d d d</sig>

<margin>Satsuma</margin> By the *Ryukyu*, or *Liquejo* Islands, one must understand that chain of islands which extends from the southwest coasts of *Satsuma* <note>a powerful feudal domain in southern Kyushu</note> toward the *Philippine Islands*. The inhabitants speak a dialect of *Chinese*, which proves their ancestral origin from *China*. Chinese merchants have traded with these islands at all times. After the recent <term>Tartarian: the Manchu or Qing Dynasty</term> conquest of *China*, many families fled there to settle and were warmly received by the inhabitants as old acquaintances and countrymen. Some time ago, these islands were invaded and conquered by the Prince of *Satsuma*, under whose authority they remain. Although they recognize the Prince of *Satsuma* as their conqueror and sovereign, and pay a small portion of their agricultural produce as tribute to his <term>Bugjos: magistrates or provincial governors</term>, they still do not acknowledge the supreme authority of the *Japanese* Emperor. Furthermore, they send a gift every year to the *Manchu* Monarch of *China* as a token of submission <note>referring to the Ryukyu Kingdom's historical status as a "tributary of two masters"</note>. Although they might be considered, in some sense, subjects of the *Japanese* Emperor, they are treated like other foreigners in regards to their trade. They are commanded to use only the harbor of *Satsuma* and are forbidden from frequenting any other port in the *Japanese* dominions. The import and sale of their goods has also been restricted to a yearly sum of 125,000 <term>Taels: a weight-based currency of silver</term>, beyond which nothing may be sold. Nevertheless, they manage to sell much larger cargoes through the secret cooperation of the *Japanese* trade directors, who themselves profit from the arrangement. The goods they import include all varieties of silk and other fabrics, along with several other *Chinese* commodities which they bring from *China* on their own <term>yonks: junks, or traditional sailing vessels</term>. They also bring products of their own country, such as corn, rice, legumes, and fruits; *Awamori* <note>original: "Awamuri"</note>, a potent type of brandy distilled from the remains of their harvest; and *Takaragai* and *Himagai* <note>original: "Takaragai, and Fimagai"</note>, which are pearl-shells and the small shells known as <term>Cowries</term> in the *Indies*. These cowries are brought primarily from the *Maldive Islands* to *Bengal* and *Siam*, where they serve as common currency. From those shells imported into *Japan* by the people of the *Ryukyu Islands*—upon whose shores they are found in great abundance—is prepared a white cosmetic varnish <note>a lead-based or shell-based face powder</note> which boys and girls use to paint themselves. They also import a type of large, flat shell, polished until almost transparent, which the *Japanese* use in place of glass for windows and to protect themselves against rain and cold, as well as several rare flowers and plants in pots, among other items.

### IV.

-><term>GODSIOMOKU: Goshuin-moku</term>. Strict Imperial Commands.<-

<margin>1.</margin>OUR Imperial Predecessors have ordered concerning you Dutchmen, that you shall have leave to come to Nagasaki, on account of the Japanese trade, every year. Therefore, as we have commanded you heretofore, you shall have no communication with the Portuguese. If you should have any, and we should come to know it from foreign countries, you shall be prohibited from navigating to Japan. You shall import no Portuguese commodities on board your ships.

<margin>2.</margin>If you intend not to be molested in your navigation and trade to Japan, you shall notify to us by your ships whatever comes to your knowledge of any endeavors or attempts of the Portuguese against us; we likewise expect to hear from you if the Portuguese should conquer any new places or countries, or convert them to the Christian Sect. Whatever comes to your knowledge in all countries you trade to, we expect that you should notify the same to our Governors at Nagasaki.

### V.
(1.)
->Prohibitions for Dejima Street.<- <note>This column translates the romanized Japanese text provided in the original manuscript.</note>

No women shall enter, with the exception of prostitutes.

(2.) No priests or mountain monks <term>Jammabus: Yamabushi, ascetic practitioners of Shugendō</term> shall enter, with the exception of the holy men of Mount Koya.

# Chap. X. The History of JAPAN.
E e e e e VI.

1. (*Desimamatz.*) *Desima*, is an Island rais'd by art <note>This refers to Dejima being a man-made or artificial island, constructed in 1634 to isolate foreign residents from the Japanese population.</note> in the harbour of *Nagasaki*, not far from the town. It was formerly the factory <term>factory: a merchant's trading post and warehouse, overseen by a "chief factor," rather than a manufacturing site</term> of the *Portuguese*. At present the *Dutch* live there. It is comprehended among the streets of *Nagasaki*, and subject to the same regulations, for which reason it is call'd *Desimamatz*, that is, the street of *Desima* <note>original: "Desimamatz," likely from Dejima-machi, with "machi" meaning a town ward or street</note>.

2. (*Koja Fisiri.*) *Koja* <term>Koja: Mount Kōya, the sacred center of Shingon Buddhism</term> is a mountain in the neighbourhood of *Miaco* <term>Miaco: Kyoto, the historic imperial capital of Japan</term>. Its Inhabitants, many thousand in number, lead an Ecclesiastical Life, and are for this reason call'd *Koja Fisiri* <note>original: "Koja Fisiri," referring to the Kōya Hijiri, or the "holy men of Kōya," who were itinerant monks</note>, that is to say, the Monks, or Clergy of the mountain *Koja*, tho' the word *Fisiri* implies, that they have not near so strict Rules to observe, as other religious Orders. This mountain is a sanctuary for Criminals, no Constables nor any Officers of Justice being suffer'd to come there <note>Historically, Mount Kōya held a status of extraterritoriality, offering asylum to those fleeing secular law.</note>. Every body is admitted, that desires it, or flies there for shelter, and afterwards maintain'd for Life, if they can but bring in thirty *Thails* <term>Thails: Taels, a unit of currency based on a weight of silver</term> for the use of the Convent, and are otherwise willing to serve the common-wealth <note>Here meaning the monastic community or general society.</note> in their several capacities. *Kobodais* <term>Kobodais: Kōbō Daishi (774–835), also known as Kūkai, the famous monk and polymath who founded Shingon Buddhism</term> was the founder of this order. Lamps are kept perpetually burning before his Idol <note>Likely referring to the Reikunōin or the Hall of Lamps at the Okunoin cemetery, where flames are said to have burned for over a millennium.</note>, and it is thought a very good and meritorious work to found such a Lamp, which may be done by a small Legacy of an hundred *Maas* <term>Maas: Mace, a smaller denomination of silver currency, equal to one-tenth of a Tael</term>, the Interest of this Money being sufficient to provide the necessary quantity of Oil. These Monks are not absolutely confin'd to this mountain, but may travel up and down the country in what manner or business they please. Very many of them betake themselves to trade and commerce. They do not indeed come to *Nagasaki*, but if they should, they must be admitted as well as other merchants.

3. (*Jammabus,*) *Jammabus* <term>Jammabus: Yamabushi, ascetic practitioners of Shugendō, a tradition that merges mountain worship with Buddhist and Shinto beliefs</term> signifies mountain priests. It is a very singular religious order, which hath been more particularly describ'd in the fifth Chapter of the third Book of this History.

# The History of JAPAN. Book IV.

### Established Regulations <note>original: "Dzio Sadamari"</note>

Whether Japanese or Foreigner, any person who violates the prohibitions <note>original: "gofatto"</note> and at any time plots an evil deed to export contraband goods <note>original: "Reimotzu"</note>, if such a person is discovered, it must be reported immediately. Even if the informant is an accomplice <note>original: "Dorui"</note>, their offense shall be pardoned and a reward <note>original: "Gofoobi"</note> shall be granted in proportion to the value of the goods. If an offender is found through another person's report, they shall be executed <note>original: "Seiqua," a term for capital punishment</note> according to the law.

Such is the decree.
--- Quarter --- Year ---

<column-break/>

### VI.

### Orders concerning Contraband Goods.

**I**f any foreigner, or Japanese, endeavours, contrary to orders, to dispose of any contraband goods <term>contraband goods: prohibited items, most notably religious artifacts, weapons, or certain luxury goods restricted by the Shogunate</term> whatsoever, and it be discovered, notice shall be given forthwith to the proper magistrates. If any of the accomplices discovers himself, and turns evidence, he shall have his Pardon, and moreover a reward proportionable to the Crime. Offenders found guilty upon the evidence of their accomplices, shall be punished according to law.

->Thus much,<-

It may not be out of place to observe, regarding the private servants of the Dutch who are appointed to wait upon them at their lodgings, that as they are generally young boys—not yet of an age to take such a solemn oath—they must find an honest citizen of **Nagasaki** who will stand as security for their good behavior. ### IX.

### Orders to be observed during the time of the Dutch Sale, posted in the main street of our island for the information of those who come to Dejima at that time.

### <term>DSJO</term>. Absolute Command.
<note>The term "DSJO" likely refers to the Japanese *Jō* (edict or article) or *Go-jō* (The Five Articles), indicating a formal government decree.</note>

**No Dutchman** shall be permitted to leave **Dejima** without permission.

**No one** shall be allowed to enter the island before the sale begins, except for the ordinary officers and servants.

**No goods** of any kind shall be carried out of the island before the sale begins. No **<term>Tsintasaki</term>** (Tent wine) <note>From the Spanish *Vino Tinto*, a dark red fortified wine popular at the time.</note> nor any **<term>Budoosju</term>** (Grape wine) <note>From the Japanese *budōshu*.</note> shall be sent out of the island without a special license.

**No Japanese arms**, nor any pictures, representations, or puppet-figures of any **<term>Musia</term>** (military figures) <note>From the Japanese *musha*, meaning a warrior or samurai.</note> or soldiers, shall be brought to **Dejima**. Pursuant to our frequently repeated and strict commands, no goods whatsoever shall be sold privately to the Dutch, nor shall any goods be bought from them in the same private manner.

When the time for the departure of the Dutch ships approaches, notice shall be given to the **<term>Ottona</term>** <note>The *Otona* was the Japanese "ward headman" or official responsible for the oversight of Dejima.</note> and to the company of interpreters regarding which goods have been sold to the Dutch. This must include a written list so that the agreed-upon sums can be paid on time, avoiding all trouble and inconvenience during the final days of their stay in the harbor.

The **Dutch and Portuguese interpreters** who frequent the island and are licensed to do so shall not plot together nor converse in private.

**No one** shall come to **Dejima** without special leave, except for the **<term>Bugjo</term>** <note>The *Bugyō*, or Governor/Commissioner of Nagasaki, who held supreme authority over the port.</note> and the officers of the island.

### LIST OF CONTRABAND GOODS <note>original: "GOTSIOOSI MONO NO OBJ O J E"</note>; that is, a list of forbidden items which the Dutch are not permitted to purchase or export from the country.

**The Imperial Crest.** <note>original: "GOMON"</note>. The Emperor’s coat of arms. All prints, pictures, goods, or fabrics bearing this emblem.
**Military Equipment.** <note>original: "Budoogu"</note>. Warlike instruments.
**Military Images.** <note>original: "Mufaige"</note>. Pictures and representations, whether printed or otherwise, of soldiers and military personnel.
**People of the Court.** <note>original: "Fejro no Giendsi"</note>. Pictures or representations of any persons belonging to the Court of the **<term>Dairi</term>** <note>The spiritual or "Ecclesiastical" Emperor residing in Kyoto, distinguished from the Shogun who held political power.</note>, or Ecclesiastical Hereditary Emperor.
**Japanese Vessels.** <note>original: "Nippon bune no kogatta narabinije"</note>. Pictures or models of Japanese ships or boats.
**Maps of Japan.** <note>original: "Nipponno Jedsii"</note>. Maps of the Empire of **Japan**, or of any part thereof. Plans of towns, castles, temples, and similar locations.
**Military Puppets.** <note>original: "Jakko kenqua Ningio"</note>. Puppets or small figures representing military men.
**Curved Knives.** <note>original: "Duitru Jurigana"</note>. Crooked knives, such as those used by carpenters.
**Hino Silk.** <note>original: "Fino Ginu"</note>. A type of silk fabric manufactured in the province of **Hino**.
**Kaga Silk.** <note>original: "Kaga Ginu"</note>. Similar silk made in the province of **Kaga**. Both of these are prepared in long rolls, similar to the silk fabrics imported from **Tonquin** <note>A historical region in northern Vietnam, a major source of silk in the 17th-century trade network.</note>.
**Woven Stuffs.** <note>original: "Tsumuggi"</note>. Another type of fabric sold in long rolls, manufactured in **Japan**.
**Fine Silks.** <note>original: "Gumai no rui"</note>. All varieties of fine silken fabrics.
**Hemp Fabrics.** <note>original: "Nuno no rui"</note>. All types of fabrics made of hemp.
**Cotton Fabrics.** <note>original: "Momen no rui"</note>. Fabrics manufactured from cotton.
**Silk Padding.** <note>original: "Mawatta"</note>. Mats or wadding made of silk.
**Silver.** <note>original: "Gin"</note>.
**Dutch-style Japanese Swords.** <note>original: "Ken Hollanda gattana Nippon gosij raje"</note>. All types of sabers, swords, and other weapons manufactured in **Japan** in imitation of the styles imported by the Dutch.

### XI.

->FORM of their PASSPORTS.<-

NAGASAKI. Name of the street. The Person's Family Name. His proper name. His age. At the bottom are several sorts of money current in the **Japanese** Empire, to wit: *A.* an **Ōban** <note>Obani</note> in gold, which goes for ten **Koban**, though it weighs but 9 and 3 quarters. It has the impression of the coat of arms of the **Imperial Court** <note>Dairi</note> in four places, and the strokes, or lines, represented in the figure, engraved in the surface. *B.* One side of the **Koban** <note>or Cobang</note>, which is likewise a piece of gold, worth about 23 and a half Dutch **Guilders** <note>Gilders</note>, that is, between 41 and 42 shillings sterling. It has, besides the lines as above, the following impressions: *a.* The coat of arms of the **Imperial Court**. *b.* A mark showing the value of the piece. *c.* **Mitsutsugu** <note>Midsutsugu</note>, the name of the master of the mint at **Edo** <note>Jedo</note> and **Suruga**, expressed in **Seal** <note>Sjo; refering to Tensho or seal-script</note> characters. *C.* The other side of the **Koban**, wherein *d* is the mark of the Inspector-general of the gold and silver money. The rest, on both sides, are stamps of private persons, whereby they may know whether or not the money passed through their hands. The **Japanese** prefer the **Koban** made at **Edo**, which have strong lines, but foreigners rather take the others. They try the goodness of them, either by applying them to the breast—to which the best will stick a little—or else by clashing them against their teeth, and some also by cutting them with scissors. *D. E.* An **Ichibu** <note>Itzebo</note> in gold, with the arms of the Emperor on one side, and the mark of the master of the mint on the other. *F.* A large lump of silver, with several impressions, such as, among others, that of **Daikoku**, or the God of riches with his hammer, barrel <note>original: "tun"</note>, and bag. These are not reduced to any certain standard, but are taken by the weight. *G.* An **Ita** or **Silver Bar** <note>original: "Schuit" or "boat," referring to the shape of the ingot</note> of silver. *H.* The upper side of a **Zeni** <note>Senni</note>, or **Penny** <note>original: "Putjes," a Dutch colonial term for small change</note>, a copper money, with the name of the **Era** <note>Nengo</note> in which it was coined. *I.* The other side of a **Zeni**. *K. # Plan of the City of Edo <note>original Latin: "Ju<unclear>...</unclear>", likely "Jedum," the Latinized name for Edo, the historical name for Tokyo.</note>

->**A Detailed Map of Urban Fortifications**<-

This engraving provides a meticulous architectural plan of a fortified settlement, showcasing the complex relationship between urban planning, defense, and water management. The city is defined by a massive, curved <term>canal</term> <note>an artificial waterway used here for both transportation and as a protective moat</note> and a series of defensive walls.

### Legend and Notable Landmarks

The following locations are identified by alphabetical markers on the plan, indicating key strategic and administrative points:

| Marker | Description of Feature |
| :--- | :--- |
| **A** | **The Central Square** — A large, rectangular building complex or plaza situated in the heart of the city, likely representing the seat of government or the palace grounds. |
| **C** | **Western Bastion** — A specific defensive structure or <term>gatehouse</term> <note>a fortified structure built over or near a city gate</note> along the western circuit of the wall. |
| **D** | **Southern Outpost** — A small, isolated building located to the south of the main fortifications, possibly serving as a guard post or customs house. |
| **L** | **Canal Fork** — A strategic point to the northwest where the external canal splits into two distinct branches. |
| **M** | **South Canal Junction** — A junction where a secondary waterway branches off toward the south, away from the primary city defenses. |
| **P** | **Perimeter Defenses** — Various points along the outer canal marking bridge crossings or fortified <term>bastions</term> <note>projections in a fortification wall that allow defenders to fire along the face of the wall</note>. |
| **R** | **Open Commons** — An undeveloped area or open field situated to the south of the city walls. |

The internal structure of the city follows a disciplined, grid-like arrangement of streets and smaller secondary canals. This layout suggests a highly organized society where space was allocated for specific administrative and residential functions. The surrounding terrain is depicted as flat ground, possibly reflecting the reclaimed marshlands that were famously transformed during the development of Edo in the 17th century.

<summary>This page presents an architectural map of a fortified city, almost certainly Edo (Tokyo), highlighting its sophisticated system of canals, defensive walls, and grid-based urban planning.</summary>

# Scenes of Chinese Life

->Plate III.<- <note>original Latin: "Tab. III."</note>

->Figure 2.<- <note>original Latin: "Fig. 2."</note>

This illustration depicts a grand, multi-storied Chinese palace or temple complex. The building is characterized by its prominent colonnaded front and a distinctive stepped or tiered roofing system, which was a hallmark of high-status architecture in the Qing Dynasty. Such structures often served as both religious centers and administrative halls.

->Figure 1.<- <note>original Latin: "Fig. 1."</note>

Featured here is a long, shallow-draft river vessel. Notably, it is equipped with a large paddle wheel at the stern, a technology used in China for centuries where manpower—often via a treadmill mechanism—propelled the ship through calm inland waters. A central canopy provides shade for passengers or cargo.

->Figure 3 and Figure 4.<- <note>original Latin: "Fig. 3. Fig. 4."</note>

These figures show smaller, specialized watercraft common to the crowded waterways of coastal and riverine China. These <term>sampans<gloss>from the Cantonese "sam pan," literally meaning "three planks," referring to the relatively flat-bottomed design of these small wooden boats</gloss></term> are shown with protective covers, serving as mobile homes or small-scale transport vessels for merchants and families.

# Plate VI <note>original Latin: "TAB. VI."</note>

->The Cupola as Constructed<- <note>original Latin: "Cupula prout ædificata"</note>

This architectural drawing provides a sophisticated "worm's-eye" perspective, looking directly upward into the interior of a massive <term>cupola<gloss>a small, dome-like structure on top of a building, often used to provide light or decoration</gloss></term>. Unlike a rounded dome, this structure is built on a square base, using receding concentric squares to create a sense of towering height and depth. 

To the left of the main structural outline, the artist has meticulously detailed the timber scaffolding or internal framework required to support such a heavy masonry or wooden feat. This suggests the plate was intended not just as an artistic rendering, but as a technical guide for architects and engineers of the period.

->Scale of 30 <term>Common Paces<gloss>a historical unit of measurement based on the length of a single step, approximately 2.5 to 3 feet</gloss></term><- <note>original Latin: "Scala 30 Passuum communium"</note>

The inclusion of a scale bar at the bottom center allows the viewer to grasp the true magnitude of the project. A "common pace" was a standard reference in early modern engineering, indicating that this structure would have been a significant landmark, likely crowning a major religious or civic building.

<summary>This page features a technical architectural perspective of a square cupola, including its internal scaffolding and a scale for measurement.</summary>

# Plate IV <note>original Latin: "Tab. IV."</note>

-> Figure 1 <-

-> The Puka'thon Pyramid <- <note>This refers to the **Phu Khao Thong** (the "Golden Mount"), a massive Buddhist monument located just outside the city of Ayutthaya.</note>

This detailed architectural engraving showcases one of the most significant structures of the Ayutthaya Kingdom. While the Latin title refers to it as a **Pyramis** (Pyramid), it is more accurately described in a Southeast Asian context as a <term>chedi<gloss>a Thai-style Buddhist monument, often containing relics, characterized by a tapering spire</gloss></term> or a <term>stupa<gloss>a hemispherical or solid structure used as a place of meditation and a reliquary in Buddhism</gloss></term>.

The structure is built upon a massive, multi-tiered square base. Each of these receding stepped terraces features ornate balustrades and smaller decorative spires at the corners, creating a sense of rhythmic verticality. From the center of the highest terrace rises the primary spire—a slender, ringed column that tapers to a sharp point. This specific design, with its "indented corners" and tall spire, is a hallmark of the architectural transition between the Khmer-influenced *prang* and the more slender Thai *chedi*.

For 17th and 18th-century European observers, such buildings were wonders of engineering and devotion, often compared to the pyramids of Egypt due to their scale and stepped profiles. The engraving captures the monument in its full, pristine state, before the structural collapses and subsequent restorations that have altered its appearance over the centuries.

<summary>This page illustrates the Phu Khao Thong (Golden Mount) in Ayutthaya, Thailand, depicting it as a massive, tiered "pyramid" with a towering central spire.</summary>
<keywords>Ayutthaya, Thailand, Siam, chedi, stupa, Phu Khao Thong, Buddhist architecture, pyramid, engraving</keywords>

# Plate IV <note>original Latin: "Tab. IV."</note>

-> Figure 1 <-

-> The Puka'thon Pyramid <- <note>This refers to the **Phu Khao Thong** (the "Golden Mount"), a massive Buddhist monument located just outside the city of Ayutthaya.</note>

-> Scale of 90 *common paces* <- <note>original Latin: "Scala 90 Passuum communium." The "common pace" was a historical unit of measure roughly equivalent to 5 feet or 1.5 meters.</note>

<margin>
V. der Gucht engraved this
</margin> <note>Michael van der Gucht (1660–1725) was a prominent Flemish engraver who worked extensively in London, providing illustrations for many historical and geographical works.</note>

The ground plan provided in Figure 2 reveals the rigorous geometric precision of the monument’s foundation. The plan illustrates a perfectly square perimeter with four monumental staircases located at the cardinal points (North, South, East, and West). These stairs lead the visitor upward through the diminishing concentric squares of the terraces. 

At the very heart of the plan sits an octagonal core, which serves as the structural base for the massive central spire. The symmetry of the design was intended to represent the Buddhist cosmology, specifically Mount Meru, the center of the universe. The use of a scale bar in "common paces" indicates that this engraving was intended for a European audience to appreciate the immense physical footprint of the structure, which spans a width of approximately 150 meters at its base.
